Read the formulas, rounding rules and limitations FORMULA TRACE · ENGINE v 1.3.1 contribution = price - direct_costs - fees exact_units = fixed_need / contribution required_inquiries = exact_units / conversion MEANING, FORMULA AND EXAMPLE What is breakeven? Breakeven is the sales level where total revenue equals total costs. The business has no operating profit or loss under the costs included in the calculation. The break-even point can be expressed as units sold or sales revenue for a stated period. This calculator focuses on business operations. Recovering startup investment, cash-flow timing and stock or options trading are different calculations. The break-even formula Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit) For revenue, divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio. Use that ratio as a decimal: 40% means 0.40. Keep the selling unit, sales mix and time period consistent, and include each cost once. Operating break-even and a profit goal are different. For operating break-even, include the fixed costs in your stated boundary and set extra profit to zero. Add a separate owner-income goal only when it is not already in costs. Adding profit gives a higher target. With positive fixed costs, zero or negative contribution cannot produce a finite break-even sales target. Review price and cost assumptions before increasing volume. A checked monthly example Fictional inputs: $4,000 fixed costs, $50 price and $30 variable cost per unit. Each sale contributes $20 (40%). The exact threshold is 200 units and $10,000 revenue . Same monthly costs; original illustrative USD example Units sold Revenue Total cost Operating result 199 $9,950 $9,970 −$20 200 $10,000 $10,000 $0 201 $10,050 $10,030 +$20 A fractional threshold must be rounded up for whole units. For example, $4,010 fixed costs ÷ $20 contribution = 200.5 units. Selling 201 units leaves $10 above those costs; rounding does not make the result exactly zero. Revenue and total cost meet at 200 units Original fictional example: revenue is 50 dollars times units, total cost is 4,000 dollars plus 30 dollars times units. Both are 10,000 dollars at 200 units. The adjoining table gives the results at 199, 200 and 201 units. 10,000 0 200 300 Units sold USD per month Break-even Revenue (blue) = $50 × units · Total cost (green) = $4,000 + $30 × units Turn the number into a usable plan Compare the target with demand and the work your team can deliver. A result can be financially sufficient but operationally impossible. Cash may also run short before invoices are collected. HOW THE CALCULATION WORKS From contribution margin to a monthly sales target you can check Calculate contribution per sale. Subtract direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and payment fees from average price. Distinguish fixed and variable costs before choosing the inputs; restaurant operators can also reconcile actual food cost from inventory and sales . Set the monthly amount to cover. Use operating fixed costs for a zero-profit operating threshold. Add owner pay only if it is not already in costs, and add optional profit only for a higher funding target. Calculate the exact sales target. Divide the monthly amount to cover by contribution per sale without prematurely rounding the result. Compare the units and revenue formulas or follow the step-by-step calculation . Check capacity and inquiry requirements. Compare required sales with team capacity and translate the sales target into required customer inquiries. WORKED SERVICE BUSINESS EXAMPLE How many customers do you need to break even? These are illustrative inputs, not market averages. Suppose a service sells for $200. Materials, labor, travel and acquisition cost $95 per job, and a 2.5% payment fee costs $5. Each completed job therefore contributes $100 toward monthly costs. With $2,400 in overhead and $1,600 in owner pay, the business needs 40 jobs ($8,000 in sales) to cover costs and owner pay. Add a $1,000 profit goal and the target becomes 50 jobs ($10,000 in sales). At a 25% inquiry-to-job conversion rate, those 50 jobs require 200 inquiries. Now check delivery: two people working 20 hours a week at 50% productive utilization provide about 87 delivery hours a month. If each job takes two hours, they can complete only 43 whole jobs. The 50-job profit target needs more capacity or a change in price, costs or the profit goal. The basic break-even formula is fixed costs divided by contribution per sale; this example separately includes owner pay, a profit target, inquiries and delivery capacity. See the U.S. Small Business Administration's break-even method . Run your own numbers in the free calculator . For receipts and bills that fall on different dates, build a separate 13-week cash flow forecast ; break-even profit is not the same as available cash. Breakeven (also written break-even) is the sales level where total revenue equals total fixed and variable costs. At that point, the business has no operating profit or loss under the assumptions entered. How do I calculate break-even revenue? For operating break-even, divide included fixed operating costs by contribution per sale, then multiply by price. MyBreakeven can also add separately entered owner pay and target profit to calculate a higher monthly target. Count each cost once and keep those targets distinct. Does the calculator include owner salary and target profit? Yes. Set target profit to zero for a zero-profit threshold and include owner compensation once in the chosen cost boundary. Add a separate owner-pay amount only if it is not already in costs. A positive profit goal gives a sales target beyond break-even. Why does business capacity matter? A financial target is not feasible if your team cannot deliver the required orders, jobs, clients or appointments. The calculator compares required volume with productive team hours. Can I use a currency other than US dollars? Yes. Select a supported currency before entering your figures. The calculator labels all amounts in that currency; it does not perform exchange-rate conversion. Are my financial figures saved? The free calculator runs in your browser. Inputs are not sent or saved automatically. Choosing Continue with these numbers carries a temporary plan to the full calculator in the same browser tab; the handoff expires after five minutes and is removed when opened. If you sign in and choose Save scenario, that scenario is stored with your account and can be deleted from your dashboard. Is operating break-even the same as recovering startup costs? No. Operating break-even covers the fixed and variable costs included for a period. Recovering equipment or launch funding is a separate cash-payback question. A positive target profit also gives a sales goal beyond operating break-even. Why can a whole-unit break-even target show a small profit? The exact threshold can be fractional. If $4,010 fixed costs and $20 unit contribution require 200.5 units, a whole-unit plan needs 201 units. That leaves $10 above the included costs; it is not an exactly zero-profit result. documents.text: RESTAURANT CUSTOMER EXPERIENCE · UNITED STATES Thai Foods Restaurant Break-Even Case Study: From Monthly Costs to Daily Table Bills A Jacksonville manager’s reported experience using a $99 average table bill to turn monthly costs and a profit goal into a daily operating target. Written by MyBreakeven Editorial Team · Published by MyBreakeven Interview source · Mr. Samule, Operational Manager at Thai Foods Published November 19, 2026 · Updated November 28, 2026 Publisher-produced case study based on organizer-supplied participant feedback. Unpaid; no benefit reported. Financial planning calculations and reported accounts results are labelled separately. AI-generated editorial illustration; not the restaurant’s premises, documents or staff. $54.56 Calculated contribution per table bill 1,476 Calculated monthly profit-target bills 50/day Reported operating target A clearer daily plan, with the calculations visible Thai Foods, described by its manager as a five-year-old full-service restaurant in Jacksonville, Florida, wanted a clearer answer to a practical question: how many table bills must the team complete to support its desired profit? Mr. Samule, Operational Manager, manages sales and the monthly budget. According to the supplied follow-up, his earlier monthly manual process did not give him a clear target. The corrected screenshot shows a $99 average table bill and a $50,000 additional monthly profit target . After the entered variable costs, each bill contributes $54.56 . Funding overhead, owner pay and the profit goal requires 1,476 whole table bills per month . The manager translated that into a plan of about 50 table bills per day across 30 open days. The useful outcome reported here is clearer target setting and attention to daily delivery. The monthly target is a conditional calculation, not a booking forecast. Open the restaurant break-even calculator for the tool, or follow the exact reconstruction below. Who used the calculator and how this account was collected The outreach organizer emailed the restaurant on November 1, 2026, and reports desktop use through November 15. Feedback was relayed from a WhatsApp call with Mr. Samule; the call date was not supplied. Business details, permissions and the accounts figure were provided to MyBreakeven through that organizer. The restaurant’s website or official profile was not supplied, and we have not independently established its identity or inspected its accounts. The organizer confirmed permission to publish the name, role, screenshot and agreed figures. They also confirmed this was an unpaid review with no benefit provided. MyBreakeven publishes this account as the maker of the calculator. It is a participant experience, separate from the Daily Outfitter founder account and the Malaysia restaurant review . The evidence consists of the corrected calculator screenshot and supplied follow-up answers. The earlier screenshot was explicitly withdrawn and is excluded. There are no raw POS exports, wage schedules, inventory records, session logs, numerical manual-calculation worksheet or independently reviewed financial statements in the evidence supplied. The corrected inputs: one table bill, one monthly period Here, one order means one table bill . Several diners can share a bill. Neither actual guest numbers nor average guests per bill were supplied. The inputs are described by the organizer as restaurant figures; we can reproduce their arithmetic but cannot verify their accounting completeness. The $24,500 overhead was described as rent, electricity and FOH-related costs. The organizer clarified that direct salaries are excluded from this total and entered separately at $10.50 per bill. A detailed FOH breakdown was not supplied. Owner pay is a separate planning allowance; its treatment in statutory accounts may differ. The fee calculation applies 6% to the entire entered $99; the actual settlement fee base, tax/tip treatment and individual channel mix were not documented. The materials figure already includes food wastage. Treat the packaging/commission and promotion amounts as the blended costs entered for this plan, not verified dine-in-only costs or market rates. Labor is treated as volume-related in this calculation. If wages are committed regardless of bills served, reclassify the committed portion into overhead and remove it from per-bill labor to prevent double counting. Input record from the corrected screenshot USD; monthly commitments and per-table-bill costs Input Supplied value Average revenue per table bill $99.00 Materials/product cost, including wastage $21.50 Direct labor per table bill $10.50 Packaging and delivery commission per table bill $3.50 Promotion cost per table bill $3.00 Payment/platform fee 6% of entered revenue Monthly operating overhead $24,500 Separate monthly owner-pay allowance $6,000 Additional monthly profit target $50,000 Existing active team members 10 Hours per member per week 40 Combined worker-hours per table bill 0.35 Open days per month 30 (reported in follow-up) Corrected screenshot supplied by the outreach organizer with reported publication permission. Lower utilization/conversion values are cropped. Select the image for the full-size file. Reconstructing the 1,476-table-bill monthly target Payment/platform fees per bill = $99 × 6% = $5.94 . Total variable cost = $21.50 materials + $10.50 labor + $3.50 packaging/commission + $3 promotion + $5.94 fees = $44.44 . Contribution per bill = $99 − $44.44 = $54.56 . This contribution funds the monthly commitments and profit goal; it is not profit on each individual bill. The total monthly funding requirement is $24,500 overhead + $6,000 owner pay + $50,000 additional profit = $80,500 . Required bills = $80,500 ÷ $54.56 = 1,475.439882…; round the final requirement upward to 1,476 bills . At that volume, modeled sales are $146,124 , variable costs are $65,593.44 and contribution is $80,530.56 . Subtracting overhead and owner pay leaves $50,030.56 under the entered assumptions, before any omitted costs and taxes. Rounding matters: 1,475 bills leave only $49,976 after overhead and owner pay, $24 below the goal. These calculations assume stable average revenue, costs and fee rates over the operating range. They do not prove actual sales will occur. Same $54.56 contribution; different funding questions Target Requirement Whole table bills Sales at $99 Overhead only $24,500 450 $44,550 Overhead plus owner pay $30,500 560 $55,440 Plus $50,000 profit goal $80,500 1,476 $146,124 Calling all three “break-even” would hide the distinction. The first covers the stated operating overhead; the last includes a substantial profit goal. For broader definitions, see restaurant contribution and break-even . Turning the monthly requirement into daily table-bill targets The restaurant reports opening 30 days per month. Dividing 1,476 by 30 gives 49.2 bills per day on average . The manager chose about 50 per day as an operating target. Fifty daily bills over 30 days would produce 1,500 bills and $148,500 modeled monthly sales at a $99 average. With unchanged costs, the modeled remainder after overhead and owner pay is $51,340 . The daily revenue arithmetic is 50 × $99 = $4,950 . The stated approximately $5,000 daily sales goal is a rounded operating goal, not a guaranteed minimum receipt. Actual bill sizes and the menu/channel mix vary. A monthly average permits quieter and busier days; it does not require identical sales every day. The reported action was to set daily table-bill targets and focus on bringing in enough visitors. No quantified increase in visitors, actual bill count or conversion was supplied. Converting bills into covers needs actual party sizes, while a demand plan needs evidence of reservations, walk-ins and completed purchases. Keep these records separate from kitchen and labor capacity. The reported November 1–15 accounts figure is a separate record The organizer reports an accounts figure of $32,721 for November 1–15, 2026 , after $12,250 allocated overhead and $3,000 owner pay , before tax. Both allocations are half their monthly planning amounts. November was still in progress when the information was collected. This is a reported after-owner-pay, before-tax result, not an independently verified statutory net-income figure or cash balance. A comparable editorial half-month plan would use $12,250 overhead + $3,000 owner pay + $25,000 profit goal = $40,250. At the same $54.56 contribution, that needs 738 bills , $73,062 sales and a modeled $25,015.28 remainder. A hypothetical 50-bill daily plan across 15 days gives 750 bills and a modeled $25,670 remainder. Neither number reproduces the reported $32,721. That difference remains unexplained because actual sales, table bills, fee bases, costs and accounting adjustments were not supplied. Do not reverse-engineer an actual bill count from the reported profit or project it into a full-month result. It also does not establish that the calculator caused higher earnings. A proper comparison needs the same period, realized averages, expense boundary and owner-pay treatment. Use the restaurant budgeting workflow and budget-versus-actual record to document that reconciliation. What the capacity display says about the 10-person team The screenshot lists 10 existing team members,40 hours per person per week and 0.35 combined worker-hours per table bill. It displays 3,565 monthly bills of capacity and 41.4% capacity needed . The percentage agrees with 1,476 ÷ 3,565 × 100 ≈41.4%. Productive-utilization and inquiry-conversion inputs are cut off in the supplied image. We retain the displayed capacity and 3,280 inquiries as screenshot observations without inventing the missing inputs or claiming a fully reproduced capacity scenario. Inquiries are not confirmed visitors or bills. The finance calculation above is independently reproducible from the visible monetary inputs. The capacity result concerns worker-hours under entered assumptions. It does not validate seats, table turns, peak kitchen throughput, customer demand or an optimal headcount. The 10 employees already existed; no staffing reduction, hiring decision or changed shift schedule was reported. Use the restaurant planning cluster to connect staffing, menu contribution and service constraints. Manager feedback: useful planning and a request for visible wastage According to the organizer’s summary of the WhatsApp call, Mr. Samule found the calculator easy to understand and helpful for business utilization and operations planning. The practical benefit described was a clearer volume target. This is a paraphrase, not a verbatim testimonial, numerical rating or independently conducted review. The organizer clarified that the earlier manual process did not give the manager an exact planning figure. A numerical matched-input manual worksheet was not supplied, so this account does not claim a measured accuracy improvement, error reduction or time saving. His specific improvement request was a separate food-wastage calculation. Wastage is already within the entered $21.50 materials cost. A useful future field would split the existing total into usable ingredient cost and wastage, or add only genuinely additional losses. Adding the same loss again would understate contribution and inflate the sales target. No separate wastage amount was supplied and no dedicated new feature is claimed here. See actual food-cost reconciliation and restaurant inventory and waste costs for related methods. What to capture at the next restaurant review Export completed table bills and realized sales for the exact period; distinguish diners from bills and separate refunds, taxes and tips. Reconcile inventory consumption, wastage and actual fees once. Keep committed payroll separate from genuinely variable labor. Save the full input screen, including utilization and conversion, alongside the dates and unit definition. Compare actual contribution with the $54.56 planning assumption before comparing profit with the target. Inspect daily and peak-service bottlenecks separately from monthly worker-hour capacity. Review payment dates in the dated cash forecast ; modeled profit does not guarantee available bank cash. Download the calculation and evidence record (CSV) . It contains the supplied inputs, editorial arithmetic and clearly labelled reported results. It is a static record, not an account export or POS ledger. Sources, method and corrections The business account comes from the outreach organizer’s supplied answers and corrected screenshot, with publication permission reported by that organizer. The image below the introduction is AI-generated editorial artwork, not a photograph of Thai Foods. The calculator screenshot is separately labelled participant-supplied evidence. The OpenStax break-even and target-profit explanation supports the general contribution method. All figures in this article are supplied case inputs or our explicitly labelled calculations; none are copied textbook cases or industry benchmarks. Our calculation methodology explains rounding and model scope. Read the case-study evidence standards or send corrections through the contact page . Frequently asked questions What does one order mean in the Thai Foods case study? One order means one completed table bill, which may cover several guests. The $99 average revenue and per-order costs use that same unit. No average party size was supplied, so table bills cannot be relabelled as individual customers. Is 1,476 table bills the restaurant’s operating break-even point? No. It is the monthly volume required to fund $24,500 overhead, $6,000 owner pay and an additional $50,000 profit target at $54.56 contribution per bill. Overhead-only break-even is 450 whole bills; funding overhead and owner pay needs 560. Why did the manager choose about 50 table bills per day? The monthly 1,476-bill target averages49.2 over30 open days. A plan of 50 each day provides 1,500 monthly bills. At the entered $99 average, that is $4,950 daily sales; about $5,000 was the sales goal rather than guaranteed collections. Did MyBreakeven independently verify the reported $32,721 profit? No. The publisher was told this was the accounts figure for November 1–15, after $12,250 allocated overhead and $3,000 owner pay, before tax. The underlying sales and cost ledger were not supplied, so it is not an audited outcome or proof the calculator increased profit. Was this a paid testimonial? The outreach organizer reported no payment, discount, free paid-plan access or other benefit for the review, and reported that Mr. Samule permitted publication. Feedback came through a WhatsApp call and is paraphrased; no verbatim written testimonial or rating was supplied. Should food wastage be added to the $21.50 cost again? No. Food wastage was already included in the entered materials cost. A separate field would need to split that total into components or identify genuinely additional losses. Adding the same wastage twice would understate contribution.

documents.text: BUSINESS FINANCIAL ANALYSIS Financial Ratios: Formulas, Types and Examples Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 18, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Explore 55 financial measures: 19 connected worked examples and 36 additional formula definitions. Match each measure to the right records, period and business question before interpreting the result. Calculate all 55 measures in the interactive calculator → Illustrative financial-analysis scene. The reference table contains the exact formulas and fictional figures. What financial ratios tell you Financial ratios compare defined financial-statement amounts to answer a specific question. Liquidity asks about near-term resources and obligations; profitability relates a profit subtotal to sales; leverage describes financing; efficiency and returns connect period activity with assets or equity. A single ratio is not a business-health score. Open the Financial Ratios Calculator to calculate the grouped measures with your own records. Choose the question before the formula A question-led map Category Question Read next Liquidity What resources support near-term obligations? Working capital Profitability Which earnings subtotal is being compared with sales? Operating margin Leverage and coverage What finances the assets, and what covers interest? Integrated leverage methods Efficiency and returns How do flows relate to the balances supporting them? Days sales outstanding One connected fictional business Cedar Supply’s original annual example uses the same inputs as the calculator defaults. It reports $200,000 net revenue, $120,000 COGS, $50,000 operating expenses including $10,000 D&A, $5,000 interest and $5,000 income-tax expense. Thus gross profit is $80,000, operating profit/EBIT $30,000, net income $20,000 and EBITDA $40,000. Net credit sales are $180,000, and the reporting period is 365 days. All amounts are fictional USD, not an industry benchmark. Closing current assets are $60,000: $10,000 cash including equivalents, $5,000 separate eligible liquid investments, $25,000 trade receivables, $18,000 inventory and $2,000 prepayments. Current liabilities are $30,000. Closing assets $200,000 equal liabilities $120,000 plus equity $80,000; defined interest-bearing debt is $60,000. Opening inventory, receivables, assets and equity are $22,000, $20,000, $180,000 and $70,000 respectively. Follow the full statement and cash reconciliation without duplicating that walkthrough here. Printable financial-ratio formula reference Print this page for the in-page reference; there is no separate eBook download. “×” means times. Ratios below use closing balances for liquidity/leverage and period flows with the stated average balances for efficiency/returns. Cash already includes equivalents; do not add them again. sheet is a snapshot; an income statement covers an interval. For inventory turnover, average inventory is ($22,000 + $18,000) / 2 = $20,000. For ROA it is ($180,000 + $200,000) / 2 = $190,000. More frequent observations may better capture seasonality. Do not compare a 90-day return with a 365-day return and call the difference an improvement without addressing the period. Zero sales or zero interest does not make the corresponding margin or coverage zero; the division is undefined. Missing values are unknown, not zero. Zero or negative equity makes conventional positive-equity leverage and return comparisons unsuitable. The calculator flags these boundaries rather than inventing a score. Different leverage formulas legitimately give different numbers Assets/equity = 2.50×, total liabilities/equity = 1.50×, and interest-bearing debt/equity = 0.75×. With positive equity and a balanced statement, assets/equity equals 1 + liabilities/equity. It does not automatically equal 1 + interest-bearing debt/equity. Use the integrated leverage selector to keep the numerators distinct. These business ratios are not trading leverage or bank regulatory-capital measures. Interpret a pattern, not a universal pass mark A current ratio can rise because more overdue invoices accumulate; a gross margin can improve while collections slow; a larger equity multiplier can lift ROE without stronger operating profit. Look at customer aging, stock quality, debt maturities and operating cash alongside the ratio. Compare the same entity, accounting policy, season and period against its own history and truly comparable businesses. No universal green threshold establishes credit eligibility. Trace EBITDA to the included expenses before interpreting its margin. COGS classification affects both gross margin and inventory turnover; operating cash flow explains why profit is not the money available to pay obligations. Common mistakes and next steps Double-counting cash, mixing total sales with credit sales, using closing inventory where an average is intended, hiding negative equity and calling working capital a percentage all change the measure. Record the numerator, denominator, dates and missing data before comparing results. Analyze the complete Cedar Supply statements or enter a matched dataset in the calculator . Sources and editorial scope The SEC’s statement guide explains the statement boundaries. BDC’s financial tools provide a practical ratio reference. Our dataset, formula table and reconciliations are original and use the definitions printed here. Published by MyBreakeven under our editorial and correction standards . If inventory rises $14,000 while cash falls from $10,000 to $6,000 and other current assets remain unchanged, that higher ratio does not prove improved payment capacity. Review the asset composition and dated cash obligations separately. A zero or negative denominator is not a healthy zero result. Additional formula reference reviewed November 18, 2026. Original worked dataset and calculator definitions are preserved. Frequently asked questions What are financial ratios? They relate financial-statement amounts to answer a defined liquidity, profitability, leverage or efficiency question. Their usefulness depends on matched periods, definitions and context. What is a good current ratio? There is no universal threshold that proves financial health. Review collection quality, inventory liquidity, payment dates, industry and financing terms. Are liabilities and interest-bearing debt the same? No. Total liabilities also include obligations such as trade payables. Label the numerator before comparing leverage. Educational examples only. documents.text: MONTHLY RECORDS · SELECTED YTD · FREE EXCEL DOWNLOAD Income Statement Template Download an editable monthly and YTD income statement Excel template with a filled example. Reconcile net revenue, COGS, operating income and net income. Published and method checked November 18, 2026 . Download income statement Excel template Try the statement example Build one matching-period income statement Fictional USD example. Enter the fourteen recognized amounts for one entity and reporting period; use explicit zeros. These inputs do not calculate tax liability or transfer into the Excel file. Gross sales Sales returns and allowances Sales discounts Cost of goods sold / services Operating payroll excluding COGS Operating rent excluding COGS Operating utilities excluding COGS Marketing expense Other operating expense Operating depreciation excluding COGS Other non-operating income Other non-operating expense Interest expense Income tax expense Net revenue $47,500.00 Gross profit $29,500.00 Operating expenses $14,500.00 Operating income / loss $15,000.00 Pretax income / loss $14,700.00 Net income / loss $11,700.00 Net margin: 24.63% . Expenses are positive inputs; losses are calculated and shown as negative results. Reset statement example Download scenario CSV Print / save PDF Browser inputs reset on reload. CSV values do not recalculate; the Excel workbook has formulas and separate inputs. AI-created editorial illustration. All example financial amounts are fictional. Prepare the records before filling the statement An income statement summarizes earned revenue and recognized expenses for a defined reporting period. Begin with one entity, a calendar year, one currency and the accounting basis adopted for the records. Reconcile the trial balance and close the period before presenting the result as actual. A draft based on unreconciled bank transactions is not equivalent to a completed accrual-basis report. Collect sales and refund records, inventory and cost-of-sales schedules, payroll, supplier invoices, accruals, prepayments, asset depreciation, financing interest and the period income-tax expense. Identify the person responsible for each schedule and unresolved difference. The worksheet helps present the amounts; it does not choose recognition policies or turn incomplete source records into an audited statement. What the Excel download contains The workbook has three sheets: Instructions, Blank Statement and Example Statement. The blank version starts without monetary assumptions. The example uses original fictional USD amounts so you can trace every subtotal. Blue input amounts on pale-yellow cells are editable; calculated outputs use formulas. Each sheet covers January through December and a separately selected year-to-date total. Set the calendar year and enter how many months belong in YTD, from one through twelve. Enter all fourteen monetary inputs for every included month, including explicit zeros. Missing selected-month inputs make YTD unavailable instead of silently treating an unknown expense as zero. Unselected later months do not block the completed earlier-month result. The browser example and downloaded workbook are separate; online edits are not transferred into the file. Map the ledger without counting expenses twice Start with gross sales and subtract recognized returns, allowances and discounts to obtain net revenue. Then deduct the adopted cost of goods sold or cost of services to find gross profit. The operating-expense categories cover payroll, rent, utilities, marketing, other operating expenses and depreciation that has not already been included in cost of sales. Keep the classification policy consistent across periods. A production wage or depreciation charge already included in COGS must not also enter operating expenses. A supplier payment for unsold inventory does not establish the current-period cost of sales by itself. Likewise, a refundable deposit and a new equipment purchase are not automatically current operating expenses. Reconcile their asset treatment and later expense recognition separately. Owner distributions, loan proceeds and loan-principal repayments also belong outside this income-statement expense calculation. Trace the fictional monthly statement The example starts with gross sales of $50,000, returns and allowances of $1,000, and discounts of $1,500. Net revenue is $47,500. COGS of $18,000 leaves $29,500 gross profit. Operating payroll of $8,000, rent $3,000, utilities $500, marketing $1,200, other operating expenses $800 and operating depreciation $1,000 total $14,500. Operating income is therefore $15,000. Add $200 of separately identified non-operating income, then deduct $100 other non-operating expense and $400 interest to obtain $14,700 pretax income. Entered income-tax expense of $3,000 leaves $11,700 net income. Net margin is $11,700 divided by positive net revenue of $47,500, or about 24.6%. These figures illustrate the presentation, not a benchmark, customer outcome, tax estimate or earnings forecast. Calculate YTD totals and margins on the right basis With the fictional example repeated for January through March and the YTD selector set to three, gross sales total $150,000, net revenue $142,500 and net income $35,100. The YTD margin is total net income divided by total net revenue. Do not average monthly margin percentages when revenue differs between months; that gives equal weight to unequal sales bases. A blank month is unknown, while an explicit zero describes a known zero amount. Complete the selected months before relying on the YTD result. The model accepts nonnegative input amounts and calculates a loss automatically when expenses exceed revenue. Margin is unavailable when net revenue is nonpositive. Tax benefits, specialized financial-industry formats, consolidated entities, OCI and earnings-per-share calculations are outside this compact statement template. Keep earnings and bank cash separate Positive net income does not demonstrate that customers have paid. Receivables, inventory, unpaid operating bills, noncash depreciation and tax timing can change the relationship between earnings and operating cash. Asset purchases and borrowing create further differences between operating profit and total cash movement. Read the completed statement together with matching balance-sheet and cash-flow records. For example, equipment paid in full can reduce cash while only the adopted period depreciation enters this expense presentation. A new loan raises cash without becoming sales. Debt principal reduces cash without becoming interest expense. Keep those distinctions in the supporting schedules instead of forcing the bank balance to match net income. The connected cash-flow analysis guide explains how to investigate the resulting pattern. Review the statement before distributing it Reconcile each subtotal to the adjusted ledger and retain the source schedules. Review unusual returns, cost classifications, missing accruals, one-off entries and period cutoffs. Compare matching months and the same presentation policy. A changed cost classification can move gross margin without changing net income, so explain the policy change before interpreting the trend as improved performance. Name the preparer, reviewer, reporting date and remaining unresolved items. Preserve a dated copy of the completed workbook and separate actuals from planning scenarios. Use the financial-reporting workflow for preparation and approval, then the financial-statement analysis guide for interpretation. This resource owns statement preparation; it does not replace a general valuation, cash forecast or accounting-framework assessment. Sources and calculation scope Definitions were checked November 18, 2026 against the SEC’s income-statement building blocks and introductory financial-statement guide. All numerical cases, workbook formulas and browser defaults are original teaching examples. The layout is a compact management worksheet rather than a claim of universal financial-reporting compliance. Use the presentation and accounting policies applicable to the actual business. The browser accepts fourteen nonnegative amounts up to one trillion each and retains them only in the current page state. Tax expense is entered from the records, not calculated from a tax rate. CSV exports contain scenario values rather than recalculating formulas. The Excel download contains formulas and its own inputs. Neither version submits financial information or automatically saves the browser scenario. SEC income-statement building blocks SEC guide to financial statements Frequently asked questions Is an income statement the same as a profit and loss statement? The names often describe the same period-performance report. Match the actual accounting basis, entity, dates and expense classifications before comparing two versions. Does the Excel template calculate monthly and YTD totals? Yes. It calculates net revenue, gross profit, operating income, pretax income, net income and margins from entered amounts. The YTD selector includes one to twelve calendar months and requires complete inputs for those months. Why does a blank input make a subtotal unavailable? A blank amount is unknown. Enter zero when the source record establishes a zero amount. This avoids presenting incomplete expenses as a complete profit figure. Can the template calculate a net loss? Yes. Expenses can exceed revenue and produce a negative profit subtotal. Input amounts are nonnegative; tax benefits and specialized signed adjustments need a separately adapted statement. Are equipment payments and loan principal operating expenses? They are not automatically income-statement expenses. Equipment may be an asset with later depreciation; loan principal is financing. Match the adopted accounting policy and supporting records. Do browser edits appear in the Excel download? No. The workbook starts with its own blank and fictional example sheets. The CSV button exports only the current browser scenario as fixed values. Connect preparation with review Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections .

documents.text: FREE EDITABLE BUSINESS PLANNING RESOURCE Business Plan Template Write a detailed business plan that connects the buyer, offer, operating capacity, funding and cash assumptions. Download a blank Word outline with a completed fictional example, then replace each claim with evidence. Published October 25, 2026 · By MyBreakeven Get the free Word template Download the editable business plan outline and example The Word file contains a blank detailed outline, executive-summary prompts, a completed Harbor Desk Services narrative and a financial example. Keep the example as a reference, then replace every prompt and fictional assumption with your own evidence. Downloads are free and require no signup. Download editable Word plan (.docx) The blank outline comes before the completed example. Write the customer, offer, operating plan and financial assumptions first, then use those checked details in the executive summary. The example uses USD labels without currency conversion. Word and Excel formats are supplied as stated; Google application compatibility has not been tested. Actual Word document preview. The completed case and its amounts are fictional. Choose the plan that matches your decision Use this detailed outline when the reader needs the evidence behind the business decision. For a short summary, use the one-page business plan template . For annual objectives and an editable longer-horizon worksheet, use the five-year business plan template . A recipient may require a different order, more detail or particular financial statements. Match the format to that request. The downloadable examples do not imply funding approval or independent accounting certification. Detailed business plan outline 1 . Executive summary Write this last. Identify the customer, offer, evidence, financial requirement and next approval. Label assumptions and describe the decision sought. 2 . Company and ownership State the purpose, stage, location or service area, ownership and responsibilities. List registrations or approvals to verify rather than assuming compliance. 3 . Customer and market evidence Define a specific buyer and problem. Record interviews, paid tests, competitor offers and dated sources. Separate addressable prospects from accepted work. 4 . Offer and delivery scope Describe the deliverable, price basis, quality standard, revision limit and exclusions. Explain variable costs and complete delivery hours. 5 . Sales and customer retention Name testable channels, spending boundaries, sales stages and retention measures. Reconcile accepted work, completed work and cash collected. 6 . Operations and management Assign delivery, review, supplier, backup and financial responsibilities. Compare the workload with available productive hours and document dependencies. 7 . Financial plan and funding Show volume, contribution, commitments, owner funding, opening cash, capital purchases and collection timing. Attach detailed statements when the reader requires them. 8 . Risks milestones and review Choose measurable approval conditions, a downside case, an owner and a review date. State the action taken when evidence contradicts the plan. 9 . Appendix and evidence register Attach only relevant dated records. Include references for each important assumption, approved decisions, historical statements if available and unresolved information. Use dated source records beside important assumptions. Record what is known, what is still estimated and who must verify it. Do not fill a market-size or customer-contract field with an invented claim because a template has space for it. How to write the executive summary Write the summary after checking the rest of the plan. It should let the reader identify the buyer and offer, the evidence, the operating requirement, the source and use of funding, the major constraint and the decision requested. Keep the full assumptions and supporting schedules in the body and appendix. Executive-summary example Harbor Desk Services is a fictional owner-operated service preparing defined document and presentation packages for small professional firms. The first-year plan tests 120 completed packages at $500 each. Sales of $60,000 leave $42,000 contribution before $12,000 operating commitments and a separate $24,000 owner cash allowance. The resulting $6,000 planning surplus is not statutory net profit. The owner proposes $15,000 cash at the start of 2027, with $3,000 equipment spending during the year. Expansion depends on paid customer tests, delivery hours and actual collection dates. Before sharing your own version, replace the business name, customer claim, price, costs, hours and funding source together. A claim of strong demand needs evidence such as paid pilots or accepted work; it cannot be inferred from the revenue target. Completed example: Harbor Desk Services This original fictional case is a defined document-and-presentation service. All prices, customer volumes and costs are assumptions. It is not a customer success story, an industry benchmark or a quotation for your location. Company and ownership The example has one owner responsible for sales, quality and cash review. Work is delivered remotely within a defined service area. The operating format and any registration, insurance, data-handling and client-contract requirements must be checked for the actual location before trading. No legal structure or approval is represented as already established. Customer and market evidence The intended buyer is a small professional firm with recurring document-formatting work but limited internal production time. Interviews and paid pilots will test scope, turnaround and willingness to pay. Buyers can use their own staff, independent contractors or design tools. The example has no measured market share, signed contracts or claimed market-size statistic. Offer and delivery scope A package includes a fixed set of pages, one briefing call, two revision rounds and final files. The assumed selling price is $500 and direct cash cost is $150 per completed package, including applicable delivery support, transaction charges and acquisition allowance. Eight productive hours include communication, revisions and handover. Extra scope requires a revised quote. Sales and customer retention The owner will test a small referral network and direct outreach to suitable firms. Inquiries, accepted quotes, completed packages and collected invoices will be recorded separately. The 120-package target is an assumption, not a conversion forecast. Marketing costs already included in direct or fixed commitments are not entered a second time. Repeat purchasing will be measured after delivery. Operations and management The first year assumes 1,200 productive hours. At eight hours per package, the practical annual ceiling is 150 whole packages, compared with 120 planned. The owner must support these hours with a workable calendar that also allows selling, administration and leave. Supplier and contractor quotes, backup arrangements, review steps and permissions are evidence to obtain. Financial plan and funding At $350 contribution per package, $12,000 operating commitments plus a $24,000 owner cash allowance require 103 whole packages, rounded up. The 120-package case leaves $6,000 after those commitments. Opening cash is $15,000, supported by a proposed owner funding source rather than an approved loan. Ninety percent of annual sales is collected within the same year and the balance in the following year in this simplified example. Year-end cash is $12,000 after $3,000 equipment cash spending; $6,000 sales remains receivable. No new funding is assumed later. Risks milestones and review Before scaling, the owner will complete paid pilots, record full delivery time and validate the collection terms. At only 90 first-year packages, the same commitments produce a $4,500 shortfall after owner allowance and $3,000 year-end cash after equipment, below the illustrative $5,000 floor. The owner will postpone discretionary spending, revise scope or seek confirmed funding before making commitments. Monthly actuals and quarterly decisions replace unsupported annual growth assumptions. Appendix and evidence register The appendix will retain interview notes, paid-pilot records, accepted scopes, supplier quotes, delivery-hour logs, collection terms and a funding record. A decision log will name each assumption, source date, owner and next review. No attachment in this fictional example is represented as an actual customer contract, quote or audited financial statement. Check the first-year financial example 2027 fictional service case, USD Measure Calculation Revenue 120 × $500 = $60,000 Contribution $60,000 − $18,000 direct costs = $42,000 After owner allowance $42,000 − $12,000 fixed cash − $24,000 owner cash = $6,000 Whole packages for commitments Round up $36,000 ÷ $350 = 103 Delivery ceiling 1,200 productive hours ÷ 8 = 150 whole packages Closing cash $15,000 + $54,000 collected − $54,000 operating and owner cash − $3,000 equipment = $12,000 Contribution is revenue less the specified direct costs. Fixed operating cash commitments are separate from the owner cash allowance. The worksheet shows the result before that allowance and the planning result after it. Accounting and tax treatment depend on the actual business arrangement. Do not describe the post-allowance result as statutory net profit. For the 2027 example, the same $350 contribution must cover $12,000 fixed commitments and $24,000 owner support. The 103-package rounded minimum is below the assumed 120 packages and 150-package capacity. Neither the target nor capacity proves demand. Include paid delivery support and owner work once within a consistent cost boundary. Test a weaker first year At 90 packages with unchanged price, costs, collection share and owner allowance, contribution falls to $31,500 and the result after commitments becomes −$4,500. Collections are $40,500. Opening $15,000 less $9,000 trading cash use and $3,000 equipment leaves $3,000 year-end cash, below the illustrative $5,000 floor. Name the spending, scope or funding response before committing. Attach the financial schedules your reader needs The Word example is a readable financial explanation. It does not replace the income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements, capital schedules or historical records a lender, investor or owner may need. Build the first year with monthly or quarterly detail and keep later annual assumptions traceable. The completed case collects $54,000 of its $60,000 first-year sales and leaves $6,000 receivable. Equipment uses $3,000 cash without automatically becoming a full current-year operating expense. Owner allowance is shown separately so the same work is not paid twice in the example. Use the dated 13-week cash forecast for payroll, supplier and settlement dates. Annual positive cash can conceal a shortage before receipts arrive. For launch costs and the initial funding gap, use the business startup cost calculator . Opening either tool does not transfer these document or workbook inputs. Review the plan before sharing or expanding Match the narrative and numbers. Update volume, scope, team hours, contribution, owner support, funding and collections together. Check evidence. Retain source dates, paid tests, accepted scopes, supplier records and delivery logs. Keep unresolved assumptions visible. Assign the next action. Give each milestone an owner, review date, measurable approval condition and response if the test fails. Compare actuals with the same plan. Review the first year monthly, record explanations and revisit the remaining years at quarterly decisions. Preserve the previous approved version. Fit the recipient’s request. Attach the statements and records they require. Remove examples from the submitted plan and identify projections as assumptions. Use the budget-versus-actual worksheet for a recurring numerical review and the rolling forecast guide when extending the next twelve months. A five-year strategic plan and a rolling operational forecast serve different review horizons. Frequently asked questions What does the free business plan template include? The editable Word file contains a blank detailed outline, executive-summary prompts, a completed fictional service-business narrative and a checked financial example. No email or account is required. How is this different from the one-page business plan? The one-page resource summarizes a decision. This detailed outline gives space for customer evidence, delivery scope, management, funding, financial assumptions, risks and an appendix. Use the shorter summary after checking the supporting plan. What belongs in an executive summary? State the customer and offer, the evidence supporting the plan, the operating and funding requirement, the main constraints and the next approval. Write it after the body and financial schedules agree. Does the Word document include complete financial statements? No. It includes a transparent annual example. Attach the income statements, balance sheets, cash flow forecasts and supporting schedules required by your reader, with monthly or quarterly first-year detail where needed. Are the example customers and prices real? No. Harbor Desk Services and all amounts are fictional planning assumptions. Replace them with your own customer evidence, accepted scopes, cost quotes, hours and collection terms. Can this guarantee a business loan? No. A recipient may require additional records, a particular format and an independent assessment. A written plan and an illustrative funding assumption are not loan approval. References and specialist templates The U.S. Small Business Administration business-planning guidance describes traditional and lean planning and the financial outlook a reader may need. This resource uses original prompts, examples and calculations; it is not an SBA-issued or approved plan. Use the existing landscaping , marketing agency or ecommerce business plan when the specialist operating assumptions fit your task. Explore all business planning resources and read our editorial and correction standards .

documents.text: FREE EDITABLE BUSINESS PLANNING RESOURCE Five-Year Business Plan Template Translate a five-year direction into annual decisions, capacity and cash assumptions. Download a Word plan and Excel annual planning worksheet with one consistent fictional case from 2027 to 2031. Published October 25, 2026 · By MyBreakeven Get the free Word and Excel files Download the editable five-year plan and annual worksheet The Word file contains a blank strategy outline, an annual objectives template and the completed Harbor Desk Services case. The separate Excel file reconciles annual operating assumptions and cash, and gives each milestone an owner and review field. Downloads are free and require no signup. Download editable Word plan (.docx) Download annual planning Excel (.xlsx) In Annual plan, replace the blue inputs while keeping the formulas. In Milestones, replace the example targets and add an owner and review date before approving a year. The cash and receivables roll forward between annual columns. The example uses USD labels without currency conversion. Word and Excel formats are supplied as stated; Google application compatibility has not been tested. Actual Word document preview. The completed case and its amounts are fictional. Choose the plan that matches your decision Use this resource for annual priorities, resources, financial assumptions and approval conditions. For the complete business narrative, use the detailed business plan template . The one-page plan is the concise decision summary. A recipient may require a different order, more detail or particular financial statements. Match the format to that request. The downloadable examples do not imply funding approval or independent accounting certification. How to build a five-year business plan Establish the starting position. Record actual customers, products, team resources, cash and unresolved constraints before setting later targets. Choose an evidence-based direction. Define the offer and buyer you intend to serve. State what would cause you to change direction. Set a separate objective for each year. Name the measurable outcome, evidence, owner and next review. A percentage growth assumption alone does not describe the work. Reconcile resources and money. Link package volume to delivery hours, costed support, price and contribution. Review owner cash and collection timing separately. Gate expansion on results. Identify which purchase, hiring or capacity decision depends on each test. Record what you will postpone if the condition is not met. Review the first year in more detail. Keep monthly or quarterly financial schedules and actual payment dates alongside the annual view. Revisit the remaining years at each quarterly review. Use dated source records beside important assumptions. Record what is known, what is still estimated and who must verify it. Do not fill a market-size or customer-contract field with an invented claim because a template has space for it. Summarize the five-year decision Summarize the starting position, intended direction, annual evidence gates, resources and cash conditions. Later annual targets are conditional plans rather than guaranteed outcomes. Make the first expansion decision clear before describing a year-five vision. Executive-summary example Harbor Desk Services is a fictional owner-operated service preparing defined document and presentation packages for small professional firms. The first-year plan tests 120 completed packages at $500 each. Sales of $60,000 leave $42,000 contribution before $12,000 operating commitments and a separate $24,000 owner cash allowance. The resulting $6,000 planning surplus is not statutory net profit. The owner proposes $15,000 cash at the start of 2027, with $3,000 equipment spending during the year. Expansion depends on paid customer tests, delivery hours and actual collection dates. The later-year package targets are 144, 168, 192 and 216. Each requires its own supported price, cost and productive-hours plan. The worksheet does not create those resources or prove that the work will sell. Completed example: Harbor Desk Services This original fictional case is a defined document-and-presentation service. All prices, customer volumes and costs are assumptions. It is not a customer success story, an industry benchmark or a quotation for your location. The plan expands only a validated offer. Productive team hours increase from 1,200 in 2027 to 2,160 in 2031. Those hours require an evidenced calendar and costed delivery support; increasing a spreadsheet input does not hire another worker. 2027 : Validate the core service Target: 120 packages at 8 productive hours each . Evidence: Paid pilot records and a workable 1,200-hour calendar . Response: Pause expansion if actual work exceeds scope or cash dates fail . 2028 : Develop repeat customers Target: 144 packages at $520 . Evidence: Repeat paid orders and documented 1,440 productive hours . Response: Review price and staffing before accepting more recurring work . 2029 : Standardize quality and handover Target: 168 packages at $540 . Evidence: Rework logs, supplier backup and 1,680 productive hours . Response: Fund added delivery support before promising the larger volume . 2030 : Expand only the validated offer Target: 192 packages at $560 . Evidence: Customer evidence and 1,920 productive hours . Response: Rebuild the plan if scope or collections change . 2031 : Review the next strategic period Target: 216 packages at $580 . Evidence: Retention, complete cost records and 2,160 productive hours . Response: Approve a new plan rather than extending the same growth line . Check the five-year operating assumptions Fictional USD annual assumptions for Harbor Desk Services ; not demand forecasts Measure 2027 2028 2029 2030 2031 Packages 120 144 168 192 216 Revenue $60,000 $74,880 $90,720 $107,520 $125,280 Contribution $42,000 $52,416 $63,504 $75,264 $87,696 Before owner allowance $30,000 $39,416 $49,504 $60,264 $71,696 After owner allowance $6,000 $13,416 $21,504 $30,264 $39,696 Whole packages for commitments 103 108 112 115 119 Package capacity 150 180 210 240 270 Contribution is revenue less the specified direct costs. Fixed operating cash commitments are separate from the owner cash allowance. The worksheet shows the result before that allowance and the planning result after it. Accounting and tax treatment depend on the actual business arrangement. Do not describe the post-allowance result as statutory net profit. For the 2027 example, the same $350 contribution must cover $12,000 fixed commitments and $24,000 owner support. The 103-package rounded minimum is below the assumed 120 packages and 150-package capacity. Neither the target nor capacity proves demand. Include paid delivery support and owner work once within a consistent cost boundary. Test a weaker first year At 90 packages with unchanged price, costs, collection share and owner allowance, contribution falls to $31,500 and the result after commitments becomes −$4,500. Collections are $40,500. Opening $15,000 less $9,000 trading cash use and $3,000 equipment leaves $3,000 year-end cash, below the illustrative $5,000 floor. Name the spending, scope or funding response before committing. Reconcile annual cash and receivables Fictional USD annual assumptions for Harbor Desk Services ; not demand forecasts Measure 2027 2028 2029 2030 2031 Opening cash $15,000 $12,000 $22,928 $40,848 $68,432 Cash collected $54,000 $73,392 $89,136 $105,840 $123,504 Operating and owner cash paid $54,000 $61,464 $69,216 $77,256 $85,584 Equipment cash $3,000 $1,000 $2,000 $1,000 $2,000 Closing cash $12,000 $22,928 $40,848 $68,432 $104,352 Uncollected sales $6,000 $7,488 $9,072 $10,752 $12,528 The workbook starts with $15,000 cash and no opening receivables. Each year collects the entered share of current sales plus all prior-year receivables. The uncollected portion rolls into the next year. All stated direct and fixed costs and the owner allowance are paid in the year. Equipment, other payments and new funding have separate cash rows. Ninety percent same-year collection and full collection of opening receivables are simplifying assumptions, not measured behavior. No bad debt, longer delay, tax, depreciation or debt schedule is supplied. Put applicable tax, principal, interest and other cash in the appropriate rows without double counting. Use the dated 13-week cash forecast for payroll, supplier and settlement dates. Annual positive cash can conceal a shortage before receipts arrive. For launch costs and the initial funding gap, use the business startup cost calculator . Opening either tool does not transfer these document or workbook inputs. Review the plan before sharing or expanding Match the narrative and numbers. Update volume, scope, team hours, contribution, owner support, funding and collections together. Check evidence. Retain source dates, paid tests, accepted scopes, supplier records and delivery logs. Keep unresolved assumptions visible. Assign the next action. Give each milestone an owner, review date, measurable approval condition and response if the test fails. Compare actuals with the same plan. Review the first year monthly, record explanations and revisit the remaining years at quarterly decisions. Preserve the previous approved version. Fit the recipient’s request. Attach the statements and records they require. Remove examples from the submitted plan and identify projections as assumptions. Use the budget-versus-actual worksheet for a recurring numerical review and the rolling forecast guide when extending the next twelve months. A five-year strategic plan and a rolling operational forecast serve different review horizons. Frequently asked questions What comes with the five-year business plan template? An editable Word outline and completed example, plus an Excel annual planning worksheet with Annual plan and Milestones tabs. The fictional case covers calendar years 2027–2031. Does Excel automatically assume a growth rate? No. Volume, price, costs, owner allowance, productive hours, collection share and cash payments are separate editable annual inputs. A larger target is not evidence of demand or available staffing. Is this a full five-year financial model? It is an annual planning worksheet for volume, contribution, capacity, owner funding and a simplified cash bridge. It does not supply an integrated balance sheet, depreciation, tax or debt schedule. Attach required financial statements separately. Why show the owner cash allowance separately? Owner cash support can be necessary without being an operating expense under the chosen business structure. The worksheet shows the operating result before that allowance, then the result and cash after it. Count the same owner work once. How are receivables collected? Each year collects the entered share of its sales plus all opening receivables. Uncollected current sales move to the next year. This simplified assumption does not model bad debt or delays longer than the following year. Does positive annual cash mean every bill can be paid? No. Annual netting can hide earlier shortages. Build a first-year monthly or quarterly plan and use the dated cash forecast for payroll, supplier payments and processor settlements. How should I update the milestones? Replace the example objectives with measurable outcomes. Assign an owner and a valid review date, retain evidence, and record the action taken when a condition fails. A populated field is not proof that a milestone was achieved. Can I use the files in Google Sheets or Google Docs? The files are supplied as Word and Excel downloads. Compatibility with Google applications has not been tested, so no native Google format or identical rendering is promised. References and specialist templates The U.S. Small Business Administration business-planning guidance describes traditional and lean planning and the financial outlook a reader may need. This resource uses original prompts, examples and calculations; it is not an SBA-issued or approved plan. How to write your landscaping business plan The same plan must explain who buys, what one visit includes, how the crew delivers it and how the quiet months are funded. Start with evidence from customers and records, then write the executive summary after the operating and cash schedules agree. Business and ownership Name the owner, service area, business structure and responsibilities. Record local registration, insurance and service-specific requirements to verify. Customers and demand Define the customer, property scope and evidence from interviews, paid trials and comparable local quotes. Separate signed work from targets. Services and pricing Define a complete visit, exclusions, revisit policy and seasonal extras. Record time and materials before setting the price. Acquisition and retention List channels, spend, qualified enquiries, conversion evidence and renewal dates. Do not count each repeat visit as a new customer. Operations and staffing Record travel, setup, worker-hours, equipment availability and weather cancellations. Assign responsibility for route and quality checks. Seasonal financial plan List active months, costs that continue off-season, owner compensation and cash collection dates. Link figures to the workbook. Funding and cash List opening cash, equipment purchases, deposits, debt payments and a minimum reserve. Explain each source of funding. Risks and response Choose specific triggers and responses for weather, route delays, repairs, late invoices and insufficient capacity. Milestones and evidence Assign an owner, date, evidence and pass condition to each launch step. Review actual visits, hours, costs and collections monthly. Add an executive summary with the customer, offer, funding need and next milestone. If a bank or investor asks for a particular format, supporting statements or a longer projection, adapt the plan to that request. This download does not imply funding approval. Completed example: Cedar Loop Lawn Care This is a fictional planning case for residential lawn maintenance within a compact service area . Figures are assumptions, not industry averages, actual customer results or a forecast of demand. Business and ownership Cedar Loop is a fictional owner-operated lawn-maintenance business serving one compact residential area. The owner handles quotes, scheduling and field delivery. Local requirements and insurance quotes remain launch conditions. Customers and demand The intended customer wants a dependable maintenance visit with a clear scope. The launch test uses homeowner interviews and paid trial visits. No signed contracts or established demand are assumed. Services and pricing The example models one comparable maintenance visit at $80, with $30 direct cost including job labor, fuel and consumables. Tree work and installations are excluded and require separate quotes. Acquisition and retention The owner will test local referrals and a service-area website. Repeat visits will be scheduled by customer and address. The 100-visit monthly target is a hypothesis, not 100 distinct customers. Operations and staffing One worker has 160 monthly hours, with 80% available for modeled delivery. Each visit requires 1.5 worker-hours including allocated travel. Capacity is only 85 whole visits, so the original sales target fails. Seasonal financial plan March through October carry 100 planned visits per month; the other four months have no modeled sales. Fixed commitments are $3,000 every month. Owner pay, tax, debt and equipment purchases are excluded until entered. Funding and cash The example starts with $10,000 cash. It collects 75% of sales in the service month and 25% next month. Early bills reduce cash before March receipts; no loan or funding approval is assumed. Risks and response Before accepting 100 visits, the owner must add feasible paid capacity or lower bookings. Any added worker changes direct cost and cash. Weather cancellations require both volume and hours to be reforecast. Milestones and evidence Days 1–30: validate demand and quote equipment and insurance. Days 31–60: log paid pilot visits and route time. Days 61–90: commit only the visit volume supported by hours, demand and the cash reserve. Check that the financial plan reconciles Illustrative USD example matching the supplied workbook Measure Calculation Active-month revenue 100 × $80 = $8,000 Contribution before monthly commitments 100 × ($80 − $30) = $5,000 Annual contribution / fixed commitments $40,000 / $36,000 Annual result before excluded items $4,000, conditional on delivering all 800 visits Productive time / required time 128 / 150 worker-hours per active month Whole-visit capacity 85; the target is 15 visits above capacity A positive annual result does not make the delivery plan feasible. The workbook deliberately exposes the 15-visit capacity shortfall. Changing active-month visits to 85 reduces annual contribution to $34,000 and the result to a $2,000 loss before excluded items. Adding staff instead needs a new cost and hours assumption. The result is sales less the specified direct costs, fixed commitments and entered additional owner pay. It excludes unentered tax, interest, depreciation and other costs. Include compensation for owner delivery work once in the chosen labor boundary. A separate owner draw can require cash without being an operating expense; the workbook's additional owner-pay row is an explicit funding allowance. Connect the plan to customer receipts and cash payments January and February each pay $3,000 commitments with no sales receipts, reducing opening cash from $10,000 to $4,000. March receipts are $6,000, direct payments $3,000 and fixed payments $3,000, leaving cash unchanged at $4,000. March ends with $2,000 uncollected sales. The workbook rolls that receipt into April. Monthly cash totals do not identify a shortfall inside a month. The workbook rolls closing cash and uncollected sales into the next month. Opening cash and receivables apply only in January. The uncollected share is assumed received in the next month; there is no automatic bad-debt or longer-delay calculation. Enter equipment, principal, tax and other cash payments in their separate monthly rows. These cash amounts do not automatically become operating expenses. Use the dated 13-week cash forecast for payroll dates, supplier deposits, staged funding and within-month cash gaps. A positive month-end balance cannot prove every payment date is covered. Replace assumptions with evidence before committing money Completed visit and route-time logs Customer confirmations and renewal dates Equipment, insurance and supplier quotes Bank receipts and unpaid invoices Cost and timing mistakes to avoid Treat eight active months and twelve months of bills separately. Keep crew elapsed time distinct from total worker-hours. Include travel once in the productivity and visit-time boundary. Price installation projects separately when their scope differs from routine maintenance. A practical 90-day review In days 1–30, validate the customer problem and gather dated quotes. In days 31–60, run a small paid test and record delivery time, costs and collections. In days 61–90, compare actual results with the same plan and approve expansion only when the demand, hours and cash assumptions are supported. Give each milestone an owner, date and measurable pass condition in your plan. Use the specialist guide for the next decision This page owns the editable business plan and its supporting financial schedule. Pricing, job costing and specialist calculations remain on their existing pages. Opening another tool does not transfer the workbook's inputs. No. The plan also describes the customer, offer, sales approach, operations, risks and milestones. Break-even is one check on its financial assumptions. Can I use the completed example unchanged? Use it to understand the structure and arithmetic. Its prices, demand, staffing and collection timing are fictional. Replace them before making a business commitment. Read our editorial standards and calculation methodology . Separate seasonal maintenance from installation commitments Write the planned service mix before forecasting the season. Recurring maintenance depends on retained routes, visits, crew-hours and collection terms. Installation work also depends on accepted scope, material orders, deposits, milestone acceptance and rework. A combined revenue target can hide the cash and staffing differences. Carry postponed bills into later periods. Keep the workbook's stated example unchanged and attach your business-specific schedules. Business and ownership Harbor Signal is a fictional small marketing studio offering a defined monthly content and reporting service. Two delivery contributors support the schedule. Their hours are capacity assumptions; direct costs must cover their paid work. Customers and demand The target buyer is a small-business owner who needs consistent content execution and reporting. The team will interview prospects and test paid pilots. Expected new clients remain assumptions until agreements are signed. Services and scope The illustrative retainer is $2,000 per client-month for one fixed scope using 20 worker-hours. Client advertising spend is excluded. Extra deliverables need a change agreement and a revised time budget. Sales and retention January starts with eight clients, loses one and adds two at the month start. Nine clients are billed for the full month. Later months assume no gains or losses; this flat forecast is editable. Delivery and staffing Two contributors each have 160 monthly hours at 65% productive utilization, giving 208 delivery hours. Nine clients need 180 hours. The $900 direct cost per client includes modeled delivery cost; the same pay is not in overhead. Revenue and operating costs Nine clients produce $18,000 revenue and $8,100 direct cost. After $6,000 monthly overhead, $3,900 remains before excluded owner pay, tax, financing and unentered costs. No industry margin benchmark is assumed. Collections and funding Opening cash is $8,000 and opening receivables are zero. Half of billed revenue is collected this month and half next month. January cash falls to $2,900 despite a positive operating result. Risks and response The studio will review client concentration and unpaid invoices monthly. An eleventh equivalent client would exceed the 208-hour allowance. New scope requires repricing or resourcing before the team commits.
