Enter explicit zeros for inapplicable costs; missing inputs make dependent results unavailable. The files use USD labels and do not convert currencies. They are Excel files; Google Sheets compatibility is not claimed. Actual document preview: the completed narrative page for Juniper Desk Supply . Download the editable file for the blank outline and financial notes. How to write your ecommerce business plan Revenue, inventory and bank receipts follow different schedules. The plan keeps product cost used in shipped orders separate from the cash spent on replacement stock. Start with evidence from customers and records, then write the executive summary after the operating and cash schedules agree. Business and ownership Describe the store, ownership, product category, sales territories and operating responsibilities. Verify location-specific obligations. Customers and demand Define buyer needs, alternatives, demand evidence and a paid validation test. Separate sessions, checkouts and shipped orders. Product and pricing Define the order basket, price, discounts, shipping collected, product cost and returns policy. Match payment fees to the charged amount. Acquisition and retention Set channels, test spend, attributable orders and repeat purchase definitions. Avoid counting platform-attributed sales twice. Supply and fulfillment Record units, purchase quantities, receipt dates, lead times, storage and dispatch capacity. Define how returned stock is handled. Order contribution and costs Show product cost, fulfillment, fees, acquisition and returns once. Keep fixed costs and owner compensation explicit. Inventory cash and funding Schedule stock purchases and settlement dates. Record opening cash and unsettled receipts. Do not deduct purchases again from operating contribution. Risks and response Set triggers for stockouts, supplier delays, ad cost, refund rates and settlement holds. Describe a funded response. Milestones and evidence Assign dates to supplier validation, product tests, launch and reorder decisions. Record actual orders, returns and bank receipts. Add an executive summary with the customer, offer, funding need and next milestone. If a bank or investor asks for a particular format, supporting statements or a longer projection, adapt the plan to that request. This download does not imply funding approval. Completed example: Juniper Desk Supply This is a fictional planning case for online shoppers buying a single comparable desk-accessory product . Figures are assumptions, not industry averages, actual customer results or a forecast of demand. Business and ownership Juniper Desk is a fictional direct-to-consumer desk-accessory store. The owner manages suppliers, fulfillment and customer service. Tax, product compliance and local registration requirements must be verified for the actual goods and location. Customers and demand The proposed customer wants one comparable desk-accessory item. Interviews, sample feedback and a limited paid launch will test demand. The model assumes 500 shipped orders per month; it does not predict traffic or conversion. Product and pricing One shipped order contains one modeled unit and charges $50 before tax, with no separate shipping receipt. Unit product cost is $20. The fee is 3.5% of the full $50 checkout amount. Acquisition and retention The sample allocates $8 acquisition cost to each shipped order. Paid and repeat orders are not modeled as different cohorts. A real store should replace this blended amount with a documented channel mix. Supply and fulfillment Opening stock is 1,000 units. January receives and pays for 600 units; later months receive 500. Each order uses one unit. Fulfillment and shipping cost $6 per order. Returned units are assumed non-resalable in this example. Order contribution and costs Costs per shipped order are $20 product, $6 fulfillment, $1.75 fees, $8 acquisition and $2 returns allowance. Contribution is $12.25; 500 orders leave $6,125 before $5,000 fixed costs. Inventory cash and funding The example begins with $20,000 cash and no unsettled sales. January stock payments are $12,000, while shipped-unit product cost is $10,000. Settlement is 90% this month and 10% next month. Risks and response The store will review stock coverage and actual refunds weekly. A negative closing inventory balance means the shipment plan is unsupported. Higher returns or acquisition costs require a revised contribution and cash forecast. Milestones and evidence Days 1–30: validate samples, buyers and supplier terms. Days 31–60: run a limited paid launch and track order costs. Days 61–90: reorder only after checking sell-through, cash reserve and delivery reliability. Check that the financial plan reconciles Illustrative USD example matching the supplied workbook Measure Calculation Shipped orders / checkout sales 500 / $25,000 Costs per shipped order $20 + $6 + $1.75 + $8 + $2 = $37.75 Contribution $12.25 × 500 = $6,125 Result before excluded owner pay and tax $6,125 − $5,000 = $1,125 January stock cash / product cost used $12,000 / $10,000 January closing inventory 1,000 + 600 − 500 = 1,100 units The $2 allowance covers modeled refunds and return handling after the full checkout amount has been recorded. It is not an additional deduction from already refund-net revenue. The cash schedule assumes the same allowance is paid in that month. Change that assumption when refunds arrive later; do not treat an accounting allowance as an observed bank payment. The result is sales less the specified direct costs, fixed commitments and entered additional owner pay. It excludes unentered tax, interest, depreciation and other costs. Include compensation for owner delivery work once in the chosen labor boundary. A separate owner draw can require cash without being an operating expense; the workbook's additional owner-pay row is an explicit funding allowance. Connect the plan to customer receipts and cash payments January settles $22,500 and leaves $2,500 unsettled. Cash payments are $12,000 stock, $3,000 fulfillment, $875 fees, $4,000 acquisition, $1,000 refunds and $5,000 fixed costs: $25,875 total. Cash falls $3,375 to $16,625. Compared with $1,125 operating result, the $4,500 difference is $2,000 added inventory cost plus $2,500 unsettled receipts. The workbook rolls closing cash and uncollected sales into the next month. Opening cash and receivables apply only in January. The uncollected share is assumed received in the next month; there is no automatic bad-debt or longer-delay calculation. Enter equipment, principal, tax and other cash payments in their separate monthly rows. These cash amounts do not automatically become operating expenses. Use the dated 13-week cash forecast for payroll dates, supplier deposits, staged funding and within-month cash gaps. A positive month-end balance cannot prove every payment date is covered. Replace assumptions with evidence before committing money Supplier quotes, purchase orders and receipt dates Shipped-unit and stock records Checkout, refund and processor settlement reports Fulfillment invoices and acquisition-cost records Cost and timing mistakes to avoid Define shipped orders and the number of units per order consistently. Do not deduct the same return through both net revenue and a reserve. Separate supplier cash payments from product cost consumed. Account for settlement holds and resalable returns when those apply. A practical 90-day review In days 1–30, validate the customer problem and gather dated quotes. In days 31–60, run a small paid test and record delivery time, costs and collections. In days 61–90, compare actual results with the same plan and approve expansion only when the demand, hours and cash assumptions are supported. Give each milestone an owner, date and measurable pass condition in your plan. Use the specialist guide for the next decision This page owns the editable business plan and its supporting financial schedule. Pricing, job costing and specialist calculations remain on their existing pages. Opening another tool does not transfer the workbook's inputs. Ecommerce break-even calculator Returns cost guide Shipping cost guide Inventory reorder and cash guide Explore all ecommerce business planning guides . For a shorter narrative, use the one-page business plan template . Frequently asked questions Are these templates free and editable? Yes. Download the Word narrative and Excel financial workbook directly without signing up. Replace the fictional example with your records. Is a business plan the same as a break-even calculation? No. The plan also describes the customer, offer, sales approach, operations, risks and milestones. Break-even is one check on its financial assumptions. Can I use the completed example unchanged? Use it to understand the structure and arithmetic. Its prices, demand, staffing and collection timing are fictional. Replace them before making a business commitment. Does the workbook show net profit or guarantee enough cash? No. The result covers only entered costs, and the cash schedule uses monthly timing assumptions. Add omitted costs and use dated cash planning for actual payment decisions. Method and sources Published and example arithmetic checked October 24, 2026. The financial schedules are original MyBreakeven examples. They have not received an independent accountant's review. The SBA business-planning guide provides general planning and market-research context; it does not supply the example numbers or endorse these templates. Read our editorial standards and calculation methodology .

documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN · BUSINESS PLANNING One-Page Business Plan Template with a Completed Example Download a concise editable Word plan or print-ready PDF. Write the business story, then check whether the customer target fits delivery capacity and cash timing. Published October 24, 2026 · By MyBreakeven Download the blank template or completed example Choose the editable Word file to write your plan, or the PDF to print it. Each supplied document is one US Letter page. No account or email address is required. The example describes a fictional service business, not a customer outcome or a tested market opportunity. Blank one-page business plan Eight short prompts for the business decision, customer, offer, marketing, delivery, financial target, cash and risks. Replace the bracketed prompts in Word, or use the PDF’s writing lines. Download blank Word template Download blank PDF Completed service-business example Northline Studio tests a fixed-scope website-update service. Its proposed monthly jobs, delivery hours and opening cash are checked below so you can see what each figure means. Download example in Word Download example PDF The Word files contain editable text, not automatic spreadsheet formulas. The PDFs are static and print-ready, not interactive PDF forms. Update the calculations when you change the assumptions. AI-generated editorial illustration. The actual downloadable document is previewed below. Completed example: a small service business with a specific launch decision Northline Studio is an invented owner-operated business considering four-hour website-update jobs for local service companies. Its plan is a November 2026 launch test. It will proceed only after paid trials test the proposed price, delivery time and collection terms. All figures below are illustrative USD assumptions. Customer and offer The intended buyer is an owner-managed service firm with an outdated booking page. The offer is a defined update package with one revision at a proposed $300 per job. Ten owner interviews and three paid trials are planned; no completed interviews, bookings or market demand are claimed. Sales and delivery The monthly target is 15 paid jobs. An assumed 25% conversion from qualified leads would require 60 qualified leads. Referrals and direct follow-up are proposed channels. The owner reserves 64 practical delivery hours after sales and administration, and each job is assumed to take four hours. Capacity is therefore 16 whole jobs, not an unlimited number of leads or sales. Finance and cash At $300 price and $100 variable cost, each completed job contributes $200. Fixed operating costs are $2,000 and the owner separately targets $1,000 of pay. Fifteen jobs cover that $3,000 planning requirement. Owner savings of $4,250 fund $1,500 setup spending plus $2,750 opening cash. First-month collections are only $2,250 against $4,500 payments, leaving $500. Decision and next review Validate price and hours before committing. If jobs take longer than four hours or customers collect later than assumed, revise scope, price, timing or commitments. Review the interview record, paid-trial results and collection terms after 30 days. A feasible arithmetic target is not evidence that customers will buy. Actual rendered preview of the completed example. Open the PDF for a full-size print view. Check the financial target before polishing the wording A concise plan still needs consistent arithmetic. Start with contribution per job, state which fixed commitments it must cover, round required jobs upward and compare that number with practical capacity. Keep owner pay separate so the label tells the reader which target they are looking at. Original price fails capacity; the revised price is a conditional test Monthly assumption or result Initial idea Revised example Price per job $250 $300 Variable cost per job $100 $100 Contribution per job $150 $200 Fixed operating costs plus owner-pay target $2,000 + $1,000 $2,000 + $1,000 Required whole jobs including owner-pay target 20 15 Hours needed at four hours per job 80 60 Practical capacity 64 hours / 16 jobs 64 hours / 16 jobs Target fits capacity? No: four jobs beyond capacity Yes: one job of spare capacity At the initial $250 price, maximum modeled contribution is 16 × $150 = $2,400. That leaves $600 of the $3,000 owner-pay-inclusive requirement unfunded. Writing “sell 20 jobs” in a financial box cannot create the missing 16 delivery hours. The revised $300 offer gives $200 contribution. Operating break-even alone is $2,000 ÷ $200 = 10 jobs. Adding the separately stated $1,000 owner-pay target increases the requirement to 15 jobs. At 16 jobs, contribution would be $3,200, leaving $200 after these specified commitments. These amounts exclude tax, interest and unlisted costs; the owner-pay target is not presented as an accounting expense classification. For this fictional example, the $100 variable cost consists of $60 outside production support, $20 platform/payment costs and $20 job-specific materials. Fixed costs total $800 workspace, $400 software and $800 marketing/administration. They exclude the owner’s delivery labor, which is represented by the separately included owner-pay target. Replace the boundary if your staffing or fee structure differs. A 25% qualified-lead conversion is only an assumption: 15 ÷ 25% = 60 qualified leads. If conversion is 15%, the same 15 jobs need 100 qualified leads. Neither a capacity calculation nor a lead target establishes demand. Keep quote and paid-order records to improve the assumption. Use the break-even calculation guide for the underlying method or the agency calculator for a fuller contribution and capacity check. The downloadable Word document does not recalculate these figures. Show when sales become usable cash The revised plan sells 15 jobs at $300, or $4,500 in the month. Suppose only 50% is collected that month and the remaining $2,250 arrives later. All $1,500 job costs, $2,000 fixed costs and $1,000 owner pay are paid during the month. There are no other modeled cash transactions. Separate startup funding, first-month cash and uncollected sales Cash item Illustrative USD Owner savings provided before launch $4,250 Setup paid before the month starts ($1,500) Opening cash after setup $2,750 First-month customer collections $2,250 First-month payments including owner pay ($4,500) Closing cash $500 Customer balance still to collect $2,250 Do not subtract the $1,500 setup spending again after using the $2,750 opening cash. It was already paid before that opening balance. Similarly, the uncollected $2,250 is not added to bank cash merely because it is included in sales. The $500 closing balance is a chosen example, not a recommended reserve. It also does not prove every payment date is funded: if all $4,500 payments precede any collection, opening cash of $2,750 is insufficient. Test the actual sequence in the 13-week dated cash forecast and review tight weeks daily. Use net cash flow to summarize a completed period, rather than treating forecasts as actual transactions. How to write a one-page business plan that remains usable Name the decision. State whether you are testing an offer, opening a location, changing a price or reviewing an existing business. Add an owner and review date. Describe one specific customer. Explain their problem and the alternatives they currently use. Separate interview evidence from assumptions. Define the paid offer. Specify the deliverable, unit, scope limits and proposed price. “Consulting” or “quality service” alone is too broad to cost. Explain how a customer reaches a paid order. Name the channel and show the assumed link from qualified leads to sales. Track actual conversion instead of inventing a large market share. Allocate practical delivery capacity. Deduct non-delivery commitments before using hours per job. A full calendar is not the same as paid utilization. Check the monthly contribution target. Keep variable costs, fixed costs and owner pay on the same period and use whole-job rounding. Separate cash from sales. Show setup spending, opening cash, collection timing, payments and the funding source. Keep a dated schedule outside the one-page narrative. Set evidence-based next actions. Name the largest uncertainty, its test, the person responsible and the next review date. Write a short answer under each heading, then remove repetition. Keep quotes, interview notes, financial schedules and contracts in a separate evidence folder. The one-page document should communicate the decision without trying to hold every supporting record. Choose a one-page summary or a more detailed business plan A one-page plan suits an initial discussion, a relatively simple offer or a frequent review. The U.S. Small Business Administration describes lean plans as a compact way to summarize key business elements. A recipient may instead require a traditional plan with more detailed research and financial information. Ask for their requirements before assuming one page is sufficient. This resource owns the concise general plan. For a specific delivery model, continue to the existing freelance business-plan financials or agency planning guides . Those pages provide deeper industry context; duplicating their full models inside this template would weaken the one-page task. Inventory and receivable balances need their own review. The working-capital guide and editable worksheet explain the balance-sheet snapshot, while the cash forecast schedules when payments become due. Keep these supporting checks separate from the concise narrative. Edit, print and review the final page The supplied DOCX and PDF files have been rendered and checked as one-page US Letter documents. Replace bracketed prompts rather than adding long paragraphs beneath them. Keep a readable font and normal margins. After editing, export a new PDF and inspect the page count, line wraps and every financial number. For Google Docs, upload a copy of the DOCX and review the converted layout before sharing. Word processors can substitute fonts and change line breaks; native Google Docs import has not been independently certified here. The static PDF gives you the supplied print layout, while the Word file is the editable starting point. Before using the plan, check that the offer’s unit matches its price and costs, the required jobs fit capacity, the cash schedule includes payment timing, the funding source is named and unresolved assumptions have a test. If the figures fail, revise the plan rather than compressing text or presenting a larger sales target as a solution. Frequently asked questions What is a one-page business plan? A concise overview of the customer, offer, sales approach, delivery model, finances, funding and next decisions. It summarizes the plan; supporting research and detailed schedules can remain separate. Is this one-page business plan template free? Yes. The blank Word and PDF files and completed fictional example are free, with no signup required. The DOCX is editable; the PDF is designed for viewing and printing. Can I edit the PDF? The PDF is a static print-ready copy, not a fillable form. Edit the Word document and export your own PDF, or print the blank PDF and write on it. Can I open the Word template in Google Docs? You can import a copy of the DOCX into Google Docs. Review font substitution, spacing and page count after conversion. Native Google Docs rendering has not been certified for this download. Is one page enough for a loan or investor application? Requirements vary. Ask the recipient what they need. This is a planning summary, not a promise of lender acceptance or a substitute for requested statements, market evidence or projections. Does owner pay belong in operating break-even? Here owner pay is a separate planning target added after fixed operating costs. The example labels operating break-even and the owner-pay-inclusive target separately; it does not assume owner withdrawals are an accounting operating expense. Why does the example need cash if its sales cover costs? Only half the first month’s sales are collected in that month, while all modeled payments are made. The uncollected balance remains a receivable; sales and bank receipts are different amounts. Will the template stay on one page after editing? The supplied blank and filled documents each render to one US Letter page. Longer answers or different fonts can add pages. Shorten the summary and retain detailed evidence separately, then inspect the exported PDF. Sources and example status The structure, templates, fictional company and calculations are original MyBreakeven material. SBA business-planning guidance provides general context on plan formats and research. It does not approve this template or verify the example’s demand, costs or funding. documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN · BUSINESS BUDGETING Budget vs Actual Excel Template: Monthly and YTD Published 2026-10-23 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . A budget vs actual Excel template compares the budget you approved before a period with the results recorded for that same period. Use the free workbook below to review one month or January through a selected month. It includes an empty report for your figures and a separate completed fictional example. The report answers “How far did we finish from the original plan?” It does not, by itself, tell you whether a difference came from activity, price, resource use or accounting timing. Keep those questions separate before deciding what to change. Download the budget vs actual Excel workbook XLSX, no macros, no account required. Two worksheets: Blank report and Filled example. This is a focused operating-result report with net revenue and included expense totals, rather than a general-ledger import or a full financial-statement model. What the workbook calculates Choose a calendar month from 1 to 12. The top report retrieves that month's budget and actual totals. A second report adds the months from January through your selection, so the budget and actual periods match. Calculated results stay unavailable until all required fields in the selected comparison are numeric. Preview of the workbook's fictional USD example. Yellow cells accept inputs. Workbook fields and their meaning Field What you enter or receive Original budget Approved monthly net revenue and included expense totals. Keep this baseline unchanged during reviews. Actuals Comparable recorded net revenue and expenses after each month closes. Both fields are needed. Operating result Net revenue less the expenses included in this report. It is not automatically after-tax net income. Raw variance Actual minus budget, using the same sign convention for every line. Percentage variance Raw variance divided by the absolute budget value. A zero budget displays n.a. Direction Higher revenue or operating result is favorable; higher included expense is unfavorable. These labels describe this comparison. Completeness Budget entries / 2 and Actual entries / 2 show whether both fields for a month are numeric. Budget vs actual example: a $3,000 operating shortfall A fictional service company budgets $30,000 revenue and $20,000 included operating expenses for January. Its budgeted operating result is $10,000. Recorded revenue is $28,000 and expenses are $21,000, leaving $7,000. All figures use the same January accounting basis and USD currency. January static budget comparison, USD Line Budget Actual Actual − budget Interpretation Net revenue 30,000 28,000 −2,000 6.7% below budget; unfavorable Included expenses 20,000 21,000 +1,000 5.0% above budget; unfavorable Operating result 10,000 7,000 −3,000 30.0% below budget; unfavorable The result bridge is −$2,000 revenue variance minus the +$1,000 expense variance, giving −$3,000. Adding the expense overrun to profit would reverse its effect. The expense percentage and the operating-result percentage use different denominators, so their percentages cannot be added. Separate the amount difference from percentage-point changes. January's operating margin is $7,000 ÷ $28,000 = 25%, compared with $10,000 ÷ $30,000 = 33.3% in the budget. That is an 8.3 percentage-point margin decrease. It is a different measure from the 30% decrease in operating-result dollars. The sample continues with February revenue of $32,000 and expenses of $20,000, followed by March revenue of $30,000 and expenses of $20,500. Selecting month 3 produces $90,000 budget revenue and $60,000 budget expenses against $90,000 actual revenue and $61,500 actual expenses. YTD operating result is $28,500 versus $30,000: a $1,500 unfavorable difference. April actuals stay blank, so selecting April does not falsely treat an unclosed month as zero. How to use the template each month Save the original. Keep an untouched downloaded copy. Work on Blank report; retain Filled example for reference. Set the calendar year and reporting month. This version uses January–December. A fiscal year beginning in another month needs a revised period mapping; changing the year alone does not create one. Enter approved budget totals. Use the yellow revenue and expense input cells for each month. Do not revise them merely to remove an unfavorable result. Close the actual period. Reconcile accounting records, credits and adjustments. Enter both actual fields for every closed month. An explicit zero records a real zero; a blank means unreported. Inspect month and YTD together. Check completeness counts before interpreting a result. YTD does not skip a missing month and call the remaining total complete. Record a reason and action. Use the monthly notes column for the main cause, evidence, owner and follow-up date. Keep a separate detailed account schedule if you need more categories. Archive the report. Save a dated copy after review. Changes to expectations belong in a rolling forecast , alongside the original budget. Investigate a variance before judging performance A lower expense total can follow fewer completed jobs. It can also reflect a supplier credit, an invoice recorded next month or a useful improvement. An “unfavorable” increase may support extra profitable activity. Read the sign first, then examine quantity, rates, mix and timing. For example, suppose 100 jobs were planned and only 80 were completed. Lower variable spending than the original 100-job budget is expected. The static report still measures the original-plan difference; it does not establish efficiency. Use the flexible budget and variance calculator to compare actual results with original rates applied to actual activity. Choose a consistent accounting basis. Under an accrual operating report, an unpaid customer invoice may be revenue while its collection happens later. Loan principal and equipment payments are not automatically operating expenses. For future payment dates and the minimum bank balance, use the 13-week cash-flow forecast . The master budget worked example shows how operating and cash schedules connect. Zero budgets, losses, returns and missing figures Zero budget: if $500 of actual expense appears against a zero budget, the amount variance is +$500 and is unfavorable under this report's convention. The percentage is unavailable. No percentage should be invented by dividing by zero. Budgeted losses: the denominator is ABS(budget). A −$2,000 budget result and −$1,000 actual result give a +$1,000 favorable difference and a +50% variance under that stated convention. This is improvement from a planned loss, not a 50% operating margin. Returns and credits: enter revenue after the returns included in your chosen accounting basis. Supplier credits reduce the related expense total. Do not subtract the same refund in net revenue and again as an overlapping expense allowance. Keep positive spending totals consistent; do not type ordinary expenses as negatives because the result formula subtracts expenses. Missing fields: do not put a dash or the word “zero” in a numeric cell. Enter 0 when the account genuinely has no activity. Leave an unknown actual blank. If a report says Unreported, inspect the entry counts and selected month before replacing formulas. Reporting controls: enter a numeric whole month from 1 through 12 and a whole calendar year from 1900 through 9999. Invalid controls leave the report unavailable. A zero-activity month still needs explicit zeros in both actual input cells; a partial entry is not a completed close. Questions about the Excel report Can I use this as a budget vs actual dashboard? The top month and YTD tables provide a compact review. This version does not import account records, show category-level charts or provide automatic bookkeeping integration. Does it update the budget to actual activity? No. The original budget remains the benchmark. The separate flexible-budget guide owns activity-adjusted comparisons. Can I open it in Google Sheets? The download is an XLSX workbook using common formulas. Native Excel and Google Sheets behavior has not been independently certified. After import, check the January result of $7,000 and March YTD result of $28,500 before relying on the imported version. Can I add account categories? Keep your category-level records in a supporting schedule and enter reconciled totals here. Inserting category rows into the report would require updating its formulas and completeness checks. Method and related resources The worked figures and workbook are original fictional MyBreakeven examples. For the underlying distinctions, see OpenStax on flexible budgets and evaluating budget differences . These references explain concepts; they do not certify this file. Continue with the contribution income statement , restaurant budgeting guide or business planning resources .

documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN How MyBreakeven calculates your business target Published October 10, 2026 · Updated October 26, 2026 Your selling price and the costs of delivering one sale determine its contribution. Monthly commitments determine how many sales you need. Available productive hours determine whether you can deliver them. Define the inputs before dividing Selling price The revenue from one consistent job, appointment, order or client period. Keep the unit and tax treatment consistent. Direct costs per sale Materials, directly attributable labor, other variable delivery costs and the acquisition allowance you enter. Monthly commitments Operating overhead plus separately entered owner pay. Add target profit only when calculating a target beyond operating break-even. Do not count the same salary or expense in two fields. Payment fees apply to the entered selling price. Include a flat per-transaction charge in another direct-cost field. Currency selection labels amounts; it does not convert exchange rates. The core formulas fee per sale = price × fee percentage ÷ 100 contribution = price − fees − materials − labor − other costs − acquisition allowance monthly target = overhead + owner pay + target profit exact sales = monthly target ÷ contribution required whole sales = round exact sales upward exact revenue = exact sales × price practical revenue = required whole sales × price If contribution is zero or negative, this model cannot calculate a finite sales target that funds monthly commitments. Change the cost mix or price before interpreting required sales. An acquisition allowance per sale is a simplified average; repeat-client and new-client economics may need separate scenarios. Reproduce this monthly example Illustrative USD assumptions, not a customer result: price $100; materials $10; direct labor $8; other costs $2; acquisition allowance $0; payment fees 3%; overhead $2,500; owner pay $1,500; target profit $0. One consistent sale and monthly cost period Step Result Fees: $100 × 3% $3 Contribution: $100 − $3 − $10 − $8 − $2 $77 Monthly target: $2,500 + $1,500 $4,000 Exact sales: $4,000 ÷ $77 51.948… Required whole sales 52 Exact / practical revenue $5,194.81 / $5,200 At 52 sales, contribution is $4,004. At 40 sales it is $3,080, leaving a $920 shortfall against these commitments. These figures exclude any cost you did not enter. Check productive hours and customer demand monthly capacity = workers × weekly hours × (52 ÷ 12) × utilization ÷ 100 ÷ worker-hours per sale whole-sale capacity = round monthly capacity downward practical inquiries = round (required whole sales ÷ conversion rate) upward Hours per sale must be total worker-hours: two people working for two hours use four worker-hours. Weekly hours are per worker. Utilization reserves time for work outside delivery. Include editing, setup or travel consistently; do not subtract the same time twice. Example: one worker × 30 weekly hours × 52/12 × 80% ÷ 2.6 worker-hours gives 40 sales per month. The target of 52 therefore exceeds capacity by 12 whole sales. At an assumed 25% inquiry-to-sale conversion, 52 sales need 208 inquiries. This is a planning assumption, not evidence those inquiries exist. Why industry and small-tool results differ The eight industry calculators share the monthly contribution and capacity model, with different input labels and example values. A focused tool may answer a different question. The cleaning contract tool, for example, averages weekly visits using 52/12 and subtracts modeled labor, supplies, travel and entered contract overhead from the contract fee. Its assumptions do not automatically add payment fees, owner pay or acquisition costs. Read each tool's own formula and limits before comparing results. Discount tools compare contribution before and after a discount. Cash-runway tools use entered cash flows, not accounting profit. The job-cost worksheet compares one job before monthly overhead. Its contribution should not be labelled final business profit. Business investment and AI automation ROI The business ROI and payback calculator uses incremental cash benefits and costs over the entered horizon. ROI = (total benefits − total costs) ÷ total costs × 100. Total costs include setup plus the running payments in that period; this differs from dividing by setup alone. With zero total cost the percentage is undefined. Fixed running cost starts in month one, including a benefit delay. Simple fractional payback = delay + (setup + fixed monthly cost × delay) ÷ active monthly net benefit, when that net benefit is positive. It assumes uniform cash movement; the table separately shows month-end recovery. For AI, paid-hours changes affect labor cash; remaining hours count as capacity and only entered extra sold work adds contribution. Do not count the same hours twice. See the AI cash-saving and capacity method and reconciled ROI examples . The model is pre-tax and undiscounted, with no financing, resale value or demand verification. Statement ratios, exact proportions and mortgage refinancing The financial ratios calculator uses explicit reporting periods and opening/closing averages. Its leverage mode distinguishes assets/equity, liabilities/equity and interest-bearing debt/equity. Missing data is not zero, and nonpositive denominators are explained rather than scored. The equivalent ratio calculator answers a mathematical question: whether all corresponding terms have the same nonzero scale. It uses exact rational arithmetic for decimals and fractions, checks every pair in three-term comparisons, and distinguishes a unique missing value from no or infinitely many solutions. The mortgage refinance calculator compares fixed-rate amortizing loans from the same current principal. It separates upfront charges, financed fees and lender credits, rounds regular P&I to cents, adjusts final payoff, and compares cumulative cash plus debt at the same holding date. Rates are entered assumptions, not lender offers. Read each tool’s own rounding and scope contract; these specialist engines do not inherit the core sales-target formula. Precision, limits and review scope Core engine version 1.3.1 uses decimal arithmetic at 40-digit precision before converting results for display. Currency normally displays two decimals. Required units round upward; capacity rounds downward. Near-zero positive contribution can produce a very large required volume; inspect the assumptions rather than treating that volume as a forecast. The capacity indicator and planning score are formula-based summaries, not probabilities of success. Demand, booking patterns, inventory payment timing, debts, taxes, replacement equipment and seasonal peaks require separate consideration when not included in your inputs. Weekly averages do not represent every calendar month. On October 10, 2026, the formulas on this page were compared with the core engine and the examples were recomputed. This is a calculation consistency check, not independent accounting certification. Report a formula or content error . Reference and next step The U.S. Small Business Administration startup-cost guide provides general context for identifying business costs. MyBreakeven's exact implementation is described above; the SBA has not endorsed this product. Follow an interactive walkthrough , then use the free business calculator with your own costs.

The purpose is to help you inspect prices, costs and delivery capacity using assumptions you can change. Responsibility and attribution Anis Ul Haq is the founder. MyBreakeven is the publisher of the site's guides. Publisher attribution does not mean every article was personally written or independently reviewed by the founder. An individual author or reviewer is named only when their contribution is recorded. AI tools assist with drafting, editing and software work. A name, credential, testimonial or business outcome must not be invented to make the content appear more authoritative. Sources and examples Worked scenarios use explicitly stated assumptions. They are not industry averages, customer results or forecasts unless the page provides evidence for that description. Source links support the associated claim; a general reference does not verify every number on a page. Real business walkthroughs require the owner's permission, a defined period and traceable inputs. Anonymized publication must still have underlying records. Quotes and endorsements require permission and accurate attribution. Case study evidence and relationships Founder accounts, independent customer experiences and hypothetical demonstrations are labelled separately. We state the business relationship, country, period, selling unit and source of each material claim. Owner-reported figures remain labelled as self-reported unless supporting records have been checked; arithmetic verification does not independently verify the business records. Retrospective reconstructions are dated and kept distinct from historical calculator outputs. Case studies separate assumptions, actions and observed outcomes, including changes in spend, offers or sales mix that limit attribution. We obtain permission for named businesses, quotes and agreed figures before publication. Missing data is identified, not filled with invented results. See the Daily Outfitter founder account and its evidence status . What a calculation check covers A calculation check compares the stated inputs, formula, units and arithmetic. It can also examine rounding and whether a worked target fits the stated capacity. It is different from a financial professional reviewing tax treatment, bookkeeping or a business's complete accounts. A review date applies to the scope stated on that page. Publication date remains the original release date; substantive edits receive an updated date. Changes to navigation alone do not establish a fresh review of every worked example. No independent professional review is implied where none is named. Corrections Email mybreakeven1@gmail.com with the page URL, the statement or formula, expected result and steps to reproduce it. Use redacted or illustrative inputs; do not email customer names, account credentials or private financial records. We assess the report against the stated assumptions and implementation. Confirmed calculation errors are corrected with an affected check and a dated note when the change materially alters the answer. Reports remain unverified until reproduced. We do not promise a response time or a resolution before examining the evidence. Recent material correction: on October 10, 2026, the salon membership example minimum was rounded upward to $89.70. At $89.69, a 3% fee and $42 cost leave $44.9993; $89.70 leaves $45.009 and meets the stated $45 contribution goal. Commercial relationships and limits MyBreakeven offers Free and Pro plans. A sponsored contribution or affiliate arrangement must be disclosed beside the relevant content. Payment does not establish the accuracy of an example or permission to claim an endorsement. Tools are planning estimates based on entered assumptions. They do not replace accounting, tax, legal or lending advice. See our calculation methods and contact options .

documents.text: THE FOUNDER OF MYBREAKEVEN Anis Ul Haq Business Planning & Business Development A business owner building practical planning tools around the decisions he encounters himself: understanding costs, setting sales targets and working through uncertainty. Founder of MyBreakeven and owner of Daily Outfitter, based in Pakistan. His background brings together business economics education, accounts management experience in the UAE and a Store Incharge role in Malaysia. Explore my background ↗ LinkedIn profile ↗ AI-assisted portrait based on a photograph supplied by Anis. Current roles Founder & business owner Academic background Master's in Business Economics Professional experience Pakistan · UAE · Malaysia 01 PROFILE Business planning shaped by running a business. Anis Ul Haq's focus is the connection between a business plan and the work required to put it into practice. Costs, pricing and sales targets matter together: a revenue goal needs a clear cost base, an achievable workload and a realistic view of customer demand. He started Daily Outfitter in November 2025 and owns the Pakistan-based clothing business. His responsibility for planning and development keeps those questions close to everyday decisions about products, offers, customer communication and operating workflows. WHY MYBREAKEVEN EXISTS From costing uncertainty to a clearer target. MyBreakeven grew out of questions in his own business: how to understand the cost of a sale, connect sales activity with a monthly goal, and make decisions when the outcome is uncertain. It turns those questions into planning models with inputs that the owner can inspect and change. The aim is to make the reasoning visible. Owners can examine what remains after direct costs, what the business needs to cover each month, and whether the required work fits the resources available. The Daily Outfitter founder account gives a more detailed example of that experience. It explains the original business problem, the actions he described and a costing reconstruction readers can explore. 02 EXPERIENCE An operating business and an international background. NOVEMBER 2025–PRESENT · PAKISTAN Owner, Daily Outfitter Visit the business ↗ Anis is responsible for Daily Outfitter's business planning and development. The business sells men's fabrics and women's clothing, with orders coming through its website and WhatsApp. His work spans product presentation, pricing and offers, digital marketing, customer communication, orders, inventory and fulfilment workflows. These connected responsibilities provide a practical context for thinking about growth: attracting orders is one part of the task; understanding their costs and organizing delivery are part of the same plan. Planning Working through costs, pricing and sales goals. Development Product offers, digital presentation and customer communication. Operations Order, stock and fulfilment workflows that support execution. Earlier professional roles His previous roles add to the background he brings to his current business work. UAE Accounts Manager Previous professional experience in accounts management. Malaysia Store Incharge Previous professional experience in a store-based role. His current focus is applying business planning and development to his own ventures, while making practical planning methods available through MyBreakeven. 03 WORKING APPROACH Connect the numbers with the business decision. MyBreakeven reflects four connected planning questions. Together, they move the discussion from a headline sales number toward the assumptions and work behind it. 01 What does each sale contribute? Start with a consistent selling unit and the costs of delivering it. Look beyond the invoice value to understand the amount available for the business's wider commitments. 02 What monthly target needs to be funded? Connect contribution with overhead, owner-income needs and a clearly defined profit goal. Keep those boundaries visible so the same cost is not counted twice. 03 Can the business deliver the required work? Compare the target with productive time and available resources. A mathematically balanced plan can still require more work than the business can complete. 04 What needs to be tested in practice? Examine demand assumptions, sales activity and operating choices. Compare scenarios, then use actual business records to review the assumptions behind the plan. For the underlying calculations and a reproducible example, see the MyBreakeven calculation methodology . 04 SELECTED WORK Explore the work behind the profile. These pages connect Anis's business experience with the product and its methods. Each serves a different purpose: use a tool, read a first-hand account or inspect the calculation process. FOUNDER · MYBREAKEVEN Business planning tools Calculators for exploring break-even, pricing, contribution, monthly sales targets and capacity using the owner's own inputs. His work connects product development with the cost and sales questions that motivated the site. In his current work, that academic background sits alongside first-hand experience of owning and developing a business. 06 RESPONSIBILITY Clear roles. Transparent methods. Anis is the founder and publisher of MyBreakeven. He leads the product's ongoing development, with software, analytics, technical SEO and AI-assisted workflows supporting its business planning purpose. His other digital project experience includes NexalyPlanner. ChatGPT and Claude assist implementation, troubleshooting and editing. documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN Cleaning business budget template Published October 11, 2026 · Updated October 24, 2026 This cleaning business budget template compares a whole month's bookings, paid payroll, direct job costs and overhead. Download a blank Excel workbook and a separate illustrative example. Both include budget and actual columns, an owner-pay allowance and a productive-capacity check. Download monthly budget template (.xlsx) Build the month from jobs and paid hours Enter the month and currency label. The workbook labels amounts; it does not convert currencies. Enter completed jobs and comparable net revenue per job, excluding taxes collected for others. Use one consistent job scope or a documented blended average. Enter total paid worker-hours and loaded hourly payroll cost. Include paid travel, admin and idle time where applicable. Count owner delivery labor here if you assign it a wage. Enter supplies and travel cost per job, payment-fee percentage, monthly fixed overhead and owner pay outside payroll. Add other job-linked costs to the relevant direct-cost amount and document them. Count every cost once. Enter target profit, productive share of paid time and total worker-hours per completed job. Do not subtract travel twice: define which hours count as productive before using this share. At month end, fill the Actual column from your records. Enter explicit zeros for inapplicable costs. Blank inputs leave results incomplete. The workbook treats all entered monthly payroll as committed for its job target. If more bookings require additional paid hours, revise payroll and capacity before relying on the target. A different per-job labor model can give a different threshold. Inspect the monthly budget example These USD assumptions illustrate the formulas. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts of bookings. One month, matching budget and actual cost definitions Input or result Budget Actual Completed jobs 80 72 Revenue per job $180 $180 Paid worker-hours 300 310 Loaded cost per paid hour $24 $24 Supplies / travel per job $12 / $10 $14 / $12 Payment-fee rate 3% 3% Fixed overhead $1,200 $1,300 Owner pay outside payroll $1,500 $1,500 Target profit $500 $500 Productive share / hours per job 80% / 3 75% / 3.2 Monthly payroll $7,200 $7,440 Contribution per job before monthly payroll $152.60 $148.60 Result after entered owner pay $2,308 $459.20 Whole jobs needed for target profit 69 73 Whole-job capacity 80 72 Budget revenue is 80 × $180 = $14,400. Each job leaves $180 − $12 − $10 − $5.40 = $152.60 before monthly payroll. Subtract $7,200 payroll, $1,200 overhead and $1,500 owner pay from $12,208 contribution to leave $2,308. Adding the $500 profit goal gives a $10,400 target: $10,400 ÷ $152.60 = 68.151… jobs, rounded upward to 69. Budget capacity is 300 paid hours × 80% ÷ 3 worker-hours = 80 jobs. Actual capacity is 310 × 75% ÷ 3.2 = 72.65625, rounded downward to 72. Actual commitments plus the profit goal need 73 jobs, so that target exceeds capacity by one whole job. The actual result is $1,848.80 below budget: eight fewer jobs lose $1,220.80 of budget contribution; $4 more supplies and travel across 72 jobs lose $288; payroll rises $240 and overhead rises $100. Together, $1,220.80 + $288 + $240 + $100 = $1,848.80. Use it as a janitorial budget template For commercial cleaning, define the unit as one completed visit or a consistent contract period. Convert contract revenue, supply costs and worker-hours to that same unit. Include paid supervision and non-delivery time in payroll, and keep periodic deep cleans separate when their scope differs materially. Do not mix a monthly contract price with per-visit costs without conversion. Compare recurring and one-time work using the cleaning profitability guide . For the quote versus one completed job, use the separate cleaning job-cost worksheet . Commercial janitorial budget: convert contracts into visits This separate fictional USD example shows the input conversion. Five identical contracts each pay $1,200 for 12 scheduled visits this month: 60 visits and $6,000 revenue, or $100 per visit. Enter 60 completed jobs only if all 60 are delivered in this reporting period. A cancelled visit, partial contract or periodic deep clean needs its own documented treatment. Independent commercial example using the workbook's committed-payroll model Workbook input or result Monthly basis Completed visits / revenue per visit 60 / $100 Paid worker-hours × loaded hourly cost 180 × $20 = $3,600 payroll Supplies / travel per visit $5 / $4 Payment fee 1% = $1 per visit Fixed overhead / separate owner pay $600 / $600 Target profit $300 Productive share / worker-hours per visit 80% / 2 Contribution before monthly payroll $100 − $5 − $4 − $1 = $90 per visit Result after entered owner pay 60 × $90 − $3,600 − $600 − $600 = $600 Whole visits for the profit target Ceiling of $5,100 ÷ $90 = 57 Whole-visit capacity 180 × 80% ÷ 2 = 72 Sixty visits use 120 productive worker-hours, within the 144-hour allowance. The remaining paid time is already in the $3,600 payroll; do not add it again as direct labor. The 57-visit target assumes payroll remains $3,600. Losing a contract may change staffing, fee rates or supplies, so recalculate rather than assuming all costs stay fixed. Record what the contract actually includes Separate client-supplied consumables from products you buy. List restocking, liners and specialist chemicals when included in your price. Include paid supervision, key collection, travel and training in the paid-hours schedule. Define productive time consistently with the hours per visit. Give periodic floor care, windows and deep cleans their own scope and hours. A quarterly service does not become a regular monthly visit simply because invoices are monthly. Keep equipment usage and replacement cash separate. Record an allocation's basis and avoid counting a purchase again as both full monthly expense and per-visit wear. At month end, reconcile completed visits to service logs, revenue to the same contract period, payroll to paid hours and supplies to usage records. Record invoice collection separately: $6,000 invoiced is not proof that $6,000 reached the bank. Use the 13-week cash forecast to schedule customer receipts against wages and supplier payments. What these results include The result is revenue less entered supplies, travel, fees, all entered monthly payroll, fixed overhead and the separate owner-pay allowance. It is not a cash-flow forecast or a tax calculation. Unentered costs, debt principal, equipment purchases and collection timing require separate planning. Productive capacity checks hours; it does not prove customers or bookings exist. Review the cleaning business monthly-expenses guide for cost classification. To test your full monthly plan, use the cleaning business break-even calculator . That calculator's per-job labor treatment differs from this workbook's committed monthly payroll: reconcile the cost boundary before comparing outputs. Frequently asked questions Is this a monthly janitorial budget template? Yes, when each job represents a consistent janitorial visit or contract period. Match revenue and job costs to that unit and use a full month of paid hours and fixed expenses. Does the template include owner pay? It has an owner-pay field outside payroll. Exclude owner labor already assigned a wage in payroll from this field so the same cost is not counted twice. What does a negative variance mean? The headline variance is actual result minus budget result. A negative number means less remained after entered costs and owner pay. It does not by itself identify the cause; compare job volume, contribution and committed expenses. Can I use the Excel file in Google Sheets? The download is an Excel workbook, not a native Google Sheets template. If you import it into another application, check its formulas and validation against the example before using your own figures.

documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN Cleaning Job Cost Worksheet: Estimate vs Actual Published October 10, 2026 · Updated October 14, 2026 A cleaning job can finish on time and still leave less money than the quote suggested. Use this worksheet to compare estimated costs with actual costs, then account for a callback, customer credit or extra work. The final result shows what remains to help cover monthly overhead. Download the free cleaning job cost worksheet (.xlsx) Includes a blank Job tab and a fictional Example tab. Use one currency throughout. What the worksheet calculates Compare revenue, paid crew-hours, loaded hourly cost, supplies, travel and payment fees. Enter additional callback costs separately. A customer credit reduces revenue; it is not also added as a cost. The worksheet shows final contribution, contribution as a share of retained revenue, and the change from your original estimate. How to use it Open the Job tab. Enter your job reference and currency label. Complete both the Estimate and Actual columns. Enter zero when a cost genuinely did not occur. Leave a required input blank only when it is still unknown. Enter total paid crew-hours: two workers working three hours means six crew-hours. Use a loaded hourly cost that consistently includes the employment costs you intend to track. Use Actual for the first visit. In the additional entries section, enter callback time, supplies and travel only if they are absent from those first-visit figures. Enter any customer credit once. Keep the original charged first-visit revenue in Actual revenue; the credit is deducted in the final result. Leave the payment-fee override blank to estimate fees from first-visit revenue multiplied by the fee rate. Enter actual net fees when you know them, including any fee retained after a refund. For extra work, include its additional processing costs either in the total actual-fee override or in extra variable costs, once. Read Final job result and Contribution change by driver. Use the driver rows to identify whether labour, travel, a callback or a credit caused the difference. Worked example: a $240 cleaning job This is a fictional illustration, not an industry benchmark. USD; first visit before callback and credit Item Estimate Actual first visit Revenue $240.00 $240.00 Paid crew-hours × loaded hourly cost 4 × $25 5 × $25 Supplies $12.00 $15.00 Travel $10.00 $14.00 Payment fees $7.20 $7.20 Contribution before overhead $110.80 $78.80 A callback adds one paid crew-hour at $25, $4 of supplies and $8 of travel: $37 in additional costs. A $20 customer credit reduces retained revenue to $220. Actual payment fees remain $7.20 in this illustration. Final variable costs are $198.20. Final contribution is $21.80 , or 9.9% of retained revenue. That is $89 less than the estimated contribution. The change is explained by $25 of extra first-visit labour, $3 of supplies, $4 of travel, the $37 callback and the $20 credit. Contribution is not net profit The result is retained revenue minus the variable costs you entered. It still needs to cover rent, software, insurance and other fixed overhead, plus any owner compensation or other costs not included in the inputs. Currency is a label; the workbook does not convert exchange rates. Common questions Do I enter a callback twice? No. If its hours or supplies are already included in Actual, do not enter them again below. What if my processor does not refund its fee? Use the actual net payment-fee override. A customer credit does not automatically reduce the fee. What if no callback or credit occurred? Keep those adjustment inputs at zero. Leave only the optional fee override blank when you want the rate-based estimate. What happens when retained revenue is zero? The currency result remains useful, but the contribution percentage displays “n.a.” because dividing by zero does not produce a meaningful margin. What if the result is negative? The entered variable costs exceeded retained revenue. Review the cost drivers and the scope of the job before changing future quotes. Can this set the right price for every cleaning business? No. Use your own labour, travel, scope, overhead and local operating assumptions. The example is not a recommended hourly rate. Continue your review Read the cleaning estimate vs actual job cost guide to investigate the difference. Use the contribution margin guide to understand the result.

documents.text: FOUNDER EXPERIENCE · E-COMMERCE · PAKISTAN How I used MyBreakeven to bring clarity to Daily Outfitter Connecting manual costing with a monthly order target for a clothing business. By Anis Ul Haq · Published October 16, 2026 Founder relationship: I founded MyBreakeven and also run Daily Outfitter , selling ladies’ and gents’ clothing in Pakistan. This is my own product-use account. What this founder account shows The problem: costs were in Excel, but the monthly order target was unclear. The practical benefit: clearer planning helped me direct team effort and customer outreach. My food cost is higher than the recipes suggest Build the ingredient standard Use purchased quantities and edible yield. Multiply recipe cost by the actual portions sold, including the real menu mix. Reconcile the period Use inventory movements and food sales for the same dates. Compare actual usage with the sold-mix standard, not a single popular dish. Investigate the difference Check counts, credits, portions, waste and staff meals before changing menu prices. A variance alone does not identify its cause. A busy menu is not covering the monthly bills Cost the full selling unit Include ingredients, packaging, genuinely variable labour and the fee basis for the selected channel. Worked check: actual food usage exceeds the standard Fictional USD example; the stated cost boundary applies Input or result Amount Opening inventory $8,000 Purchases / supplier credits $18,000 / $0 Closing inventory $6,000 Food sales / theoretical usage $60,000 / $18,200 Actual usage / food-cost percentage $20,000 / 33.33% Usage variance / percentage-point gap +$1,800 / +3.00 points Actual usage is $8,000 + $18,000 − $6,000 = $20,000. The theoretical $18,200 represents the actual sold mix in this fictional example. Its 30.33% of sales differs from actual food cost by 3 percentage points, not 3% of food spending. Reconcile records before interpreting the $1,800. The result does not establish waste, theft, staff performance or a price increase. It also excludes payroll and overhead. documents.text: SALON BUSINESS PLANNING Salon guides for pricing, repeat visits and chair capacity Cost a service, review a membership or check whether available appointments can fund your target. Find my next decision Run your own numbers Plan the whole business → Required monthly appointments, revenue, owner pay and productive capacity. Measure rebooking → Repeat-visit assumptions and appointment demand. Estimate no-show losses → Missed revenue and contribution after avoided costs. Cost hair color products → Product use and waste per appointment. Product cost is one appointment input. Rebooking describes repeat visits; no-show losses depend on costs actually avoided. The whole-business plan also needs monthly commitments and deliverable capacity. Start with the problem in your records Follow the steps for your decision. The examples below use fictional USD amounts; replace them with your own records. More rebookings are not becoming more completed visits Define the repeat-visit cohort Keep baseline visits, the booking window and follow-up delivery period separate. Adjust for attendance and available slots. Check missed-slot economics Separate equivalent refills, costs avoided and costs already incurred. Gross missed revenue is not the same as contribution lost. Test the whole diary Bring the completed service mix into the monthly plan with committed payroll, owner pay and stylist capacity. A membership or colour service is consuming the diary Cost the products actually mixed Record grams used, developer and waste. Product cost does not include every appointment expense. Cost the full appointment Include paid stylist time, preparation, cleanup and fees consistently; keep committed payroll separate. Reserve capacity for membership use Translate member-months into redeemed appointments, especially full-use and peak-time scenarios. Collections alone do not establish deliverable profit. Gather these records before you calculate Completed baseline visits, rebookings and the defined follow-up window. Actual attendance, cancelled slots, equivalent refills and retained non-refundable fees. Products used, avoidable commission or labour, processing fees and committed payroll. Service duration, preparation/cleanup, stylist skills and spare slots in the delivery period. Keep customer identities and private financial details out of shared copies. If a figure is missing, mark the result provisional rather than treating the missing cost as zero. Worked check: spare slots cap the rebooking gain Fictional USD example; the stated cost boundary applies Input or result Amount Baseline completed visits / current to target rebooking 200 / 40% to 60% Additional bookings / assumed attendance 40 / 80% Expected visits / spare slots 32 / 25 Delivered additional visits 25 Ticket / avoidable cost / percentage fee $80 / $25 / 3% Contribution per visit / added contribution $52.60 / $1,315 The rate change creates 200 × (60% − 40%) = 40 extra bookings. Attendance reduces these to 32 expected visits, but 25 spare slots cap the model. Each completed visit leaves $80 − $25 − $2.40 = $52.60. The seven visits beyond spare capacity are excluded. These are fictional assumptions, not a prediction about reminder software. Additional contribution still needs to help fund overhead; assess stylist skill and service duration as well as slot counts. documents.text: LANDSCAPING BUSINESS PLANNING Landscaping business guides for pricing, costs and capacity Build a service quote, check a lawn route or plan your monthly target. Choose the guide that matches the decision, then test it with your own costs and available hours. Find my next decision FOLLOW ONE CONNECTED DECISION From a job quote to a route, monthly target and cash plan 1. Price the work Match the scope, material quantities, worker-hours and machine-hours. A two-person crew working three hours uses six worker-hours. Build the estimate 2. Check route time Include driving, unloading and service time. Keep crew elapsed hours separate from each person’s paid hours. Review route density 3. Test the whole month Monthly commitments, owner allocation and target profit need enough contribution across every planned service. Calculate the monthly target 4. Check payment dates Map supplier deposits, payroll, seasonal gaps and actual collection dates. Profit does not pay a bill before collection. Build a dated cash forecast Worked crew-hour and weather-capacity check All values below are fictional planning assumptions. A two-person crew has 8 paid elapsed hours per day, with 1.5 hours of driving/loading and 0.5 hours for breaks and administration. That leaves 6 elapsed site hours, or 12 worker-hours. A repeat job requiring 2 people for 1.5 hours consumes 3 worker-hours, so the day supports 4 such jobs before any further delay. Twenty scheduled days would provide 80 jobs. If four days are explicitly reserved for weather, training or maintenance, 16 workable days provide 64 jobs. Do not subtract the same time twice through an additional utilization percentage. At an assumed $95 contribution per job and $5,700 of monthly overhead plus owner allocation, 60 jobs cover the target. Capacity of 64 leaves only 4 jobs of room, not evidence that demand or cash is sufficient. Buying a machine can change both capacity and cash. Compare equipment cost per machine-hour , seasonal cash planning and CAPEX versus current expense before counting an asset payment or depreciation twice. Decision paths and original capacity example reviewed November 18, 2026. Run your own numbers Plan the whole business → Required monthly jobs, revenue, owner pay and crew capacity. Check one lawn route → Route revenue, service and driving time, crew costs and allocated overhead. A route estimate covers one route. A monthly break-even plan also needs the rest of the business costs, target income and workable capacity. Write the business plan and check its financial schedule Download the landscaping business plan template with a completed Word example and editable Excel schedules for revenue, capacity and cash. Use your own customer evidence and costs. Start with the problem in your records Follow the steps for your decision. The examples below use fictional USD amounts; replace them with your own records. The completed job did not match the estimate Preserve the original job comparison Match cost categories and distinguish worker-hours, crew elapsed hours and equipment hours. Separate added scope from an overrun Include added and genuinely avoided costs alongside extra customer revenue and credits. Review the equipment allowance Use the stated operating/ownership boundary and productive machine hours. Do not count fuel or depreciation twice. A profitable route is not funding the quiet months Check one route Include service and driving time, the crew cost basis and the stated overhead allocation. Make active months fund annual commitments Keep the full-year target alongside active-month contribution and achievable workload. Check crew capacity and cash dates Separate available productive worker-hours from machine hours and collection timing. Do not assume every available hour sells. Gather these records before you calculate Accepted scope, quoted revenue, change approvals and supplier credits. Estimated and actual worker-hours, loaded rates and machine operating hours. Materials used, travel, disposal, subcontractors and equipment-cost boundaries. Annual commitments, active service months, productive crew capacity and payment dates. Keep customer identities and private financial details out of shared copies. If a figure is missing, mark the result provisional rather than treating the missing cost as zero. Worked check: annual commitments exceed seasonal capacity Fictional USD example; the stated cost boundary applies Input or result Amount Job price / direct cost before percentage fee $120 / $60 Payment fee / job contribution $3.60 / $56.40 Annual commitments / active service months $24,000 / 8 Required annual whole jobs 426 Even monthly target / capacity 54 / 50 jobs Contribution at 400 delivered jobs / annual gap $22,560 / −$1,440 Annual break-even is $24,000 ÷ $56.40, rounded upward to 426 jobs. An even $3,000 active-month target needs 54 whole jobs; scheduling 54 in each of eight months would deliver 432, slightly above the annual minimum. Capacity of 50 per active month permits only 400. The $1,440 gap is under these fictional assumptions. Use your actual service mix and season. Quiet months still need a dated cash plan; annual profitability cannot establish that payroll is funded on its due date. Start with the decision you are making, and keep each cost in one place. The guides include hypothetical worked examples; their figures are not local market rates.
