documents.text: MYBREAKEVEN · PRO HELP CENTER MyBreakeven Pro calculator: complete user guide Follow the exact path from your Pro dashboard to advanced break-even decisions. Every visual below maps to a real section of the product. Go to Pro dashboard Open calculator inputs Updated October 8, 2026 · Illustrated screen maps are guides, not live screenshots. 1. Where is Pro on the website? Path: Sign in → Dashboard → look for the PRO PLAN badge → choose Open advanced analysis . That button opens the homepage calculator at its Pro section. The same dashboard card includes Step-by-step guide with visuals so you can return here anytime. Visual 1 · Where Pro users find the tools 01 · Sign in Dashboard PRO PLAN Open advanced analysis Step-by-step guide with visuals → 02 · Calculator page Business model + Currency Enter your assumptions Read results and planning tools → 03 · Scroll to Pro PRO INTELLIGENCE Advanced dashboard PRO DECISION STUDIO tabs This is an illustrated navigation map. The wording matches the buttons and sections on the site. Sign in with the same email linked to your subscription. If you are already signed in, choose Dashboard at the top right of the site. On the dashboard, confirm you can see PRO PLAN under your email. The Pro card is visible even if you have no saved scenarios. Choose Open advanced analysis . The page opens at PRO INTELLIGENCE . Scroll up to edit the calculator assumptions; scroll within Pro to reach the PRO DECISION STUDIO tabs. For help while using the Pro panel, choose Visual step-by-step guide in its heading. You can also find this guide from Pricing . 2. Fill the calculator, step by step Visual 2 · Calculator screen map A Business model Cleaning, restaurant, e-commerce and five other models B Currency Choose USD or another listed currency before entering money C Operating model · 14 input fields Price and per-sale cost → monthly goal → capacity and conversion Optional · Build my costs Below Inquiry-to-job conversion · preview a breakdown, then Use these costs D Visual feasibility report Contribution, workload and demand E Planning tools Save, compare, export, decision brief F PRO INTELLIGENCE Forecast, sensitivity, capacity, heatmap and seven decision tabs The Pro section appears below the calculator results and planning tools. Your inputs update the analysis immediately. On the calculator page , select Business model . There are eight models: cleaning, landscaping, photography, agency/freelancer, mobile detailing, e-commerce, restaurant and salon. Field labels and the sales unit change to fit the model. Select Currency before entering amounts. Changing currency changes the symbol and code, but does not exchange-convert numbers. Enter all money fields in that one currency. Under the operating model, replace the example values in all 14 fields. Reset example restores that industry's sample values, so save a plan first if you want to keep your entries. Optional: open Build my costs below the inputs. Choose a service, split materials and other expenses into their named rows, and enter direct pay as a total or hours × hourly pay. Count total team-hours, including your own time. Review the direct-cost total and Current/New comparison (or start with zero costs), then choose Use these costs . This replaces the material, labor, other-cost and delivery-hours fields; acquisition, percentage fees and monthly totals stay separate. Save scenario keeps an applied breakdown, and Pro PDF/CSV reports include it. Keep monthly totals separate from per-sale costs. A $500 monthly software bill belongs in overhead; a $5 fee on each order belongs in a per-sale cost field. Price and per-sale costs Field on calculator What to enter Average price per job What a customer pays for one job. The label changes with the selected model (order, session, client or appointment). Materials / product cost Supplies or goods consumed by one sale. For a $180 cleaning job, enter the supplies cost for one job. Direct labor Cost of performing one sale; do not enter the whole team's monthly payroll here as well. Other variable cost Per-sale travel, packaging, equipment use, delivery or similar costs. Lead generation cost Estimated acquisition cost per booked sale. The label varies by business model. Payment and platform fees Percentage of the selling price charged on each transaction. Enter 2.9 for 2.9%. Monthly goal Field on calculator What to enter Monthly operating overhead Rent, software, insurance and other monthly costs that do not rise with each sale. Monthly owner pay What the owner wants to take home each month, separately from the target profit. Target monthly profit Profit above overhead and owner pay. Enter 0 if you only want to cover those costs. Delivery and demand Field on calculator What to enter Active team members Whole number of people who can deliver the work. Hours per team member / week Working hours for one person, before applying productive utilization. Delivery hours per job Total working hours used by all people for one sale, including the owner. Two people working two hours each use four team-hours. The unit name changes with the model. Productive utilization Percent of working time available to deliver work, after admin and downtime. Enter 75 for 75%. Inquiry-to-job conversion Percent of inquiries that become sales. If 20 of 100 inquiries buy, enter 20%. 2a. Build the cost of one sale Where: on the calculator, below Inquiry-to-job conversion , choose Build my costs . This optional tool is available without Pro or sign-in. It helps you add up expenses instead of guessing one total. Under What are you costing? , choose your service or product type. Names change with your industry; changing the type rebuilds the preview from current calculator totals, not market rates. Choose Start with zero costs to enter your own breakdown. Otherwise, the current materials and other-expense totals start in the first row of their group. Split those totals across the rows; do not add the same amount twice. Open 1. Materials / products and enter what one sale uses. Use 0 for items you do not pay for. Open 2. Labor and delivery time . Enter the total labor cost, or choose Calculate hours × hourly pay . Add each person's working hours, including preparation and travel. Two people working two hours each use four team-hours. If your pay is already in monthly owner pay, count your hours but enter 0 hourly pay. Treat payroll already in overhead the same way. Open 3. Other expenses . Add travel, equipment use or the expenses named for your industry. Keep monthly bills in overhead. Read the total and What will change when you apply? table. Current means the calculator values now; New means your preview. Editing the preview does not change results. Choose Use these costs . The new materials, labor, other expenses and team-hours replace those four calculator inputs. Results recalculate. Restore current calculator totals discards preview edits and reloads the values currently in the calculator; it does not undo a previous apply. Worked Cost Builder example · fictional USD amounts $15 supplies + $5 disposables + 3 hours × $20 = $60 labor + $12 travel + $8 equipment = $100 direct cost per job The calculator receives materials $20, direct labor $60, other expenses $20 and delivery time 3 team-hours. Customer acquisition and percentage fees are added separately. Monthly overhead, owner pay and target profit remain separate. 3. Read the result before opening advanced tools The Visual feasibility report sits immediately below the calculator inputs. It shows unit economics, team capacity and the inquiry demand needed for the selected target. After that, the Planning tools section gives you scenario comparison, exports and the Pro analysis panel. Worked example · why the target changes $100 selling price − $50 total per-sale costs and fees = $50 contribution per sale If monthly overhead is $1,000, owner pay $500 and target profit $500, the required contribution is $2,000. Divide $2,000 by $50 to get 40 sales , or $4,000 target revenue . At 25% inquiry conversion, those 40 sales need about 160 inquiries . Compare required sales with the Capacity result. If the team can deliver only 30 sales, the plan has a capacity gap even though the arithmetic reaches your profit goal. Review price, hours or team size. Whole units are rounded up; exact units can be fractional because they are mathematical thresholds. In Planning tools, Pro users see Conservative , Current plan and Optimized scenarios, a variable-cost increase slider, and the Executive Decision Brief . The built-in scenarios are assumption changes, not forecasts of customer behavior. Use Copy brief or Download brief if you want an action summary. 4. Use the Advanced break-even dashboard Open PRO INTELLIGENCE . Set Expected monthly jobs (or your model's sales unit) to your realistic sales plan, then set Monthly growth rate . Those two controls drive the planned-profit and 12-month outlook. Change the main calculator fields above to update all Pro cards. Visual 3 · What to read inside Pro Costs + owner-pay revenue Target-profit revenue Margin of safety Profit after owner pay Expected monthly jobs Monthly growth rate 12-month outlook Risk sensitivity Capacity solver Price × volume heatmap Offer Mix Price Guard Break-Even Ladder Acquisition Hire Break-Even Timeline Monthly Monitor These are the actual names of the cards and tabs. Select a tab to open its inputs and results. Four headline cards Costs + owner-pay revenue covers overhead and owner pay. Target-profit revenue additionally includes the profit goal. Margin of safety shows how far planned revenue sits above costs + owner-pay revenue; at or below that point its displayed cushion is zero. Profit after owner pay uses your expected units and contribution per sale, then subtracts monthly overhead and owner pay. It is before personal taxes. Forecast and sensitivity 12-month outlook compounds the growth rate you enter and holds price and costs constant. Risk sensitivity changes one input at a time and shows how target revenue moves. Not viable means that changed case loses positive contribution. Capacity solver Check the estimated Capacity-safe minimum price , Additional team members , planned revenue and safety cushion. These are calculated from the current hours and utilization, not a hiring recommendation. Price × volume heatmap Read across price changes from −10% to +10% and down sales volumes from 80% to 150% of the current target. Green cells show modeled profit; red cells show modeled loss. Compare several combinations before treating a price cut as safe. 4a. Find a price for your realistic sales volume Where: sign in with Pro, scroll to PRO DECISION STUDIO , select Price Guard and read Pricing Plan above the discount controls. These prices answer: “At the number of sales I can deliver, what price covers my costs and income goal?” Enter real per-sale costs, payment fees, monthly overhead, owner pay, profit goal and team hours in the main calculator. Cost Builder can help with the per-sale costs. Enter Expected monthly jobs (or your industry's sales unit) in Pricing Plan. Replace the starting sample with your own estimate of customer demand. This input is shared with the advanced dashboard and saved/exported planning assumptions. Read the volume actually used. If expected sales exceed whole team capacity, pricing uses the lower deliverable volume. Capacity is a working-time limit, not a promise of bookings. Read the two prices below and compare the current-price profit at the same volume. Expand See the calculation in simple steps to follow the costs, fees and monthly amount per sale. Worked Pricing Plan example · fictional USD amounts Per-job costs including acquisition: $98. Payment fee: 2.9%. Monthly overhead: $3,200. Owner pay: $4,500. Profit goal: $1,000. Expected demand: 131 jobs. Available capacity: 97 whole jobs. Both prices use 97 jobs. Cover expenses and pay yourself $182.68 per job Covers per-sale costs and fees, $3,200 overhead and $4,500 owner pay. It does not include the extra $1,000 profit goal. Also earn your target profit $193.30 per job Covers the same costs and owner pay plus the $1,000 monthly profit goal. At the current $180 price and 97 jobs, monthly profit after owner pay is −$252.34 . At $193.30 and 97 jobs, it is $1,000.35 . Prices round up to cents so the displayed price covers the entered goal. Follow the target-price calculation: ($3,200 overhead + $4,500 owner pay + $1,000 profit) ÷ 97 jobs = about $89.69 needed per job toward monthly goals. Add $98 per-job costs, then divide by 0.971 to allow for the 2.9% fee. The calculator keeps full precision before rounding the final price up to $193.30. Change volume or costs to test another case. A blank or zero sales input needs correcting before pricing can be calculated. If available capacity is zero, enter realistic team hours and utilization. PDF/CSV use the same pricing assumptions shown on screen. 5. Open each Pro Decision Studio tool Below the charts, find PRO DECISION STUDIO . Select one of its seven tabs. Each tab has its own inputs; editing the main calculator above also updates the baseline used by these tools. 01 Offer Mix What to do: Open the Offer Mix tab. Edit each offer's name, price, variable cost, sales mix and delivery hours. Use Add offer for another service; remove an offer with its delete button. How to read it: Read weighted contribution, total sales, revenue and the capacity gap in hours. Shares are normalized, so a 70:30 mix stays proportional. A zero or loss-making offer must be corrected before the mix can be calculated. When to use it: Use this when a cleaning company sells standard and deep-clean jobs at different prices. 02 Price Guard What to do: Open Price Guard. Enter Expected monthly sales inside Pricing Plan; this same input also updates the dashboard and reports. Replace the starting example with your own sales estimate. How to read it: Cover expenses and pay yourself shows the minimum price for per-sale costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Also earn your target profit adds your selected monthly profit. When expected sales exceed whole team capacity, the plan uses the lower deliverable volume and states it clearly. The current-price comparison uses that same volume. Expand See the calculation in simple steps for a breakdown, or Per-sale cost floor for direct costs only. No monthly sales target is shown for that floor. PDF and CSV include the same planning inputs. Prices round up to cents; these minimums do not predict demand or recommend lowering a profitable price. When to use it: With 131 expected cleaning jobs but capacity for 97, pricing is calculated for 97 jobs. Then use the existing Test discount slider to compare discount trade-offs. 03 Break-Even Ladder What to do: Open Break-Even Ladder. Move Safety volume buffer between 0% and 30%. How to read it: Follow the four levels: expense coverage, owner-paid, target profit and safety buffer. Whole units are rounded up for a practical sales target. When to use it: Use the ladder to separate keeping the business open from paying yourself and meeting a profit goal. 04 Acquisition What to do: Enter monthly channel spend, monthly leads, lead conversion and purchases per customer. How to read it: Check customers acquired, CAC, contribution per customer and the purchases or leads needed to recover marketing spend. This channel view replaces the base per-sale acquisition estimate with spend-derived CAC rather than charging both. When to use it: If 100 leads at 20% conversion yield 20 customers, $1,000 spend means $50 CAC per customer. 05 Hire Break-Even What to do: Enter monthly pay, payroll burden, other monthly cost, one-time onboarding, productive hours and expected extra sales. How to read it: Read the hire's total monthly cost, extra sales and leads required, utilization needed and monthly net benefit. Payback is meaningful only if monthly net benefit is positive. When to use it: Use it before hiring a fourth worker, then compare the required jobs with demand you can realistically generate. 06 Timeline What to do: Enter startup investment, starting monthly sales and assumed monthly volume growth. How to read it: Review the monthly operating floor, the first month that reaches target profit and the month cumulative operating profit recovers the investment. The table shows months 1–12; the model can evaluate up to 60 months. When to use it: Run a 0% growth case alongside an optimistic case to see how sensitive payback is. 07 Monthly Monitor What to do: Select a month. Enter completed sales, revenue, variable costs including fees, fixed overhead, owner pay and inquiries, then choose Save / update month. How to read it: Compare actual profit, revenue and volume with the plan snapshot saved for that month. Up to 24 months are kept in this browser, separately for your account, model and currency. Records do not sync across devices. When to use it: At month-end, enter actual figures and check whether a cost increase or lower volume explains the gap. 6. Save, compare and export your work On a valid calculator result, find PLANNING TOOLS and choose Save scenario . Enter a name in the Scenario name field, using up to 80 characters, then choose Save plan . Wait for the saved confirmation before opening Dashboard. Cancel closes the name form. A Pro account can keep up to 100 saved scenarios. Return to Dashboard . The saved card offers Open , Rename and Delete . Open reloads its inputs into the calculator; wait for those saved inputs to appear before editing. Editing an opened plan and choosing Save scenario creates a new saved plan, so use a name that distinguishes the revised version. The original saved plan keeps its existing inputs. The Pro Command Center above the list summarizes your plans and offers search, model, currency and sort filters. Tick Compare on two or three saved cards. The comparison shows revenue, exact units, capacity and score. PRO COST DRIFT compares changes with the first selected plan as its baseline. Use the same currency when comparing money amounts. From Planning tools choose Download CSV for scenario numbers, advanced metrics, sensitivity, a 12-month forecast and pricing-plan assumptions. Exact fractional targets and practical whole targets are labelled separately. For example, the cleaning preset needs 114 whole jobs and 380 inquiries at 30% conversion; its exact financial threshold is 113.31 jobs and 377.70 inquiries. Applied Cost Builder details are included. The PDF report also includes the pricing inputs and applied cost breakdown. If forecast sales exceed whole delivery capacity, the report warns that more capacity would be required. Forecast profit is after owner pay and requires the displayed sales to be delivered; it does not predict demand. Choose Print / Save PDF to open a print-ready report, then select your browser's PDF destination. On the dashboard, Export all CSV downloads a list of saved plans. PLANNING TOOLS Save scenario → Scenario name → Save plan Download CSV Print / Save PDF DASHBOARD Open · Rename · Delete Compare up to 3 Export all CSV 7. Common problems and answers Where is the Pro calculator? I only see the free calculator. Both plans use the same homepage inputs. After signing in with a Pro account, the advanced section unlocks below Planning tools. Dashboard → Open advanced analysis jumps to it. You can also use this direct section link . Do I need Pro to use Build my costs? No. Open it below the calculator inputs without signing in. Pro is needed for Pricing Plan in Price Guard and PDF/CSV exports. Why did editing Build my costs not change my results? You are editing a preview. Check the Current/New table and choose Use these costs. The four totals replace existing inputs; they are not added on top. Why does Pricing Plan use fewer sales than I entered? Expected sales can exceed the jobs your team can deliver. Pricing Plan uses the lower whole-unit capacity and explains the volume used. Lower your sales assumption if you expect fewer bookings than that capacity. Why do I see FREE PLAN despite a paid receipt? Confirm the email on the receipt matches your sign-in email. Refresh Dashboard once. If it remains Free, email support with the receipt and account email so the subscription can be checked. Avoid buying a second subscription. Why do results disappear or say the plan is invalid? Complete all numeric fields. Price, delivery hours and whole-number team size must be positive; conversion must be above zero; percentages cannot exceed 100. Each sale must retain positive contribution after variable costs and fees. Do currency and industry changes convert or preserve my entries? Currency changes the label without converting values. Changing business model loads that model's example assumptions; save your current scenario first if you need to preserve it. Why is the forecast different from my real sales? The 12-month line compounds your chosen growth rate; it does not forecast customer demand. Try slower growth and higher costs to see the range of possible outcomes. Why did Monthly Monitor disappear on another browser? Monthly Monitor uses local browser storage for each account, model and currency. It does not sync. Dashboard saved scenarios are stored with your account and can be opened after sign-in. How can I change or cancel my Pro subscription? Sign in, open Dashboard and choose Manage subscription beside the PRO PLAN badge. Start with one realistic plan Enter your real price and costs, check that your team can deliver the required sales, save the baseline, then test a price or demand change in Pro. documents.text: ABOUT MYBREAKEVEN Know the number. Then see if the plan can actually work. MyBreakeven turns your costs, pricing and workload into a monthly target you can inspect—not a promise, and not a black-box forecast. Run your numbers ↗ Read the guides → WHY IT EXISTS A break-even number is useful only when the business can deliver it. A spreadsheet may show that the math balances. The next question is whether you have enough hours, crew capacity and qualified demand to reach that target. MyBreakeven keeps those questions in one practical planning flow for owner-operators. Who publishes these guides MyBreakeven publishes the guides and calculator explanations on this site. Anis Ul Haq is the founder . Worked examples show stated planning assumptions; they are not customer results or a forecast for your business. Read the editorial and correction standards and calculation methodology . Send calculation errors, unclear assumptions or content corrections to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . 01 Your assumptions stay visible Every result begins with the costs, prices and capacity you enter. Change an input and see what moves. 02 The formulas do the math Deterministic calculations produce the numbers. Explanations add context; they do not replace the formula. 03 Feasibility comes next Compare required sales with productive hours and the qualified leads implied by your conversion assumption. This can reveal a capacity gap; it does not establish that customers will book. FROM IDEA TO DECISION One clean path through the numbers. Use the result as a planning baseline, then revise it when your real costs or capacity change. 01 Choose your model Start with the calculator built around how your business sells and delivers work. 02 Enter real assumptions Add fixed costs, per-sale costs, owner pay, pricing and available capacity. 03 Read the whole result Review the chosen revenue target alongside whole sales, required inquiries and productive workload. 04 Test a safer case Raise a delivery cost, reduce productive hours or lower your conversion assumption, then compare the target again. READY WHEN YOU ARE Put your own assumptions through the model. Open the free calculator ↗

documents.text: PRIVACY Privacy Policy How MyBreakeven handles information when you use our calculators and website. Effective September 30, 2026 Calculator data The free calculator runs in your browser. Typing or changing financial assumptions does not send them to our servers. Choosing Continue with these numbers uses same-tab session storage for a temporary handoff to the full calculator; it expires after five minutes and is removed when opened. If you sign in and choose Save scenario, the scenario name, industry, currency and financial inputs are stored with your account in Supabase so you can reopen them. You can export or delete saved scenarios from your dashboard. Website information Our hosting and security providers may process standard technical data such as IP address, browser type, device information, requested pages and timestamps to operate, protect and diagnose the website. Messages you send If you contact us, we use the information in your message to reply, provide support and improve the product. Optional accounts If you create an account, our authentication provider processes your email address, encrypted authentication credentials, verification status and security session data. MyBreakeven never receives your plain-text password. Account controls You may request access, correction or deletion of account information by emailing mybreakeven1@gmail.com. Authentication records may be retained where reasonably required for security, fraud prevention or legal compliance. Analytics With your permission, Google Analytics measures pages viewed, approximate location, device and browser information, traffic sources and interactions. We do not send calculator inputs, account passwords or saved scenario contents to Google Analytics. You can reject optional analytics without losing access to the service. Error monitoring We use Sentry to receive technical error details needed to diagnose failures. Default personally identifiable information, session replay, logs and performance tracing are disabled. Query strings, request headers, cookies, request bodies and user identity are removed before an error is sent. Service providers We use carefully selected providers for hosting, analytics, authentication, email and subscription payments through Polar. Each provider processes data for its stated service and under its own applicable terms. Your choices You may ask about, correct or request deletion of personal information you have directly provided by emailing mybreakeven1@gmail.com.

documents.title: Other Comprehensive Income: Reconcile OCI, AOCI and Equity
documents.summary: Separate net income, current-period OCI and accumulated OCI. Follow a limited US GAAP debt-security reclassification through a checked equity reconciliation.
documents.headings: What is other comprehensive income? State the framework before deciding where a gain belongs Separate net income, OCI, comprehensive income and AOCI Define the original net-of-tax teaching inputs Reconcile current-period comprehensive income without double counting Trace the reclassification to its source and earnings line Reconcile the flow to closing corporate equity Read the note rather than only the OCI headline Use a component-level evidence and review record Use this as a reconciliation, not a classification decision Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Other Comprehensive Income: Reconcile OCI, AOCI and Equity Published November 26, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 By MyBreakeven Editorial Team . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Separate net income, current-period OCI and accumulated OCI. Follow a limited US GAAP debt-security reclassification through a checked equity reconciliation. Accounting Financial statements OCI What is other comprehensive income? OCI is current-period income or expense presented outside net income under the applicable accounting requirements. AOCI is the related accumulated equity balance. Comprehensive income equals net income plus current-period OCI. An unrealized gain is not automatically OCI. In the original net-of-tax teaching case, $9,800 net income + $800 current OCI = $10,600 comprehensive income. Opening AOCI $3,000 + $800 = $3,800 closing AOCI. Follow the supplied classification assumptions and reclassification bridge below; this is not guidance for deciding which real transactions qualify. AI-created editorial illustration. The numerical case is fictional; no independent accounting certification is implied. State the framework before deciding where a gain belongs This guide uses a limited US GAAP presentation example for a corporation. It assumes the underlying accounting assessment has already established that the modeled noncredit gains on available-for-sale debt securities belong initially in OCI. It does not choose an investment classification, calculate a credit-loss allowance or determine when an instrument qualifies for a particular treatment. The FASB April 2025 OCI Taxonomy Implementation Guide illustrates OCI, accumulated balances and reclassifications, while explicitly stating that it is not authoritative recognition guidance. Its examples assume the reporting criteria are met. The applicable accounting requirements and the entity’s qualified advisers determine a real reporting treatment. This teaching example does not reproduce or certify a current complete Codification assessment. Do not use a taxonomy label, this worksheet or an old investment example as permission to route an unwanted operating loss outside net income. Separate net income, OCI, comprehensive income and AOCI Four labels used throughout this bounded example Measure Period or balance? Question answered Net income Current-period flow What is the result included in earnings? OCI Current-period flow What qualifying items are outside net income this period? Comprehensive income Current-period flow What is net income plus OCI? AOCI Accumulated equity balance What related amounts remain accumulated at the reporting date? AOCI is separate from retained earnings in this example’s equity reconciliation. Net income flows into retained earnings through the close, while OCI changes the accumulated OCI component. A gain is not automatically OCI merely because it is unrealized. Classification follows the relevant requirements; different securities and transactions can have different earnings treatment. Avoid applying this debt-security illustration to shares, ordinary customer invoices or any other asset without a fresh assessment. Define the original net-of-tax teaching inputs All amounts below are fictional USD inputs, not a company result or market observation. Assume opening AOCI is $3,000, all attributable to the modeled eligible component. Current-period net income before the specified reclassification is $9,000. A new qualifying holding gain of $1,600 is initially reported in OCI. A separate prior accumulated gain of $800 is now appropriately reclassified into net income upon the assumed sale. All supplied gain amounts and income figures are after their separately determined income-tax effects. No tax rate is prescribed and no current/deferred-tax journal is calculated. Assume no credit losses, impairment, hedging, noncontrolling interest, other OCI components or opening corrections. These boundaries isolate the presentation arithmetic; they do not turn the example into a complete US GAAP accounting model. Reconcile current-period comprehensive income without double counting Original flow and accumulated-balance reconciliation; all USD figures net of tax Movement / result Amount Net income before the assumed reclassification 9,000 Prior gain reclassified into net income +800 Net income including the reclassification 9,800 Current gain initially reported in OCI +1,600 Reclassification adjustment in OCI −800 Net current-period OCI 800 Comprehensive income 10,600 Opening AOCI 3,000 Closing AOCI 3,800 Net income becomes $9,000 + $800 = $9,800. Current-period OCI is $1,600 − $800 = $800. Comprehensive income is $9,800 + $800 = $10,600. Closing AOCI is $3,000 opening balance + $800 current-period OCI = $3,800. Retain the minus sign on the OCI reclassification: the previously accumulated gain cannot be counted again in current comprehensive income simply because it is now included in net income. Trace the reclassification to its source and earnings line The FASB explanation of ASU 2013-02 describes greater visibility over amounts reclassified from AOCI and affected earnings lines; it does not create eligibility for an otherwise unsupported OCI item. For the assumed sale, retain the investment reference, accumulated gain being released, disposal evidence, tax treatment and the specific net-income line receiving the $800. The numerical transfer adds $800 to the period’s net income and subtracts $800 through OCI, leaving total comprehensive income unchanged by the transfer itself. Before that transfer, this case would show $9,000 net income and $1,600 OCI, also totaling $10,600. The release can change the composition of equity once income closes, without creating another $800 of new total equity. It is not an $800 bank receipt by itself; sale cash and the carrying amount require their separate asset record. Reconcile the flow to closing corporate equity Add fictional opening retained earnings of $40,000 and paid-in capital of $50,000. Assume $2,000 validly declared dividends, no new shares and no other equity movements. Opening total equity is $50,000 + $40,000 + $3,000 = $93,000. Closing retained earnings is $40,000 + $9,800 − $2,000 = $47,800. Paid-in capital stays $50,000 and closing AOCI is $3,800. Separate equity components; USD Component Opening Closing Paid-in capital 50,000 50,000 Retained earnings 40,000 47,800 AOCI 3,000 3,800 Total equity 93,000 101,600 The independent total is $93,000 + $10,600 comprehensive income − $2,000 dividends = $101,600. Declared dividends are an owner distribution, outside this modeled comprehensive-income flow. Adding comprehensive income to equity and then adding net income a second time would overstate the change by $9,800. Use each component once. Read the note rather than only the OCI headline Look for the component, opening amount, current movements, reclassification, tax basis and closing balance. Determine whether a positive amount means gain, release of a loss or a presentation convention in that particular table. An AOCI loss can coexist with current positive OCI when a prior loss is recovering or being reclassified; a positive period flow does not imply the accumulated balance is positive. A 2026 SEC-filed issuer note provides a real example of separately presenting beginning balance, OCI before reclassification, reclassified amounts and ending AOCI. It is evidence of that issuer’s disclosure, not an SEC endorsement or a universal policy for every company. This guide deliberately uses independent fictional amounts rather than relabeling the issuer’s figures as a small-business benchmark. Use a component-level evidence and review record Record reporting framework, instrument or component, recognition-policy reference, period, opening balance, current gain/loss, release, related earnings line, tax basis, closing balance and reviewer. Reconcile the statement of comprehensive income, equity statement and note. If the underlying recognition, tax allocation or release condition is unresolved, stop at the provisional schedule instead of using a plug to force agreement. The retained-earnings guide explains the earnings and dividend bridge, while the accounting-equation example covers total balances. Use statement analysis to read the resulting reports. This source and arithmetic verification does not claim external professional sign-off or replace the entity-specific accounting assessment needed for a compliant filing. Open the editable OCI reconciliation record . This manual record does not calculate or save entries; print it before leaving. Use this as a reconciliation, not a classification decision This published guide explains the relationship between supplied net income, OCI and equity amounts. It is not an entity-specific accounting opinion or a certified reporting assessment. A real investment classification, tax effect or filing decision requires the applicable framework and qualified review; no such assessment is supplied here. Continue with business net income , retained earnings , the accounting equation and the reporting workflow . For organizing a profit statement, use the income-statement template ; it does not prepare a statement of comprehensive income. Frequently asked questions What is the difference between OCI and AOCI? OCI is a current-period flow; AOCI is the accumulated equity balance. This case adds $800 net current OCI to $3,000 opening AOCI to reach $3,800. Is every unrealized investment gain reported in OCI? No. The applicable requirements and classification determine the treatment. The guide assumes only a qualifying available-for-sale debt-security noncredit-gain case. Why is the $800 gain subtracted in OCI when included in net income? It was already accumulated through OCI. The reclassification adjustment prevents the same gain from being counted twice in comprehensive income. Does the reclassification create another $800 total-equity gain? No. In the modeled transfer, net income rises $800 and OCI falls $800, leaving total comprehensive income unchanged by the transfer itself. Are the example’s values before or after tax? They are supplied after-tax amounts. The guide does not choose a tax rate or calculate the underlying tax allocation. Does this worksheet establish US GAAP compliance? No. It checks a limited reconciliation after recognition eligibility and tax effects are assumed to have been determined. Entity-specific policy, disclosure and professional review remain separate. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Capacity Planning: Demand, Bottlenecks and Deliverable Work
documents.summary: Match demand with worker-hours, machine time and bottlenecks. Follow a checked capacity case, compare alternatives and keep a practical review record.
documents.headings: Capacity planning starts with a deliverable unit Separate theoretical, practical and committed capacity Worked example: enough labor, but a machine bottleneck Compare feasible throughput with demand and deadlines Test the cost of the actual constraint-relieving option Allow for changing mix, rework and peak loading Connect the resource plan to controlled people and product records Review the plan after disruption and before expansion Keep an editable decision record Sources, scope and review Continue with budgets, forecasts and performance Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Capacity Planning: Demand, Bottlenecks and Deliverable Work Published November 20, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Match demand with worker-hours, machine time and bottlenecks. Follow a checked capacity case, compare alternatives and keep a practical review record. Capacity Planning Business operations Worked example Capacity planning matches a defined workload with the usable resources and time needed to complete it. In the worked case, labor supports 50 jobs but a shared machine limits the week to 40; demand for 46 jobs therefore needs a real change in routing, resources or promises. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. The numerical case below is an original fictional planning example, not a customer result, market benchmark or professional determination. All monetary figures use USD. Use the same unit and period throughout, and replace assumptions with source records. Capacity planning starts with a deliverable unit Capacity planning compares the work customers need with the resources and time that can deliver it. Define a completed unit first: one inspected repair, one finished batch or one accepted client assignment. An inquiry is demand evidence, not completed output. A paid hour is an input, not a sale. Without those boundaries, a team can appear fully booked while promising more completed work than its process can release. Choose one planning window and write its opening backlog, new demand, due dates and completion standard. A monthly total is useful for commitments, but a weekly or daily schedule exposes concentrated deadlines. Keep capacity available in the period separate from capacity already committed to existing customers. Do not count an unfinished job as both opening backlog and new demand. Separate theoretical, practical and committed capacity Theoretical capacity assumes the resource is available for every stated hour. Practical capacity removes identified time that cannot produce the defined unit. Committed capacity is the portion already promised. These are different records, not competing answers. If maintenance is explicitly removed from machine hours, do not also apply a utilization allowance that removes that same maintenance again. Count worker-hours for each person working an hour. Two people on a three-hour assignment use six worker-hours, even though only three elapsed hours pass. Machine time and inspection time may run partly alongside labor, so document which resource is occupied at each stage. A total-hours estimate alone cannot establish the slowest stage. Worked example: enough labor, but a machine bottleneck A fictional repair team has three technicians, each scheduled for 35 paid hours in the week: 105 worker-hours. Identified leave uses nine hours, training six hours and administration 15 hours, leaving 75 productive worker-hours. Each completed job consumes 1.5 technician worker-hours. Labor could therefore support 50 jobs. These are stated planning assumptions, not wage, productivity or industry benchmarks. The process also needs one shared machine and a final inspection. The machine has 24 usable hours and needs 0.6 hour per job, supporting 40 jobs. Inspection has 18 usable hours and takes 0.3 hour per job, supporting 60. Assuming every job follows these stages and no other constraint applies, practical weekly throughput is the smallest stage capacity: 40 completed jobs. Fictional weekly capacity by resource Resource Usable time Time per job Whole-job capacity Technician labor 75 worker-hours 1.5 worker-hours 50 Shared machine 24 machine-hours 0.6 machine-hour 40 Inspection 18 inspection-hours 0.3 inspection-hour 60 Compare feasible throughput with demand and deadlines Suppose confirmed demand is 46 jobs for that same week. The bottleneck can support only 40, leaving six beyond the base plan. Buying more technician hours does not by itself release those six jobs because labor is not the limiting resource. Before accepting the due dates, check machine scheduling, alternate routing, subcontracting or a revised customer promise. Write the gap as six jobs and 3.6 machine-hours: 46 × 0.6 minus 24. That shortfall is not 3.6 technician hours. Keep material availability and the inspected completion standard unchanged when comparing options. A busy upstream stage can create a queue at the machine without increasing finished output. NIST’s supply-chain research illustrates why bottleneck and flow-time analysis concern the process, not just isolated resource use. Test the cost of the actual constraint-relieving option Assume a vetted subcontractor can perform only the machine step for six jobs, with no extra internal machine time. The additional charge is $28 per job, or $168. The 46 jobs still require 69 technician hours and 13.8 inspection hours, within the stated 75 and 18. If contribution before that additional charge is $65 per job, the base 40-job plan contributes $2,600. Completing 46 with the subcontract step contributes $2,990 less $168 = $2,822. The incremental contribution is $222 before any extra transport, quality failures, overhead or other unentered cost. This is a conditional comparison, not a reason to outsource automatically. Record supplier capacity, turnaround, acceptance checks and responsibility for defects. Use relevant differential costs to compare actual alternatives rather than treating every shared allocation as avoidable. Allow for changing mix, rework and peak loading Averages can hide unequal resource use. A job family needing twice as much machine time cannot be scheduled as if it were an ordinary job. List demand by routing and resource-hours, then sum each resource’s load. If rework occurs, measure its actual resource consumption and check whether the original standard already includes it. An unexplained cushion is harder to review than a documented range. A promised completion date also depends on sequence and available inputs. Forty jobs spread evenly through the week differ from 40 all arriving on Friday afternoon. Preserve the daily schedule and queue age alongside the weekly arithmetic. Identify which assumptions are commitments and which depend on an unconfirmed order, delivery or employee availability. Connect the resource plan to controlled people and product records A skills matrix matters because employees are not interchangeable hours. Document who can perform the constrained step, who can approve inspection and what supervised training is still needed. The small-business HR workflow owns role, training and approval records; the capacity plan consumes their current approved availability. It should not silently redefine pay, leave or employee classification. Product or service revisions can change processing time. Link the routing to the released version described in product lifecycle management . If a new revision needs a longer test, update the capacity standard when that revision takes effect. Keep the labor-cost question separate too: gross pay and net pay explain a paycheck boundary, not how many productive hours a person can deliver. Review the plan after disruption and before expansion A broken machine can move the constraint or remove the base plan entirely. The business continuity plan should state which work must resume first and which alternate route has been tested. Do not count an emergency workaround as normal capacity merely because it exists on paper. Record its activation time, usable output and full operating costs. For expansion, compare added output with supported demand, incremental contribution and payment dates. Equipment bought this month may require commissioning and training before releasing any work. The business expansion guide connects that investment to cash and capacity. At each review, preserve the original plan, record actual completed output and investigate differences in mix, availability, rework or cycle time before replacing the assumptions. Keep an editable decision record Open the printable capacity planning record . Record the evidence, calculation, responsible role and next review before making a commitment. This is a manual worksheet: fields accept typing, but do not calculate, submit information or save after reload. Print or save a PDF while the entries are present. Use non-sensitive aliases rather than employee identifiers, account numbers or confidential customer records. Sources, scope and review Owns demand-versus-resource capacity, bottleneck routing and completion planning; not an employee-cost calculator, staffing recommendation or expansion investment model. Primary references checked November 20, 2026. The sources explain the underlying concepts; the figures, scenarios and decision records were constructed independently for this guide. Applicable policies, contracts and local requirements need their own qualified review. NIST: supply-chain flow time and bottlenecks — Process and bottleneck context, not the source of the fictional weekly figures. Frequently asked questions What is capacity planning in a small business? It is the comparison of demand and deadlines with the usable people, equipment and process time needed to deliver a defined completed unit. Why is capacity not the same as utilization? Capacity describes feasible output under stated assumptions. Utilization describes how much of a resource’s available time or output capacity is used. High utilization at a non-bottleneck does not prove higher finished throughput. How is the bottleneck found in the example? Labor supports 50 jobs, the machine 40 and inspection 60. With the stated shared routing and no other constraint, the machine limits the process to 40 completed jobs. Should leave and a utilization allowance both reduce capacity? Only if they represent different unavailable time. Removing the same leave, maintenance or administration twice understates capacity. Does the subcontract option guarantee a better result? No. The fictional comparison adds $222 contribution after the stated $168 extra charge, but depends on supplier capacity, quality, timing and the absence of further unentered costs. Can gross pay be used as the productive-hours denominator? No. Gross pay is an earnings amount, while productive hours measure usable work time. Keep pay, employer cost, time availability and completed output as separate records. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Business Continuity Plan: Critical Work, Recovery and Testing Published November 20, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a business continuity plan around critical work, dependencies and tested recovery. Separate canceled contribution from delayed cash in an original case. Business Continuity Plan Business operations Worked example A business continuity plan identifies the minimum essential service to maintain or restore, who can act, the dependencies required and how recovery will be tested. It turns disruption priorities into a usable operating sequence rather than a list of risks alone. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. The numerical case below is an original fictional planning example, not a customer result, market benchmark or professional determination. All monetary figures use USD. Use the same unit and period throughout, and replace assumptions with source records. A business continuity plan names the minimum service to restore A business continuity plan explains how an organization will maintain or resume its most important operations during disruption. Start with the service customers need, the point at which interruption becomes unacceptable and the people authorized to act. A directory of emergency contacts is useful, but it does not establish that orders, payroll or essential records can be recovered. Keep three tasks connected but distinct. A risk assessment considers possible events and their consequences. Emergency response protects people and addresses immediate hazards. Continuity planning specifies the minimum operating service, dependencies, workarounds and recovery sequence. The business risk assessment guide owns the risk comparison; this guide owns the practical operating recovery record. Use a business impact analysis to set priorities List critical activities and ask what happens as each remains unavailable. Record missed obligations, customer disruption, safety implications, contribution lost, extra operating costs and cash delays separately. The impact of losing a scheduling system at payroll cutoff can differ from losing it during a quiet afternoon. State the timing and workload instead of assigning a generic severity label alone. Name the dependencies required to deliver the minimum service: staff skills, workspace, equipment, suppliers, communications, power, access permissions and usable records. Include external providers whose restoration you cannot control. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security describes continuity as a lifecycle that includes analysis, strategies, documented responsibilities and testing. Our operational cases below are independent teaching examples, not a certified continuity standard. Distinguish recovery time from acceptable data loss A recovery time objective is the targeted time to restore a defined service level. A recovery point objective describes the acceptable point to which data can be restored, often expressed as a maximum period of data loss. Neither is the same as a backup frequency promise, the time to start working on the problem or the time at which every backlog item is completed. For an illustrative order-entry service, management sets a six-hour recovery-time objective and a two-hour recovery-point objective. A test restores usable service after eight hours and restores a snapshot from three hours fifteen minutes before interruption. The test misses the service objective by two hours and the data objective by one hour fifteen minutes. Record these as gaps; do not change the objectives simply to make a failed test look successful. Worked example: lost jobs, deferred jobs and extra costs A fictional service business normally completes 40 jobs per day, each with $90 revenue and $55 avoidable variable cost. Contribution is $35 per completed job. A two-day disruption affects 80 planned jobs. A tested manual workaround completes 12 on day one and 20 on day two, or 32 jobs. The shortfall against the original two-day plan is 48 jobs. Of those 48,18 customers cancel and 30 agree to a later date. The business plans six extra jobs per day over the next five days to recover those 30 deferred jobs, with separate evidence that people and equipment can provide the extra capacity. Workaround activation costs $320 and the additional recovery effort costs $240. These are assumed incremental costs, not wage rates, legal overtime calculations or supplier quotations. Fictional disruption impact, USD Item Calculation Impact Canceled-job revenue 18 × $90 $1,620 revenue not earned Avoided canceled-job variable cost 18 × $55 $990 cost avoided Lost contribution on cancellations 18 × $35 $630 contribution lost Deferred collections 30 × $90 $2,700 moves to later dates Workaround and recovery costs $320 + $240 $560 incremental cost Total contribution reduction plus extra cost $630 + $560 $1,190 adverse effect Do not count delayed revenue as permanently lost profit The normal 80-job plan would contribute $2,800. The 32 jobs completed during disruption contribute $1,120; the 30 later completed jobs contribute $1,050. Combined contribution is $2,170 before the additional $560 response cost, leaving $1,610. Compared with the original $2,800, the adverse effect is $1,190. This cross-check assumes the deferred jobs retain the original revenue and variable cost and no further work is canceled. The $2,700 deferred collection is a dated cash issue, not an extra permanent loss on top of the $630 canceled contribution. If a customer later cancels, change the classification with evidence. Put the actual collection dates and response payments in the cash-flow forecast . Do not assume insurance pays the shortfall, covers these costs or pays before bills fall due; policy and claim terms require separate review. Write a workaround that can be used under pressure For each critical service, record the activation condition, named decision role, backup role, required access, minimum inputs, step sequence, approval and return-to-normal checks. Store an accessible copy in a way that does not depend entirely on the service being unavailable. Keep confidential credentials and personal contact details out of a public worksheet or an uncontrolled printed pack. A manual order log needs a unique temporary identifier, customer commitment, status and later reconciliation owner. When the primary system returns, reconcile the manual items before importing them to avoid duplicate work or duplicate customer charges. The product lifecycle management record can identify which released product instructions remain valid during a change; the continuity pack should refer to an approved version rather than an obsolete attachment. Validate people, training and recovery capacity A backup person must have the relevant training, permissions and actual availability. Merely writing a second name does not demonstrate that the person can approve payments, restore a machine or complete an inspection. Use the small-business HR workflow to keep role and training records aligned with the continuity plan. Respect separation between requesting, approving and reconciling an emergency payment. A recovery promise also needs a deliverable schedule. The six extra jobs in the example must fit after ordinary commitments, with materials and inspection time available. The capacity planning guide tests that load against bottlenecks. Payroll recovery has another boundary: gross pay versus net pay distinguishes earnings, deductions and employee payment, so restoring a net bank file alone is not proof that the underlying payroll record is complete. Exercise the plan, record failure and close the actions Choose a realistic scenario and a defined test scope. A tabletop exercise checks whether people understand the decision sequence; a restore test checks whether usable records and service can actually return. Record start time, achieved service level, restored-data date, missing permissions, reconciliation errors and customer commitments. Do not describe an unperformed restore as tested recovery. Assign each gap a named role, due date, interim control and retest criterion. Review the pack when suppliers, systems, staff responsibilities or product versions change. Archive the superseded plan with its review record and clearly mark the current version. A continuity plan is useful when it exposes an unworkable assumption early, not when every box is marked complete without evidence. Keep an editable decision record Open the printable business continuity plan record . Record the evidence, calculation, responsible role and next review before making a commitment. This is a manual worksheet: fields accept typing, but do not calculate, submit information or save after reload. Print or save a PDF while the entries are present. Use non-sensitive aliases rather than employee identifiers, account numbers or confidential customer records. Sources, scope and review Owns business impact analysis, operating recovery, dependencies and test evidence; not a duplicate risk-assessment guide, emergency-response procedure, insurance determination or cybersecurity implementation manual. Primary references checked November 20, 2026. The sources explain the underlying concepts; the figures, scenarios and decision records were constructed independently for this guide. Applicable policies, contracts and local requirements need their own qualified review. Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: developing a business continuity plan — General continuity lifecycle and recovery context; not a claim of compliance. Frequently asked questions What belongs in a small-business continuity plan? A defined minimum service, business impacts, recovery priorities, dependencies, authorized roles, tested workarounds, reconciliation steps and a review record. How does a continuity plan differ from a risk assessment? A risk assessment compares possible events and consequences. A continuity plan explains which essential service resumes first and how people, records and dependencies support that recovery. Are recovery time and recovery point the same? No. Recovery time concerns how quickly a stated service level is restored. Recovery point concerns the acceptable age or loss of restored data. Each needs its own test evidence. Why is $2,700 deferred collection not added to the $1,190 loss? The 30 deferred jobs are assumed to be completed later at their original economics. Their receipts move in time; the permanent contribution reduction comes from 18 canceled jobs plus the specified extra response costs. Does a backup prove the business can continue? No. The records must be accessible, restorable and usable by authorized people alongside the other operating dependencies. A backup file alone does not establish recovered service. How often should the plan be reviewed? Choose a review cycle appropriate to the operation and update it when important people, systems, suppliers, duties or product versions change. This guide does not prescribe a universal legal testing interval. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Gross Pay vs Net Pay: Read the Paycheck and Reconcile the Payment Published November 20, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Understand gross pay, net pay and employer cost with a checked paycheck example. Reconcile deductions, reimbursements, pay frequency and bank deposits. Gross Pay vs Net Pay Business operations Worked example Gross pay is earned pay before employee deductions; net pay is what remains after those deductions. Employer cost and the bank deposit can differ from both. Reconcile one pay period before comparing salaries, budgets or income figures. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. The numerical case below is an original fictional planning example, not a customer result, market benchmark or professional determination. All monetary figures use USD. Use the same unit and period throughout, and replace assumptions with source records. Gross pay is earned pay; net pay is the employee payment Gross pay is the earnings amount before employee deductions. Net pay is what remains after the deductions included in the payroll calculation. A bank deposit can contain an additional reimbursement or be split between accounts, so the deposited amount is not always the same as net wages. Start with the pay period and earnings record rather than identifying a number solely by where it appears on a bank statement. The IRS tutorial describes gross earnings, take-home pay, payroll taxes, income-tax withholding and other withheld amounts. This guide uses those general distinctions, but does not calculate a tax return, select withholding elections or estimate current federal, state or local tax rates. The deduction amounts in the case are deliberately supplied assumptions, not a tax-table result. Read one pay period before comparing annual figures Write down the dates covered, payment date, earning units and rate. An hourly worker might have regular earnings, a bonus or an adjustment from a previous period. A salaried worker may see a period amount derived from an annual salary. Confirm how the payroll system defines the period; do not mix a weekly gross number with monthly deductions or a year-to-date net number. Distinguish current-period values from year-to-date totals on the same statement. A prior correction may affect this payment without changing the work performed in the current week. If the employer issues a replacement payroll calculation, preserve which version is final and whether the first payment was reversed. A duplicated bank payment is a reconciliation problem, not extra earned gross pay. Worked paycheck: a transparent gross-to-net bridge In an original fictional example, a worker earns 36 regular hours at $25 per hour, giving $900, plus a $120 bonus. Gross pay is therefore $1,020. The payroll record lists a $40 employee benefit deduction, $60 employee retirement contribution, $206 combined tax withholding and a $15 authorized after-tax deduction. The tax withholding is an input, not computed from a rate in this article. Total employee deductions are $40 + $60 + $206 + $15 = $321. Net pay is $1,020 minus $321 = $699 . The classification of a deduction may affect a particular taxable-wage base, but this simple bridge does not establish any base. Different taxes can use different rules. Check the actual payroll calculation rather than assuming every deduction reduces every tax base. Fictional current-period paycheck, USD Line Calculation or input Amount Regular earnings 36 × $25 $900 Bonus Supplied earnings $120 Gross pay $900 + $120 $1,020 Employee benefit and retirement deductions $40 + $60 −$100 Combined tax withholding Supplied assumption −$206 Authorized after-tax deduction Supplied assumption −$15 Net pay $1,020 − $321 $699 Reconcile the bank payment without inventing taxable treatment Assume a separately approved $45 expense reimbursement is paid alongside the $699 net wages. The combined employee bank transfer is $744. Record two components: $699 payroll net and $45 reimbursement. This example does not determine whether that reimbursement is taxable or how the employer should report it; the supporting documents and applicable policy need their own review. If the worker sees only $744 at the bank, calling all of it take-home wages would overstate the net-pay figure in this record. Conversely, a split deposit could send part of the $699 to a second account. Match payment identifiers and component records before assuming a difference is an error. Do not place personal account numbers or employee tax identifiers in a public worksheet. Employer cost is a third number, not the missing net pay For this teaching example only, suppose the employer separately incurs $80 of employer payroll taxes and $120 of employer-funded benefits. Modeled employer cost before the separate reimbursement is $1,020 gross wages + $80 + $120 = $1,220 . The employee’s $321 deductions are already part of the $1,020 gross amount; adding them to employer cost again would count the same wages twice. Total cash associated with the payroll and reimbursement is $1,265 when all the listed obligations are paid: $744 to the employee plus $521 to tax, benefit, retirement and other recipients. Those payments may occur on different dates. This is a cash-allocation cross-check, not a statutory expense classification. Use employee compensation or the employee-cost calculator for the broader employer-cost question. Compare pay frequencies with their actual schedules A payment every two weeks is different from one twice a month. In a separate fictional schedule with 26 equal payments of $1,500 net, annual net receipts are $39,000 and the monthly average is $3,250. A two-payment calendar month has $3,000, while a three-payment month has $4,500. The average is not a promise that the bank receives $3,250 in every month. A twice-monthly schedule with 24 equal $1,500 payments totals $36,000 annually and $3,000 monthly. The examples compare schedules, not the pay of the same job. Verify the actual calendar, unpaid periods and adjustments before annualizing. A debt-to-income comparison normally starts with a stated gross-income denominator; it should not silently substitute these net deposits or treat them as an approval decision. Investigate a difference by tracing the affected line If gross pay seems wrong, compare approved hours, rate changes, bonus instructions and the period covered. If gross is correct but net differs, compare deduction amounts and any correction or advance recovery. A final bank mismatch calls for checking deposit splits, reversals, reimbursements and payment dates. Preserve the original statement, corrected version and explanation rather than changing a number merely to make the reconciliation balance. The small-business HR workflow can identify who approves hours, pay changes and employee instructions. HR records should support a clear payroll handoff, not give every manager access to confidential deduction information. Use role-based access and a named reviewer for changes. This workflow discussion does not decide employment status, overtime eligibility or whether a particular deduction is lawful. Keep pay, capacity and recovery records connected A paycheck reports earnings and deductions; it does not measure productive time. Paid hours may include time away from the deliverable service, and a person’s take-home pay cannot be used as an hourly business-cost estimate. The capacity planning guide keeps the usable-hours calculation separate from the payroll record. Match the period when comparing staffing costs with a delivery plan. Payroll is also a continuity dependency. The business continuity plan should identify authorized recovery of approved inputs, payroll records and payment reconciliation without exposing employee details. When product or workflow changes require training, product lifecycle management preserves the approved instruction version; payroll and time records separately show what was actually paid. None of those records should be replaced by an estimated average without retaining its basis. Keep an editable decision record Open the printable gross pay vs net pay record . Record the evidence, calculation, responsible role and next review before making a commitment. This is a manual worksheet: fields accept typing, but do not calculate, submit information or save after reload. Print or save a PDF while the entries are present. Use non-sensitive aliases rather than employee identifiers, account numbers or confidential customer records. Sources, scope and review Owns US-oriented gross-pay, net-pay and payment-record definitions with hypothetical arithmetic; not a tax-rate estimator, withholding election tool, personal tax calculation or employer-cost model. Primary references checked November 20, 2026. The sources explain the underlying concepts; the figures, scenarios and decision records were constructed independently for this guide. Applicable policies, contracts and local requirements need their own qualified review. IRS: gross pay, net pay and withholding — General paycheck definitions only; no current tax rates are used. IRS: understanding employment taxes — Distinguishes employment-tax responsibilities; this guide does not make a filing or compliance determination. For an agreed partial-month housing charge, use the separate prorated rent calculator with the correct dates and rate basis. A payroll deduction calculation does not establish the rent due under a lease. Frequently asked questions What is the difference between gross pay and net pay? Gross pay is earned pay before employee deductions. Net pay is the payroll amount remaining after those deductions. A bank transfer may also include reimbursements or represent only one part of a split deposit. Is the $206 tax withholding a current tax estimate? No. It is a supplied fictional amount used to demonstrate a reconciliation. The guide does not calculate federal, state or local taxes or select withholding elections. Why is the example bank transfer $744 but net pay $699? The fictional transfer combines $699 net wages and a separately approved $45 reimbursement. Its actual tax and reporting treatment is not determined by this arithmetic example. Are employee deductions an extra employer cost? They are already within gross wages in the example. Employer-funded taxes or benefits are separate additions. Counting the same withheld wages again would duplicate cost. Is biweekly pay the same as twice-monthly pay? No. The illustrative 26-payment schedule and 24-payment schedule have different annual totals at the same per-payment amount. Check the actual pay calendar before annualizing. Can this guide estimate my actual take-home pay? No. It explains the record boundaries and hypothetical arithmetic. Actual pay depends on verified earnings, elections, deductions and applicable payroll requirements. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
