documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Customer Acquisition Cost: Formula, Channels and Recovery Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate customer acquisition cost with matched costs and new-customer cohorts. Compare channels, repeat contribution and cash recovery in a checked example. Business finance Worked example Practical record Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, divides the defined acquisition spending by the matched number of new customers. Use the same cost boundary, customer definition and acquisition window before comparing channels. Then test whether collected customer contribution can recover that spending; revenue, ad ROAS and a low headline CAC answer different questions. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical cases are original fictional USD teaching examples, not market benchmarks, customer results, offers or forecasts. Replace each assumption with dated evidence. Define a customer, a period and the included costs Write what counts as a newly acquired customer before opening the advertising report. A paid order, an account registration and a sales-qualified lead are different events. Decide how cancellations, duplicate accounts, related companies and first-time buyers are treated. A repeat order from an existing customer should not automatically become a second new customer just because it came through another campaign. State whether the numerator includes media only, externally paid acquisition cost or a fuller sales-and-marketing cost boundary. Creative work, agency fees, sales effort and allocated support can change a comparison. Preserve both cash expenses and any separately measured internal effort rather than quietly treating unpaid owner time as free or as a second cash payment. A fully loaded analytical figure and a cash-only figure can both be useful if named correctly. Use the same declared boundary for both channels and keep a reconciliation to source invoices, payroll or time records. Do not include recruiting costs merely because a sales employee was hired. Cost per hire uses completed hires as its denominator; CAC uses new customers. Reconcile two channels and shared acquisition work In a fictional quarter, Channel A spends $3,000 on media, $600 on creative and $1,400 on attributed sales work to acquire 50 paying new customers. Its direct acquisition cost is $5,000 and direct CAC is $100. Channel B spends $1,600, $400 and $1,000 respectively to acquire 20 new customers. Its direct cost is $3,000 and direct CAC is $150. Assume each new customer appears once and the groups do not overlap. A shared $800 acquisition task is allocated $500 to A and $300 to B using documented work hours. The resulting fuller boundary gives A $5,500/50 = $110 and B $3,300/20 = $165. Together, $8,800 over 70 new customers gives blended CAC of $125.71 after presentation rounding. Do not average $110 and $165 without weighting the customer counts. Original quarterly USD case; unique acquired customers Measure Channel A Channel B Combined Direct acquisition spend $5,000 $3,000 $8,000 Allocated shared acquisition work $500 $300 $800 Defined acquisition total $5,500 $3,300 $8,800 New paying customers 50 20 70 CAC on this boundary $110 $165 $125.71 The allocation moves the channel comparison but does not change the $8,800 total. An allocation chosen to make a favored channel look better is not evidence of improved performance. Record the allocation basis and show a sensitivity if the shared work cannot be reliably traced. Separate media CAC, blended CAC and incomplete cohorts The same case has $4,600 media spend. Dividing that by the same 70 attributed new customers gives $65.71 media-only acquisition cost per customer. It does not replace the $125.71 fuller-boundary figure. If some customers actually came from unpaid or untracked sources, the numerator and denominator must be rebuilt before calling this a paid-channel metric. A platform-reported conversion count is not sufficient evidence that all those buyers are new. Attribution also has a time boundary. Spending late in a quarter can produce conversions in the next quarter. A same-period spending divided by same-period customer ratio is a period diagnostic; it may not describe a mature acquisition cohort. Preserve the two dates and explain the approach. Do not silently move spend to improve one period while retaining the customers in another. For a channel test, track stable customer IDs internally using appropriate access controls, then bring only non-sensitive aggregate counts into a planning record. Reconcile CRM, payment and campaign systems before comparing the results. The printable record attached here is not a customer database and should not contain names, email addresses, payment details or other personal records. Follow acquired customers from net sales to contribution Suppose each of the 70 new customers completes one first order with $200 net revenue after discounts and returns. The order has $90 COGS, $20 variable delivery and $10 payment fees, leaving $80 contribution before acquisition spending. Initial cohort contribution is therefore 70 × $80 = $5,600. Against $8,800 acquisition cost, the initial unrecovered amount is $3,200. A $200 order does not mean a $125.71 CAC has already paid back. Use the gross-to-net sales reconciliation before calculating this contribution. Gross profit and gross margin explains why a gross-profit subtotal may still exclude delivery fees, selling costs or other amounts relevant to customer recovery. State which costs change with the orders and do not count a sales expense both in CAC and again in the per-order contribution. A customer-profitability review can extend the cost-to-serve analysis after acquisition. It should retain the acquisition record rather than rewrite the original CAC whenever a customer becomes more expensive to support. For an actual staffing or software change used to lower CAC, differential cost analysis separates avoided payments from unchanged allocations. Measure cohort recovery without assuming perfect retention In the next month, assume 60 of the original customers generate $40 collected contribution each, adding $2,400. In month three, only 50 generate the same $40, adding $2,000. Cumulative contribution is $5,600, then $8,000, then $10,000. The $8,800 acquisition outlay is first recovered at a modeled month-end in month three. This is a teaching scenario, not a retention benchmark or promise that new customers will reorder. The first-order values above assume the contribution is collected in that month. If invoices remain unpaid, keep earned contribution and bank cash recovery in separate columns. Refunds, bad debt, servicing effort and future retention spending can change the result. The calculation does not estimate lifetime value, and a business should not extrapolate three observed months into perpetual customer earnings. Test a downside using explicit lost customers or lower repeat contribution. If month three produces only 15 × $40 = $600, cumulative contribution is $8,600 and the cohort is still $200 short. Reporting an average payback based on the successful customers alone would hide the acquisition cost of those who never returned. Keep the original 70-customer cohort intact. Choose an action that improves economics, not just the ratio A lower CAC can come from cheaper acquisition, a more complete cohort, changed attribution or a broader customer definition. It can also arrive with smaller orders, weaker repeat contribution or a delivery problem. Review these explanations before increasing spending. There is no universal good CAC or universally correct lifetime-value-to-CAC target for every business model, margin and collection cycle. Use the record to choose one action, its owner and an evidence date: improve qualification, change a channel, revise creative, reduce sales friction or stop an unproductive campaign. Preserve a comparable baseline and the exact numerator/denominator. An expansion plan should use acquisition cost and timing consistent with its proposed customer volume. A valuation forecast should not assume sustained customer growth after eliminating the spending required to obtain it. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Customer Acquisition Cost review record . Use it to preserve the assumptions, supporting records, reconciliation and next action in this guide. It does not automatically calculate, save entries after reload or submit information. Print or save a copy when complete, and use fictional or non-sensitive planning data. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. Source concepts and original teaching cases are separate. This guide supports planning and record review; it is not an appraisal, accounting-policy election, legal determination or lending recommendation. Shopify: customer acquisition cost — First-party metric and acquisition-cost context; no Shopify statistics or benchmarks are used. SBA: business planning — Customer and marketing evidence context; channels and recovery cases are original. Frequently asked questions Does CAC equal cost per lead? No. CAC uses defined new customers; cost per lead uses leads. Conversion and qualification connect the two but do not make their denominators interchangeable. Should repeat orders count as new customers? Usually not under the same new-customer definition. Track repeat contribution separately while preserving the original acquisition cohort. Why is blended CAC not the average of channel CAC figures? The combined ratio is total included cost divided by total matched customers. An unweighted average ignores different customer counts. Can internal sales work be included? Yes under a declared fuller cost boundary with supported allocation. Show whether the amount is actual cash expense or an analytical time cost and avoid double counting. Is positive ROAS enough to show acquisition has paid back? No. ROAS compares attributed revenue with ad spend. CAC recovery needs contribution after relevant costs and the actual timing of collections. What happens when no new customers were acquired? CAC is undefined for a zero-customer denominator. Report the spending and zero customers separately rather than presenting zero cost or a fabricated finite ratio. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Gross Profit and Gross Margin: Formula and Reconciliation
documents.summary: Calculate gross profit dollars and gross margin percentage from net sales and COGS. See both formulas in one example and reconcile inventory costs.
documents.headings: Gross profit dollars and gross margin percentage for the same period State what your gross-profit subtotal includes Build the net-revenue side of the example Reconcile inventory to cost of goods sold Calculate gross profit, margin and the different markup base Show what gross profit has not paid for Turn the reconciliation into a useful operating review Build your own review record Sources and scope Continue with pricing and customer profitability Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Gross Profit and Gross Margin: Formula and Reconciliation Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate gross profit and gross margin from net revenue and matched COGS. Reconcile a checked inventory case and separate fees, contribution and net income. Gross profit dollars and gross margin percentage for the same period If net sales are $10,000 and cost of goods sold is $6,000, gross profit is $4,000. Gross margin is $4,000 ÷ $10,000 = 40%. Use net sales after discounts and returns, and match the period used for COGS. Rent, sales staff and other operating costs still need to be deducted where applicable. Reconcile inventory costs with the COGS calculator Compare margin with markup on a unit cost Business finance Worked example Practical record Gross profit is net revenue minus the cost of goods sold or cost of sales on the stated reporting basis. Gross margin is that gross profit divided by net revenue. Reconcile both inputs for the same period before interpreting the percentage, and keep selling costs, financing, tax and customer cash separate from the gross-profit subtotal. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical cases are original fictional USD teaching examples, not market benchmarks, customer results, offers or forecasts. Replace each assumption with dated evidence. State what your gross-profit subtotal includes Start with the business, period and accounting policy. A retailer’s inventory purchases do not necessarily equal its cost of goods sold for the period, because some stock remains unsold. A service business needs a supported cost-of-sales policy for delivery labor and other included costs. Consistency matters when comparing periods or companies; the same label can conceal different cost classifications. Use net revenue after the applicable sales deductions as the denominator, not gross billings or bank deposits. The net-revenue guide owns the sales reconciliation. This guide then subtracts the matched cost of sales and interprets the resulting subtotal. If you need to solve a selling price from a target margin, use the existing margin-versus-markup calculator rather than treating this explanatory page as another competing price tool. Write down whether factory or delivery overhead is in cost of sales and whether payment fees are presented as selling expenses. Do not move a recurring cost below gross profit simply to make the percentage rise. A comparison is useful only after you understand the reporting boundary and any genuine change in the policy. Build the net-revenue side of the example A fictional retailer has $50,000 gross earned sales for a month, $2,000 sales discounts and $3,000 recognized customer returns. Assume these are complete, non-overlapping deductions under the stated case. Net revenue is $50,000 − $2,000 − $3,000 = $45,000. The return figure is the customer sales value, not the inventory cost of the goods coming back. A goods return can have a separate stock-cost entry if returned items qualify for recovery. The closing inventory record in the next section already includes any supported recovered stock, so no second retail-price deduction is made from COGS. Damaged goods and refund obligations need their own evidence and applicable accounting treatment. A simple revenue reduction does not explain the entire physical inventory movement. Reconcile credited sales with dated invoices, approved discounts and return records. Separate customer refunds from supplier purchase credits. Separate tax collected for a government under the stated agency arrangement from earned sales. Customer acquisition analysis and forecasts should begin with the same defined sales basis instead of switching between headline orders and collected amounts without explanation. Reconcile inventory to cost of goods sold The retailer begins with $18,000 inventory, records $26,000 purchases and $2,000 qualifying freight-in, and receives $1,000 supplier purchase credits. A supported closing count and cost valuation gives $14,000 ending inventory. Available cost is $18,000 + $26,000 + $2,000 − $1,000 = $45,000. Subtracting closing inventory leaves $31,000 COGS. The amounts are original assumptions, not an industry example copied from a source. Original monthly USD inventory-to-COGS bridge Cost record Amount Opening inventory $18,000 Purchases $26,000 Qualifying freight-in $2,000 Supplier credits −$1,000 Available cost $45,000 Closing inventory −$14,000 Cost of goods sold $31,000 The $45,000 available-cost total happens to equal this case’s net revenue, but those are independent calculations. A valid stock-cost schedule does not require available cost to equal sales. Use the inventory-valuation guide for cost-flow choices and the COGS guide for a fuller stock movement reconciliation. Investigate missing counts, duplicate supplier invoices, unsupported freight classification or receipts booked after the cut-off. A percentage produced from an unreconciled stock balance is not a reliable pricing signal. Keep physical units and monetary costs traceable, even when a summary statement displays only dollars. Calculate gross profit, margin and the different markup base Gross profit is $45,000 − $31,000 = $14,000. Gross margin is $14,000/$45,000 × 100 = 31.11% after presentation rounding. If someone instead divides the same $14,000 by $31,000, the result is 45.16%. That second ratio is markup on the defined COGS base, not gross margin. The profit numerator is the same; the denominator changes the question. Use full precision for intermediate values and label the displayed rounding. Adding item-level gross-margin percentages without weighting their revenue does not reproduce the business margin. For a mixed range, combine net sales and matched costs first, or calculate a properly revenue-weighted result. A change in product mix can move gross margin even if no individual product price changed. If net revenue is zero, a gross-margin percentage is not defined. A positive sales figure with COGS above sales gives negative gross profit and a negative gross margin. Do not turn an undefined ratio into zero, and do not suppress the loss because it looks unusual. Preserve dollar totals next to every ratio so a reader can see scale. Show what gross profit has not paid for Assume the $14,000 gross profit must also cover $1,350 payment fees, $4,000 selling payroll and $2,500 premises rent, all outside COGS under this particular case’s classification. Operating profit is $14,000 − $1,350 − $4,000 − $2,500 = $6,150. After a separately assumed $500 interest expense and $1,000 income-tax expense, net income is $4,650. The tax amount is a teaching input, not a tax-rate calculation or filing instruction. These subtotals explain why a business can have a healthy-looking gross margin and modest final earnings. They do not establish what is in the bank: sales can remain uncollected, inventory purchases can precede sales, and loan principal or equipment payments can use cash without being the same period’s operating expense. The earnings-to-cash comparison follows those separate boundaries. Gross margin is also not automatically contribution margin. Suppose $4,000 of the $31,000 COGS is fixed production overhead and the remaining $27,000 changes with the modeled activity. If the $1,350 payment fees are the only other variable costs, contribution is $45,000 − $27,000 − $1,350 = $16,650. This different subtotal supports a different decision; see contribution versus gross margin . Turn the reconciliation into a useful operating review When gross margin moves, compare net selling price, discounts, returns, stock costs and mix on a consistent period basis. Check a matched set of products or jobs before concluding that all prices need to increase. A supplier-credit timing issue, a stock write-down or an unusual returned order can explain a change without indicating a new sustainable margin. For a proposed operating change, differential cost asks which future amounts actually change. For an added location, expansion planning adds capacity and cash timing. For a potential sale, valuation reviews normalized transferable earnings rather than applying a price multiple blindly to this month’s gross profit. The gross-profit bridge remains one controlled input to those decisions, not a substitute for their other records. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Gross Profit and Gross Margin review record . Use it to preserve the assumptions, supporting records, reconciliation and next action in this guide. It does not automatically calculate, save entries after reload or submit information. Print or save a copy when complete, and use fictional or non-sensitive planning data. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. Source concepts and original teaching cases are separate. This guide supports planning and record review; it is not an appraisal, accounting-policy election, legal determination or lending recommendation. OpenStax: income-statement presentation — Gross-profit and operating-subtotal context; no textbook numerical examples are reproduced. IFRS Foundation: IFRS 15 — Revenue-recognition framework context; the simplified deductions are fictional. Frequently asked questions What is the gross-profit formula? Net revenue minus matched cost of goods sold or cost of sales, using a defined business, period and reporting basis. What is the gross-margin formula? Gross profit divided by net revenue, multiplied by 100 for a percentage. Net revenue must be nonzero for the ratio to be defined. Are margin and markup the same? No. Margin uses net revenue as its denominator; markup uses the stated cost base. A 31.11% margin in this example is a 45.16% markup on COGS. Do purchases equal COGS? Not necessarily. Opening inventory, purchases and qualifying adjustments must reconcile with ending inventory and supported goods outflows. Does gross profit equal bank cash? No. Collection dates, inventory payments, financing and capital spending can separate the income-statement subtotal from cash movements. Is gross margin the same as contribution margin? No. Gross margin follows the cost-of-sales reporting boundary; contribution separates variable costs under the relevant operating model. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Differential Cost: Relevant Costs Between Alternatives
documents.summary: Compare differential costs on the same horizon, separate sunk and committed amounts, and reconcile cash and opportunity-cost results in a checked example.
documents.headings: Write two comparable alternatives before classifying a cost Build a monthly process comparison Put the one-time setup on the same horizon Show the cost of a real scarce-resource alternative Test the assumptions that could reverse the answer Create an auditable choice rather than a preferred answer Build your own review record Sources and scope Continue with cost accounting and cost behavior Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Differential Cost: Relevant Costs Between Alternatives Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare differential costs on the same horizon, separate sunk and committed amounts, and reconcile cash and opportunity-cost results in a checked example. Business finance Worked example Practical record Differential cost is the cost difference between defined alternatives over the same decision horizon. Compare future amounts that change because of the choice, then include differential revenue and any supported opportunity cost. Keep sunk spending, unchanged commitments and arbitrary allocations visible but outside the incremental difference. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical cases are original fictional USD teaching examples, not market benchmarks, customer results, offers or forecasts. Replace each assumption with dated evidence. Write two comparable alternatives before classifying a cost A useful comparison begins with specific operating alternatives and a common period, output, quality requirement and service obligation. “Buy a machine” is incomplete unless the alternative states how the same required work would otherwise be delivered. A lower-cost process may not be comparable if it changes product quality, reliability, staff safety or the agreed delivery date. Use a row for every amount, including those that ultimately cancel. Label whether it is a future cash payment, an accounting allocation, a sunk amount or a separately stated opportunity cost. A fixed cost is relevant when the decision changes it; a variable cost can be irrelevant when it is identical under both alternatives. The label alone does not settle the decision. This page owns the general comparison framework. The make-or-buy guide applies it to sourcing, while marginal cost measures the change in cost between output levels. A differential analysis can compare processes producing the same output, so it need not be a cost-per-added-unit calculation. Build a monthly process comparison A fictional workshop must package 2,000 units per month. Process A uses $1.20 materials, $0.80 paid labor and $0.30 variable support per unit, or $2.30 × 2,000 = $4,600. Management also allocates $1,000 existing premises cost to the work. The lease payment remains unchanged under either process for the decision horizon, so the allocation is shown but contributes zero to the difference. Process B needs $0.95 materials, $0.50 paid labor and $0.20 variable support per unit, or $1.65 × 2,000 = $3,300, plus a new $900 monthly machine lease. Future recurring cash cost is therefore $4,200. Assume the labor amounts are genuinely avoidable payments rather than released salaried time. A proposed saving that merely frees committed employee hours needs a separate capacity argument. Original monthly USD comparison at equal required output Cost Process A Process B B minus A Materials $2,400 $1,900 −$500 Avoidable paid labor $1,600 $1,000 −$600 Variable support $600 $400 −$200 New machine lease $0 $900 +$900 Relevant recurring total $4,600 $4,200 −$400 Unchanged premises allocation $1,000 $1,000 $0 Process B reduces the defined recurring cash cost by $400 a month. The $1,000 allocation is not a saving: the business still pays it. If the new machine also needs different maintenance, insurance, power or staffing, obtain those amounts before treating $400 as the complete difference. Put the one-time setup on the same horizon Assume B additionally requires a future $2,400 installation payment before operation. A previous $600 feasibility study has already been paid and cannot be recovered whichever alternative is chosen. The future installation is included in the decision; the $600 study is a sunk amount shown in the background record. Do not treat the study as a new payment, and do not choose B simply to justify money already spent. For twelve identical operating months, A costs 12 × $4,600 = $55,200. B costs 12 × $4,200 + $2,400 = $52,800. On that stated future cash boundary, B saves $2,400 over the year. Dividing the setup by the $400 recurring saving gives six months of simple setup-cost recovery, but this does not value time, risk, taxes, later lease commitments or disposal proceeds. Keep the cash dates in a separate column. A $2,400 annual advantage does not mean the opening installation is funded. Use the business ROI and payback tool for its explicitly defined return questions, and capital budgeting for longer dated investment cash flows. Do not combine a one-month cost difference with an unexplained multi-year investment commitment. Show the cost of a real scarce-resource alternative Suppose operating B uses 100 hours a month of a specialist whose available time would otherwise earn $300 monthly contribution on confirmed alternative work. This is a separately supported opportunity cost, not a new invoice. Including it reduces B’s monthly economic advantage from $400 to $100. Over twelve months, $4,800 recurring cash saving − $2,400 setup − $3,600 forgone contribution = a $1,200 economic disadvantage. The cash-payment view and economic comparison can therefore point in different directions without an arithmetic error. Report both with their boundaries: $2,400 lower directly modeled payments, but $1,200 worse after the stated forgone contribution. The opportunity amount should reflect the best feasible alternative, its contribution after relevant costs, and the portion actually displaced. Do not use gross sales as the lost profit. If that specialist has no saleable alternative work, the $300 assumption fails and should not remain as an automatic surcharge. If the hours could earn a different amount, show the revised result. Expansion planning uses the same discipline when a new location attracts work away from an existing operation. A scarce resource requires evidence, not an invented hourly charge. Test the assumptions that could reverse the answer The recurring $100 economic advantage before setup disappears if B needs more than $100 additional monthly relevant cost. For example, an omitted $120 maintenance commitment produces a $20 recurring disadvantage after the stated opportunity cost. This is a sensitivity on a defined missing amount, not a claim that all maintenance is fixed or all new machines require that charge. At a different output level, rebuild materials and labor from quantities and verify whether the $900 lease, staffing and quality obligations remain unchanged. Never extend a per-unit rate beyond its supported range without checking capacity steps. Average cost per unit can describe a period’s total spread across output, but an average that falls when volume rises is not proof of an avoidable payment. A lower defect rate or more dependable delivery might justify a higher measured cost, but quantify only what can be supported and preserve the nonfinancial requirements separately. A process that fails mandatory specifications is not an acceptable option merely because its spreadsheet cost is lower. Use the original baseline to distinguish evidence updates from changed decision rules. Create an auditable choice rather than a preferred answer Before approving a choice, reconcile the cost rows with supplier quotations, staff schedules, lease terms and available alternative work. Identify the reviewer, date and expiry of each quote. State whether installation is refundable, whether the lease extends beyond the comparison horizon and what happens if output is delayed. The plan should expose a missing input instead of silently filling it with zero. Connect the comparison with the gross-profit statement without altering its accounting classifications merely to match this decision table. Net revenue remains the sales basis for a differential-revenue case. Valuation may use maintainable future costs over a different horizon, so the same allocation or commitment can need a different treatment there. Write the boundary first, preserve the evidence and choose only after the cash, capacity and contractual conditions have been reviewed. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Differential Cost review record . Use it to preserve the assumptions, supporting records, reconciliation and next action in this guide. It does not automatically calculate, save entries after reload or submit information. Print or save a copy when complete, and use fictional or non-sensitive planning data. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. Source concepts and original teaching cases are separate. This guide supports planning and record review; it is not an appraisal, accounting-policy election, legal determination or lending recommendation. OpenStax: relevant information for decisions — Relevant, sunk and opportunity-cost concepts; all packaging amounts and alternative work are original. SBA: business planning — Evidence and operating-plan context; no prescribed cost or decision threshold is claimed. Frequently asked questions Is every variable cost relevant? No. A cost that is equal under both alternatives does not change the comparison. Relevance depends on the choice and horizon, not the accounting label alone. Can a fixed cost be differential? Yes. A new lease or an avoidable fixed commitment is relevant when one alternative changes the future amount. Should a sunk feasibility study affect the choice? An unavoidable past payment is not a new cost difference. Keep it in the evidence record without letting it justify an otherwise weak alternative. Is released employee time automatically a cash saving? No. Show an actual avoidable payment separately from usable capacity or forgone contribution. Do not count the same time benefit twice. What is an opportunity cost? The supported benefit from the best feasible alternative that the choice prevents. It is not necessarily a bank payment and should be presented separately. Can I compare alternatives over different periods? Align their horizon, output, timing and obligations first. A monthly operating saving cannot be compared directly with a multi-year total commitment. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Net Revenue: Discounts, Returns and Gross-to-Net Reconciliation
documents.summary: Reconcile gross sales, discounts, returns and allowances to net revenue. Follow the same example into receivables, processor fees and bank cash.
documents.headings: Define the revenue event before subtracting deductions Reconcile a simple gross-to-net sales record Do not subtract every expense just because revenue is called net Follow net credit sales into the customer ledger Reconcile processor settlement and borrowing separately Use the bridge to improve a decision without changing its meaning Build your own review record Sources and scope Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Net Revenue: Discounts, Returns and Gross-to-Net Reconciliation Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Reconcile gross sales, discounts, returns and allowances to net revenue. Follow the same example into receivables, processor fees and bank cash. Business finance Worked example Practical record Net revenue is the revenue amount remaining after the applicable sales deductions on a stated reporting basis. Reconcile earned gross sales, discounts, returns and allowances without subtracting unrelated operating costs. Then follow receivables, collections and fees separately: net revenue, gross profit, net income and bank deposits are different measures. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical cases are original fictional USD teaching examples, not market benchmarks, customer results, offers or forecasts. Replace each assumption with dated evidence. Define the revenue event before subtracting deductions State the period, business scope and accounting basis. A quote is not necessarily earned revenue, an invoice can be issued before or after the relevant performance, and a customer payment can settle an earlier period. The net-revenue bridge starts with a supported sales record under the applicable recognition policy, not automatically the bookings total in a sales dashboard. Specify whether discounts are already reflected in invoice amounts. If the ledger begins with discounted invoices, subtracting the same discount again understates revenue. Identify customer returns, price allowances and other contract-related adjustments by reference and date. Refund cash can move in another period, and an estimate of future returns needs the applicable policy and supporting evidence rather than an arbitrary percentage. This guide is a planning reconciliation, not a complete application of every revenue-recognition rule. IFRS 15 provides an authoritative recognition framework; US GAAP and local requirements must be identified for the actual reporting task. The numerical case below assumes its recognition and deduction decisions are already supported. It does not decide them from the word “net.” Reconcile a simple gross-to-net sales record A fictional merchant records $40,000 gross earned credit sales excluding separately accounted-for sales tax. Approved sales discounts are $2,000, recognized returns are $2,500 and customer price allowances are $500. Assume these are distinct amounts, complete for the case and not already netted into the starting balance. Net revenue is $40,000 − $2,000 − $2,500 − $500 = $35,000. Original USD case; sales values, not inventory costs Sales record Deduction Running revenue Gross earned sales Starting amount $40,000 Approved discounts −$2,000 $38,000 Recognized customer returns −$2,500 $35,500 Price allowances −$500 $35,000 Attach the approval, invoice or credit reference for each deduction. A return can also create a separate inventory-cost consequence, but the retail sales refund is not a substitute for that stock entry. An allowance lets the customer retain goods or accept a price adjustment under the stated circumstances; it need not represent a physical return. A net-revenue ratio such as $35,000/$40,000 = 87.5% describes this bridge only. It is not a profit margin, tax rate or collection percentage. Report the $5,000 total deduction alongside the ratio so the reader can see scale and investigate whether discounts, returns or allowances are driving the result. Do not subtract every expense just because revenue is called net In this case, product cost, employee wages, premises rent and payment-processing charges are expenses or other cost records rather than the sales deductions shown above. Subtracting them here would create a different subtotal and conceal the gross-to-net sales bridge. Gross profit subtracts matched COGS from net revenue; operating and net-income measures include further defined expense categories. Contract facts can change presentation. A platform collecting on behalf of another party may have a principal-versus-agent question; shipping charges and incentives can need careful analysis. Do not assume that every amount withheld by an intermediary must reduce revenue, or that every amount collected from the customer belongs to the merchant. Preserve the contract and identify the applicable reporting framework. For the worked merchant, assume it acts as principal for its goods and separately accounts for $2,800 tax collected for the relevant authority. That tax is outside the $40,000 tax-exclusive sales base; it is not an extra deduction from the $35,000 net-revenue total. The amount is supplied as an assumption, not a jurisdictional tax calculation or determination. Follow net credit sales into the customer ledger Suppose opening trade receivables are $6,000, current net credit sales are $35,000, customer receipts applied to those accounts are $31,000 and supported write-offs are $1,000. On the deliberately simplified tax-exclusive receivables boundary, closing receivables are $6,000 + $35,000 − $31,000 − $1,000 = $9,000. The tax ledger is kept separately in this case so it is not silently mixed with the table. A $31,000 receipt total includes whatever opening and current customer balances it settles. It is not evidence that current-period revenue is $31,000 or that all current sales were collected. The write-off also does not automatically become another sales return: distinguish credit loss from a price concession or approved customer credit using the actual facts and policy. Use the receivables process to preserve invoice allocation and the credit-loss guide for the allowance and write-off boundary. Reconcile the ending customer ledger with the control account before using a collection ratio. Do not replace missing cash-application detail with an unsupported claim that the remaining $9,000 is all overdue. Reconcile processor settlement and borrowing separately Assume the merchant’s processor collects the $31,000 customer receipts in the receivables example and withholds $930 documented fees. Its bank settlement is $30,070. Under the case’s expense presentation, the $930 is recorded separately and net revenue remains $35,000. If the processor holds a reserve or pays on a different date, add those movements to the settlement record rather than forcing the bank amount to equal sales. Assume the separately tracked $2,800 tax collection is remitted in full in the same period through separate cash movements. Its equal inflow and outflow add zero net cash; it is outside the tax-exclusive processor settlement just described. The merchant also receives $5,000 loan proceeds. Bank inflows from settlement and borrowing are $35,070, but borrowing is not customer revenue. With $4,000 opening bank cash and $22,000 supplier plus $7,000 payroll payments, closing cash is $4,000 + $30,070 + $5,000 − $22,000 − $7,000 = $10,070. No claim about final accounting profit follows from that bank balance. Invoice funding can make this distinction especially important: an advance against a receivable is not automatically a second sale. Cash versus profit break-even explains why a sales target and this month’s payment requirement can differ. Keep revenue, liabilities, expenses and settlement timing in separate schedules that reconcile. Use the bridge to improve a decision without changing its meaning Review discounts and returns by consistent customer cohort, product or contract. A temporary discount might increase gross orders while reducing earned net revenue or order contribution. A reduction in refund cash might be a timing delay rather than an improvement in returns. Record the cause, support and period before comparing channels or changing price. Customer acquisition cost needs a matched new-customer denominator; order revenue alone does not establish acquisition recovery. An expansion forecast should use the same discount and return assumptions as the existing operation when estimating new sales. A valuation should not apply an earnings story built on unreconciled gross billings. Maintain a monthly control: starting sales ledger, separately referenced deductions, net-revenue total, customer-account movement and processor-to-bank settlement. Assign an owner to unexplained differences and retain the original entries. If a policy or estimate changes, explain it and preserve comparability instead of rewriting old periods merely to make a trend look smoother. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Net Revenue review record . Use it to preserve the assumptions, supporting records, reconciliation and next action in this guide. It does not automatically calculate, save entries after reload or submit information. Print or save a copy when complete, and use fictional or non-sensitive planning data. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. Source concepts and original teaching cases are separate. This guide supports planning and record review; it is not an appraisal, accounting-policy election, legal determination or lending recommendation. IFRS Foundation: IFRS 15 — Revenue-recognition and consideration context; simplified sales assumptions are original. OpenStax: income-statement presentation — Separation of revenue, cost of sales and operating subtotals; no textbook case values are reused. Frequently asked questions Is net revenue the same as net income? No. Net revenue concerns the sales amount after applicable deductions. Net income reflects the further expenses, other income, financing and tax included on the stated reporting basis. Are card fees always a revenue deduction? No. This merchant case presents documented processor fees separately as expense. Actual contract facts and the applicable reporting framework determine presentation. Can I subtract discounts twice? No. If the starting invoice or ledger sales balance already reflects a discount, do not deduct it again in the gross-to-net bridge. Does a loan receipt increase net revenue? No. Borrowing creates cash and an obligation under its terms; it is not a new customer sale. Do receivable write-offs equal customer returns? Not necessarily. Distinguish credit losses from approved sales returns, allowances and price concessions using the actual facts and policy. Should net revenue equal bank deposits? No. Receivable timing, opening balances, processor fees, reserves, other receipts and funding can separate earned revenue from bank movements. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Inventory Valuation Methods: FIFO, Weighted Average and Profit
documents.summary: Compare inventory valuation methods with a reconciled FIFO and weighted-average example, framework boundaries, write-downs and a practical review record.
documents.headings: What the main inventory valuation methods mean Follow two purchase batches through a month-end sale Why periodic and moving averages can diverge Keep IFRS, US reporting and tax choices separate Test recoverability separately from the cost-flow method A practical inventory-valuation close Build your own review record Sources and scope Continue with cash flow, working capital and stock Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Inventory Valuation Methods: FIFO, Weighted Average and Profit Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare inventory valuation methods with a reconciled FIFO and weighted-average example, framework boundaries, write-downs and a practical review record. Business finance Worked example Practical record Inventory valuation assigns supported costs to the units sold and the stock still held. FIFO, weighted average and specific identification can allocate the same purchase cost differently. First establish the accounting framework and inventory record; then reconcile cost of goods sold plus ending inventory to the total available cost. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical examples are original fictional USD teaching cases. They are not market rates, customer results, eligibility determinations or forecasts. Replace assumptions with dated records. What the main inventory valuation methods mean FIFO assigns the earliest available costs to sold units. Weighted average spreads a supported average cost across interchangeable units. Specific identification traces an individual item’s actual cost, useful when the item can be reliably distinguished. LIFO assigns later costs first where the applicable framework permits it; it is not an IFRS option. The physical shelf-picking order and the accounting cost-flow assumption are related operating decisions, but they are not automatically the same record. Use the inventory movement guide to establish what was received, sold, returned or lost. This page starts after those quantities reconcile. A costing method cannot repair an inaccurate count, and choosing a method solely to produce a preferred margin is not a sound close process. Follow two purchase batches through a month-end sale A retailer begins with 100 identical units costing $10 each and purchases 100 more at $14. Assume no freight, rebates, returns, damage, tax or other acquisition adjustments. There are 200 units with $2,400 total cost. The retailer sells 150 units for $20 each, giving $3,000 revenue, and physically counts 50 remaining units. All purchases occur before the sale, so periodic weighted average and a moving average updated before this sale have the same result here. Original USD case; 200 units available, 150 sold, 50 remaining Checkpoint FIFO Periodic weighted average Cost per assigned unit Old layer $10; new layer $14 $2,400 / 200 = $12 Cost of goods sold 100 × $10 + 50 × $14 = $1,700 150 × $12 = $1,800 Ending inventory 50 × $14 = $700 50 × $12 = $600 Cost reconciliation $1,700 + $700 = $2,400 $1,800 + $600 = $2,400 Gross profit $3,000 − $1,700 = $1,300 $3,000 − $1,800 = $1,200 Gross margin $1,300 / $3,000 = 43.33% $1,200 / $3,000 = 40.00% The $100 gross-profit difference is matched by the $100 difference in ending inventory. It is an allocation difference within the same $2,400 pool, not an extra $100 bank receipt. Neither gross profit figure deducts selling expenses, payroll outside COGS, interest or income tax. The COGS bridge connects this allocation with the income statement. Why periodic and moving averages can diverge Now consider a different sequence using the same opening stock and purchase prices: sell 50 units before the second purchase, buy the 100 units at $14, then sell another 100. A perpetual moving-average record first expenses 50 × $10 = $500. The remaining 50 old units cost $500; adding the $1,400 receipt leaves $1,900 over 150 units, or $12.666666… each. The next 100 sales release $1,266.67 after presentation rounding, leaving $633.33 inventory. Total COGS is $1,766.67. A periodic average calculated once across the entire period still produces $1,800 COGS and $600 ending inventory. The two schedules have different averaging dates. Retain full precision in the ledger and reconcile the displayed cents to the $2,400 control total; do not average the two quoted purchase prices without weighting their quantities. Record transaction dates before comparing systems. Keep IFRS, US reporting and tax choices separate IAS 2 uses specific identification for appropriate distinct items and FIFO or weighted average for ordinarily interchangeable inventory. Its measurement rule compares cost with net realisable value, which considers expected selling proceeds less completion and selling costs. US reporting and US tax rules have their own requirements; LIFO availability in a US context is not permission to use it under IFRS. The IRS also has method-change procedures and particular small-business inventory provisions. Identify which statements or return you are preparing, the documented policy and any required approval before changing methods. A planning spreadsheet is not an accounting-policy election. Apply the same supported basis consistently to comparable inventory; explain a real policy change instead of silently replacing last month’s costs. Product and period costs addresses which costs enter inventory in the first place. Test recoverability separately from the cost-flow method In a separate IFRS illustration, the 50 closing FIFO units carry $700 cost. New evidence supports $12 expected selling price per unit and $1 selling cost, with no completion cost. Net realisable value is 50 × ($12 − $1) = $550. The assumed comparison therefore indicates a $150 write-down. Under the $600 average-cost carrying amount, the difference to the same $550 recovery estimate would be $50. This is a separate valuation adjustment, not another purchase or an immediate cash payment. Document the evidence date, affected items, estimated recovery and applicable framework. Do not spread one damaged product’s estimate across unrelated healthy inventory. US measurement can depend on the inventory method and reporting rules, so do not apply this IFRS illustration as a universal US tax instruction. A practical inventory-valuation close Reconcile opening quantity plus supported receipts minus supported outflows to the counted closing quantity. Build the cost pool from the policy’s qualifying costs and supplier adjustments, each counted once. Apply the documented method to dated transactions; keep original source invoices. Check COGS plus closing inventory against available cost before separate adjustments. Review loss, obsolescence and recoverability evidence, and distinguish write-downs from physical losses. Reconcile the expense with accrual timing and supplier cash payments separately. If the control total fails, resolve the missing movement or duplicated cost before using the resulting margin to change prices. The margin-versus-markup guide then helps interpret the correctly defined cost base. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Inventory valuation review . It stays in the browser, does not automatically calculate and does not save entries after reload. Print or save a copy of your completed record. Use fictional or non-sensitive planning data; this is not a payroll, tax, lending or grant submission system. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. The original case and decision record are separate from the source guidance; follow the applicable framework, current terms and local requirements. OpenStax: periodic inventory costing — Cost-flow concepts; the batches and arithmetic above are original. IFRS Foundation: IAS 2 — IFRS cost-formula and recoverability boundaries. IRS Publication 538 — US tax accounting-method context; not a method election through this record. Frequently asked questions Is FIFO always the best inventory method? No. Framework permissions, item characteristics, reliable records and consistent policy matter. A method producing a higher profit this month is not automatically the appropriate one. Is weighted average the average of supplier price quotes? No. Weight supported cost by the corresponding quantities. In the case, $2,400 over 200 units is $12 per unit. Does a higher inventory value create cash? No. The example reallocates the same purchase cost between COGS and remaining stock. Customer and supplier cash payments need a separate schedule. Can LIFO be used under IFRS? No. IAS 2 does not permit LIFO. A US reporting or tax choice must be evaluated under its own rules rather than transferred to IFRS. Why can moving average differ from periodic average? Moving average updates after receipts and applies the rate to subsequent issues. Periodic average uses the whole period’s cost pool. Intervening sales can therefore change the allocation. Does a write-down change the quantity on the shelf? Not by itself. A valuation adjustment changes carrying value. A physical loss also needs a supported quantity movement and must not be counted twice. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Recruitment Strategies for Small Business: Cost and Hiring Quality
documents.summary: Build a small-business recruitment strategy from workload, role evidence and a comparable hiring funnel. Track cost, productive capacity and hiring quality.
documents.headings: Start with work that a new hire can actually take over Choose channels for the role and document the comparison Compare qualified hiring outcomes rather than raw applications Include internal recruiting and onboarding time once Use a consistent selection record and a realistic offer Review the hire at 30, 60 and 90 days Build your own review record Sources and scope Continue with hiring, payroll and employee costs Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Recruitment Strategies for Small Business: Cost and Hiring Quality Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a small-business recruitment strategy from workload, role evidence and a comparable hiring funnel. Track cost, productive capacity and hiring quality. Business finance Worked example Practical record A recruitment strategy connects a real workload gap with a defined role, a fair selection process and a funded onboarding plan. Choose channels by qualified outcomes and delivery readiness, not applicant volume alone. Measure hiring expense separately from the recurring cost and capacity of the person who joins. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical examples are original fictional USD teaching cases. They are not market rates, customer results, eligibility determinations or forecasts. Replace assumptions with dated records. Start with work that a new hire can actually take over List the recurring tasks, quality standard, required schedule and decision authority before writing an advert. A founder who needs production support may still be the bottleneck for approvals. Hiring another producer will not remove an approval queue unless the role and handoff address it. Separate an enduring workload gap from a temporary deadline or an inefficient process. For an original agency case, signed work requires 240 delivery hours next month and the current team can provide 180. The initial gap is 60 hours. A proposed hire has 160 paid monthly hours, but the plan allows 40 for onboarding, 30 for internal work and 10 for leave or other downtime. Planned delivery capacity is only 80 hours . If the founder must supervise for 20 hours that would otherwise support delivery, the net increase is 60, exactly the stated gap. This is a capacity hypothesis, not a promise of first-month productivity. Choose channels for the role and document the comparison Employee referrals can reach people familiar with the work; targeted job boards can reach a defined skill group; general job boards widen reach; schools, workforce organizations and professional communities may support different experience levels. A specialist recruiter adds an external service and contractual cost. An internal move may shorten some onboarding but create another vacancy. None is universally the cheapest or best source. Publish the same essential role requirements and evaluate the relevant work evidence consistently. The EEOC’s small-business guidance addresses consistent screening and nondiscriminatory hiring. A referral is an introduction, not a reason to lower the standard or ignore other qualified applicants. Establish an accessible contact route for application-process needs and use current guidance for the rules that apply. Compare qualified hiring outcomes rather than raw applications Suppose one role is advertised in two channels over the same four-week window. Counts below are original assumptions, not channel benchmarks. “Qualified” means meeting the role’s documented criteria, and a start means the person actually begins work. Keep the same cost boundary in both rows. Original recruitment funnel; illustrative USD Channel Applicants Qualified Interviews Starts External cash cost Targeted board 40 12 6 1 $600 Referral program 10 5 3 1 $500 The board’s qualified share is 12 ÷ 40 = 30%, versus 5 ÷ 10 = 50% for referrals. Cash cost per start is $600 and $500, respectively. Those small counts do not prove that referrals always perform better, nor that either hire will stay or deliver the work. A second observation window and role-specific outcomes are more informative than treating two starts as a universal ranking. Include internal recruiting and onboarding time once The example team also spends 20 interview and administration hours valued at $30 each, adding $600 allocated internal cost. Combined recruiting cost is $600 + $500 + $600 = $1,700, or $850 across two starts. External cash spending is still $1,100: the allocated time is not automatically an additional bank payment. Record whether that time was existing salary, overtime or outside contractor work. Then budget onboarding separately. If a new employee earns $4,000 in a month, that entire payroll commitment still exists even when only 80 of 160 paid hours are productive. Do not add the same salary again as an “onboarding loss” in the cash budget. Use cost per hire versus employee cost and the employee cost calculator for their separate cost boundaries. Use a consistent selection record and a realistic offer Translate the role into a small set of observable criteria: for example, accuracy of a work sample, explanation of a relevant process, schedule fit and experience needed for a specific duty. Ask comparable job-related questions and retain evidence supporting the evaluation. Do not turn an informal “culture fit” label into a substitute for the requirements. Explain the scope, pay structure, reporting relationship and expected ramp-up before acceptance. Screening, accommodations, background checks and record retention have legal requirements that depend on the facts and jurisdiction; the linked EEOC material is a starting point, not a promise that this illustrative process establishes compliance. Keep applicant identifiers and sensitive details out of a public planning worksheet. Review the hire at 30, 60 and 90 days Agree in advance what successful independent work looks like. Track whether the employee started, completed the relevant training, met the work standard and stayed through the review date. Separate time-to-fill from time-to-productivity. A fast start can still need a long supervised ramp-up. In the capacity case, if the hire supplies only 50 rather than 80 delivery hours and the founder still gives up 20, the net increase is 30. Total effective capacity becomes 180 + 30 = 210, leaving 30 of the 240 required hours unsupported. The next decision may be a scope or schedule change, not another advert. Connect the review to growth and capacity planning , the complete compensation budget and the payroll handoff . A hiring strategy is complete only when the work, cost and handoff make sense together. Frequently asked questions Which recruitment strategy is best for a small business? The appropriate mix depends on the actual role and evidence from qualified applicants, starts and later performance. No channel is universally best or cheapest. Is cost per applicant a useful success measure? It can describe one stage, but cheap applications may not meet the role. Track comparable qualification, interviews, starts and later work outcomes. Does recruiting cost include the employee salary? Routine salary after joining belongs in the employee-cost budget. Recruiting cost may include supported recruiting staff time, but avoid counting the same salary twice. Do 160 paid hours mean 160 delivery hours? No. Onboarding, internal duties, leave and supervision reduce the productive hours available for the modeled work. Can referrals skip normal screening? A referral should still be assessed against the same documented role criteria. Use current nondiscrimination and other applicable hiring guidance. What should the hiring review record contain? Record the role, dated workload gap, channel cost boundary, comparable funnel counts, onboarding assumptions and later job-related outcomes. Keep personal applicant data in a suitable private system. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Business Loans: Compare Types, Total Cost and Cash-Flow Fit Published November 17, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare business loan structures using net proceeds, payment timing and total cost. Follow a checked repayment example and build an offer-comparison record. Business finance Worked example Practical record A business loan supplies cash that must be repaid under a contract. Compare what reaches the business, every required payment and the cash source for repayment. A lower monthly payment can come with a longer commitment and higher total cost. Start with the use of funds before comparing lenders or headline rates. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Numerical cases in this guide are fictional. All numerical examples are original fictional USD teaching cases. They are not market rates, customer results, eligibility determinations or forecasts. Replace assumptions with dated records. Match the borrowing structure to the business use A term loan generally provides a defined advance repaid over an agreed schedule. A line of credit permits draws within an approved facility, subject to its terms and availability. Equipment financing links funding to an asset purchase; an asset-backed facility may depend on eligible collateral. The financing label alone does not establish affordability, approval, legal classification or whether a personal guarantee is required. Questions to ask before choosing a product Structure Planning question Contract detail to check Term loan Does the repayment period match the funded use? Payment dates, rate changes, fees and prepayment terms Revolving line Will cash collections support repayment and later redraws? Draw conditions, maturity, renewal and unused-line charges Equipment financing Will the asset support the payment through its useful work? Deposit, security, final payment and ownership terms Invoice-backed funding Which invoices are eligible and who collects? Advance, reserve, recourse, collection and fee basis For a business without operating history, use startup loan readiness . For a short collection gap, use working-capital loans . Invoice financing versus factoring explains why selling a receivable and borrowing against it are not interchangeable descriptions. Compare offers on the same amount and dates Record gross principal, fees withheld, fees paid separately, net usable proceeds, the entire payment schedule, any final balloon, interest basis and security requirements. Keep an offer expiry date and link each amount to the written document. A quote that funds $20,000 and one that leaves $19,600 after a fee do not provide the same usable cash. Do not compare a factor rate, a flat fee and an annual interest rate as if they were the same measure. Ask for the total repayment and a supported annualized disclosure when available; the calculation method and included charges matter. Faster approval or a lower advertised payment does not answer the question of total cost or repayment capacity. A checked $20,000 term-loan illustration Assume a fictional $20,000 principal, a fixed nominal annual rate of 12%, twelve equal end-of-month payments, monthly rate 1%, and no balloon. A separate $400 origination fee is withheld at funding. This is a teaching assumption, not a lender offer or quoted APR. Usable funding is $19,600. For principal P, monthly rate r and n payments, payment = P × r ÷ [1 − (1 + r) −n ] . At zero interest, use P ÷ n. Here the unrounded payment is $1,776.9757735668…, displayed as $1,776.98. Multiplying the unrounded amount by twelve gives $21,323.71 total repayment after presentation rounding. Interest is $1,323.71; adding the $400 fee gives $1,723.71 modeled borrowing cost relative to usable proceeds. Actual cent-rounded servicing schedules can adjust the final payment. First-payment reconciliation using unrounded model values Item Calculation Displayed USD Opening principal Given $20,000.00 Month-one interest $20,000 × 1% $200.00 Month-one principal reduction Payment − interest $1,576.98 Remaining principal Opening − principal reduction $18,423.02 Net cash received Principal − withheld fee $19,600.00 The $400 withheld fee is included once in the proceeds comparison. Do not subtract it again as a later cash payment unless the agreement actually requires another charge. Likewise, repayment principal is not automatically an operating expense in a profit-margin calculation. Why a longer term can lower payments but increase cost With the same hypothetical principal and 12% nominal rate, extending the schedule to 24 end-of-month payments produces an unrounded $941.4694444653… payment. The displayed monthly burden falls to $941.47, but unrounded total payments rise to $22,595.27. With the same $400 withheld fee, modeled total borrowing cost becomes $2,995.27, versus $1,723.71 for twelve months. The lower payment does not make the longer option cheaper. This comparison holds the rate, principal and fee constant to isolate term. Real offers can change all three. A variable-rate agreement also needs a rate-stress scenario and the exact reset terms. Do not extend the life of borrowing merely to make a spreadsheet’s first month look comfortable without reviewing the full commitment. Test repayment against cash available on the payment date Suppose the business expects $2,300 monthly cash available after operating payments and its planned owner cash need, before this new debt. A $1,776.98 payment leaves about $523.02. If collections are $700 lower while other payments stay the same, only $1,600 is available and the payment creates a roughly $176.98 shortfall. This is a deliberately defined cash test, not a lender’s debt-service ratio or approval rule. Use a dated cash forecast rather than treating invoices or accounting profit as cash in the bank. Record existing debt, tax dates, asset purchases and minimum reserves separately. Funding proceeds increase cash and debt; they do not prove that an unprofitable offer has become profitable. Cash versus profit break-even explains the boundary. A proposed collateral value also needs a defined basis. Inventory valuation methods establish accounting costs, but the provider’s eligible borrowing base can differ from inventory carrying value. A grant eligibility review is a separate route and an unawarded application is not a substitute for confirmed repayment cash. Prepare a decision record before accepting terms Write the funded purpose, amount and date required, with the expected repayment source. Reconcile financial records, existing debt, cash forecast and ownership information requested by the provider. Compare net proceeds and every payment on matching dates, not just the rate label. Review guarantees, security, default provisions, collection rights, minimum fees and early-exit terms with appropriate support. Test delayed receipts, lower contribution and any rate reset before making a commitment. SBA-backed lending is subject to program and lender requirements. The official 7(a) program page describes permitted uses and eligibility context; a government guarantee to a lender is not a grant to the business or an approval promise. This guide does not rank lenders or assume a universal credit-score cutoff. Build your own review record Open the editable, printable Business loan offer comparison . It stays in the browser, does not automatically calculate and does not save entries after reload. Print or save a copy of your completed record. Use fictional or non-sensitive planning data; this is not a payroll, tax, lending or grant submission system. Sources and scope Primary references checked November 17, 2026. The original case and decision record are separate from the source guidance; follow the applicable framework, current terms and local requirements. SBA: loans — Official overview of lender-delivered SBA-backed options. SBA: 7(a) loans — Program uses and eligibility context; the rate and repayment example are invented. FDIC: small-business financing module — Financing structure and comparison context. Frequently asked questions Is the lowest monthly payment the cheapest business loan? Not necessarily. A longer schedule can reduce each payment while increasing total interest and the time the business is committed. Are loan proceeds business revenue? Borrowed principal generally creates cash and a repayment obligation rather than sales revenue. Keep financing and operating results separate. Is a flat factor rate the same as APR? No. A flat multiplier or fee does not describe the timing-sensitive annual cost by itself. Compare the complete schedule and the provider’s supported disclosures. What if an origination fee is withheld? Gross principal and usable cash differ. In the example, $20,000 less a $400 withheld fee leaves $19,600, with the fee counted once. Does SBA backing mean automatic approval? No. Program and lender criteria still apply. Review the current official program and the written lender requirements. Can this example determine the loan I should take? No. It illustrates a comparison method. Your actual terms, security, cash timing and repayment evidence require their own review.
