documents.summary: Model a penetration pricing launch with acquisition cost, repeat orders and a clear exit price. Compare incremental contribution, retention and capacity risks.
documents.headings: Use a launch price for a defined adoption problem Build the first-order contribution before counting customers Calculate the repeat orders needed to recover the deficit Separate new demand from buyers who would have paid full price Stress-test cost, capacity and the return to normal price Review the cohort against a precommitted stop condition Use the printable working record Sources and method boundaries Continue with pricing and customer profitability Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRICING GUIDE Penetration Pricing: Launch Offer and Payback Trade-Off Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Model a penetration pricing launch with acquisition cost, repeat orders and a clear exit price. Compare incremental contribution, retention and capacity risks. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Penetration pricing uses an initially low price to encourage adoption when entering a market. A useful launch plan shows what the introductory order contributes, what acquiring that buyer costs and how much repeat business is needed before the cohort recovers its launch spending. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Use a launch price for a defined adoption problem A lower introductory price may reduce a buyer’s hesitation to try an unfamiliar offer. It does not establish that customers will remain when the normal price begins. Define whether the offer introduces a product, geography or customer segment, and state the normal price, eligibility, duration and purchase limits clearly. This approach differs from premium launch skimming, a permanent low-cost position or a simple clearance sale. In the decision record, identify why the adoption benefit might outweigh the contribution sacrificed. The pricing strategy comparison helps choose whether a temporary introductory offer fits the objective at all. Build the first-order contribution before counting customers A fictional online seller tests an introductory price of $30, followed by a stated $45 normal price. Every order has $18 fulfillment and product cost, a 3% payment fee and a $0.30 flat fee. Assume one order per customer at launch, no refunds, no taxes and no extra shipping subsidy. The variable cost assumptions apply equally to launch and repeat orders. Original launch cohort; USD Item Calculation Result Launch contribution per order 30 − 18 − 0.90 − 0.30 10.80 Normal-price contribution per order 45 − 18 − 1.35 − 0.30 25.35 Contribution sacrificed per discounted order 25.35 − 10.80 14.55 100 first orders 100 × 10.80 1,080.00 Acquisition campaign cash Given campaign assumption 1,500.00 Cohort contribution after campaign 1,080 − 1,500 −420.00 The 100 launch orders generate $3,000 sales but still leave a $420 cohort deficit after the campaign. Calling the launch profitable because each order has positive contribution would omit the acquisition spend. Conversely, assigning the same $1,500 again to repeat orders would count that campaign twice. Calculate the repeat orders needed to recover the deficit If later qualifying orders earn $25.35 each and require no additional acquisition spending, the cohort needs ceiling($420 / $25.35) = 17 repeat orders. Sixteen produce $405.60 and leave $14.40 unrecovered; 17 produce $430.95 and leave $10.95 after the original deficit. With at most one repeat per original customer, that is a 17% observed repeat-customer threshold within the chosen horizon. Twenty repeat orders produce $507 contribution and a net $87 after the original $420 gap. Ten produce $253.50 and leave a $166.50 deficit. These are incremental cohort results before ordinary fixed overhead. They are not lifetime value estimates or a calendar payback date; timing requires the actual repeat-order schedule. Investment payback uses a separate cash-recovery method for projects. Separate new demand from buyers who would have paid full price Suppose, in a separate variation, 20 of the 100 launch buyers would otherwise have bought immediately at $45. Discounting those 20 sacrifices 20 × $14.55 = $291 of contribution on existing demand. Only 80 first orders are incremental; they contribute $864. Relative to no campaign and those 20 full-price orders, first-period incremental contribution after the $1,500 campaign is $864 − $291 − $1,500 = −$927. To recover that incremental gap from genuinely additional normal-price repeats requires ceiling($927 / $25.35) = 37 orders. Do not automatically count every repeat as incremental either: some may have happened without the promotion. Use a credible comparison or explicitly label the baseline as uncertain. The 17-order cohort threshold and 37-order incremental variation answer different questions. Stress-test cost, capacity and the return to normal price If the launch attracts 150 orders but only 100 can be fulfilled within promised service levels, the extra demand is not automatically a gain. Backlogs can create support cost, refunds and lost trust. Model the next capacity step before expanding the campaign. Restrict the pilot to a volume the business can serve and track actual refund, replacement and shipping costs. Set a transition date or number of eligible orders, and record the price customers will face next. A plan that assumes all discount buyers accept $45 has assumed away the central risk. Test repeat contribution at the actual charged price and acquisition cost at the actual acquired-customer count. Discount volume requirements shows how price reductions change the contribution needed from additional sales. Review the cohort against a precommitted stop condition Create a dated cohort record with first order, channel, campaign cost, discount, subsequent purchases, refunds and variable costs. Close the observation window before comparing retention rates, so customers who have not had time to repeat are not treated like mature customers. Keep customer data only in the business’s appropriate systems; the downloadable record here uses aggregate planning fields. For this case, a useful stop condition would flag a growing campaign deficit or repeat contribution below the stated recovery target at the review date. The worksheet does not decide whether to keep spending. Link the cohort result to the full cash forecast and fixed-cost budget before approving another launch. All case data, comparisons and decision checkpoints are original MyBreakeven examples. Reviewed November 11, 2026. No external professional review is claimed. OpenStax: penetration and other pricing approaches Frequently asked questions What is penetration pricing? It is an initially low market-entry price intended to encourage adoption. The offer needs a defined transition and an economic recovery plan. Does positive contribution on the first order mean the campaign pays back? No. In this case each launch order contributes $10.80, but 100 orders leave a $420 deficit after the $1,500 campaign. How many repeat orders recover the base cohort deficit? Seventeen normal-price repeats at $25.35 contribution recover the $420 gap, assuming no additional acquisition spending and unchanged costs. Is 17% repeat purchasing always enough? No. It is only the stated 100-customer, one-repeat-per-customer example. Different costs, refunds, timing and cannibalization change the threshold. Why does the cannibalization variation require 37 orders? It compares against 20 buyers who would have paid full price. That opportunity-cost adjustment increases the modeled incremental gap to $927. When should the introductory price end? Define an eligibility limit and transition date before launch, communicate the next price and review actual repeat demand and contribution before extending the offer. documents.title: Cost-Plus Pricing: Markup, Margin and Fee Boundaries
documents.summary: Calculate cost-plus pricing from a clear cost base, distinguish markup from margin, and include payment fees without counting overhead twice or assuming sales.
documents.headings: Define the cost base and the volume that supports it Apply markup and reconcile the resulting margin Solve the price when fees are charged on revenue Test the allocated fixed cost against actual volume A mathematically valid quote still needs a demand test Keep a quote record that can be audited later Use the printable working record Sources and method boundaries Continue with pricing and customer profitability Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRICING GUIDE Cost-Plus Pricing: Markup, Margin and Fee Boundaries Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate cost-plus pricing from a clear cost base, distinguish markup from margin, and include payment fees without counting overhead twice or assuming sales. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Cost-plus pricing adds a stated markup to a defined cost base: price = cost × (1 + markup). The method is only meaningful when the base, planned volume and treatment of fees are explicit. A markup on cost is different from a profit margin measured as a percentage of revenue. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Define the cost base and the volume that supports it A quote based only on direct materials is not comparable with one based on materials, labor and allocated support. State whether the base is variable cost, full production cost or a wider internal planning cost. A markup percentage without that definition is incomplete. For a fictional workshop, materials are $24 per item, direct labor is $16 and variable production overhead is $5. Its variable production cost is $45 per unit. Monthly fixed production support is $3,000 and selling/administrative commitments are $2,000. At a planning volume of 500 units, the $5,000 fixed pool allocates $10 per unit, giving an internal pricing base of $55. This is a management planning base, not a claim that every $55 belongs in financial-reporting inventory. See product versus period costs for that distinction. Apply markup and reconcile the resulting margin With a 30% markup on the $55 base, the candidate price is $55 × 1.30 = $71.50 before any fee adjustment. The dollar amount over that base is $16.50, so its base-relative margin is $16.50 / $71.50 = 23.08%, not 30%. A 30% margin on selling price would instead require $55 / 0.70 = $78.571… before fees. Same $55 internal cost base; USD per unit Method Calculation Price / interpretation 30% markup on cost 55 × 1.30 71.50 Margin from that markup 16.50 / 71.50 23.08% before omitted fees 30% margin on revenue 55 / (1 − 0.30) 78.58 rounded upward, before fees Margin versus markup gives the general conversion. Keep the denominator visible whenever a quote or target uses “percent profit.” Solve the price when fees are charged on revenue Assume each item is sold in its own transaction and the payment provider charges 3% of selling price plus $0.30 per transaction. To retain the original $16.50 markup amount over the $55 base after fees, solve P × 0.97 − $0.30 − $55 = $16.50. Therefore P = ($71.50 + $0.30) / 0.97 = $74.020618… . A cent-based quote must round upward to $74.03. At $74.03, the 3% fee is $2.2209 and the retained amount over the base is $16.5091. At $74.02 it is only $16.4994. The algebra uses unrounded fees; actual processor rounding can change cents and should be reconciled from settlement records. If multiple items share one checkout, allocate the single fixed transaction fee across that order instead of charging it repeatedly to each item. If the goal were a 30% margin after those fees over the $55 base, solve P = ($55 + $0.30) / (1 − 0.03 − 0.30) = $82.537313… , or $82.54 upward. The denominator must be positive. This target is materially different from a 30% markup. Test the allocated fixed cost against actual volume At the $74.03 quote, contribution before the $5,000 fixed pool is $74.03 × 0.97 − $0.30 − $45 = $26.5091 per item. At 500 sales, total contribution is $13,254.55 and modeled operating profit is $8,254.55. At 300 sales, contribution is $7,952.73 and profit is $2,952.73. The fixed pool remains $5,000 in both scenarios. Volume sensitivity at one fee-adjusted price; USD Sold units Fixed allocation per sold unit Total contribution Profit after fixed pool 500 10.00 13,254.55 8,254.55 300 16.67 displayed 7,952.73 2,952.73 188 26.60 displayed 4,983.71 −16.29 189 26.46 displayed 5,010.22 10.22 Whole-unit break-even is 189 sales. Do not subtract the original $10 allocation inside contribution and then subtract the full $5,000 again. The pricing allocation helps construct a quote; the period profit bridge uses variable cost per sale and the fixed pool once. Contribution margin provides the bridge. A mathematically valid quote still needs a demand test A customer may reject $74.03 if competing alternatives solve the same problem for less. A supplier’s cost increase does not guarantee a buyer will accept the markup. Conversely, a customer may value a differentiated offer above the calculated cost-plus price. Use the quote as one candidate within a broader pricing decision , not evidence of willingness to pay. Check labor duration, waste, returns, shipping subsidies, capacity steps and actual payment terms. If a cost is already in the $45 variable amount, do not add it again through a second burden rate. If fixed capacity expands at 600 units, do not extrapolate the same pool indefinitely. Document the volume range for which the quote is valid. Keep a quote record that can be audited later Record the cost-base date, included categories, planned volume, fixed pool, markup denominator, fee schedule and rounding rule. State exclusions and quote expiry in the customer offer where relevant. Compare the fulfilled job or item with the original estimate so the next quote reflects real costs. Use the worksheet to reconcile both the unit calculation and the total period result. A retained markup amount over an allocated base is not the same as a guaranteed cash surplus: receivables, inventory purchases and tax payments can create a different cash pattern. OpenStax: cost-based pricing within pricing policy Frequently asked questions What is the cost-plus pricing formula? Price equals the defined cost base multiplied by one plus the markup rate. Revenue-based fees require a separate algebraic adjustment if the markup amount must remain after fees. Does a 30% markup produce a 30% margin? No. Before other costs, a 30% markup corresponds to 30 / 130, or about 23.08% margin. Why does the example quote $74.03 rather than $71.50? It adds room for a 3% revenue fee and $0.30 fixed fee while retaining the original $16.50 markup amount over the $55 base. Should I subtract allocated overhead again in the profit calculation? No. In the example, contribution subtracts the $45 variable cost and fees; the $5,000 fixed pool is then subtracted once for the period. Can I use one fixed transaction fee for every item? Only if each item is a separate transaction. Allocate the actual single checkout fee when several items share an order. What if the market will not pay the calculated price? Reconsider the scope, costs, positioning or viability. Cost-plus arithmetic does not establish demand or compel customers to cover the cost base. documents.headings: Compare the project with a credible do-nothing alternative Use different methods for different questions Compare two mutually exclusive equipment projects Resolve value and affordability separately Stress-test savings and the required return Keep an approval and post-investment review record Use the printable working record Sources and method boundaries Continue with investment decisions and cost of capital Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Capital Budgeting: Compare Business Investment Projects Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare capital budgeting projects using dated cash flows, NPV, payback and a funding limit. Follow an equipment case with downside and discount-rate checks. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Capital budgeting evaluates long-term uses of business cash, such as equipment or expansion. Build incremental project cash flows, discount them at a justified rate and compare value, recovery time, funding limits and execution risk before choosing an alternative. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Compare the project with a credible do-nothing alternative Define the decision first: replace equipment, add capacity, outsource or continue with the current setup. Count the cash changes caused by the decision. Include installation, training, incremental maintenance, working capital, disposal costs and forgone alternatives where relevant. A sunk feasibility study paid last month is not a new cash outflow caused by today’s choice. A forecast needs dates as well as amounts. Set a common evaluation horizon or handle different lives explicitly. State whether flows are nominal or real, before or after tax and available to the firm or only equity owners. Match the discount rate to that basis. Depreciation is not itself a cash payment, although tax consequences may change cash flows in a fully specified model. Use different methods for different questions Capital budgeting decision methods Method What it answers Boundary Net present value (NPV) Value of forecast net cash flows after required return Depends on the cash schedule and discount rate Payback period How long forecast cash takes to recover initial outlay Simple payback ignores time value and later cash Internal rate of return (IRR) Rate that makes modeled NPV zero Unusual cash-flow signs can create multiple or no useful roots Profitability index Present value relative to initial outlay A ratio can mis-rank mutually exclusive projects Funding / execution review Can the business finance and deliver the project? Positive NPV alone does not establish affordability Use the payback method for the recovery schedule and profitability index for its ratio interpretation. This guide’s main task is to put those measures into one project-selection record. Compare two mutually exclusive equipment projects A fictional workshop can select one of two machines or keep its existing setup. Project A requires $24,000 now and provides $10,000 net cash savings at each of the next three year-ends. Project B requires $18,000 now and provides $7,200 at those same dates. The savings are incremental cash after operating costs. For this deliberately simplified, no-tax case, assume no additional working capital, salvage value, financing cash flows or later maintenance outlays. The 8% discount rate is a stated illustrative assumption, not a current market estimate. Same three-year horizon and end-year timing; USD Time Project A cash Project B cash Now, t = 0 −24,000 −18,000 End of year 1 10,000 7,200 End of year 2 10,000 7,200 End of year 3 10,000 7,200 NPV = initial signed cash flow + Σ[year-t cash flow / (1 + rate)^t]. At 8%, the three-payment present-value factor is 2.577096987. A’s inflows have present value $25,770.97, leaving NPV $1,770.97. B’s inflows have present value $18,555.10, leaving NPV $555.10. A produces $1,215.87 more modeled value, provided the extra funding and operational requirements can be met. Resolve value and affordability separately Simple payback is 2.4 years for A and 2.5 for B if each year’s savings accrue evenly within the year. If savings arrive only at year-end, both first recover their initial outlay at the end of year 3. State which timing interpretation is being reported; do not present a fractional recovery date with a year-end-only cash assumption. If the available project budget is $20,000 with no additional financing, A is infeasible despite its higher NPV. B fits the limit, but accepting it still depends on the credibility of the savings and the cash reserve the business needs outside the project. An indivisible $24,000 machine cannot be funded by allocating 83% of its forecast cost and assuming the full savings. Do not deduct interest in an unlevered project cash flow and also use a financing-inclusive discount rate without reconciling the framework. WACC describes a firm-capital benchmark; a project with different risk may need a different justified rate. Stress-test savings and the required return NPV sensitivity; same timing and horizon, USD Rate / scenario Project A Project B 8%, base savings 1,770.97 555.10 10%, base savings 868.52 −94.67 12%, base savings 18.31 −706.81 8%, A savings fall to 8,000 −3,383.22 B base remains 555.10 The A downside changes operating savings only, leaving initial cost and timing unchanged. Do not silently combine it with a different rate or additional machine life. At 8%, A’s level annual cash savings must reach approximately $9,312.80 to make NPV zero. This is a useful supplier-and-operations question: what observable throughput, labor reduction or defect improvement supports that saving? Keep an approval and post-investment review record Retain competing quotes, implementation milestones, cash-flow sources, discount-rate rationale and sensitivity cases. Assign owners for installation timing and operating benefits. If the claim is labor savings, distinguish cash payroll actually avoided from hours released for other work; spare hours are not automatically cash inflow. Set a review date after commissioning to compare actual incremental cash with the approved forecast. Explain variance from volume, price, downtime and maintenance rather than changing the original forecast retrospectively. A positive modeled NPV is conditional evidence, not a promise of realized return or a reason to disregard liquidity and execution risks. It is the process of evaluating and choosing long-term business investments using forecast cash flows, required return, funding and implementation considerations. Why use cash flows rather than accounting profit? Project value depends on the timing of cash committed and recovered. Accounting allocations such as depreciation need reconciliation to the actual cash and tax effects. Which project has the higher NPV in the example? At the assumed 8% rate and three-year horizon, A has $1,770.97 NPV and B has $555.10. A needs $6,000 more upfront funding. Why might the business choose B? If the project budget is strictly $20,000 with no further funding, A is not feasible. B still requires a credible savings case and adequate remaining liquidity. Does simple payback replace NPV? No. Payback highlights cash-recovery timing but ignores time value and cash after recovery. NPV evaluates the full specified cash schedule at a required return. Can I use company WACC for every project? Not automatically. The discount rate must fit project risk, currency, tax basis, timing and the type of cash flow being discounted. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Payback Period: Cash Recovery and Its Limits Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate payback for equal and uneven cash flows, handle partial years and end-year timing, and compare discounted recovery with the limits of simple payback. Copy an uneven cash-flow payback schedule into Excel Paste the three columns below into Excel starting at A1. The opening outlay is negative. Find the first cumulative total at or above zero. Here the balance after Year 2 is −$2,000 and Year 3 adds $5,000. Estimated payback is 2.4 years if that inflow accrues evenly during Year 3. If cash only arrives at year-end, recovery occurs at the end of Year 3. Excel cash-flow schedule Year Net cash flow Cumulative cash flow 0 -10000 =SUM($B$2:B2) 1 3500 =SUM($B$2:B3) 2 4500 =SUM($B$2:B4) 3 5000 =SUM($B$2:B5) Test uneven and discounted cash flows in the Business ROI Calculator Microsoft’s Excel running-total instructions Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet The payback period is the time forecast net cash inflows take to recover an initial investment. For equal positive annual flows, divide the outlay by annual net cash inflow. For uneven flows, use a cumulative schedule; fractional years require an explicit within-year timing assumption. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Use the shortcut only for a level cash-flow pattern For an investment with a single initial outlay and equal positive net annual cash inflows, simple payback = initial investment / annual net cash inflow. A fictional $24,000 outlay with $8,000 a year gives three years. Net cash inflow means additional receipts or cash costs avoided less additional cash spending; it is not gross sales or accounting profit. If $8,000 is a forecast profit after depreciation, reconcile that measure to cash before dividing. Exclude financing receipts from project operating benefits. A loan can fund the purchase but does not make the machine recover its cost economically. State the project life: an apparent five-year payback is not achieved by equipment that stops producing cash after year 4. Build a cumulative schedule for uneven cash flows Consider a different fictional project with $30,000 paid now. Its net cash inflows are $9,000 in year 1, $12,000 in year 2, $15,000 in year 3 and $8,000 in year 4. No other cash flows, residual value or taxes are included. The unrounded cumulative schedule identifies the first recovery crossing. Original uneven cash-recovery case; USD Time Net cash flow Cumulative after initial outlay Still unrecovered Now −30,000 −30,000 30,000 Year 1 9,000 −21,000 21,000 Year 2 12,000 −9,000 9,000 Year 3 15,000 6,000 0 Year 4 8,000 14,000 0 At the end of year 2, $9,000 remains. If year-3 cash arrives evenly, the fraction is $9,000 / $15,000 = 0.6 year, giving payback of 2.6 years. That is 7.2 months into year 3 under a 12-month interpolation convention. If all $15,000 instead arrives on the final day of year 3, the cash recovery date is the end of year 3, not 2.6 years. Avoid averaging away a cash-flow delay The four-year average inflow is ($9,000 + $12,000 + $15,000 + $8,000) / 4 = $11,000. Dividing $30,000 by $11,000 gives 2.727… years, which does not reproduce the cumulative schedule. The shortcut has hidden when the cash arrives. A monthly model is more informative for seasonal or milestone payments. Use the actual planned receipts and payments when available, and report the first period with nonnegative cumulative cash. If annual or quarterly totals are the only evidence, do not invent a precise day of recovery. The uncertainty is in the forecast, not something extra decimal places resolve. Compare discounted payback on a stated time basis For a separate discounted calculation, treat all annual cash flows as year-end receipts and assume a 10% annual discount rate. Discounted cash in year t is CFt / 1.10^t. Keep unrounded values through the cumulative calculation and round only the displayed amounts. Discounted recovery at an assumed 10%; USD Year Nominal cash Present value Cumulative PV of inflows 1 9,000 8,181.82 8,181.82 2 12,000 9,917.36 18,099.17 3 15,000 11,269.72 29,368.90 4 8,000 5,464.11 34,833.00 The $30,000 outlay is not recovered in discounted terms by the end of year 3. It is recovered at the end of year 4 under the explicit year-end receipt assumption. A conventional interpolation of annual discounted values would give about 3.12 years, but that is an approximation, not the actual receipt date in this schedule. Discounted payback can also fail to occur within the project life even when simple payback does occur. Do not confuse recovery with total project value Suppose another project has the same $30,000 outlay and years 1–3 flows, but no year-4 inflow. Its simple payback remains 2.6 years under even year-3 accrual; the first recovery crossing is unchanged. Yet it loses $8,000 nominal later cash and $5,464.11 present value at 10%. A payback ranking alone misses that difference. Use capital budgeting to compare the full horizon, NPV and funding constraints. Cost-benefit analysis helps document costs, benefits and noncash considerations. The payback method is especially useful as a liquidity screen when paired with a separate value and risk review. Report an unrecovered balance honestly If cumulative inflows never reach the initial outlay during the modeled life, report “not recovered within the forecast horizon” and the remaining amount. Do not return zero, a negative payback period or an annual-average result beyond the project’s supported life. For a zero initial outlay, clarify whether the question is meaningful before interpreting immediate recovery. Multiple later outflows require more than a first-crossing check. A project may briefly recover, then need a major overhaul that takes cumulative cash negative again. Show the full schedule and the later deficit. Record the selected timing convention, sources, review date and any cash that is uncertain or conditional before using the result to approve spending. For equal positive annual net inflows, initial outlay divided by annual net cash inflow. Uneven flows require a cumulative schedule. How is the example’s 2.6 years calculated? Two years pass before $9,000 remains unrecovered. Dividing that by year 3’s $15,000 gives 0.6, assuming year-3 cash arrives evenly. Can I use average annual cash flow for uneven receipts? It can give the wrong crossing. In this case the average shortcut gives about 2.73 years instead of the 2.6-year evenly accrued schedule. What if receipts occur only at year-end? Report the first actual year-end when cumulative cash recovers the outlay. The nominal example recovers at year 3 and the discounted example at year 4. What does discounted payback change? It discounts future cash before accumulating it. The result depends on the assumed rate and receipt timing and can be longer than simple payback. Does a short payback mean the best investment? No. It omits value after recovery and simple payback omits time value. Review full-horizon NPV, funding and risk separately. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE WACC: Weighted Average Cost of Capital Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate WACC from debt and equity weights, reconcile the tax assumption, and test sensitivity. See when a company-wide rate does not fit a project cash flow. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet WACC is a weighted estimate of the required return across a firm’s financing sources. With only debt and common equity, WACC = [E / (D + E)] × Re + [D / (D + E)] × Rd × (1 − T). The weights, required returns and usable tax benefit must describe a consistent capital structure and valuation basis. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Define the financing sources before using the formula E is the relevant equity value; D is interest-bearing debt value. Re is the estimated required equity return, Rd is the relevant current debt cost and T represents the tax assumption applied to deductible interest. Market-value weights are normally used in the standard valuation framework, rather than mixing book equity with market debt without explanation. Accounts payable is not automatically another interest-bearing capital component. If preferred shares, leases or other financing are material, their treatment needs explicit reconciliation. This guide uses only debt and common equity, so those two weights must sum to 100%. A spreadsheet that leaves 15% of capital unassigned has not estimated a complete weighted average. Reconcile a two-source capital mix The fictional case uses an as-of-date equity value of $600,000 and debt value of $400,000. The chosen Re is 12%, Rd is 7%, and T is 25%, with an assumed fully usable interest tax benefit. All rates and values are illustrative assumptions, not current market observations or a tax opinion. No preferred shares, leases or excess-cash adjustment is included. Original WACC case; capital values in USD Component Value / input Weight Weighted contribution Common equity 600,000; Re 12% 60% 7.20 percentage points Debt 400,000; Rd 7% 40% 2.10 percentage points after tax Total financing 1,000,000 100% WACC 9.30% After-tax debt cost is 7% × (1 − 25%) = 5.25%. WACC is 60% × 12% + 40% × 5.25% = 7.20% + 2.10% = 9.30%. Enter rates consistently: 12% is 0.12 in decimal arithmetic. The weighted debt contribution is 2.10 percentage points, not the full 5.25% debt rate. Test whether the tax shield is actually supported The 25% input is not a universal business tax rate. Entity form, losses, deduction limits, jurisdiction and timing can alter whether and when interest reduces tax. If the case has no usable tax benefit, set that benefit to zero for the modeled horizon: WACC becomes 60% × 12% + 40% × 7% = 10.00%, rather than 9.30%. Do not both reduce the debt rate for the tax shield and subtract the same financing benefit again from an otherwise unlevered cash-flow forecast without a consistent framework. A business with uncertain taxable income needs an evidence-based treatment, not a convenient lower rate. Record the source and date of any professional tax assumption used in a real model. Show what changes the result Change one stated input at a time; base weights otherwise retained Scenario Equity contribution Debt contribution WACC Base: Re 12%, Rd 7%, T 25% 7.20% 2.10% 9.30% Re rises to 14% 8.40% 2.10% 10.50% Rd rises to 9% 7.20% 2.70% 9.90% No usable tax benefit 7.20% 2.80% 10.00% Debt weight 50%, rates held only for illustration 6.00% 2.625% 8.625% The last row is a mechanical sensitivity, not a prediction that more borrowing makes financing cheaper. Leverage can change equity risk, debt pricing and distress costs. Holding Re and Rd constant while changing the weights does not capture those effects. Present it as a limited scenario, not an optimized capital structure. Match the rate to the cash being valued WACC can be a starting point for discounting unlevered cash available to the firm when the project has comparable operating risk and the assumed financing policy remains relevant. Equity-only cash flows need an equity required return instead. The cost-of-equity guide explains that component and its model assumptions. Currency, nominal-versus-real treatment, tax basis and period length must also match. A 9.3% annual nominal USD rate should not be copied into a monthly real cash-flow model unchanged. For unusually risky expansion, a stable existing-business WACC can understate the project hurdle. Capital budgeting shows how a rate assumption affects project comparisons. Handle private-company values as estimates, not quotes A private firm may not have an observable traded equity value or beta. Document how values and target weights were estimated, why comparable businesses are relevant and how sensitive the result is to reasonable alternatives. Owner capital still has an opportunity cost even when the business pays no dividend this year. Do not plug retained earnings from the balance sheet into E and describe the result as a market-value WACC. A range can be more honest than a point estimate when inputs are uncertain. Keep debt terms, valuation assumptions, review date and exclusions alongside the calculation so a later reviewer can reproduce it. WACC is a required-return estimate; it is not a promised borrowing rate, accounting expense or guaranteed realized return. OpenStax: WACC equation, financing weights and estimation limits OpenStax: required returns on debt and equity Frequently asked questions What is WACC? It is a weighted estimate of required returns across the firm’s financing sources, often debt, common equity and any preferred capital. What is WACC in the fictional example? 9.30% using 60% equity at 12%, 40% debt at 7%, and an assumed fully usable 25% interest tax benefit. Why multiply debt cost by one minus the tax rate? The standard formula models an interest tax benefit. Its applicability and timing need support; it is not automatic for every entity or loss-making firm. Is a lower WACC always achieved by adding debt? No. Changing leverage can change required equity return, debt cost and financial risk. A constant-rate weight sensitivity is not a financing recommendation. Can I discount equity cash flows with WACC? Not without reconciling the framework. Equity cash flows normally use the cost of equity, while WACC is used with matching firm-level cash flows. Is book equity an observable market value? No. For a private business, values and target weights need a documented estimation method and sensitivity analysis. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost of Equity: Inputs, Formula and Assumptions Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Estimate cost of equity with CAPM, align risk-free rate, beta and market premium assumptions, and compare a dividend-growth cross-check with clear limitations. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Cost of equity is the return equity investors require for taking the business’s equity risk. A common estimate is CAPM: Re = risk-free rate + beta × equity market risk premium. It is a model-dependent required return, not a guaranteed gain or a cash interest bill owed to shareholders. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Distinguish required return from accounting profit Equity holders receive the residual outcome after other claims. They may accept retaining earnings rather than receiving cash now, but that does not make the funding free. Cost of equity represents the return required for bearing that risk; actual returns can be above or below it, including a loss. It is not the same as historical return on equity, a net-profit margin or the dividend yield alone. Those measures describe different denominators and cash patterns. Use an equity required return with matching cash flows to equity holders; combine it with other financing costs only within a consistent WACC calculation . Define each CAPM input and its evidence CAPM input record Input Meaning Evidence and consistency check Risk-free rate, Rf Time-value baseline with minimal default risk in the chosen framework Record currency, maturity, as-of date and nominal/real basis Beta, β Equity sensitivity to systematic market risk Record comparable business, sample, leverage and market definition Equity risk premium, ERP Expected market return above Rf State source, horizon and estimation method Cost of equity, Re Rf + β × ERP Use a consistent set, not unrelated dates and currencies If a source gives total expected market return Rm rather than a premium, calculate ERP = Rm − Rf before multiplying by beta. Adding Rm as though it were already a premium counts the risk-free component incorrectly. Beta is not a volatility percentage or a direct measure of every operational risk. Calculate an original CAPM example Assume a fictional annual nominal USD model with Rf = 4%, beta = 1.2 and ERP = 5%. These are deliberately selected teaching inputs, not today’s Treasury yield or an observed company estimate. Re = 4% + 1.2 × 5% = 10%. The beta-adjusted premium contributes six percentage points; the risk-free component contributes four. If the total expected market return were presented as 9%, the same result follows: ERP = 9% − 4% = 5%. The incorrect expression 4% + 1.2 × 9% would produce 14.8%, a different number caused by a definition error. Retain the input labels in the worksheet, not just three unlabeled cells. CAPM sensitivity with Rf fixed at 4% Beta / premium ERP 4% ERP 5% ERP 6% Beta 0.8 7.2% 8.0% 8.8% Beta 1.2 8.8% 10.0% 11.2% Beta 1.6 10.4% 12.0% 13.6% This range shows sensitivity, not a confidence interval or a prediction of actual shareholder returns. Changing beta may reflect leverage or business comparability as well as a different risk judgment. Use dividend growth as a separate cross-check when it fits For a firm with a sustainable constant dividend-growth assumption, a different model is Re = next-period dividend / current share price + growth rate. A fictional current annual dividend of $2, next-year growth of 3%, and a $30 share price give next dividend $2.06. Re = $2.06 / $30 + 3% = 9.8667%, or about 9.87%. Using the current $2 dividend without growing it first would produce 9.67%. This model is unsuitable when the business has no meaningful sustainable dividend policy, growth is unstable or the price and distribution assumptions are inconsistent. Do not average 10% CAPM and 9.87% dividend growth mechanically to manufacture precision. Investigate what assumptions differ and whether both methods actually describe the business. Explain a private-company estimate without inventing a traded beta A private business does not automatically have an observable market beta or share price. An analyst may use comparable firms, adjust for leverage and evaluate business differences; those choices need documentation and appropriate expertise. A single industry beta copied without its date, capital structure and selection rationale is weak evidence. Small-firm, country, liquidity or company-specific adjustments are sometimes considered in practice, but adding arbitrary premiums can double count risks already reflected in cash-flow scenarios or other inputs. This introductory case does not prescribe such add-ons. Show a sensitivity range and make the unresolved assumptions visible rather than presenting a personal target return as a market-derived estimate. Match the estimate to the decision and review it A $100 one-year equity cash flow discounted at 10% has present value $100 / 1.10 = $90.91. Discounting the same flow at the case’s highest sensitivity rate of 13.6% gives $88.03. The difference illustrates why the required-return assumption matters; it does not value an entire company or establish an investment recommendation. Use capital budgeting to connect project cash, funding and risk. Record rate currency, as-of date, horizon, source methodology and whether the cash flows are nominal, real, levered or unlevered. Revisit the estimate after material business-risk, financing or market-input changes. A documented model is more useful than an unexplained “standard” percentage. Re = Rf + beta × equity market risk premium. If given total expected market return, subtract Rf to obtain the premium first. What is the example’s cost of equity? 10%, from fictional inputs of 4% risk-free rate, 1.2 beta and 5% market risk premium. Is cost of equity the same as dividend yield? No. A constant-growth dividend model combines next-period dividend yield with expected sustainable growth; CAPM uses systematic risk inputs. Can retained earnings have zero equity cost? Retained earnings still have an opportunity cost to owners. An absence of current dividends does not imply shareholders require no return. Can a private business use a public-company beta unchanged? It needs a documented comparability and leverage assessment. A public beta is not automatically an observed beta for a private company. Is the estimated required return guaranteed? No. It is an assumption-dependent estimate used in a valuation or decision framework. Actual returns may be much lower, including losses. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Small-Business Inventory Management: Cash and Stock Records Published November 11, 2026 Updated November 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Reconcile inventory receipts, sales, returns and damage in a small-business stock record. Link available units, purchase commitments and cash in a clear case. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Small-business inventory management tracks what stock exists, where it is, whether it can be sold and what purchasing will commit in cash. A reliable routine reconciles movements to physical counts before turning the balance into buying decisions. AI-created editorial illustration with topic title. Worked numbers in this guide are fictional teaching cases. All numerical examples are original fictional teaching cases in USD, not market benchmarks or promised outcomes. Assumptions are stated beside the calculations; replace them with your own dated evidence. Start with one stock identity and a movement record Give each distinct item a stable SKU, unit of measure and location. A case of 12 and a single unit cannot share a quantity field without a conversion rule. Record receipts when accepted, sales when stock leaves the relevant stage, returns when assessed and damage or other adjustments with reasons. Identify who owns each entry and source document. Do not rely on an invoice list alone. A supplier invoice can arrive before the goods, and a customer order can reserve units before shipment. Keep physical on-hand, committed stock, available stock and incoming purchase orders distinct. The same carton should not be counted in transit, in receiving and on the shelf simultaneously. Reconcile a one-SKU stock movement A fictional retailer starts a week with 120 units of one SKU. It accepts 80 purchased units, ships 140 sold units, receives five customer-returned units that pass inspection and can be resold, and writes off three damaged units. All units carry the same $12 cost, so this case deliberately avoids competing valuation methods, freight adjustments, taxes and currency effects. Original weekly stock record; units and USD at uniform $12 cost Movement Unit change Running on-hand Cost movement Opening stock 120 120 1,440 opening Accepted purchase receipt +80 200 +960 inventory Customer shipments −140 60 −1,680 to cost of goods sold Resellable returns +5 65 +60 inventory; reverse related cost Damage write-off −3 62 −36 inventory; loss Closing stock 62 62 744 carrying amount Quantity reconciliation: 120 + 80 − 140 + 5 − 3 = 62 units. Cost reconciliation: $1,440 + $960 − $1,680 + $60 − $36 = $744. The net cost released on sold goods is $1,620; the $36 damage loss is separately identified in this teaching record. The returns’ selling-price refunds and sales recognition belong in the sales ledger and are not calculated from the $12 cost. Investigate the difference between the ledger and the shelf At the count, physically observed stock is 60 units instead of the expected 62. The two-unit difference represents $24 at the uniform cost. Do not immediately label it theft or add a balancing purchase. Freeze the relevant movement window and check receiving, shipments, unit conversions, returns and locations for missing or duplicated entries. Suppose the team finds two shipped units whose dispatch record never reached the inventory ledger. Post the supported shipment movement through the normal sales/cost workflow. If no cause is established, follow the business’s approval policy for the count adjustment and retain the unresolved reason. The revised 60-unit balance carries $720, but the classification of the $24 difference depends on the evidence. Separate available stock from a purchasing promise Use the reconciled 60 on-hand units for this separate availability decision. Fifteen are already committed to unshipped customer orders. Available to promise is 60 − 15 = 45 units. A purchase order for 50 more units is incoming, not available on the shelf. The inventory position for a defined replenishment model may include that incoming quantity, but customer promises must reflect receipt timing and reliability. Availability and purchasing at the same review date Record Units / amount Meaning Physical on-hand after reconciliation 60 units Stock currently held Committed customer orders 15 units Reserve against on-hand Available to promise now 45 units 60 − 15 Open purchase order 50 units Not yet received Supplier commitment at $12 each 600 USD Payment timing tracked separately The $600 purchase commitment is not another $600 closing stock asset before receipt in this simplified record. Nor is it automatically a cash payment today. Record the supplier’s payment terms and expected receiving date in the cash forecast. The reorder-point and cash-flow guide handles order timing and stock protection in detail. Connect stock decisions to cash and product condition Slow stock can tie up cash while the inventory ledger still reports a positive balance. Review age, expiry, condition and actual demand by SKU. An inventory balance is not cash ready to spend, and damaged or obsolete units should not remain available to promise simply because they still have a system quantity. Count discrepancies, returns and stockouts can expose different operational causes. A recurring receipt mismatch needs a receiving fix; repeated stockouts may indicate lead-time or demand errors. Holding cost per SKU considers the cost of keeping stock. The COGS bridge connects the cost ledger to sold units without treating all purchases as immediate expense. Use a practical daily, weekly and monthly control routine Daily, record accepted receipts, dispatches, reservations and inspected returns with source references. Check negative quantities and duplicate SKUs before accepting new orders. Keep damaged or quarantined units distinguishable from sellable stock. For multiple sales channels, confirm that a sale updates the shared availability record in time to prevent double selling. Weekly, cycle-count selected high-value or high-movement items, reconcile open orders and review upcoming supplier payments. Monthly, reconcile the stock subledger to accounting, review aging and adjustment approvals, and document any policy changes. These frequencies are illustrative starting points, not universal rules; item value, perishability and transaction volume should shape the routine. A spreadsheet can support a small operation if responsibilities, backups, access and reconciliation are clear. More software does not repair undefined units or unrecorded returns. Use the worksheet to document the movement bridge and an action owner before deciding whether a process or system change is required. Australian Government: stock records, stocktakes and inventory control OpenStax: merchandise inventory and cost-of-goods-sold context Frequently asked questions What should a small-business inventory record include? A stable SKU, unit of measure, location, dated receipts and issues, returns, adjustments, commitments and supporting references. How is closing stock calculated in the example? 120 opening + 80 receipts − 140 shipments + 5 resellable returns − 3 damaged units = 62 expected units. Why is the physical count only 60? The example investigates a two-unit difference rather than inventing a cause. A supported missing shipment or an approved unexplained adjustment requires different evidence. Are incoming purchase orders available stock? Not yet on hand. Track their expected receipt and reliability separately when making customer promises and replenishment decisions. Does a supplier purchase commitment reduce cash immediately? Not necessarily. Payment timing depends on terms. The case tracks the $600 commitment separately from receipt, inventory recognition and cash payment. Is this an inventory valuation-method guide? No. The worked record uses a uniform $12 cost to isolate movement control. Different valuation and impairment policies require their own accounting analysis. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Accrued Expenses: Recognize, Reconcile and Settle Unpaid Costs Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Record unpaid period costs with supported accruals, reconcile the liability and compare direct settlement with optional reversing entries in a checked example. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Accrued expenses are costs incurred but not yet paid. When the cost and obligation have not already been recorded, a supported cutoff adjustment recognizes them; the later invoice or payment must clear the balance without counting the same expense twice. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Start with the consumed service and reporting cutoff Accrual recognition follows the transaction facts and applicable reporting policy, rather than waiting automatically for a supplier invoice. OpenStax’s adjusting-entry discussion illustrates an expense paired with a payable when an incurred cost remains unrecorded. This guide applies that basic mechanism to a service business; it does not determine whether a complex legal claim, uncertain bonus or tax obligation satisfies its own recognition requirements. Ask what work was received, which dates it covers and what evidence supports the amount. A future service in an unsigned proposal is not an incurred expense merely because management expects to buy it. A bill already entered in accounts payable also needs no second expense accrual. Distinguish an omitted liability from a different label for an existing one. Build an accrual record that another preparer can follow Use a unique reference, counterparty, service period, expense account, liability account, estimate basis, supporting record and responsible reviewer. For payroll, retain approved work dates and the unpaid portion. For utilities, use relevant consumption evidence and the supported billing basis. For professional work, retain the accepted delivery or documented service performed, not only an annual purchase budget. Search both the general ledger and supplier subledger before posting. An approved $700 supplier bill already recorded as expense and accounts payable stays outside the new-accrual total below. The payment can still be outstanding without creating another $700 expense. Review supplier statements and invoices received after cutoff as completeness evidence, with their actual service dates. Recognize three original November accruals Every amount in this example is an original fictional USD teaching input. At November 30, six wage days have been earned at $200 per day but remain unpaid. November utilities consumed are supported at $450. A consultant has completed accepted November work priced at $900, with the invoice to arrive in December. Assume all three are operating expenses, no opening accruals, no payroll withholdings, sales tax, foreign currency or other adjustments. Original November 30 expense-accrual record; USD Cutoff Evidence / item Amount Adjustment November 30 Six unpaid November wage days 1,200 Dr wage expense / Cr wages payable November 30 Consumed utilities; supported estimate 450 Dr utilities expense / Cr utilities payable November 30 Accepted consulting work; invoice pending 900 Dr consulting expense / Cr accrued services November total Expense and new liability 2,550 No cash entry at accrual The total is $1,200 + $450 + $900 = $2,550. Relative to omitting these entries, November expense rises $2,550, November profit falls $2,550 and liabilities rise $2,550. The posting itself changes no cash balance. It is not a payment and does not establish that cash is available for the due dates. Allocate the later payment to the correct periods Suppose December payroll pays $2,000 for ten days: the six November days plus four December days. Without a reversing entry, debit Wages Payable $1,200, debit December Wage Expense $800 and credit Cash $2,000. November’s expense stays $1,200; December receives only its four-day $800 portion. Assume the final utilities invoice is exactly $450 and consulting invoice exactly $900. If invoice processing transfers these accruals into supplier payables, debit their accrual liabilities and credit Accounts Payable, without another expense. Their payments subsequently debit Accounts Payable and credit Cash. A direct debit to the accrued liability on payment is another workflow; select the actual system path and reconcile it, rather than posting both alternatives. Compare an optional reversal with direct settlement OpenStax’s reversing-entry appendix describes reversal as an optional aid for specified accruals. For the wage example, a December 1 reversal debits Wages Payable $1,200 and credits Wage Expense $1,200. The payroll system then debits Wage Expense $2,000 and credits Cash $2,000. December’s net wage expense is still $800: $2,000 less the $1,200 reversal. These are alternative methods for the same obligation. Do not reverse the accrual and also debit that cleared payable in the payment entry. That would remove the liability twice. Track which exact journal is scheduled to reverse, its date and whether the normal invoice or payroll feed will use expense. A temporary expense credit after reversal is not a cash receipt or an approved cost reduction. Investigate a changed invoice before choosing the period An estimate needs a documented update process. In an independent variation, the utility invoice arrives before November statements are finalized and provides better evidence that the November service cost was $480, rather than $450. Assuming that evidence belongs to the same recognition period, increase November utility expense and payable by $30. The revised three-item November accrual becomes $2,580. Do not automatically call every difference a December expense, and do not rewrite issued statements without assessing the applicable correction and subsequent-event policy. Retain the original estimate, new document, timing and reason for the adjustment. An estimate revision, duplicate invoice and prior-period error are different diagnoses; the invoice date alone does not resolve them. Reconcile liability movements independently from cash Base case only: liability and expense checkpoints; USD Checkpoint Accrued liability Recognized expense / cash Opening before the three items 0 No case expense yet November adjustments 2,550 November expense 2,550; cash 0 Later settlement of November portions 0 after all settle Liability reductions 2,550 Combined November and December wage portion Not another liability Expenses 2,550 + 800 = 3,350 All base payments No remaining case liability Cash paid 2,000 + 450 + 900 = 3,350 A liability-to-payables transfer changes the ledger location, not the overall obligation. Reconcile both accounts together so a transferred item is not reported as an unpaid accrual and a supplier payable simultaneously. New December accruals, if any, would require separate records; the zero closing figure assumes none within this deliberately bounded case. Use the accrual schedule as a close and payment handoff At each close, check service cutoff, source evidence, duplicate references, estimate approval, reversal settings and later settlement. Give unresolved items an owner and next evidence date. Preserve the final record so the next preparer can understand why the balance exists, not just copy last month’s amount. The accrual-accounting overview explains revenue, cash and prepayments together. Use the payable workflow for supplier approval and the ledger record for journal references. The accounting cycle connects the reviewed adjustment to statements; this guide’s task is the supported unpaid expense and its later clearance. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. Sources and scope Primary references below support the stated definitions or framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OpenStax: accrued-expense adjusting-entry mechanism OpenStax: optional reversing entries and the settlement trail Frequently asked questions Does an accrued expense require an invoice first? Not necessarily. The service or cost must meet the applicable recognition requirements, and the amount needs support; an invoice date alone does not determine the expense period. Is an unpaid bill already in accounts payable another accrual? It is already an obligation. Do not post the same expense again merely to rename an accounts-payable balance as an accrual. Are reversing entries mandatory? No. The case compares direct settlement with an optional specified reversal; both reach the same period expenses when implemented consistently. Why is December wage expense only $800 on a $2,000 payment? Six $200 days were already recognized in November. The payment covers those $1,200 plus four December days worth $800. What if the actual invoice differs from the estimate? Investigate the service period, evidence and statement timing. The guide’s separate $480 variation updates November by $30 before finalization; it does not prescribe every difference as a current-period expense. Does the accrual entry reduce cash immediately? No. It records expense and a liability. The later payment changes cash and clears the appropriate liability. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Retained Earnings: Reconcile Profit, Dividends and Equity Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Reconcile opening retained earnings, net income and declared dividends. Separate cash, contributed capital and any supported opening-balance adjustments. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Retained earnings is a cumulative equity balance built from earnings retained in the corporation, adjusted for distributions and any separately supported opening-balance items. It is not a bank account or a promise that the balance can be distributed. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Identify the corporation and the balance being reconciled Retained earnings belongs within corporate shareholders’ equity. OpenStax’s equity comparison distinguishes the retained-earnings movement from the broader statement of changes in equity. A sole proprietor’s owner-capital record or drawings account should not be relabeled automatically as the corporate dividend example below. Use the same entity, reporting period and currency for the opening balance, net income and distributions. The opening retained-earnings figure should agree to the previous closing ledger and financial statements, subject to any separately justified restatement. Net income is the period’s accounting result after its included income-tax expense; it is not revenue, EBITDA or customer collections. Verify the source statement rather than inserting a desired target profit. Build one original retained-earnings rollforward This original fictional USD case starts with $32,000 retained earnings. The corporation reports $12,000 net income for the period and validly declares $5,000 cash dividends. Assume no stock dividends, treasury-share transactions, opening corrections or other retained-earnings movements in the base case. The example assumes the declaration has been appropriately authorized; it does not assess legal distribution capacity. Base corporate retained-earnings bridge; USD Movement Amount Opening retained earnings 32,000 Current-period net income +12,000 Cash dividends declared in period −5,000 Closing retained earnings 39,000 Closing retained earnings is $32,000 + $12,000 − $5,000 = $39,000. A positive $7,000 change in this account reflects these modeled income and distribution movements. It does not mean cash increased by $7,000. Keep each input traceable to its ledger, closing journal or board record, with sign conventions shown. Use declaration and payment dates without counting twice OpenStax’s cash-dividend entries distinguishes the declared obligation from later payment. In this case, declaration reduces retained earnings by $5,000 and creates Dividends Payable $5,000. If the system first uses a temporary Dividends account, its closing transfer must produce the same retained-earnings reduction, rather than a second $5,000 deduction. Suppose $3,000 is paid during the period and $2,000 remains payable. The payment debits Dividends Payable $3,000 and credits Cash $3,000. It does not reduce retained earnings again. A retained-earnings schedule that subtracts $5,000 declared and another $3,000 paid would incorrectly show $36,000 rather than $39,000. Review both the authorization and settlement trail. Cash dividends are distributions, not operating expenses used to calculate the $12,000 net income. Reconcile available cash through its own movements Separate fictional cash schedule for the same period; USD Cash movement Amount Running cash Opening cash 15,000 15,000 Net operating cash movement +9,000 24,000 Equipment purchase −8,000 16,000 New share capital received +10,000 26,000 Cash dividends paid −3,000 23,000 Closing cash is $23,000 while retained earnings is $39,000. Operating cash differs from net income because receipts, payments and noncash or accrual items can occur on different dates. The equipment payment changes cash and the asset record, while share proceeds are an owner contribution. Neither becomes an extra retained-earnings credit merely because money entered or left the bank. The unpaid $2,000 dividend remains a liability and belongs in future payment planning. This cash schedule is a limited reconciliation, not a complete statement of cash flows or proof that every balance-sheet account is correct. Verify restricted balances and commitments before describing any amount as usable. Reconcile retained earnings inside total equity Assume opening paid-in capital is $70,000 and opening accumulated other comprehensive income is $1,200. New shares add $10,000 paid-in capital, while a separately measured current-period OCI loss of $400 reduces that accumulated component to $800. The OCI amount is a supplied assumption for this bridge; this article does not decide its underlying classification. Separate equity components, not three cash accounts; USD Component Opening Movement Closing Paid-in capital 70,000 +10,000 share contribution 80,000 Retained earnings 32,000 +12,000 income −5,000 dividends 39,000 Accumulated OCI 1,200 −400 OCI 800 Total equity 103,200 +16,600 net movement 119,800 The total bridge is $103,200 + $12,000 net income − $400 OCI + $10,000 share capital − $5,000 declared dividends = $119,800. Crediting share proceeds to retained earnings would misclassify equity even if total equity still agreed. A balanced accounting equation alone does not prove the component classification is right. Keep any opening-balance correction separate and supported An error affecting issued prior statements requires an applicable-framework and materiality assessment. It is not a general permission to post unexplained differences to retained earnings. SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin 108 discusses how prior-year errors can affect current financial statements for SEC registrants; that scope must not be treated as a universal bookkeeping shortcut. In an independent alternative, assume a completed accounting assessment requires a $3,000 net-of-tax reduction to opening retained earnings. Show the previously reported $32,000, the separately labeled −$3,000 correction and adjusted opening $29,000. Adding $12,000 current net income and deducting $5,000 declared dividends then gives $36,000. Do not combine that alternative with the base $39,000 result or hide its effect inside this period’s expenses. Document the actual treatment and disclosures required. Interpret a deficit without turning it into a cash measure A debit retained-earnings balance is often described as an accumulated deficit. For a separate fictional case, opening retained earnings of $4,000 plus a $9,000 net loss and no distributions produces a $5,000 deficit. The arithmetic identifies the equity balance; it does not establish insolvency, liquidity, company value or whether the company can continue trading. Likewise, positive retained earnings does not prove dividend permission, sufficient usable cash or absence of lender restrictions. Review the actual jurisdiction, governing documents, financing agreements and obligations before a distribution decision. An accounting rollforward answers how the balance moved. A funding or legal-capacity assessment uses additional evidence and should not be replaced by this formula. Close the reconciliation and retain the evidence Agree opening balance to the prior close, net income to the final income statement, declarations to authorization and distributions to the liability/payment ledger. List every other movement separately; unresolved differences need an owner and correction trail. Retain the version used for reporting rather than changing last period’s figures silently. Use the accounting-cycle guide for the full close, accrued-expense schedule for omitted period costs and accounting-equation guide for total-balance context. The statement-analysis guide addresses interpretation after these components reconcile. Retained earnings remains a permanent balance carried forward, rather than an expense account reset to zero each month. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. Sources and scope Primary references below support the stated definitions or framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OpenStax: retained earnings and the broader equity movement OpenStax: declaration and payment entries for cash dividends SEC SAB 108: prior-year misstatement assessment for registrants, not a universal posting rule Retained earnings and AOCI are different balances The other comprehensive income guide traces a separate accumulated-equity component. In its fictional case, net income affects retained earnings while current OCI changes AOCI. Adding comprehensive income and then adding net income again would double-count earnings. Frequently asked questions What is the basic retained-earnings formula? Under the stated base case, opening retained earnings plus net income minus declared dividends equals closing retained earnings. Other supported movements must be shown separately. Is retained earnings the cash available in the bank? No. The case closes with $39,000 retained earnings and $23,000 cash. They reconcile different records and can differ substantially. Do newly issued shares increase retained earnings? They normally belong in contributed-equity accounts under the applicable treatment, rather than current profit or retained earnings. The example credits the $10,000 share contribution to paid-in capital. Should paid dividends be deducted again after declaration? No. The $5,000 declaration already reduces retained earnings. The later $3,000 payment reduces the payable and cash. Can I use retained earnings to fix any unexplained difference? No. Determine the cause, period, framework and materiality. A supported opening correction must be separately identified and receive the required treatment. What does negative retained earnings prove? It identifies an accumulated deficit under the recorded movements. It does not by itself establish the company’s usable cash, insolvency or distribution rights. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.summary: Calculate marginal cost from matching changes in cost and output. Reconcile a fictional batch example, a capacity step and an additional-order decision.
