documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Marginal Cost: Calculate Added Output and Capacity Steps Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate marginal cost from matching changes in cost and output. Reconcile a fictional batch example, a capacity step and an additional-order decision. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Marginal cost measures the change in a defined total cost divided by the change in output. State the interval: a batch average can differ sharply from the cost of the very next unit when a capacity commitment is triggered. Marginal cost calculator Use matching cost boundaries and comparable output. The quotient is an average across the added output interval, not necessarily the cost of the very next unit. Fictional example. Use one currency and a consistent unit; labels do not convert amounts. Initial total cost Final total cost Initial output Final output Change in total cost 1,200 Added output 50 Cost per added unit 24 Reset fictional example Inputs stay in this page’s memory and reset on reload. For an actual choice, compare differential costs between alternatives and capacity before expanding . AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define both changes before dividing OpenStax distinguishes marginal cost from average cost : one compares changes in cost and output; the other spreads a defined total across output. For a finite interval, marginal cost = (new total cost − original total cost) / (new quantity − original quantity). Use quantities of the same product, quality and period. If output does not change, this quotient is undefined rather than zero. Write the decision beside the calculation. Increasing monthly production from 200 to 250 comparable units is different from replacing a machine or discontinuing a service. A historical cost comparison can describe what happened without identifying a causal cost function. Changes in input price, product mix or specifications must be explained before attributing the entire difference to added output. Build an explicit fictional production-cost schedule The original USD case assumes one homogeneous product and a single month. Up to 300 units, included production cost is $4,800 committed period cost plus $18 for each unit. Producing any amount above 300 and up to 360 requires an additional $1,200 capacity commitment for that month. The $18 unit rate is unchanged. These are constructed teaching assumptions, not supplier quotes or an industry cost benchmark. Original interval calculations; USD per added unit Output interval Total cost, before → after Cost change Output change Interval cost / unit 200 → 250 8,400 → 9,300 900 50 18.00 250 → 300 9,300 → 10,200 900 50 18.00 300 → 320 10,200 → 11,760 1,560 20 78.00 320 → 360 11,760 → 12,480 720 40 18.00 At 200 units, total cost is $4,800 + $3,600 = $8,400. At 300, it is $10,200. At 320, it becomes $4,800 + $1,200 + $5,760 = $11,760. The 300-to-320 increase therefore costs $1,560, not simply 20 × $18. Separate an interval average from the next unit For 300 to 320 units, $1,560 / 20 = $78 per additional unit on average across that batch . The 301st unit alone triggers the full $1,200 capacity payment plus $18 unit cost: its modeled incremental cost is $1,218. Units 302 through 320 then add $18 each, once the same capacity has been obtained. Twenty units total $1,218 + 19 × $18 = $1,560. Calling $78 the cost of every individual added unit would hide the step. Conversely, treating $1,218 as the repeating cost of units 302 onward would charge for the same commitment repeatedly. Compare the actual feasible batch with its alternative, and record whether the capacity commitment has already been made. This piecewise schedule does not have a smooth derivative at the threshold. Ask which commitments the decision really changes ACCA’s relevant-cost guidance distinguishes unchanged existing allocations from additional commitments caused by a decision. In this case, the original $4,800 is payable under either monthly output alternative. It cancels from the comparison. The new $1,200 does not cancel when comparing 300 units with a proposal that requires capacity above 300. After that $1,200 has become unavoidable for the stated month, a later decision within the obtained 360-unit limit has a different starting position. Do not silently use that later position to approve the original capacity purchase. Also do not assume capacity can be cancelled, renewed or reused on favorable terms without evidence. A fixed cost can be unchanged for one decision and avoidable for another horizon. Test the whole additional order, not one attractive unit rate Assume a separately accepted offer pays $65 for each added unit and initially adds no other selling or fulfillment cost. A 20-unit order above the 300-unit baseline yields $1,300 additional revenue against $1,560 additional production cost: the difference is −$260 . Comparing $65 with the existing 300-unit average of $34 would incorrectly approve this production-only case. A 60-unit order using the same new capacity yields $3,900 additional revenue. Cost rises from $10,200 at 300 to $12,480 at 360, an increase of $2,280; the difference is $1,620 before omitted order costs. If accepting it displaces another order with $300 otherwise obtainable contribution, the incremental advantage falls to $1,320 before those other costs. That opportunity effect is a decision comparison, not a second supplier invoice. Check the information the quotient cannot supply Confirm the delivery deadline, staffing, usable capacity, material availability and accepted specifications. At 361 units this model supplies no cost estimate; extending its last $18 rate beyond the 360-unit limit would invent evidence. A new shift, overtime rate or subcontractor quote needs a new alternative and cost schedule. Separate the purchase date from consumption, expense recognition and payment timing when converting the case into accounting or cash records. The order example deliberately excludes financing, tax and any additional marketing, warranty, packing or delivery costs. Add actual decision-changing amounts before approval. A positive added-order difference does not show that the entire business earns a profit, pays every bill on time or should buy a long-lived asset. Neither market demand nor a sustainable selling price comes from dividing a cost change by units. Preserve an auditable incremental-cost record Record both output alternatives, the matched period, cost categories, capacity threshold, existing commitments and new commitments. Reconcile the beginning and ending cost totals to their underlying assumptions. Retain a dated quote or operating record for each material change, an owner for unresolved items and a decision deadline. Compare actual added cost and accepted output after delivery without rewriting the original approval assumptions. Use average cost per unit for the total spread across output, cost control for investigating actual price and usage changes, and fixed versus variable costs for classification. The CVP guide tests a stated operating range, while growth scenarios connect extra demand to resources. Keep the worksheet’s incremental decision separate from the full-period result. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. Sources and scope Primary references below support the stated definitions or framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OpenStax: average and marginal cost definitions ACCA: relevant costs and changed commitments OpenStax: cost behavior and relevant ranges Frequently asked questions Is marginal cost always total cost divided by units? No. That is average cost for a defined total. Marginal cost uses the cost change divided by the output change. Is the $78 batch cost the cost of the 301st unit? No. The fictional 301st unit triggers $1,218. The $78 figure averages $1,560 over the full additional 20 units. Are fixed costs always excluded? No. Unchanged commitments cancel from a decision comparison, but a new avoidable capacity commitment caused by the order must be included. Can the formula be used when output change is zero? The finite-change quotient is undefined when the denominator is zero. Investigate the cost change on its own basis. Does a price above historical average cost guarantee a useful order? No. Check the actual incremental batch cost, new capacity, other order costs and any displaced alternative. Can I use the last unit rate beyond the capacity limit? Not without evidence. The example stops at 360 units; a higher output requires a supported new cost alternative. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Average Cost per Unit: Match Costs, Output and Capacity Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate average cost per unit using matched costs and output. Check fixed-cost spreading, capacity steps, unsold units and the limits of a unit average. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Average cost per unit is a defined cost total divided by the matched quantity of output. Label the cost boundary, product and period before interpreting the result or comparing it with another month. Average cost calculator: AFC, AVC and total Costs and output must describe the same period and comparable units. Fixed/variable describes behavior; this split does not automatically establish inventory accounting cost. Fictional example. Use one currency and a consistent unit; labels do not convert amounts. Total fixed cost Total variable cost Matching output Total cost 10,000 Average fixed cost 6 Average variable cost 14 Average total cost 20 AFC + AVC = ATC: 6 + 14 = 20 per matching unit. Reset fictional example Inputs stay in this page’s memory and reset on reload. Reconcile the same cost basis with gross profit and gross margin ; period averages do not price the next order automatically. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define the cost total and output denominator OpenStax defines average total cost as total cost divided by output. For a management production report, use production costs and comparable units produced within the same period and scope. A cost pool for one product cannot be divided by another product’s units. With zero output, an average per produced unit is undefined even when committed costs remain payable. State whether the numerator includes materials, labor, production support, selling costs or financing. “Cost per unit” alone leaves those choices unanswered. If the report instead measures all operating cost per delivered service, use that explicit label and a matching service denominator. A production average, customer-service average and purchase-price average can all be useful while answering different questions. Calculate a fictional homogeneous-product month The original USD illustration assumes one comparable finished product, no opening or closing work in process, no scrap and a single month. Committed production costs are $6,000, and included variable production cost is $12 for each completed unit. At 1,000 units, the variable pool is $12,000 and the total is $18,000. Average production cost is therefore $18 per completed unit . A possible supporting cost record is $7,000 materials, $4,000 job-varying labor, $1,000 variable production support and $6,000 committed production costs. The first three categories sum to $12,000. These amounts are constructed assumptions, not observed manufacturer data. Selling and administration of a separately assumed $2,500 are excluded from this production total; including them creates a different $20,500 numerator and a different management metric. Independent output alternatives; USD and comparable finished units Output Committed costs Variable costs Total Committed / unit Variable / unit Total / unit 800 6,000 9,600 15,600 7.50 12.00 19.50 1,000 6,000 12,000 18,000 6.00 12.00 18.00 1,200 6,000 14,400 20,400 5.00 12.00 17.00 1,400 8,400 16,800 25,200 6.00 12.00 18.00 Explain a lower average without claiming a cash saving At 800 units the same $6,000 plus $9,600 variable cost gives $15,600, or $19.50 each. At 1,200 units, $20,400 divided by 1,200 gives $17. The $6,000 commitment has not been reduced. Its assigned amount falls from $7.50 to $5 per unit because the denominator increases, while the assumed variable amount stays $12 per unit. OpenStax’s cost-behavior discussion emphasizes the activity range behind a fixed-cost assumption. In this case, producing more units to lower the reported average is not a saving if the extra units cannot be sold or require funding. Additional materials and labor still consume resources. Compare total commitments, usable output and demand rather than rewarding a smaller allocated amount in isolation. Recheck the average when the cost structure steps The example’s original capacity ends at 1,200 units. Producing 1,400 requires another $2,400 monthly commitment, making committed costs $8,400. Variable cost is 1,400 × $12 = $16,800. Total cost becomes $25,200 and average returns to $18 . Carrying the old $6,000 commitment into this alternative would report $22,800 / 1,400, or about $16.29, and omit the capacity requirement. The 1,200-to-1,400 increase costs $4,800 for 200 additional units, an interval incremental cost of $24. That differs from the $18 average across all 1,400. Use the marginal-cost method when evaluating the added batch. Verify how long the new capacity is committed, its usable output and its payment dates before treating this alternative as achievable. Do not quietly replace production with sales If the 1,000-unit case sells only 800 units, $18,000 divided by 800 equals $22.50. That is not the original average production cost per unit produced: it divides the whole production pool by a smaller sales denominator. It could describe a deliberately labeled cost-pool-per-unit-sold indicator, but it should not silently replace the $18 production measure. For a simple internal allocation assigning the entire $18,000 uniformly to those 1,000 identical units, 800 units represent $14,400 and 200 remaining units represent $3,600. Those two allocations reconcile to $18,000. This arithmetic is not a complete US GAAP or tax inventory valuation: capitalization, overhead allocation, impairment, abnormal costs and other framework requirements need separate assessment. Use the COGS guide for the inventory movement rather than assuming all production spending is the current cost of sales. Make changes in quality, mix and measurement visible Compare accepted good output with the same specification and unit of measure. A kilogram, an individual component and a boxed set are not interchangeable units. A change toward larger or more complex products can raise the average while each product’s own process improves. Separate product families or use an explicitly justified cost driver instead of blending unlike output into a persuasive single figure. Trace invoices, material consumption, time records and production support to the period. A late supplier payment does not prove the current production cost fell. A batch with more rework can look cheaper per attempted unit while costing more per accepted unit. Preserve both counts where relevant and explain which is in the denominator. The clean teaching case deliberately excludes those complications; a real report must document them rather than inherit the example’s assumptions. Use the average alongside the decision it supports An average is a summary, not a selling-price rule or a guarantee of profit. A price must be tested against the whole offer, demand, relevant costs, capacity and commercial commitments. Allocated historical cost alone cannot identify the incremental cost of a rush order. Likewise, a profitable income statement does not establish that supplier and payroll payments can be funded before customer receipts clear. Record the cost categories, output basis, time window, capacity assumptions, excluded items and reviewer beside every reported average. Use cost control to investigate price and usage differences, job-order costing when jobs require separate cost records, and CVP analysis for operating recovery within a stated range. Recompute a new average only after changed assumptions and quantities have been reconciled to their source records. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . OpenStax: average total cost and output OpenStax: cost behavior, relevant ranges and cost classifications Frequently asked questions What is the formula for average cost per unit? Divide a defined cost total by the matching quantity of comparable output for the stated period. The label must explain which costs and output are included. Does lower fixed cost per unit mean the fixed bill fell? Not necessarily. The same committed amount can be spread across more units while the total payment remains unchanged. Should I divide production cost by units sold? Use produced units for an average production cost per unit produced. A sales-based indicator needs its own explicit cost and denominator definition. What happens when output is zero? The per-produced-unit average is undefined. Committed costs can still exist and should be reported separately. Is $18 automatically the correct inventory valuation? No. It is the fictional case’s simple internal allocation. Actual financial-reporting and tax valuation requirements require their own review. Does the average establish the cost of the next order? No. Use a matching incremental alternative, including capacity steps and other decision-changing amounts. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost Control: Investigate Differences and Verify Actions Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Control costs with matched records, clear action owners and verified results. Reconcile a fictional volume, usage and price case without double counting. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Cost control connects a supported cost difference to an investigation, a responsible action and a measured result. Compare matching activity and scope before calling higher spending waste or a lower supplier rate a saving. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define the control question before assigning blame Choose the product, period, accepted-output measure, cost pool and standard being reviewed. Record who approved the standard and which actual documents support consumption and price. A report of “spending above budget” cannot by itself distinguish extra useful output, a changed specification, higher input prices or inefficient usage. Keep approved changes visible rather than altering last month’s standard to remove the variance. ACCA’s controllability discussion distinguishes an operation’s result from the matters a particular manager can influence. Apply that distinction to the investigation: a supplier-market shock is not automatically the buyer’s fault, and a lower-rate material is not automatically the production team’s improvement. Name the decision owner while retaining the full business effect, including quality and delivery consequences. Reconcile output, usage and price in one original case The fictional USD case budgets 1,000 accepted units, each using two kilograms of one material at $5 per kilogram: $10,000. Actual accepted output is 1,100 units. The business consumes 2,310 kilograms at $5.20, so actual material cost is $12,012. Assume purchases equal consumption, no opening or closing material inventory, no purchase credits, no mixed products and unchanged specifications. Those constraints keep the consumption-price bridge comparable. Original material-cost bridge; positive movements increase cost Stage Independent calculation USD Original standard at 1,000 units 1,000 × 2 kg × $5.00 10,000 Output-volume movement 100 extra units × 2 kg × $5.00 +1,000 Standard at actual 1,100 units 2,200 kg × $5.00 11,000 Usage effect at standard price 110 extra kg × $5.00 +550 Price effect on actual usage 2,310 kg × $0.20 +462 Actual material cost 2,310 kg × $5.20 12,012 Of the $2,012 increase over the original amount, $1,000 reflects 100 more accepted units at the standard usage and price. The remaining $1,012 compares actual cost with the $11,000 standard allowed for actual output. It requires investigation; it is not automatically an amount that can be saved. Allocate the price–usage interaction once OpenStax’s materials-variance framework separates price and quantity effects against a defined standard. In this example, excess consumption is 2,310 − 2,200 = 110 kilograms. Valued at $5, it gives $550. The actual-usage price effect is 2,310 × ($5.20 − $5.00) = $462. Together they reconcile the $1,012 difference at actual output. An alternative display can separate pure price on the allowed 2,200 kilograms, $440; pure usage at standard price, $550; and the 110 × $0.20 interaction, $22. That also totals $1,012. The first display already includes the $22 interaction in its $462 price component. Adding it again would overstate the difference. Do not mix a purchase-price variance on inventory acquisitions with a consumption-usage variance without reconciling inventory movements. Investigate records and operations before choosing a response Check the price invoice, unit conversions, freight or discounts included, actual receipts and supplier credit notes. Compare material issues, returned unused material, count adjustments and accepted output to the same cutoff. Investigate whether the 110-kilogram excess reflects real scrap, a changed design, measurement error, a poor standard or an unrecorded return. A favorable variance can also be a warning if quality or customer scope has been reduced. Investigation and action ownership for this case Question Evidence Action lead Why did the comparable kilogram price change? Matched quote, invoice and purchase terms Procurement with finance review Why did usage exceed 2 kg per accepted unit? Material issues, returns, scrap and quality records Operations and quality Why were 100 more accepted units produced? Demand authorization and completion records Sales / production planning Did the approved product scope change? Specification version and approval Product / contract owner Agree what each lead can actually change and by when. Do not evaluate one department only on a narrow favorable rate while its decision pushes a larger cost or delay elsewhere. Test whether a cheaper rate reduces the whole cost A fictional supplier option reduces the kilogram price from $5.20 to $5.05 but requires 2.2 kilograms per accepted unit under its tested usage assumption. At the same 1,100 units, consumption becomes 2,420 kilograms and cost becomes $12,221. That is $209 more than $12,012 despite the lower price. Confirm comparable quality, usable output and delivery before calling the quote a saving. A separate process trial instead reduces usage to 2.05 kilograms at unchanged $5.20. It consumes 2,255 kilograms and costs $11,726, a $286 reduction. If the trial also incurs $400 expense in this same period, its first-period included cost is $12,126: $114 above the original actual case. Later benefits may justify the trial, but they need evidence and a stated horizon. Do not promise $286 monthly savings indefinitely from one pilot. Verify the result without confusing expense and payment Write the chosen action, test cost, owner, completion date, expected mechanism and stop condition before implementation. Specify whether the claimed improvement reduces physical consumption, a contractual rate, a recurring commitment or only an allocated charge. Keep supplier payment timing in the cash forecast. Delaying a payable can help current cash while leaving the cost unchanged; consuming existing stock can reduce this month’s purchases without demonstrating lower usage. After the action, compare matching accepted output, specification, usage and prices. Separate an external market-price movement from the effect attributed to the project. Reconcile one-time trial expense, recurring benefit and actual cash movements to their own periods. Preserve the original baseline and disclose whether a later approved standard is different. Check complaints, rework and throughput so a smaller cost number is not accepted at the expense of the intended service. Keep control actions connected to the wider model The output is a short action record, not a large variance report without a next step. Leave unresolved differences visible with evidence needed, a responsible person and review date. Escalate a missing document or a failed quality check before increasing the intervention. A cost pool can be fully reconciled while its rate assumptions or operating response still need investigation. Use the flexible-budget guide for its broader activity-adjusted tutorial; this page owns the investigation and action workflow. Use cost-driver evidence to select a meaningful activity measure, average cost per unit to interpret the whole-period spread, and marginal cost to evaluate changed output and commitments. The bookkeeping close supplies the reconciled underlying record. Close an action only when its result and remaining uncertainty are recorded. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OpenStax: materials price and quantity effects ACCA: controllability and performance measures ACCA: decision-changing cash flows and commitments Frequently asked questions Is every increase over the original budget waste? No. In the case, $1,000 of the $2,012 increase reflects extra accepted output at standard usage and price. Other differences need investigation. Should the $22 interaction be added to the $462 price effect? Not in the first decomposition. The $462 actual-usage price effect already contains that interaction; adding it again double counts it. Does a lower material price guarantee a saving? No. The fictional $5.05 option uses more material and costs $209 more at the same accepted output. Does a favorable usage difference always mean better performance? No. It can reflect a changed specification, less service, measurement error or quality effects. Confirm comparable accepted output and evidence. Is a payment delay a cost saving? Not necessarily. It changes cash timing; the obligation and recognized cost can remain unchanged. Evaluate any actual fees or negotiated changes separately. Who should own a cost-control action? Assign someone with authority over the proposed response, supported by finance and affected teams. Distinguish controllable actions from the full operation’s result. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost-Benefit Analysis: Incremental Cash, Discounting and Decision Evidence Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare incremental costs and benefits against a baseline. Check a discounted example, uncertainty, payback and nonfinancial conditions before deciding. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Cost-benefit analysis compares the additional consequences of a decision with a defined alternative. Identify who bears each cost, when each benefit occurs and what cannot credibly be monetized before interpreting a total or ratio. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define the decision and the alternative first Write the question in operational terms: should a workshop replace its manual scheduling process with a specified system for the next three years? Compare that option with continuing the present process, including the costs and performance reasonably expected without the change. A baseline is not automatically zero cost or zero improvement. Include a lower-cost repair or smaller pilot if it could meet the same objective. This guide uses an original fictional USD business case, not a vendor quote, observed customer result or investment recommendation. Its perspective is the workshop’s incremental operating cash before financing and income tax. A social benefit-cost analysis can include effects on other parties and therefore have a different boundary. OMB Circular A-94 is a federal-program methodological reference; it does not set this private business’s hurdle rate or approval policy. Build a cost-and-benefit register without double counting Include future changes caused by choosing the option: setup, integration, training, recurring fees, transition disruption, decommissioning and any supported residual proceeds. Identify a resource’s next-best use when an opportunity cost matters. A nonrefundable study fee already paid before the decision is normally outside the future incremental comparison; an unpaid cancellation obligation or avoidable next stage can still be relevant. Record the reason for each inclusion or exclusion. Do not value the same released labor twice as both avoided payroll and additional delivery contribution. If payroll continues, freed hours are capacity, not automatically cash savings. Include incremental sales only through their additional cash contribution after the associated costs, rather than adding gross revenue and ignoring fulfillment. Use a separate nonfinancial record for effects that lack a defensible monetary estimate. A precise spreadsheet cannot turn an unsupported claim into evidence. Reconcile a dated three-year teaching case Assume $18,000 implementation plus $2,000 transition cash at time zero. Each year-end brings $12,000 of avoided external-service payments relative to the baseline and $4,000 incremental operating payments. Assume identical nominal dollar amounts each year, a three-year horizon, no taxes, financing, terminal proceeds or working-capital change. These exclusions keep the arithmetic inspectable; a real proposal must assess them rather than presume they are immaterial. Original incremental case; USD and year-end timing Date Gross benefit Incremental cost Net cash PV of net at 8% Today, t=0 0 20,000 −20,000 −20,000.00 End of year 1 12,000 4,000 8,000 7,407.41 End of year 2 12,000 4,000 8,000 6,858.71 End of year 3 12,000 4,000 8,000 6,350.66 Total, unrounded calculation 36,000 32,000 4,000 616.78 NPV Undiscounted benefits total $36,000 and costs total $32,000, producing a $4,000 net benefit. That sum treats a dollar received in year three like a dollar spent today, so it is a screening total rather than the discounted decision result. Preserve the gross benefit and cost columns even when a net cash column is convenient. Discount benefits and costs on the same basis For a stated rate r and end-of-year amount in year t, present value equals amount / (1 + r) t . Use the same timing convention, currency and price basis across the comparison. Nominal cash amounts require a compatible nominal rate; constant-price amounts require a compatible real rate. Do not add an inflation forecast to cash flows and then discount them with an unrelated real assumption. At an illustrative 8% nominal rate, the three-year discount-factor sum is 2.577096987. Present-value benefits are $30,925.16. Present-value costs are $20,000 + $4,000 × 2.577096987 = $30,308.39. NPV is $616.78, and the explicitly defined benefit-cost ratio is PV benefits / PV costs = 1.02035. Calculate from unrounded values and round displayed amounts only. An OMB Appendix C rate is not automatically appropriate for this business. Keep ROI, payback and NPV as separate questions A simple undiscounted return defined here as net benefit / total incremental cost is $4,000 / $32,000 = 12.5% over the full three-year horizon. It is not an annual return or an internal rate of return. Other ROI conventions can use a different denominator, so show yours rather than comparing unlabeled percentages. The ROAS-versus-ROI guide separately explains campaign return boundaries. After two annual net receipts, $4,000 of the initial $20,000 remains unrecovered. Assuming benefits accrue uniformly within year three gives an interpolated simple payback of 2.5 years. Under the actual year-end-only timing in the table, recovery occurs at the third payment. Discounted payback must use discounted cash and still does not capture benefits beyond its cutoff. Use profitability index for that separate capital-ranking question, with its own numerator definition. Test the fragile assumptions and nonfinancial conditions At the same $8,000 annual net cash, illustrative rates of 4%, 8% and 12% give NPVs of $2,200.73, $616.78 and −$785.35. If annual gross benefit is only $10,000 while operating cost remains $4,000, NPV at 8% becomes −$4,537.42. The gross annual benefit required for zero NPV under these assumptions is about $11,760.67. These are original scenario calculations, not probability estimates. The GAO cost-estimating guide recommends documenting assumptions and sensitivity rather than presenting one estimate without its drivers. Link each scenario to a question that can be investigated: supplier price, implementation delay, usable capacity or actual baseline spending. Keep service reliability, data-access requirements, accessibility and exit feasibility as explicit criteria. A positive NPV does not override a failed mandatory requirement, and unsupported scores should not be disguised as dollar benefits. Approve a testable decision and review actual results Record the chosen alternative, dated input evidence, cash owner, accepted uncertainty and stop conditions. Before a full commitment, a bounded pilot can test whether the assumed external-service payment really disappears and whether the replacement meets its delivery requirement. State what result would change the decision instead of selecting a threshold after the pilot outcome is known. After launch, compare actual incremental payments and achieved benefits with the original baseline. Preserve the prior version when revising the forecast. Feed payment dates into the cash-flow forecast . Benefits can arrive late even when the three-year total looks acceptable. The worksheet is a manual evidence record, not an automatic financial appraisal. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. Sources and scope Primary references below support the stated definitions or framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OMB Circular A-94: federal benefit-cost method; private-case rate is independently assumed OMB current circular index and 2026 Appendix C listing GAO: documented assumptions and sensitivity analysis Frequently asked questions What is cost-benefit analysis? It compares the additional costs and benefits of a defined option with a stated alternative, including timing, uncertainty and relevant nonfinancial effects. Is the benefit-cost ratio the same as ROI? No. This case defines BCR as present-value benefits divided by present-value costs, while its simple ROI uses undiscounted net benefit divided by total incremental cost. Is an 8% discount rate recommended for my business? No. It is a fictional teaching assumption. Select and support a rate consistent with the decision, price basis and risk treatment. Should time saved be counted as cash saved? Only when a supported cash consequence follows. If payroll continues, released time can be capacity rather than an avoided payment. Does payback include every benefit? No. Payback asks when the initial amount is recovered under its timing convention and can ignore later benefits and other decision effects. Can a positive NPV override a legal or operational requirement? No. Treat mandatory requirements and unmonetized consequences explicitly rather than allowing a financial subtotal to erase them. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.headings: Define what the ABC model will explain Build pools whose activity records can be checked Apply each rate and reconcile the complete allocation Explain the difference from one machine-hour rate Report an unused-capacity scenario separately Do not turn an allocated saving into an automatic cash saving Maintain the model as an evidence-backed operating record Download the editable worksheet Sources and scope Continue with cost accounting and cost behavior Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Activity-Based Costing: Reconcile Cost Pools, Drivers and Product Costs Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a reconciled activity-based costing example with three pools, two products and a separate unused-capacity scenario. Test drivers before using the result. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Activity-based costing traces resource costs to activities and then assigns activity costs to the products, services or customers that use them. Its value depends on a defensible cost boundary, meaningful drivers and a complete reconciliation. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define what the ABC model will explain Start with the decision and cost object. A product-cost model, a customer cost-to-serve model and a quote for one job can need different pools. Write which ledger costs are included and which remain outside the model. Direct materials or directly traced labor must not be added to an overhead pool and then charged to the product a second time. OpenStax’s ABC lesson describes assigning indirect costs through activity pools and drivers. This guide supplies a separate original fictional USD manufacturing case with two products and three support pools for one period. It does not reuse a source’s numerical case, claim that an allocation measures avoidable cash or prescribe an external-reporting inventory policy. Use the customer profitability guide when customer-specific support is the question. Build pools whose activity records can be checked The fictional factory has $18,000 setup support, $12,000 inspection and $30,000 machine support: $60,000 included overhead. The case assumes these pools are mutually exclusive and fully reconciled to the selected ledger accounts. Setup counts are appropriate only under its assumption that setups require sufficiently similar resources; inspection and machine support use hours rather than units sold. Original pool budget and matched activity quantities Pool Cost USD Total driver Calculated rate Product A driver Product B driver Setup support 18,000 40 setups 450 / setup 10 30 Inspection 12,000 200 inspection hours 60 / hour 120 80 Machine support 30,000 2,000 machine hours 15 / hour 1,500 500 Total resources 60,000 Different driver units Do not add rates — — Keep costs and activity in the same period. Record whether the quantities are budgeted or actual, what a setup includes, how hours are captured and who reviews incomplete logs. A count generated by software can still omit rework or combine different activity definitions. A driver should explain resource consumption for the chosen pool, not merely correlate with revenue. Apply each rate and reconcile the complete allocation For each pool, rate = included pool cost / selected driver quantity. Product allocation = pool rate × product driver consumption. These units matter: dollars per setup cannot be added directly to dollars per inspection hour. Apply the rates separately, then add the dollar allocations. A zero denominator with a nonzero pool is an unresolved model condition, not permission to return a zero rate. Original ABC allocation; USD except units Pool or measure Product A Product B Reconciliation Setup support 4,500 13,500 18,000 Inspection 7,200 4,800 12,000 Machine support 22,500 7,500 30,000 Total ABC overhead 34,200 25,800 60,000 Units produced 1,000 500 1,500 Overhead per unit 34.20 51.60 Not an additive total Product A receives $4,500 + $7,200 + $22,500 = $34,200. Product B receives $13,500 + $4,800 + $7,500 = $25,800. The allocations sum to $60,000, and each pool also reconciles individually. Dividing by 1,000 and 500 completed units gives $34.20 and $51.60 overhead per unit. This case has no work in process, losses or unallocated base-case cost. Explain the difference from one machine-hour rate A single-rate comparison would allocate $60,000 / 2,000 machine hours = $30 per machine hour. That assigns $45,000 to A and $15,000 to B, or $45 and $30 per unit. Relative to that method, ABC shifts $10,800 from A to B without changing total included overhead. B has fewer machine hours but more setups, which is why the mix of activities changes the assignment. Assume separately traced manufacturing costs of $26 per A unit and $34 per B unit. The base-case ABC assigned manufacturing costs become $60.20 and $85.60 per unit; the single-rate comparison gives $71 and $64. These are assigned manufacturing costs, not contribution margins, market prices or complete business profits. Nonmanufacturing costs, demand and capacity remain outside this comparison. A more complicated method is useful only if the resulting decision information justifies maintaining the evidence. Report an unused-capacity scenario separately The base case divides the machine-support pool by its specified 2,000 used hours. Now consider a separate management scenario in which the same $30,000 resource budget supplies 2,500 practical machine hours, but only 2,000 are used. A practical-capacity rate is $12 per hour. A receives $18,000 machine support and B $6,000; $6,000 is shown separately as unused machine capacity. Keeping setup and inspection allocations unchanged gives A $29,700 and B $24,300, totaling $54,000 assigned plus $6,000 unused = $60,000 supplied. Harvard Business School’s capacity discussion explains why resource use and resource supply need separate visibility. This alternative management model is not a direction to capitalize or expense amounts under a particular reporting standard. Preserve its denominator and separate it from the full-allocation base case rather than silently switching the rate. Do not turn an allocated saving into an automatic cash saving Stopping Product B would remove its recorded activity demand from this model, but not necessarily its share of paid staff, machinery or facility commitments. Identify which resources can actually be reduced, when contracts can change and whether released capacity has a better use. A cost transfer between products changes the report even when the next bank payment is identical. Test driver quality before changing price or mix. If B’s thirty setups include many short changeovers while A’s ten are unusually long, setup count may distort the assignment; measure duration or split genuinely different activities. If inspection hours reflect defects, retain the distinction between necessary inspection and avoidable rework. Reconcile the proposed action to CVP assumptions only after identifying which costs change with activity and which remain committed. Maintain the model as an evidence-backed operating record Preserve pool account mappings, driver definitions, quantity sources, rate version and reconciliation. Investigate any variance between budgeted resource cost, applied activity cost and actual ledger spending instead of hiding it in the unit price. Document treatment of facility-sustaining activity and excluded costs; forcing every cost through an arbitrary driver can make a complete-looking model less informative. Update when process design, product mix, resource prices or capacity changes materially, and retain the previous version for comparison. A small pilot with a few consequential pools can reveal whether better records alter the decision before every minor expense is modeled. The cost-driver guide supports driver investigation; job order costing supports a job-level cost sheet. This worksheet records assumptions and allocations manually and does not calculate rates or audit source records automatically. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. Sources and scope Primary references below support the stated definitions or framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 9, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. OpenStax: activity pools, drivers and allocation mechanics Harvard Business School: resource use, supply and unused capacity Frequently asked questions What is the activity-based costing formula? For each pool, divide the included cost by the selected driver quantity, multiply by each object’s usage and reconcile the resulting allocations. Must every pool use the same driver? No. A setup count, inspection hour and machine hour can represent different resource demands; their definitions and evidence must match their pools. Does ABC change the total overhead incurred? Allocation alone changes who receives the included cost, not the underlying total spending. Separate actual resource changes from reporting transfers. Why is Product B more costly under this example’s ABC model? It uses thirty of forty setups despite using fewer machine hours, so multiple drivers assign it more setup support than the single-rate comparison. Is unused capacity a cash saving? Not automatically. Cash changes only when the resource supply or other relevant cash consequence changes; unused availability can also support future work. Is this an automatic external-reporting inventory calculation? No. It is a management-costing illustration. Financial-statement inventory must follow the applicable recognition, allocation and measurement requirements. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Absorption vs Variable Costing: Inventory and Profit Reconciliation Published November 9, 2026 Updated November 9, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare absorption and variable costing using two months of production and sales. Reconcile fixed manufacturing overhead, inventory and operating profit. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Absorption and variable costing differ in how fixed manufacturing overhead enters product cost and current-period expense. Reconcile production, sales and inventory before explaining a profit difference between the two reports. AI-created topic illustration; worked examples are fictional and independently reconciled. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Separate manufacturing cost from selling and administration In the simplified methods compared here, both reports include variable manufacturing cost in units produced. Absorption costing also assigns fixed manufacturing overhead to inventory; variable costing charges that fixed manufacturing amount to the period instead. Selling and administrative costs remain outside manufacturing inventory in this case. Fixed marketing expense must not be absorbed merely because it is fixed. OpenStax’s comparison explains the basic timing difference. The following two-month USD case is original fictional teaching material, not a company result. It assumes one homogeneous product, no work in process, returns, scrap, taxes, financing, valuation write-down or overhead spending variance. Actual financial reporting needs the applicable inventory policy and classification review; the exercise does not establish tax treatment or compliance for a particular entity. Calculate one supported manufacturing rate Assume direct materials $12, direct labor $5 and variable manufacturing overhead $3 per completed unit. Variable manufacturing cost is therefore $20. Fixed manufacturing overhead is $6,000 per month. The selected normal-capacity illustration is 1,000 units each month, equal to actual production in both months, giving $6 fixed manufacturing overhead per unit. Absorption manufacturing cost is $26 per unit; variable manufacturing cost is $20. Selling price is $40 per unit sold. Variable selling cost is $2 per unit sold, and fixed selling/administrative cost is $3,000 monthly. Keep the production denominator separate from the sales denominator: manufacturing allocation uses the specified production/capacity basis, while variable selling expense follows sales in this case. Direct labor is assumed variable for this exercise only; a real workforce arrangement can behave differently and must be classified from its facts. Reconcile the physical units before comparing income Month one starts with zero finished goods, produces 1,000 units and sells 800, leaving 200. Month two starts with those 200, produces another 1,000 and sells 1,100, leaving 100. The identity beginning units + units completed − units sold = ending units holds for each month. No unit can be sold twice or disappear solely because the reporting method changes. Original physical movement; completed identical units Measure Month 1 Month 2 Opening finished goods 0 200 Completed production 1,000 1,000 Units available 1,000 1,200 Units sold 800 1,100 Closing finished goods 200 100 Both methods use the same physical quantities, price and selling costs. Because all manufacturing rates are constant and the units are identical in this case, cost-flow assumptions do not change its numerical bridge. If costs vary between periods, opening layers must retain their own fixed-overhead content; multiplying every historical unit by today’s rate would be an unsupported shortcut. Prepare the two reports from the same facts Month-one sales are $32,000. Absorption COGS is 800 × $26 = $20,800. After $1,600 variable selling and $3,000 fixed selling/administration, operating profit is $6,600. Variable costing deducts $16,000 variable manufacturing COGS and $1,600 variable selling to reach $14,400 contribution, then deducts $6,000 fixed manufacturing and $3,000 fixed selling/administration, giving $5,400. Original comparison; USD; cost lines are positive deductions Line M1 absorption M1 variable M2 absorption M2 variable Sales 32,000 32,000 44,000 44,000 Manufacturing cost of goods sold 20,800 16,000 28,600 22,000 Variable selling expense 1,600 1,600 2,200 2,200 Fixed manufacturing expense shown separately 0 6,000 0 6,000 Fixed selling/admin expense 3,000 3,000 3,000 3,000 Operating profit 6,600 5,400 10,200 10,800 Closing inventory 5,200 4,000 2,600 2,000 Month-two sales are $44,000. Absorption COGS is 1,100 × $26 = $28,600, and variable manufacturing COGS is $22,000. The same $2,200 variable selling and $3,000 fixed selling/administration apply to both reports. Variable costing additionally shows the month’s $6,000 fixed manufacturing charge separately. Do not subtract the full $6,000 again from absorption profit after its inventory/COGS allocation. Explain the profit bridge through inventory Use amounts, not only the direction of unit movement: absorption profit − variable profit = fixed manufacturing overhead in ending inventory − fixed manufacturing overhead in beginning inventory, under this case’s assumptions. In month one the bridge is 200 × $6 − $0 = $1,200, so $6,600 − $5,400 = $1,200. Absorption defers that amount in the 200 units still held. Month two starts with $1,200 of fixed overhead in inventory and ends with 100 × $6 = $600. The bridge is $600 − $1,200 = −$600, matching $10,200 − $10,800. More prior fixed overhead leaves inventory through sales than enters the closing balance. Across both months, absorption profit is $16,800 versus $16,200 variable profit; the remaining $600 difference equals fixed overhead still included in the final inventory. This is an expense-timing difference, not $600 newly collected cash. Do not inflate inventory by ignoring capacity or exclusions Normal capacity is not interchangeable with whatever production denominator produces the most favorable profit. The Australian standard setter’s AASB 102 paragraphs 12–13 , an IFRS-aligned reference for the specified Australian reporting scope, describe production-overhead allocation and normal-capacity treatment, including unallocated overhead when relevant. Do not silently treat that framework-specific reference as a US tax rule. For US nongovernmental GAAP, confirm current applicable requirements in the FASB Accounting Standards Codification ; pre-Codification summaries are not the current authority. If actual output falls or idle capacity appears, reassess the allocation and expense treatment instead of automatically dividing the full pool by fewer units. Likewise, a management decision to produce extra stock requires demand, storage, obsolescence and funding evidence. Higher absorption profit caused by inventory growth does not show that customer sales or economic performance improved. The example assumes actual equals the selected normal capacity specifically to isolate timing without an unresolved volume variance. Use the comparison for the decision it can support A variable-costing report can make cost behavior and contribution visible for a defined internal decision, but it must not omit fixed commitments when assessing total profitability. An absorption unit cost includes assigned fixed manufacturing cost, so it is not automatically the incremental cost of one extra order. Identify spare capacity, additional setup, avoidable resources and opportunity cost before accepting or rejecting work. Use the existing contribution income statement guide for its presentation format and COGS guide for inventory-to-expense reconciliation. This page owns the manufacturing-method timing bridge. Preserve the unit movement, cost classification, capacity basis, opening inventory layers and fixed-overhead bridge with the close. The downloadable worksheet is a manual working record; it neither calculates the reports automatically nor determines the inventory policy appropriate for a reader’s business. In the simplified comparison, absorption includes fixed manufacturing overhead in product cost; variable costing expenses that fixed manufacturing amount in the period. Why is absorption profit higher in month one? The $1,200 fixed manufacturing overhead in the 200 unsold units remains in absorption inventory instead of becoming current-period expense. Why is absorption profit lower in month two? Opening inventory releases $1,200 fixed overhead while closing inventory retains $600, making absorption profit $600 below variable profit in that month. Should fixed selling expense be included in inventory? Not in this case. The fixed manufacturing versus nonmanufacturing boundary matters; being fixed does not itself make a cost inventoriable. Can the inventory unit change always be multiplied by today’s overhead rate? Only when the relevant fixed-overhead content and other assumptions make that shortcut valid. Different opening cost layers require their actual amounts. Does an absorption-profit increase prove cash generation? No. Inventory timing can change reported profit while using cash to fund unsold goods. Review demand, capacity, carrying value and cash separately. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Accrual Accounting: Revenue, Expenses and Cash Timing Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare earned revenue, incurred expenses and cash timing using one reconciled service-business example. Track receivables, prepayments and customer advances. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Accrual accounting records revenue and expenses in the periods to which they belong under the accounting framework, rather than using cash dates alone. Separate the delivery, billing and settlement evidence before comparing profit with a bank balance. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Identify what happened before choosing the date For this introductory financial-reporting example, assume an accepted service gives an unconditional right to payment and all relevant recognition conditions are satisfied in November. The invoice is issued later. The invoice date by itself does not determine when revenue is earned. If payment depends on additional performance, a contract asset or another treatment may be relevant; do not automatically call every unbilled amount accounts receivable. Likewise, distinguish a service consumed, an asset purchased and an advance paid. A December payment for November work can settle an existing obligation. Insurance paid in advance can provide coverage over several periods. These distinctions organize the evidence; they are not an election of a permissible US tax method. Use four transactions with separate accounting and cash dates Original November 2026 accrual case; USD Event November recognition Cash / billing date Illustrative posting Accepted November service; unconditional payment right $5,000 earned in November Invoice Dec 1; collect Dec 15 Dr receivable / Cr revenue 5,000 November payroll earned $1,800 November expense Pay December 5 Dr wage expense / Cr payable 1,800 Insurance paid November 1; twelve months coverage $100 November expense; $1,100 prepaid $1,200 November payment Dr insurance expense / Cr prepaid 100 at close Customer advance for December service No November revenue from this advance $2,400 November receipt Dr cash / Cr contract liability 2,400 The insurance initially creates a $1,200 prepaid asset. One month of coverage is then consumed, leaving $1,100. The $2,400 advance is assumed refundable or deliverable under the contract and wholly unearned at November 30. It is not extra November sales merely because money arrived. No sales tax, bad-debt adjustment, depreciation or other expenses are included in this deliberately limited example. Reconcile November profit, cash and balances Earned revenue is $5,000. Included expenses are $1,800 payroll plus $100 insurance, so accrual profit is $3,100 . Operating receipts less payments in this case are $2,400 − $1,200 = $1,200. The $1,900 difference between profit and this operating cash movement is explained by $5,000 new receivable, $1,100 remaining prepaid, $1,800 unpaid wages and $2,400 customer advance: $3,100 − $5,000 − $1,100 + $1,800 + $2,400 = $1,200. Add a separate $10,000 owner cash investment at the beginning. Closing cash becomes $11,200, not $3,100. Assets are $11,200 cash + $5,000 receivable + $1,100 prepaid = $17,300. Liabilities are $1,800 wages + $2,400 advance = $4,200. Equity is $10,000 investment + $3,100 profit = $13,100. Thus $17,300 = $4,200 + $13,100. This is a financial-reporting illustration. A simple cash receipts/payments view of these transactions is not a complete tax-basis income computation. Loan principal, equipment purchases, deposits, constructive receipt and applicable tax rules can require additional analysis. Carry the balances into December without counting twice On December 15, collecting the $5,000 reduces the receivable and increases cash; it does not recognize the same service revenue again. Paying $1,800 wages settles the November payable. Consuming another month of insurance reduces the prepaid asset by another $100. Recognize the advance as earned only when the assumed December service conditions are satisfied, not automatically because the calendar changed. Preserve references from each settlement to its original transaction. Use the receivable workflow for collection allocation and the liability schedule for unpaid obligations. A balanced entry can still contain the wrong period or classification. Use a cutoff review before reading the result At month end, inspect accepted work, invoices issued before or after cutoff, services received but unbilled, unused prepayments and unfulfilled customer promises. Document the reporting basis and reviewer. Reconcile opening balances plus movements to closing schedules; do not replace missing evidence with an arbitrary journal to make profit look reasonable. The accounting cycle connects adjustments to statements. Bookkeeping for small business covers the routine evidence collection, and the cash forecast handles future payment timing. IRS Publication 538 is the separate official reference for tax accounting methods; this guide makes no blanket eligibility or change-of-method claim. Check recognition, billing and settlement against separate evidence The OpenStax adjustment framework distinguishes accrued items from deferred items. Apply that distinction to the four case records: accepted work supports the revenue assessment; payroll evidence supports the wage accrual; the insurance contract supports the unused coverage; and the customer agreement supports the unearned advance. A bank statement establishes a receipt or payment, but does not establish that every recognition condition was satisfied. For a real close, create one row per event with the performance or consumption date, invoice date, due date, settlement date and account reference. Explain any difference rather than forcing all five dates to match. If an invoice includes work still to be delivered, review the separate obligations before assigning the entire invoice to revenue. If an amount is disputed, identify whether the problem concerns the transaction price, the recognition conditions or collectibility; those are different questions. The case’s $3,100 profit, $1,200 operating cash movement and $11,200 closing cash answer three defined questions. The owner’s $10,000 investment belongs in the funding bridge, not service revenue. Compare each reconciliation with the same reporting cutoff and included transactions. IRS Publication 538 is a separate federal tax-method reference; it does not turn this introductory financial-reporting case into a tax return. Not necessarily. Recognition depends on the framework and transaction facts; an invoice date alone is insufficient. Is an advance payment always revenue? No. In this example it remains an obligation until the service is earned under the stated assumptions. Does collecting a receivable increase revenue again? No. It normally converts a previously recognized receivable into cash. Does this determine which tax method I may use? No. Tax eligibility and changes of method need a separate review of current official rules and your circumstances. Can a customer invoice contain both earned and unearned amounts? Yes. Assess the underlying delivery obligations and applicable recognition rules; the invoice total alone does not settle that question. Which evidence supports the insurance adjustment? The coverage period and amount in the insurance agreement, together with the payment and prior prepaid balance, support the allocation. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Bookkeeping for Small Business: A Monthly Record Workflow Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Organize transaction evidence, reconcile cash and customer balances, review adjustments and close the month with an original bank-reconciliation example. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Small-business bookkeeping turns supported transactions into consistent records and reconciled balances. A useful monthly routine collects evidence, posts transactions once, resolves differences and preserves a reviewed closing package. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Build the record around evidence rather than the bank feed Keep an identifiable link between each posting and the underlying sale, supplier bill, receipt, payroll record or agreement. The IRS describes supporting business documents as the evidence behind entries. Its tax-record guidance is not a substitute for your financial-reporting policy, but it reinforces why a bank description alone may not explain what a transaction represents. Assign a unique reference, reporting date, amount, currency, counterparty and account. Separate business and personal activity appropriately. A bank feed entry can match an invoice payment already recorded; importing it as another sale would duplicate income. Keep unidentified items in a visible investigation list rather than assigning convenient categories. Separate daily capture from the monthly close A practical sequence with observable completion evidence Frequency Work Evidence of completion Daily / weekly Collect and match documents; post invoices and payments Unique references; no unexplained duplicates Weekly Review customer and supplier open items Detail reconciles to control accounts Month end Reconcile cash, cards, loans and relevant stock Dated schedules with differences explained Month end Review accruals, prepayments and asset schedules Approved adjustments linked to evidence Close Review reports and preserve the version Reviewer, unresolved issues and next actions Frequency depends on transaction volume and commitments, not a universal deadline invented by this guide. A business with payroll this week may need cash review before the formal month-end close. The formal close should use a consistent cutoff across reports. Reconcile a bank difference without inventing a plug Original cash-reconciliation case, USD Record / adjustment Amount Reason Cash book before omitted bank fee $9,750 8,000 opening + 6,200 receipts − 4,450 payments Unrecorded bank fee −$50 Post supported fee once Adjusted cash book $9,700 Agrees to adjusted bank evidence Statement balance $9,850 Statement at same month-end cutoff Deposit in transit +$250 Already in books; absent from bank Outstanding payment −$400 Already in books; absent from bank Adjusted statement $9,700 9,850 + 250 − 400 The $50 fee is missing from the books, so it needs a supported book entry. The $250 deposit and $400 outstanding payment are already recorded in the books; adding or subtracting them there again would duplicate their effects. Their role is to explain the statement timing. Both adjusted views reach $9,700 . An equal result does not validate every payment. Verify the recipient, amount and business purpose. Investigate old reconciling items and retain evidence of later clearing. Do not force unexplained differences into fees or owner equity. Reconcile detail before accepting the report totals In a separate customer subledger example, $3,000 opening receivables + $6,000 invoices − $5,200 allocated collections = $3,800 closing gross receivables. If the GL says $3,600, identify the $200 difference before treating the report as reconciled. Check credits, manual journals, duplicate invoices and unapplied receipts. This is independent of the bank example’s total receipts. Use AR records and AP records for their respective workflows. Match asset cost and accumulated depreciation to an asset register. Check prepayment periods and accrued obligations. An account can reconcile mathematically while its valuation or classification still needs review. Preserve the close and the unresolved-action list Review unusual balances and changes against actual operations. Retain the trial balance, reconciliations, adjustment support and reports with their cutoff date. Assign an owner and deadline to each remaining issue. A lock date is useful only when corrections are still made through a controlled, documented process rather than silently changing prior reports. The general ledger template supplies posting references and account-level balances; the accounting cycle explains adjustments and closing. The statement-analysis guide addresses interpretation after the records are prepared. Check the actual retention requirements for each document type; this article does not assert a single period for every business record. Build a close package that another person can reproduce The IRS recordkeeping guidance allows a system suited to the business, while requiring records that support the amounts reported. It does not require this guide’s particular spreadsheet, chart of accounts or monthly timetable. Keep the document that explains a transaction alongside its posting reference; a category selected in an app is not the underlying evidence. For the $9,700 cash reconciliation, preserve the original statement, opening book balance, receipts and payments, the omitted $50 fee, and the $250/$400 timing items. The reviewer should be able to reach the same adjusted balance without asking the preparer to remember what happened. Retain subsequent clearing evidence for the timing items. If a payment remains outstanding unusually long, record the investigation rather than deleting it to make the schedule shorter. A practical close package also contains customer and supplier detail, the bank reconciliation, asset and loan schedules, approved adjustments, the trial balance and the reports actually reviewed. Make the cutoff and version visible. Record who prepared and reviewed each reconciliation and which issues remain open. Retention is a separate decision: IRS retention guidance has different conditions for different records, so a blanket “discard everything after three years” instruction would be misleading. Consider other applicable contractual or legal requirements before disposal. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . Frequently asked questions Is the bank feed the whole bookkeeping system? No. It does not by itself explain unpaid invoices, noncash adjustments or the purpose and period of every transaction. Should deposits in transit be entered again? Not if already recorded correctly. Use them to explain timing between books and statement. Can I close with an unexplained difference? Record it as unresolved and investigate; do not conceal it with an unsupported balancing entry. Does this guide recommend accounting software? No. It defines the evidence and reconciliation workflow independently of a product. Must every business use the same chart of accounts? No. The chart should support the business and reporting requirements, with consistent account identities and documented mappings. Is a bank-feed category sufficient supporting evidence? Not by itself. Retain the invoice, receipt, agreement or other evidence explaining the amount, purpose and reporting period. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides.
