documents.summary: Trace one service-business month through journal entries, ledger balances, adjustments, financial statements and closing with checked trial-balance totals.
documents.headings: Quick answer Record six supported events before adjusting Keep the adjustment evidence distinct Compare unadjusted and adjusted trial balances Prepare statements from the adjusted balances Close temporary accounts without deleting history Use each report for its own question Use a stage-by-stage completion test before carrying balances forward Download the editable worksheet Sources and scope Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Accounting Cycle: From Transactions to Closed Statements Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Trace one service-business month through journal entries, ledger balances, adjustments, financial statements and closing with checked trial-balance totals. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer The accounting cycle connects transaction evidence to journal entries, ledger accounts, adjustments, statements and closing. Keep the unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing balances separate so each stage has a traceable purpose. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Record six supported events before adjusting This fictional sole-proprietor service business begins with zero balances. The owner invests $10,000 cash. It buys $900 supplies on account, earns and invoices $4,000 of accepted services, collects $2,500 of that receivable, pays $600 rent for the month, and receives $1,200 for future services. No tax, depreciation, inventory for resale or owner drawings are included. Journal entries preserve the two-sided effect of each event. For example, supplies purchased on account debit Supplies and credit Accounts Payable by $900. Collecting $2,500 debits Cash and credits Accounts Receivable; it does not record another sale. Post each journal reference into the appropriate ledger accounts. Keep the adjustment evidence distinct At month end, a supported count shows $600 supplies remain, so $300 has been used. Employees have earned $700 unpaid wages. Of the $1,200 advance, $400 is now earned under the case’s service-recognition assumptions. Record three adjustments: Dr Supplies Expense / Cr Supplies $300; Dr Wages Expense / Cr Wages Payable $700; Dr Customer Advance Liability / Cr Service Revenue $400. These entries change the period’s result and balances without creating a cash transaction at the adjustment date. Preserve the count, payroll cutoff and delivery evidence. Adjusting to a desired profit number is not a valid substitute for that support. Compare unadjusted and adjusted trial balances Original trial-balance comparison, USD Account Unadjusted balance Adjusted balance Normal side Cash 13,100 13,100 Debit Accounts receivable 1,500 1,500 Debit Unused supplies 900 600 Debit Rent expense 600 600 Debit Supplies expense 0 300 Debit Wages expense 0 700 Debit Accounts payable 900 900 Credit Wages payable 0 700 Credit Customer advance liability 1,200 800 Credit Owner capital 10,000 10,000 Credit Service revenue 4,000 4,400 Credit Debit / credit totals 16,100 each 16,800 each Balanced The unadjusted trial balance totals $16,100 on each side. After adjustments, both sides total $16,800 . Equal totals show posting equality, not proof that the right accounts and periods were used. An omitted event or a wrong but balanced entry can escape this test. Prepare statements from the adjusted balances Recognized revenue is $4,400. Expenses are $600 rent + $300 supplies + $700 wages = $1,600, leaving $2,800 profit. Closing equity before any drawings is $10,000 investment + $2,800 profit = $12,800. Assets are $13,100 cash + $1,500 receivables + $600 supplies = $15,200. Liabilities are $900 AP + $700 wages + $800 unearned advance = $2,400. The balance sheet reconciles: $15,200 = $2,400 + $12,800. Cash increased $13,100 from zero, which differs from profit because owner funding, collections, credit purchases and the customer advance have different effects. The cash-flow statement and reporting framework require their own classification; do not copy the profit subtotal into a cash balance. Close temporary accounts without deleting history For this illustrative sole-proprietor closing convention, debit Revenue $4,400 and credit Income Summary. Debit Income Summary $1,600 and credit the three expense accounts. Transfer the remaining $2,800 credit from Income Summary to Owner Capital. Revenue, expenses and Income Summary then have zero balances; capital is $12,800. There are no drawings to close in this case. The post-closing trial balance contains $15,200 debit assets and $15,200 credit liabilities/equity. Real systems may automate closing or use different equity accounts; do not post these manual entries on top of an automated close. Preserve the transaction history and the reports used for approval. Use each report for its own question The journal explains what was recorded; the ledger groups postings by account. The trial balance checks aggregate equality; the statements report the resulting position and performance. The bookkeeping routine gathers evidence and reconciles detail. Accrual accounting explains why dates can differ. Keep the prior period’s closing balances as the next period’s opening balances and record correction references. Use statement analysis after the close to interpret the result, rather than treating interpretation as another posting step. Use a stage-by-stage completion test before carrying balances forward The OpenStax closing-entry explanation separates temporary revenue and expense accounts from permanent balance-sheet accounts. The teaching case uses owner capital because it is a sole-proprietor illustration. A corporation may use retained earnings and different distribution accounts. Follow the entity and system actually used instead of copying equity-account names without checking them. Treat each stage as a separate control. The unadjusted trial balance must trace to posted journals. Each adjustment needs its own evidence and reference. Statements must reconcile to the adjusted balances. The closing journals must reset only the intended temporary accounts. Finally, permanent balances must agree with the next period’s opening records. A list of stage names without these links does not demonstrate a completed close. In this case, $4,400 revenue less $1,600 expenses produces $2,800 profit before closing. Transferring that amount to capital changes where the result is recorded within equity; it does not create another $2,800 of business performance. The $15,200 post-closing debit total is smaller than the $16,800 adjusted debit total because the expense balances have been closed, not because $1,600 cash disappeared at closing. Keep both reports so that difference can be explained. Reversing selected accruals, when the system uses that procedure, is also separate from closing all temporary accounts. They show distinct stages: before adjustments, after adjustments and after temporary accounts are closed. Does a balanced trial balance prove correctness? No. Omissions, wrong classification and incorrect timing can still leave equal totals. Does closing delete old transactions? No. It resets temporary balances under the selected closing convention while preserving history. Should I manually close software that already closes automatically? Do not duplicate automated closing. Follow the actual system and reporting policy. Why do adjusted and post-closing trial-balance totals differ? Temporary accounts have been closed. In this case the $1,600 expense debit balances disappear from the post-closing trial balance while the result is transferred to equity. Does transferring profit to capital earn the profit again? No. It transfers an already measured result within the accounting records; it is not a new revenue or cash event. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Use an editable account-level ledger with posting references, debit and credit columns, a checked cash example and a matching trial-balance reconciliation. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer A general ledger groups posted transactions by account. A useful template records the date, journal reference, explanation, debit, credit and running balance, then ties the closing account to independent evidence and the trial balance. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Use one account identity and one balance convention The downloadable HTML template is editable and printable. It includes a completed Cash ledger and a blank working record with evidence and reviewer fields. It does not automatically calculate, post journals, create a trial balance or save edits. This limitation is deliberate: users must verify each result rather than assuming a blank manual template is an accounting application. Set the account name/number, period, currency, opening balance and normal side. For a debit-balance account, running balance equals opening balance + debits − credits. A credit-balance account can instead use opening credit balance + credits − debits. Label the sign convention. Debit does not universally mean money received, and credit does not universally mean a cash payment. Retain the journal behind the account detail Original supporting journal; each entry balances, USD Ref Event Debit Credit J01 Owner contribution Cash 5,000 Owner capital 5,000 J02 Equipment bought for cash Equipment 1,800 Cash 1,800 J03 Accepted service invoiced Receivable 2,200 Revenue 2,200 J04 Part collection of J03 Cash 1,600 Receivable 1,600 J05 Period service expense paid Expense 250 Cash 250 J03 does not appear in the Cash account because it creates a receivable rather than a cash receipt. It must still appear in the receivable and revenue ledgers. A cash-only record cannot replace a complete general ledger. Keep document references separate from journal references when the two identify different evidence. Check the completed Cash account Original account 100 Cash; opening zero; USD debit-balance convention Date Journal ref Description Debit Credit Running balance Nov 1 J01 Owner contribution 5,000 0 5,000 Dr Nov 3 J02 Equipment purchased 0 1,800 3,200 Dr Nov 12 J04 Customer invoice collection 1,600 0 4,800 Dr Nov 18 J05 Period expense paid 0 250 4,550 Dr Debits total $6,600 and credits $2,050. The closing Cash debit balance is $4,550 . Do not add a later bank-feed match as another $1,600 collection. Trace the existing receipt to J04 and the related customer invoice. For a nonzero opening balance, retain evidence that it equals the prior period’s reviewed closing account. An unexplained opening balance can make every subsequent row appear orderly while the account remains wrong. Reconcile the other ledgers and the trial balance Closing balances from the same five entries, USD Account Debit Credit Cash 4,550 0 Receivables 600 0 Equipment 1,800 0 Expense 250 0 Owner capital 0 5,000 Revenue 0 2,200 Total 7,200 7,200 The receivable closes at $2,200 − $1,600 = $600. Revenue less the included expense is $1,950. Assets are $4,550 + $600 + $1,800 = $6,950; equity is $5,000 + $1,950 = $6,950, with no liabilities in this case. Equal trial-balance totals still require evidence and classification review. Match Cash to a bank reconciliation, the receivable control to customer detail and Equipment to the asset register. A bank statement is not evidence for every GL account. Document and resolve differences rather than making unsupported entries to match a total. Maintain references and corrections as the ledger grows Use unique journal references, preserve the original entry and show the approved correcting or reversing entry. Keep dates and account names consistent. A sorted display is not an audit trail if someone can silently replace prior amounts. In a live system, access control, backups and period locks need a separate design. Use the bookkeeping workflow for the monthly evidence package and the accounting cycle for adjusting and closing. Customer detail and supplier detail support their respective control accounts. This template does not choose the recognition policy for every transaction. Read normal balances without treating debit and credit as cash directions The OpenStax journal and posting explanation defines journal entries before their transfer to individual accounts. Debits and credits are the two sides of an entry; their effect depends on the account. Cash and an ordinary receivable normally carry debit balances, while a payable normally carries a credit balance. A contra-asset such as accumulated depreciation has a different normal side from the related asset. Use the template as one account’s working record, not a substitute for the whole double-entry system. Every journal reference needs the complete balanced entry in its supporting record. For J03, the absence of cash movement explains why the invoice is missing from the Cash ledger, but it must still be present in Receivables and Revenue. If only bank-feed transactions were imported, the books would omit that unpaid revenue and receivable even though Cash looked correct. Check a ledger in both directions: trace selected source documents forward to the journal and ledger, then trace selected ledger lines back to their documents. Compare the date, account, amount and counter-account, not just the existence of a reference. An unusual credit in Cash may be an ordinary payment; an unusual credit balance in a customer account may require investigation or reclassification. The normal-side label helps interpret the balance but cannot replace that review. Preserve approved corrections as traceable entries instead of silently replacing the original row. Verify running balances and totals independently. Can I reconcile every account to the bank? No. Different accounts require different evidence, such as customer detail or an asset register. Does a debit always mean a cash receipt? No. Debit and credit effects depend on the account and transaction. Does debit always mean cash received? No. Debit identifies one side of an entry. For example, buying equipment for cash debits Equipment and credits Cash. Can one Cash ledger represent every transaction? No. Credit sales and other noncash events can affect other accounts without appearing in Cash. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Depreciation Methods: Asset Cost, Useful Life and Profit Impact Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare straight-line, units-of-production and declining-balance depreciation using asset cost, residual value and life assumptions, with checked effects. Turn your depreciation method into a schedule Record opening carrying value, depreciation expense and closing carrying value for each period. A $12,000 asset with $2,000 residual value and a five-year life has $2,000 annual straight-line depreciation for full years. The first year closes at $10,000 and the fifth at $2,000. Reconcile the asset schedule to accumulated depreciation and document partial periods or changes in estimates. Carry cost, residual value and useful life into the calculator, then select the method you want to compare. This is a book depreciation example. Compare full-year book schedules in the calculator Build a straight-line depreciation schedule Reconcile accumulated depreciation Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Depreciation allocates a depreciable asset’s cost over its estimated useful life under the reporting policy. Choose a method that reflects the expected consumption pattern; depreciation is not a direct estimate of market value or a cash reserve for replacement. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define the asset and depreciable amount first Start with supported capitalized cost, the date the asset is available for its intended use, useful life, residual value and the relevant consumption pattern. Distinguish repairs and period expenses from costs that meet capitalization requirements. Do not classify an item as an asset only because you prefer a smaller current expense. The original example uses equipment with $14,000 capitalized cost, $2,000 estimated residual value and a five-year useful life. The depreciable amount is $12,000. The example assumes a full first year available for use, no impairment, revaluation, disposal or estimate change, and USD financial-reporting amounts. It is not a tax-depreciation election or industry life recommendation. Compare methods on exactly the same starting asset Original first-year comparison; three alternative policies, not cumulative charges Method Year-one allocation Closing carrying amount Calculation Straight line $2,400 $11,600 12,000 depreciable base / 5 years Units of production $3,000 $11,000 12,000 / 60,000 units × 15,000 units Double declining balance $5,600 $8,400 40% × 14,000 opening carrying amount Straight line allocates $2,400 in each full year under unchanged estimates. Units of production uses a selected total life output of 60,000 units and first-year output of 15,000: $12,000 / 60,000 × 15,000 = $3,000. The 40% double-declining rate is twice the five-year straight-line rate and applies to opening carrying amount. Residual value is enforced as a floor; it is not subtracted again before applying that rate. Do not add the three charges. They are alternative methods for the same asset. Their different first-year amounts reflect different assumed consumption patterns, not three separate costs to post. Test whether the method fits the consumption evidence A reasonably even time-based consumption pattern may support straight line. A measurable usage relationship may support units of production when output records and lifetime capacity estimates are credible. A declining pattern requires support for higher earlier consumption; choosing it only to lower reported profit is not a method-selection argument. For the declining-balance illustration, full-year charges are $5,600, $3,360, $2,016, $1,024 and $0 after capping at the $2,000 residual. Total allocation is $12,000. The fourth year’s uncapped 40% amount would exceed the remaining depreciable amount, so it is limited. Another documented policy might switch methods; this schedule assumes no switch. Separate expense, inventory, cash and carrying amount If revenue before depreciation is $30,000 and other included period expenses are $20,000, the pre-depreciation result is $10,000. Treating all depreciation as a period expense in this simplified service case gives results of $7,600, $7,000 or $4,400 under the three alternatives. The asset acquisition cash payment is the same $14,000 in all three cases; the allocation itself does not pay another $2,400, $3,000 or $5,600. In production settings, depreciation can enter manufacturing overhead and inventory before reaching cost of goods sold. Do not force every asset’s depreciation into a separate current OPEX line. Reconcile the actual capitalization and expense policy. The COGS guide retains its cost boundary. Maintain estimates and keep the specialist schedules separate Document the selected method, estimate evidence, reviewer and effective date. Review a change in expected life, residual amount or use under the relevant accounting framework; do not erase prior history or call every revision an error. Impairment and disposal are different questions and can change the carrying amount outside ordinary depreciation. Use the straight-line tutorial for partial periods and a complete dated schedule. Use the accumulated-depreciation rollforward for balances and asset removals. The accounting cycle shows where supported adjustments enter statements. Tax deductions, bonus depreciation and section 179 require separate current tax guidance and are outside this financial-reporting illustration. Separate a reporting method from a tax deduction and an asset valuation The OpenStax method comparison supports the straight-line, usage and declining-balance mechanics used here. The choice concerns cost allocation under a reporting policy. It does not establish the asset’s resale value, a replacement-funding balance or a tax deduction. The case explicitly keeps the $14,000 acquisition cash amount the same under all three alternatives. For a real asset, retain the purchase and installation evidence, readiness date, approved life and residual assumptions, method rationale and review history. For a usage method, reconcile the period’s production measure to the same unit definition used for total estimated output. Do not use machine-hours for one input and saleable units for the other. For declining balance, retain the residual cap and the policy on any method switch rather than allowing a formula to drive carrying amount below its intended floor. Compare the effects using a common cutoff and cost boundary. The first-year service-case results of $7,600, $7,000 and $4,400 assume all depreciation reaches that period’s expenses. They cannot be copied unchanged into a manufacturer’s result if some allocation remains in unsold inventory. For federal tax, IRS Publication 946 addresses separate eligibility, basis, recovery-method and convention rules. A financial-statement five-year life is not proof that the same five-year tax treatment applies. Keep the reporting schedule and any tax schedule separately reconcilable. Frequently asked questions Does depreciation measure market value? No. It allocates cost under a reporting policy. Market valuation and impairment are separate analyses. Can I post all three methods together? No. The table compares alternatives for one asset. Does depreciation create replacement cash? No. The noncash allocation does not fund a bank account. Are these useful lives or tax rates recommended for my business? No. They are fictional assumptions; actual reporting and tax treatment need their own evidence. Is a depreciation schedule a replacement fund? No. Depreciation is an accounting allocation. A replacement-funding plan requires a separate cash decision. Can units-of-production inputs use different units? No. The period usage and estimated lifetime usage must use a consistent measure for the ratio to be meaningful. documents.summary: Reconcile asset cost, current depreciation and disposal removals to closing accumulated depreciation and carrying amount using a checked original example.
documents.headings: Quick answer Distinguish the period allocation from the balance Reconcile gross cost and accumulated depreciation independently Remove both the disposed cost and its accumulated balance Tie the rollforward to individual asset evidence Use a balance reconciliation for the right decision Keep impairment, disposal and ordinary depreciation as separate movements Download the editable worksheet Sources and scope Continue with assets and depreciation Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Accumulated Depreciation: Balance-Sheet Rollforward and Disposal Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Reconcile asset cost, current depreciation and disposal removals to closing accumulated depreciation and carrying amount using a checked original example. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Accumulated depreciation is the cumulative depreciation recorded against an asset or asset group that remains on the books. Reconcile opening balance, current allocations and removals separately from gross asset cost to explain the closing carrying amount. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Distinguish the period allocation from the balance Depreciation expense or capitalized depreciation is a current-period movement. Accumulated depreciation is a balance at a date. Gross cost and accumulated depreciation generally remain separate in a cost-model asset register; their difference supports carrying amount, subject to other relevant adjustments. Accumulated depreciation is not a liability owed to a supplier. This fictional rollforward assumes a cost model, no impairment, revaluation, foreign exchange, transfers or estimate changes. The stated $6,000 allocation has all been treated as period expense for simplicity and includes depreciation through the disposal date. A manufacturing asset register can require a separate inventory-cost reconciliation. Reconcile gross cost and accumulated depreciation independently Original asset-group rollforward, USD Line Amount / balance Opening gross asset cost 50,000 Additions at supported cost 10,000 Disposed asset cost removed −12,000 Closing gross asset cost 48,000 Opening accumulated depreciation 18,000 credit Current period depreciation 6,000 credit movement Accumulated depreciation removed on disposal 8,400 debit movement Closing accumulated depreciation 15,600 credit Closing carrying amount 32,400 Gross cost closes at $50,000 + $10,000 − $12,000 = $48,000. Accumulated depreciation closes at $18,000 + $6,000 − $8,400 = $15,600 . The resulting carrying amount is $48,000 − $15,600 = $32,400. Adding the $6,000 again to closing accumulated depreciation would duplicate the period allocation. The opening carrying amount was $32,000. Add $10,000 cost, subtract $6,000 depreciation and subtract the disposed asset’s $3,600 carrying amount: $32,000 + $10,000 − $6,000 − $3,600 = $32,400. The gross and net reconciliations agree. Remove both the disposed cost and its accumulated balance The disposed asset has $12,000 cost and $8,400 accumulated depreciation at sale, leaving $3,600 carrying amount. Suppose it sells for $4,000 with no selling costs. The illustrative entry debits Cash $4,000 and Accumulated Depreciation $8,400, credits Asset Cost $12,000 and Gain on Disposal $400. Debits and credits both total $12,400. The $4,000 receipt is sale proceeds, not all gain. The $8,400 debit removes the disposed asset’s contra balance; it is not negative current depreciation. If only cost were removed, the remaining register would retain depreciation belonging to an asset no longer held. If the period allocation already runs through the disposal date, do not record it a second time. Tie the rollforward to individual asset evidence Assign a durable asset ID to cost, in-use date, method, life, residual value, accumulated balance and disposal record. Reconcile opening IDs plus additions less removals to the closing register. Check fully depreciated assets still used: they may remain in the register until disposal, with cost offset by accumulated depreciation under the policy. A total can reconcile while a disposed asset remains wrongly assigned to an active location. Verify ownership, use and disposal approvals as well as arithmetic. Do not infer a gain, loss or impairment solely from a low carrying amount. Those conclusions require separate transaction and valuation evidence. Use a balance reconciliation for the right decision Use the methods overview when evaluating the consumption pattern. Use the straight-line schedule to compute a method-specific time allocation. The ledger template supports posting references, while the close workflow connects the register to statements. This article explains a financial-reporting balance. Tax basis, accumulated tax depreciation and proceeds treatment may differ and are not determined here. Preserve both schedules when required rather than overwriting financial-statement balances with tax amounts. Keep impairment, disposal and ordinary depreciation as separate movements The OpenStax long-term-asset discussion treats a revised estimate and a disposal as separate events. The $15,600 closing accumulated balance in this guide is an allocation-and-removal reconciliation under the stated cost-model assumptions. It is not an appraisal of the remaining assets and does not, by itself, establish their recoverable or market values. For the disposed item, retain its asset ID, $12,000 cost, $8,400 accumulated allocation through disposal, $4,000 proceeds and any disposal costs. The $400 gain follows only because the case assumes no selling costs and no other carrying-amount adjustments. If costs or another relevant adjustment exist, reconcile them before calculating the result rather than treating gross sale proceeds as net gain. Do not remove another active asset’s accumulated balance simply because its amount makes the group total reconcile. The closing gross-cost and accumulated schedules should agree on which asset IDs remain. A fully allocated asset can still be in use; a physical count may identify that fact without creating a new cost or rewriting its previous allocation. Conversely, an item with a positive carrying amount may have been disposed of or lost. Investigate the actual event. Where impairment or another adjustment applies under the reporting framework, show it separately; the simplified equation “cost less accumulated depreciation” is not a universal complete valuation model. Frequently asked questions Is accumulated depreciation an expense for this month? No. It is a cumulative balance. Current-period depreciation is one movement in that balance. Does a disposal remove only the original cost? No. Remove the associated accumulated depreciation as well, after updating through the disposal date as required. Is the sale receipt the gain? No. Compare net proceeds with the relevant carrying amount. Must a fully depreciated asset disappear from the register? Not merely because it is fully depreciated; confirm the actual disposal and applicable policy. Does a low carrying amount prove impairment? No. Carrying amount alone does not establish an impairment conclusion; the applicable framework and evidence require a separate assessment. Why retain asset IDs in the rollforward? They help ensure that disposed cost and accumulated balances belong to the same item and that closing balances relate to assets still recorded. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Straight-Line Depreciation: Formula, Partial Periods and Schedule Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate straight-line depreciation with supported cost, residual value, useful life and partial periods. Reconcile a complete editable sixty-month schedule. Check the full-year schedule with your own asset Enter cost, residual value and useful life in the calculator, then select straight-line. Compare its annual expense and final carrying value with your worksheet. The interactive schedule uses full years. Use this guide’s worked calendar-year schedule for the in-service month and partial periods. Open the Business Depreciation Calculator Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Straight-line depreciation allocates the depreciable amount evenly across the selected time-based useful life. Annual allocation equals cost minus residual value, divided by life in years; a partial-period schedule must use an explicit start date and time convention. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define cost, life, residual and in-use date For this independent service-asset case, capitalized cost is $14,000, residual value $2,000 and useful life five years. The asset is available for intended use on April 1, 2027. The example adopts a whole-month convention beginning that date and assumes no impairment, disposal, method switch or estimate change. These are teaching assumptions, not mandatory asset lives or a universal partial-month rule. The purchase invoice can precede readiness for use. Keep evidence of the in-use date and explain any capitalization policy. Tax conventions can differ from this financial-reporting month count; do not automatically apply a tax half-year or mid-quarter convention to this schedule. Compute the annual and monthly amounts once Depreciable amount = $14,000 − $2,000 = $12,000. Annual straight-line depreciation = $12,000 / 5 = $2,400 . Monthly amount = $2,400 / 12 = $200. Equivalently, $12,000 / 60 months = $200 per month. The full-year rate is 20% of the depreciable amount, not 20% of cost without considering residual value. April through December includes nine months under the stated convention, so 2027 allocation is $200 × 9 = $1,800. Nine months is not a universal rule for every April purchase; it follows this exact in-use date and policy. Reconcile the complete calendar-year schedule Original sixty-month straight-line schedule; amounts in USD Calendar period Months Period allocation Closing accumulated Closing carrying amount 2027 Apr–Dec 9 1,800 1,800 12,200 2028 12 2,400 4,200 9,800 2029 12 2,400 6,600 7,400 2030 12 2,400 9,000 5,000 2031 12 2,400 11,400 2,600 2032 Jan–Mar 3 600 12,000 2,000 Total 60 12,000 12,000 closing 2,000 residual The six calendar rows cover only five years of useful life: 9 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 3 = 60 months. Four full intervening calendar years allocate $9,600. The first $1,800 and final $600 complete the $12,000 depreciable amount. Closing carrying amount stops at the $2,000 residual; do not charge another full $2,400 in 2032. Exact carrying amounts from the original dated schedule. Post the allocation without inventing another cash payment If the first nine months are all period expense in this service example, debit Depreciation Expense and credit Accumulated Depreciation by $1,800 for 2027. The original asset cost remains $14,000, accumulated depreciation becomes $1,800 and carrying amount is $12,200. No cash leaves the bank merely because that entry is posted. Production assets may contribute depreciation to inventory costs instead. The example does not prescribe that classification for every business. Keep acquisition cash, capitalization, current allocation and eventual expense recognition traceable rather than automatically treating them as one payment. Handle changes and rounding with a documented policy Reassess estimates when supported facts change. A change in remaining life or residual value may change future allocation; do not silently rewrite old months or automatically treat an estimate revision as an error. An actual disposal or impairment also requires its own analysis. Use the applicable framework and approval process. For a monthly amount that is not exact to cents, retain calculation precision and reconcile the final allocation to the intended residual. Do not round every input repeatedly and then allow the schedule to drift below its floor. This worksheet is manual and does not enforce that check automatically. Keep the method tutorial separate from the balance rollforward The depreciation overview compares time, usage and declining patterns. The accumulated-depreciation guide reconciles additions, current allocations and removals. The bookkeeping close provides the recurring review routine. Record your cost evidence, readiness date, life, residual, convention and reviewer in the downloadable schedule. If any is unknown, the result is provisional; a precise formula cannot supply missing business evidence. Distinguish a changed estimate from an error in the original schedule The OpenStax discussion of revised estimates illustrates allocating a remaining depreciable amount over a revised remaining life. That is a different task from correcting an arithmetic error. Keep the original approved schedule and document why new information changes an estimate; do not simply overwrite its life or residual assumptions without an effective date. In the unchanged case here, April 2027 through March 2032 contains exactly sixty whole months. A genuine revision would require a separately documented carrying amount at the revision date, supported remaining life and updated residual estimate. Use those facts for the future schedule under the applicable policy. A mistake in the original cost, a wrongly entered start date and newly learned usage information are not automatically the same type of change. Before using a partial-period result, verify the year, available-for-use date, convention, reporting cutoff and rounding treatment. Reconcile the first partial period and final residual, not just the annual formula. A tax convention cannot be selected solely because it creates the same first-year amount as this teaching case: IRS Publication 946 is the separate federal tax reference. Likewise, a switch to a usage method or an actual disposal requires its own decision. The manual worksheet preserves a working record but does not automatically implement any of these changes. Frequently asked questions Why does a five-year asset appear in six calendar years? The first and last calendar years are partial. The schedule still contains exactly sixty months. Does straight line use cost without residual value? The depreciable amount is cost less the supported residual estimate. Is purchase date always the depreciation start date? Not necessarily. Check readiness for intended use and the applicable reporting policy. Does this calculate a tax deduction? No. It is a financial-reporting illustration with a stated time convention. Does new useful-life information mean the original accounting was necessarily wrong? No. New information can support a change in estimate. An original error requires a separate assessment and treatment. What should be checked before using a partial-year result? Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build an illustrative receivables aging estimate and reconcile opening allowance, write-offs, recoveries and the provision needed for the closing balance. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer An allowance for doubtful accounts reduces gross receivables to a supported carrying amount for expected credit losses. Estimate the required closing balance, then reconcile the existing allowance before calculating the provision; the required balance is not automatically this period’s expense. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. State the reporting framework and current policy choices This educational example uses US GAAP credit-loss terminology for ordinary trade receivables. It is not a complete ASC 326 model or a substitute for entity-specific accounting review. Aging percentages are fictional assumptions, not prescribed rates. Assess relevant experience, current conditions, customer-specific evidence and the applicable forecasting requirements. FASB ASU 2025-05 introduced optional simplifications for in-scope current receivables and contract assets. A current-conditions practical expedient and, for qualifying nonpublic entities using it, a subsequent-collections policy election require their own scope and disclosure assessment. The example below assumes neither election. Do not infer that every entity must use the same forecast or subsequent-cash treatment. Build the closing estimate from a defined receivables population Original November 30 aging illustration; USD, due-date buckets Bucket Gross balance Assumed loss rate Estimated allowance Not past due 50,000 1% 500 1–30 days past due 20,000 4% 800 Over 30 days past due 10,000 15% 1,500 Total gross receivables 80,000 Illustrative rates only 2,800 required closing allowance The three amounts reconcile to $80,000 gross AR. The required closing allowance is $500 + $800 + $1,500 = $2,800 , giving a $77,200 net carrying amount. Review whether similar risk characteristics support the grouping and whether any balance needs separate assessment. Avoid applying both a pooled rate and a second specific allowance to the same exposure without reconciling the overlap. A bucket percentage must have a defensible basis and an update process in a real model. The arithmetic alone does not establish a compliant loss estimate. Preserve how credits, disputes, write-offs and subsequent evidence affect the population and rates. Reconcile the existing allowance before recording the provision Original allowance movement before and after estimation, USD credit-positive convention Movement / target Amount Opening allowance credit 1,200 Write-offs debited to allowance −700 Reinstatement on recovery +200 Credit balance before new provision 700 Required closing allowance 2,800 Current provision credit needed 2,100 Opening credit $1,200 − $700 write-offs + $200 recovery reinstatement leaves $700 credit before the new provision. To reach $2,800, record a $2,100 provision: Dr Credit Loss / Bad Debt Expense, Cr Allowance. Recording the entire $2,800 as new expense would overstate this example’s provision by $700. If the pre-adjustment allowance instead had a $300 debit balance, reaching $2,800 credit would require a $3,100 credit provision. Keep debit and credit signs visible; subtracting an unsigned balance can produce the wrong answer. Reconcile gross and net AR as well as the allowance For the same fictional period, opening gross AR is $60,000. Add $40,000 credit sales, deduct $19,300 ordinary collections and $700 write-offs, reinstate $200 recovered receivable and collect that $200. Closing gross AR is $80,000. Total collections are $19,500, including the recovery; do not deduct that recovery twice. Opening net AR is $60,000 − $1,200 = $58,800. Add $40,000 credit sales, deduct $19,500 cash collections and $2,100 provision to get $77,200 closing net AR. A write-off against an existing allowance reduces gross AR and allowance together, so it does not by itself create a second net-AR loss in this model. Keep approval, evidence and estimation separate Support write-offs and recoveries with approved customer records. Reconcile the detailed customer ledger to the gross AR control, and the allowance schedule to its own control account. A customer promise is not collected cash; a write-off is not a cash payment. Document the estimate owner, review date and changes in assumptions. Use the receivable workflow for invoice detail and the bad-debt expense guide for the event-by-event provision, write-off and recovery entries. The current-assets guide explains gross versus net presentation. Tax deductibility is a separate determination and is not established by an allowance entry. Apply the current policy scope before treating an aging table as an estimate The official FASB ASU 2025-05 summary states that the optional changes apply to specified current receivables and contract assets arising under Topic 606. The effective annual periods begin after December 15, 2025, with early adoption permitted. This case does not elect the options; its arithmetic is not evidence that another entity’s population or policy qualifies. Before using a real aging matrix, reconcile the population to the gross receivable control, separate credit balances and disputed items for review, and record how due dates are assigned. Keep the loss-rate support, risk grouping, current information and any forecasting assessment together with the calculation. A rate copied from an online article is an unsupported input even when the multiplication is exact. A customer’s overdue status and an approved write-off are also different facts. The $2,800 target is a closing allowance balance. The current $2,100 provision follows from the existing $700 credit after the specified write-off and recovery events. If the pre-adjustment allowance were already higher than the supported target, investigate the evidence and policy rather than forcing another positive expense simply because a table has a positive estimated loss. Keep a signed rollforward: opening allowance, provision or release, write-offs, recoveries and other explained movements. Reconcile the net receivable as well as the gross population so an adjustment is not counted twice. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . Frequently asked questions Is the required allowance the same as this period’s expense? Not necessarily. Reconcile the existing debit or credit balance and intervening movements first. Are the 1%, 4% and 15% rates recommended? No. They are fictional inputs to demonstrate arithmetic, not a compliant estimate for another business. Does writing off an already provided balance create another expense? Under this allowance example, it reduces gross AR and allowance together rather than recognizing the expense twice. Does the guide apply every current US GAAP simplification? No. The case assumes neither ASU 2025-05 election; eligibility, consistency and disclosures require separate review. Do the optional FASB changes cover every financial asset? No. ASU 2025-05 describes a specified scope for current receivables and contract assets arising from Topic 606 transactions. Must every adjustment to an allowance increase expense? No. Compare the supported closing requirement with the signed existing balance and movements; the evidence can require a provision or a release under the applicable policy. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Bad Debt Expense: Provision, Write-Off and Recovery Published November 7, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Separate bad-debt expense recognition, an allowance write-off and a later recovery with balanced entries and a reconciled gross, allowance and net-AR example. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Bad debt expense recognizes a credit-loss provision under the selected accounting policy. A later write-off and recovery are different events. Under an allowance approach, do not record the same expected loss again as expense when the customer balance is removed. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Identify whether you are estimating, writing off or collecting This original example uses a US GAAP-style allowance approach for trade receivables, solely to explain posting mechanics. It does not build the full expected-credit-loss estimate. Opening gross AR is $25,000 and allowance is $1,500 credit. Assume a separately supported review requires a $900 current provision before the later events below; there are no other sales, ordinary collections, credits or tax effects. The allowance guide owns estimation, including current FASB policy choices. A percentage of sales or a textbook aging table should not automatically be described as complete current US GAAP compliance. Keep the entity’s applicable method and approval evidence visible. Record each event with its own balanced entry Original allowance-method entries, USD Event Debit Credit Cash at this step Provision Credit loss / bad debt expense 900 Allowance 900 None Approved write-off Allowance 1,200 Customer receivable 1,200 None Reinstate recovered balance Customer receivable 300 Allowance 300 None Collect recovered balance Cash 300 Customer receivable 300 Receipt 300 The provision reduces current profit by $900 under this case’s expense convention. The write-off uses the existing allowance. Reinstatement restores the customer item before the supported receipt is allocated. Do not treat the recovered $300 as another sale or automatically reverse $300 of expense without examining the actual policy and allowance estimate. A write-off decision requires documented authorization and the relevant accounting assessment. It is not created merely by reaching an arbitrary number of days overdue. Collection rights, customer communications and tax treatment can involve separate considerations. Follow gross AR, allowance and net AR through the sequence Original event-level balance bridge; no other movements Stage Gross AR Allowance Net AR Cash movement Opening balances 25,000 1,500 credit 23,500 0 Record 900 provision 25,000 2,400 credit 22,600 0 Write off 1,200 23,800 1,200 credit 22,600 0 Reinstate recovered 300 24,100 1,500 credit 22,600 0 Collect recovered 300 23,800 1,500 credit 22,300 +300 The $1,200 write-off reduces gross AR from $25,000 to $23,800 and allowance from $2,400 to $1,200, leaving net AR unchanged at $22,600 . Reinstating $300 increases both balances and still leaves net AR at $22,600. Collecting $300 then changes the composition of assets: net AR becomes $22,300 and cash increases $300. Across the full sequence, opening net AR $23,500 − $900 provision − $300 recovered cash collection = $22,300. The write-off is not a $1,200 cash payment, and the recovery is not $300 new revenue. Reassess the closing allowance under the actual reporting policy after all relevant evidence is considered. Do not confuse an allowance provision with direct write-off treatment A direct write-off presentation records an expense when a specific receivable is removed, rather than first using an allowance. That timing differs from the modeled sequence. It is not presented here as an unrestricted alternative for financial reporting or as automatic tax treatment. Method suitability, materiality, framework and current requirements need their own review. Financial-reporting expense, customer-ledger removal and tax deduction can occur under different conditions. Recording an allowance or approving a customer write-off does not itself prove a tax deduction is available. This guide intentionally makes no deduction amount, eligibility or filing claim. Reconcile and preserve the recovery trail Retain customer ID, original invoice, provision policy, write-off approval, reinstatement reference, bank evidence and cash allocation. Check the customer subledger against gross AR and the allowance rollforward against its control account at the same cutoff. If a receipt cannot be identified, investigate rather than attaching it to a convenient written-off balance. Use the collection workflow for payment matching, the general ledger record for posting references and the accounting cycle for the reviewed close. A clear audit trail keeps estimation uncertainty separate from an observed bank receipt. Keep an allowance write-off separate from a tax-worthlessness conclusion The OpenStax uncollectible-account illustration distinguishes estimation from a later removal of a customer balance. This guide demonstrates that mechanical distinction. It does not present its two-step reinstatement and collection sequence as the only recovery presentation permitted under every accounting policy. For each event, identify what actually changed. The $900 provision changes the allowance estimate and included period expense. The $1,200 write-off removes a customer item and uses the existing allowance. The $300 reinstatement restores that item in the illustrated process; the subsequent $300 receipt must match bank evidence. Keep those references together so an automated receipt import cannot create a second collection, a second expense or a new sale. An internal credit approval, a financial-reporting estimate, a customer-ledger write-off and a federal tax deduction do not share an automatic trigger. If tax treatment is needed, use the IRS bad-debt topic and the applicable business-debt guidance for the taxpayer and facts. Do not assume an unpaid invoice was previously included in taxable income, especially where a different tax accounting method is used. The numerical case intentionally makes no deductible-amount claim. Preserve the accounting trail even if legal collection activity or a tax assessment follows a different timetable. Frequently asked questions Does a write-off always create new bad debt expense? Not under this allowance example. It uses a balance that was already provided. Is a recovered debt new sales revenue? Not simply because cash arrived. Trace the original receivable and the applicable recovery treatment. Is a write-off a cash outflow? No. Removing the receivable does not itself move cash. Does an accounting expense prove tax deductibility? No. Tax conditions and financial-reporting entries require separate analysis. Does this guide prescribe the only permitted recovery entry? No. It illustrates a two-step reinstatement and receipt sequence; use the policy appropriate to the entity and accounting framework. Does a customer-ledger write-off automatically create a federal deduction? No. The applicable tax conditions and accounting-method history require a separate determination. documents.headings: Quick answer Define the objective before listing risks Build a register that can produce an action Calculate exposure without calling it a reserve Stress the dated cash position separately Choose, test and review the response Make the likelihood estimate and control decision auditable Download the editable worksheet Sources and scope Continue with strategy, growth and risk Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Business Risk Assessment: Financial Impact and Response Plan Published November 6, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a business risk register with impact ranges, control costs, owners and response triggers. Compare expected exposure with a dated cash stress case. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer A business risk assessment identifies events that could prevent an objective, estimates their impact and likelihood over a defined horizon, and assigns a response owner. Use a risk register to turn the assessment into dated decisions, not just a colored score. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Define the objective before listing risks Start with an observable objective: for this fictional workshop, deliver accepted jobs over the next quarter while keeping available cash above a chosen $6,000 floor. Name the horizon and which operations are included. “Economic risk” is too broad to assign; “the sole component supplier fails to deliver before a committed customer date” identifies an event, a dependency and an exposure. Separate the cause, event and consequence. An unreliable supplier is a cause; a missed delivery is an event; replacement freight, idle labor and a delayed customer receipt are consequences. Record existing controls before estimating the remaining exposure. A business risk register can sit within enterprise risk management, but this small-business worksheet is not a certified ERM or cybersecurity standard. Build a register that can produce an action Original quarterly workshop risk register; ranges are management assumptions Event Assumed probability Impact / cash effect Proposed control cost Owner Review trigger Supplier interruption 10–20% / quarter $12,000–$20,000 Backup supplier test: $600 Ops lead Lead time > 14 days Customer delay 15–30% / quarter $8,000 receipt shifted Milestone verification: $200 Collections lead Invoice disputed > 5 days Equipment failure 5–10% / quarter $3,000–$7,000 Service/backup review: $300 Workshop lead Failed inspection The probabilities are deliberately uncertain assumptions, not observed frequencies. Add evidence dates, control status and an assessment confidence note. A control described as planned is not an effective control until implemented and tested. Keep inherent exposure and residual exposure as separate versions, with a reason for any estimated reduction. Calculate exposure without calling it a reserve At a selected 15% probability and $16,000 loss, the supplier event has a simple probability-weighted exposure of $2,400 per quarter . If a tested backup arrangement reduced the assumed probability to 8%, holding severity constant, exposure would be $1,280. The modeled reduction is $1,120; less a $600 control cost leaves $520 in this narrow comparison. It does not prove the control will work or that spending $600 is the best decision. Do not multiply an ordinal “likelihood 4” by an ordinal “impact 5” and label 20 as dollars. Do not add overlapping consequences twice, such as total lost sales plus the full profit lost on those same sales. Identify which costs stop when delivery stops. Consider correlated events: one outage could delay both the supplier and the customer. A simple sum of independent-looking scores can conceal that dependency. Stress the dated cash position separately Suppose opening available cash is $14,000. Planned receipts of $18,000 and payments of $20,000 give $12,000 closing cash. A receipt delay of $8,000 gives $4,000, below the selected $6,000 floor by $2,000. The customer may still owe the money; moving its clearing date is a funding problem, not automatically an $8,000 permanent loss. Re-run the following periods when the receipt clears. Combine plausible disruptions and test payment order near the low point. A probability-weighted loss cannot tell you whether payroll clears on Friday. Use the financial contingency plan for response funding and the dated cash-flow forecast for timing. Choose, test and review the response Compare avoiding the activity, reducing exposure, transferring a defined part or consciously accepting the residual risk. Check the actual contract or insurance scope before treating a transfer as effective. Record cost, implementation date, responsible person and evidence of a test. A second supplier that has not qualified the component is still an unresolved dependency. Review when a trigger occurs and at a scheduled cutoff. Preserve the prior estimate so a changed forecast cannot erase the original decision. Close an action only after its evidence exists; keep the risk open if the underlying exposure remains. Tie the major unresolved conditions to the feasibility decision rather than assigning every risk a low score to justify proceeding. Make the likelihood estimate and control decision auditable A probability needs an event definition and a time unit. In this original example, interpret 15% as the assumed chance of at least one specified supplier interruption during the next quarter, with $16,000 as the modeled loss if it occurs. This is a deliberately simplified single-event model. A recurring incident count requires a frequency model instead; do not multiply a probability of at least one event by an assumed number of incidents without explaining the change. The December 2025 NIST risk-estimation revision addresses cybersecurity risk, while the Canadian public-service register illustrates context, controls, residual exposure and ownership. Neither supplies this workshop’s probabilities. Record the evidence behind the original estimate and the assumptions behind the proposed 8% residual estimate. Until the backup supplier passes its qualification test, retain the uncontrolled scenario in the decision record. For a fair comparison, charge the $600 control cost against the same quarter used for the $1,120 modeled exposure reduction. If the $600 is one-time setup but benefits last longer, build a multi-period comparison rather than repeating or omitting the setup arbitrarily. Also test the cost on the actual payment date: a control can improve a probability-weighted comparison while worsening this week’s cash low point. Approval should state who accepts the remaining exposure, what evidence would invalidate the estimate and which trigger starts the contingency action. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is a risk score the same as expected loss? No. An ordinal ranking is a prioritization aid. A monetary expected-loss estimate needs explicit probabilities, amounts and a consistent horizon. Should I hold the expected loss as cash? Not automatically. Size the funding response using dated commitments, severe plausible scenarios and the chosen cash floor. Does moving a customer receipt create a loss? A delay changes timing. A loss requires a separate assessment of recoverability and costs. When should the register be updated? At its scheduled review and whenever a material trigger, incident, dependency or control changes. Is the 15% probability a published industry rate? No. It is a fictional quarterly assumption used to explain the method. A real assessment needs dated evidence and an explicit event definition. Can a one-time control cost be compared with an annual benefit directly? First align the time horizon. Record setup and recurring costs separately and model benefits over the same periods. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Online Business Ideas: Compare Services, Products and Ecommerce Published November 6, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare online services, digital products and ecommerce using contribution, owner-hours, demand evidence and the time between paying costs and collecting cash. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Choose an online business idea by testing the customer problem, delivery work, contribution and cash cycle. Services, digital products and ecommerce can each be workable, but an online sale does not remove acquisition, support or collection costs. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Choose the operating model before the platform Consider a narrowly scoped editing service, a specialist spreadsheet template or a curated physical accessory. Each needs a defined buyer and evidence that the offer solves a problem. The service sells a delivery commitment; the download sells a usable digital asset; ecommerce adds sourcing, stock and fulfillment. These are examples to test, not a ranking of profitable opportunities. A marketplace can supply discovery and payment tools while creating fees, competition and platform dependence. Your own site offers different control but still needs a way to attract qualified customers. Do not choose by the platform headline alone: write who buys, why, what they receive, when they pay and what you must do after the sale. Put three models on a consistent cost boundary Original per-sale examples; before fixed overhead, income tax and unpaid owner time Model Net price Included variable costs Contribution Resource constraint Cash issue Client service $600 engagement $90 delivery + $150 acquisition $360 12 owner-hours Approval and collection Digital download $40 sale $4 delivery/support + $12 acquisition $24 60 setup hours + support Refunds and ongoing updates Stocked ecommerce $80 order $42 goods + $10 delivery/fees + $12 acquisition $16 Inventory and fulfillment Supplier payment before settlement The service contribution is $600 − $90 − $150 = $360, or $30 per owner-hour over twelve hours. The download leaves $24 per sale. At 100 sales, that is $2,400 before recovering setup work and fixed costs. Valuing 60 creation hours at a selected $25 adds a $1,500 planning requirement; that is an explicit owner-time assumption, not a cash invoice or market wage. The ecommerce order contributes $16 after the included costs. A hypothetical $800 monthly fixed commitment requires 50 orders merely to cover that commitment at unchanged unit economics. Refunds, damaged stock and owner pay still need their own included or separately identified treatment. A higher revenue total can coexist with a weaker cash position. Collect evidence matched to the model What a small test must reveal Model Test Evidence beyond a click Reason to revise Service One tightly scoped paid pilot Accepted output, time log, collection Revisions exceed scope Digital product Small usable sample and paid release Buyer can use the file; support requests Purchase depends on misleading claims Ecommerce Small stock batch Net receipts, returns, delivery cost Unsold inventory absorbs cash Interest is useful but not equivalent to an order. Record prospects who declined as well as buyers. A successful pilot demonstrates that one transaction worked under its conditions; it does not establish a repeatable acquisition cost or a large market. Set a test budget and decision date before seeing the result. Trace cash before calling a model low-cost For a separate ecommerce batch of 50 units, paying $42 goods cost per unit uses $2,100 before sales. If only 30 units sell, 20 units remain in stock. Do not expense or ignore that stock solely to make a launch cash estimate match a per-order contribution table. Shipping, acquisition, fees, refunds and settlement delays need their own dates. The startup cost calculator organizes one-time and recurring cash requirements. A digital product avoids physical stock but can still require software, licensed materials, design effort, support and maintenance. A service may require no inventory but be capped by qualified delivery hours. Test the bottleneck that actually constrains the model. Choose the next test rather than an earnings promise Reject a model if you cannot deliver it competently, access the intended customers or tolerate its funding gap. Verify relevant professional and local requirements for the actual activity. Do not infer permission to offer regulated services from an idea list. Compare the best-supported alternatives in the general business-idea screen . After selecting a model, use the online launch workflow to test checkout and delivery. Use the business model canvas to record dependencies. Keep the chosen model provisional until repeat transactions show that its demand, costs and support burden can coexist. Test the rights, dependency and cash behind the offer Before paying for a supposedly automated store or template package, identify exactly what you will own or be permitted to use: the domain, customer relationship, source files, product images, software account and supplier arrangement. Record restrictions on commercial use and resale. An attractive mockup does not establish that the seller owns the materials or that a marketplace will permit the proposed activity. The FTC’s business-opportunity warning describes the danger of unsupported online-store earnings promises. Treat projected revenue as an assumption until supported by records that also show costs and unsuccessful outcomes. Check the seller, cancellation terms, references and any applicable disclosure obligations before buying an opportunity. A third-party service’s claim is not evidence that your own account, inventory or delivery system can achieve its result. Use the existing original ecommerce case to separate unsold stock from lost cash. Paying $2,100 for fifty units and selling thirty leaves twenty units costing $840 in the simplified stock record. Cash has already left for all fifty, but that does not make the remaining twenty units another acquisition expense for each of the thirty sold. Investigate damage or unsellability separately. For a digital download, retain a dated version and test the file in the promised application; for the service, log revisions and unpaid selling time. The next decision is whether repeat orders remain deliverable at the recorded net economics, not whether the model can be described as passive income. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Which online business is most profitable? There is no universal answer. Compare actual demand, included costs, owner time and cash needs for a specific offer. Are digital downloads passive income? Creation, updates, support, acquisition and refund handling can require ongoing work. Does a marketplace remove marketing costs? No. Fees, advertising, listing effort and customer support can still affect the economics. Should I start with a large inventory order? Use supplier terms, test evidence and the downside cash schedule to decide; a small batch can limit an unproven commitment. Does an automated-store provider guarantee a usable business? No. Verify account control, permitted activity, delivery responsibilities, total costs and the evidence behind earnings claims. Are the twenty unsold units automatically a loss? Not in this simplified inventory example. They remain stock subject to the applicable measurement assessment, although their purchase has already used cash. Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Launch a defined online offer with a small demand test, checked payment and delivery workflow, checked unit-economics case and a launch acceptance worksheet. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Start an online business by defining one offer and customer, validating demand, checking the requirements for that activity, and testing a complete payment-to-delivery workflow before scaling. Measure net receipts and delivery capacity alongside sales. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Write a testable offer and acceptance boundary Specify the deliverable, exclusions, net price, turnaround, revision limits and how acceptance is recorded. For the fictional pilot here, a $300 service package takes six delivery hours and $40 job-specific cash costs. Record when the buyer can cancel and how a refund or complaint will be handled. Do not promise outcomes that you cannot substantiate. Use the online model comparison if the model is undecided. This guide starts after that choice. It does not require a custom store: the first workflow can be simple if it supports accurate terms, appropriate records and a reliable way to fulfill the offer. Run one bounded demand test Original service pilot; all five orders are completed and accepted Measure Case value Evidence / boundary Qualified inquiries 20 Fictional inquiry log; illustrative only Paid orders 5 25% of inquiries in this case only Net sales 5 × $300 = $1,500 Accepted service package Delivery cash costs 5 × $40 = $200 Tools and job inputs Acquisition test spend $250 One test channel Pilot surplus after included costs $1,050 Before owner time and overhead Owner delivery time 5 × 6 = 30 hours $35 pilot surplus per delivery hour Five divided by twenty is a 25% conversion for this fictional teaching pilot, not a forecast or a platform benchmark. The $1,050 is not take-home pay. It excludes owner selling time, general administration, fixed subscriptions, tax and setup work. If delivery takes eight hours instead of six, 40 hours produce $26.25 pilot surplus per delivery hour with other inputs unchanged. At a selected 40-hour delivery ceiling, six-hour jobs permit at most six whole packages, before checking demand. Seven need 42 hours. Record a stop rule for spend, late work, refunds and capacity. A profitable five-order sample does not justify multiplying the result by all website visitors. Check the activity and selling locations SBA launch guidance separates registration, IDs, permits, banking and insurance. The IRS startup checklist is explicitly not exhaustive and points to state requirements. Record which official state and local offices apply to your actual business, where customers are served and what evidence remains outstanding. This article does not decide entity choice, tax nexus or professional licensing for you. For a business operating at home, also check workspace, property and capacity constraints . For US merchandise orders, the FTC explains requirements concerning advertised shipping times, delay consent and refunds. Read the applicable rule before making a shipping promise. Do not treat that merchandise-specific reference as a universal rule for every digital or professional service. Test order, payment, delivery and reversal together Launch acceptance record Stage Test evidence Failure to resolve before wider launch Offer Customer sees scope, total and timing Hidden costs or unavailable promise Payment Authorized test matches order amount Duplicate charge or wrong currency Delivery Buyer receives correct item or access Broken file or missed handoff Reversal Refund/credit traced to order Refund missing from records Records Order, fees and settlement reconcile Bank receipt treated as gross sales Use authorized test transactions or a processor’s documented test environment; do not fabricate a customer review. Check the workflow on a phone and keyboard. For downloads, open the delivered file on the intended application. For services, test booking and approval. For merchandise, verify packaging, tracking and return handling. Reconcile the first orders before increasing spend If the processor settles less than gross customer charges, identify fees, refunds, taxes and timing rather than editing invoice amounts to match the bank. Keep gross activity and settlement deductions traceable. Use the receivable process for unpaid customer invoices and the payable process for supplier obligations. Prepare a dated cash plan including setup payments, settlement delays and owner withdrawals separately from the defined operating result. For the detailed physical-store funding boundary use the ecommerce startup-cost guide . Continue with measurable business goals only after the delivery system and records are working. Set separate launch tests for merchandise and service promises For US merchandise covered by the FTC’s order rule guidance , a seller needs a reasonable basis for its stated shipping time; when no shipping time is stated, the usual rule is shipment within thirty days after a properly completed order. If timely shipment becomes impossible, follow the applicable delay-consent or cancellation/refund procedure. This is not a universal thirty-day delivery rule for every online transaction, and the FTC guidance identifies exemptions and special cases. Services are outside this merchandise rule. For the original service pilot, make the delivery promise testable: what file or work product is due, how the buyer confirms receipt, which revisions are included and who handles a failed handoff. A payment receipt establishes a payment event; it does not by itself prove completed service performance. Keep the five fictional orders labeled as teaching data when presenting the 25% inquiry conversion. Replace them with genuine dated business records before describing a real customer result. The $1,050 includes a one-off $250 test budget, so it is a defined pilot surplus rather than standard sales-minus-variable-cost contribution margin. The launch decision should have separate evidence for offer accuracy, payment, fulfillment and customer communications. The FTC review-rule Q&A explains why businesses must avoid fake or false testimonials and incentives conditioned on a particular review sentiment. Ask genuine buyers for their actual experience; a test order, generated persona or fictional worked case must not become a customer endorsement. Record unresolved launch defects with an owner and retest the repaired step before increasing demand. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven.
