SBA: launch requirements IRS: startup checklist and state-level requirements FTC: merchandise shipping and delay requirements Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Do I need a custom website to test an offer? Not necessarily. Use a channel that can present accurate terms, accept appropriate payments and support reliable delivery and records. Can I forecast a 25% conversion rate from this case? No. The fraction describes only the fictional twenty-inquiry pilot. Is processor settlement the same as revenue? No. Fees, refunds, tax amounts and timing can make the bank deposit differ from recorded sales. When should I increase advertising? After checking delivery capacity, net economics, refunds, settlement timing and the quality of repeat demand. Does the FTC’s usual thirty-day shipping rule cover my consulting service? The cited rule concerns covered merchandise orders, not services. Service promises still need their own applicable contractual and legal assessment. Can the fictional five-order pilot be described as a client result? No. It is a teaching example. Actual result claims need genuine underlying records and an accurate description of what was measured. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Start a Home-Based Business: Workspace, Costs and Capacity Published November 6, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Plan a home-based business with separate workspace, incremental costs, operating limits, capacity and a location-specific verification record. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer A home-based business needs a workable location, a clear boundary between household and business activity, and enough delivery capacity to cover its commitments. Check the actual property and local requirements before assuming that working from home removes premises costs or restrictions. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Verify the proposed activity at the actual address List customer visits, employees, storage, deliveries, noise, equipment and signage before asking the relevant authority what is permitted. Arizona Commerce’s location checklist illustrates why residential zoning and property restrictions matter even for an online business. It is an Arizona reference, not permission for another city or state. Obtain current information for your actual location. Keep a dated verification record: office contacted, activity described, response, reference number and unresolved conditions. Review lease or property restrictions and relevant insurance coverage. A quiet desk-based activity and a home food-production operation need different checks. Do not substitute a generic startup checklist for activity-specific requirements. Design the work boundary and safe capacity Specify a dedicated work area, storage maximum, customer handoff method and working hours. Separate business records and customer data from shared household access. Identify equipment, internet or power dependencies and the practical fallback if a failure prevents a promised delivery. Avoid counting every hour at home as productive capacity. In this case, the owner has 56 hours available monthly, reserves 16 for administration and selling, and can deliver in the remaining 40. At two hours per completed job, that permits 20 jobs. Family commitments, interruptions and rework could lower that ceiling. Test actual completion times before accepting the maximum schedule. Separate incremental cash from household allocations Original home-based service budget; no tax deduction claim Item Amount / quantity Scope One-time equipment $900 Cash before launch Workspace adaptation $300 Cash before launch Monthly incremental commitments $350 Software, utilities and cover in this case Net price per job $120 Accepted service output Relevant cash cost per job $25 Included job inputs Contribution per job $95 Before owner income and fixed costs Practical job capacity 20 40 available delivery hours / 2 hours Selected owner-income goal $1,500 / month Separate planning requirement Startup cash here is $900 + $300 = $1,200. It is separate from the monthly $350 commitments. A fair-use share of existing household rent may help an internal full-cost view, but it is not necessarily an additional cash payment caused by starting. Document whether each amount is new cash, an allocation or an owner-time allowance. The treatment for a tax return is a separate question for the applicable rules and adviser. At $95 contribution, covering $350 monthly commitments takes four whole jobs because $350 / $95 is about 3.68. Adding the separate $1,500 owner-income planning goal needs twenty jobs because $1,850 / $95 is about 19.47. That uses the entire delivery capacity. It leaves little room for rework and does not fund additional owner benefits or tax. Test a slower job before relying on the plan At 2.5 hours per job, forty delivery hours permit sixteen jobs. Sixteen × $95 − $350 = $1,170 toward the stated owner goal, leaving a $330 gap against $1,500. The business can cover its narrow overhead while failing the owner-income target. Do not label “above operating break-even” as “enough to support the owner.” If all twenty jobs sell at the planned scope, $2,400 sales less $500 job cash costs and $350 commitments leaves $1,550 before the separate exclusions. Recovery of the $1,200 startup spending requires additional analysis over time; do not deduct it twice as both a one-time launch payment and monthly fixed cash. Set a review routine before accepting more work Reconcile accepted jobs, hours, refunds, stock if any and cleared cash weekly. Limit bookings by productive hours and property constraints, not website demand alone. Record when you will revisit price, scope, equipment or location. Expansion can create a new permit, insurance or capacity question rather than being a simple multiplication of sales. Use the general startup roadmap for wider launch decisions and the online delivery test for digital channels. The startup cost calculator records launch cash; the risk assessment records operational dependencies. Separate premises permission, tax treatment and usable capacity Keep three decisions in different records: permission to conduct the activity at the address, the cash required to operate it, and any tax deduction. The SBA location guidance notes that zoning can apply to home businesses; the Arizona source is only an example for that jurisdiction. A permitted home activity does not automatically qualify its owner for a federal home-office deduction, and a possible deduction does not create local operating permission. IRS Topic 509 describes qualifying business uses and the exclusive-and-regular-use tests that apply to many home-office claims, with specific exceptions such as qualifying storage and daycare. Do not infer a deduction merely from calling a room an office or allocating household rent in a planning budget. Preserve the relevant use records and review the actual tax requirements separately from this original operating case. In the fictional capacity case, twenty jobs need forty delivery hours, leaving none of that delivery allowance unused. The sixteen hours already reserved for administration and selling must not be counted again as spare delivery capacity. Log actual booked time, completed jobs, cancellations and rework for the same month. If a job needs 2.5 hours, the sixteen-job ceiling leaves only $1,170 after the stated $350 commitments. Changing tax assumptions cannot repair that physical capacity shortfall. Revisit price, scope, scheduling or the owner-income target using evidence from completed work before accepting a fully loaded calendar. No. Check the actual activity and location, along with applicable property restrictions. Is household rent an incremental business cash cost? Only the actual additional payment belongs in that view. An internal allocation and tax treatment answer separate questions. Does covering monthly overhead mean the owner earns enough? No. Test the separate owner-income requirement and realistic capacity. Can I use all time at home as delivery hours? No. Allow for selling, administration, breaks, household constraints and rework. Does permission to work from home establish a tax deduction? No. Local operating permission and federal tax qualification are separate questions. Are the sixteen administration hours spare delivery capacity? No. They are already reserved in this example. Using them for jobs would require a revised plan for the administration and selling work. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Assets, Liabilities and Equity: Accounting Equation Examples Published November 6, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Follow eight reconciled transactions through assets, liabilities and equity. Separate profit, borrowing, customer collections and owner withdrawals. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer The accounting equation is assets = liabilities + equity. Assets show recognized resources, liabilities show obligations, and equity is the residual interest. Every recorded transaction must preserve the equality even when cash, profit and debt move differently. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Read the equation as a relationship, not a valuation The SEC financial-statement guide describes the balance sheet as a snapshot. Book equity is the accounting residual; it is not a promise of the price a business could sell for. A resource can be useful without all of its economic value appearing as a recognized asset. The equation alone does not tell you whether customer demand, liquidity or future profitability is strong. Owner investment and earned income both can increase equity but represent different activity. Borrowing increases an obligation rather than creating revenue. An owner withdrawal reduces the owner’s interest; it is not automatically an operating expense. This simplified service example uses an accrual view with no tax, inventory, depreciation, interest or other omitted period adjustments. Trace eight transactions without losing the balance Cumulative balances immediately after each transaction, USD Transaction Total assets Total liabilities Equity Owner invests $18,000 $18,000 $0 $18,000 Borrow $6,000 $24,000 $6,000 $18,000 Buy $5,000 equipment for cash $24,000 $6,000 $18,000 Earn and invoice $4,000 service $28,000 $6,000 $22,000 Collect $2,500 of that invoice $28,000 $6,000 $22,000 Incur $1,200 unpaid expense $28,000 $7,200 $20,800 Pay $700 of the expense $27,300 $6,500 $20,800 Owner withdraws $800 $26,500 $6,500 $20,000 Buying the equipment exchanges $5,000 cash for $5,000 equipment: total assets do not change in this simplified initial-recognition example. Earning the service creates $4,000 receivable and increases equity through income. Collecting $2,500 exchanges receivable for cash without earning the revenue again. Incurring the unpaid $1,200 expense increases liabilities and reduces equity; paying $700 later reduces cash and the liability together. The last row balances: $26,500 = $6,500 + $20,000. An equal balance is necessary, but it does not prove that the correct accounts, period or amounts were used. Recording the same wrong amount on both sides still balances. Reconcile the closing accounts and equity bridge Closing account detail; check against the transaction log Asset account USD Liability / equity account USD Cash 20,000 Loan 6,000 Accounts receivable 1,500 Unpaid expense 500 Equipment 5,000 Owner equity 20,000 Total 26,500 Total 26,500 Cash is $18,000 + $6,000 − $5,000 + $2,500 − $700 − $800 = $20,000. Equity is $18,000 investment + $4,000 earned revenue − $1,200 expense − $800 withdrawal = $20,000. Included profit is $2,800, while cash increased $20,000 from zero because investment, borrowing and asset purchases also affect cash. Do not use the cash change as profit. Exact closing-account diagram of this fictional example. Find errors the equality will not reveal Use source documents to confirm that a customer collection has not been recorded as new revenue. Check that a bank loan was not posted to sales and that an equipment payment was not automatically treated as an immediate period expense. Review whether an unpaid invoice belongs to the period. Each error can leave a superficially balanced ledger. A negative equity balance is possible and needs analysis of accumulated losses, distributions and the relevant accounting basis. It is not a negative cash balance by definition. Likewise, an asset-heavy business can have little available cash. See current asset classification and current liability classification before interpreting short-term coverage. Use the equation inside a complete close Start from reconciled opening balances, post supported transactions, complete necessary period adjustments and compare detailed accounts with the statement totals. Retain the prior version and the reason for every correction. Do not force a difference into equity just to make the statement balance. The AR workflow and AP workflow help support two common balances. Continue with financial statement analysis for the relationship among performance, balances and cash. This primer does not replace journal-entry policy, a full closing checklist or specialist review. Trace a real document through all four financial statements The SEC’s financial-statement primer distinguishes a reporting-date balance sheet from statements covering a period. Use that distinction when explaining the original eight transactions: the $6,000 borrowing belongs in the liability balance and cash movement, not in sales. The $2,500 customer collection reduces an existing receivable without adding another $2,500 of earned income. The identity of the bank transaction is insufficient without its source document. For each actual entry, retain the date, economic event, supporting document, debit, credit and reviewer. OpenStax’s transaction-analysis lesson shows how supported events affect the equation. The article’s owner-investment and withdrawal labels describe a simplified owner-equity case; a corporation would normally use its own share-capital, retained-earnings and distribution accounts. Changing the entity’s account labels does not authorize classifying a dividend as wages or a loan as revenue. A useful final check is to explain the difference between $2,800 included profit and $20,000 closing cash without a plug. Owner investment contributes $18,000; the loan contributes $6,000; equipment acquisition uses $5,000; part of earned revenue remains in the $1,500 receivable; $500 of expense remains unpaid; and the owner withdraws $800. Each belongs in its own bridge. A proposed market sale price or an estimate of employee expertise must not be inserted into the balance sheet simply to increase equity. Recognition and measurement require the applicable accounting policy, not an attractive valuation story. Download the editable worksheet Download the printable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed case and a separate blank working record. It does not calculate automatically. Edit in your browser, then print or save a completed copy before closing; your edits are not sent to MyBreakeven. SEC: balance-sheet relationship OpenStax: transaction-analysis method Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Reconcile the accumulated OCI component of equity Equity may include separate accumulated OCI alongside paid-in capital and retained earnings. Follow the limited OCI-to-equity example to check the arithmetic of those supplied components; it does not determine accounting classification or tax treatment. Frequently asked questions Is equity the same as cash? No. Equity is assets less liabilities under the accounting basis. Cash is one asset. Does collecting an invoice create revenue again? Not when the revenue was already recognized. It exchanges receivable for cash. Does a loan increase profit? Borrowed principal creates an obligation; it is not earned revenue. Does a balanced equation prove the accounts are correct? No. Wrong accounts, duplicated transactions or incorrect timing can still preserve equality. Why are the closing cash balance and included profit different? Investment, financing, asset purchases, unpaid customer and supplier balances, and withdrawals affect cash and equity differently. Can a corporation reuse the owner-equity labels unchanged? Use accounts appropriate to the legal entity and reporting framework. Share capital, retained earnings and distributions require their own supported records. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Current Assets: Classification, Examples and Liquidity Limits Published November 6, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Classify cash, receivables, inventory and prepayments at one reporting date. Reconcile a current-assets schedule and separate its total from available cash. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer Current assets are assets expected to be realized or consumed within the applicable short-term classification period, commonly one year or the normal operating cycle if longer. Classify and measure each balance before adding it; current does not mean immediately spendable cash. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Start with dates and restrictions Use the actual reporting basis and operating cycle. A routine retailer’s inventory may be current even though it has not sold, while equipment used for several years is normally outside this category. For this fictional short-cycle business, all included inventory and prepayments relate to the next twelve months. Unusual operating cycles and restricted balances require policy-specific review. Ask what the asset is, when it is expected to be realized or used, what restriction applies and what supports its carrying amount. A label in a software account is not sufficient evidence. Principlesofaccounting’s classified-balance-sheet lesson explains the one-year or longer operating-cycle boundary; this schedule is an original application, not a universal classification ruling. Reconcile a same-date current-assets schedule Original reporting-date classification, USD Balance Amount Classification Evidence Available cash $12,000 Current Reconciled bank/cash records Gross trade receivables $9,000 Current before allowance Customer invoice ledger Receivable allowance −$600 Reduces carrying amount Documented assessment Inventory $7,000 Current in this case Count and cost records Prepaid insurance consumed in next 12 months $1,200 Current Policy dates Total current assets $28,600 Sum once Same reporting date Equipment carrying amount $15,000 Noncurrent Fixed-asset schedule Long-term restricted deposit $2,000 Noncurrent in this case Restriction over 12 months The current total is $12,000 + $9,000 − $600 + $7,000 + $1,200 = $28,600 . Net receivables are $8,400. Do not add both $9,000 gross receivables and $8,400 net receivables. The allowance is a reduction of the carrying amount, not an additional bank account or a customer credit note. The $15,000 equipment and $2,000 deposit excluded from current assets remain relevant to total assets. In this deliberately limited schedule, total listed assets are $45,600. Excluding them from one subtotal does not remove them from the balance sheet. Separate current assets from cash available for payments Only the stated $12,000 is currently available cash in the example. Receivables need collection; inventory needs sale and settlement; prepaid insurance supplies future coverage rather than cash to pay a supplier. The $28,600 subtotal therefore cannot be read as the amount available for tomorrow’s payroll. Prepare a separate dated view. If $5,000 of receivables clears next week and $3,000 stock requires a slow sales cycle, list those events on their expected dates. Do not invent a collection date from the fact that an item is current. Review customer disputes and stock condition before treating all balances as equally recoverable. Check measurement without double-counting adjustments Reconcile cash to statements, the customer detail to the control account and physical stock to inventory records. Assess returns, damage, expiry and valuation under the applicable policy. Check the unused period on each prepayment. A prepaid annual bill should not remain at its original full amount after some of the coverage has been consumed. For a separate sensitivity, reducing this example’s inventory carrying amount by $1,000 would reduce current assets from $28,600 to $27,600, all else unchanged. It does not create a $1,000 cash payment on the adjustment date. Do not deduct the same adjustment again if the listed inventory is already net of it. Use the classification in the next decision Compare the category with current liabilities at the same cutoff. The working-capital guide owns the defined difference; the financial-ratios hub owns ratio interpretation. This article supplies account classification, not a recommended ratio or cash reserve. Use invoice and collection records to explain the receivable balance and the accounting equation to reconcile total assets with obligations and equity. Keep the reporting schedule and cash forecast connected without pretending they answer the same question. Document the reporting basis before interpreting the subtotal This is a classified-balance-sheet teaching case for a US business with a short operating cycle, not a complete rulebook for every reporting framework. OpenStax’s classification lesson explains the introductory one-year-or-longer-operating-cycle boundary. A maturity date alone is insufficient for every unusual asset: document the asset’s purpose, restriction, expected realization or consumption and the applicable policy. Do not take an issuer’s taxonomy label in a filing as the accounting standard itself. Create a review line for each original balance. The $9,000 gross receivable needs invoice and settlement support; the $600 allowance needs a separate estimate; $7,000 inventory needs count, cost and condition evidence; $1,200 prepaid insurance needs the unconsumed coverage schedule. These records support different judgments. A current classification does not validate the amount, and a supported carrying amount does not establish that the item can pay tomorrow’s bill. Reconcile the net $8,400 receivable once rather than adding its gross and net presentations. For the $2,000 deposit excluded from current assets, the example assumes a genuine long-term restriction consistent with the stated reporting policy, rather than merely an account named restricted cash. Confirm the contract, permitted withdrawals and release conditions. If those facts change, reassess classification before recalculating the subtotal; do not change a label only to improve working capital. Preserve current and noncurrent portions where the policy requires them. Use the same reporting date and accounting basis for the liability comparison, then build a separate collection and payment calendar from actual expected dates. Sources and scope The references below support the stated definitions, educational mechanics or specifically identified framework. The worked case, numbers and decision records are original MyBreakeven material. Reviewed November 8, 2026; no external professional sign-off is claimed. Principlesofaccounting: classified balance sheets OpenStax: introductory current-asset classification and liquidity; not an accounting standard Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Are all current assets cash? No. Receivables, inventory and prepayments can be current without being available cash. Should I add gross and net receivables? No. Use a consistent presentation and deduct the applicable allowance once. Is equipment a current asset because I paid cash? Payment method does not determine classification; consider how the asset is held and used. Does an inventory write-down spend cash? The adjustment itself changes the carrying amount. Its cash consequences belong in a separate transaction and forecast analysis. Is a taxonomy description in a company filing the accounting standard? No. It is a filing-related label or definition, and its presence on a regulator’s site does not make it regulator-authored accounting guidance. Does a current label validate the carrying amount? No. Classification and measurement require different evidence, such as dates and restrictions versus valuation and recoverability. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Reconcile a liability schedule and separate recognition from cash payment dates. Build the total from supported balances, then create a separate due-date schedule for cash planning. Read the source-backed application and limits . Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Distinguish recognition from the next payment date An obligation can exist before the supplier sends its invoice. A payment can settle an old obligation without becoming a new expense. Some obligations, such as customer advances, may be settled by delivering goods or services rather than paying the same amount in cash. These differences matter when converting a balance sheet to a cash plan. OpenStax describes common current-liability categories, including payables, accrued wages, unearned revenue and current debt portions. Debt terms, covenant issues, refinancing and unusual operating cycles can require specialized classification analysis. This simplified example assumes no such complications; it does not determine treatment for a particular loan. Add each obligation once at the reporting cutoff Original classification schedule, USD Obligation Balance Supporting evidence Trade accounts payable $8,000 Supplier terms / invoice due dates Accrued payroll $2,500 Earned before cutoff; payable next run Other accrued expense $900 Service received; not duplicated in AP Tax collected / payable $1,100 Separate obligation; verify due dates Customer advance $2,000 Undelivered service next month Current portion of loan principal $3,000 Contractually due in next 12 months Total current liabilities $17,500 Same cutoff Remaining long-term loan principal $9,000 Noncurrent in this simplified case The current total is $8,000 + $2,500 + $900 + $1,100 + $2,000 + $3,000 = $17,500 . The loan balance is $12,000 in total: $3,000 current and $9,000 noncurrent in this case. Adding the entire $12,000 again to current liabilities would duplicate the current portion and misclassify the rest. The $900 accrued expense is explicitly outside the supplier ledger here. When an invoice for that same service is posted, reconcile or reverse the accrual under the accounting policy. Leaving both as independent obligations would overstate the total. A disputed invoice still needs an assessment; withholding payment alone does not decide whether a liability exists. Turn the balance into a payment calendar carefully Separate near-term settlement illustration Item Cash due within next 30 days Other settlement Supplier bills 5,000 3,000 later Payroll 2,500 None in this case Accrued service 900 None Tax amount 1,100 Check actual statutory date Loan principal 250 Remaining current principal later Customer advance Not assumed to be 2,000 cash outflow Deliver the service; refund conditions reviewed Listed 30-day cash total 9,750 Not the 17,500 liability total The $9,750 is the sum of the listed near-term payments, not all costs of fulfilling the advance and not the whole next-month business budget. Add relevant future service-delivery cash and other commitments separately. Do not add the $2,000 advance as both an automatic cash repayment and all fulfillment costs unless the actual scenario requires both. Investigate omissions before interpreting coverage Review goods or services received near the cutoff, payroll earned but unpaid, lender schedules, customer advances and tax control accounts. Match supplier statements to detail and document differences. Check whether a credit note has been posted and whether payments in transit are represented consistently. A low payable balance can reflect an omitted bill rather than strong finances. Current classification and overdue status answer different questions. A bill due next month and a bill overdue for sixty days can both be current. Maintain due dates, dispute status and payment evidence so a single balance cannot hide urgent exceptions. Connect classification to cash and account workflows Use the AP approval and reconciliation workflow for supplier records. Compare with current asset classifications at the same date before using working capital or a ratio. A positive subtotal difference does not prove that cash arrives before the bills. The accounting equation example separates borrowing from profit. The cash-flow forecast uses payment and collection dates. Keep forecast commitments that are not yet recognized liabilities visibly separate from the accounting total. Separate the recognized balance, debt terms and settlement plan This original schedule is an introductory classified-balance-sheet case for a short-cycle US business. OpenStax’s current-liability lesson supports the listed common categories. Do not extend the simplified $3,000-current/$9,000-noncurrent loan split to a loan with different terms. Read contractual maturities, demand clauses, covenant compliance and relevant refinancing evidence under the applicable reporting framework before assigning the portions. A lender’s informal expectation of renewal is not the same evidence as an executed right or agreement. Build a debt register with opening principal, new borrowings, principal repaid, closing principal, interest, next payment and classification assessment. Interest and principal answer different questions. The $250 principal payment in the original thirty-day schedule does not assert that no interest will be paid; the $9,750 total includes only the listed items. Add any actual interest and other omitted commitments to the separate cash plan without quietly changing the supported accounting balances. For customer advances, reconcile opening liability plus new receipts less amounts earned, approved refunds and other supported movements. The $2,000 advance in this case remains a service obligation at cutoff; it is not assumed to require an immediate $2,000 cash repayment. Its fulfillment can still require future payroll or supplies, so excluding that automatic refund is not permission to exclude delivery cash. Record refund conditions and delivery evidence. The classification schedule, the expense budget and the dated cash forecast should reconcile through explained differences rather than being forced into one identical total. Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build an invoice-to-collection workflow with a reconciled customer ledger, credits, due-date aging, disputes and cash application. Includes an editable record. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer The accounts receivable process tracks customer amounts from a valid invoice through credits, collections and reconciliation. Keep each invoice, due date, receipt allocation and open balance connected so the total can be explained from individual customer records. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Numerical examples and diagrams are original fictional teaching cases. All amounts and operating results below are original fictional teaching examples in USD. They are not customer results, industry averages or forecasts. Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Agree the terms and evidence before billing Record the customer identity, approved scope, delivery or acceptance evidence, invoice contact and agreed payment terms. Establish who can approve a credit change or adjustment. An invoice date is not proof that the full revenue-recognition criteria were met; the accounting basis and delivery facts still matter. Microsoft’s receivables process documentation distinguishes invoicing, customer payments, credits and settlement. This article supplies a small original invoice ledger, not an assessment of customer creditworthiness or a debt-collection legal procedure. Use appropriate professional support for disputed obligations and regulated collection activity. Keep a reconciled invoice-level record Original gross customer ledger; no tax, allowance or write-off in this case Invoice Invoice date Due date Invoice Applied cash Credit Open Status on Nov 6 A-101 Oct 1 Oct 31 $5,000 $2,000 $0 $3,000 6 days overdue A-102 Oct 20 Nov 19 $4,000 $0 $500 $3,500 Not yet due A-103 Sep 15 Oct 15 $3,000 $1,000 $0 $2,000 22 days overdue Total As of Nov 6, 2026 Due-date aging $12,000 $3,000 $500 $8,500 Reconcile to control account Open gross receivables are $12,000 invoices − $3,000 allocated collections − $500 approved credit = $8,500 . A-102’s credit reduces its balance to $3,500; it is not a $500 receipt. Record the credit’s reason and approval. This ledger does not include an expected-credit-loss allowance; a financial-statement carrying amount may need a separate supported adjustment. Check every customer row and the overall movement. At an opening gross AR of $7,000, new invoices of $5,000, collections of $3,000 and credits of $500 produce the same $8,500 closing control balance. The movement is a separate summary of this month’s activity, not a second set of invoices to add to the ledger. Original gross-AR movement; credits are separate from collections. Age balances using one explicit date policy Using due dates and a November 6 cutoff, A-101 is six days overdue, A-103 twenty-two days overdue and A-102 not yet due. Thus $5,000 is 1–30 days overdue and $3,500 is not yet due. The aging total is $8,500. A report aged from invoice date would show different buckets, so label the basis before comparing reports. Separate disputes, promises to pay and collection estimates from posted cash. A customer email promising $2,000 does not reduce the open balance. Assign a dispute owner, required evidence and next contact date. Preserve the original terms and any approved change; do not rewrite a due date simply to improve the aging report. Match the receipt without earning revenue twice For A-101, apply the $2,000 receipt to that invoice and retain its bank reference. A general transfer from a customer may need remittance evidence before allocating across several invoices. Keep unidentified receipts visible for investigation under the accounting policy instead of guessing an allocation. If a processor settles $970 against a supported $1,000 invoice and withholds a documented $30 fee, the settlement may require $970 cash plus $30 fee to clear the $1,000 receivable. Do not leave a fictional $30 customer debt or reduce sales without examining the actual settlement. Refunds, withholding and currency differences need their own documented treatment. Reconcile detail, control account and bank evidence At cutoff, total the customer detail and compare it with the general-ledger AR control account. Explain manual journals, unapplied cash, credits, duplicates and timing differences. Separately reconcile bank activity. The AR control balance is not expected to reconcile to the bank balance: it represents unpaid customer amounts, while the bank balance represents cash held. Re-run the detail after corrections, retain the reconciliation and have an appropriate reviewer investigate unresolved differences. Feed expected clearing dates into the cash forecast . For definitions use current assets ; for the customer-versus-supplier distinction use AR versus AP . The AP workflow handles money owed to suppliers, without netting unrelated customers and vendors. Resolve unapplied cash and report exceptions without hiding balances Run three linked but separate records: the invoice and credit ledger, the receipt-allocation record, and the bank reconciliation. Microsoft’s receivables process documentation separates invoices, credits, customer payments, prepayments, refunds and settlement. It describes a product workflow rather than prescribing a universal accounting policy. Your control record should still explain which event occurred, who approved it and how it links to the customer balance. For a separate original receipt example, a customer sends $1,200 against a supported $1,000 invoice. Apply $1,000 to that invoice and investigate the remaining $200 using remittance evidence. Do not increase revenue or create a second invoice merely to absorb the receipt. The balance may be an advance, an overpayment awaiting refund or another supported item; decide from the facts and accounting policy. Preserve both the gross bank receipt and its allocations so the customer account does not appear settled through an unexplained journal. At review, list outstanding disputes, unallocated receipts, approved-but-unposted credits and promised payments with owner and next action. Reconcile those exceptions to the same cutoff as the $8,500 gross ledger. Keep any allowance assessment separate from cash collection; the OpenStax receivable examples distinguish earned sales from later settlement. A write-off or allowance change can alter a reported balance without collecting cash. Collection speed should not be improved cosmetically by changing due dates, netting unrelated parties or silently removing disputed invoices. No. Keep it as a collection expectation until a supported transaction is posted. Should receivables equal the bank balance? No. Reconcile customer detail to the AR control account and bank cash separately. Does a credit note count as collected cash? No. It reduces the customer balance for its approved reason without creating a receipt. Should I age invoices from their date or due date? Choose and label a consistent policy. This guide’s overdue buckets use contractual due dates. How should a receipt larger than the invoice be handled? Allocate the supported invoice amount and investigate the excess using remittance evidence. Do not invent sales to absorb the difference. Can gross receivables and the bank balance happen to be equal? Yes, numerically by coincidence. They represent different accounts and are reconciled to different supporting records. Business finance Worked example Practical worksheet Quick answer The accounts payable process verifies supplier obligations, records approved invoices and credits, schedules authorized payments and reconciles the remaining balance. Match what was ordered, received and billed before paying, and preserve evidence for exceptions. Read the source-backed application and limits . Use your own dated records and applicable accounting policies. Capture the invoice and validate the supplier record Use a controlled intake location and record supplier, invoice number, currency, date, terms, purchase reference and total. Check duplicates using more than a file name: the same bill can arrive as a PDF, reminder and statement. A supplier statement summarizes activity; it is not automatically a new expense. Separate supplier-detail changes, invoice approval and payment release where practical. Verify a requested bank-detail change through a previously trusted contact route, not only the new email. In a very small business, an independent owner review of the evidence can compensate for limited staffing, but it should be an actual recorded check. Match receipt and price, then resolve exceptions Microsoft’s invoice-matching documentation distinguishes price comparison with the purchase order from the additional receipt-quantity check. Choose controls that fit the purchase. A service may need approved completion evidence instead of a warehouse receipt; a non-PO bill needs a documented authorization route, not automatic approval. For an independent goods example, a purchase order requests 100 components at $20, but the receiving record shows only 90 accepted. A supplier invoice for $2,000 raises a $200 quantity exception. Investigate the missing ten and request correction or evidence before approval. Do not silently change the receipt to 100 to make the documents agree. Recognition of goods received and treatment of any dispute still follow the accounting policy. Reconcile the supplier balances and monthly movement Original gross AP detail; no tax, foreign exchange or unresolved accrual in this case Invoice Invoice date Due date Invoice Applied payments Credit Open Status V-201 Oct 15 Nov 14 $4,000 $1,500 $0 $2,500 Receiving checked V-202 Oct 20 Nov 19 $3,000 $0 $300 $2,700 Credit approved V-203 Sep 25 Oct 25 $2,000 $1,000 $0 $1,000 12 days overdue Total As of Nov 6, 2026 Due-date policy $9,000 $2,500 $300 $6,200 Compare supplier detail to GL The ledger closes at $9,000 invoices − $2,500 allocated payments − $300 approved credit = $6,200 . V-203’s remaining $1,000 is twelve days overdue on November 6. The credit on V-202 is not a payment; retain the supplier reference and reason. A dispute flag is not permission to delete a supported obligation. The separate month movement is $4,500 opening AP + $4,500 new bills − $2,500 payments − $300 credits = $6,200. Compare that result with the supplier-detail total and GL control balance. Do not add the opening balances to a closing ledger that already includes them. Original AP reconciliation; payments and supplier credits remain distinct. Authorize the payment without duplicating the expense Prepare a proposed payment run with invoice references, due dates, available cash and hold reasons. Review agreed discounts against actual terms; do not assume delaying every payment improves the business. A planned payment is not a completed bank transaction. Retain release approval and settlement evidence, then allocate the payment to the correct invoice. If $1,500 of V-201 is paid after that invoice was already recorded, reduce cash and the payable. Posting another $1,500 expense at payment would duplicate the cost. A purchase can instead relate to inventory, equipment or a prepayment, so the AP workflow must not force every bill into operating expense. Close with supplier, ledger and cutoff checks Compare supplier statements with internal invoices, payments and credits. Investigate missing invoices, unallocated payments, duplicates and payments in transit. Reconcile supplier detail to the AP control account at the same cutoff. Review received goods and completed services not yet invoiced, keeping necessary accruals separate until matched so they are not counted twice. Use liability classification for the reporting boundary and the customer collection workflow for incoming amounts. The AR-versus-AP comparison explains the distinction. Feed actual supplier due dates into the cash plan ; a reconciled $6,200 balance does not itself say which payments are due tomorrow. Keep matching tolerance and payment authority separate Microsoft’s matching documentation distinguishes two-way price checks from three-way checks that also compare receipt quantities. In the original case, ninety accepted units at $20 support $1,800 of received goods, while the $2,000 invoice contains a $200 quantity exception. A system tolerance is a configured review threshold, not proof that an incorrect invoice is economically correct or that missing goods arrived. Retain the original invoice, receiving record, exception decision and supplier correction. SAP’s reconciliation example illustrates keeping the original document and the reconciliation trail separately. A documented partial payment, credit or corrected invoice must explain its effect on the remaining supplier balance. Resolving a matching icon does not itself show that a bank payment was authorized or settled; those events need their own references. Protect supplier-master changes as a separate control. The FBI’s IC3 guidance recommends verifying account-change requests through another channel. For an actual payment run, confirm changed bank details through a previously trusted contact route, retain the verification and review the payee independently of invoice approval. If only one person operates the business, keep a visible callback and approval record rather than treating the sender’s email as confirmation. After settlement, allocate the receipt or payment reference to the invoice, reconcile the resulting $6,200 example balance, and investigate any unexplained supplier-statement difference before closing the period. documents.text: Landscaping PRACTICAL GUIDE Landscaping Working Capital: Fund the Seasonal Cash Gap Published November 5, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a dated landscaping cash schedule for materials, payroll and customer receipts. Test the funding gap, minimum cash floor and delayed-payment scenario. Business finance Planning Worked example Quick answer Landscaping working-capital needs depend on when materials, crew payroll and overhead must be paid compared with when customer cash clears. Build a dated cash schedule, find its lowest balance and test a delayed-receipt case before choosing a funding amount. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Financial cases are original fictional teaching examples. All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Separate the balance-sheet measure from the seasonal funding gap Net working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. That balance-sheet measure is useful, but it does not say whether Friday’s payroll clears before Monday’s customer payment. A profitable landscaping job can require temporary funding if plants, soil, fuel and labor are paid first. Start the cash schedule with reconciled, available business cash. List each receipt by its expected clearing date and each payment by its actual due date. Include equipment purchases, debt payments and owner withdrawals in separate lines when relevant. Those lines affect funding even though they do not all belong in operating profit. Do not count an unapproved credit limit or a customer promise as cleared cash. A spring ramp-up with materials paid before collections Illustrative April 2027 cash schedule; no borrowing in this base case Week ending Opening cash Receipts Payments Closing cash April 2 $12,000 $2,000 $10,000 $4,000 April 9 $4,000 $4,000 $11,000 −$3,000 April 16 −$3,000 $12,000 $8,000 $1,000 April 23 $1,000 $10,000 $7,000 $4,000 Week one includes $6,000 materials, $3,000 payroll and $1,000 other payments. Week two includes $4,000 materials, $5,000 payroll and $2,000 other payments. Total receipts are $28,000 and total payments $36,000, so $12,000 + $28,000 − $36,000 = $4,000 closing cash. The lowest weekly closing balance is −$3,000. A negative forecast is a funding warning, not an instruction to let a bank account overdraw. If management chooses a $5,000 minimum cash floor, the additional cash needed at the lowest weekly close is $5,000 − (−$3,000) = $8,000 . The floor is a choice for this case, not a landscaping-industry standard. Check daily order within each week: a Monday payroll before a Friday receipt can create a deeper trough. Delay one receipt without inventing a second payment Move $6,000 of the April 16 receipts to April 23. Week-three receipts become $6,000 and week-four receipts $16,000. Closing balances become $4,000, −$3,000, −$5,000 and $4,000. The total month’s receipts and closing cash are unchanged, but the low point falls to −$5,000. Keeping the same floor now needs $10,000 additional cash at that weekly close. Do not add the late receipt to the later week while leaving it in the original week. Reconcile every scheduled invoice to one open receipt record. Record evidence for customer approval, invoice disputes, deposits and clearing delays. A deposit may also carry delivery or refund obligations; it is not automatically earned profit. Same final cash, different seasonal low point. Exact chart of the original fictional example. Match the response to the timing and the underlying margin Possible management responses include staging materials by job, agreeing milestone billing before work starts, aligning valid supplier terms with collections or evaluating a documented funding facility. Compare actual fees, repayment dates, availability conditions and the downside forecast. This schedule does not establish eligibility or recommend a lender. Re-run the later weeks after any payment deferral or borrowing. Moving a supplier bill does not remove it, and a draw creates a repayment obligation. If each job loses money after its relevant costs, short-term funding only delays that problem. Check the seasonal landscaping break-even guide for operating recovery and the working-capital calculation guide for account definitions. Keep a seasonal review tied to job and bank records Reconcile cash, open invoices, purchase commitments and payroll dates at the same cutoff. Update the next 13 weeks by clearing date, with daily detail near the tightest dates. Separate confirmed work from unaccepted quotes and isolate customer concentration. Assign an owner and deadline to each proposed funding or collection action. Archive the forecast, compare cleared results and investigate date or amount differences. Use the 13-week cash-flow forecast for the dated model and the landscaping business plan for the wider operating assumptions. Extend the horizon through winter commitments instead of stopping the forecast at the first profitable month. If the seasonal gap exposes a larger operating constraint, use the feasibility study to separate demand, capacity and funding conditions. Reconcile a funding draw through the later repayment BDC’s cash-management guidance supports anticipating when receipts and payments occur. It is Canadian business education, not a statement of US lender eligibility. In this guide’s original case, the $8,000 requirement is a top-up to the chosen $5,000 weekly-close floor; it is not a recurring weekly expense, a recommended reserve or an approved credit limit. If an $8,000 draw is inserted immediately before the base case’s lowest weekly close, that close rises from −$3,000 to $5,000. The borrowing increases cash and an obligation; it does not create customer revenue. Carry the draw through every later balance and add principal repayments, interest and fees on their expected payment dates. Drawing $8,000 again in every later week would invent additional funding. Match the assumed availability date with the facility’s actual written conditions before treating the proceeds as usable. Check within-week order as well. A Monday payment before a Friday receipt can need more funding than a weekly-close table reveals. Include later repayment dates, off-season commitments and any customer refund obligation. If a payment is deferred to protect April cash, it remains a payment in the later schedule. Keep confirmed funds, conditional offers and applications separate. Approve a response only after both the low point and the repayment period can meet their actual obligations. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . It includes the completed case and blank fields for your evidence, assumptions, dates and decision. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. Sources and method The linked sources support the general framework. The calculations, operating constraints and decision examples here are original MyBreakEven teaching material. BDC: anticipating cash receipts and payments Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is working capital the same as a seasonal cash reserve? No. Net working capital is a balance-sheet difference. The seasonal funding schedule tracks dated available cash and a separately chosen floor. Does a profitable landscaping contract fund its own payroll? Not necessarily. Payment timing can require cash before the customer settles. Test dates as well as margin. Should the monthly closing balance determine the facility size? Not by itself. Check the lowest daily balance, availability conditions, the downside case and the later repayment schedule. Is $5,000 a recommended minimum cash reserve? No. It is an explicit teaching assumption. Choose a floor using the actual business commitments and risk. Does the $8,000 funding need recur every week? No. It is the additional amount needed at the base case’s lowest weekly close to reach the chosen floor. Carry any actual draw forward and schedule its repayment; do not invent a new draw each week. Does a line-of-credit approval guarantee usable cash on every date? No. Check the actual availability conditions, remaining undrawn amount and timing in the written agreement. The forecast does not establish eligibility or approval. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

Compare models by what must be true Six starting points to investigate, not earnings recommendations Model Customer problem Main constraint First evidence to collect Recurring home cleaning Reliable scheduled cleaning Travel, crew time and rework Local paid trial and repeat booking Bookkeeping support Timely organized business records Competence, access and scope Owner interviews and defined pilot Product photography Usable catalog images Editing time and revisions Paid sample with acceptance criteria Plant-care visits Maintained office plants Route density and replacement costs Nearby-site trial and travel log Made-to-order alterations Clothing fit or repair Skilled production hours Paid job with measured completion time Specialty resale Hard-to-find selected products Inventory, returns and cash cycle Small-batch sell-through and net receipts These models have different operating burdens. A home service can avoid inventory while still needing transport, insurance and practical schedule capacity. A digital service can avoid a storefront while creating customer-acquisition, software and revision costs. A product business can show sales growth while cash remains tied up in unsold stock. Use disqualifying constraints before scoring enthusiasm Write your available cash, weekly hours, required personal income, relevant skills, geographic reach and unacceptable commitments. Exclude ideas that cannot meet those constraints under a plausible downside case. For regulated or sensitive work, verify the actual professional, insurance and local requirements before accepting customers. A broad idea list cannot establish permission to practice. Then compare demand evidence, contribution per constrained hour, startup commitments, time to collection and repeatability. Keep unknowns visible instead of assigning a precise score to an unsupported guess. A signed paid pilot is stronger evidence than compliments from friends, but a single pilot still does not prove recurring demand. Compare two fictional pilots on the same cost boundary Original pilot economics; both cases exclude general overhead and income tax Measure Cleaning visit Photography package Price $180 $450 Assumed job-varying cash delivery costs $55 $90 Contribution before owner time $125 $360 Total owner-hours including travel/admin 4 12 Contribution per owner-hour $31.25 $30.00 Pilot startup purchases $600 $1,800 The photography package has a larger ticket, but $360 divided by 12 hours is $30 per hour; cleaning yields $125 divided by four, or $31.25. Neither figure is take-home pay. They must still cover the included owner-income requirement, fixed costs, idle time and any omitted commitments. If the cleaning visit needs five hours instead of four, contribution per hour falls to $25. Suppose a month offers 80 practical owner-hours and 20 hours are needed for prospecting and general administration outside those job totals. The remaining 60 hours support at most 15 four-hour visits or five twelve-hour photography packages. Customer demand might be below either ceiling. Avoid multiplying a full calendar by a price before checking all the hours. Design a small test with a stop rule Choose one customer segment and one tightly specified offer. Ask how the customer currently solves the problem, what causes dissatisfaction and how buying decisions are made. Compare actual alternatives and test a paid delivery at the intended price where practical. Record acquisition effort, delivery time, changes, refunds and collection dates. Before the test, set a spending ceiling and a decision rule. For example: test three paid jobs, keep total test cash below a chosen $400 limit and investigate any job that needs over five hours. Those are fictional experiment settings, not universal validation thresholds. If the test misses the rule, revise scope or stop; do not redefine success after seeing the result. Turn the best-supported model into a funding plan Obtain dated supplier quotes and identify one-time, recurring and refundable amounts. Include operating shortfalls before customers pay, a separately chosen reserve and the owner’s own living needs outside the business budget. Avoid adding the same startup payment to both setup spending and the cash-gap total. The startup cost calculator helps organize cash needs; the business plan template records the chosen model. When you need a demand schedule, use the small-business sales forecast . Choose the idea because the evidence and constraints fit, then preserve the assumptions so the first month’s actual results can challenge them. After selecting an offer, follow the startup roadmap . For a client engagement, use the proposal and delivery-cost record before committing to scope. Keep a demand-evidence record before comparing owner income The SBA planning guidance connects customer research with competitor analysis. Apply that framework to a specific offer: record the customer group, the problem, the alternative supplier, matched service scope and date of each conversation or test. Compare nearby alternatives on the same scope; a public price for a different package is not an equivalent benchmark. Separate an interview, a request for a quote, an accepted order, completed delivery and cleared payment. They answer different questions and must not be added together as equal proof of demand. Record the cost and owner time needed to acquire the first buyer, not just the time spent delivering. In the fictional cleaning case, $125 spread over four job-related hours gives $31.25 per hour before general overhead, idle time and owner requirements. That is an offer-level comparison, not an authentic earnings average for cleaners. The case assumes the $55 and $90 cash delivery costs vary with the relevant jobs. If a real cost is a committed salary, a sunk purchase or allocated shared overhead, classify it separately before interpreting variable-cost contribution. A paid pilot may expose delivery or pricing problems but does not establish market-wide demand or repeatable income. Set the next test, maximum cash exposure and review date while keeping unsupported inputs labeled as assumptions. Retain failed tests as well as successful ones so the selection record reflects the evidence available at the time. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . There is no universal answer. Price, cost scope, owner-hours, repeat demand, fixed commitments and cash timing change the result. Can a service business start without cash? Even an inventory-light service may need tools, transport, insurance, software or a cash bridge before payment. Estimate the actual requirements. Are the six ideas ranked? No. They are different models to screen against your skills, constraints and customer evidence. Does a paid pilot prove the idea will work? It supplies useful evidence, but repeat demand, acquisition costs and delivery consistency still need testing. Are the example hourly figures actual industry earnings? No. They divide fictional price less the specified job-varying costs by assumed owner-hours. General overhead, non-job time, owner requirements and other omitted costs still need consideration. Can I count interviews and orders as the same demand evidence? No. Record their distinct stages. Interest, accepted scope, completed work and cleared payment support different conclusions. Interview likely buyers and compare local alternatives. A large market estimate is not a list of customers who will buy from you. Keep confirmed orders, customer interest and assumptions in separate categories. Test price and scope together. Record the time and cash required to deliver a paid pilot, including revisions, travel, payment fees and customer support. Choose a spending ceiling and a date to decide whether to continue. Reconcile setup spending and early operating cash Fictional launch plan for a small service business Cash requirement Amount Boundary Tools and setup purchases $2,400 Paid before opening Security deposit $600 Cash paid; not assumed expense First two months operating shortfall $2,000 Receipts less payments after setup Chosen cash cushion $1,500 Separate management assumption Total initial funding need $6,500 No setup amounts counted twice Owner cash committed $4,500 Confirmed available source Unfunded difference $2,000 Resolve before commitments The funding need is $2,400 + $600 + $2,000 + $1,500 = $6,500. Subtracting $4,500 confirmed owner cash leaves $2,000 unresolved. That difference is not automatically an approved loan. Reduce or stage commitments, obtain documented funding or postpone launch until the dated schedule works. Include any financing fees, interest and repayments when a specific option is assessed. The $2,000 shortfall means operating cash outflows exceed receipts by that amount during the two-month schedule, after excluding the separately listed setup payments. If your forecast already contains those setup payments, do not add them a second time. Budget household living costs separately and confirm what the owner must withdraw from the business. Check whether the offer can cover the monthly requirement Suppose one service sells for $250 and its defined job-linked costs are $100. Contribution is $150 per completed job. Covering $1,200 monthly business overhead requires eight jobs before owner compensation, interest and tax under that cost boundary. Adding a separately chosen $2,400 owner-income planning requirement raises the combined target to 24 jobs: ($1,200 + $2,400) ÷ $150. If delivery takes four hours per job, 24 jobs require 96 job-hours, plus selling and administration outside the quoted job time. Check your practical calendar and expected demand. A personal income target is not necessarily a deductible accounting expense; label it as a planning requirement. The startup calculator helps organize launch assumptions without replacing that distinction. Complete the requirements for the actual business Use the SBA’s launch guidance as a starting point to identify questions about structure, name registration, tax identifiers, banking, permits and insurance. Requirements depend on activity, state and locality. Verify current obligations with the relevant government agencies and advisers before trading; there is no single checklist that grants permission for every US business. Keep business transactions identifiable from the start. Establish invoice numbering, supplier records, receipt storage, expense categories and bank reconciliation. Confirm who maintains the books and how payroll or customer deposits will be handled if relevant. Do not choose a structure solely from a generic cost comparison without considering the actual ownership and obligations. Launch with a short review cycle and a visible cash cutoff Confirm the offer, price, delivery scope and customer acceptance process. Resolve the funding schedule and distinguish committed funds from applications. Check required registrations and operational permissions for the real location. Record the first invoices, receipts, delivery costs and work hours. Compare the first month with the original assumptions and approve the next commitments. That does not mean every individual researching an idea needs every identifier, entity or permit. Establish the actual activity, ownership, business location, employee plans and customer locations before checking which requirements apply. For each applicable registration or permission, record the issuing agency, official source, current status, renewal date and supporting document. A bank account or tax identifier does not itself authorize every regulated activity. Separate preparatory research from commitments that depend on a permission being effective. Verify unresolved state, local or activity-specific questions with the actual agency and suitable advisers; a generic launch article cannot resolve them for an unidentified business. IRS Publication 583 explains business recordkeeping and supporting documents. For the fictional launch, trace the $4,500 owner contribution separately from customer receipts or loans. Preserve the quotes and payment dates behind the $6,500 need and the $2,000 unfunded difference. Identify which forecast already contains tools, deposits and early operating shortfalls so no cash item is added twice. Record customer invoices, supplier bills, receipts and bank movements from the first transaction. Check applicable retention requirements by record type instead of assuming a single universal period. Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Work through a nine-block business model example, reconcile its revenue and delivery costs, and turn assumptions into tests using an editable record. Business finance Planning Worked example Quick answer A Business Model Canvas summarizes how one business model serves customers and earns revenue through nine connected blocks. Its value comes from testing the relationships between those blocks, including whether the proposed price, costs and delivery capacity can work together. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Financial cases are original fictional teaching examples. All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Fill the nine blocks for one model Original fictional example: recurring small-office cleaning Block Illustrative hypothesis Evidence needed Customer segments Nearby offices needing after-hours cleaning Buyer interviews and site criteria Value propositions Consistent scoped service with documented completion Pilot and customer acceptance Channels Local referrals and direct outreach Cost and conversion records Customer relationships Named contact and monthly scope review Retention and issue records Revenue streams Monthly contracted service fee Accepted terms and collections Key resources Trained crew, transport and equipment Available hours and quotes Key activities Scheduling, cleaning, checks and invoicing Time log and quality checks Key partners Supply vendor and backup support Actual availability and terms Cost structure Job-linked labor/supplies plus period overhead Cost ledger and commitments The framework is associated with Alexander Osterwalder, Yves Pigneur and Strategyzer. Use the official Strategyzer canvas for the original tool and its applicable usage terms. The table and worksheet here are an independently written case and evidence record, not an official Strategyzer template. Connect the customer promise to the operating numbers Assume ten office customers each pay $600 a month: revenue is $6,000. Each requires eight worker-hours at an assumed job-varying loaded delivery cost of $30 per hour, so delivery labor is $2,400. Supplies are $30 per customer, or $300. Contribution after those included delivery costs is $3,300. Subtract $1,800 defined monthly overhead for an illustrative $1,500 operating result before omitted financing and tax items. Ten customers need 80 worker-hours. If practical delivery capacity is 96 hours, the same eight-hour scope supports at most 12 whole customers, before considering route and scheduling constraints. A promise of unlimited additional service contradicts the cost and capacity blocks. Do not count the same salaried labor in both the $30 hourly rate and the $1,800 overhead. Change a block and follow the consequences Suppose the value proposition changes to include two extra worker-hours per customer at the same fee. Ten customers now require 100 hours, exceeding the stated 96-hour capacity. At the same $30 cost rate, delivery labor becomes $3,000, contribution $2,700 and the result after unchanged overhead $900. That arithmetic does not make the schedule feasible: an actual capacity response may add further cost. The choice could require a narrower scope, a justified price change, a different customer segment or additional resources. Update channels and relationship expectations as well as the spreadsheet. A model canvas should expose those dependencies rather than hide them behind separate attractive statements. Rank assumptions by consequence and missing evidence Mark every statement as observed, supported by a limited test or still assumed. Customer willingness to pay, delivery time and repeat purchase deserve early attention because they can change several blocks at once. Write a test with a customer group, offer, cost ceiling, measured outcome and decision date. For the cleaning case, time a fully scoped pilot including travel and inspection, then obtain a separate repeat-service decision. An enthusiastic survey response is not equivalent to paid recurring demand. Archive the original canvas and change only the blocks the evidence affects; record why each version differs. Use the right next document for the decision A canvas describes the model; a feasibility study examines whether it should proceed under actual constraints. A business plan organizes the chosen venture’s operating and funding story. A sales forecast translates demand assumptions into a dated volume schedule. None of those documents independently proves a profitable business. Continue with the business plan template , the customer profitability method for cost-to-serve differences or the sales forecast for demand and capacity. Keep the canvas focused on one coherent model so its assumptions can be challenged together. The feasibility study tests whether the model can proceed; strategic planning records which customers and resource priorities the business will choose. Trace each changed promise through the connected blocks The official Strategyzer canvas guidance treats the model as connected hypotheses that should be dated and revised as evidence changes. Put one accountable owner and version date on the record. Attach a short evidence reference to important assumptions rather than hiding every uncertainty in one general notes field. In the original cleaning case, expanding from eight to ten worker-hours per customer changes the resources, activities and cost blocks immediately. Ten customers would require 100 hours against 96 available. The $900 result after unchanged overhead does not resolve that four-hour operational shortage. A new distant segment can also change travel, channels, the support relationship and the acceptable price. Do not revise only the revenue block while leaving the delivery system unchanged. State what actual change supplies the missing capacity and recheck its cost before committing to the promise. This numerical example assumes the $30 loaded delivery rate varies with the included worker-hours and that its underlying labor is not also counted in overhead. A real salaried employee’s allocated rate may be useful for estimating full service cost without being an avoidable payment for one more customer. Mark that distinction before using the amount as variable-cost contribution or a cash forecast input. A completed canvas describes the proposed model; paid delivery, customer acceptance and repeat decisions test different parts of it. Archive the original and explain each changed block. Use the official source for its own tool and usage terms; this article’s evidence record is an independently written example. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is a Business Model Canvas the same as a business plan? No. The canvas summarizes one model and its assumptions. A plan develops the chosen operating and funding approach in more detail. Do all nine blocks have to be certain before drafting? No. Label assumptions and test important unknowns. Filling every block does not validate the model. Can revenue streams alone demonstrate profitability? No. Reconcile delivery costs, shared commitments and practical capacity. Also check when customer cash arrives. Is the downloadable worksheet an official canvas? No. It is an original MyBreakEven case and evidence record. The article links to Strategyzer for the official tool and terms. Does a completed canvas prove the business is feasible? No. It records connected hypotheses. Customer demand, delivery capacity, costs and funding still require evidence and their own decision review. Is an internal hourly labor rate always a variable cash payment? No. A loaded or allocated rate can include committed salary or shared costs. Identify the actual cost behavior and avoid counting its underlying amount again in overhead. Build the delivery cost case before promising the scope, then turn the agreed details into the appropriate written engagement. Read the source-backed application and limits .
