Use a proposal the client can evaluate Editable proposal sections and the question each answers Section What to write Review control Client objective Specific problem and agreed success evidence Confirm the buyer recognizes it Deliverables Named outputs, quantities and formats Define completion for each output Scope and exclusions Included work and explicit boundaries Avoid unlimited revisions Schedule Milestones and client inputs Identify dependencies and decision dates Price Fee, assumptions and applicable tax treatment Reconcile included and optional amounts Payment Amounts, milestones and due-date basis Match contract and invoice terms Acceptance Authorized parties, scope approval and date Obtain suitable engagement review A proposal can answer a request for proposals or start a conversation with a potential buyer. In either case, adapt it to the decision the client must make. A business plan explains the venture to owners or funders; a client proposal offers a defined engagement. Do not substitute a generic company history for an answer to the client’s requirement. Check a fictional fixed-fee project before quoting A catalog photography proposal includes 20 finished images, one agreed background treatment and one consolidated correction round within the stated scope. The seller estimates 20 production hours plus ten planning, communication and editing hours. At an internal loaded rate of $40, included labor is $1,200. Add $300 studio and materials and $150 travel for a defined delivery cost of $1,650. At a $2,400 fee, project surplus after those included costs is $750, or 31.25% of the fee. Markup on that same $1,650 cost is 45.45%. The percentages use different denominators. Neither establishes net company profit because shared overhead and other omitted costs still need coverage. The $40 rate must represent the chosen cost basis consistently. Show how one scope change affects the quote Ten extra hours at the same internal rate add $400. If the fee stays $2,400, included delivery cost becomes $2,050 and project surplus falls to $350, or 14.58%. If the client also needs new props, travel or a new deadline, the cost change may be larger. An undefined revision promise makes the original estimate unreliable. State which customer inputs are required, how feedback is consolidated, what counts as an accepted output and how requested changes are evaluated. Record the proposed impact on scope, delivery dates and fee before commencing additional work. This teaching template does not establish enforceable contract terms for every jurisdiction. Connect milestones to actual cash requirements An illustrative 40% / 40% / 20% payment schedule splits the $2,400 fee into $960, $960 and $480. The schedule must be negotiated, documented and matched to the work and invoice dates. A milestone described in a proposal is not a cleared payment. Test the cash schedule if the second installment arrives late. Do not promise the client an unsupported revenue increase to justify the price. Use measurable deliverable acceptance or explicitly labeled scenarios instead. Taxes, intellectual property, confidentiality, cancellation and liability depend on the actual engagement; resolve those terms with suitable review rather than treating this example as a complete legal agreement. Complete and review the proposal before sending Replace the sample client, objective, deliverables and assumptions. Recompute all hours, costs, optional items and the total fee. Check the planned completion date against practical capacity and client dependencies. Reconcile milestone amounts to the total and record the due-date basis. Review commercial and legal terms for the actual engagement and retain the accepted version. Use the downloadable worksheet as an editable proposal record, including blank acceptance fields. The customer profitability guide helps evaluate account support beyond the initial job, while the contribution-margin method explains sales less variable costs, a different boundary from a loaded full-cost estimate. Use the cash forecast to test payment timing. When demand for the engagement grows, compare growth options against delivery capacity before promising a wider scope. Turn deliverables and changes into an acceptance record Salesforce’s proposal guide supports organizing client-specific scope, timing, price and acceptance. It is vendor education, not legal authority. For the 20-image case, identify the product list, final file format, dimensions, agreed background and the person authorized to approve delivery. Write observable completion criteria instead of promising an undefined “professional result.” Record which products, brand files and approvals the client must supply before production can proceed. Explain how a delayed input changes the proposed schedule. Give an additional image or correction request its own reference, estimated extra hours, impact on delivery and proposed fee decision. Confirm that decision before starting the additional scope. A recorded request alone is not evidence that the customer accepted a changed fee. Keep the accepted version and its supporting correspondence together so subsequent invoices can be traced to the same scope. The $40 internal loaded rate is an estimating assumption. It can include costs that do not vary with one additional project, so the $750 and $350 differences are labeled project surplus after included costs rather than automatically treated as textbook variable-cost contribution. Check which underlying salaries or shared costs are already in the rate before adding overhead. The $960, $960 and $480 installments sum to the $2,400 fee, but due dates are not receipt dates. Map cash timing independently, including a delayed second installment. Review intellectual property, cancellation, liability and other engagement-specific terms with appropriate expertise rather than treating the worksheet as a complete enforceable agreement. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. Frequently asked questions What should a business proposal include? A client objective, defined deliverables, scope boundaries, schedule, price, assumptions, payment basis and an acceptance process suited to the engagement. Is the project surplus percentage the same as markup? No. Here project surplus divided by fee and project surplus divided by included cost use different denominators. Standard contribution margin uses variable costs; this example instead uses its stated loaded project-cost boundary. Can this worksheet replace a contract? It is a teaching and drafting record. Whether additional terms or a separate agreement are needed depends on the actual engagement and applicable law. How should I handle extra revisions? Define the original revision scope, then review and document the effect of additional work on cost, price and delivery dates before proceeding. Is the $750 example surplus the company’s net profit? No. It is the fee less the specified project costs. Shared overhead, financing, tax and any omitted costs still need consideration; the internal loaded-rate basis also matters. Does a customer request automatically approve an extra fee? No. Record the requested change, proposed scope/date/fee effect and the actual acceptance before beginning additional work. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Choose a growth mechanism before choosing a spending budget Growth choices to test against actual evidence Option Evidence needed Cost or constraint to test Retain existing customers Repeat purchase and churn records Support effort and retention incentives Improve price or scope Buyer acceptance and offer comparison Lost volume and delivery changes Sell more through the current channel Conversion and demand records Acquisition cost and practical capacity Add a channel or segment Pilot with separately tracked economics Fees, returns and collections Add an offer for existing buyers Problem and willingness-to-pay evidence Development, training and complexity Increase delivery capacity Verified backlog and bottleneck Fixed commitments and ramp-up cash Compare options using the same period and cost boundary. A discount may increase orders while lowering total contribution. A new channel may bring demand but add commissions or slower settlement. Retention can reduce replacement selling effort, but it still needs a defined offer and service budget. Test the actual mechanism rather than applying a generic growth percentage. Compare price, volume and capacity in one fictional business Independent monthly cases; baseline price 200, job cost 100, overhead 6000 Case Jobs / price Revenue Contribution Overhead Result Baseline 100 / $200 $20,000 $10,000 $6,000 $4,000 Price +5%, same volume 100 / $210 $21,000 $11,000 $6,000 $5,000 Volume +20%, same costs 120 / $200 $24,000 $12,000 $6,000 $6,000 Volume +20%, new capacity cost 120 / $200 $24,000 $12,000 $8,500 $3,500 Each job takes two worker-hours. Baseline work requires 200 hours; 120 jobs require 240. If practical capacity is 220, the simple volume case is infeasible without a resource or scope change. The last case assumes a specific $2,500 added monthly commitment and adequate capacity, showing a result below baseline despite higher sales. The price case assumes no volume loss solely to isolate the price effect; customer acceptance still needs evidence. Growth result before a separately specified campaign expense depends on the capacity cost. Exact chart of the original fictional example. Fund the ramp before treating the result as available cash Suppose the extra 20 jobs require $2,000 additional delivery payments before customer cash clears. A $1,000 campaign payment and $2,500 capacity payment are also due before those receipts. The incremental pre-collection cash requirement is $5,500, before fees, timing differences or a chosen reserve. This is a cash schedule, not another $5,500 expense to subtract from the monthly result. The table already includes the $2,000 delivery cost and $2,500 capacity cost, but excludes the separately specified $1,000 campaign. If that campaign is an additional expense of the same month, the fourth-row result after campaign expense is $2,500; its payment date alone does not establish the expense period. Map every incremental receipt and payment to a date. Distinguish a one-time setup purchase from a recurring capacity commitment. Test customer payment delays and the period after a promotion ends. Review the financial contingency plan for triggers if the growth assumptions fail. Set limits and compare a pilot with its original case Choose one offer, channel or segment for the first test. Record incremental acquisition spending, accepted price, realized delivery hours, refund or rework costs and collection dates. Keep comparable existing activity visible: a new channel can shift customers from an existing channel rather than create entirely new demand. Set an exposure ceiling, review date and response to missed assumptions before launching the test. For example, investigate if delivery rises above the planned two hours or if additional sales require capacity earlier than expected. Those are case-specific controls. Do not claim a pilot caused all extra sales without a defensible comparison. Decide using profit, bottlenecks and cash together Approve a next step only when the demand evidence, defined contribution, operational plan and dated cash schedule reconcile. List commitments that cannot be reversed quickly and verify funding conditions. A positive forecast under an unapproved staffing plan is still an unresolved decision. Use CVP scenarios for cost ranges, the sales forecast for demand and capacity, and ROAS versus ROI when evaluating a paid campaign. Link growth choices to an archived operating forecast so the next review can explain what actually changed. Translate an approved growth choice into measurable business goals , and record the resource trade-off in the strategic plan . Reconcile the separate campaign between profit and cash BDC’s growth guidance links expansion with resource and cash requirements. Apply that principle without treating cash receipt as the universal revenue-recognition rule. The original table isolates price, volume and capacity. Its fourth row’s $3,500 result is before a separately specified campaign expense. The fourth row already includes the extra 20 jobs’ $2,000 delivery cost and the $2,500 additional monthly capacity commitment. If the later $1,000 campaign payment represents an additional expense of this same month, that row’s result after campaign expense is $2,500. A payment alone does not determine its accounting period: a genuine prepayment or a different covered period needs its own treatment under the applicable basis. Keep the $3,500 before-campaign comparison and any after-campaign result explicitly labeled instead of mixing them in one table. In the stated cash scenario, the delivery, campaign and capacity payments are all due before the incremental customer receipts, so the pre-collection outlay is $5,500. Do not subtract that full amount again from $3,500: delivery and capacity are already included in the fourth row. The $1,000 campaign is the newly specified item, whose expense treatment must be stated separately. Map the subsequent receipts, any repayments and the period after the campaign ends. A funded expansion can still reduce profit; a profitable expansion can still require cash before collection. Reconcile both views to the same underlying commitments before increasing the next spending limit. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . Additional fixed commitments, weaker prices, delivery costs or channel costs can outweigh the extra contribution. Should I spend more on ads first? Identify the growth mechanism and current bottleneck first. Additional demand may create a capacity or cash problem rather than a better result. Does the price scenario predict a 5% increase will work? No. It holds volume constant to isolate arithmetic. Actual willingness to pay and retention need evidence. How should I compare growth options? Use matching periods and cost boundaries, then check demand evidence, practical capacity, cash dates and downside exposure. Why is the growth table’s $3,500 result different from $2,500 after campaign expense? The $3,500 row includes the delivery and added capacity costs but excludes the separate $1,000 campaign. If that campaign is an additional expense of the same period, the after-campaign result is $2,500. Should I subtract the $5,500 cash requirement again from the table result? No. The delivery and capacity costs are already in the fourth row. Reconcile cash payment dates and expense periods item by item; a payment does not by itself establish the expense period. documents.summary: Assess demand, delivery capacity, economics and funding with a worked feasibility study. Use explicit proceed, revise or stop conditions and an editable record.
documents.headings: Quick answer Define the decision and the alternatives Test five connected forms of feasibility Work through a constrained service venture Compare explicit revisions instead of forcing a yes Write a conditional decision that can be checked State which evidence would reverse the decision Download the editable decision record Sources and method Continue with business ideas and launch Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Business Feasibility Study: Should This Venture Proceed? Published November 5, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Assess demand, delivery capacity, economics and funding with a worked feasibility study. Use explicit proceed, revise or stop conditions and an editable record. Business finance Planning Worked example Quick answer A business feasibility study investigates whether a defined venture can work under real market, operating, financial and funding constraints. Its output is an evidenced proceed, revise or stop decision with conditions, rather than a document written to justify a decision already made. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Financial cases are original fictional teaching examples. All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Define the decision and the alternatives Specify the offer, customer, delivery model, location where relevant, decision horizon and commitments under consideration. Include a smaller pilot or postponement as real alternatives. A study of “starting a business” is too broad to test supplier quotes, customer acceptance or the cash required before launch. Decide in advance which evidence would change the answer. Separate confirmed facts from estimates and unknowns. Name the owner, date and source for important assumptions. Feasibility investigates whether the venture should proceed; the subsequent business plan develops how an accepted option will operate. Test five connected forms of feasibility Decision questions and evidence Area Core question Useful evidence Market Will the defined customer buy at this scope and price? Paid pilot, buyer interviews and alternatives Technical / operational Can the team deliver the required quality and volume? Timed process, supplier quotes and capacity Organizational / requirements Can the actual team operate within relevant obligations? Competence, permissions and adviser checks Economic Does defined contribution cover the requirement? Reconciled costs, price and scenarios Funding / timing Can commitments be paid when due? Dated cash schedule and verified funding Passing one area does not pass the others. A popular product can fail a practical delivery test; a positive accounting result can still require more startup cash than is available. Obtain current specialist input for material location or activity requirements instead of copying a general statement that permits are “easy.” Work through a constrained service venture Consider a fictional monthly service priced at $300 with $120 relevant delivery cost per job. Contribution is $180. Period overhead is $5,400, so operating break-even is 30 whole jobs. A separately chosen $3,600 owner-income planning requirement raises the combined recovery target to 50 jobs: ($5,400 + $3,600) ÷ $180. Each job takes three delivery hours. At 120 practical delivery hours a month, the business can complete only 40 jobs before other constraints. At 40 jobs, revenue is $12,000, delivery costs $4,800 and contribution $7,200. After $5,400 overhead, the result is $1,800, below the chosen owner-income requirement. Calling the idea feasible because it passes 30-job operating break-even would conceal that unmet requirement. Break-even does not establish capacity feasibility. Exact chart of the original fictional example. Compare explicit revisions instead of forcing a yes One option is a $330 price with unchanged $120 job cost. Contribution becomes $210, and the combined $9,000 requirement needs 43 whole jobs after rounding up, still above 40-job capacity. Another option reduces the scoped delivery time to two hours, if quality and customer acceptance can be maintained. At the original $300 price, capacity becomes 60 jobs and the 50-job recovery target becomes operationally possible, but demand remains unproven. Test revised scope rather than assuming the same job can be rushed without consequence. If the narrower offer loses customers or adds rework, update both the demand and cost cases. Funding remains a separate test: a $9,000 startup cash need against $7,000 confirmed funds leaves $2,000 unresolved even if the revised operating case works. Write a conditional decision that can be checked The original model should not receive unconditional approval: the owner-income requirement exceeds the capacity-supported result and a funding gap remains. A reasonable study output is “revise and test the narrower scope, obtain demand evidence at that scope, and resolve the dated $2,000 funding gap before launch commitments.” Record who must deliver each piece of evidence and by when. Use the startup cost calculator for launch cash, CVP analysis for the cost range and business plan template after choosing a viable alternative. Archive rejected options as well as the approved one so later reviewers can see the trade-offs. If a revised model passes the decision conditions, continue with the launch roadmap ; use the seasonal funding case for an example of dated operating cash needs. State which evidence would reverse the decision Iowa State Extension’s feasibility guidance examines whether a proposed idea can proceed using the resources and risks involved. The five connected tests in this article are its working structure, not a compulsory universal five-part standard. Its owner-income requirement is a planning recovery target, not automatically a deductible accounting expense. Give each decision condition a source, accountable owner and review date. For the original three-hour service, a forecast of 50 jobs does not resolve the 40-job practical capacity limit. A revised two-hour scope must be demonstrated at the required quality and accepted price. Include rework, inspection and added supervision before approving the new 60-job ceiling. A supplier quote should identify its scope, expiry, payment dates and assumptions; a favorable amount from a different specification is not equivalent support. Funding must still resolve the separate $2,000 startup gap. Compare proceed, pilot, revise and postpone on the same horizon and cost definitions. Record which commitments are difficult to reverse and the maximum exposure before the next evidence check. State the specific result that would stop further spending: missing permissions, a failed delivery test, insufficient buyer acceptance or unavailable funding can each matter. A “not yet supportable” conclusion is useful rather than a reason to manufacture a positive business plan. Preserve rejected alternatives and the evidence behind the decision. The university page is educational material; its authors state they no longer provide feasibility-study assistance, so use it as a reference rather than a promise of an available advisory service. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . It includes the completed case and blank fields for your evidence, assumptions, dates and decision. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. Sources and method The linked sources support the general framework. The calculations, operating constraints and decision examples here are original MyBreakEven teaching material. Iowa State University Extension: feasibility study purpose and scope Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions How does a feasibility study differ from a business plan? A study investigates whether and under which conditions to proceed. A business plan develops the chosen operating and funding approach. Does break-even prove feasibility? No. Capacity, demand, owner requirements, funding dates and other constraints can still fail. Can the answer be revise rather than yes or no? Yes. State the exact changes, evidence needed and commitments that must wait. Are the cost figures industry averages? No. All figures are fictional assumptions constructed to expose the capacity and funding decision. Are the guide’s five feasibility areas an official universal standard? No. They organize this guide’s market, delivery, organizational, economic and funding investigation. A real study should include the issues material to the actual venture. Does a forecast of 50 jobs resolve a 40-job capacity ceiling? No. Demonstrate a workable change in price, scope, resources or the required recovery target, then recheck demand, quality and funding. documents.title: Business Goals: Translate Targets into Drivers and Cash
documents.summary: Turn business goals into measurable drivers, ownership and review dates. Reconcile a service growth target with delivery hours, contribution and cash needs.
documents.headings: Quick answer Separate a goal, a forecast and an action Translate a fictional revenue target into work Check contribution and the payment cycle Give each goal a measure, owner and guardrail Review progress without rewriting the original target Keep the same measurement definition through every review Download the editable decision record Sources and method Continue with strategy, growth and risk Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Business Goals: Translate Targets into Drivers and Cash Published November 5, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Turn business goals into measurable drivers, ownership and review dates. Reconcile a service growth target with delivery hours, contribution and cash needs. Business finance Planning Worked example Quick answer A useful business goal names an outcome, its baseline, a measure, an owner and a review date. Translate the target into customer activity, delivery capacity and cash requirements before treating it as an achievable commitment. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Financial cases are original fictional teaching examples. All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Separate a goal, a forecast and an action A goal is an intended result. A forecast is the current evidence-based expectation. An action is something the team will do to influence the result. “Reach $24,000 monthly revenue” is a goal; “current customer evidence supports $21,000” is a forecast; “test one referral offer by the end of the month” is an action. Keep those statements separate so an ambitious goal does not become an unsupported forecast. The SMART framework helps make objectives specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. It does not independently verify demand, resource availability or cause and effect. Write the baseline and source beside the target, including the reporting period and cost or revenue boundary. Translate a fictional revenue target into work A service business currently completes 80 jobs per month at $250: revenue is $20,000. Its goal is $24,000 at the same price within the chosen three-month planning period. That requires 96 jobs, an increase of 16, or 20%. At three worker-hours per job, required delivery time rises from 240 to 288 hours. Practical available delivery capacity is 270 hours. The target therefore needs 18 additional hours, a valid scope change or a different price/volume mix. A goal can be clear and measurable while still exceeding capacity. Confirm whether the 270 hours already excludes general administration, absence, travel or rework; do not subtract those twice. Check contribution and the payment cycle Assume the defined relevant delivery cost is $100 per job. Each job contributes $150 before period overhead and other omitted costs. Sixteen extra jobs add $2,400 contribution if price and cost remain unchanged. That amount is not an approved hiring budget unless the added-capacity plan, overhead effect and owner requirements have been tested. If those extra jobs require $1,600 delivery payments before customer collections, the growth plan needs a dated cash bridge. A $400 referral test paid in advance increases the illustrative pre-collection outlay to $2,000. Avoid subtracting the $1,600 delivery cost twice from the projected result: it is already included in contribution. Cash timing and profit use the same underlying events in different views. Give each goal a measure, owner and guardrail Original example goal record; targets are management choices Field Example Evidence / control Outcome 96 completed jobs per month by review date Accepted job and completion records Baseline 80 jobs at 250 Same period and revenue basis Driver Qualified inquiries, acceptance and repeat work Track distinct customers and denominators Capacity 288 required hours vs 270 available Resolve 18-hour shortfall Cash 2000 illustrative pre-collection outlay Confirm dates and available funds Owner / review Operations owner; weekly driver review Monthly outcome and quality review Guardrail No unapproved scope or quality decline Rework, complaints and actual hours Use a small set of leading measures the team can act on and lagging measures that show the outcome. Calls made alone may rise without useful orders; completed sales alone may hide refunds or unpaid balances. Choose denominators carefully and avoid changing the definition after the target is missed. Review progress without rewriting the original target Preserve the approved baseline, goal and forecast. At review, explain differences in volume, price, time, contribution and collection dates. Record whether a missed result reflects demand, delivery limits, changed assumptions or execution. Revise the next forecast using new evidence while retaining accountability for the original goal. Use the sales-forecast method for expected demand, rolling forecasting for refreshed assumptions and the cash forecast for payment dates. Put the corrective action, responsible person, deadline and next evidence check next to the goal rather than in a separate forgotten task list. Choose the underlying growth mechanism before assigning an activity target. The strategy example shows how to prioritize scarce resources. Keep the same measurement definition through every review BDC’s SMART explanation supports clear criteria and alignment with available resources. For this guide’s original goal, define whether a job counts when booked, delivered, accepted or paid. Those stages are not interchangeable, even if each appears in the same customer system. State the calendar period and treatment of cancellations, refunds and rework. Use the same definition for the 80-job baseline and the 96-job target. A higher price can raise revenue without the same job increase, while a booking target can be met even when the resulting work exceeds available delivery time. Identify whether $250 is the gross quoted price or revenue after any agreed credits. If a definition changes, retain a reconciliation to the earlier series rather than claiming the resulting measurement jump is operating improvement. Assign a data owner for the job record and an action owner for the referral test; they may be different people. Keep the current forecast beside the intended target. Do not raise a forecast solely to match an ambition. At three hours each, 96 jobs still require 288 hours against 270 available: the 18-hour gap remains until a real capacity, scope or price/volume decision resolves it. Record the revised assumption, approval date and resulting cost or cash effect. Review completed activity, service quality, case-defined margin and payment timing together. Clear goal wording helps coordination; it cannot independently supply missing demand or delivery resources. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . It includes the completed case and blank fields for your evidence, assumptions, dates and decision. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. Sources and method The linked sources support the general framework. The calculations, operating constraints and decision examples here are original MyBreakEven teaching material. BDC: SMART objectives and resource alignment Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is a revenue goal a sales forecast? No. The goal is intended performance. A forecast estimates what current evidence supports. What makes a business goal achievable? Verify demand, delivery resources, cost assumptions and dated cash availability, rather than relying on wording alone. How many goals should I set? Choose a manageable set with clear ownership and measures. The right number depends on the business and review capacity. Should I change the goal after missing it? Preserve the original record, explain the variance and approve any future revision explicitly. Do not erase the comparison. Can I compare booked jobs with a completed-job baseline? Not without a clear reconciliation. Bookings, delivery, acceptance and payment measure different stages; retain the same definition for the goal and baseline. Does a SMART goal automatically make 96 jobs achievable? No. The fictional case still has an 18-hour delivery shortfall, and actual demand and cash evidence must support any revised operating plan. documents.title: Strategic Planning for Small Business: Choices, Resources and Review
documents.summary: Build a small-business strategy around customer choices, trade-offs and resources. Compare two original options and use a quarterly review record.
documents.headings: Quick answer Start with the decision the business needs to make Compare choices using the same scarce resource State what the business will decline or defer Fund a short list of connected initiatives Use a quarterly review to challenge the choice Record the scarce-resource decision and its review trigger Download the editable decision record Sources and method Continue with strategy, growth and risk Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Strategic Planning for Small Business: Choices, Resources and Review Published November 5, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a small-business strategy around customer choices, trade-offs and resources. Compare two original options and use a quarterly review record. Business finance Planning Worked example Quick answer Small-business strategic planning chooses which customers to serve, how the business will compete and where limited resources will go. A workable strategy makes trade-offs explicit, funds a few coherent priorities and defines how evidence will trigger a review. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. AI-created topic illustration. Financial cases are original fictional teaching examples. All business names, amounts and operating results in the worked examples are fictional teaching assumptions in USD. They are not industry averages, actual customer results or forecasts for your business. Start with the decision the business needs to make Review the actual customer mix, contribution, delivery process, cash cycle and bottleneck. Separate recurring strengths from a one-time favorable month. Use customer evidence and relevant alternatives to identify where the business has a defensible advantage, rather than filling a long SWOT list with untested claims. State the central choice in one sentence. For a fictional service company, the choice is whether to concentrate on nearby repeat office customers or pursue a wider premium project market. Both can sound attractive. The strategy must explain which one receives scarce management attention and practical delivery hours first. Compare choices using the same scarce resource Illustrative monthly steady-state cases, before separate setup cash Choice Nearby repeat offices Wider premium projects Customer volume 20 accounts 12 projects Revenue per customer $500 $900 Relevant delivery cost per customer $250 $450 Total revenue $10,000 $10,800 Contribution $5,000 $5,400 Delivery hours per customer 5 10 Total delivery hours 100 120 Contribution per delivery hour $50 $45 Defined common overhead $3,000 $3,000 Illustrative operating result $2,000 $2,400 At 120 practical delivery hours, the premium-project option fully uses the stated capacity; the repeat-office option uses 100 hours. Premium projects produce $400 more monthly result under the assumptions, but lower contribution per delivery hour and no spare delivery capacity. Those facts do not automatically choose the winner: customer evidence, volatility, sales effort and execution risk remain material. State what the business will decline or defer If the company chooses nearby repeat offices, it might prioritize route density, consistent scope and renewal discipline, while deferring distant custom work. That choice needs evidence that the nearby market can support the volume and accepted price. The 20 unallocated hours may provide resilience or future capacity; they do not become revenue without customers. If it chooses premium projects, it must support the longer delivery scope and potentially different sales and collection cycle. In a separate startup scenario, the repeat-office approach needs $2,000 setup cash and premium projects need $6,000. Those are original assumptions to test, not deductions from the steady-state result. Map the actual cash timing and avoid judging the choice on one monthly profit number alone. Fund a short list of connected initiatives For the repeat-office choice, coherent initiatives could include validating a compact service area, standardizing the service checklist and measuring renewals. Allocate hours, budget and an owner to each. Do not simultaneously approve a distant custom-sales push if it consumes the resources the chosen strategy needs. Write a one-page action record: choice, evidence, initiative, resources, owner, deadline, outcome measure and review trigger. Connect the operating assumptions to the budget and cash forecast. A list of activities without a resource limit is not an allocation decision. Hiring, leases and other harder-to-reverse commitments need their own explicit decision case. Use a quarterly review to challenge the choice At the chosen review date, examine whether the customer and delivery assumptions held. Track contribution per constrained hour, customer retention, actual selling effort, collection delays and service quality. Compare matching periods and definitions. A missed target may need a tactical adjustment, a revised assumption or a different strategic choice; identify which before adding more initiatives. The business plan explains the wider venture, rolling forecasting refreshes operating expectations and customer profitability analysis tests cost to serve. Preserve the original strategy and review evidence so the next quarter’s changes are deliberate rather than reactions to whichever new opportunity appears first. Use the goal-to-driver record to assign ownership after making the strategic choice. The growth comparison tests the cost of added capacity. Record the scarce-resource decision and its review trigger BDC’s strategy guidance connects priorities to named actions, responsibility, timing and measures. Apply that structure to an explicit resource choice. University of Nevada, Reno Extension also treats strategic planning as fundamental direction and decisions, rather than simply a list of tasks. Record which of the original two options receives the next available hours and setup cash, what is deferred and what evidence could change the choice. Nearby offices use 100 of the stated 120 delivery hours. The remaining 20 can provide resilience or be offered to additional buyers, but unused capacity is not already revenue. Premium projects use all 120 hours and generate $400 greater modeled monthly result. They also need $4,000 more assumed setup cash. Neither difference by itself settles the strategic choice; compare buyer evidence, collection timing, service quality and the cost of acquiring the work. Assign each approved initiative an owner, due date, budget and outcome measure. Check that the same manager-hours or cash are not allocated to incompatible initiatives. A material customer loss, unavailable worker or failed price assumption may warrant review before the next chosen quarterly meeting. Record the trigger and the decision authority in advance. Separate a tactical adjustment within the selected model from a change in the model itself, and preserve the old version for comparison. Do not infer a compulsory review cadence or document length from one educational source. The business needs a usable record of its choices, commitments and evidence. Download the editable decision record Download the printable HTML worksheet . It includes the completed case and blank fields for your evidence, assumptions, dates and decision. It does not calculate automatically. Edits stay in the open browser until you print or save your completed copy; keep your original separately. Sources and method The linked sources support the general framework. The calculations, operating constraints and decision examples here are original MyBreakEven teaching material. BDC: strategic choices, priorities and action planning University of Nevada, Reno Extension: strategic planning Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is strategic planning a list of growth targets? No. It chooses customers, competitive approach and resource priorities, including what the business will defer. Should I always choose the highest monthly profit option? Compare demand confidence, capacity, selling effort, cash commitments and risk as well as the stated result. How does strategy differ from the operating budget? Strategy chooses priorities and trade-offs. The budget translates the chosen activities into a defined financial period. How often should a small business review strategy? Choose a cadence suited to the business and revisit material failed assumptions promptly. The example uses a quarterly formal review. Do the unused 20 hours automatically create more office revenue? No. They are capacity, which may provide resilience or be offered to buyers. Additional accepted demand and its delivery/cash requirements still need evidence. Must a small business wait until a quarterly meeting to review strategy? No. Quarterly review is this example’s chosen cadence. A material failed assumption can justify an earlier review under a documented decision process. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.title: Customer Profitability Analysis: Revenue, Cost to Serve and Decisions
documents.summary: Measure customer profit with a reconciled cost-to-serve example. Separate avoidable costs, shared overhead and cash timing before changing an account.
documents.headings: Quick answer Define the period and the cost boundary Reconcile three customers to the business total Choose drivers that explain actual work Test an action instead of automatically dropping the customer Build a monthly account review that can be audited Test the incremental effect before removing an account Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with pricing and customer profitability Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Customer Profitability Analysis: Revenue, Cost to Serve and Decisions Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Measure customer profit with a reconciled cost-to-serve example. Separate avoidable costs, shared overhead and cash timing before changing an account. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Customer profitability analysis compares a customer’s net revenue with the direct and shared costs of serving that customer during the same period. Show the defined service subtotal and allocated profit separately before deciding whether a relationship should change. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Define the period and the cost boundary Start with a customer-month, quarter or year. Use earned revenue after discounts, credits and returns for that period. Keep collections in a separate dated view: an unpaid invoice can create accounting revenue without available cash. Define whether your result includes acquisition spending, account support, general overhead and owner work. Defined customer service subtotal = net revenue − directly traceable delivery and service costs. Then subtract assigned shared service costs to obtain the specifically defined allocated result. Label the boundary; do not call a partially costed margin company net income. A customer’s lifetime value uses a different horizon and needs retention assumptions. Reconcile three customers to the business total Fictional monthly customer ledger Measure Customer A Customer B Customer C Total Net revenue $6,000 $4,000 $2,000 $12,000 Direct delivery $2,400 $2,000 $1,200 $5,600 Support hours 10 20 30 60 Support at $40/hour $400 $800 $1,200 $2,400 Customer subtotal after assigned support $3,200 $1,200 −$400 $4,000 General overhead allocated $900 $600 $300 $1,800 Allocated result $2,300 $600 −$700 $2,200 The support pool is $2,400 divided by 60 practical support hours, giving $40 per hour. General overhead is allocated by revenue only to reconcile the remaining $1,800. Its allocation is a reporting choice, not evidence that the cash disappears when a customer leaves. Total revenue of $12,000 less $5,600 delivery, $2,400 support and $1,800 overhead equals $2,200. Choose drivers that explain actual work Use order lines for processing, support time for assistance, shipments for dispatch and documented collection effort for chasing overdue balances. Do not allocate every pool by sales simply because sales is available. Record the pool amount, source ledger, included activity, denominator and each customer’s usage. The sum of allocations must equal the amount assigned; idle capacity or unassigned overhead should remain visible. For acquisition cost, choose and disclose a treatment. Expensing all campaign spend in the acquisition month may be useful for that month’s result; spreading it over an assumed relationship produces a different managerial measure. Neither choice should silently mix lifetime acquisition cost with one month’s revenue. Test an action instead of automatically dropping the customer Customer C looks loss-making after allocation. Suppose a standard-order policy removes ten support hours. At the chosen $40 rate, the ledger shows $400 less assigned support and a zero customer subtotal after assigned support. But if salaried staff are still paid, near-term cash does not improve by $400. Instead, released hours may let the same team serve better work. Before repricing or exiting, list contract commitments, collection risk, rework, spare capacity and costs genuinely avoided. Compare a scoped service level, paid rush requests, minimum order or staged price change with the current account. A negative allocated result is a reason to investigate, not an automatic customer termination rule. Build a monthly account review that can be audited Reconcile customer net revenue to the sales ledger. Trace delivery, refunds and customer-specific effort from source records. Allocate only identified service pools using documented drivers. Show unassigned overhead and reconcile the complete business result. Choose an action, name an owner and review the next period’s actuals. Use the agency client profitability guide for a service-account application, and the cleaning contract profit calculator for a contract-specific cost boundary. Check those records against the broader contribution income statement . Test the incremental effect before removing an account The customer ledger above is a management allocation, not a standard contribution-margin income statement. A conventional contribution margin subtracts variable costs from sales; a traceable customer cost can be fixed, and a support allocation can remain payable after the customer leaves. The OpenStax relevant-cost framework supports comparing future amounts that actually differ between alternatives. Extend Customer C with another explicitly fictional assumption: its $1,200 direct delivery cost disappears if the account ends, but all support salaries and general overhead remain. Removing C loses $2,000 revenue and avoids only $1,200 cost. The business result falls by $800, from $2,200 to $1,400, before any replacement work. The account’s negative $700 allocated result therefore does not mean closure saves $700. Now test released capacity separately. If the team can sell replacement work, list its achievable revenue, additional materials, delivery hours and collection date. Deduct transition costs or contract penalties where supported. Compare that complete alternative with retaining C; do not count both a salary saving and revenue from the same retained employee without explaining the staffing arrangement. Keep three columns in the decision record: amount assigned in the reporting ledger, cash actually avoided by the decision, and capacity released. Ask the delivery manager to confirm each assumption and reconcile the chosen action to the next month’s actual cost and customer service evidence. Frequently asked questions Is a high-revenue customer always profitable? No. Discounts, delivery effort, exceptions, support and collection work can consume the apparent margin. Compare consistently costed results for the same period. Should shared overhead determine whether to drop a customer? Not by itself. Test avoidable costs and released capacity; allocated overhead may remain after the account leaves. Which cost driver should I use? Choose a documented measure that explains the activity, such as support hours or shipments. Reconcile the allocated pool and show any unassigned cost. Can profit be positive while collections are late? Yes. Accrual revenue and the defined customer service subtotal do not establish available cash. Track invoice due dates and receipts separately. Why can dropping a customer reduce business profit despite a negative allocated result? The customer may still cover costs that remain payable after departure. In the added fictional case, removing $2,000 revenue avoids only $1,200 delivery cost, reducing the business result by $800. Is a directly traceable cost automatically variable? No. Traceability identifies the customer or activity; cost behavior describes how the amount changes with activity or a decision. A dedicated salary can be traceable and fixed. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE ROAS vs ROI: Follow One Campaign from Revenue to Profit Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare ROAS and ROI using one campaign ledger. Include refunds, product costs and creative fees, and state the investment denominator before comparing returns. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer ROAS divides attributed conversion revenue by ad spend. ROI compares a defined net profit with a defined investment cost. A high ROAS can coexist with a loss when product, fulfillment, refunds and campaign costs absorb the revenue. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Write both formulas and state what each includes ROAS = attributed conversion revenue ÷ advertising spend. A 4× result means $4 attributed revenue for each $1 of media spend; it is not $4 profit. Where a platform tracks non-revenue conversion value, call the metric conversion-value ROAS rather than cash sales. ROI = net return ÷ defined investment cost × 100%. Net return subtracts the costs included in that definition. Some teams report campaign profit divided by media/marketing investment; others divide by all included costs. Both can be interpretable, but only if the numerator and denominator are explicit and comparable. Work through one completed campaign Original fictional campaign, one matched reporting window Ledger item Amount Treatment Net attributed revenue $12,000 After credits/returns in this example Ad spend $3,000 Media only Product costs $5,400 Cost of fulfilled sales Fulfillment and transaction fees $1,800 Additional sale-linked costs Creative and campaign support $1,200 Separate from media Included total cost $11,400 Sum of all four cost lines Profit after included costs $600 $12,000 − $11,400 ROAS is $12,000 ÷ $3,000 = 4×, or 400% . Total-cost ROI is $600 ÷ $11,400 = 5.26% . A separately labelled marketing-investment return is $600 ÷ ($3,000 + $1,200) = 14.29% . The different percentages do not conflict: their cost bases differ. The case excludes general company overhead, interest and tax, so $600 is not represented as company net income. Find the threshold implied by this exact ledger Product and fulfillment costs total $7,200, or 60% of net revenue. The pre-marketing contribution ratio is 40%. Ignoring the separate creative/support cost, media-only break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5×. Including $1,200 creative/support and holding $3,000 media spend fixed requires revenue of ($3,000 + $1,200) ÷ 0.40 = $10,500, or 3.5× media ROAS . This threshold assumes a stable cost ratio, net revenue definition and campaign support budget. If returns, order mix or fulfillment rates change, recalculate. Use the existing break-even ROAS calculator and its formula explanation for the threshold task rather than creating a second ROAS tool. Keep the sales result constant and change the economics If fulfillment and fees increase by $900, profit falls from $600 to −$300 while ROAS remains 4×. Included costs become $12,300 and total-cost ROI becomes −2.44%. That is why creative changes that raise revenue can still damage profit when they also increase discounts, returns or expensive deliveries. Track net revenue, contribution before media, campaign profit and cash settlement together. Compare cohorts only after a consistent conversion/return window. An order reported today may be returned later, and a payment processor can settle cash on another date. Do not turn attribution into proof of incremental sales Attributed conversions follow a platform’s measurement model. They do not establish how many sales would have happened without advertising. Separate branded/returning-customer attribution from a documented incrementality test. Do not combine overlapping platform revenue totals as though every order were unique. Before increasing spend, verify currency, revenue events, refunds, attribution windows, cost imports and the investment definition. Review ecommerce unit economics and the business ROI calculator when the decision includes more than advertising. Reconcile the reported return to orders, attribution and cash Google Ads’ ROI example includes production and advertising costs in its stated investment base. That supports the total-cost version used above; it does not make every marketing team’s differently defined return interchangeable. Keep a named numerator, denominator and measurement window beside every percentage. For this fictional $12,000 campaign, prepare an order-level bridge from gross tracked value to $12,000 net attributed revenue. Show cancellations, credits and returns once. If the conversion tag sends profit or an assigned lead score rather than revenue, label the platform value accordingly; a 4× value-to-cost ratio then cannot be described as four sales dollars per advertising dollar. Incrementality is a separate question. Google’s conversion-lift documentation distinguishes experiment-based additional value from attribution-based credit. As an independent teaching calculation, suppose a valid experiment estimated $4,500 incremental revenue against $3,000 media spend: incremental revenue ROAS would be 1.5×. The same ledger could still show 4× attributed ROAS because the numerators answer different questions. This invented experiment result is not a measurement of the site or a customer. Before scaling, reconcile finance revenue, platform settings and the experiment’s uncertainty. Also check unsettled processor amounts and the expected return window. A correct reported ratio cannot replace evidence of additional demand, profitable fulfillment or enough cash to fund orders before collections arrive. No. A 400% ROAS is 4× attributed value divided by media spend. ROI uses net return and a separately defined investment denominator. Which result should I use for scaling? Review contribution and campaign profit, attribution quality, capacity and cash timing together. A revenue ratio alone does not establish profitable incremental growth. Should refunds change the revenue input? Use a consistently defined net revenue measure and a matched return window. Do not subtract a refund again if it is already netted in the input. Does reported ROAS prove advertising caused the sales? No. Attribution assigns credit under a model. Incrementality requires evidence about sales that would not have happened without the campaign. Can the same campaign show 4× attributed ROAS and 1.5× incremental ROAS? Yes, if a valid experiment supports the different incremental numerator. The added amounts are fictional arithmetic, not evidence that any actual campaign achieved those results. What if conversion value is a lead score rather than revenue? Label the ratio conversion value divided by spend. Do not present a score-based conversion value as sales revenue, profit or received cash. documents.summary: Build a sales forecast from units, price and customer evidence. Check capacity, separate bookings from cash and compare scenarios with an editable worksheet.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Sales Forecast Formula: Build a Capacity-Checked Small-Business Plan Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a sales forecast from units, price and customer evidence. Check capacity, separate bookings from cash and compare scenarios with an editable worksheet. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer A practical sales forecast sums expected units multiplied by net selling price for each offer and period. Build the unit assumptions from customer evidence, check delivery capacity, and keep revenue recognition and collection dates separate. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Choose a method that matches the evidence you have For repeat services, begin with opening customers, expected completed work and known renewals. For a product line, use expected sold units and net unit prices. For a qualified pipeline, sum opportunity value multiplied by a documented close probability for the relevant period. Historical growth can supply a baseline, but unexplained percentage growth is not customer evidence. Forecast sales = Σ(expected units × net unit price). A weighted pipeline is an expectation across uncertain outcomes, not a promise that a fractional contract will close. Do not add the same sale again when it appears in both a customer schedule and the pipeline. Build a two-offer month before applying a growth rate Fictional planning month Offer Completed jobs Net price Revenue Hours/job Worker-hours Recurring service 40 $180 $7,200 2 80 One-off service 12 $300 $3,600 4 48 Total 52 Mixed $10,800 Mixed 128 The team has 160 scheduled worker-hours, of which 80% are realistically productive: 128 hours . The base case uses every productive hour. A target of 60 recurring jobs and 12 one-off jobs would need 168 hours, so demand or sales ambition alone cannot support it. Keep worker-hours distinct from elapsed clock hours when several people attend a job. Use scenarios that change the actual drivers Demand scenarios with the same illustrative prices Scenario Recurring jobs One-off jobs Revenue Hours needed Capacity status Downside 32 8 $8,160 96 32 hours available Base 40 12 $10,800 128 At capacity Demand upside 48 16 $13,440 160 32 hours beyond capacity The upside is a demand case, not an executable delivery forecast. It needs 32 more productive hours, a revised offer mix or rescheduling. If overtime or contractors add cost, update contribution and cash along with sales. If cancellations are already incorporated in completed-job assumptions, do not subtract them a second time. Separate signed work, delivered revenue and cash received A signed $3,000 agreement in November might be delivered in December and collected in January. Keep separate columns for signed bookings, the revenue period under the applicable accounting treatment, and the expected receipt date. The illustrative tables use completed service work as the sales basis; they are not tax-method guidance. Once sales are built, send dated receipts into the cash-flow forecast . Use the rolling forecast guide to update the horizon as actual months close. These are linked tasks, not interchangeable templates. Measure forecast error and improve the assumptions Freeze a dated forecast version before the month begins. Compare actual units, net price, mix, cancellations and timing against that version. If actual revenue is $10,200 against $10,800, the dollar error is −$600 and the shortfall versus forecast is 5.56%. This stated denominator is forecast revenue; a metric using actual revenue would produce a different percentage. Review persistent bias rather than rewriting the old forecast to match actuals. For a new business, replace weak assumptions with paid pilots, signed scope, customer interviews and observed conversion rates as evidence accumulates. Retain the source date and owner of each assumption in the business plan evidence register . Calibrate pipeline probability and reconcile it to delivery Salesforce’s forecasting guidance recommends maintaining opportunity detail and using historical evidence when adjusting close probabilities. A stage label alone does not prove a reliable chance of winning. Record when each estimate was made, the expected close date and any unresolved condition. Consider an additional fictional pipeline: one $10,000 opportunity at an assumed 30% close probability and another $20,000 opportunity at 60%. Their weighted total is $15,000. Actual bookings from these two all-or-nothing opportunities could be $0, $10,000, $20,000 or $30,000. The $15,000 expectation is neither a partial signed contract nor a receipt guaranteed for next month. Correlated customer decisions can also make a downside scenario more severe than the weighted total suggests. Assign probable delivery dates only after checking the work. The existing two-offer base already requires all 128 productive worker-hours. Adding a newly won contract to that month without moving another job or obtaining supported additional capacity would overstate executable revenue. Preserve a demand view and a feasible delivery view, then send the feasible invoices and payment terms into cash planning. After closing the period, compare the dated opportunity list with wins, losses, slippages and delivery evidence. Investigate systematically optimistic close dates or stage probabilities. Keep the original forecast unchanged so later edits do not erase the forecast error being measured. Use the worksheet with your own records Download the printable, editable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed example and a blank table. Open it in a browser, edit the blank fields, calculate the outputs using the stated method and print to PDF or paper. It does not automatically calculate results or replace your accounting records. Method references and source notes The method references below support the definitions. The examples, assumptions and decision checks on this page are independently constructed. Salesforce: forecasting methods and review process Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Connect a startup financial model without creating another forecast A startup financial model connects a sales forecast, cost assumptions, planned income statement and dated cash forecast. Keep one explicit scenario: a fictional 100 orders × $80 gives $8,000 monthly sales; variable costs 100 × $30 give $3,000; $4,000 fixed operating expense leaves $1,000 operating profit under that boundary. A $6,000 equipment payment would reduce cash separately; depreciation and debt service need their own treatment. That $1,000 profit is not proof of $1,000 cash collected or enough capacity to deliver 100 orders. Add payment dates, startup purchases, funding and realistic worker-hours. Use the existing business-plan template , five-year projections resource , startup cash calculator and cash forecast as connected parts; do not add their separate funding goals together without reconciling the same costs. Frequently asked questions Can a sales target be used as a forecast? A target states an ambition. A forecast estimates an outcome from stated evidence and assumptions. Keep both visible rather than treating the target as proof. Does the forecast show cash available? Not by itself. Put delivery, invoice and collection dates into a separate dated cash schedule. How should I handle an upside above capacity? Label it a demand scenario and calculate the additional worker-hours or other constrained resources before treating it as deliverable revenue. What error denominator does the example use? It divides the revenue shortfall by forecast revenue. State the denominator because using actual revenue produces another percentage. Does $15,000 weighted pipeline mean $15,000 will be delivered next month? No. It is an expectation from stated opportunity values and assumed probabilities. Wins, timing, recognition and delivery capacity need separate evidence. Can I add won pipeline to the base without another capacity check? Only if the original base did not already include those jobs and sufficient delivery resources remain. This example’s base uses all 128 productive worker-hours. documents.title: Cost Volume Profit Analysis: Break-Even, Target Profit and Capacity
documents.summary: Test price, costs, volume, sales mix and capacity with CVP analysis. Reconcile break-even and target profit before accepting a higher fixed-cost commitment.
documents.headings: Quick answer Start with one consistent unit and cost boundary Reconcile the profit at several volumes Check the capacity step before trusting the target A sales mix changes what an average unit means Know when the straight-line model stops answering the question Measure the safety margin inside the relevant capacity range Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with break-even and sales risk Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost Volume Profit Analysis: Break-Even, Target Profit and Capacity Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Test price, costs, volume, sales mix and capacity with CVP analysis. Reconcile break-even and target profit before accepting a higher fixed-cost commitment. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Cost-volume-profit analysis tests how price, variable costs, fixed costs and sold volume combine to produce operating profit. Break-even is its zero-profit case; the useful business decision also checks demand, product mix and the capacity range. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Start with one consistent unit and cost boundary Operating profit = units × (net price − variable cost per unit) − fixed operating costs. Contribution per unit is net price less variable cost. The contribution ratio divides that contribution by price. Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by positive unit contribution. Required units for a profit target equal (fixed costs + target operating profit) divided by unit contribution. If contribution is zero or negative, selling more of the unchanged offer does not cover positive fixed costs. Keep every amount in the same period and currency. Owner wages included in fixed costs must not be added again as a separate profit goal. Drawings and financing require separate cash treatment. Reconcile the profit at several volumes Original fictional monthly case: $120 price, $72 variable cost, $9,600 fixed costs Sold units Sales Variable cost Contribution Operating profit 150 $18,000 $10,800 $7,200 −$2,400 200 $24,000 $14,400 $9,600 $0 250 $30,000 $18,000 $12,000 $2,400 300 $36,000 $21,600 $14,400 $4,800 Unit contribution is $48, the contribution ratio is 40%, and exact break-even is 200 units or $24,000. A $4,800 operating-profit target requires 300 units. A $5,000 target would require 304.1667 units mathematically; 305 whole units produce $5,040 profit under the unchanged assumptions. Exact chart of the original fixed-cost range. Rebuild the cost line when capacity adds another commitment. Check the capacity step before trusting the target Suppose existing resources can deliver only 260 units. Selling 300 requires another $2,400 monthly capacity commitment. The fixed-cost base becomes $12,000 and 300 units now produce $2,400, not $4,800. To recover the original $4,800 target at the same price and variable rate requires 350 units . That second target also needs its own capacity and demand check. A discounted price of $110 leaves only $38 contribution at the original $72 variable rate. With the original $9,600 fixed base, break-even becomes 252.6316 exact units, or 253 whole units. These comparisons isolate a changed assumption; combining them without rebuilding the full model would misstate the answer. A sales mix changes what an average unit means For two offers contributing $40 and $70 per unit, a 3:2 unit mix creates a five-unit bundle with $260 contribution. At $10,400 fixed cost, break-even is 40 bundles: 120 units of the first offer and 80 of the second. The weighted unit contribution is $52. If the mix changes, that average no longer applies. Use the existing multiple-product break-even guide for the mix calculation. The contribution income statement reconciles cost behavior; the target-profit guide owns the detailed units-and-sales task. Know when the straight-line model stops answering the question Simple CVP assumes stable price and variable cost per unit, a relevant fixed-cost range, meaningful cost classification and a stated mix. Inventory changes, capacity tiers, waste, payment fees and channel commissions can require a more detailed model. Profit is not available cash: collection delays, inventory purchases, debt principal and capital expenditure must also be scheduled. Use flexible budget variance analysis to compare actual performance at actual volume rather than blaming a revenue shortfall on cost control. Treat a feasible profit target as a plan to test, not proof that buyers will order it. Measure the safety margin inside the relevant capacity range The ACCA CVP explanation treats margin of safety as the excess of budgeted or actual sales over break-even sales. It should use the same price, cost assumptions and sales mix as the break-even calculation. It is a sales buffer under that model, not a cash reserve or a probability of avoiding loss. At 250 units in the original fictional case, sales are $30,000 and break-even sales are $24,000. The margin of safety is 50 units or $6,000. Dividing $6,000 by $30,000 gives 20%. A loss of 50 sales units reaches zero operating profit under the original $48 unit contribution and $9,600 fixed-cost base. This statement assumes no simultaneous price, mix, variable-rate or fixed-cost change. A capacity change requires a fresh calculation. The case’s additional $2,400 commitment raises fixed costs to $12,000, so the revised break-even is 250 units at $48 contribution. At 300 units, the revised result is $2,400 and the revised margin of safety is 50 units, or 16.67% of 300. The old 200-unit threshold no longer explains that committed cost structure. Record exactly when the extra commitment becomes unavoidable. If a capacity purchase has already been agreed, returning to a lower sales volume may not restore the old fixed-cost base immediately. Show the applicable range, commitment date and exit terms beside each scenario rather than selecting whichever fixed-cost assumption produces the preferred answer. Open it in a browser, edit the blank fields, calculate the outputs using the stated method and print to PDF or paper. It does not automatically calculate results or replace your accounting records. Method references and source notes The method references below support the definitions. The examples, assumptions and decision checks on this page are independently constructed. ACCA: CVP calculations, graphs and assumptions FAO: CVP and decision making Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is CVP the same as break-even analysis? Break-even is the zero-profit case within CVP. CVP also compares target profits and changes in volume, price, costs and mix. Why can a correct target still fail? It may exceed capacity, rely on unsupported demand or cross a fixed-cost step. A profit model also does not establish cash availability. What if contribution per unit is negative? With the same price and variable rate, additional units deepen the contribution shortfall. Resolve the economics before dividing fixed costs by contribution. Why does the product mix matter? Each offer can contribute a different amount. The weighted contribution is valid only for the stated mix and cost range. Does a 20% margin of safety mean a 20% chance of loss? No. It describes the modeled sales reduction to break-even using a stated denominator, not a probability. Demand uncertainty requires separate analysis. Can I retain the old break-even after committing to more fixed capacity? No. Recalculate using the applicable committed fixed costs and check whether reducing sales also removes that commitment.
