documents.summary: Calculate recruiting cost per completed hire, then build a first-year employment budget. Include internal time consistently without double-counting onboarding.
documents.headings: Quick answer Define the recruiting numerator and the hires denominator Calculate a completed two-hire campaign Build the employment budget separately Distinguish hiring efficiency from hiring quality Keep a recruiting ledger that can be reproduced Reconcile recruiting, compensation and the first-year cash calendar Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with hiring, payroll and employee costs Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost per Hire vs Employee Cost: Two Different Budgets Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate recruiting cost per completed hire, then build a first-year employment budget. Include internal time consistently without double-counting onboarding. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Cost per hire divides the recruiting costs included in a defined period by completed hires in that period. Employee cost measures the ongoing cost of employing someone. The two budgets answer different questions and should not be added without checking shared items. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Define the recruiting numerator and the hires denominator Cost per hire = (included external recruiting costs + included internal recruiting costs) ÷ completed hires. External costs may include job ads, agency fees and screening. Internal costs may include recruiting staff and documented interviewer time. Use one written cost policy so months and roles can be compared. For this example, count completed starts as hires and report accepted offers separately. If another internal report uses a different counted event, disclose it and reconcile the difference before comparing cost-per-hire results. An open vacancy is not a hire. When a period has costs but zero hires, the ratio is undefined; report the spend and zero denominator rather than returning $0 cost per hire. Multi-month campaigns need a reconciliation so costs and outcomes are not silently moved between periods. Calculate a completed two-hire campaign Original fictional recruiting period Item Calculation Cost Job advertising Campaign invoices $1,200 Agency/screening Separate invoice records $1,800 Recruiter effort 30 hours × $40 $1,200 Manager interviews 20 hours × $60 $1,200 Total recruiting cost External $3,000 + internal $2,400 $5,400 Completed hires Two starts 2 Cost per hire $5,400 ÷ 2 $2,700 The hourly values are planning assumptions, not current pay benchmarks. If interviewer salary is already in the internal recruiting pool, do not add the same hours again. A cash-only view might show $3,000 external spend, but it omits $2,400 of valued staff effort; label the two views rather than comparing them as identical metrics. Build the employment budget separately For one illustrative role, assume $48,000 salary, $4,800 employer charges, $3,600 benefits, $1,200 equipment/software and $1,000 incremental onboarding paid time outside both the salary and recruiting amounts. The first-year employment budget before recruitment is $58,600 . Adding the separately assigned $2,700 recruitment cost gives $61,300 . These are chosen amounts, not a payroll tax or benefit rate. A hiring bonus, relocation payment, training time or recruiter salary must appear only once under the adopted boundary. Recurring-year cost can differ from first-year cost because recruiting and equipment are not necessarily repeated. Distinguish hiring efficiency from hiring quality A lower cost per hire does not prove a better hire. Compare like roles and channels, then review acceptance, start dates, retention and observed job performance. A cheap process with repeated replacement hires can cost more overall. Small samples also move sharply: one additional start changes a two-hire denominator by 50%. Time to fill, recruiting conversion yield and cost per productive hour answer other questions. A team may hire quickly but lack work, onboarding capacity or cash to support the position. Use the employee cost calculator for recurring and productive-hour economics, and the dated cash forecast for the payroll funding period. Keep a recruiting ledger that can be reproduced Choose the reporting period and the counted hire event. List invoices and internal hours with an owner and source reference. Document shared-cost allocation and any excluded costs. Reconcile hires, costs, open campaigns and timing differences. Compare channels only after matching cost and role definitions. Keep applicant records secure and use job-related review criteria. The financial worksheet does not determine employment-law obligations, eligibility or candidate suitability. Reconcile recruiting, compensation and the first-year cash calendar The official SHRM teaching excerpt separates external recruiting spending, internal staffing resources and hires during the evaluated period. Its dated publication supports the metric’s components; it is not a current market cost-per-hire benchmark. The two completed starts remain the counted event in this guide’s fictional $2,700 case. Retain one row per counted hire, including role, actual start, source and the recruiting campaign reference. Maintain a separate accepted-offer count: a candidate who accepts and then never starts should not silently become a completed start in this example. Explain any cutoff policy for a recruiting campaign spanning several periods, and use the same policy when comparing channels. The BLS National Compensation Measures concepts define compensation through wages/salaries and employee benefits. This article’s employment budget is broader because it also includes equipment, software and separately defined onboarding. Consequently the $58,600 subtotal should not be presented as a BLS compensation statistic or compared directly with an hourly benefits benchmark without reconciling those boundaries. Build a dated funding schedule as well as an annual total. A $1,200 equipment payment before the employee starts can create a larger first-month cash need than an annual average suggests. Check whether the $1,000 onboarding amount is genuinely additional; if the same paid hours already sit within the $48,000 salary, remove the duplicate. Retain jurisdiction-specific employer charges as supported inputs rather than applying the example’s amounts as universal payroll rates. Frequently asked questions Does cost per hire include annual salary? The employee’s ongoing annual salary belongs in the employment budget, not automatically in recruiting cost. Recruiting staff effort can be part of internal recruiting costs. What if no one was hired? Report recruiting spend and zero completed hires. Division by zero does not produce a meaningful cost-per-hire result. How should internal interview time be valued? Use a documented, consistently applied hourly cost or internal rate. Keep it separate from cash-only recruiting spend and avoid adding the same staff cost twice. Is lower cost per hire always better? No. Role mix, timing, sample size, retention and hiring outcomes affect the comparison. A low ratio can conceal repeated replacement hiring. Should an accepted offer that never starts count among the two starts? No. This guide’s example counts completed starts. Track accepted offers separately and disclose any different policy used in another report. Is the $58,600 budget a BLS compensation benchmark? documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Financial Contingency Plan: Cash Triggers, Actions and Funding Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a financial contingency plan with dated cash scenarios, triggers, owners and verified funding. Test an original cash-gap example and response worksheet. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer A financial contingency plan defines what the business will do when cash assumptions fail: the trigger, decision owner, dated response and funding actually available. It complements the cash forecast and operational continuity plan; it is not a promise that emergency finance will be approved. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Connect a risk to a date and an accountable action Choose a planning horizon that captures your payment commitments. List opening usable cash, expected receipts and committed payments by week or date. Separate restricted balances, unapproved borrowing and expected insurance recoveries from cash available to pay bills. Identify which receipts depend on customer acceptance, processing delays or unresolved disputes. For each risk, record the event, a measurable trigger, the owner, the response deadline, the action’s cash effect and the dependency that could prevent it. A reserve target should follow the business’s downside timing and tolerance, not an unexplained percentage copied from another company. Model the shortage before assuming a funding solution Original fictional four-week cash case, before corrective action Case Opening usable cash Receipts Payments Closing cash Base $18,000 $8,000 $20,000 $6,000 Customer delay $18,000 $2,000 $20,000 $0 Delay plus repair $18,000 $2,000 $22,500 −$2,500 Use a chosen $5,000 minimum cash floor for this case. The base case stays $1,000 above it. The customer-delay case needs $5,000 of timely improvement to restore the floor, and the combined downside needs $7,500. These are aggregate four-week checks; a payroll payment before the week-four receipt may create an earlier, larger need. The dated worksheet must test that ordering. Build a response that can actually occur before the bill Illustrative response to the combined downside Action Cash improvement Evidence needed Move discretionary equipment purchase $2,000 Purchase not committed; no penalty Reschedule a supplier payment by agreement $1,500 Written acceptance and new due date Available credit draw $4,000 Existing facility, conditions met, timely draw Total improvement $7,500 Do not count unconfirmed actions Revised closing cash $5,000 −$2,500 + $7,500 Deferring a payment shifts the obligation into a later period; it does not eliminate the cost. Add the new payment date and debt service to later weeks. Avoid showing credit as ordinary revenue. If the lender can suspend the line or the business fails its conditions, the draw must not appear as dependable cash. Write an escalation ladder with a decision owner An illustrative green level is forecast cash at or above the chosen floor, with a weekly review. Amber begins when a dated forecast falls below that floor or a material receipt slips: the finance owner confirms collection status and pauses uncommitted discretionary spending. Red is an inability to meet a critical due payment: the owner escalates immediately, verifies financing and contacts the affected counterparties before making unsupported promises. The numbers and color levels belong to this fictional case. In a real plan, set them around payroll, critical suppliers, legal commitments, funding terms and operational resilience. Do not advise missing tax or wage obligations as a routine liquidity tactic. Rehearse the plan and reconcile it after each review Test a delayed receipt, a lost customer, an equipment failure and a funding source that is unavailable at the same time. Keep source evidence for cash, counterparties, approvals and facility conditions. Check after the event whether the action occurred on time and whether a temporary fix created another shortage. Use the 13-week cash forecast for dated payments, the cash-flow recovery guide for causes and responses, and your business plan for the assumptions and owners. The broader business continuity task also covers staffing, systems, premises and recovery priorities; this article owns the financial response. Turn the four-week closing balance into a dated funding test The SBA emergency-preparedness material covers risk assessment, a business-specific response plan and practice. It supports preparation; it does not establish this example’s $5,000 cash floor or promise financing. Those amounts must follow the business’s actual commitments and decision policy. A positive month-end balance can conceal an earlier shortage. Extend the fictional base with dated movements: begin at $18,000, pay $12,000 in week one, then $8,000 in week two, and receive $8,000 in week four. Closing cash is still $6,000, but week-two cash reaches −$2,000. Restoring the selected $5,000 floor before that payment requires $7,000 of timely additional cash or agreed payment changes, rather than the $1,000 month-end buffer suggested by the aggregate base. Apply the same timing test to each response. If a $4,000 credit draw can arrive only in week three, it does not solve the week-two payment. If a supplier agrees to defer $1,500, record the replacement due date and include it in the next forecast period. Distinguish removing a genuinely uncommitted purchase from merely postponing an existing obligation. Keep the last evidence date beside every available-funding line. Check draw conditions, approvals and settlement delays before treating it as usable. Assign an alternative action if any condition fails, and rehearse the decision before the critical payment date. Disaster assistance, insurance claims and hoped-for receivable collections remain conditional until their amount and timing are supported. Frequently asked questions How large should the emergency reserve be? Base it on dated downside cash needs, commitments, available financing and risk tolerance. The illustrative $5,000 floor is not a universal recommendation. Can expected insurance or a new loan be counted as available cash? Only with a supportable amount and timing, and after relevant conditions are met. Pending approval is not immediately available cash. Does rescheduling a supplier bill remove the cost? No. It moves the cash obligation to another date, subject to agreement. Include that later payment when checking the next forecast periods. How often should the plan be reviewed? Choose a cadence that matches the payment risk, and review immediately when a material assumption fails. The example uses more frequent escalation under stress. Can month-end positive cash hide an earlier negative balance? Yes. The added fictional sequence closes at $6,000 but reaches −$2,000 in week two before its week-four receipt. Does a later credit draw fix an earlier missed payment automatically? No. Cash must be usable by the payment deadline, and any draw conditions or settlement delays must be considered. documents.summary: Compare receivables and payables with matched entries. Reconcile an invoice, credit and partial payment without confusing revenue, expense and cash.
documents.headings: Quick answer Compare the direction, classification and supporting records Follow an invoice, credit and partial payment The payment changes cash without creating the same revenue twice Reconcile the open balances instead of relying only on totals Choose the detailed workflow after understanding the difference Complete the merchandise record without confusing the two prices Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with receivables, payables and credit risk Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Accounts Receivable vs Accounts Payable: One Invoice, Two Ledgers Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare receivables and payables with matched entries. Reconcile an invoice, credit and partial payment without confusing revenue, expense and cash. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Accounts receivable is an amount customers owe your business; accounts payable is an amount your business owes suppliers. The same credit transaction can create the seller’s receivable and the buyer’s payable, but each business keeps its own ledger and payment dates. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Compare the direction, classification and supporting records Ordinary trade-account comparison; the accounting framework still applies Question Accounts receivable Accounts payable Who owes whom? Customer owes the business Business owes supplier Usual balance-sheet category Asset Liability Main evidence Sales invoice, credit, receipt Supplier bill, credit, payment Normal increase entry Debit AR Credit AP Cash event when settled Business receives cash Business pays cash Trade balances are often current, but classification depends on the operating cycle and terms. A debit or credit is an accounting direction, not a synonym for good or bad. Customer deposits and prepayments can require other accounts; do not force every balance into ordinary AR or AP. Follow an invoice, credit and partial payment In a fictional accrual-basis example with no tax, Harbor Supplies delivers $3,000 of materials to a customer on November 5, with payment due December 5. The customer receives and records the materials as inventory. On November 12, a valid $300 return is accepted. On November 25, the customer pays $1,000. The remaining open balance is $1,700 . Matched entries; seller inventory/COGS entries are outside this comparison Event Seller ledger Buyer ledger Invoice / delivery Debit AR $3,000; credit revenue $3,000 Debit inventory $3,000; credit AP $3,000 Accepted return Debit sales returns $300; credit AR $300 Debit AP $300; credit inventory $300 Partial payment Debit cash $1,000; credit AR $1,000 Debit AP $1,000; credit cash $1,000 Open amount $3,000 − $300 − $1,000 = $1,700 $3,000 − $300 − $1,000 = $1,700 The seller’s inventory cost and related cost-of-sales reversal are excluded from this narrowly matched ledger example because the acquisition cost was not given. A complete accounting record must include them where applicable. Sales tax, foreign currency, discounts, impairment and framework-specific recognition require additional treatment. The payment changes cash without creating the same revenue twice The seller’s invoiced net sales in this case are $2,700 after the return, but the cash collected so far is $1,000. The receipt reduces AR; it is not another $1,000 of accrual revenue. The buyer’s payment reduces AP; it does not automatically create another expense. Buying inventory is also different from recognizing cost of goods sold when that inventory is sold. The outstanding $1,700 affects collection or payment planning. Put its expected settlement date into the cash forecast . The balance alone does not say whether it is overdue; compare it with the agreed due date and any dispute or amendment. Reconcile the open balances instead of relying only on totals For AR, opening balance plus invoices less credits, receipts and applicable write-offs should explain the closing ledger. For AP, opening balance plus accepted bills less credits and payments should explain the closing ledger. Reconcile customer/supplier subledgers with the control account, then match settlement amounts to the bank. Review unapplied receipts, duplicate bills, unmatched credits and cut-off errors. Keep disputed amounts visible. Amounts due from and to the same counterparty should not be netted casually: applicable offsetting rules and agreements matter. Use aging buckets based on a consistently stated method, such as days past due. Choose the detailed workflow after understanding the difference AR management concerns invoicing, collection, disputes and customer credit exposure. AP management concerns approved bills, valid suppliers, due dates and controlled disbursement. This comparison does not replace either full process. For the collection-speed calculation, use DSO ; for the broader balance relationship, use working capital . Keep the historical cash-flow statement separate from the forecast of future dates. Complete the merchandise record without confusing the two prices The receivable and payable use the invoice selling amount for the transaction between the two businesses. The seller also keeps a separate inventory-cost record. OpenStax’s perpetual-inventory sales entries illustrate both the revenue entry and the separate cost-of-sales entry; customer settlement subsequently reduces the receivable. To complete the fictional Harbor example, add a new explicit assumption: the delivered goods cost Harbor $1,800, and the accepted return contains resalable goods originally costing $180. At delivery Harbor records Dr Cost of Goods Sold $1,800 / Cr Inventory $1,800. On the resalable return it records Dr Inventory $180 / Cr Cost of Goods Sold $180. Net seller cost of goods sold is $1,620, and $2,700 net sales minus that cost gives $1,080 gross profit before other expenses. These new cost amounts are teaching assumptions, not a markup inferred from the original invoice. The buyer initially records its $3,000 acquisition at the supplier’s selling price; the $300 return leaves a $2,700 purchase amount in this restricted example. That is not the same as Harbor’s $1,620 cost of goods sold. The buyer must then trace what it retains, uses or sells before recognizing its own expense under the applicable policy. The $1,000 settlement still leaves both trade accounts open at $1,700 and creates no second sale. Match the agreed due date, bank receipt/payment and credit reference independently. A correct account balance does not prove the returned inventory was resalable or justify using the seller’s cost in the buyer’s ledger. Use the worksheet with your own records Download the printable, editable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed example and a blank table. Open it in a browser, edit the blank fields, calculate the outputs using the stated method and print to PDF or paper. It does not automatically calculate results or replace your accounting records. Method references and source notes The method references below support the definitions. The examples, assumptions and decision checks on this page are independently constructed. Stripe: accounts payable and accounts receivable fundamentals Xero US: accounts receivable definition Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Are accounts receivable revenue? A credit sale can create revenue and AR at recognition, but AR is the outstanding asset balance. Collecting that balance is not another sale. Is paying accounts payable always a new expense? No. Payment settles the liability. The related asset or expense was recognized according to the original transaction and applicable accounting method. Does a partial payment change the original invoice revenue? Not by itself. In the stated accrual example it reduces the open receivable/payable and moves cash. A valid credit or correction is a separate event. Should balances with the same counterparty be netted? Do not net them casually. Check the applicable accounting offsetting rules and agreements, and retain the underlying records. Why are the seller’s cost and buyer’s inventory purchase different? The seller measures its own inventory cost; the buyer records the acquisition price charged by the supplier, subject to its accounting policy. They are different cost records. Does the original $3,000 invoice reveal the seller’s profit? No. The seller’s inventory cost and other expenses are needed. The added $1,800 and $180 cost assumptions create a fictional complete example; they are not facts inferred from the invoice. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. documents.summary: Calculate CPI from earned value and actual cost. Check weighted totals, separate project cost performance from margin and compare remaining-work forecasts.
documents.headings: Quick answer Define planned value, earned value and actual cost Calculate cost and schedule performance separately Choose an estimate-at-completion assumption explicitly Aggregate dollars before calculating portfolio CPI Turn the ratio into a corrective project decision Test the remaining efficiency needed to meet a chosen budget Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with budgets, forecasts and performance Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Cost Performance Index: Earned Value, Actual Cost and Forecast Limits Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate CPI from earned value and actual cost. Check weighted totals, separate project cost performance from margin and compare remaining-work forecasts. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Cost Performance Index, or CPI, equals earned value divided by actual cost for the same project scope and status date. It measures the budgeted value of completed work per dollar of actual cost; it does not measure sales revenue or profit margin. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. Define planned value, earned value and actual cost Planned value is the approved budget for work scheduled by the status date. Earned value is the approved budget for work actually completed by that date, using a defensible completion method. Actual cost records what that completed work has cost on a consistent accounting basis. Match scope, cut-off and currency before dividing. CPI = EV ÷ AC. Below 1 means the measured work has consumed more actual cost than its budgeted value; above 1 means the opposite. A zero actual-cost denominator needs investigation, not a fabricated finite index. Missing supplier accruals can make CPI look artificially favorable. Calculate cost and schedule performance separately Original fictional project status date Measure Amount / result Meaning Budget at completion (BAC) $100,000 Approved project budget Planned value (PV) $60,000 Budgeted work scheduled so far Earned value (EV) $50,000 Budgeted completed work Actual cost (AC) $62,500 Cost recognized to the status date CPI 0.80 $50,000 ÷ $62,500 Cost variance −$12,500 EV − AC Schedule performance index 0.8333 EV ÷ PV The project has earned $0.80 of budgeted work for each actual dollar. CPI does not mean a 20% profit loss, and the schedule index does not directly convert into days late. In this example, cost performance and scheduled completion both require investigation, but they describe different dimensions. Choose an estimate-at-completion assumption explicitly If all remaining work can be delivered at its original remaining budget, EAC is AC + (BAC − EV): $62,500 + $50,000 = $112,500 . If the same cost efficiency is assumed to continue across the total project, EAC is BAC ÷ CPI: $100,000 ÷ 0.80 = $125,000 . The $12,500 gap is an assumption difference, not an arithmetic error. A bottom-up remaining estimate of $58,000 would instead produce EAC of $120,500. Document supplier commitments, remaining quantities, rework and resource rates behind that estimate. Do not select the most reassuring formula without checking what is causing the variance. EAC is a forecast, not a confirmed final invoice. Aggregate dollars before calculating portfolio CPI Suppose work package A has EV $30,000 and AC $25,000, so CPI is 1.2. Package B has EV $20,000 and AC $37,500, so CPI is approximately 0.5333. The simple average of the two indices is 0.8667, but project CPI is ($30,000 + $20,000) ÷ ($25,000 + $37,500) = 0.80 . Weighting follows the underlying totals. Verify completion evidence rather than treating dollars spent as percentage complete. An expensive early purchase can increase actual cost while little eligible work is earned; a milestone-based rule can delay earned value. State those rules and apply them consistently. Turn the ratio into a corrective project decision Confirm baseline, completion evidence and status-date cut-off. Investigate quantity, rate, productivity, scope and rework causes. Re-estimate the remaining work from supported inputs. Choose and fund the response; log approved scope changes. Review the next status date without erasing the original baseline history. Use job-order costing for recorded job cost and budget variance analysis for driver-specific performance. CPI is a project earned-value measure, separate from a business operating margin . Test the remaining efficiency needed to meet a chosen budget CPI describes cost performance achieved to date. The separate to-complete performance index, or TCPI, asks what efficiency the remaining work would need to meet a selected funding target. PMI’s TCPI paper explains the remaining-work numerator and the different denominators for the original budget and an approved revised estimate. Using the existing fictional status, $50,000 of budgeted work remains: $100,000 BAC minus $50,000 EV. Only $37,500 remains within the original budget: $100,000 minus $62,500 AC. Thus TCPI to the original BAC is $50,000 / $37,500 = 1.3333. That would require substantially better remaining cost efficiency than the measured 0.80 CPI; it is a requirement, not proof the team can achieve it. If the selected revised target is the $125,000 EAC, its remaining funding is $62,500 and TCPI becomes $50,000 / $62,500 = 0.80. That matches the continued-efficiency assumption used to derive this EAC. A $120,500 bottom-up EAC gives $58,000 remaining funding and TCPI approximately 0.8621. Each denominator must identify the target being tested; changing the forecast does not erase the original approved baseline. When the selected target has no remaining funding, this ratio is undefined or infeasible for positive remaining work. Investigate scope, accrual cutoff, remaining commitments and corrective resources before using the result. Do not interpret 1.3333 as a required percentage margin, a promised productivity improvement or a schedule completion date. Use the worksheet with your own records Download the printable, editable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed example and a blank table. Open it in a browser, edit the blank fields, calculate the outputs using the stated method and print to PDF or paper. It does not automatically calculate results or replace your accounting records. Method references and source notes The method references below support the definitions. The examples, assumptions and decision checks on this page are independently constructed. PMI: earned-value data, CPI and executive action Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Can CPI be used as a profit margin? No. Earned value is budgeted completed work, not customer revenue. A CPI of 0.8 is not an 80% margin. Does EAC equal BAC divided by CPI in every situation? No. That formula assumes the measured cost efficiency continues. A remaining-at-budget or bottom-up estimate uses different assumptions. Can I average work-package CPI values? Calculate total earned value divided by total actual cost. A simple average of ratios can misstate the project because packages have different cost weights. What happens when actual cost is zero? The division is undefined. Investigate missing costs, timing or completion rules rather than presenting a finite CPI value. Is TCPI the same as CPI? No. CPI measures achieved earned value per actual cost. TCPI divides budgeted remaining work by funds remaining under a specified target. What does 1.3333 TCPI mean in this case? The original budget would require about $1.3333 of budgeted remaining work for each remaining actual dollar. It does not show that this required performance is attainable. documents.summary: Calculate profitability index from discounted cash flows. Reconcile NPV, compare project scale and avoid ranking indivisible investments by a ratio alone.
documents.headings: Quick answer State the cash-flow convention before calculating PI Discount the same project year by year A ratio above one is not an annual return Use NPV and constraints when comparing alternatives Build a defensible project cash schedule Test feasible project combinations and make the PI convention explicit Use the worksheet with your own records Method references and source notes Continue with investment decisions and cost of capital Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Profitability Index: Discounted Cash Flows and Project Selection Published November 4, 2026 Updated November 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate profitability index from discounted cash flows. Reconcile NPV, compare project scale and avoid ranking indivisible investments by a ratio alone. Business finance Worked example Decision worksheet Quick answer Profitability index compares the present value of a project’s future net cash flows with its positive initial investment. Under the stated conventional setup, PI above 1 corresponds to positive NPV, but the ratio alone does not select the best combination of projects. Read the source-backed application and limits . Worked business amounts are fictional teaching examples. Topic illustration. All financial examples in the article are fictional. Every amount in the worked case is an original fictional USD planning assumption. It is not an industry benchmark, a customer result or a prediction. State the cash-flow convention before calculating PI PI = present value of future net project cash flows ÷ initial investment. Here the investment occurs at time zero, future amounts are net incremental project cash flows, and discounting uses end-of-year timing. NPV = present value of future net cash flows − initial investment. With these conventions and a positive initial outlay, PI = 1 + NPV ÷ initial investment. Some sources use a different numerator or treat later investment outlays separately. Do not compare such ratios without reconciling the definitions. A zero initial investment makes this version undefined. Nonconventional cash flows and multiple later capital commitments need an explicitly rebuilt model. Discount the same project year by year Original fictional project; 10% illustrative discount rate Time Net project cash flow Discount calculation Present value 0 −$20,000 Initial investment −$20,000.00 Year 1 $9,000 9000 ÷ 1.10 $8,181.82 Year 2 $9,000 9000 ÷ 1.10² $7,438.02 Year 3 $9,000 9000 ÷ 1.10³ $6,761.83 Future PV total $27,000 nominal Sum of unrounded PV $22,381.67 PI is $22,381.6679 ÷ $20,000 = 1.1191 . NPV is $2,381.67 . Retain unrounded discount factors until the final display. The 10% rate is an illustrative input, not a recommended return, borrowing quote or risk-adjusted rate for your business. A ratio above one is not an annual return A PI of 1.1191 means about $1.1191 of discounted future net cash flows for each $1 initially invested in this defined case. It is not an 11.91% annual ROI. Project timing, risk, taxes, replacement needs and a suitable discount rate affect the interpretation. Accounting profit and EBITDA are not substitutes for incremental project cash flow. At the same 10% discount rate, reducing each future annual cash flow to $8,000 gives future PV of about $19,894.82, PI of 0.9947 and NPV of −$105.18. A modest assumption change crosses the acceptability threshold, so retain a sensitivity table rather than only the base-case label. Use NPV and constraints when comparing alternatives Consider project A requiring $10,000 with future PV $13,000: PI is 1.30 and NPV $3,000. Project B requires $30,000 with future PV $36,000: PI is 1.20 and NPV $6,000. If the projects are mutually exclusive and risk, timing and other constraints are comparable, choosing the higher ratio alone would miss B’s larger dollar NPV. Under a fixed budget with indivisible projects, evaluate feasible combinations. Dividing a project into fractions is not automatically possible. Include dependencies, available funding, staff capacity, required assets and strategic obligations. A ratio ranking can assist analysis; it is not a universal capital-allocation rule. Build a defensible project cash schedule Specify the decision and the alternative being compared. List incremental cash inflows, operating outflows, working-capital changes, later investment and terminal recoveries. Use consistent timing, currency, nominal/real treatment and tax assumptions. Document the chosen discount rate and review sensitivities. Reconcile PI to NPV and confirm feasibility before approval. Use the present-value guide for discounting, the business investment calculator for its stated return/payback measures, and the cash forecast to check funding dates. A discounted value result does not ensure cash is available to buy the asset. Test feasible project combinations and make the PI convention explicit OpenStax’s discounted-cash-flow explanation provides the PV-of-net-future-cash-flows divided by initial-investment convention used here. Another convention reports NPV divided by investment. Under this guide’s positive time-zero outlay setup, those figures differ by one: 1.1191 versus 0.1191 for the base case. They can preserve rankings within that setup while using different acceptance thresholds. For a separate fictional indivisible-project decision, let a $30,000 budget fund A at $20,000 outlay and $26,000 future PV, or B and C at $15,000 outlay and $19,200 future PV each. Assume all PV amounts already use consistent risk, timing and rate assumptions; there are no dependencies or repeat opportunities. A has PI 1.30 and $6,000 NPV. B and C each have PI 1.28 and $4,200 NPV. Ranking only by PI selects A first and leaves $10,000 that cannot buy B or C, producing $6,000 total NPV. Choosing B plus C uses the whole $30,000 budget and yields $8,400 total NPV. The arithmetic demonstrates why a ratio ranking is insufficient when projects cannot be split. It is an original constrained-choice illustration, not an observed investment recommendation. List every feasible combination, include required companion investment and compare total NPV under the same stated assumptions. If future funding is also constrained, a single time-zero ratio may miss another bottleneck. Revisit working-capital recovery, terminal costs and discount-rate sensitivity before interpreting a rounded PI near its threshold as a robust decision. Use the worksheet with your own records Download the printable, editable HTML worksheet . It contains the completed example and a blank table. Open it in a browser, edit the blank fields, calculate the outputs using the stated method and print to PDF or paper. It does not automatically calculate results or replace your accounting records. Method references and source notes The method references below support the definitions. The examples, assumptions and decision checks on this page are independently constructed. CFI: profitability-index formula and interpretation Wall Street Prep: PI calculation and comparison limits Source review: November 8, 2026. Official guidance, publisher explanations and software workflows have different scopes. The linked application section identifies their use. Numerical business cases remain original fictional teaching examples, not observed customer results or market benchmarks. Frequently asked questions Is PI minus one an annual return? No. It expresses discounted value relative to initial outlay under the selected horizon and rate, not a compound annual return. Should I always choose the highest PI? No. Mutually exclusive projects, different scale, indivisibility and funding constraints can change the best feasible choice. Reconcile NPV and the actual decision constraints. What cash flows belong in PI? Use the explicitly defined incremental project cash flows, timing and rate. Include later investment and terminal effects consistently with the chosen convention. Why keep unrounded discount factors? Rounding each year early can change the reported total. Sum unrounded present values, then round the displayed PI and NPV. Why do some sources report a PI of 0.1191 rather than 1.1191? They may use NPV divided by initial investment rather than PV of future net cash flows divided by initial investment. Reconcile the definition and threshold before comparison. Why does the lower-PI pair beat the highest-PI project here? The projects are indivisible. B plus C fits the $30,000 budget and gives $8,400 total NPV, while A leaves unusable funding and gives $6,000. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant OWNER REVIEW & CASE STUDY Restaurant Break-Even Calculator Review: Lessons from 5 Malaysian Owners Published October 30, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Five Malaysian restaurant owners reported faster break-even planning. Examine the evidence, then test an RM-based restaurant plan against food costs, delivery fees and capacity. Restaurant break-even calculator Restaurant profit planning Malaysia restaurant user feedback Illustrative promotional artwork, not participant evidence or a verified screenshot of current features. See the product-scope section for what the calculator supports. THE RESTAURANT OWNER'S VERDICT Useful when the question is “How many orders must we actually sell?” The strongest signal from this five-owner evaluation is clearer sales planning: translating restaurant costs into a break-even volume and a higher profit target. Participants reported faster calculations and greater confidence. The evidence supports an early usability signal; it does not establish higher restaurant profits or independently certified accuracy. Best fit: an owner who can supply realistic selling prices, complete per-order costs and monthly commitments. Needs extra work: a changing menu mix, delivery contracts, peak-service bottlenecks and a dated cash-flow plan. Test your restaurant's own numbers Inspect our worked example first What five Malaysian restaurant owners actually reported The supplied evaluation describes five owners using mobile and desktop between October 12 and October 27, 2026 . No individual restaurant names, menus, device records or participant-level worksheets were supplied. The calendar dates are retained as provided; we cannot establish how many sessions or active testing days each owner completed. Reported calculation time 120 → 15 min 105 minutes less per evaluated calculation Reported confidence 3/10 → 8/10 Five points higher on the supplied scale Participant group 5 owners A small self-reported evaluation The time reduction is (120 − 15) ÷ 120 × 100 = 87.5% . This is a comparison of the supplied averages, not a controlled productivity benchmark. We do not know the range, median, error rate or timing protocol. Confidence scores measure perception rather than financial performance. Evidence ledger: what the supplied feedback can support Reported observation Useful interpretation Evidence boundary 120 to 15 minutes Planning felt faster for evaluated tasks No raw timing logs or matched task sheets Confidence: 3/10 to 8/10 Owners felt more comfortable setting targets No validated confidence instrument or control group Ease of use: 10/10 reported Positive usability feedback No individual score distribution or device breakdown Participants said they checked calculations A reason to investigate accuracy further No supplied raw scenarios or external audit Recommend and reuse intentions Positive stated intent Future usage and retention were not measured Profit, cash flow and business survival No measured outcome available No claim of increased earnings or causal business impact “It is wonderful tool can help restaurant businesses to find out there exact breakeven point and give clear idea that how you can go to achieve your goal” Original wording supplied as collective feedback. No verified individual attribution is available; this is not presented as five separately documented testimonials. A worked RM example: from one restaurant order to a monthly target Hypothetical editorial example—not a participant's restaurant or a Malaysian market benchmark. All money below is in Malaysian ringgit (RM), and the sales unit is one completed order. There is no currency conversion. The underlying arithmetic is currency-independent; the example does not verify Malaysian tax, SST or payroll compliance. One RM30 order Average selling price RM30.00 Ingredients RM10.50 Genuinely variable labor RM2.50 Other variable costs RM1.40 Payment fee: 2% × RM30 RM0.60 Total variable cost RM15.00 Contribution per order RM15.00 The monthly requirement Fixed operating commitments RM18,000 Separate owner-pay allowance RM3,000 Additional operating profit target RM6,000 Total planning requirement RM27,000 Assume 26 open days. The owner allowance is included separately only because it is absent from fixed commitments. Classify committed payroll with fixed costs and variable labor with orders; never charge the same work twice. Operating break-even: RM18,000 ÷ RM15 = 1,200 orders , or RM36,000 revenue. Including the separate owner allowance requires 1,400 orders . Funding both that allowance and RM6,000 additional profit requires RM27,000 ÷ RM15 = 1,800 orders , or RM54,000 revenue. RM54,000 revenue 1,800 orders × RM30 − RM27,000 variable costs 1,800 × RM15 = RM27,000 contribution RM18,000 overhead + RM3,000 owner allowance + RM6,000 target Monthly contribution bridge at the illustrative target. It excludes costs not entered and is not a cash-flow forecast. The 1,800-order target averages 69.23 orders over 26 days. 70 orders per open day is a rounded planning pace, not an assertion that every service has equal demand. At 1,560 orders (60 per open day), contribution would be RM23,400: RM2,400 remains after the included overhead and owner allowance, leaving the RM6,000 target short by RM3,600. For the general method, use our restaurant break-even guide . For table-service counts, use the covers-per-night guide . One order can cover several guests; do not label an order target “customers” without an explicit conversion. Stress tests: where a restaurant plan becomes fragile Each row below funds the same RM27,000 monthly requirement. Unless stated otherwise, only the named assumption changes. Whole-order targets are rounded upward; daily paces are the monthly target divided by 26 and rounded upward again. The delivery fee is an illustrative combined percentage assumption, not any platform's quoted commission. Illustrative RM scenarios: RM27,000 requirement, 26 open days Scenario Contribution/order Orders/month Pace/day Base plan RM15.00 1,800 70 Ingredients +20% RM12.90 2,094 81 Price −10% RM12.06 2,239 87 Delivery channel RM6.10 4,427 171 70% base / 30% delivery RM12.33 2,190 85 Food cost pressure: a 20% increase in the RM10.50 ingredient cost adds RM2.10 per order. At the original 1,800-order volume, that removes RM3,780 from monthly contribution. Use the food cost calculator to reconcile actual inventory usage; use the recipe cost calculator for ingredient-level costing. Discount pressure: a 10% price reduction lowers price to RM27. The 2% fee falls to RM0.54, but ingredients and other per-order costs remain unchanged. Contribution becomes RM12.06. Higher sales volume is useful only if incremental contribution and capacity support the promotion. Delivery pressure: at RM30, a 25% combined percentage fee is RM7.50. With an extra RM2 packaging cost, contribution is RM6.10. Do not stack the original 2% on top when the combined assumption already includes it. Actual contracts can use different fee bases, subsidies, taxes or fixed charges; enter those terms rather than copying this example. Menu and channel mix: with 70% base orders and 30% delivery orders, weighted contribution is (0.70 × RM15) + (0.30 × RM6.10) = RM12.33. The resulting 2,190-order target assumes that mix stays stable. A best-selling menu item cannot represent the whole business if lower-contribution orders dominate. Download the worked scenario table (CSV) . These are static editorial examples, not saved calculator sessions or participant data. Check the kitchen, worker-hours and demand before accepting the target Suppose the team has four people, 40 hours each per week, 75% productive utilization and 0.25 total worker-hours per order. The calculator's annualized monthly convention gives 4 × 40 × (52 ÷ 12) × 75% ÷ 0.25 = 2,080 orders of worker-hour capacity . “Total worker-hours” means combined work across staff, not simply the elapsed time a ticket spends in the kitchen. The 1,800-order base target fits that entered capacity at roughly 86.5%. The 2,094-order food-cost case is already 14 orders over it, and the 4,427-order delivery case is far beyond it. More staff or equipment may change both capacity and cost; rerun the financial requirement after adding those commitments. Worker-hour capacity is only one constraint. Check peak tickets per hour at the slowest station, preparation capacity, delivery collection congestion, opening days, seats and realistic table turns. Separately test whether demand can produce the required orders. A monthly total can fit while a Friday dinner service still fails. Keep cash planning separate too: rent deposits, debt principal, equipment purchases and settlement delays can create a cash shortage even when the included operating costs break even. Use the restaurant budgeting guide to build the broader operating plan. What is supported now—and what this review has not verified The current product source supports a restaurant planning workflow for per-order costs, percentage fees, fixed commitments, owner pay, a target profit and productive worker-hour capacity. Its restaurant examples distinguish dine-in, direct takeaway and delivery. Account features are separate from the participant evidence. Product scope checked against the current implementation Capability Scope of this review Contribution and required order volume Present in the current calculation engine; worked examples here are checked against that engine. Capacity check Productive worker-hours, not a verified seat-layout or kitchen simulation. Saving, comparison and reports Free-account saving and Pro saving/comparison/export options are described in the product. Account limits and entitlements belong to the current pricing and user guide. Dedicated food-wastage analysis A participant improvement request; not established here as a shipped dedicated module. Avoid counting ingredient losses twice. Malaysian localization RM worked arithmetic; no verified tax engine, local compliance certification or Malaysian price benchmarks. The featured artwork is promotional illustration. Its “before/after” panels and feature labels are not proof of an account fix, a participant's screen or a verified list of current entitlements. Confirm current features on Free and Pro pricing and the Pro user guide . The improvement requests that matter most Participants asked for clearer visual comparisons and specific food-wastage costs. The useful next standard is decision clarity: show what changes contribution, how far the target sits from workable capacity, and whether wastage is already inside actual ingredient costs. Their request does not prove that those enhancements were tested or released. A repeatable owner checklist for your next planning review Define the unit and period. Choose orders, meals or covers, keep all inputs consistent, and use the same month for commitments and revenue. Use records before assumptions. Take sales and discounts from the POS, ingredients from recipes and inventory, fees from settlement statements, and committed payroll and rent from actual obligations. Reconcile the variable-cost boundary. Include packaging, incremental labor and order-related promotions. Check that payment fees, delivery commission and wastage appear once each. Separate three targets. Record operating break-even, owner-pay funding and additional profit funding so a busy month does not hide an unpaid owner. Stress the weakest assumptions. Test ingredient increases, discounts and a delivery-heavy mix. Keep the same unit and requirement when comparing scenarios. Check capacity at service level. Compare the target with worker-hours, the slowest kitchen station and realistic demand, then update costs for any expansion. Compare actuals with the plan. Review orders, contribution per order and cost changes after the month closes. Preserve the input date and source records so another person can reproduce the calculation. If you want to assess the tool itself, time the same defined task manually and with the calculator, use identical inputs, check both outputs and record errors as well as minutes. Report device, task, units and assumptions alongside any score. That produces more useful evidence than a general “easy to use” rating. Method, sources and editorial accountability Participant evidence: the supplied five-owner evaluation summarized above. Original participant-level files and independent verification were not available. This review is published by the maker of the tool. Formula reference: the U.S. Small Business Administration break-even analysis guidance explains fixed costs divided by price less variable cost and the single-product assumption. We adapt that arithmetic to explicitly stated restaurant orders; the SBA source is not an endorsement of this product. Editorial calculations: the RM examples, channel assumptions and capacity inputs were constructed for this article and checked against the current MyBreakeven calculation engine. They are separate from participant results. Corrections and evidence: see our editorial standards . Send a reproducible calculation or evidence correction to mybreakeven1@gmail.com ; do not send confidential customer or employee data. Verdict: encouraging small-group feedback for a clearer planning workflow. The practical test is whether your inputs produce a reproducible target that covers the intended commitments and fits a workable service—not whether a calculator displays a reassuring number. Build your restaurant break-even plan Check food-cost performance Work backward from kitchen capacity to an affordable order cost The existing RM example needs RM27,000 monthly contribution and models capacity of 2,080 orders. Rather than assuming the kitchen can always serve more orders, solve the other direction: RM27,000 ÷ 2,080 = RM12.980769 contribution per order . At RM30 revenue per order, the maximum combined variable cost is RM17.019231. Keep full precision until the final display; a cost rounded upward to RM17.02 would fall slightly short. Capacity-constrained check using the existing teaching assumptions Input or scenario Calculation Decision Base variable cost RM15 2,080 × RM15 contribution = RM31,200 RM4,200 above the stated requirement Food-cost stress: RM17.10 variable cost 2,080 × RM12.90 = RM26,832 RM168 below requirement Required contribution at capacity RM27,000 ÷ 2,080 ≈ RM12.9808 Change cost, price, mix or verified capacity The food-cost stress therefore cannot be solved merely by scheduling the modeled maximum. The RM168 is a contribution shortfall against the full stated requirement, which includes the owner-pay and profit targets; it is not automatically an accounting loss. Test a feasible change and recalculate variable fees when price changes. Use the restaurant cash forecast separately for supplier and payroll dates. Repeat the test without inventing another user result Save the order definition, dated supplier inputs, fee basis, fixed-cost period and capacity assumptions. Run the RM30/RM15/RM27,000 baseline, then change only food cost and check the result independently. Label this a reproducibility check, not new participant evidence. An order is not necessarily a customer or cover: if a fictional bill serves two diners, 70 bills represent 140 covers, but that conversion cannot be applied to the original study without evidence. The five-owner account above remains user-reported with its stated limitations. Frequently asked questions Is this an independent restaurant calculator review? No. MyBreakeven published this review using feedback supplied from five Malaysian restaurant owners. Raw participant worksheets, individual timing records and independently audited restaurant profits were not supplied. Does the reported 87.5% reduction mean restaurant profits increased? No. It is the relative reduction from a reported 120 minutes to 15 minutes of calculation time: (120 − 15) ÷ 120 × 100. Actual profit improvements were not measured. Can I use the restaurant break-even calculator with Malaysian ringgit? The break-even arithmetic works with RM when every monetary input uses RM and the same time period. The worked example here uses RM throughout; it does not demonstrate Malaysian tax, SST, payroll or accounting compliance. Should I plan in orders or customers? Use one unit throughout. An order can include several guests, so average revenue and variable costs per order cannot be combined with a guest-count target. Convert orders into covers only with a stated guests-per-order assumption. How do delivery app fees affect restaurant break-even? Subtract percentage fees and order-specific packaging or promotional costs from revenue before calculating contribution. The hypothetical RM30 delivery case here leaves RM6.10 contribution and needs 4,427 orders to fund RM27,000; actual contract terms will differ. Can a profitable-looking sales target exceed restaurant capacity? Yes. Positive contribution does not guarantee enough worker-hours, kitchen throughput, seats or customer demand. Compare the target with each relevant constraint and recalculate any extra fixed or variable costs required to expand capacity. Are food-wastage analysis and seats-per-service planning verified premium features? This review does not establish that. The verified product scope is described separately from participant requests and promotional artwork. Dedicated food-wastage accounting and physical seat-capacity checks were not verified in this review. What if required restaurant orders exceed kitchen capacity? Work backward from the capacity limit to required contribution per order. Test price, costs, sales mix or evidenced capacity changes; do not assume unlimited additional orders or remove owner pay silently. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: FIRE vs Coast FIRE vs Barista FIRE: Which Target Are You Measuring?
documents.summary: Compare FIRE, Coast FIRE and part-time-income targets with the same spending assumptions. Check current living costs, growth dates and real purchasing power.
documents.headings: Three labels, three different questions Keep one spending target and one money basis Why the Coast milestone depends on time A Barista scenario needs an earned-income end date Turn the label into a cash-flow plan Common mistakes Method and sources Separate a Coast portfolio from the bridge that pays current bills Stress the Coast assumption before changing work hours Continue with retirement and refinancing decisions Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE FIRE vs Coast FIRE vs Barista FIRE: Which Target Are You Measuring? Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare FIRE, Coast FIRE and part-time-income targets with the same spending assumptions. Check current living costs, growth dates and real purchasing power. Financial independence Worked examples Planning assumptions FIRE targets portfolio-funded living costs; Coast FIRE targets enough invested today to grow toward a later retirement without more retirement deposits; Barista FIRE still relies on earned income. Reaching a Coast milestone does not mean you can stop paying today’s bills. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Three labels, three different questions Choose the question before comparing balances Approach Portfolio task Income still needed FIRE Fund the spending assigned to the portfolio under a chosen withdrawal plan Other income only if explicitly included in the plan Coast FIRE Grow existing assets to a future retirement target with no new retirement deposits Current living expenses, taxes, healthcare and other goals Barista FIRE Combine portfolio withdrawals with continuing earned income The assumed part-time income, after its costs and taxes These are informal planning labels, not standardized account types. State the cash flows instead of assuming everyone uses the same definition. The FIRE calculator models accumulation while saving; the Coast FIRE calculator tests the zero-further-deposit milestone. Neither validates a retirement withdrawal strategy or employment income. Keep one spending target and one money basis In this original fictional USD example, portfolio-funded annual retirement spending is $40,000 in today’s purchasing power, including the taxes and healthcare allocated to it. A selected 4% initial withdrawal fraction gives $40,000 / 0.04 = $1,000,000 . This is an arithmetic scenario, not a safe-rate recommendation. At 3% the same spending requires $1,333,333.33; at 5% it requires $800,000. For the Coast comparison, choose a 5% effective annual real growth assumption, after fees. There are no new deposits or withdrawals during growth. A 7.625% effective nominal return, zero additional fee and 2.5% inflation produce exactly the same real assumption: 1.07625 / 1.025 − 1 = 5%. Actual returns will not follow a fixed path. Why the Coast milestone depends on time One $1 million real target at age 65; zero further deposits Current age Years to target Required invested today at assumed 5% real growth 35 30 $231,377.45 45 20 $376,889.48 65 0 $1,000,000.00 At 45, $1,000,000 / 1.05^20 = $376,889.48. Under that fixed assumption it grows to the later target. Withdrawing current living expenses from this same balance would break the no-withdrawal projection. At zero real growth the Coast threshold is the full $1 million; negative real growth can make the required starting balance greater than the later target. Use Future Value to reconcile a growth projection only after matching nominal/real rates and contribution timing. Entering a real return and then applying inflation again would remove inflation twice. A Barista scenario needs an earned-income end date Suppose the same person expects $24,000 a year of spendable part-time earnings after work expenses and taxes. During that employment period, the portfolio-funded gap is $40,000 − $24,000 = $16,000. At the selected 4% fraction, $16,000 / 0.04 = $400,000 . This reduced arithmetic target depends on continuing earnings and is not interchangeable with the full $1 million target. If that work ends at 60, its $24,000 does not continue automatically. A dated plan must replace it through later benefits, lower spending, a larger portfolio or other evidenced income. Do not assume a particular employer provides health insurance or that a part-time job is guaranteed. Our two retirement calculators do not model this changing earned-income bridge. Turn the label into a cash-flow plan Write down the earliest withdrawal date, the last planned contribution date and when each income stream starts and stops. Separate an accessible bridge fund from assets with withdrawal restrictions. Keep emergency cash and home equity outside invested assets unless the plan explicitly and realistically uses them. Recalculate after a material change in spending, family needs, fees or time horizon. Common mistakes Comparing a nominal future million with a today-dollar target; treating gross wages as spendable income; subtracting a later pension from today’s bill; and withdrawing from a supposedly untouched Coast portfolio all change the question. A target can be met in an accumulation model while the withdrawal plan remains exposed to market losses. Read the withdrawal-rate and retirement-risk guide before interpreting target attainment. Method and sources Investor.gov’s compound-interest tool provides a public reference for principal, contributions, time and compounding. Our targets and age comparisons are original calculations. Investor.gov explains how fund expenses reduce returns . These examples use stated net-real assumptions and do not choose investments or a suitable withdrawal rate. Separate a Coast portfolio from the bridge that pays current bills Coast FIRE assumes the designated retirement assets can grow without further contributions or withdrawals until the target date. It does not pay living costs during that wait. In a separate fictional example, someone aged 45 spends $40,000 a year and earns $28,000 after tax from part-time work until age 55. The annual funding gap is $12,000 for ten years: $120,000 of cumulative withdrawals at a zero real return . That bridge is separate from the untouched Coast portfolio. Independent bridge illustration; constant purchasing-power dollars Stage Spending less earnings Funding question Age 45–54: ten annual periods $40,000 − $28,000 = $12,000/year Ten beginning-year gaps total $120,000 at 0% real return Age 55–64: ten annual periods $40,000 − $0 = $40,000/year Another $400,000 at 0% real return if no other income Age 65 onward Use actual income and spending assumptions Recalculate the long-term portfolio requirement The $520,000 combined gap is an undiscounted scenario total, not a recommended cash reserve. Earnings, tax, benefits, inflation and investment outcomes could change it. If bridge withdrawals come from the same assets called “Coast,” the original untouched-growth calculation no longer applies. Use a dated cash-flow model rather than counting one portfolio twice. Stress the Coast assumption before changing work hours For an independent $1 million real target in 20 years, required untouched assets are about $376,889 at 5% real growth, $553,676 at 3%, and $1 million at 0%. These are $1,000,000 ÷ (1+r) 20 , with no deposits, withdrawals, fees or taxes. Lower growth can materially change the decision. Compare the present-value assumptions and the withdrawal-risk checks before treating any scenario as permission to retire. Frequently asked questions Does Coast FIRE mean I can retire today? No. The pure Coast projection leaves retirement assets invested without withdrawals or further deposits. Current expenses still need funding. Is Barista FIRE always a $400,000 target? No. That amount follows only from this guide’s $16,000 portfolio spending gap and selected 4% fraction. Income duration and later spending require a separate dated plan. Can I compare the FIRE and Future Value tools directly? Only with matched cash-flow timing, rate conventions and money basis. The FIRE tools use real purchasing power; fixed nominal deposits are a different scenario. What happens if the part-time income stops? The portfolio-funded spending gap increases unless another income source or a spending change replaces it. Model that end date instead of assuming the smaller target lasts forever. Can I spend from my Coast FIRE portfolio before retirement? You can model withdrawals, but then it is no longer the untouched Coast growth scenario. Recalculate the dated portfolio path and avoid counting the same money as both retirement capital and a separate bridge. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
