documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE FIRE Withdrawal Rates: Horizon, Sequence Risk and a Spending Plan Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Test withdrawal-rate assumptions against retirement length, return order, tax, healthcare and asset access. Follow an original two-year sequence-risk example. Retirement risk Worked examples Planning assumptions A selected withdrawal rate converts spending into a portfolio target; it does not guarantee that withdrawals will last. Retirement length, return order, fees, taxes, healthcare, accessible assets and willingness to change spending all need a separate drawdown plan. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Define the withdrawal rule before selecting a percentage An initial withdrawal fraction divides the first year’s portfolio withdrawal by the starting retirement portfolio. A fixed-real rule then adjusts that dollar withdrawal for inflation. Withdrawing the same percentage of each year’s changing balance is a different policy: income falls when assets fall. Neither is described adequately by writing “4%” without a rule. Original arithmetic sensitivity; not recommended rates Annual portfolio-funded spending Selected initial fraction Implied starting target $40,000 3% $1,333,333.33 $40,000 4% $1,000,000.00 $40,000 5% $800,000.00 The FIRE calculator uses this target for accumulation. It does not run a market-return simulation, forecast ruin or model retirement withdrawals. A higher selected fraction lowers the target mathematically; it does not establish a safer plan. Same returns, different order, different remaining money Start with a fictional $100,000 portfolio. Withdraw $10,000 at the beginning of each of two years. Ignore fees, taxes and inflation to isolate return order. Both paths use the same −20% and +25% annual returns. Independent two-year sequence demonstration; USD Path Year 1 after withdrawal and return Year 2 after withdrawal and return Loss first (100,000 − 10,000) × 0.80 = 72,000 (72,000 − 10,000) × 1.25 = 77,500 Gain first (100,000 − 10,000) × 1.25 = 112,500 (112,500 − 10,000) × 0.80 = 82,000 Both portfolios paid the same $20,000 in withdrawals, yet the second ends $4,500 higher. Without withdrawals, 0.80 × 1.25 = 1, and both would end at $100,000. Selling assets early reduces the capital available for recovery. The $10,000 withdrawal is deliberately a teaching amount, not a recommended retirement policy. Plan for the full horizon and uncertain lifetime Retiring at 40 can require funding far more years than retiring at 65. A withdrawal finding for a specified horizon, asset mix and modeled success definition cannot simply be relabelled a lifetime guarantee. Include the possibility of living longer, a survivor’s changed expenses and late-life care. A smooth average return suppresses the return-order effect shown above. The Coast FIRE calculator is even narrower: it projects untouched retirement assets to a chosen future age. Its zero-contribution milestone does not test the years after withdrawals begin. Compare FIRE, Coast and part-time-income scenarios before choosing which result to use. Build a spending boundary that includes the actual bills Separate essential expenses from discretionary spending and dated one-off costs. If annual living expenses are $40,000 but another $6,000 of withdrawal-funded taxes and $4,000 of healthcare are omitted, the required withdrawal is $50,000. At the same selected 4% fraction, the arithmetic target rises from $1 million to $1.25 million. These costs are fictional, not tax or insurance estimates. For taxable withdrawals, after-tax spending and gross withdrawals can differ. Do not apply one generic tax rate to every account or treat all benefits as tax-free. Include fees once: if a return assumption is already net of the same investment expense, do not subtract it again. Separate total wealth from accessible retirement funding Write a dated inventory of liquid funds, account types, expected benefits and access restrictions. Home equity does not pay a bill without a real sale or financing plan. An emergency reserve already committed to short-term needs should not also be counted as invested retirement capital. Early US retirement-plan distributions can carry additional tax unless an applicable exception is met; exceptions and account rules require individual verification, not a blanket assumption. Specify what changes after a poor market year A flexible policy might reduce a named discretionary expense, postpone a purchase or revisit withdrawals at an agreed review point. It helps only if the budget actually has room to change. Write the trigger and affordable floor instead of promising that all spending can be cut. Test loss-first paths, higher costs and delayed other income separately; do not multiply arbitrary stress tests into a supposed success percentage. Common mistakes Using a withdrawal rate as an expected investment return; comparing fixed-real with percentage-of-balance policies; ignoring a longer horizon; counting restricted assets as immediately spendable; and interpreting a target age as a retirement authorization can each mislead. Preserve the base scenario and document changed assumptions. References and model boundary Investor.gov’s fund-fee bulletin explains the expense drag on investment returns. IRS Topic 558 describes additional tax and exceptions for early distributions from retirement plans other than IRAs; it is not a substitute for the rules for your account. Morningstar’s withdrawal-strategy discussion is further reading on horizon and spending policies; we do not quote a current recommended rate or claim its research validates these examples. The sequence and spending calculations above are original. Translate spending flexibility into an explicit dollar rule “Spend less after a bad year” is not a reproducible plan until the timing and spending boundary are stated. Consider a separate one-year illustration: a $1 million starting portfolio, a $40,000 withdrawal at the beginning of the year, and a −20% return afterward. The ending balance is ($1,000,000 − $40,000) × 0.80 = $768,000 . This excludes fees, taxes and inflation; all spending amounts below must use the same convention. Next-year spending choices at the same $768,000 opening balance Illustrative rule Next withdrawal Share of opening balance Keep $40,000 nominal spending $40,000 5.2083% Reduce $10,000 discretionary spending by 20%; retain $30,000 essential spending $38,000 4.9479% Take 4% of the new balance $30,720 4.0000% The last choice leaves only $720 above the assumed $30,000 essential budget. A lower withdrawal rate is not evidence that the household can live on the result. With 2% inflation, retaining the original purchasing power would instead require $40,800; do not silently compare a nominal cut with an inflation-adjusted baseline. Write down the trigger, floor and review date A usable policy identifies the balance measurement date, whether withdrawals precede returns, the essential-spending floor, which expenses can change and when the plan is reviewed. The 20% discretionary cut here is an arithmetic illustration, not a tested safe-withdrawal policy. Longer horizons, taxes, fees, market sequences and changing income require separate modeling. Schwab’s sequence-risk explanation illustrates why return order matters. Compare the FIRE income stages and keep cash-flow feasibility separate from a portfolio target. Frequently asked questions Does the FIRE calculator prove a withdrawal rate is safe? No. It is an accumulation projection with a selected target fraction. It does not model variable market returns or retirement drawdowns. Why can the same average returns lead to different outcomes? Withdrawals change how much remains invested between returns. In the worked loss-first path, less capital participates in the recovery. Should taxes and healthcare be in my spending input? Include the portion you expect the portfolio to fund. Record other income and its dates separately, and avoid counting a cost twice. Is a withdrawal percentage the same as a return assumption? No. A withdrawal rule describes cash taken from assets; a return assumption describes their growth or loss. They have different roles in the plan. Does a flexible withdrawal rule guarantee retirement success? No. State its trigger, spending floor, timing and assumptions, then test affordability and adverse scenarios. A smaller withdrawal can still fail to cover essential spending. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: How to Analyze Financial Statements: One Business, Three Reconciliations
documents.summary: Analyze an income statement and two balance sheets. Reconcile ratios, average balances and why $20,000 fictional profit adds only $2,000 cash.
documents.headings: Prepare, reconcile, then interpret the reports Start with the reporting perimeter Read the annual income statement Make both balance sheets balance Use period flows and average balances consistently Explain three different leverage answers Reconcile $20,000 net income to $27,000 operating cash Turn the reconciliation into questions, not a health score Common mistakes Sources and accounting boundary Turn a ratio into a question you can verify in the records Compare periods on the same basis Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How to Analyze Financial Statements: One Business, Three Reconciliations Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Analyze an income statement and two balance sheets. Reconcile ratios, average balances and why $20,000 fictional profit adds only $2,000 cash. Financial statements Worked examples Planning assumptions First reconcile the statements, then calculate measures using matching dates and periods, and finally explain the difference between profit and cash. Our fictional business earns $20,000, generates $27,000 operating cash and increases cash by $2,000 after investing and financing. Prepare, reconcile, then interpret the reports Before comparing ratios, match the entity, dates, currency and accounting basis. Reconcile the income statement to the ledger, cash-flow closing cash to the balance sheet, and net income to retained earnings after distributions and other equity changes. An unexplained difference needs a source record, not a plug. Planning connections reviewed November 18, 2026. Existing calculation methods and article dates are preserved. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Start with the reporting perimeter Cedar Supply is an original fictional teaching business. All figures are USD for one 365-day year, with opening and closing balance sheets for the same entity. Net credit sales are $180,000 of $200,000 total revenue; the remaining $20,000 sales are cash sales. There are no acquisitions, exchange effects, asset disposals or other undisclosed movements. Interest and income taxes paid are operating cash flows here, with no change in their payables. This is a deliberately simplified US-style presentation, not a complete set of financial statements. Use the Financial Ratios reference hub for definitions, and the grouped ratios calculator to reproduce this dataset. Its defaults use these input amounts. A real review also needs accounting notes, revenue policies, estimates, commitments and comparable prior-period data. Read the annual income statement Cedar Supply annual income statement; fictional USD Line Amount Net revenue 200,000 Cost of goods sold 120,000 Gross profit 80,000 Operating expenses, including 10,000 D&A 50,000 Operating profit / EBIT here 30,000 Interest expense 5,000 Income-tax expense 5,000 Net income 20,000 EBITDA: 20,000 + 5,000 + 5,000 + 10,000 40,000 Revenue less $120,000 COGS gives $80,000 gross profit. Subtracting $50,000 operating expenses gives $30,000 operating profit. Here EBIT equals operating profit because no other non-operating items exist. After $5,000 interest and $5,000 income-tax expense, net income is $20,000. Included D&A is $10,000, so EBITDA is $40,000. Rebuild that subtotal in the EBITDA calculator ; do not add debt principal or add D&A twice. Make both balance sheets balance Cedar Supply balance sheets at the beginning and end of the same year; USD Line Opening Closing Cash and cash equivalents 8,000 10,000 Separate liquid short-term investments 5,000 5,000 Trade receivables 20,000 25,000 Inventory 22,000 18,000 Operating prepayments 0 2,000 Total current assets 55,000 60,000 Net property, plant and equipment 125,000 140,000 Total assets 180,000 200,000 Trade payables 20,000 20,000 Current interest-bearing debt 10,000 10,000 Total current liabilities 30,000 30,000 Long-term interest-bearing debt 50,000 50,000 Non-interest-bearing shareholder loans 30,000 40,000 Total liabilities 110,000 120,000 Equity 70,000 80,000 Liabilities plus equity 180,000 200,000 Opening assets $180,000 equal $110,000 liabilities plus $70,000 equity. Closing assets $200,000 equal $120,000 liabilities plus $80,000 equity. Cash equivalents are already in cash; the separate $5,000 investment line is not another copy of that cash. Non-interest-bearing shareholder loans are liabilities, but are excluded from the narrowly defined interest-bearing debt input. Use period flows and average balances consistently Selected reconciled measures; see the hub for the full reference Question Calculation Result Liquidity at closing 60,000 / 30,000 Current ratio 2.00× Assets excluding inventory/prepayments (10,000 + 5,000 + 25,000) / 30,000 Quick ratio 1.3333× Inventory efficiency 120,000 / ((22,000 + 18,000) / 2) 6.00 turns in this year Collection period ((20,000 + 25,000) / 2) / 180,000 × 365 45.625 days Return on assets 20,000 / ((180,000 + 200,000) / 2) × 100 10.5263% for this year Return on equity 20,000 / ((70,000 + 80,000) / 2) × 100 26.6667% for this year An opening-to-closing average uses two observations, not every daily balance. Seasonal swings can make it unrepresentative; use more frequent observations when available. A 90-day flow divided by an annual balance convention is not automatically comparable with this 365-day example. Do not assume missing opening inventory is zero. Explain three different leverage answers At closing, the equity multiplier is $200,000 / $80,000 = 2.50×. Total liabilities/equity is $120,000 / $80,000 = 1.50×. Interest-bearing debt/equity is ($10,000 + $50,000) / $80,000 = 0.75×. The first equals 1 plus the second because assets = liabilities + equity. It does not equal 1 plus the third because trade payables and non-interest-bearing shareholder loans are also liabilities. Inspect these methods in the integrated leverage selector . A high ROE can reflect a smaller equity base and greater financing exposure rather than better operations. Negative equity makes a conventional positive-equity comparison unsuitable; it is not a strong score. Reconcile $20,000 net income to $27,000 operating cash Indirect operating cash bridge under the stated policy; USD Item Signed amount Net income 20,000 Add included noncash D&A +10,000 Increase in trade receivables −5,000 Decrease in inventory +4,000 Increase in operating prepayments −2,000 Change in trade payables 0 Operating cash flow 27,000 Equipment purchases are $25,000, with no disposals. Net PPE therefore rolls forward as $125,000 + $25,000 − $10,000 depreciation = $140,000. Financing receives $10,000 additional non-interest-bearing shareholder loans and pays $10,000 dividends, net zero. Thus cash rises by $27,000 − $25,000 + $10,000 − $10,000 = $2,000, from $8,000 to $10,000. Equity rolls forward as $70,000 + $20,000 net income − $10,000 dividends = $80,000. The $2,000 cash change is not the $20,000 profit or $40,000 EBITDA. Our operating cash flow guide and cash flow statement guide explain their separate cash classifications. Do not classify every current account as an operating adjustment or treat a new loan as sales. Turn the reconciliation into questions, not a health score Check receivables aging before concluding that $25,000 will be collected promptly. Ask whether inventory reductions reflect efficiency, shortages or a write-down; this fictional bridge assumes no write-down. Review loan terms and related-party repayment demands rather than treating non-interest-bearing financing as risk-free. Compare margins and turnover with the company’s own history and genuinely comparable businesses, including reporting policies and seasonality. Common mistakes Mixing total and credit sales in DSO, confusing total liabilities with interest-bearing debt, annualizing a short period silently, treating profit as distributions available and interpreting one ratio in isolation can reverse the decision. Follow the DSO method or the existing working-capital guide when those specific balances need investigation. Sources and accounting boundary The SEC’s financial-statement introduction distinguishes reporting-period flows, dated balance sheets and cash flows. BDC’s financial tools organize business-ratio questions. Cedar Supply, its statement amounts, the 19-measure reference and all reconciliations are original. This teaching example omits the full notes, disclosures and complexities needed for actual reporting or lending. Turn a ratio into a question you can verify in the records In the Cedar Supply ledger above, operating cash flow is $27,000 and net income is $20,000. The cash-conversion ratio is 27,000 ÷ 20,000 = 1.35 . That observation does not prove high earnings quality: a temporary inventory reduction or delayed supplier payment can also lift cash. Ask which reconciliation lines explain the result and whether they can recur. Cedar Supply follow-up workpaper; same original annual ledger Observation Independent check Evidence to request Gross profit $80,000 on $200,000 revenue 40% common-size gross margin Product mix, returns, purchase costs and cutoff Operating cash flow $27,000 135% of $20,000 net income Receivable aging, inventory roll-forward and payment dates Capital expenditure $25,000 $27,000 − $25,000 = $2,000 Asset invoices and maintenance/replacement commitments Cash increases only $2,000 27,000 − 25,000 + 10,000 − 10,000 Borrowing and dividend records matched to bank The $2,000 operating-cash-less-capex subtotal uses one simple free-cash-flow convention. It is not cash freely distributable after every commitment. The borrowing and dividend bridge still matters, and a cash-conversion ratio is unstable or misleading when net income is close to zero or negative. Compare periods on the same basis In a separate two-period illustration, revenue rises from $100,000 to $120,000 while cost of sales rises from $60,000 to $78,000. Sales grow 20%, but gross margin falls from 40% to 35%; gross profit grows only from $40,000 to $42,000. Investigate price, mix, input cost and accounting-policy changes before calling the sales growth an improvement. These figures are not another Cedar Supply year. The SEC financial-statement guide explains the role of notes and management discussion. Reconcile findings with the earnings-to-cash comparison and cash-flow statement . Frequently asked questions Why use average assets instead of closing assets for ROA? The income covers a period. A matched opening/closing average is a simple estimate of the assets supporting that period, although seasonal businesses may need more observations. Does the $27,000 operating cash mean owners can withdraw $27,000? No. Equipment purchases, financing, liquidity needs and other commitments remain. This example finishes with a $2,000 cash increase after its stated movements. Why is interest-bearing debt smaller than total liabilities? Total liabilities also include payables and non-interest-bearing loans here. State the debt definition before comparing ratios. Do two balance sheets explain every cash movement? Not by themselves. You also need transactions and supporting records to distinguish cash from noncash changes, investing, financing and operating adjustments. Is operating cash flow above net income always a good sign? No. Identify the working-capital and noncash drivers, compare consistent periods and inspect the notes. Inventory liquidation or delayed payments may temporarily improve the ratio. documents.title: Find a Missing Value in Equivalent Ratios: All Four Positions
documents.summary: Solve a missing term in any position, verify cross products and distinguish a unique answer from inconsistent, invalid and nonunique zero cases.
documents.headings: Four-step check: how to find a missing value in a ratio Label positions and units before multiplying Solve the unknown in every position Work through 3:5 = x:20 without a shortcut Retain exact fractions until the final display A zero can mean a solution, no solution or no unique solution Check every known constraint in three-term ratios Common mistakes and next practice Method reference Check labels and units before cross-multiplying Know when a proportional model does not apply Continue with ratios and marketing returns Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Find a Missing Value in Equivalent Ratios: All Four Positions Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Solve a missing term in any position, verify cross products and distinguish a unique answer from inconsistent, invalid and nonunique zero cases. Ratio math Worked examples Planning assumptions For a:b = c:d with valid nonzero denominators, use ad = bc, isolate the missing value, then substitute it back into the original ratios. A zero coefficient needs a consistency check before any division. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Four-step check: how to find a missing value in a ratio First write both ratios with the same quantity order . Second mark the unknown as x and identify known nonzero denominators if treating ratios as fractions. Third find a common scaling factor or solve by cross multiplication. Fourth substitute x into the original statement , not only the rearranged equation. For 3:5 = x:20 , 5 × 4 = 20, so x = 3 × 4 = 12 ; equivalently, 3 × 20 = 5 × 12 = 60. Three original checks: one solution, none, or nonunique (two-term fraction convention) Question Equation Verified outcome 3:5 = x:20 60 = 5x x = 12; denominator values 5 and 20 are valid 0:5 = 3:x 0 = 15 No solution, regardless of x 0:5 = 0:x 0 = 0 Not unique: any nonzero x is allowed when x is a fraction denominator Common error: a zero cross-product does not automatically mean x = 0. A proportion can also be impossible or have multiple valid x values. Use the exact ratio calculator in Solve mode to verify the typed position; use ratio-table word problems when the task gives repeated quantities rather than a single unknown. Label positions and units before multiplying Suppose a:b = c:d means a/b = c/d, with b and d nonzero. Equivalent ratios multiply every component by the same nonzero factor. Keep the same unit order on both sides: flour:water cannot be compared directly with water:flour. Use the exact equivalent ratio calculator in solve mode with exactly one blank or x. This guide explains the reasoning; the tool performs exact rational checks. Solve the unknown in every position One relation, four placements; each worked answer is independently substituted Missing position Example Cross-product equation Solution and check a x:5 = 12:20 20x = 5 × 12 = 60 x = 3; 3/5 = 12/20 b 3:x = 12:20 3 × 20 = 12x x = 5; 3/5 = 12/20 c 3:5 = x:20 3 × 20 = 5x x = 12; 3/5 = 12/20 d 3:5 = 12:x 3x = 5 × 12 x = 20; 3/5 = 12/20 In general, a = bc/d, b = ad/c, c = ad/b and d = bc/a, but only when the divisor is nonzero and the original relation is valid. The algebraic product equation alone can admit an invalid denominator, so always check the original fractions after solving. Work through 3:5 = x:20 without a shortcut First write 3/5 = x/20. Multiply both sides by 5 × 20 to get 3 × 20 = 5x. Thus 60 = 5x, so x = 12. The scale from 5 to 20 is four; the corresponding first term must also scale by four, from 3 to 12. Checking 3 × 20 = 5 × 12 = 60 verifies the answer. Adding 15 to both 3 and 5 would give 18:20, which is not the same ratio: 3 × 20 = 60 whereas 5 × 18 = 90. Equivalent ratios preserve multiplicative relationships, not equal differences. Retain exact fractions until the final display For (1/2):(3/4) = x:3, the equation is (1/2) × 3 = (3/4)x. Dividing by 3/4 gives x = 2 exactly. Multiplying both original components by four also gives 2:3. For 0.1:0.3 = 1:x, exact decimal conversion gives 1:3 = 1:x, hence x = 3. Rounding a fraction such as 1/3 before checking equality can create a false disagreement. A zero can mean a solution, no solution or no unique solution Zero cases under the fraction convention b ≠ 0 and d ≠ 0 Relation Constraint Conclusion 0:5 = x:20 0 × 20 = 5x Unique x = 0; both fractions valid 0:5 = 0:x 0 = 0 Any nonzero x satisfies it; no unique value 0:5 = 3:x 0 = 15 No solution 3:x = 6:0 The known denominator is zero Invalid fraction proportion 0:0 = 0:5 0/0 is undefined Invalid, not an equivalent zero ratio Colon notation may be used for component vectors even when a later component is zero. That is a different convention from dividing a by b. The calculator accepts nonzero ratio vectors and checks proportional components; if a second term is zero, do not interpret its result as a defined fraction with a zero denominator. It rejects an all-zero vector such as 0:0. State the convention your exercise uses. Check every known constraint in three-term ratios For 2:3:4 = 6:9:x, the first two components agree on a factor of three; the third requires x = 12. In 2:3:4 = 6:10:x, the known pairs already conflict because 2 × 10 ≠ 3 × 6. No choice of x repairs them. Never solve from one convenient pair and ignore contradictory known terms. Common mistakes and next practice Reversing one ratio, adding rather than scaling, rounding before cross multiplication and accepting an answer that makes a denominator zero are common errors. Write unit labels and substitute your answer. Then practice ratio tables, recipes and stock problems to connect the symbols to quantities. Method reference OpenStax’s proportions lesson defines equality of fractions with nonzero denominators and the cross-product method. Our four-position, fraction and zero-case examples are original. A valid algebraic answer still needs the units and domain restrictions from the question. Check labels and units before cross-multiplying A correct proportion can still answer the wrong question if the quantities are reversed. Suppose a fictional materials instruction uses 250 grams of A for 1.5 kilograms of B. Convert B to 1,500 grams first: A:B = 250:1,500 = 1:6. For 900 grams of B, A is 900 ÷ 6 = 150 grams . Verify 150 × 1,500 = 250 × 900 = 225,000 using the matched gram units. Independent practice with an explicit check Question Answer Verification A:B = 250 g:1,500 g; B = 900 g A = 150 g 150/900 = 1/6 4 items cost $10 at a constant unit price; cost of 7? $17.50 10/4 = 17.50/7 = $2.50/item 3 red:5 blue; exactly 11 blue, whole objects only 6.6 red mathematically; no exact whole-object solution Rounding to 7 gives 7:11, not 3:5 Keep item counts, currency and units in the labels. A statement written as B:A must be reversed on both sides; changing only one side produces the reciprocal answer. Before solving, estimate whether the unknown should be smaller or larger than the known quantity. After solving, substitute it back into the original statement. Know when a proportional model does not apply The $17.50 price assumes no setup charge, discount threshold or minimum order. If a seller adds a fixed $5 charge, the total bill does not scale with item count even though the per-item component does. Use ratio tables and proportionality checks to detect that difference. The Math Is Fun proportion examples illustrate matching quantities before solving. These fictional materials quantities teach arithmetic only; they are not a safety, chemical or food-production instruction. Frequently asked questions Can the unknown be the second term? Yes. Solve the cross-product equation for that term, then check that the resulting denominator is nonzero under a fraction convention. Does 0 = 0 mean x is zero? No. It means the equation supplies no unique value. Domain restrictions still apply; in 0:5 = 0:x, x must be nonzero for the fraction interpretation. Why use fractions instead of rounded decimals? Exact fractions preserve equality. Rounding intermediate values can make equivalent ratios appear different. Can a third component contradict the solved value? Yes. Every known proportional constraint must agree. A solution from one pair cannot repair an inconsistent second pair. Can I round a ratio answer to a whole object? Only if an approximate allocation is allowed. A fractional answer can mean no exact whole-object solution; rounding changes the original ratio and should be disclosed. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Equivalent Ratio Tables and Word Problems: Recipes and Stock
documents.summary: Build equivalent ratio tables with one scale factor. Follow original 5:2 recipe and 2:1 stock examples, quantity bars and part-to-whole checks.
documents.headings: Equivalent ratio tables: try the question before revealing the method Keep one scale factor across each row See the parts before changing the quantity A 2:1 stock allocation is a separate family Why 5:2 and 2:1 are not equivalent Convert units before comparing columns Translate a word problem into a table Common mistakes Reference and example scope Test whether the table is proportional before filling a blank Combine batches using quantities, not averaged ratios Continue with ratios and marketing returns Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Equivalent Ratio Tables and Word Problems: Recipes and Stock Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build equivalent ratio tables with one scale factor. Follow original 5:2 recipe and 2:1 stock examples, quantity bars and part-to-whole checks. Ratio applications Worked examples Planning assumptions An equivalent-ratio table multiplies every component by the same factor. For a 5:2 mix, factors 1, 2 and 3 give 5:2, 10:4 and 15:6. A 2:1 mix belongs to a different family: 5:2 is not equivalent to 2:1. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Equivalent ratio tables: try the question before revealing the method The multiplier must apply to every component of the same row . When a total is provided instead of one component, divide by the sum of ratio parts before scaling. Keep dimensions consistent: convert kilograms to grams before treating two measurements as comparable mass values. These are proportional-math demonstrations, not food-safety recipes or purchasing forecasts. Three new ratio-table practice questions with verified answers Question Working Answer and check 5:2 mixture, 28 g total: how much of each? 7 total parts; 28 ÷ 7 = 4 g per part 20 g first + 8 g second = 28 g; 20:8 = 5:2 3:4 stock, 24 red units: how many blue units? Red is four parts, so one part = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 18 blue; 18:24 = 3:4 2:1 allocation, 25 indivisible units: exact split? Three parts; 25 ÷ 3 is not an integer No exact whole-unit allocation of all 25; 24 can split into 16 and 8 with one left over if allowed Problem-solving shortcut: label each component, calculate a single part, then multiply every quantity by that part and verify the sum. If the missing term is inside one proportion rather than a full table, see the four-position x tutorial . You can generate and check exact scaled ratios without rounding decimal inputs. Keep one scale factor across each row Flour:water by mass; original fictional recipe Scale factor Flour (g) Water (g) Total mixture (g) 1 5 2 7 2 10 4 14 3 15 6 21 10 50 20 70 20 100 40 140 Both component columns scale together, and the total scales by the same factor. The total is seven parts, so flour is 5/7 of the mixture and water is 2/7. The ratio 5:2 does not mean flour is 5/2 of the total. This is a mathematical mass example, not a tested cooking or food-safety recipe. See the parts before changing the quantity Flour: 5 parts Water: 2 parts Each block is one equal mass part. Seven blocks make the complete mixture; labels preserve the quantities without relying on color. For 350 g total at 5:2, one part is 350 / 7 = 50 g. Flour is 5 × 50 = 250 g ; water is 2 × 50 = 100 g . Check 250 + 100 = 350 and 250 / 100 = 5/2. If instead you are given 350 g flour, the required water is 350 × 2/5 = 140 g; the question’s starting quantity changes the calculation. A 2:1 stock allocation is a separate family Fictional shelf plan: blue:red units, no losses Multiplier Blue units Red units Total 1 2 1 3 3 6 3 9 6 12 6 18 12 24 12 36 Allocate 36 units in a 2:1 ratio. There are three total parts, so each part is 12 units. Allocate 24 blue and 12 red. For 37 indivisible units, an exact 2:1 allocation of all stock is impossible: 37/3 is not an integer. You could allocate 36 and leave one unassigned, if the task permits; do not round the components independently and still claim an exact ratio. Why 5:2 and 2:1 are not equivalent Cross products give 5 × 1 = 5 and 2 × 2 = 4. Because those differ, no common nonzero scaling factor changes 5:2 into 2:1. The first mix has 5/7 ≈ 71.43% of its first component; the second has 2/3 ≈ 66.67%. Compare component order and units before concluding two mixes are the same. Use the equivalent ratio calculator to check both families or generate scaled rows. For a missing entry, use the stepwise missing-value method . A table is useful for repeated scaling; cross multiplication checks an isolated unknown. Convert units before comparing columns A fictional mix contains 0.5 kg dry material and 200 g liquid, measured by mass. Convert 0.5 kg to 500 g first: 500:200 simplifies to 5:2. Calling the raw numbers 0.5:200 would compare different units and misstate the relationship. Do not convert mass to volume without an appropriate density; a gram is not automatically a milliliter. Translate a word problem into a table Name both quantities and choose their order. Identify whether the supplied number is one component or the whole. Divide by its corresponding base component to find the scale factor, multiply all other components, then verify the total and original relationship. If a result must be a whole stock unit, test divisibility before rounding. For example, if the 5:2 row has 60 g water, the factor is 60/2 = 30. Flour is 5 × 30 = 150 g and total mass is 210 g. If the task gives a 210 g total, divide by seven first and reach the same row. These are equivalent descriptions of that one case, not interchangeable instructions for every starting number. Common mistakes Adding the same amount to both components, mixing a component-to-component ratio with a component-to-total fraction, reversing the order, ignoring units and rounding indivisible stock can all invalidate a table. Recipe proportions alone do not price ingredients or establish nutrition, shelf life or business profitability. Reference and example scope OpenStax’s proportion applications supplies the equality-of-ratios method and consistent quantity-order principle. All table rows, the 350 g illustration and the indivisible-stock problem above are original. They teach proportional reasoning rather than financial leverage or accounting ratios. Test whether the table is proportional before filling a blank Equivalent-ratio rows share one constant quotient for the same ordered quantities. Equal increases alone are insufficient. Consider a fictional printing bill with a $5 setup charge plus $2 per item. One, two and three items cost $7, $9 and $11. The total rises by $2 each time, but the cost-per-item ratios are 7, 4.5 and about 3.6667; this is not an equivalent-ratio table . Two different models; fictional USD example Items No setup: $2 × items With $5 setup: $5 + $2 × items 1 $2 $7 2 $4 $9 3 $6 $11 6 $12 $17 Doubling three items to six doubles the no-setup total from $6 to $12. It does not double the setup-price bill from $11 to $22: the correct bill is $17 because the setup happens once. Write the model before using a scale factor. Combine batches using quantities, not averaged ratios A separate fictional batch A has 2 red and 3 blue counters; batch B has 8 red and 2 blue. Together they contain 10 red and 5 blue, giving 2:1. Averaging the two red-to-blue quotients, (2/3 + 8/2) ÷ 2 = 7/3, gives the wrong combined ratio because the blue quantities differ. Add corresponding quantities first, then simplify. If batch sizes are unknown, their combined ratio is not determined. For a missing row, check labels, units, one common scale factor and whether fractional objects are permitted. Use the missing-value worked solutions to verify the result by cross-products. A business cost table may contain both fixed and variable components; an equivalent-ratio shortcut should not replace the full cost model. Frequently asked questions Is 5:2 equivalent to 2:1? No. Their cross products are 5 and 4. Equivalent examples include 5:2 = 10:4 and 2:1 = 6:3. What if I know the total rather than one component? Add the component parts, divide the total by that sum, then multiply each component by the resulting one-part quantity. Can I round a stock allocation? Only if the task allows an approximation, and then label the resulting ratio as approximate. Exact allocations of indivisible units require whole-number component counts. Can mass and volume units be mixed in a ratio table? Keep units consistent. Convert kilograms to grams when comparing masses; converting mass to volume needs an appropriate density. Does a table with equal increases always show equivalent ratios? No. A fixed starting charge can produce equal increases while the quotient changes. Test the same ordered quotient in every row before scaling. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Mortgage Refinance Break-Even: Payment Savings vs Cost at Sale

documents.headings: A refinance can cost more at year one and save later Which mortgage refinance break-even should you calculate? documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PROFITABILITY GUIDE Mortgage Refinance Break-Even: Payment Savings vs Cost at Sale Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare simple fee recovery with cash paid plus debt remaining at the same holding date. Reconcile an original fixed-rate example and an early-sale warning. Refinance decisions Worked examples Planning assumptions Simple payment break-even divides eligible net upfront fees by positive monthly payment savings. A fuller same-date comparison adds cash paid and remaining principal for each loan. Those measures can give different answers, especially when loan terms change. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. A refinance can cost more at year one and save later Use the same exit month for both options. This worked scenario starts with a $250,000 unpaid balance, 6.5% fixed current note rate, 300 months remaining, a 5.5% fixed new note rate, 300 new months and $6,000 upfront charges, with no financed fees or additional monthly costs. The figures below are generated and regression-checked against our amortization engine, not lender quotes. Economic savings = current cumulative cash + unpaid balance − refinance cumulative cash − unpaid balance − net upfront fees Common exit date Advantage What this means Month 12 $3,501.93 extra cost Upfront fees have not been recovered by this exit date. Month 36 $1,472.58 saving The remaining-debt-adjusted comparison favors refinancing. Month 60 $6,394.53 saving At the assumed five-year exit, modeled saving is positive. The first nonnegative same-date savings month is month 29 in this example. That threshold is not guaranteed to persist for every input or future interest-rate environment. The simpler fee ÷ monthly payment difference does not include the remaining loan balance. Change holding period and fees in the interactive refinance calculator ; review shorter versus longer mortgage terms if the new payoff date differs. This is an undiscounted comparison; it does not estimate taxes, investment returns or home-price changes. Which mortgage refinance break-even should you calculate? Two legitimate comparisons answer different questions . The payment-savings method asks when lower monthly payments repay eligible fees paid today; the common-date method asks which mortgage has less cash spent plus principal still owed on the same exit date. They are not interchangeable, particularly when you change the length of the loan. Illustrative decisions; compare like with like Your question Method What can go wrong How many months until $6,000 fees recover from $250 monthly payment savings? $6,000 ÷ $250 = 24 months when savings remain constant and fees are not financed Ignores changes in remaining debt; a shorter term with a higher payment has no positive-payment-saving threshold Would I be ahead at sale in month 60? Compare each option's cumulative payment cash and unpaid principal at month 60, including net upfront fees once Comparing monthly payments alone can mistake postponed principal for true savings Are two lender offers comparable? Match loan type, remaining/new terms, note rate, closing charges, credits, mortgage insurance and holding dates Different cash-to-close and escrow assumptions may distort the comparison The refinance calculator provides both a conditional simple threshold and the fuller cash-plus-debt schedule. Check the closing-fee reconciliation before entering financed fees. The CFPB recommends comparing loan estimates including rate, costs, lender credits and borrower cash-to-close. These figures are hypothetical and not a lender offer. Start with the narrow payment-savings question If net upfront transaction fees are $6,000 and a stable monthly saving is $250, simple recovery is $6,000 / $250 = 24 months . At month 18 only $4,500 of payment savings has accumulated, leaving $1,500 unrecovered on that cash basis. A planned sale at month 18 arrives before this 24-month threshold. This method assumes savings persist, both schedules are still in their relevant payment periods, and no fees are financed into principal. With no positive monthly saving there is no simple payment-savings break-even. That does not prove a shorter loan has no cost advantage. Use the mortgage refinance calculator to inspect both cash and balances. Compare cash and debt at one common date For the current loan, cost at holding date h = payments through h + remaining principal at h. For the refinance, cost = net upfront fees + new payments through h + new remaining principal at h. Subtract refinance cost from current cost; a positive difference favors refinancing under these assumptions. The common starting debt cancels from the difference. These are undiscounted comparative amounts, not a market valuation. They include principal so that a loan cannot look cheaper merely by postponing repayment. Keep the same property and initial debt, and account separately for taxes, insurance and other housing expenses that differ. Cash-out borrowing is outside this rate-and-term example. Reconcile one fictional five-year comparison Current balance is $250,000, fixed note rate 6.5%, with 300 months remaining. The new loan is $250,000 at an assumed 5.5% fixed note rate for 300 months. Upfront transaction fees are $6,000, financed fees and lender credits are zero, and the holding period is 60 months. Other housing costs and mortgage insurance are zero in both comparison inputs. These are fictional rates, not lender offers. P&I rounded to cents; interest retains precision internally; USD Measure Keep current Refinance Monthly principal and interest $1,688.02 $1,535.22 60 payments $101,281.20 $92,113.20 Principal after payment 60 $226,405.26 $223,178.73 Net upfront fees $0.00 $6,000.00 Cash plus remaining debt $327,686.46 $321,291.93 The refinance advantage at month 60 is $6,394.53 using full-precision balances before rounding. Payment savings are $152.80 per month, so the simple threshold is ceil($6,000 / $152.80) = 40 months. Payment savings of $9,168 less fees give only $3,168; the additional $3,226.53 of lower remaining debt explains the rest of the same-date advantage. Check the date you actually expect to exit A recovery date beyond the planned sale or another refinance is not recovered within your plan. Test shorter, likely and longer holding dates. A first favorable date need not remain favorable at all later dates if a long new term continues after the old loan would be paid off. Inspect the schedule rather than treating break-even as a permanent guarantee. Financed fees change the debt path Rolling $5,000 of fees into a $250,000 refinance creates $255,000 new principal. Do not also put that same $5,000 in upfront fees. The fee and its interest are reflected in payments plus remaining debt; a simple division using zero upfront cost would hide the economic cost. Classify each charge using the closing-cost and financed-fee ledger . What this comparison leaves out The model assumes fixed-rate fully amortizing loans, scheduled monthly payments and no extra principal, prepayment penalties, cash-out, ARM resets or tax effects. Note rate/12 drives interest; APR is not the accrual rate. Temporary escrow/prepaid cash affects liquidity but is excluded from irreversible transaction fees here; refund timing is not modeled. Opportunity cost and discounting can change a decision and require explicit assumptions. Common mistakes Using the original current-loan term instead of months remaining; comparing payments without payoff balances; counting financed charges twice; and comparing 60 months of one option with a full lifetime of another are inconsistent. For a term change, read the shorter-versus-longer-term comparison before relying on the lower-payment label. Sources and independent arithmetic CFPB’s Loan Estimate explainer distinguishes principal-and-interest payments, other housing charges and closing disclosures. OpenStax explains loan amortization . We independently reconciled the fictional schedules with a separate Decimal implementation using rounded regular payments and an adjusted final payoff. Actual lender timing and rounding may differ. Calculate an original payment before comparing refinancing For an original fixed-rate loan and a separate tax, insurance and HOA budget, use the mortgage payment calculator . The refinance model here answers a different question: transaction costs, remaining principal and alternatives at the same exit date. A lower payment alone does not establish lower financing cost. Frequently asked questions What if I sell before the simple break-even month? The assumed payment savings have not recovered the eligible upfront fees by that date. Also compare balances and total cash at your actual holding date. Does no monthly saving mean refinancing cannot reduce costs? No. A shorter term can have higher payments and lower interest or remaining debt. Evaluate matched-date cost and affordability separately. Is payment break-even the same as total-cost break-even? No. Simple recovery ignores differences in principal remaining, while a same-date cost comparison includes them. Why not use APR in the payment formula? The scheduled interest accrues using the note rate under this model. APR is a broader financing-cost disclosure and is not the monthly accrual rate. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Refinance Closing Costs and Financed Fees: Reconcile the Quote Published October 26, 2026 Updated October 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Classify upfront fees, financed charges, credits, points and escrow in a fictional quote. Reconcile new principal and closing cash without double counting. Refinance costs Worked examples Planning assumptions Upfront fees use cash; financed fees increase the new loan balance; lender credits offset specified charges; escrow and prepaids need separate timing treatment. A low cash-to-close figure does not mean a refinance has no cost. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Reconcile three ledgers before you calculate Do not assume total closing costs , new mortgage principal and cash needed today mean the same thing. Here is a controlled $250,000 refinance payoff example with $6,000 transaction charges, $1,000 lender credit, $2,000 of charges rolled into the new loan and $2,500 temporary escrow/prepaid funding. Educational ledger; confirm actual disbursement on the lender's disclosures Ledger Calculation Outcome Net transaction cost $6,000 fees − $1,000 credit $5,000 New principal $250,000 unpaid balance + $2,000 financed fees $252,000 Upfront transaction fees $5,000 net fees − $2,000 financed $3,000 Closing liquidity $3,000 upfront fees + $2,500 escrow/prepaids $5,500 Enter $3,000 as upfront fees, $2,000 as financed fees and $2,500 as escrow/prepaids in the refinance calculator ; do not also enter the $1,000 credit because it has already been netted against the stated upfront amount. Alternatively, enter $4,000 upfront, $2,000 financed and $1,000 credits: both methods yield $3,000 net upfront fees. The calculator accepts these as separate buckets. Verify actual quote figures using the CFPB Loan Estimate guide ; payoff interest, prepaid dates and escrow refunds may change the real cash-to-close figure. Transfer a refinance Loan Estimate to the calculator without double-counting Start with the quoted loan amount, fixed note rate, term and mortgage-insurance line . Then identify each charge that is actually financed or actually paid upfront; a single charge cannot belong to both groups. Lender credits reduce eligible upfront charges under this simplified model. Escrow and certain prepaids may change liquidity without being identical to irreversible lender fees. A real closing disclosure has further payoff and timing adjustments this calculator does not model. Practical field mapping for this educational calculator Loan Estimate / quote item Where it belongs Check before typing Origination, points and other quoted transaction charges Upfront fees or financed fees Confirm which portion is actually rolled into new principal Lender credit Credits toward upfront fees Do not enter a rebate exceeding the fee bucket or assume cash back Escrow/prepaid funding Separate closing-liquidity assumption Verify prepaid periods, payoff adjustments and possible refunds; don't call it free Mortgage insurance / tax / insurance / HOA Matching monthly cost assumptions Some charges are not lender-controlled and may not stop on payoff In the already worked fictional ledger, $6,000 charges − $1,000 lender credit = $5,000 net transaction fees ; $3,000 is paid at closing and $2,000 added to debt. Adding $2,500 separately for temporary escrow/prepaids produces $5,500 cash needed and $252,000 new principal on a $250,000 payoff baseline. These totals are a controlled example, not a substitute for a lender's cash-to-close calculation. Check CFPB's Loan Estimate field explainer and then compare the loan schedule . Reconcile a fictional quote before comparing rates Assume a $250,000 outstanding balance with no accrued payoff interest, cash-out, cash-in or other payoff adjustments in this teaching ledger. A fictional quote has $6,000 of irreversible transaction charges. $2,000 is financed and $4,000 is allocated upfront before a $1,000 lender credit. Temporary escrow/prepaid cash is $2,500. Original simplified refinance closing ledger; USD Item Treatment Amount Origination, including any quoted points Transaction charges 2,000 Appraisal Transaction charges 600 Title and settlement Transaction charges 2,400 Recording and other included transaction fees Transaction charges 1,000 Total transaction charges 4,000 upfront + 2,000 financed 6,000 Lender credit Offset upfront charges here −1,000 Net cash transaction fees 4,000 − 1,000 3,000 Temporary escrow/prepaids Separate liquidity assumption 2,500 Cash required in this simplified ledger 3,000 + 2,500 5,500 New loan principal 250,000 + 2,000 financed fees 252,000 Reconciliation: $6,000 charges − $1,000 credit = $5,000 net transaction fees , comprising $3,000 cash and $2,000 financed. Cash to close here is $5,500, not $5,000, because the separate $2,500 liquidity item is not the financed-fee amount. Real payoff interest and lender adjustments need their own lines; this is not a replacement Loan Estimate. Enter each charge once in the calculator In the refinance calculator , enter upfront fees 4,000, financed fees 2,000, credits 1,000 and temporary escrow/prepaid cash 2,500. With starting balance 250,000, it displays net upfront fees 3,000, new principal 252,000 and cash needed 5,500. Enter the actual quoted note rate and term separately. The schedule includes financed principal once; never add that same 2,000 to the upfront fee field. Points have a price and a quoted rate trade-off A discount point is 1% of the quoted loan amount. On the $252,000 new principal in a separate points example, one point is $2,520; half a point is $1,260. These are arithmetic illustrations, not additional charges to add to the $6,000 ledger above. Use the quote’s actual points amount inside the correct fee bucket. A point does not buy a universal fixed rate reduction. Compare complete offers for the same loan type and holding periods, including note rate, charges and credits. A lender credit can accompany a different rate; increasing a credit while leaving all other quote terms unchanged is not necessarily an offer a lender will make. Escrow, prepaids and payoff timing are separate questions An escrow deposit funds a reserve for bills; it is not automatically a new irreversible fee like an appraisal. Prepaid interest and prepaid tax or insurance items have different periods and economic treatment. Review what is being paid, which dates it covers, whether it replaces a payment you would otherwise make and whether any old escrow is refunded. Our calculator groups temporary closing liquidity separately and excludes it from the comparative transaction-cost subtotal. It does not forecast refunds, daily interest, tax benefits or different prepaid periods. If a supposedly temporary item is actually an incremental unrecoverable cost, this simplified exclusion will understate it: reconcile it separately or use a fuller dated cash model. Do not classify every prepaid line as recoverable cash. Low upfront cash can shift cost into rate or principal A quote described as “no closing cost” can fund charges through a larger balance or a lender-credit trade-off. It does not establish that the lifetime or same-date cost is zero. A new $252,000 principal has $2,000 more debt than the $250,000 baseline before the first payment, and interest can accrue on the extra principal. Use the payment and same-date break-even methods for the holding-date comparison. When fees are financed, rely on the full cash-plus-balance schedule rather than zero cash fees divided by payment savings. Build an offer-by-offer comparison For each quote, retain its date, rate-lock assumptions, note rate, term, principal, financed charge allocation, upfront fee allocation, credits and separate closing liquidity. Compare the expected shortest, likely and longest holding dates. Check whether costs are financed, paid now, paid earlier or omitted from the simplified ledger. A different term also changes balances: see the term-choice guide . Common mistakes Counting the same fee as both financed and upfront, treating a credit as unrestricted cash back, applying point percentages to the wrong principal, entering APR as note rate and labelling all cash to close as unrecoverable cost make comparisons unreliable. This calculator limits credits to the upfront fee bucket and does not model cash rebates. Primary references CFPB’s Loan Estimate explainer helps identify the payment, closing costs and estimated cash to close. CFPB’s points and lender-credit explanation describes their rate/cost trade-offs. All dollar amounts and allocations in our quote are fictional. Ask the lender to reconcile the actual disclosure, payoff and timing items before a transaction. Frequently asked questions Are financed closing costs free? No. They increase the new principal and can increase interest. Include them once through the new loan schedule. Should I enter all cash to close as fees? No. Separate transaction fees from escrow, prepaids and payoff adjustments according to their actual treatment and timing. Does one point always reduce the rate by a fixed amount? No. One point describes 1% of loan amount; the rate reduction depends on the actual lender offer. Can a lender credit exceed upfront fees in this model? No. The supported rate-and-term model offsets only the entered upfront fee bucket and does not create an unrestricted cash rebate. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
