documents.summary: Compare remaining mortgage term with shorter and longer refinance examples. Check payments, lifetime interest and remaining debt at the same five-year date.
documents.headings: Compare payment burden and debt remaining at the same sale date Refinance to a shorter or longer term: make three separate checks Use months remaining, not the original mortgage term Compare payment pressure and remaining lifetime interest Bring every option to the same five-year date Distinguish affordability from comparative borrowing cost Let payments stop at payoff Keep fee financing and extra-payment ideas explicit Common mistakes Sources and arithmetic conventions Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Refinance to a Shorter or Longer Term: Compare Payments and Debt Published October 26, 2026 Updated October 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare remaining mortgage term with shorter and longer refinance examples. Check payments, lifetime interest and remaining debt at the same five-year date. Mortgage term choice Worked examples Planning assumptions A shorter term can raise payments while reducing interest and remaining debt. A longer term can lower payments while extending borrowing. Compare the current loan’s remaining months, each proposed term and cash plus debt at one common holding date. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Compare payment burden and debt remaining at the same sale date For the same hypothetical $250,000 payoff and 5.5% new fixed note rate, the new loan term changes both monthly obligations and principal still owed after five years. Each version includes $6,000 upfront charges and is compared with keeping a 6.5% current mortgage with 300 months remaining. Original tested engine figures at month 60; all figures approximate to cents New term Monthly P&I Unpaid balance at month 60 Advantage vs current loan 15 years $2,042.71 $188,222.40 $10,901.46 saving 25 years $1,535.22 $223,178.73 $6,394.53 saving 30 years $1,419.47 $231,151.68 $5,366.58 saving The shorter loan reduces principal faster but demands a larger monthly payment. The longer loan has the smallest required payment among these options but leaves more debt at month 60. Thus affordability, lifetime interest and cost at sale are three separate decisions ; no row is automatically best for every household. Adjust the term in the calculator and consult the common-date refinance break-even explanation before comparing different terms. No tax benefits, early PMI cancellation or extra payments are assumed. Refinance to a shorter or longer term: make three separate checks Check 1 — monthly affordability: can required principal and interest plus other housing obligations fit recurring cash flow? Check 2 — loan payoff: how many months remain on the current loan, and when would each new loan actually finish? Check 3 — planned holding period: what will you have paid and still owe on the same likely sale or next-refinance date? Fictional $250,000 balance, 5.5% new fixed note rate, $6,000 upfront fees; 60-month horizon New term Monthly P&I Debt at month 60 Month-60 cost advantage vs existing loan 15 years (180 months) $2,042.71 $188,222.40 $10,901.46 25 years (300 months) $1,535.22 $223,178.73 $6,394.53 30 years (360 months) $1,419.47 $231,151.68 $5,366.58 These are the same independently reconciled fixtures as the detailed article below. The 15-year refinance has a higher payment but less unpaid principal at month 60; the 30-year refinance has the lowest modeled new payment but the most remaining debt of these new offers. A smaller payment is not proof of a cheaper mortgage or greater lifetime savings. Reproduce each term in the calculator and compare fee recovery with holding-date debt . The CFPB recommends looking at both short and long expected holding horizons . Use months remaining, not the original mortgage term A current 30-year mortgage with 25 years left has 300 remaining payments, not 360. Restarting it at 360 in the baseline gives the current option time it no longer has. The following original fictional comparison uses $250,000 outstanding at 6.5% with 300 months remaining. New fixed-rate quotes use assumed 5.5% for 180, 300 or 360 months, with $6,000 upfront fees, no financed charges or credits, and a 60-month holding date. No extra principal or other housing costs are included. Rates are illustrative, not current offers. Compare payment pressure and remaining lifetime interest Original fixed-rate schedules; regular P&I rounded to cents; USD Option Term from today Monthly P&I Interest through its own payoff Keep current 300 months $1,688.02 $256,404.43 Shorter new term 180 months $2,042.71 $117,687.42 Same new term 300 months $1,535.22 $210,565.19 Longer new term 360 months $1,419.47 $261,011.49 The shorter refinance raises P&I by $354.69 per month; the longer one lowers it by $268.55. Yet the longer schedule has $4,607.06 more lifetime interest than keeping the current loan, before its $6,000 upfront fee. The shorter schedule has less lifetime interest, but the higher payment must fit the household’s actual cash commitments. Lifetime totals span different durations and are not a same-date cost comparison. Bring every option to the same five-year date After payment 60; include fees once and retain the debt still owed; USD Option Payments through 60 Balance at 60 Upfront fee Cash + balance + fee Keep current $101,281.20 $226,405.26 $0.00 $327,686.46 180-month new term $122,562.60 $188,222.40 $6,000.00 $316,785.00 300-month new term $92,113.20 $223,178.73 $6,000.00 $321,291.93 360-month new term $85,168.20 $231,151.68 $6,000.00 $322,319.88 Using unrounded balances, refinance advantages at month 60 are $10,901.46, $6,394.53 and $5,366.58 respectively. Rounded table components can differ from a total by a cent. The shortest loan has the highest paid cash but the lowest remaining debt. The longest has the lowest payment but owes $4,746.42 more principal than the old loan at month 60. That balance difference is why payment savings alone are incomplete. Distinguish affordability from comparative borrowing cost A lower modeled cost cannot make an unaffordable monthly payment feasible. Conversely, a lower payment may be useful for liquidity but is not proof of lower total interest. Record your holding date, minimum reserve and other commitments before preferring a term. The comparison is undiscounted and assumes the same starting property and debt; it does not value the investment return on payment differences or apply tax deductions. Reproduce each option by changing only new term in the refinance calculator . Review its cash and balance table, then download the complete monthly schedule. The guide’s examples use the same cents-rounded regular payment, unrounded internal interest and adjusted final payment convention. Let payments stop at payoff At a horizon beyond month 180, the shorter loan’s principal-and-interest payments stop after payoff. The other options may continue. At horizons beyond both payoff dates, include actual cumulative payments and zero remaining balances for both. Taxes, insurance and HOA do not disappear when the mortgage ends; enter supported housing-cost assumptions separately. The calculator does not infer early mortgage-insurance cancellation. Keep fee financing and extra-payment ideas explicit This comparison pays fees upfront. Financing them would change the new principal and schedule: use the closing-cost ledger to classify them once. Paying extra on a longer mortgage is another possible scenario, but this calculator does not model extra principal or prepayment penalties. Do not claim the scheduled 360-month row proves the result of an extra-payment strategy. Common mistakes Restarting the current loan at its original term, calling a lifetime total a five-year saving, ignoring debt remaining at sale and treating a higher payment as automatically worse are common errors. Read the break-even guide for why a shorter loan may have no simple payment-savings threshold while still reducing matched-date cost. Sources and arithmetic conventions OpenStax’s amortization explanation gives the fixed-payment principal-and-interest relationship. CFPB’s Loan Estimate explainer separates loan terms and P&I from other payment components. Our term scenarios were independently reconciled with a Decimal schedule. They are educational comparisons, not recommendations, underwriting decisions or savings guarantees. Frequently asked questions Can a shorter refinance cost less even if the payment rises? Yes. Faster principal repayment can reduce interest and debt at the holding date, but the higher payment must be affordable. Why compare balances after five years? If you sell or repay then, the remaining principal still has to be settled. A lower payment may have deferred rather than eliminated that debt. Does a longer term always cost more? No universal rule covers all rates, fees and holding periods. In this example it costs more over its full life but less than keeping the old loan at the five-year comparison date. Does the calculator include an extra-payment strategy? No. These schedules use contractual payments only. Extra principal, payment recasting and prepayment penalties need a separate supported model. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: EBITDA vs Net Income vs Cash Flow: A Reconciled Example
documents.summary: Compare EBITDA, net income and operating cash flow using one reconciled business example. Trace receivables, inventory, interest, tax and equipment cash.
documents.headings: EBITDA, net income and cash flow answer different questions Compare the three measurement boundaries Start with one complete fictional income statement Reconcile net income to EBITDA Follow the cash bridge to operating cash flow Equipment and loans sit outside this operating subtotal Choose the measure that matches the decision Common mistakes that change the answer Sources and reporting scope Stress cash collection while keeping reported earnings unchanged Make the cash bridge reviewable Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE EBITDA vs Net Income vs Cash Flow: A Reconciled Example Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare EBITDA, net income and operating cash flow using one reconciled business example. Trace receivables, inventory, interest, tax and equipment cash. EBITDA Net income Operating cash flow Quick answer: Harbor Supply’s fictional annual example has $130,000 EBITDA, $80,000 net income and $70,000 operating cash flow. The reconciled statement below explains each boundary. Enter your own earnings records in the EBITDA calculator . Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. EBITDA, net income and cash flow answer different questions EBITDA measures earnings before interest, income taxes, depreciation and amortization; net income retains those included expenses; operating cash flow reconciles profit with operating cash movements. They are different measures, not competing labels for money in the bank. In the original example below, the same year produces $130,000 EBITDA, $80,000 net income and $70,000 operating cash flow. Use the EBITDA calculator to rebuild the earnings bridge. Use this guide to understand why the cash answer differs. All amounts below are fictional USD for a simplified nonfinancial business under a stated US-style classification. They are not margins or performance benchmarks. Compare the three measurement boundaries Read the subtotal before comparing companies Measure Included here Does not prove EBITDA Net income with included interest, income taxes and D&A added back Cash collected, debt-service capacity or money available to distribute Net income Recognized revenue and period expenses, including D&A, interest and tax That customers have paid or inventory has been funded Operating cash flow Operating receipts/payments or an indirect reconciliation Cash remaining after all investing and financing activity A lender agreement or management report may define a measure differently. Preserve its actual definition and reconcile it instead of assuming that identically named numbers use the same accounting perimeter. Start with one complete fictional income statement Harbor Supply annual teaching example; USD Line Amount Net revenue 1,000,000 Cost of goods sold 600,000 Operating expenses including D&A 290,000 Operating profit / EBIT in this example 110,000 Interest expense 10,000 Income-tax expense 20,000 Net income 80,000 Included depreciation / amortization 15,000 / 5,000 The operating expenses contain $20,000 D&A and $270,000 other operating expenses. There are no additional non-operating gains, foreign-exchange items or discontinued operations in this simplified statement. Thus operating profit and EBIT agree here; that equality should not be assumed for every company. The check is $1,000,000 − $600,000 − $290,000 − $10,000 − $20,000 = $80,000 net income. Keep inventory and COGS on a consistent accrual basis. Reconcile net income to EBITDA $80,000 + $10,000 interest + $20,000 income taxes + $15,000 depreciation + $5,000 amortization = $130,000 EBITDA . Dividing by $1,000,000 net revenue gives 13% EBITDA margin. Net margin is 8%; operating margin is 11%. These percentages use the same revenue denominator but different profit numerators. Do not add back payroll, rent or materials merely because they are operating costs. Do not add back debt principal: principal was not an income-statement expense in the first place. If depreciation is already excluded from a starting subtotal, adding it again inflates earnings. Follow the cash bridge to operating cash flow Indirect method; annual operating balance changes in USD Reconciliation Signed amount Net income 80,000 Add included noncash D&A +20,000 Increase in trade receivables −25,000 Increase in operating inventory −10,000 Increase in supplier payables +5,000 Operating cash flow 70,000 Receivables grew because recognized sales exceeded collections; inventory absorbed funds; supplier credit partly funded operating purchases. Interest and income tax paid are operating in this illustrative policy, and their payable balances do not change. There are no other operating-balance changes or noncash adjustments. Real statements require every applicable reconciling item. The operating cash flow guide develops direct and indirect calculations. The working capital guide explains why a growing current-asset balance can consume cash. Cross-check from EBITDA: $130,000 − $10,000 operating interest paid − $20,000 operating income tax paid − $25,000 receivables increase − $10,000 inventory increase + $5,000 payables increase = $70,000 operating cash flow. This second route agrees because the example has no interest/tax payable changes or other adjustments. Do not subtract D&A again: EBITDA already excludes it. Equipment and loans sit outside this operating subtotal Suppose the business pays $40,000 for equipment and repays $15,000 loan principal, with no other investing or financing movements. Operating cash of $70,000 less those payments leaves a $15,000 total cash increase. The $40,000 purchase is investing; the $15,000 principal repayment is financing under the example policy. Neither is automatically a new full current-year operating expense. Under a stated operating-cash-flow-minus-capital-expenditure convention, the intermediate amount is $30,000 before the principal repayment. A report calling a number “free cash flow” must disclose its definition. EBITDA is not that $30,000 amount. See the complete cash flow statement for reconciliation to the opening bank balance. Choose the measure that matches the decision Use the EBITDA bridge to compare defined earnings across matched periods, then review its exclusions. Use net income for the period’s bottom-line accounting result. Use operating and total cash-flow schedules for payment timing, asset purchases and funding. None alone establishes what owners can safely withdraw. Compare the same company perimeter, reporting duration and revenue basis. A growth business can have improving EBITDA and deteriorating collections simultaneously. Keep that diagnosis separate from the sales volume needed to break even. The operating margin calculator answers the operating-profit percentage question. Common mistakes that change the answer Adding D&A twice, using cash tax paid as a substitute for accrued tax expense, treating all current accounts as operating working capital and subtracting equipment purchases twice can each create a false bridge. Reconcile missing data rather than entering a convenient zero. If an Adjusted EBITDA report removes unusual costs or gains, read the add-back evidence guide . A claimed one-off does not disappear from bank cash simply because management adjusts an earnings measure. Sources and reporting scope SEC guidance on EBIT and EBITDA establishes the net-income starting point and distinct naming of adjusted measures. OpenStax explains the indirect cash-flow reconciliation . Our Harbor Supply statement and arithmetic are original. The illustrative US-style interest/tax classification is explicit, not a universal IFRS presentation template. Apply the adopted reporting framework and professional advice where required. For actual dated collections and payments, use the 13-week cash forecast . Stress cash collection while keeping reported earnings unchanged Use the original $130,000 EBITDA, $80,000 net income and $70,000 operating cash flow case above as the baseline. In a separate sensitivity, assume an additional $25,000 of already-recognized sales remains in receivables at period end instead of being collected. Hold revenue, recognized expenses, taxes and every other operating-cash bridge item constant. Operating cash flow falls to $45,000 ; EBITDA and net income remain unchanged under those assumptions. Collection-timing sensitivity on the existing teaching baseline, USD Measure Baseline Extra $25,000 uncollected EBITDA 130,000 130,000 Net income 80,000 80,000 Operating cash flow 70,000 45,000 Operating cash / net income 87.5% 56.25% Additional receivables relative to baseline 0 25,000 This isolates timing; it assumes the sales still qualify for recognition and does not model a credit loss, refund or change in tax cash payments. If collectability deteriorates, the earnings assumptions may also need revision. The extra receivable is not deducted from earnings a second time merely because it has not yet become cash. Make the cash bridge reviewable For each adjustment, show opening balance, closing balance, change and its sign in the cash reconciliation. A receivable increase generally uses operating cash relative to recognized sales; a payable increase can temporarily support cash relative to recognized costs. Review each underlying transaction and the applicable reporting framework rather than inferring cash from EBITDA alone. Financing proceeds and principal repayments belong in their appropriate cash-flow categories, not in an improvised EBITDA calculation. Use the statement-analysis workpaper to investigate the drivers, the adjustment register for separately defined earnings changes, and a dated liquidity plan when payroll arrives before customer cash. A strong EBITDA margin cannot establish that those payments are funded. Frequently asked questions Is EBITDA the same as operating cash flow? No. EBITDA excludes selected expenses but does not automatically account for collections, inventory, payables or all operating cash adjustments. Can EBITDA be positive while cash falls? Yes. Uncollected sales, inventory investment, equipment payments and debt principal can absorb cash even when the earnings subtotal is positive. Why is depreciation added back in the cash bridge? Included depreciation reduced net income without being a cash payment in that period. The actual asset purchase is classified separately. Does operating income always equal EBIT? No. They agree in the fictional example because no separate non-operating items exist. Reconcile the actual statement before using either starting subtotal. Can EBITDA stay unchanged while operating cash falls? Yes. In a collection-timing sensitivity, more already-recognized revenue can remain in receivables. Reconcile the working-capital change and assess collectability separately. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Adjusted EBITDA and Add-backs: Build an Evidence-Based Bridge
documents.summary: Build a signed Adjusted EBITDA bridge with documented add-backs and deductions. Check recurring costs, gains, owner compensation and double counting.
documents.headings: What Adjusted EBITDA changes Keep standard and adjusted earnings separate Reconcile a complete signed example Build an adjustment evidence register Owner compensation needs a replacement-cost view Repeated one-offs and future savings need scrutiny Adjusted EBITDA is not cash flow or a valuation Review the bridge before using it Show the disputed adjustment as a range rather than a hidden certainty Record a decision and a reason for each item Source and methodology Continue with bookkeeping and financial statements Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Adjusted EBITDA and Add-backs: Build an Evidence-Based Bridge Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a signed Adjusted EBITDA bridge with documented add-backs and deductions. Check recurring costs, gains, owner compensation and double counting. Adjusted EBITDA Add-backs Reconciliation Quick answer: keep base EBITDA separate from signed extra adjustments. In the independent example, 130,000 + 12,000 − 5,000 = 137,000 Adjusted EBITDA; appropriateness still needs evidence. Build the separately labelled calculator bridge . Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. What Adjusted EBITDA changes Adjusted EBITDA starts with a defined EBITDA subtotal and applies separately identified adjustments. A cost adjustment usually increases the subtotal; removing an included gain decreases it. The resulting measure depends on the chosen definition and is not automatically comparable across businesses. Begin with the EBITDA calculator and preserve the standard earnings bridge before adding adjustments. This guide evaluates the evidence behind that second bridge. It does not endorse an adjustment for a transaction, covenant or public filing. Keep standard and adjusted earnings separate Standard EBITDA adds back the included interest, income taxes, depreciation and amortization to net income. A proposed litigation, owner-pay or restructuring adjustment is a further policy choice; it does not belong silently inside the standard formula. The calculator labels base EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA separately. A negative adjustment is allowed because unusual income may need to be removed. Do not use the same positive-only “add-back” field for every event and hide its direction. Reconcile a complete signed example Separate fictional annual scenario; USD, not the Harbor Supply ledger Bridge line Signed amount Evidence to retain Base EBITDA 130,000 Net-income/D&A reconciliation Remove included special legal expense +12,000 Invoice, matter description and selected policy Remove included nonrecurring gain −5,000 Ledger entry and underlying transaction Adjusted EBITDA 137,000 130,000 + 12,000 − 5,000 This independent scenario assumes both the $12,000 expense and $5,000 gain already affected the net income underlying base EBITDA. The legal-cost adjustment is an illustrative proposal, not a conclusion that all legal fees are nonrecurring. If the gain did not enter the starting earnings, subtracting it here would be a second adjustment. At $1,000,000 matched net revenue, base margin is 13% and adjusted margin is 13.7%. The $7,000 increase is a change in the selected performance measure, not $7,000 new cash received. Reproduce the bridge: in the EBITDA calculator, retain the base example, open “Adjusted EBITDA — separate signed items”, then add a uniquely described $12,000 expense adjustment and a −$5,000 gain adjustment. The base must remain $130,000 while the separately adjusted result becomes $137,000. Renaming the same invoice does not make a duplicate economic adjustment valid. Build an adjustment evidence register A reviewable adjustment needs more than a number Field Question Event and reporting date What happened, and is it in this period? Starting treatment Where did it affect net income or base EBITDA? Signed amount Is this an expense add-back or an income deduction? Recurrence Has the same class of cost occurred before or been budgeted again? Replacement economics Will a replacement employee, system or supplier still cost money? Reporting purpose What definition does the contract or reporting framework require? Retain the ledger reference, invoice, approval and written rationale with the calculation. Unique descriptions reduce duplicate entries but software cannot verify whether an event is genuinely unusual or whether a buyer will accept the adjustment. Owner compensation needs a replacement-cost view An owner’s salary is not automatically removable. If the owner performs necessary work, someone must still deliver it after a sale or management change. An adjustment based on replacement economics may remove only an evidenced excess over comparable necessary compensation, with employer costs and role scope considered. For example, $90,000 included owner compensation and a documented $70,000 replacement cost suggest a $20,000 difference under that chosen normalization policy, not a $90,000 saving. This is a hypothetical arithmetic example, not a salary benchmark or accepted valuation adjustment. Owner draws are not another wage expense merely because cash leaves the business. Repeated one-offs and future savings need scrutiny A category called “one-time” every year may be part of the ongoing cost of operating. A future system saving is not necessarily a valid adjustment to historical earnings. Show expected savings in a separate forecast with implementation costs and a start date. Do not remove ordinary rent, marketing, payroll or maintenance simply to reach a target margin. Stock compensation, impairment, acquisition costs and restructuring can have purpose-specific treatment; this simple tool does not decide the appropriate policy or contractual EBITDA definition. Adjusted EBITDA is not cash flow or a valuation Even a well-documented adjustment does not erase cash already paid. Debt service, working capital and capital investment remain separate. Read the reconciled profit-versus-cash example before treating adjusted earnings as distributable money. A valuation also needs a defensible approach, risk assessment, debt/cash treatment and transaction perimeter. The calculator supplies no market multiple and no automatic sale price. For scenario planning, keep projected benefits separate from actual historical records. Review the bridge before using it Check that the starting EBITDA reconciles, every signed item affected that starting figure, recurring economics remain visible, gains are treated consistently with expenses, and no item appears twice. Compare prior periods using the same definitions or explain a change. Keep base and adjusted subtotals side by side. If an item is disputed, show the scenario with and without it instead of presenting a single adjusted number as an independently verified fact. Return to the itemized calculator to test the arithmetic. Show the disputed adjustment as a range rather than a hidden certainty Continue the independent signed example above: base EBITDA is $130,000, the proposed special legal-cost adjustment is +$12,000 and the included nonrecurring gain removal is −$5,000. The displayed $137,000 depends on accepting the legal adjustment. If that item is disputed, show both cases; do not omit the gain deduction to make the conservative case look stronger. Same ledger, two adjustment judgments; fictional USD Line Legal item accepted Legal item not accepted Base EBITDA 130,000 130,000 Special legal expense adjustment +12,000 0 Remove included gain −5,000 −5,000 Adjusted subtotal 137,000 125,000 Margin on the same $1 million net revenue 13.7% 12.5% The $12,000 range is a definition/evidence difference, not an extra $12,000 cash reserve. Both scenarios retain the same underlying earnings and actual payments. A private transaction agreement can specify its own definition; a worksheet cannot establish what a buyer, lender or regulator must accept. Record a decision and a reason for each item Keep an evidence status such as supported, disputed or excluded; the ledger reference; the signed amount; replacement costs; recurrence history; and the reviewer/date. Check the prior two reporting periods for similar costs. This is an investigation aid, not a rule that two quiet years make a cost nonrecurring. If a proposed saving has not entered historical earnings, put it in a separately dated forecast with implementation costs rather than quietly adding it to this historical bridge. The SEC non-GAAP interpretations discuss recurring operating expenses, consistent period treatment and gains as well as charges in their public-reporting context. Keep that scope distinct from private deal negotiations. Compare the cash reconciliation before using either adjusted subtotal as a measure of available money. Source and methodology SEC non-GAAP interpretations, including sections 100 and 103 , discuss potentially misleading adjustments and the naming/reconciliation of EBIT, EBITDA and adjusted measures. Public-company rules have a defined scope; this guide does not imply every private-company worksheet is an SEC filing. The numbers, adjustment register and commentary here are original teaching material. Consult the actual agreement and qualified accounting advisers for a reporting or transaction decision. Frequently asked questions What is an EBITDA add-back? It is an identified adjustment that increases a specified EBITDA measure, normally for an expense already included in the starting earnings. Whether it is appropriate depends on evidence and purpose. Can Adjusted EBITDA be lower than EBITDA? Yes. Removing included unusual income or applying other signed deductions can lower the adjusted subtotal. Can I add back all owner salary? Not automatically. Necessary owner work may require paid replacement; draws are not the same as included salary expense. Does the calculator approve my adjustments? No. It checks arithmetic and input structure. It does not verify records, recurrence, contract terms or professional acceptance. How should a disputed EBITDA add-back be presented? Show the signed bridge both with and without the disputed item, retain consistent gain deductions and disclose the definition and evidence. Neither subtotal creates cash or proves acceptance by another party. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Present Value vs Future Value: Compare Money on One Date
documents.summary: Compare present and future value with a matched-date example. Understand compounding, discounting, inflation and the limits of fixed-rate projections.
documents.headings: Present value and future value reverse the timeline Use consistent formulas and periods Follow one amount forward and backward Put each cash flow on a timeline Discounting and inflation adjustment are different tasks Apply the timeline to a business reserve Avoid misleading comparisons Choose the right next calculation Compare payment alternatives at one valuation date Match an annual rate to monthly payment dates Sources and assumptions Continue with investment decisions and cost of capital Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Present Value vs Future Value: Compare Money on One Date Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare present and future value with a matched-date example. Understand compounding, discounting, inflation and the limits of fixed-rate projections. Present value Future value Time value of money Quick answer: at a matched 5% effective annual rate, $10,000 today grows to $11,025 in two years; discounting that same future amount returns $10,000. Project a balance with your own assumptions . Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Present value and future value reverse the timeline Future value moves a stated amount forward using a chosen growth rate; present value moves a future cash flow back using a chosen discount rate. Both require dated cash flows and matched period units. Neither establishes what an uncertain investment will actually return. Use the Future Value calculator when the question is what today’s amount plus regular deposits could become. This guide explains the comparison of dates; it does not add a separate present-value solver. Use consistent formulas and periods For a single amount, FV = PV × (1+i) n and PV = FV ÷ (1+i) n . Here i is the effective rate for one period and n is the number of those periods. A monthly rate must be paired with months, not years. A nominal annual rate compounded monthly is not generally the same as the same numerical effective annual rate. Convert using the stated convention before comparing offers. The calculator displays its selected effective period rate so the result is reproducible. Follow one amount forward and backward Original fictional example; 5% effective annual rate, USD Date or action Calculation Value Today Starting balance 10,000.00 End of year 1 10,000 × 1.05 10,500.00 End of year 2 10,500 × 1.05 11,025.00 Discount year-2 value to today 11,025 ÷ 1.05² 10,000.00 The forward and reverse calculations agree because the rate, dates and cash flow are matched. If a different discount rate is appropriate for the future payment’s risk, the reverse value will change. An arithmetic identity is not proof that a proposed return or payment is reliable. Reproduce the single-amount example: enter $10,000 starting amount, zero recurring contribution, 24 months, 5% effective annual rate and 0% inflation in the Future Value calculator. The nominal result is $11,025; the default recurring deposit must be replaced with zero. For this isolated cash flow, a zero rate leaves present and future values equal; a negative rate above −100% makes the future amount smaller. The discounting formula still requires the same dates and rate convention. Put each cash flow on a timeline Date-aware comparison Time Lump-sum path Additional contribution path 0 Initial principal Initial principal, plus any beginning contribution 1 First period growth Growth plus the contribution at its selected time 2 and later Continue same stated convention Each contribution grows only after its own deposit date A deposit made near the end does not earn all the earlier years of returns. Calculate each cash flow from its own date or use a correctly matched annuity formula. See the payment-timing comparison for beginning versus end contributions. Discounting and inflation adjustment are different tasks Discounting can represent the selected required return for a dated cash flow. Inflation adjustment expresses purchasing power. To restate a nominal ending balance in today’s money, divide it by (1+assumed inflation) years . Do not subtract the same inflation adjustment twice. At 5% nominal effective growth and 2% inflation, the exact annual real growth factor is 1.05 ÷ 1.02, or about 2.9412% real growth, rather than exactly 3%. Both return and inflation are assumptions. Real-life spending baskets and returns vary. Apply the timeline to a business reserve A business planning to replace equipment can project a reserve from current cash and fixed contributions. Label the target’s date and whether the replacement quote is today’s price or an assumed future price. Keep the reserve calculation separate from the project’s operating return. The Business ROI and payback calculator evaluates modeled project costs and cash benefits. It does not use the same question as a future savings balance. A positive project ROI also does not guarantee cash arrives before the equipment payment. Use a dated cash forecast for that funding question. Avoid misleading comparisons Do not compare one offer’s annual effective rate with another nominal rate as if they were identical. Do not use 6% annually as 6% monthly. Do not inflate a today’s-money target and then compare it with an already inflation-adjusted balance. Do not assume a high expected return is a deposit guarantee. Fees, tax timing, withdrawals, uncertain cash flows and changing contributions can require a more complete model. The current Future Value tool excludes fees and taxes rather than producing an unsupported after-tax forecast. No 401(k)-specific contribution or withdrawal rules are included. Choose the right next calculation Known principal, deposits and horizon: use Future Value . Same deposits but changed timing: use the annuity timing guide . A completed business reporting period: use the cash flow statement . A project’s cash costs and benefits: use ROI/payback. Record rates, time units, payment dates, rounding and exclusions with your result. That record makes later comparisons meaningful; a bare future balance does not. Compare payment alternatives at one valuation date A larger later payment is not automatically more valuable today. In an independent fictional choice, option A pays $10,000 today and option B pays $11,500 at the end of year three. Assume both amounts are comparable before fees and taxes and use a chosen 5% effective annual discount rate. Option B has present value $11,500 ÷ 1.05 3 = $9,934.13 , below $10,000 today under that rate. Independent offer comparison; USD and common date t=0 Effective annual discount assumption PV of $11,500 in three years Compared with $10,000 today 3% $10,524.13 Higher by $524.13 5% $9,934.13 Lower by $65.87 Break-even rate ≈ 4.768955% $10,000.00 Equal by construction The equal-value rate is (11,500 ÷ 10,000) 1/3 − 1. It is not a forecast return or a recommendation to accept either offer. Payment risk, liquidity needs, fees and tax treatment may differ. The comparison only answers the stated dated-cash-flow arithmetic. Match an annual rate to monthly payment dates If 5% is an effective annual rate, its equivalent monthly rate is 1.05 1/12 − 1 ≈ 0.407412%. Discounting for 36 months at that monthly rate gives the same $9,934.13. Using 5% ÷ 12 instead assumes a nominal annual rate compounded monthly and changes the result. Record the convention with the amount and date. For several equal payments, use the ordinary-versus-due payment timeline ; do not treat all receipts as one final lump sum. For a business decision with operating costs, compare cash timing and break-even as separate questions. The original single-amount example above remains a formula check, not an investment promise. Sources and assumptions OpenStax explains future value and compounding ; its annuity chapter explains periodic payments and their dates . The timelines and numerical cases here are original fictional illustrations. Treat the rate as an entered scenario, not a current quote or recommended asset return. Compare risk and terms independently before using any real financial product. Frequently asked questions Is present value always lower than future value? With a positive rate and positive time for one positive cash flow, yes. At zero rate they agree; a negative effective rate can reverse the relationship. Is present value just inflation adjustment? No. A discount rate can reflect a selected required return and risk, whereas inflation adjustment expresses purchasing power under an inflation assumption. Can I compare monthly and annual rates directly? Only after converting them to a common effective period and matching the cash-flow dates. Does a future value projection guarantee the balance? No. A fixed-rate calculation follows entered assumptions. Actual returns, deposits, fees and tax can differ. What discount rate makes two lump-sum offers equal? For a payment today P and one future payment F after n years, the equal-value effective annual rate is (F/P)^(1/n) − 1 when the positive amounts and dates fit that model. It does not establish a suitable investment return. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Ordinary Annuity vs Annuity Due: Payment Timing Explained
documents.summary: Compare end-period and beginning-period payments with timelines and worked examples. Match contribution frequency, compounding and valuation date.
documents.headings: The difference is when each payment happens Draw the payment dates first Apply the matched-period annuity formulas Compare two $1,000 annual deposits Check a short monthly example Contribution frequency is not compounding frequency Use timing without assuming it is free money Check the common timing mistakes Sources and next step Check present value and future value against the same payment dates Reproduce the timing in a spreadsheet Continue with investment decisions and cost of capital Frequently asked questions
documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Ordinary Annuity vs Annuity Due: Payment Timing Explained Published October 26, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare end-period and beginning-period payments with timelines and worked examples. Match contribution frequency, compounding and valuation date. Ordinary annuity Annuity due Contribution timing Quick answer: ordinary payments occur at period end; due payments occur at the beginning. Two $1,000 annual deposits at 5% finish at $2,050 versus $2,152.50 respectively. Compare timing in the calculator . Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. The difference is when each payment happens An ordinary annuity has payments at the end of each period; an annuity due has payments at the beginning. For otherwise identical deposits and a positive period rate, beginning payments have one extra period of growth at the common ending date. “Annuity” here means a regular cash-flow pattern, not a recommendation to buy an insurance product. The Future Value calculator supports both timing conventions. Enter the same principal, contribution, rate and horizon before changing only the timing option. Draw the payment dates first Two annual contributions valued at the end of year 2 Time Ordinary / end Due / beginning Start of year 1, t=0 No contribution First contribution End of year 1 / start of year 2, t=1 First contribution Second contribution End of year 2, t=2 Second contribution; value total Value total; no third contribution Both paths contain exactly two contributions. Do not accidentally put a third payment at the final date in the beginning case. A deposit count error can matter more than the interest calculation. Initial principal is a separate cash flow and is not another recurring contribution. Apply the matched-period annuity formulas For n equal end-period payments P and effective period rate i: FV ordinary = P × [(1+i) n − 1] ÷ i . Beginning-period future value is FV due = FV ordinary × (1+i) . Add PV × (1+i) n separately for initial principal. At i=0, both contribution totals are P×n. The due multiplier applies to the contribution stream, not the existing principal. For a negative valid effective rate, beginning contributions can finish lower because they experience the negative rate for longer. Compare two $1,000 annual deposits Original fictional USD example; 5% effective annual rate Payment Ordinary value at t=2 Due value at t=2 First 1,000 1,000 × 1.05 = 1,050 1,000 × 1.05² = 1,102.50 Second 1,000 1,000 1,000 × 1.05 = 1,050 Total 2,050 2,152.50 The $102.50 difference is payment timing under the stated assumptions. It is not an extra deposit or a guaranteed bonus. If there is also $10,000 initial principal, both paths add the same $11,025 principal future value; do not multiply that amount by another 1.05. Check a short monthly example With no initial principal, $100 per month, two months and 1% effective monthly growth, end-month deposits finish at $100×1.01 + $100 = $201 . Beginning deposits finish at $100×1.01² + $100×1.01 = $203.01 . To reproduce a monthly rate through an annual input, use a matched convention: 12% nominal compounded monthly gives 1% per month. An effective annual rate of 12% gives a smaller monthly effective rate. Keep these labels visible rather than dividing every annual rate by twelve. Zero-rate check: with no starting principal, twelve $100 monthly deposits and a 0% rate, both timing choices finish at $1,200. With a negative effective monthly rate of −1%, two $100 deposits instead finish at $199 at period end and $197.01 at period beginning. Earlier deposits experience the negative rate for longer, so “annuity due is higher” applies only to a positive rate. Contribution frequency is not compounding frequency A bank or projection may quote monthly compounding while the user deposits quarterly. The effective quarterly rate must represent the growth across that three-month payment interval. Under the calculator’s disclosed equivalent-rate convention, nominal j compounded m times a year converts to payment-period rate (1+j/m) m/p −1 for p payments per year. The tool requires whole contribution periods. Annual contributions need a horizon made of whole years, quarterly contributions whole quarters and monthly contributions whole months. It does not invent a fractional final deposit. Use timing without assuming it is free money Beginning contributions may reduce cash available for payroll or suppliers earlier in the period. A savings projection does not check those operating commitments. For a replacement reserve, choose deposit dates the business can actually fund and compare them with the payment calendar. Use the dated cash forecast for short-term liquidity and present versus future value to compare money on a common date. Payment timing and product risk remain separate decisions. Check the common timing mistakes Do not mix rent paid at the beginning with a formula assuming end payments. Do not give the final ordinary deposit a full extra period of growth. Do not add n+1 deposits to a horizon defined as n contribution periods. Do not multiply the whole balance, including existing principal, by the due adjustment. Schedules may display cents while the engine retains precision. Sum unrounded values when reconciling; a one-cent display difference across independently rounded rows is not an extra return. Download the tool’s CSV with its assumptions when saving a scenario. Sources and next step OpenStax discusses ordinary annuities and annuities due . The payment timelines, business application and numerical examples here are original teaching cases. Return to the Future Value calculator to change contribution timing while keeping all other inputs constant. The fixed-rate model does not forecast market returns or decide whether an annuity product suits your circumstances. Check present value and future value against the same payment dates In a separate three-payment example, pay $100 each year at a 10% effective annual rate. Ordinary payments occur at t=1, 2 and 3; due payments occur at t=0, 1 and 2. Value both streams at t=0 for present value and t=3 for future value. Each stream contains exactly three payments. Independent three-payment verification; USD, rounded only for display Measure Ordinary: t=1,2,3 Due: t=0,1,2 Present value at t=0 100/1.1 + 100/1.1² + 100/1.1³ = 248.69 100 + 100/1.1 + 100/1.1² = 273.55 Future value at t=3 100×1.1² + 100×1.1 + 100 = 331.00 100×1.1³ + 100×1.1² + 100×1.1 = 364.10 Cross-check 248.685199… × 1.1³ = 331 273.553719… × 1.1³ = 364.10 For this positive rate, both due values equal the corresponding ordinary value multiplied by 1.1. This shifts the payment stream one period earlier; it does not add a fourth payment or shift an unrelated starting principal. Discounting the ending total back three years gives its corresponding present value when the same rate and dates are used. Reproduce the timing in a spreadsheet With no separate initial principal, =FV(10%,3,-100,0,0) gives $331 and =FV(10%,3,-100,0,1) gives $364.10. For the present values, =PV(10%,3,-100,0,0) and =PV(10%,3,-100,0,1) give about $248.69 and $273.55. The negative payment is the outflow sign convention; the last argument selects end or beginning timing. Use the common-date comparison to audit the result. OpenStax’s annuity treatment explains the underlying dated-payment method. These are fixed-rate teaching calculations, with no tax, fee or market-return assumptions added. Frequently asked questions Which has higher future value, ordinary annuity or annuity due? For the same positive period rate, dates and contribution count, annuity due is higher because each payment grows for one extra period. At zero rate they agree. Does the due multiplier apply to my starting balance? No. It applies to the recurring payment stream. Initial principal follows its own full-horizon growth formula. Can contributions and compounding have different frequencies? Yes, with a disclosed effective-rate conversion and consistent payment intervals. The calculator supports annual, quarterly and monthly contributions. Does this calculator price an insurance annuity? No. It models equal periodic cash flows at a constant assumed rate, without product-specific fees, guarantees or contract terms. How can I check an annuity result without trusting one formula? List every payment date, grow or discount each payment separately to one common date and add the results. Verify the payment count and compare that total with the matched-period formula. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cash Flow Statement: Format, Example and Preparation Published October 25, 2026 Updated November 4, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Learn the cash flow statement format with a complete example, direct and indirect reconciliation, balance-sheet checks and an editable CSV close schedule. Cash flow Financial statements Small business Check the profit-to-cash reconciliation The teaching bridge below starts with net income and separately explains noncash expense, operating working capital, asset purchases and financing. It does not classify every possible transaction or replace the full statement. Planning connections reviewed November 18, 2026. Existing calculation methods and article dates are preserved. Profit-to-cash teaching bridge Fictional matching-period USD records. Positive receivables/inventory changes consume cash; a positive operating-payables change retains cash. Assume no other adjustments, tax timing, interest classification differences, FX or noncash investing/financing transactions. Net income / loss Noncash depreciation included in profit Increase / (decrease) in operating receivables Increase / (decrease) in inventory Increase / (decrease) in operating payables Cash asset purchases Cash loan proceeds Cash loan principal repaid Opening cash Operating cash flow $9,800.00 Investing cash flow -$6,000.00 Financing cash flow $3,500.00 Net cash change $7,300.00 Closing cash $22,300.00 Reset bridge example This bridge does not submit or retain inputs after reload. Review the quality and timing of the cash-flow result separately. AI-generated editorial image; all figures in the guide are separate, original fictional examples. A cash flow statement explains how cash changed during a completed reporting period. It groups movements into operating, investing and financing activities, then reconciles opening to closing cash. Unlike an income statement, it follows cash movements rather than simply recognizing sales and expenses. Unlike a forecast, it reports what happened. For the fictional Cedar Supply example, March 2026 profit is $9,000, operating cash flow is $2,000, equipment uses $12,000 and net financing provides $10,000. Total cash movement is zero, so opening and closing cash are both $10,000. The unchanged balance hides a reliance on new borrowing. All amounts are USD teaching assumptions, not customer results or industry benchmarks. Cash flow statement format: the three sections Classify the activity before totaling the payment Section Question Examples in a nonfinancial business Operating What did ordinary business activity collect and pay? Customer receipts; supplier and employee payments Investing What cash went into or came from long-term assets? Equipment bought for cash; cash proceeds from a sale Financing What cash came from or returned to capital providers? Loan proceeds; debt principal repaid; owner capital or distributions Cash flow means money moving during an interval. Cash is a balance at a date. The statement links the two: closing cash = opening cash + operating cash flow + investing cash flow + financing cash flow , with foreign-exchange or other required reconciling effects separately identified when applicable. This example has none. Use one consistent cash and cash-equivalent perimeter at both dates. Transfers between included bank accounts are internal movements, not new receipts or expenses. A complete cash flow statement example Cedar Supply is an invented US-style nonfinancial reseller. The simplified example treats interest paid and income tax paid as operating cash flows, equipment purchases as investing, and debt principal and owner distributions as financing. It has no foreign exchange, restricted cash, cash-equivalent trades, business combinations, leases, asset sales or noncash acquisitions. Do not apply these simplified classifications to another reporting framework without checking its rules. Cedar Supply — statement of cash flows, March 2026, USD Activity / line Cash inflow / (outflow) Cash received from customers 88,000 Cash paid to suppliers (53,000) Cash paid to employees (19,000) Other operating cash payments (11,000) Interest paid (1,000) Income taxes paid (2,000) Net cash from operating activities 2,000 Equipment bought for cash: investing (12,000) New loan proceeds: financing 15,000 Loan principal repaid: financing (3,000) Owner distributions: financing (2,000) Net cash from financing activities 10,000 Net change in cash 0 Opening cash, March 1 10,000 Closing cash, March 31 10,000 Operating receipts of $88,000 less $86,000 operating payments give $2,000. Then $2,000 − $12,000 + $10,000 = $0 net change. Add this to the $10,000 opening balance. Neither the $15,000 loan nor the owner distribution belongs in revenue or operating profit. Original reconciliation of the fictional statement; values in USD. Direct versus indirect method: the same operating total The direct method groups actual operating receipts and payments. The indirect method reconciles accrual profit to operating cash by adjusting for noncash items, operating asset and liability changes, and other items requiring reclassification. These are alternative presentations of the operating section; they do not create different closing cash balances. Here the income statement is $100,000 revenue − $55,000 COGS − $20,000 payroll − $10,000 other operating expense − $3,000 depreciation − $1,000 interest − $2,000 tax = $9,000 net income . The indirect bridge is $9,000 + $3,000 depreciation − $12,000 receivables increase − $5,000 inventory increase − $1,000 prepayment increase + $7,000 supplier-payables increase + $1,000 payroll-accrual increase = $2,000 OCF . Depreciation is added back because it reduced profit without being a current cash payment. It is not a cash receipt. The equipment payment is reported separately in investing. The operating cash flow guide shows opening and closing balances and derives each cash payment, with an editable reconciliation checker. How to prepare a cash flow statement from your records Set the dates and perimeter. List included bank accounts, cash and qualifying equivalents; reconcile both endpoints to their records. Collect supporting schedules. Use the income statement, comparative balance sheets, bank and cash ledgers, receivable/payable roll-forwards, fixed-asset register, borrowing records and equity movements. Identify actual cash events. Separate accrual entries, write-offs and other noncash movements from bank payments. Do not treat every balance-sheet difference as cash. Build the operating section. Choose the presentation, classify operating balances and cross-check unusual movements. Reconcile direct and indirect views when both are available. Build investing and financing. Use gross proceeds and cash payments where required. Check loan principal separately from interest and owner distributions separately from payroll. Reconcile closing cash. Investigate differences and document excluded noncash transactions and framework-required disclosures. A simple bank export will not identify all accrual adjustments or tell you whether a payment buys an asset. For example, a $12,000 payable increase caused by equipment acquired on credit must not be added into operating cash as though it were an unpaid inventory bill. Use transaction detail, not a universal “current liabilities” shortcut. Check the statement against the balance sheet The same fictional case balances at both dates, USD Item March 1 March 31 Cash 10,000 10,000 Trade receivables 20,000 32,000 Inventory 15,000 20,000 Prepaid operating costs 2,000 3,000 Net equipment 30,000 39,000 Total assets 77,000 104,000 Supplier payables 12,000 19,000 Payroll accruals 3,000 4,000 Income tax payable 1,000 1,000 Loan principal outstanding 20,000 32,000 Equity 41,000 48,000 Total liabilities and equity 77,000 104,000 Net equipment rises by $9,000: $12,000 purchases less $3,000 depreciation. Debt rises by $12,000: $15,000 borrowed less $3,000 repaid. Equity rises by $7,000: $9,000 net income less $2,000 distributions. These supporting roll-forwards explain why total asset growth is much larger than the change in cash. How to read the result without confusing cash and profit Ask where the money came from before deciding whether a positive balance is healthy. Cedar Supply earned $9,000 but generated only $2,000 operating cash. It also spent $12,000 on equipment. New borrowing, net of repayments and distributions, kept the bank balance unchanged. Without that $10,000 net financing, modeled closing cash would be zero; the example does not establish that operations can fund the same investment repeatedly. Negative investing cash may represent productive expansion, while positive investing cash may come from selling equipment. Positive operating cash may be temporary if overdue bills have increased. Review several comparable periods, customer collections, inventory and payment obligations. A statement alone cannot show whether a payroll payment earlier in the month was covered; it aggregates the completed period. Statement, forecast and profit report answer different questions Choose the right next task Record Time basis Use Cash flow statement Completed reporting period Explain cash sources and uses and reconcile balances Cash flow forecast Expected future payment dates Identify when receipts may fail to cover payments Income statement Recognized revenue and expenses for a period Measure accounting performance Break-even model Assumed activity, price and included costs Test the sales contribution required to cover a chosen cost scope Use the net cash flow calculator to total already-classified activity amounts and compare calculated cash with an observed closing balance. It does not classify the ledger or prepare every required statement disclosure. Then carry verified closing cash into the 13-week cash forecast . The profit-versus-cash guide covers the separate profitability question. Common cash flow statement mistakes to catch Checks before sharing the report Mistake Why it fails Correction Treating sales as receipts Unpaid invoices have not supplied cash Reconcile trade receivables, credits and collections Subtracting depreciation as a cash payment It is already a noncash expense Add back the included expense in the indirect bridge Putting loan proceeds in operating income Funding is not a sale Classify the actual funding flow separately Using all current assets in one adjustment Cash and non-operating items may be included Use operating balances with transaction support Netting a bank transfer into revenue Included-account transfers do not change total cash Eliminate both sides within the perimeter Forcing an unexplained balance to zero A plug conceals missing or misclassified events Resolve the source record or retain an explicit difference Download the statement example and close checklist Download the cash flow statement CSV . It is an editable values schedule containing the fictional direct statement, indirect bridge, balance-sheet checks and source-record fields. It contains no spreadsheet formulas or automated classifications. Save an untouched example, copy it for your reporting dates and replace every amount. Recalculate subtotals and reconcile them to the source records before using the result. Continue with the complete cash-flow statement , the operating cash flow calculation or cash-flow problems and management according to the question you need to answer. Reporting basis and sources The SEC financial statements introduction provides the reporting context; its cash flow statement building blocks describes the two operating presentations. The worked Cedar Supply records, calculations and commentary are original teaching material. They are a simplified US-style illustration, not a complete filing template. For IFRS users, consult IAS 7 and the adopted reporting requirements. IFRS 18 applies for annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with earlier application permitted; related IAS 7 amendments change the indirect-method starting subtotal and interest/dividend classification requirements. A net-income bridge should not be copied unchanged into an IFRS 18 reporting package. Sources checked October 25, 2026. Verify working-capital balances before the cash reconciliation The working-capital calculation and balance-sheet example separates current balances, operating balances and bank cash. Match those account definitions before using changes in the operating section. Keep earnings and cash subtotals distinct The reconciled EBITDA, net-income and cash-flow comparison follows one original statement through its earnings and operating-cash bridges. An EBITDA result is not the statement’s closing bank balance. Check invoice cut-off before explaining the cash movement Keep three dates for a material credit transaction: delivery/recognition, invoice due date and bank settlement. A receipt against an opening receivable increases cash while reducing that asset; it is not another sale. A supplier payment settles a payable rather than automatically creating a second expense. Reconcile the subsidiary invoice ledgers to the balance-sheet control accounts before using their movements in the operating-cash bridge. Illustrative cut-off checks; these do not change the statement example above Record Question to resolve Evidence Customer credit Was the return recognized in the correct period? Accepted credit and original invoice Unapplied receipt Is cash posted without clearing the right receivable? Bank receipt and customer remittance Supplier bill Was an unpaid obligation omitted from the closing ledger? Accepted delivery and supplier invoice Keep this close control separate from the forecast of future receipts and payments . The historical reconciliation must agree before its balances become forecast inputs. Frequently asked questions What are the three parts of a cash flow statement? Operating activities describe ordinary business cash; investing covers items such as long-term asset purchases; financing covers capital raised or returned. Their totals reconcile opening and closing cash, with other required reconciling effects identified separately. Is a cash flow statement the same as a cash flow forecast? No. The statement explains a completed period. A forecast places expected future receipts and payments on dates. Use verified closing actual cash as the next forecast opening balance. Can a profitable business have low operating cash flow? Yes. In the fictional example, net income is $9,000 but OCF is $2,000 because operating assets absorb cash, partly offset by increased operating liabilities. Does the CSV automatically prepare a compliant statement? No. It is a values-only teaching schedule. You must classify and verify records, calculate results and meet the reporting framework and recipient requirements separately. Are cash-equivalent and interest classifications universal? No. Follow the applicable framework, transaction facts and reporting period. This example states its simplified US-style nonfinancial-business assumptions; IFRS presentation requirements can differ.
