documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Operating Cash Flow: Formula, Calculation and Example Published October 25, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate operating cash flow with direct and indirect methods, a reconciled example, working-capital sign rules and a checker with current-values CSV. Cash flow Financial statements Small business TRY THE RECONCILIATION Operating cash flow checker Start with the fictional $2,000 example. Enter changes as closing minus opening: an increase is positive and a decrease negative. Use the same period and operating classifications in both views. Amounts are USD; no conversion is performed. Noncash and other adjustments are signed totals already verified against your records. Include each adjustment once. The checker does not identify omitted accounts, classify tax or interest, or prepare a complete cash flow statement. Net income (signed) Net noncash adjustment (signed) Change in operating receivables Change in inventory Change in operating prepayments Change in operating supplier payables Change in other operating liabilities Other reconciliation adjustment (signed) Direct operating cash receipts Direct operating cash payments Other operating liabilities include only the relevant signed accrual/tax-payable changes under your chosen policy. Borrowing and cash balances are excluded. Enter zero explicitly when a relevant input is zero. Indirect operating cash flow $2,000.00 Direct operating cash flow $2,000.00 Difference: indirect − direct $0.00 Totals match. This checks the arithmetic, not source-record completeness or compliance. Download current values (CSV) Reset example AI-generated editorial image; all figures in the guide are separate, original fictional examples. Operating cash flow (OCF) is the cash generated or used by operating activities during a stated period. It is also called cash flow from operations or CFO. It separates day-to-day business cash generation from investing and financing movements. Revenue, net income and EBITDA each measure something different; none can simply be relabeled as OCF. Cedar Supply, our fictional reseller, reports $100,000 March sales and $9,000 net income but only $2,000 operating cash flow . Below, actual receipts minus payments and a net-income reconciliation reach the same amount. All USD inputs are invented for instruction. The example uses a simplified US-style nonfinancial-business policy with interest and income tax paid in operations, no interest payable movement, and no foreign-exchange or noncash balance changes. Operating cash flow formula: choose the presentation Direct OCF = operating cash receipts − operating cash payments. Use actual collections rather than booked sales and actual payments rather than recognized expenses. Keep capital purchases and debt principal outside that operating subtotal under the example policy. Indirect OCF = net income + included noncash adjustments − increases in operating assets + increases in operating liabilities + other signed reconciliation adjustments. Decreases reverse the signs. “Other adjustments” may remove investing or financing gains/expenses according to the reporting framework. The formula is a reconciliation structure, not permission to include cash, borrowings or every current account in working capital. For the full operating/investing/financing layout, use the cash flow statement guide . This page focuses on calculating and diagnosing its operating section. Worked example: start from opening and closing balances Cedar Supply operating balances, March 2026, USD Operating account Opening Closing Change: closing − opening Trade receivables 20,000 32,000 +12,000 Inventory 15,000 20,000 +5,000 Prepaid operating costs 2,000 3,000 +1,000 Supplier payables for inventory 12,000 19,000 +7,000 Accrued payroll 3,000 4,000 +1,000 Income tax payable 1,000 1,000 0 Income is $100,000 sales − $55,000 COGS − $20,000 payroll − $10,000 other operating expense − $3,000 depreciation − $1,000 interest − $2,000 tax = $9,000. All sales are on credit before collection; there are no sales returns, VAT/sales tax flows, credit losses, acquisitions or other balance changes in this intentionally limited example. Inventory payables relate only to inventory, payroll accruals only to payroll, and the prepayment only to the other-expense line. Indirect method: reconcile $9,000 profit to $2,000 cash Signed adjustments to the same March net income, USD Bridge line Effect on OCF Running total Net income 9,000 9,000 Add back depreciation +3,000 12,000 Receivables increased −12,000 0 Inventory increased −5,000 −5,000 Prepaid operating costs increased −1,000 −6,000 Inventory supplier payables increased +7,000 1,000 Payroll accruals increased +1,000 2,000 Tax payable unchanged 0 2,000 Receivables rising means some recognized sales remain uncollected. Inventory rising means more cost is held in stock rather than released into this period’s COGS. Higher prepaid costs mean cash paid exceeds the related current expense. Higher supplier payables and payroll accruals mean some recognized costs have not yet been paid. These explanations depend on the stated clean roll-forwards; real movements need reconciliation for write-offs, reclassifications, acquisitions and exchange differences. Original signed indirect bridge. Depreciation is an adjustment, not cash received. Direct method: derive receipts and payments independently Cash reconstruction from the same records, USD Cash line Calculation Amount Customer collections 100,000 sales + 20,000 opening AR − 32,000 closing AR 88,000 Inventory purchases 55,000 COGS + 20,000 closing stock − 15,000 opening stock 60,000 Supplier cash payments 60,000 purchases + 12,000 opening AP − 19,000 closing AP 53,000 Employee cash payments 20,000 expense + 3,000 opening accrual − 4,000 closing accrual 19,000 Other operating payments 10,000 expense + 3,000 closing prepayment − 2,000 opening prepayment 11,000 Interest cash payment 1,000 expense; no payable change 1,000 Tax cash payment 2,000 expense + 1,000 opening payable − 1,000 closing payable 2,000 Total operating cash payments 53,000 + 19,000 + 11,000 + 1,000 + 2,000 86,000 Operating cash flow 88,000 receipts − 86,000 payments 2,000 Purchases are $60,000 but supplier cash paid is $53,000; COGS is $55,000. Those three numbers are not interchangeable. There is no $3,000 depreciation payment in the direct view. If your indirect and direct totals differ, check the period, account scope, signs and missing adjustments before concluding that one method produces more cash. Working-capital signs: use operating changes only Effect in a clean operating reconciliation Account movement Indirect effect Reason to investigate Receivables or inventory increase Subtract Recognized sales remain uncollected, or cash is held in stock Receivables or inventory decrease Add Collections or inventory release may exceed current sales/cost recognition Operating payable or accrual increase Add Some recognized operating costs remain unpaid Operating payable or accrual decrease Subtract Cash settles prior obligations as well as current costs Borrowing increases Not an operating adjustment here Financing source; not unpaid operating expenditure Cash increases Do not subtract as working capital It is the result being explained Do not use total net working capital from a balance sheet mechanically. It may include cash, debt, tax or non-operating items with different classification requirements. A supplier-finance arrangement also needs its actual terms and the applicable reporting rules reviewed. The working-capital calculation guide addresses the balance-sheet liquidity measure; the operating bridge is a narrower cash-reconciliation task. Is positive or negative operating cash flow good? Positive OCF means this period’s included operating receipts exceed its operating payments. It does not prove bills were paid on time or that the result will repeat. In Cedar Supply, the $8,000 combined increase in supplier and payroll obligations supports the cash result. A separate scenario with those increases removed and everything else unchanged would produce −$6,000 OCF . That scenario isolates payment timing; it does not claim the suppliers have agreed to any terms. Negative OCF can accompany a planned inventory build or receivables growth, but also recurring losses or poor collections. Identify the cause, the dated funding need and the evidence of eventual recovery. Repeated borrowing to cover negative contribution does not repair the underlying economics. Use the cash-flow diagnosis and recovery example to separate a timing gap from a business-model problem. There is no universal healthy OCF threshold for every company or month. OCF versus net income, EBITDA and net cash flow Keep the metric boundary visible Measure What it reflects What Cedar Supply shows Net income Accrual revenue and expenses including depreciation, interest and tax in this example 9,000 EBITDA, simple example definition Net income + interest + tax + depreciation; no amortization here 15,000; not cash and not a universal adjusted-EBITDA definition Operating cash flow Included operating cash generation after the stated classifications 2,000 Net cash change Operating + investing + financing in this no-FX example 0 Subtracting equipment expenditure from OCF is a separate cash measure and does not change OCF itself. Cash-flow ratios, valuation and the full free-cash-flow task have their own scope. Before comparing companies, check period length, seasonality, policies, acquisitions and the denominator definitions rather than comparing an isolated number. Download the operating reconciliation record Download the OCF reconciliation CSV . It contains opening and closing operating balances, the signed indirect bridge, the direct reconstruction and evidence columns. It is a values-only record rather than a formula workbook. The checker above exports your currently valid inputs and computed totals separately; neither file automatically extracts accounts from your ledger. Before closing the period, tie net income to the income statement; tie balance changes to supporting ledgers; remove noncash and non-operating changes; compare the two operating totals; and investigate every difference. Carry the verified operating subtotal into the net cash flow calculator alongside investing and financing. Then use a dated forecast to examine future payment coverage. Method, reporting policy and sources The SEC cash flow building blocks supports the direct/indirect distinction. All Cedar Supply calculations are original. The SEC financial statements introduction explains how the cash and accrual reports connect. This article uses the stated simplified US-style basis, not a universal compliance formula. IAS 7 has related amendments under IFRS 18 , effective for annual periods beginning January 1, 2027 or later, with early application permitted. Those amendments change the indirect-method starting subtotal and interest/dividend requirements. Check which version and adopted framework applies before using a net-income bridge for formal reporting. Sources checked October 25, 2026. Check the account scope behind the working-capital adjustment Use the net, trade and operating working capital comparison to verify the included accounts before adjusting cash flow. Its change-in-working-capital example explains why collecting an invoice and writing one off do not have the same cash effect. Reconcile earnings before interpreting cash The EBITDA calculator traces net income and included add-backs. Follow the EBITDA versus net income versus cash-flow example to see why the earnings subtotal and operating cash can differ. Operating cash flow or operating capital: choose the right calculation Operating cash flow measures included operating cash generated during a period. Operating working capital is a defined balance of operating current assets less operating current liabilities at a date. Use the working-capital guide for account boundaries; use the direct and indirect reconciliations above for the cash-flow calculation. Borrowing, total cash change and operating capital are not interchangeable names for OCF. Separate operating cash ratios and free cash flow For a defined cash-coverage measure, operating cash-flow ratio = cash from operations ÷ current liabilities . A fictional $48,000 annual operating cash flow divided by $40,000 closing current liabilities gives 1.2 times. This compares a period flow with a point-in-time balance. If a comparison instead uses average liabilities, label that basis and use it consistently. Zero liabilities make this ratio undefined; negative operating cash flow remains negative. A common simple free-cash-flow convention is operating cash flow minus cash capital expenditure . With $48,000 operating cash flow and $15,000 cash equipment purchases, that convention gives $33,000. Depreciation is not the same as cash CAPEX; do not subtract the original asset purchase twice. State whether sale proceeds, leases, interest, acquisitions or other items change the chosen definition. The SEC’s non-GAAP interpretation, question 102.07 , notes that free cash flow has no uniform definition. It is not a universally standardized subtotal, cash available for unlimited owner distributions, or the same as net change in cash. Reconcile the stated formula to the cash-flow statement and debt/other commitments before interpreting it. The cash-flow analysis guide considers quality and liquidity; net cash flow includes operating, investing and financing movements for the completed period. Frequently asked questions What is the operating cash flow formula? The direct approach subtracts operating cash payments from operating receipts. A net-income indirect bridge adds included noncash adjustments, subtracts operating asset increases, adds operating liability increases and includes other required signed adjustments under the stated policy. Why is an increase in receivables subtracted? In the clean example, recognized sales exceed collections by the receivables increase. Subtracting that increase converts the accrual sales effect to cash. Noncash or acquisition changes need separate reconciliation. Is depreciation a source of operating cash? No. Adding back depreciation reverses an expense that reduced net income without a current cash payment. It does not create a new receipt. Can operating cash flow be negative when net income is positive? Yes. Inventory, receivables, prepayments and payments of older obligations can absorb more cash than current profits provide. Identify timing, balance movements and recurring operating economics. Does the checker classify accounts or verify compliance? No. It checks entered signed adjustments and compares them with a separately entered direct operating total. You must verify the dates, reporting policy and completeness of the source records. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cash Flow Problems: Causes, Solutions and a Recovery Plan Published October 25, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Diagnose cash flow problems with a four-week example, tested timing fixes, a weekly review routine and an editable recovery action plan for your business. Cash flow Financial statements Small business AI-generated editorial image; all figures in the guide are separate, original fictional examples. A cash flow problem occurs when available cash on the required dates cannot cover payments you must make. A profitable month can still contain a payroll shortfall. Cash flow management means maintaining reliable records, forecasting collection and payment dates, assigning corrective actions and checking whether those actions actually worked. Start with the next uncovered obligation, its date and the evidence behind expected receipts. Do not begin with “increase sales” or count an unapproved loan as available cash. This guide uses an original four-week USD example where a business ends the month with $7,000 yet falls to −$2,000 in week two. The remedy is tested against the timing gap and a chosen $3,000 operating floor, not a universal reserve rule. Find the first shortfall before choosing a solution Reconcile usable opening cash. Check cleared balances, transfers, restricted funds and any amounts unavailable for operating payments. Keep an undrawn facility or loan application separate from cash already received. List the next dated obligations. Include payroll, supplier settlements, tax, debt service, owner withdrawals and committed purchases. Record the actual due date and whether a change is agreed. Review receipt evidence. An invoice issued, a sale booked, a payment promised and a cleared receipt are different stages. Separate confirmed, expected and uncertain collections. Calculate the lowest balance. Compare every dated step with zero and with your chosen cash floor. Check daily ordering when a weekly subtotal is close. Assign the response. Give each action an owner, deadline, evidence needed and fallback if it fails. Warning signs include repeated unpaid invoices, a rising overdue supplier list, emergency borrowing for routine payments, inventory that cannot be sold promptly, and a forecast that changes without explanations. These are investigation triggers, not proof that the company has failed. Begin with source records so a missing bank entry is not mistaken for a commercial problem. Seven cash flow problems: diagnose the cause and the trade-off Match the action to the evidence Problem What to check Potential action and limitation Customers pay later than planned Invoice acceptance, aging, disputes and actual payment history Resolve disputes and follow up; bring receipts forward only with credible customer confirmation Sales do not contribute enough Price less relevant delivery, product, fee and acquisition costs Reprice or change scope; extra low-contribution sales may deepen the gap Stock absorbs cash Inventory age, sell-through, purchase commitments and returns Reduce or reschedule purchases; do not assume all inventory sells at its recorded value Growth runs ahead of funding Deposit terms, staffing, lead times and settlement delays Stage orders or expansion; new revenue can require cash before collection Fixed commitments exceed affordable capacity Leases, subscriptions, payroll and cancellation terms Remove avoidable spending; cutting essential capacity can impair collections or delivery Debt, tax or one-off payments bunch together Actual repayment and due-date schedules Discuss permitted changes early; borrowing adds costs and later obligations Forecast and records are unreliable Missing events, cutoff errors, duplicate receipts and undocumented assumptions Reconcile actuals and revise dates; software cannot repair unsupported inputs A temporary timing gap has an identifiable receipt or event that could close it. A structural gap persists even after realistic collections and payment dates are used because prices, costs or fixed commitments do not support operations. Many businesses have both. Separate them before accepting a funding proposal as the whole solution. Worked example: a positive month-end balance hides a week-two gap Assume $8,000 usable opening cash, a chosen $3,000 floor and the following four-week forecast. The $14,000 receipt in week three includes a collectible $4,000 invoice that may be accelerated. Week-two payments include a discretionary $4,000 equipment purchase that has not yet been irrevocably committed. This is an illustrative forecast, not an actual company ledger. Base case before any financing or remedial action, USD Week Opening Receipts Payments Closing Headroom above 3,000 1 8,000 4,000 9,000 3,000 0 2 3,000 6,000 11,000 −2,000 −5,000 3 −2,000 14,000 6,000 6,000 3,000 4 6,000 8,000 7,000 7,000 4,000 The modeled negative balance is an unmet funding requirement, not evidence that a bank will permit an overdraft. Month totals are $32,000 receipts and $33,000 payments. Opening $8,000 plus the net −$1,000 gives $7,000 month-end cash, but that total conceals week two. The amount needed to avoid a negative weekly balance is $2,000; the amount needed to retain the chosen $3,000 floor is $5,000 . Neither amount is a loan recommendation. Original four-week teaching example. The same month-end cash can conceal a very different low point. Test a recovery plan without double-counting money Consider two explicit changes: collect $4,000 in week two instead of week three, after confirming the customer’s payment, and move the $4,000 discretionary equipment payment from week two to week three if operationally and contractually feasible. These are timing changes. Neither creates extra sales or permanently saves the purchase cost. Revised forecast after both agreed timing changes, USD Week Opening Receipts Payments Closing Headroom above 3,000 1 8,000 4,000 9,000 3,000 0 2 3,000 10,000 7,000 6,000 3,000 3 6,000 10,000 10,000 6,000 3,000 4 6,000 8,000 7,000 7,000 4,000 Total receipts remain $32,000; payments remain $33,000; closing cash remains $7,000. The lowest weekly closing cash rises from −$2,000 to $3,000. Do not leave the accelerated $4,000 in week three or erase the deferred purchase entirely. That would invent money. Check actual within-week receipt and payment order before relying on the weekly totals. Sensitivity: independent outcomes, same opening cash and floor Scenario Lowest weekly closing cash Shortfall to chosen floor Neither change succeeds −2,000 5,000 Only 4,000 receipt acceleration succeeds 2,000 1,000 Only 4,000 payment deferral succeeds 2,000 1,000 Both succeed 3,000 0 Both assumed, but accelerated receipt slips back to week 3 2,000 1,000 The last scenario shows why a promise is not a cleared receipt. If either action is unconfirmed, retain a fallback with its own timing and consequences. A price discount used to accelerate payment would change the receipt amount and possibly profit; it cannot be modeled as a date-only change. Use an action register with evidence and a fallback Example management actions, not completed commitments Action Owner / deadline Evidence and fallback Confirm accelerated 4,000 collection Accounts lead before week-two payment cutoff Written customer confirmation and later bank clearance; if late, re-test the 1,000 floor gap Review equipment timing Operations owner before placing the order Confirm week-three delivery is workable and supplier terms permit it; otherwise retain original payment Protect mandatory payments Owner with accountant / payroll lead before due date Verify actual obligations and permitted options; do not assume payroll, tax or debt can simply be skipped Reconcile forecast to actual cash Bookkeeper at each weekly close Record cleared transactions once; explain date/amount variances and re-date only outstanding amounts The owner field creates responsibility; it does not prove an action was completed. Keep a status such as proposed, agreed, cleared or failed. If obligations cannot be met, obtain timely professional help on the actual business circumstances rather than silently treating overdue liabilities as free funding. Build a weekly cash flow management routine Close the completed week. Compare the forecast closing balance with reconciled actual cash on the same account basis. Separate timing, amount, missing-event and classification differences. Preserve the earlier forecast so changes remain explainable. Roll the horizon forward. Update the remaining 13 weeks with outstanding receipts, actual supplier terms, payroll and tax dates, committed spending and documented funding conditions. Maintain a downside case for delayed collections. A facility limit is not the same as funds available at the needed time. Review the drivers. Track overdue receivables, aged stock, near-term obligations, contribution by offer, lowest cash balance and forecast accuracy. Use comparisons consistent with seasonality and scope; avoid inventing a universal reserve, ratio or “safe” number of negative months. Record a decision. Approve the action, owner, deadline and fallback. At the next review, compare the claimed saving or accelerated receipt with what cleared. Use the free 13-week forecast and Excel template for the dated schedule and the actual-to-forecast cutoff example to avoid duplicated events. When growth or pricing is the real problem Suppose a job sells for $500 but its relevant product, delivery, fees and acquisition costs total $520. The contribution is −$20 before monthly overhead. Ten extra jobs add $200 to that shortfall even if customers eventually pay in full. Faster collection changes timing; it does not make the job contribution positive. Recheck the cost scope, price and capacity before scaling the offer. A positive-contribution offer can still require funding when inventory and labor are paid before customers settle. Test deposits, milestones and order staging against customer acceptance, refund obligations and delivery capacity. A deposit can improve near-term cash but creates work or refund obligations; it is not automatically earned revenue. The contribution-margin guide checks unit economics, while the startup cost calculator combines launch cash, early shortfalls and a separately chosen reserve. Download the four-week scenario and action record Download the cash-flow recovery CSV . It includes the base and revised weekly values, sensitivity results and an action register with evidence and owner fields. It is a values-only teaching record, not a formula workbook. Copy it, replace the dates and amounts, and recalculate each carry-forward. Use the 13-week tool for a longer dated forecast; the four-week example is not a replacement for that owner. Continue with the complete cash-flow statement , the operating cash flow calculation or cash-flow problems and management according to the question you need to answer. Use the completed cash flow statement to explain where actual cash came from. Use operating cash flow to distinguish underlying cash generation from borrowing or asset sales. Keep completed-period reporting separate from the proposed recovery forecast. Evidence and source notes The cause-and-action discussion was checked against the small-business guidance published by QuickBooks and Xero . Their recurring themes include collections, margins, inventory, growth and forecast discipline. The weekly scenario, floor choice, calculations, sensitivity tests and action register here are original fictional teaching material. No survey percentage or universal business-failure claim is used. Sources checked October 25, 2026. Measure whether the recovery action actually happened The four-week recovery above works only if the $4,000 customer receipt really moves to week two and the $4,000 equipment payment really moves to week three. A task marked “followed up” is not the same evidence as a cleared receipt or agreed payment change. Record a named owner, deadline, expected cash-date effect and the source record for each action. Action control for the existing four-week teaching case Control point Expected evidence Forecast response Before week-two payroll Customer confirms $4,000 payment date Keep receipt uncertain until evidence supports it Before the equipment due date Supplier agreement and delivery consequences Move payment only if the change is feasible and agreed Bank reconciliation after week two Actual receipt and payment entries Replace estimates with actuals and explain variances If either action fails Fallback amount and availability date Re-test the $1,000 floor shortfall shown above The $1,000 is the shortfall to the chosen $3,000 floor when only one action succeeds; it is not automatically a borrowing request. Funding that arrives after the affected payment date does not fix that date’s gap. Keep loan approval, cash receipt and subsequent repayment separate. Distinguish a delayed receipt from a lost receipt If the accelerated $4,000 merely returns to week three, total four-week receipts remain $32,000 and final cash remains $7,000 under the original timings. If it is instead never collected within the four-week horizon, receipts fall to $28,000 and final cash falls to $3,000 with other totals unchanged. The first issue is timing; the second changes the horizon total and may also require a collectability assessment. Do not call both events the same variance. Roll the plan weekly, archive the forecast version and record actual-versus-forecast differences by amount and date. Use the 13-week forecast review method for a practical rolling example and the cash-flow statement to reconcile completed periods. A forecast action should close a documented gap rather than merely improve a headline month-end balance. Frequently asked questions Can a business have cash flow problems while making a profit? Yes. Profit recognition and cash collection occur at different times. Stock purchases, receivables, capital spending and debt payments can create cash shortfalls even when a period shows profit. What should I do first if cash is short? Reconcile available cash, list imminent obligations and verify expected receipt dates. Calculate the first uncovered payment and assign evidence-based actions with a fallback rather than relying on an unapproved loan or unconfirmed receipt. Does more sales revenue always solve a cash shortage? No. Negative-contribution sales worsen the economic gap, and growth can require inventory or payroll cash before collection. Check price, costs, timing and capacity separately. How much cash reserve should every small business hold? There is no single reserve suited to every business. Choose and document a floor based on actual obligations, volatility and access to funding, then stress-test payment dates. The example’s $3,000 is an assumption, not a benchmark. Can I simply delay supplier, payroll or tax payments? Do not assume a delay is permitted. Check obligations, terms and consequences, discuss feasible changes early and obtain appropriate professional advice when mandatory payments cannot be met. The worked deferral is a discretionary purchase under an explicit feasibility assumption. What evidence shows a cash recovery plan worked? Reconcile the actual bank movement and agreed payment dates against the saved forecast. Separate timing shifts from permanently changed receipt or payment totals and re-test the lowest cash point. documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Operating Expenses: Examples, Formula and COGS Comparison Published October 23, 2026 Updated November 5, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Classify operating expenses, separate COGS and equipment cash, and reconcile a checked expense report to operating income and margin. Operating expenses Financial reporting Cost classification AI-generated editorial illustration of a routine operating-expense review. Operating expenses are the costs of supporting a business's operations under the reporting convention you use. This guide uses OPEX excluding cost of goods sold : selling and administrative expenses are deducted after gross profit. That boundary matters because some reports use “operating costs” more broadly to include both COGS and OPEX. Check the line definitions before comparing amounts. For the original fictional monthly example below, net revenue is $50,000, COGS is $20,000 and OPEX is $18,000. Gross profit is $30,000; operating income is $12,000. The purpose is to classify each amount once and reconcile the result, rather than label every bank payment an expense. These USD figures are invented teaching inputs, not industry averages or tax guidance. Operating expenses formula: define the subtotal first OPEX = gross profit − operating income = net revenue − COGS − operating income. Use the formula only when the income statement has that same boundary. An independently reported operating charge outside your selected OPEX subtotal must be reconciled separately. Reversing a statement is not a substitute for checking its account classifications. In the example, $50,000 − $20,000 − $12,000 = $18,000. Total included operating costs are $38,000: $20,000 COGS plus $18,000 OPEX. Calling the full $38,000 “OPEX” and then subtracting COGS again would reduce operating income to −$8,000 incorrectly. The operating profit margin calculator keeps COGS and OPEX separate in its statement-building mode. Operating expenses list: classify the function and behavior separately The same bill can have different classifications in different businesses. “Direct or indirect,” “COGS or period expense” and “fixed or variable” answer different questions. A factory's building depreciation may enter production cost, while head-office depreciation may be an administrative expense. Neither label proves that the amount is avoidable if one order is lost. Examples to investigate using contracts, account policy and actual use Cost Function in this guide Behavior to verify Office rent Administrative OPEX for this example; production premises may have a different treatment Fixed within the stated lease and capacity range Advertising and marketing Selling OPEX here A committed campaign differs from a per-sale commission Salaries and wages Administrative salaries here; production or delivery labor may be in cost of sales Guaranteed payroll, paid hours and piece rates behave differently Depreciation and amortization Operating allocation included once in the appropriate cost function Method and usage affect behavior; the expense is distinct from asset cash payments Software and communications Administrative OPEX here Base subscription plus per-seat or usage charges can be mixed or stepped Bad-debt expense Often operating in a trading business; follow the actual reporting policy Do not subtract the same loss twice through revenue and expenses Interest and income tax Outside operating income in this nonfinancial business illustration Reconcile separately; specialized businesses can use different presentations See fixed, variable and mixed costs for behavior and COGS calculation for the inventory boundary. This page owns the operating-expense classification task; it does not replace those guides. A checked operating expense report Assume a fictional business records the following six OPEX categories for one month. Administrative payroll is already loaded with the employer costs included in this example. The depreciation line is outside COGS. No category below is added again as another operating charge. Original fictional monthly OPEX schedule, USD Category Amount Administrative payroll 8,000 Office rent 3,000 Marketing 2,500 Software and communications 1,000 Insurance and professional services 1,500 Operating depreciation outside COGS 2,000 Total OPEX excluding COGS 18,000 Reconcile $8,000 + $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,000 + $1,500 + $2,000 = $18,000. Then connect the schedule to the income statement: $50,000 net revenue − $20,000 COGS = $30,000 gross profit; $30,000 − $18,000 = $12,000 operating income. Operating margin is $12,000 ÷ $50,000 × 100 = 24% . A $1,000 non-operating gain is outside this operating subtotal and does not change its margin. COGS, OPEX and capital expenditure: three different boundaries For a reseller, purchasing inventory does not necessarily create COGS immediately: unsold items remain in inventory under the chosen accounting basis. COGS relates to the goods sold during the period. OPEX in this guide is the separate operating-period subtotal. A capitalized equipment purchase creates an asset, with subsequent depreciation recognized over its useful life according to the applicable policy. Suppose the business pays $12,000 for office equipment and recognizes $2,000 depreciation this month under the explicitly assumed schedule. Do not add $12,000 equipment cash and $2,000 depreciation together into this month's OPEX merely because both relate to the same asset. The assumed $2,000 is part of the existing schedule, not an additional charge. Whether a purchase qualifies for capitalization and its actual depreciation schedule require the business's policy and supporting facts. Likewise, a loan principal payment reduces debt; it is not OPEX. Loan interest is a separate non-operating expense in this example. The master budget connects operating results, asset purchases, debt and payment dates. A classification example does not establish a tax deduction or universal filing treatment. Operating expense ratio: name what is in the numerator OPEX ratio excluding COGS = $18,000 ÷ $50,000 = 36%. COGS is 40% of revenue, so the complete reconciliation is 40% COGS + 36% OPEX + 24% operating margin = 100%. A report using all operating costs in its numerator would instead show 76%. Both fractions can be calculated, but calling them the same metric would conceal a different cost scope. The phrase “operating expense margin” is ambiguous. State the numerator instead of inventing a new profitability measure. Real-estate operating-expense ratios can use different income and expense conventions and are outside this trading-business example. At zero revenue the ratio is unavailable; zero revenue does not mean expenses are zero. Compare matching periods and consistent accounts before interpreting an increase. Three scenarios: lower OPEX is not the only route to a better result Independent changes from the original baseline, USD Scenario Revenue COGS OPEX Operating income / margin Baseline 50,000 20,000 18,000 12,000 / 24% More sales, same 40% COGS rate and same OPEX 60,000 24,000 18,000 18,000 / 30% Higher sales but weaker cost control 60,000 27,000 22,000 11,000 / 18.33% Documented $2,000 OPEX reduction, no other change 50,000 20,000 16,000 14,000 / 28% The first growth case assumes existing capacity supports the sales. The second earns less operating income despite higher revenue. The cost-reduction case holds sales and quality unchanged solely to isolate the arithmetic. It is not proof that cutting support causes no lost customers or future repairs. Test the operational consequence before accepting the projected saving. A reclassification can change gross margin without changing operating income Move $2,000 of a correctly identified operating cost from OPEX to COGS in a comparison with otherwise identical totals. COGS becomes $22,000, OPEX $16,000 and gross profit $28,000. Operating income remains $12,000 and operating margin stays 24%. Gross margin changes from 60% to 56%; the OPEX ratio changes from 36% to 32%. The business has not saved $2,000. Document justified policy changes and restate comparisons where appropriate. This is why a low OPEX ratio alone does not establish efficiency. Review the cost boundary, recognition period and actual work performed. Do not move expenses between accounts simply to display a preferred ratio. Close the expense schedule before changing the budget Match accounts to a documented COGS/OPEX/non-operating/capital classification. Check unpaid accrued services, prepayments and credits against the reporting period. Reconcile each schedule category to its supporting ledger and total the selected accounts. Check depreciation appears once and inventory cash payments are not substituted for COGS. Compare the approved budget with actual expenses at a suitable activity level. Record explanations and an owner for justified corrective actions. For an operating expense budget, forecast the actual drivers and commitments rather than applying the same sales growth rate to every category. The flexible-budget guide distinguishes activity effects from spending differences. Use the operating-margin calculator to test the reconciled statement and the contribution statement when the question is fixed versus variable recovery. Use the editable expense-classification schedule Download the expense-classification CSV . It contains the six fictional category amounts, reporting function, cost-behavior notes and evidence fields. It is an editable record schedule, not a formula workbook or automated accounting classifier. Replace the example amounts, document the period and classifications, then reconcile the total yourself or use the calculator. Preserve evidence of any split between production and administrative functions. Method and sources The SEC financial-statements introduction explains income-statement and cash-flow distinctions. The SEC income-statement building blocks explains depreciation. Cost-behavior definitions are supported by OpenStax . Figures, schedules and scenarios here are original illustrations; they are not copied company results. Reconcile operating expenses to cash paid Recognized expense is not automatically the cash paid in the same period. The direct operating cash example derives supplier, payroll and prepayment cash from supporting balances. Use the cash flow statement to keep equipment cash and loan principal in their stated separate activity categories. Is payroll an operating expense or part of COGS? Classify payroll by the work and the reporting policy, not simply by the fact that an employee was paid. Under this article’s separate COGS/OPEX convention, directly attributable production payroll may enter inventory or COGS, while administrative payroll belongs in the separate OPEX subtotal. The applicable accounting basis and actual duties determine the treatment. In an independent illustration, a $12,000 payroll consists of $9,000 production work and $3,000 administration. Allocate those amounts once according to the documented basis; do not put the entire $12,000 into OPEX and then add $9,000 again to COGS. This separate classification example does not change the $18,000 OPEX schedule above. Payment dates also do not determine the recognition period: reconcile unpaid payroll and accruals using the operating-cash reconciliation . Frequently asked questions Is COGS an operating expense? In a broad operating-cost total it can be included. This guide uses OPEX excluding COGS and subtracts those two subtotals once each. Follow the actual statement labels. Is depreciation an operating expense? Operating depreciation belongs in the appropriate operating cost function. It may already be included in COGS; do not add it again as administrative OPEX. Are interest and income tax operating expenses? They are outside operating income in this nonfinancial-business illustration. Specialized reporting can differ, so check the actual presentation. Are restructuring costs always non-operating? No. An unusual or infrequent cost is not automatically outside operations. Check its nature and the applicable presentation; this calculator does not create an adjusted earnings figure. Is rent fixed or an operating expense? Those labels describe different dimensions. Office rent is administrative OPEX in the example and fixed within its lease range; production rent may be in manufacturing cost. What about bad debt and SG&A? SG&A is generally an operating-period subtotal under this presentation. Bad-debt treatment depends on the business and reporting policy; avoid deducting the same effect in both net revenue and expenses. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Rolling Forecast: How to Build a 12-Month Plan Published October 23, 2026 Updated November 5, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a rolling forecast with dated monthly assumptions, a worked service-business example and a free Excel template. Keep forecasts separate from the budget. Forecasting Budgeting Business planning What is a rolling forecast? A rolling forecast updates future assumptions and adds a new end period after a period closes. A rolling 12-month forecast after March covers April through the following March. Keep the original budget and archived prior forecasts for comparison. Download the rolling forecast Excel workbook or inspect the worked example . Conceptual illustration of updating a rolling 12-month plan; the display is not a screenshot of the downloadable workbook. A rolling forecast maintains a forward planning window as time passes. After a month closes, record its actual results, update the remaining assumptions and add a new future month. A 12-month horizon therefore stays 12 months long instead of shrinking toward December. Its practical value is a current view of what the business expects next. Keep the approved budget available for accountability and preserve earlier forecast versions for learning. Rewriting an old forecast after seeing the actual result removes the evidence needed to improve forecast accuracy. Download a dated rolling forecast template Download the rolling forecast Excel workbook The editable XLSX contains one operating forecast and a dated input schedule. It forecasts completed jobs, net price, variable cost and fixed operating expenses for the 12 months after the last closed month. A fictional service example is included. It does not model receivables, tax, debt, inventory, cash balances or a full three-statement forecast. The workbook retrieves drivers by absolute month. It does not simply move date headers over stationary assumptions. Rolling forecast versus annual budget and flexible budget Three planning questions, three different comparisons Method Question What changes Original annual budget What did we approve before the year? Keep the approved version for comparison. Rolling forecast What do we now expect over the next fixed-length window? Update future assumptions and add the new end month. Flexible budget What would original rates imply at actual activity? Use actual activity with original budget rates. For example, a January–December annual budget still measures that calendar year in September. A rolling 12-month forecast prepared after September closes normally covers October through the following September. A latest estimate for January–December, containing nine months of actuals and three months of forecast, is a useful annual view, but its future window is only three months. Compare recorded results with the original plan in the budget vs actual Excel template . Investigate activity and same-activity performance in the flexible budget guide . Neither comparison is replaced by a fresh forecast. Worked example: refresh the forecast after March Assume a fictional service firm originally expects 100 comparable jobs each month at $200 net revenue per completed job. Variable operating inputs are $80 per job and fixed operating expenses are $9,000 per month. The example excludes interest, tax, depreciation and owner distributions. Any owner salary included in actual operations must appear once in the relevant expense boundary. Under those assumptions, monthly revenue is $20,000, variable expense is $8,000 and contribution is $12,000. Operating result is $3,000. Twelve identical months would produce $240,000 revenue and $36,000 operating result; a flat pattern is an illustration rather than evidence that demand or seasonality will behave that way. March closes at $18,000 revenue and $17,000 included operating expenses, giving $1,000 operating result. Review the completed jobs, realized prices and invoices before changing expectations. For April, management now assumes 90 jobs at $205, with $85 variable cost per job and the same $9,000 fixed commitment. May through the following March remain at the original monthly assumptions in this miniature example. April refresh: original assumptions versus current forecast, USD Line Original April Updated April Difference Completed jobs 100 90 −10 jobs Net price / job 200 205 +5 Variable cost / job 80 85 +5 Revenue 20,000 18,450 −1,550 Variable expense 8,000 7,650 −350 Contribution 12,000 10,800 −1,200 Fixed operating expense 9,000 9,000 0 Operating result 3,000 1,800 −1,200 The calculation is 90 × $205 = $18,450 revenue; 90 × $85 = $7,650 variable expense; $18,450 − $7,650 − $9,000 = $1,800 operating result. Lower total variable expense accompanies fewer jobs, even though variable cost per job increases. Treating the $350 total reduction as demonstrated efficiency would miss that change. Explain the $1,200 change with the actual drivers Start from the original $3,000 operating result. Ten fewer jobs at the original $120 contribution per job reduce the result by $1,200. The $5 price increase across 90 forecast jobs adds $450. The $5 increase in variable cost across those same 90 jobs subtracts $450. Fixed expenses do not change. The bridge is $3,000 − $1,200 + $450 − $450 = $1,800. This ordering keeps the effects additive and uses forecast volume for the two rate changes. That bridge explains a change between two forecast assumptions. It is not a realized price or efficiency variance and should not be presented as a customer outcome. Record the evidence behind each revised driver before deciding that its new value is more reliable. With April at $1,800 and the next eleven months at $3,000, the forward 12-month operating result is $34,800. Forward revenue is $238,450. The $1,200 reduction from the prior flat expectation belongs to the April assumption changes. March actual result stays in the dated history and is not added to this April–March future total. How to build and refresh a rolling forecast Define the decision and horizon. Choose the months needed for staffing, pricing or funding decisions. This file uses monthly operating results over 12 future months. Close the period. Reconcile actuals to the same expense and revenue definitions used in the model. Keep actuals in dated rows. Archive the previous version. Save its as-of date, assumptions and expected result before changing anything. Review the drivers. Update completed jobs, net price, variable cost and fixed commitments with operational evidence. Do not apply the same growth rate to every row without justification. Advance the cutoff. Change Last closed month to a date within the month just closed. The next 12 calendar months become the forward window. Add the new end-month inputs. Match each driver row to its absolute month. Review all months still in the window, including renewals and seasonal changes. Check constraints. Compare required worker-hours with realistic capacity, and separately check sales demand and collection timing. Record the reason and action. Explain material changes with an owner, evidence and review date. Decide whether to adjust price, scheduling, commitments or cash plans. Using this workbook without losing date alignment The dated schedule initially covers January 2026 through June 2027. Future assumptions are editable yellow cells. Historical actual revenue and expenses occupy separate columns in the same dated schedule. Forecast output retrieves a driver's row by matching its month, so advancing the cutoff from March to April makes the output begin in May and preserves April's drivers in April's input row. The example's last closed month is March 2026. Its update date is an editable example date, not the file's publication date. Adapt the schedule dates and as-of date to your own reporting cycle before using it. The template does not automatically copy forecast values into actuals or declare a period closed. Before the window extends beyond June 2027, add the necessary dated input rows and extend the formulas' referenced ranges. Otherwise the report explicitly returns Missing / duplicate month or Incomplete. Changing only the visible dates does not supply new drivers. Keep each month unique and enter all four driver fields, including explicit zero where it is a valid assumption. In the dated input schedule, store each month as its first calendar day, such as April 1, 2026. Apply a month display format rather than typing a text label such as “Apr-26.” The cutoff accepts a spreadsheet date within the last closed month. A text or missing cutoff leaves the forecast incomplete. A duplicated month is also incomplete: the model must not silently choose one of two competing driver rows. These files use common spreadsheet formulas, but native Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets behavior has not been independently certified. Check April revenue of $18,450, April operating result of $1,800 and the forward result of $34,800 after opening or importing the example. Archive a copy before testing a later cutoff. What changes in a quarterly rolling forecast? A four-quarter forecast drops the closed quarter and adds a new quarter at the far end. A monthly model can still support a quarterly management review: group three correctly dated months into each quarter and refresh their drivers together. This workbook presents monthly results; it does not include an automatic quarterly output. Define whether the horizon means four future quarters or the current partly completed quarter plus future quarters. Those boundaries produce different windows. For a seasonal business, retain month-level assumptions even when the board receives quarterly totals, because three equal months may hide a concentrated payroll or demand pattern. Benefits, workload and limits A regularly refreshed view can expose a future shortfall earlier, connect hiring to expected work and keep planning relevant across a year-end. Those benefits depend on disciplined source data and useful assumptions. Updating a spreadsheet more often does not independently make uncertain customer demand accurate. Use a manageable set of drivers and assign an owner to each material assumption. Frequent refreshes create work, and constant revisions can blur performance accountability if budgets and forecasts are mixed. Preserve the budget, explain changes and review prior forecast errors at the same lead time rather than selecting whichever version looks best after the fact. For the service example, 90 jobs at two delivery hours require 180 hours. If practical delivery capacity is 160 hours, the forecast needs a feasible staffing, scheduling or scope change. Expected revenue is also different from cash collected. Translate collection delays and supplier-payment dates into the 13-week cash-flow forecast before treating operating profit as available bank cash. A short monthly forecast review Ask four questions: What actually closed? Which future assumption changed? Which constraint or cash date matters? What decision follows? Keep the reconciliation and next action beside the model. A forecast that shows a gap but assigns no response is an incomplete planning process. For error review, compare an archived one-month-ahead forecast with the matching month's actual result. Record amount differences and the drivers behind them. Avoid percentage accuracy measures with zero actuals unless you define a suitable alternative; do not quietly count an unavailable percentage as perfect accuracy. Method and further reading The workbook, service assumptions, calculation bridge and workflow are original MyBreakeven examples. ACCA's rolling-budget discussion supports the fixed-horizon distinction and describes the extra maintenance involved. OpenStax explains the different purpose of a flexible budget . For a wider set of connected schedules, see our master budget example . Build the sales-demand evidence before changing the rolling forecast Use the small-business sales forecast to document unit demand, net prices and practical delivery capacity before revising the dated driver rows. Keep the original forecast version, the new assumption and its evidence separate. The existing workbook still owns the rolling cutoff and month matching; the sales-demand guide supplies assumptions rather than replacing that logic. Frequently asked questions Does a rolling forecast replace the annual budget? It can be used alongside the approved annual budget. The budget preserves the agreed target; the rolling forecast records current future expectations. How often should I update it? Use a cadence that matches the decision and data quality. This example refreshes monthly after the actual period closes. A quarterly review may be sufficient for a different business. Is this a rolling cash-flow forecast? This template forecasts operating revenue and included expenses. It does not model collection dates, financing or closing cash. Use a dated cash-flow schedule for those tasks. Can I change the dates for a new year? Update the absolute dated input schedule and its referenced ranges, then set the last closed month. Do not move date headings over unchanged input positions. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Master Budget: Components, Worked Example and Cash Bridge Published October 22, 2026 Updated October 23, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . See master budget components, a worked income and balance-sheet example, and a cash budget bridge. Use the calculator and editable CSV with clear assumptions. Budgeting Cost accounting Worked example Master budget: the connected plan A master budget coordinates sales, resources, operating income, cash timing and the projected financial position. In the fictional service example below, $6,000 operating income leaves $3,800 closing cash before financing, a $200 gap to the stated cash floor. The calculator shows this limited operating-to-cash bridge, not a complete master budget. Operating budget to cash bridge A simplified one-period service-business worksheet within a master budget. This is not a complete manufacturing master budget or balance sheet. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Planned equivalent jobs Expected completed jobs recognized as sales in the planned period. Net sales price per job Exclude collected sales tax; use one currency. Variable operating cost per job Assumed paid in this period with no inventory or payable timing. Fixed cash operating costs Assumed expensed and paid now; excludes depreciation, interest, tax and owner distributions. Opening available cash Before the receipts and payments below. Current sales collected this period (%) 0–100; the rest of current sales remains uncollected. Collections from opening receivables Cash collected from earlier sales, excluded from current sales revenue. Other cash payments Debt principal, tax or distributions outside the operating result; count once. Equipment / capital cash payments Excluded from this simplified operating expense result. Minimum desired closing cash A planning floor; the gap is not an approved credit facility. Reset fictional example Currency changes labels only; it does not convert amounts. All defaults are fictional USD examples. Inputs stay in this browser. One-period reconciliation Budgeted net sales USD 36,000.00 Variable operating expenses USD 16,000.00 Contribution USD 20,000.00 Operating income USD 6,000.00 Total cash receipts USD 31,800.00 Total cash payments USD 33,000.00 Closing cash before financing USD 3,800.00 Gap to desired cash floor USD 200.00 Current sales collections: USD 28,800.00 . Current sales still uncollected: USD 7,200.00 . Opening-receivable collections belong in cash receipts once, not current sales. Defaults produce $6,000 operating income but only $3,800 closing cash, a $200 gap to the $4,000 floor. The model assumes all variable and fixed operating expenses are cash-paid in this period and no inventory changes. It omits depreciation, opening unpaid bills, financing proceeds/interest and a full budgeted balance sheet. Use separate schedules when those exist. A collection delay changes cash without automatically changing earned revenue. This worksheet does not forecast demand, certify capacity or approve borrowing. Illustrative editorial scene. All numerical business examples use fictional USD assumptions. A master budget is the coordinated set of operating and financial schedules used to plan one business period. It connects expected sales, required resources, planned income, cash timing and the projected financial position. A single expense list is only one piece. For an owner, the practical question is whether the same plan works in three places: the sales diary, the delivery schedule and the bank account. A profitable plan can still need funding before customers pay. Start with a shared set of assumptions and make every schedule use the same dates, currency and business boundary. What belongs in a master budget? The operating side plans sales and the costs of delivering them. The financial side plans collections, payments, capital spending, financing and the resulting balance sheet. Inventory businesses need additional schedules that a simple service company may not use. The following is a working checklist, not permission to omit a schedule that matters to your business. Master budget components and their dependencies Schedule What it establishes Feeds into Sales budget Expected units, mix and net selling prices Delivery or production, collections and income Production / delivery plan Required output and staffing; inventory changes if applicable Materials, labor and overhead Materials, labor and overhead budgets Resource quantities, rates and period commitments Product cost, operating income and payments Selling and administration Operating expense assumptions and noncash items Income and cash-payment schedules Budgeted income statement Revenue and expenses on the stated accounting basis Profit plan and balance-sheet bridge Collections and cash payments When money is expected to move Cash budget Capital expenditure and financing Equipment payments, borrowing, repayments and interest Cash budget and projected balance sheet Budgeted balance sheet Expected assets, liabilities and equity Final consistency check The usual starting point: the sales budget Expected sales normally drive the initial operating schedules. Record quantity and net price by offer rather than applying one growth percentage to every expense. Then check whether delivery capacity, materials, customer demand and credit terms support the proposal. A sales target remains an assumption until supported by evidence. For example, a fictional service company plans 200 equivalent visits at $180, giving $36,000 net sales. Each visit requires $80 of variable operating inputs, and monthly fixed cash operating costs are $14,000. The unit is a completed comparable visit, not an inquiry, invoice line or unpaid quotation. Combining different services requires separate unit economics and a realistic sales mix . Master budget example: service operating schedules The miniature example below assumes no inventory, no depreciation and all included operating expenses paid in the same month. Its deliberately narrow assumptions make the profit-to-cash bridge visible; it is not a complete set of financial statements. Fictional service operating plan Line Working USD Net sales 200 × 180 36,000 Variable operating expenses 200 × 80 16,000 Contribution 36,000 − 16,000 20,000 Fixed cash operating expenses Period commitments 14,000 Operating income 20,000 − 14,000 6,000 Suppose delivery takes 1.5 paid hours per visit. The plan requires 300 delivery hours, plus time outside that task boundary. A $32 loaded delivery rate would consume $9,600 of the $16,000 variable budget only if those hours and costs actually vary with visits. Do not add that $9,600 again on top of the $80 per visit if it is already included. Use the direct-labor budget boundary to distinguish job hours from a full annual hiring cost. The planned contribution of $100 per visit covers $14,000 at 140 visits, under unchanged assumptions. That break-even check tests the operating target, while the delivery-hours check tests a different constraint. Neither proves that 200 customers will book. Keep the contribution format linked to the same expense list so a wage or subscription is not counted twice. Why $6,000 profit can leave a cash gap Opening cash is $5,000. The company collects 80% of current sales, or $28,800, and $3,000 from opening receivables. It pays the $30,000 operating expenses above, $1,000 of other cash obligations outside this operating result and $2,000 for equipment. The $1,000 could include a debt-principal payment; it is explicitly not another operating expense in this example. Same plan: cash before financing Line USD Opening cash 5,000 Current sales collected 28,800 Opening receivables collected 3,000 Total cash available 36,800 Operating cash payments 30,000 Other cash payments 1,000 Capital expenditure 2,000 Closing cash before financing 3,800 Desired minimum cash 4,000 Gap to minimum 200 The uncollected $7,200 of current sales remains outside this month's receipts. Opening receivable collections are cash now but not new sales now. A $2,000 equipment purchase uses cash without automatically becoming a $2,000 operating expense. If depreciation exists, include its appropriate income effect and exclude it from cash payments; the small worksheet above intentionally does not model that additional schedule. If current collections fall to 70%, receipts decrease by $3,600. Closing cash becomes $200 while the stated operating income remains $6,000; the cash-floor gap grows to $3,800. This is a timing scenario, not a forecast. A funding gap does not create an approved loan, and borrowed principal does not become sales revenue. Record financing, interest and covenants in a separate schedule. Complete the example with a budgeted balance sheet To extend the same service example, assume opening receivables of $3,000, equipment at a $10,000 carrying amount, debt principal of $6,000 and equity of $12,000, alongside the $5,000 opening cash. For this illustration, the entire $1,000 of other cash payments is debt principal. There are no payables, inventory, depreciation, interest, tax, owner contributions or distributions. Same fictional service example: opening and budgeted closing balances, USD Balance Opening Closing Bridge Cash 5,000 3,800 5,000 + 31,800 receipts − 33,000 payments Accounts receivable 3,000 7,200 3,000 + 36,000 sales − 31,800 collections Equipment, carrying amount 10,000 12,000 10,000 + 2,000 capital purchase; no depreciation assumed Total assets 18,000 23,000 Cash + receivables + equipment Debt principal 6,000 5,000 6,000 − 1,000 principal repayment Equity 12,000 18,000 12,000 + 6,000 operating income under the stated zero-interest/tax assumptions Liabilities plus equity 18,000 23,000 Equals total assets at both dates The $7,200 closing receivable is the uncollected part of current sales, not additional cash. Principal repayment reduces debt, while the equipment payment increases the asset under these assumptions. The balance sheet now agrees with the cash budget and income plan. This is an explanatory extension of the example; the calculator and CSV do not automatically generate these balance-sheet schedules. How manufacturing changes the plan A manufacturer must connect sales to production and inventory. For an independent illustration, planned sales of 500 units, desired ending finished goods of 80 and opening finished goods of 50 require 530 units of production : 500 + 80 − 50. Materials purchases then depend on production requirements and raw-material inventory, not sales alone. Product costs, inventory valuation and payment timing need separate reconciliations. A service-delivery worksheet cannot silently stand in for those inventory schedules. Likewise, a cash budget alone cannot supply a budgeted balance sheet. Start from the opening balances, bridge receivables, inventory, payables, equipment, financing and equity, then check that projected assets equal liabilities plus equity. The complete master-budget checklist above retains that final check even though the embedded tool does not automate it. Prepare, approve and review the plan Choose the period and accountable owner for each assumption. Separate an approved budget from later forecast versions. Build sales quantities and prices, then check resources and the relevant cost range. Prepare the operating schedules and an income statement with all costs accounted for once. Map collections, payments, equipment and financing to actual expected dates. For weekly timing, extend the cash-flow forecast . Complete the projected balance-sheet bridge and reconcile cash to the cash budget. Keep the approved starting plan. Use a flexible budget at actual activity to distinguish activity changes from same-activity performance. A master budget coordinates the plan before the period. A flexible budget recalculates allowed revenue and cost at another activity level. A rolling forecast updates expectations. Do not overwrite the original target and then call the revised plan a favorable variance. Download the editable operating-to-cash bridge Download the formula-based operating-to-cash bridge CSV . Import into Excel or Google Sheets, replace the labeled input rows and recalculate. Incomplete, nonnumeric or invalid inputs leave results blank. This file follows the same fictional example and stated scope as the calculator; a CSV cannot preserve spreadsheet styling. Check the imported sheet: keep the row positions and formulas in column B unchanged. Enter the collection percentage as 80, not 0.8. The default results should show $6,000 operating income, $3,800 closing cash and a $200 cash-floor gap. If an input is missing, the status requests numeric inputs and calculated results remain blank; an explicit zero is a valid entry where the input permits it. Build a delivery and labor schedule behind the sales target The existing 200-visit plan has $80 of variable inputs per visit. To make that assumption operational, suppose each comparable visit needs 1.5 paid delivery hours at $24 and $44 of other variable inputs. This is an original breakdown of the same illustrative $80, not an additional expense: $36 labor + $44 other inputs = $80. The period requires 300 delivery hours, $7,200 variable labor and $8,800 other variable inputs. Together they reproduce the original $16,000 variable expense. Check the available delivery hours before accepting the sales plan. If only 280 hours can be used under the same service standard, capacity is 280 ÷ 1.5 = 186.6667 equivalent visits, or 186 complete visits if partial jobs cannot be sold. The original 200 visits require 20 more delivery hours. Do not quietly assume those hours are available at the original $24 rate: overtime, subcontracting, scheduling changes or an additional employee can change both costs and feasibility. Capacity is a ceiling under the assumptions, not a forecast of demand. Supporting schedule for the original fictional monthly service plan Schedule line Working Budget Net sales 200 visits × $180 $36,000 Paid delivery hours 200 × 1.5 hours 300 hours Variable delivery labor 300 hours × $24 $7,200 Other variable inputs 200 visits × $44 $8,800 Operating income $36,000 − $7,200 − $8,800 − $14,000 $6,000 This labor breakdown assumes hours and their payments genuinely vary with visits. A guaranteed monthly payroll cannot be charged here and again inside the $14,000 fixed commitment. Review paid non-delivery time, employer costs and owner delivery work explicitly. The cost-behavior guide owns that classification question; this schedule shows how the agreed classifications feed the master plan. What if current-month collections fall from 80% to 60%? Keep the original sales, expenses, opening balances, equipment purchase and debt repayment unchanged. At 60% current-period collection, current receipts fall to $21,600. Adding the same $3,000 collection of opening receivables gives $24,600 total receipts. Closing cash becomes $5,000 + $24,600 − $33,000 = −$3,400 before financing . Meeting a $4,000 minimum cash floor would require $7,400 of additional funding or other justified cash changes. Operating income stays $6,000 because this scenario changes collection timing, not recognized sales or expenses. Closing receivables rise to $14,400: $3,000 opening + $36,000 sales − $24,600 collections. Relative to the 80% case, cash is $7,200 lower and receivables are $7,200 higher. The negative cash figure is a funding requirement in a planning schedule, not a claim that a bank will permit an overdraft. If a new $7,400 borrowing is explicitly approved and received in the period, closing cash becomes $4,000 and closing debt becomes $12,400: original $6,000 debt − $1,000 principal paid + $7,400 new borrowing. With $14,400 receivables and $12,000 equipment, assets total $30,400; $12,400 debt plus $18,000 equity also totals $30,400. This simplified extension still excludes interest and fees. Add their actual terms before treating a financing proposal as complete. Never force a balance-sheet tie by entering an unexplained cash plug. Use a handoff check between schedules Match the sales schedule's revenue to the income budget and its collection basis to the cash budget. Match labor hours to the delivery schedule, and labor cost to the correct wage and employer-cost scope. Match the cash budget's equipment payments to additions in the asset schedule, and principal payments to debt rather than operating expense. Each handoff should name its source assumption and period. The existing calculator and downloadable cash bridge can reproduce the 60% scenario by changing the collection input to 60. They do not calculate the new borrowing or extended balance sheet automatically. Keep those supporting schedules separately. Use the rolling forecast for updated forward expectations and flexible budgeting for the same-activity performance review after the period closes. Preserve the approved master-budget baseline. Method and sources OpenStax explains the relationship among operating budgets and the financial-budget schedules . This guide's scenarios, figures, tables and simplified calculator are original fictional illustrations. Frequently asked questions What is a master budget? A coordinated set of operating and financial budgets for a period, connecting sales, resources, income, cash and projected financial position. What is normally prepared first? The sales budget usually provides the starting activity and revenue assumptions. Resource constraints and financing can require revisions. Is a cash budget the whole master budget? No. Cash timing is one financial schedule; operating budgets and a projected balance sheet also matter. Does the calculator build a complete master budget? No. It is a simplified service operating-to-cash bridge with no inventory, depreciation, financing model or full balance sheet. How does a master budget differ from a flexible budget? The master budget coordinates the period plan; a flexible budget recalculates expected results at a changed activity level. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
