documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cost Drivers: Business Examples and Allocation Calculator Published October 22, 2026 Updated November 6, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Understand cost drivers with business examples, the allocation formula and a two-pool calculator. Compare bases without treating allocations as savings. Budgeting Cost accounting Worked example Cost drivers: activity and allocation A cost driver is an activity or condition associated with resource use; a measurable driver can also be the base for assigning a defined cost pool. The two-pool example assigns $600 of scheduling support and $150 of order administration to one job, totaling $750. An allocated share is not automatically an avoidable cash cost. Two-pool cost driver allocation calculator Allocate two distinct cost pools to one job using consistent, same-period activity denominators. Selecting a driver requires evidence before doing the arithmetic. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Pool A: scheduling support cost A distinct pool; exclude anything already traced directly or in Pool B. Pool A total driver quantity Default: 200 delivery hours across all jobs. Must be positive. Job share of Pool A driver Default: 20 of the same delivery hours. Cannot exceed total. Pool B: order administration cost A second distinct pool; default $3,000. Pool B total driver quantity Default: 100 orders in the same period. Must be positive. Job share of Pool B driver Default: 5 of those orders. Cannot exceed total. Reset fictional example Currency changes labels only; it does not convert amounts. All defaults are fictional USD examples. Inputs stay in this browser. Allocation, not avoidable savings Pool A rate: 30 USD per driver unit. Pool B rate: 30 USD per driver unit. Pool A allocated to this job USD 600.00 Pool B allocated to this job USD 150.00 Total allocated cost USD 750.00 Pool cost assigned to other activity USD 8,250.00 Defaults: $6,000 ÷ 200 hours × 20 hours = $600; $3,000 ÷ 100 orders × 5 orders = $150. This job receives $750, leaving $8,250 across other activity. Assigning all jobs with the same bases should reconcile to the $9,000 pool total before rounding. Do not interpret an allocated fixed cost as a saving if this job disappears. A budgeted-capacity denominator can leave idle-capacity cost separately; this widget instead assumes total observed or planned allocable activity for the same period. It does not estimate causal relationships or calculate department step-down allocations. Illustrative editorial scene. All numerical business examples use fictional USD assumptions. A cost driver is an activity or condition associated with resources being consumed and costs being incurred. In accounting, a driver can also be the measurable base used to assign an activity's cost to jobs, customers or products. A useful allocation base should reflect how the underlying work uses resources; an easy-to-count number is not enough by itself. For a small business, this helps answer why two customers with similar revenue consume different amounts of support. Delivery hours, number of orders, visits, setups and inspections can each explain different activities. The goal is a clearer decision, not a more complicated spreadsheet for its own sake. Cost drivers in business: choose the activity first Candidate drivers to investigate, not universal rules Activity / pool Possible driver What to verify Scheduling support Delivery hours or number of scheduled visits Does complexity or travel explain more work than hours alone? Order administration Orders processed Are bulk and custom orders equally demanding? Equipment running Machine hours Separate standby costs from usage and maintenance steps Batch preparation Number of setups Check whether setup duration differs materially Quality checks Inspections or inspection hours Match effort to the type and depth of checks Premises support Floor area for a space-related pool Allocation does not make the rent avoidable Start with the task, identify the resources it consumes, then choose a measurable activity unit. One business may need order counts for administration and labor hours for delivery support. Combining both costs into one revenue-based rate can hide differences between customers. A sales-dollar base may sometimes be practical, but demonstrate why it represents resource use rather than choosing it automatically. A driver does not make every cost variable Suppose a dispatcher has a $6,000 monthly commitment while delivery activity varies from 180 to 220 hours. Assigning that commitment using hours does not imply that the bill falls when one hour disappears. Within that staffing range, the total may stay fixed. At a larger volume, another shift could create a step cost. Distinguish the behavior of the bill from the rule used to distribute it. A cost object is what you want to measure: a job, product, customer or branch. A cost pool collects a defined group of costs. The driver is the measured activity used for that pool. A cost rate connects them: pool cost ÷ total driver quantity . The assigned amount is the rate times the cost object's driver usage. The units must cancel correctly: dollars per hour times hours gives dollars. Cost object, cost pool and cost driver: three different questions Use a cost object, pool and driver from the same defined period Term Question it answers Example Cost object Whose cost are we measuring? One identified customer's job Cost pool Which support costs are grouped? $6,000 monthly scheduling support Cost driver / allocation base Which measured activity assigns that pool? Delivery hours, if records support that choice Activity rate How much is assigned per driver unit? $6,000 ÷ 200 hours = $30/hour A job's 20 delivery hours are its usage, not the denominator for the whole pool. Using $6,000 ÷ 20 would assign the entire pool to that job. At $30/hour, its assigned scheduling support is $600. Keep order counts in their own pool: hours and orders cannot be added into one denominator. Worked example: two pools, one customer job A fictional service business tracks two separate monthly support pools. Scheduling costs $6,000, allocated over 200 delivery hours. Order administration costs $3,000, allocated over 100 orders. One customer's work uses 20 of those hours and five of those orders. Neither pool includes directly traced job materials or labor, and no cost appears in both pools. Two activity pools assigned to one job Pool Rate Job usage Assigned cost Scheduling $6,000 ÷ 200 = $30/hour 20 hours $600 Order administration $3,000 ÷ 100 = $30/order 5 orders $150 Total Two separate activity bases Do not add hours to orders $750 The remaining $8,250 belongs to other activity under this allocation convention. If all jobs' usage adds to 200 hours and 100 orders, their unrounded allocations should total $9,000. Calculate with unrounded rates and round displayed currency at the end. A reconciliation difference can indicate missing activity, a duplicated expense, an inconsistent date range or premature rounding. Imagine a second customer also has $10,000 revenue but uses only ten hours and two orders. The same rates assign $300 + $60 = $360. Charging both customers an identical revenue share would erase this $390 difference. That observation supports an investigation of support work; it does not establish which customer is more profitable without their direct costs and other relevant commitments. How to select and test a driver Define a pool with one coherent resource story and one reporting period. Keep direct costs outside it if already charged to jobs. List candidate activities from operational records. Check whether the data are complete and collected consistently. Inspect jobs with unusually high or low costs. Ask whether volume, complexity, rush work or setup duration explains the difference. Compare candidate allocations with known work patterns. Look for systematic undercharging of difficult jobs, not merely a tidy average. Test several periods and the relevant capacity range. A correlation may reflect a third factor and does not by itself prove causation. Retain a reconciliation and review changes with the people doing the work. Use fewer pools when extra detail does not improve a decision. Do not infer a cost driver from just the highest and lowest invoice. The high-low method estimates a linear cost relationship from two activity observations; it neither proves a causal driver nor supplies a full activity-based costing design. Observed activity versus budgeted capacity The embedded calculator assigns a same-period pool using a total activity quantity that includes the selected job. That is why job usage cannot exceed that total. With $6,000 and 200 observed hours, the rate is $30. If you instead choose 250 practical-capacity hours, the rate becomes $24. At 200 hours of use, only $4,800 is assigned and $1,200 remains as unused-capacity cost under that convention. Those are different denominators answering different questions. Document which one is used. Do not force unused-capacity cost into every remaining job without considering the pricing and capacity decision. A separate job-order cost sheet can apply a predetermined rate; its actual job activity may exceed the budgeted base because that denominator is a plan rather than an observed total. Manufacturing and service boundaries A manufacturing example may assign setup support by setups, equipment support by machine hours and inspection support by inspection effort. These are candidate bases, not claims that every factory uses the same model. Product design, batch size and automation can change the appropriate relationship. A labor-hour rate becomes less informative if most support work follows machines or batches. This small-business guide introduces driver selection and pool arithmetic. It does not implement manufacturing inventory records, joint-product costing, reciprocal service departments or step-down departmental allocations. For a broad accounting query, use the definition and driver tests here; a specialist manufacturing implementation needs additional evidence and a separately designed scope. Using the result without inventing savings If a customer leaves, the $750 assigned amount is not automatically cash saved. The dispatcher may remain employed, software may remain subscribed and space may remain leased. Compare the costs that actually change, the capacity released and any feasible alternative use. The make-or-buy relevant-cost guide separates avoidable costs from common commitments. Use cost allocation alongside client profitability to identify service patterns and price discussions. For contribution and break-even planning, return to fixed and variable behavior ; transferring a full allocated cost into a variable-cost input can double-count fixed overhead and overstate the volume required. How one rate can shift cost between two jobs Consider an independent fictional month with $6,000 delivery-support cost and $3,000 order-administration cost. Two jobs account for all recorded activity. Job A uses 150 delivery hours and 10 orders; job B uses 50 hours and 90 orders. Totals are 200 hours and 100 orders. Assume the operations records support delivery hours for the first pool and comparable order counts for the second. A single delivery-hour rate assigns the combined $9,000 pool at $45 per hour. A receives $6,750 and B receives $2,250. With separate activity pools, delivery support is $30 per hour and order administration is $30 per order. A receives $4,500 + $300 = $4,800; B receives $1,500 + $2,700 = $4,200. Both methods assign exactly $9,000, but the single rate puts $1,950 more on A and $1,950 less on B than the two-pool model. Independent same-month allocation comparison, USD Cost object One hours-based rate Two supported activity pools Single rate minus two pools Job A 6,750 4,800 +1,950 Job B 2,250 4,200 −1,950 Total 9,000 9,000 0 The comparison shows sensitivity to the assignment rule. It does not prove that $4,800 and $4,200 are exact causal costs. If order handling effort differs greatly, counting orders equally may still hide complexity. Test the records and the purpose of the report before adopting the more detailed method. A neat reconciliation alone cannot establish a good driver. Why the driver can change an account discussion Suppose each job separately has $10,000 net revenue and $4,000 directly traced costs, with no other costs included in this particular report. Under the single rate, A's revenue less traced and assigned costs is −$750 while B's is $3,750. Under two pools, A shows $1,200 and B $1,800. The combined result remains $3,000. Only the distribution changes. A manager looking only at the first report might pressure the labor-heavy account while missing the administrative demands of the order-heavy account. The corrected question is whether the selected activity measures represent support consumption. These report subtotals are not contribution margin or full business profit. Do not classify the $9,000 pool as variable just because it is assigned using activity. For broader account reporting use client profitability ; for a decision about outsourcing use relevant make-or-buy costs . Check the activity records before changing the rate Define whether an order means a customer request, an accepted order or each internal revision. Count cancelled work consistently with the resources it used. Reconcile total job hours with approved records, identify unassigned internal support and make sure a customer is not omitted from the denominator while its costs remain in the pool. If direct support has already been traced to a job, remove the same amount from the shared pool. For the two-job example, all work is assigned by design. In a real report, retain a clearly identified internal or unassigned category when it reflects actual records. Do not silently spread missing activity across paying customers. If the denominator is incomplete, fix or qualify the report rather than treating its inflated rate as evidence that each job became expensive. Refresh the model when the work changes Review a driver when software automates routine orders, inspections become more complex, customer mix changes or a new shift changes staffing commitments. Keep the old and proposed definitions with effective dates. Recalculate the same historical sample under both policies so users can distinguish changed allocation from changed operations. A policy change should not be described as a cash saving without a separate check of the underlying bills. The existing two-pool calculator can reproduce A by entering pools 6,000 and 3,000, totals 200 and 100, and job usage 150 and 10. Change only usage to 50 and 90 for B. Each result is for one selected job; the widget does not retain a multi-job ledger or automate the single-rate comparison. Keep a separate reconciliation of all jobs to the pools. This guide owns driver selection and allocation arithmetic, while job order costing owns how a documented rate enters a job cost sheet. Method and source OpenStax's cost-driver lesson discusses activity measures and cost assignment. The examples and two-pool calculator here are original illustrations, not industry benchmarks or statistically estimated causal models. Keep customer and supplier administration traceable Before creating a new support pool, distinguish routine invoices from disputed or corrected work. The receivable record preserves customer invoice, credit and collection evidence; the payable record preserves supplier matching and approval exceptions. If exception handling consumes materially different effort, investigate measured time rather than assuming every invoice uses equal resources. Those records support a candidate driver; they do not by themselves prove a causal rate or a cash saving. Frequently asked questions What are cost drivers in accounting? Activities or conditions associated with resource use; measurable drivers can also form bases for assigning defined cost pools to jobs, products or customers. Is revenue always a good cost driver? No. Test whether it reflects the activity consuming the resource. Hours, orders, setups or inspections may explain a particular pool better. Does an allocated cost disappear when a job stops? Not necessarily. Fixed commitments may remain; check actual avoidability and alternative capacity use separately. Can a cost driver be nonfinancial? Yes. Hours, orders, visits and setups are activity quantities rather than money amounts. Does the tool prove which driver causes cost? No. It performs allocation arithmetic after you choose consistent pools and bases; it does not estimate causality or step-down departmental allocations. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Job Order Costing: Cost Sheet, Example and Calculator Published October 22, 2026 Updated November 6, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Use the job order costing formula, a worked job cost sheet and calculator. Compare process costing, check applied overhead and download the editable CSV. Budgeting Cost accounting Worked example Job order costing: the cost-sheet formula Assigned job cost equals direct materials plus direct labor plus applied overhead. The worked ten-unit order uses $1,200 materials, $720 labor and $900 applied overhead: $2,820 total, or $282 per equivalent unit. Its $180 revenue surplus is before excluded period costs and is not contribution margin. Job order cost sheet calculator Add direct materials, traced labor and applied overhead for one identifiable job. Keep the overhead base consistent with its budgeted rate. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Direct materials for this job Net issued materials after returns; excludes materials in the overhead pool. Direct labor hours for this job Approved time records traced to this job. Direct labor cost per hour Consistent burden boundary; do not also include the same burden in overhead. Budgeted overhead pool Default $6,000 for the period, not the actual job overhead bill. Budgeted total overhead-base quantity Default 200 direct labor hours. Must be positive and use the same base as job usage. Actual job overhead-base usage Default 30 direct labor hours; this may differ from the budgeted total. Completed equivalent units in this job Must be positive. Per-unit cost is meaningful only for comparable units. Job net revenue for comparison Exclude collected sales tax; zero makes the margin percentage undefined. Reset fictional example Currency changes labels only; it does not convert amounts. All defaults are fictional USD examples. Inputs stay in this browser. Applied-cost job result Predetermined overhead rate: 30 USD per overhead-base unit. Direct labor USD 720.00 Applied overhead USD 900.00 Total assigned job cost USD 2,820.00 Assigned cost per equivalent unit USD 282.00 Revenue minus assigned job cost USD 180.00 Assigned-cost margin 6% Defaults: $1,200 materials + 30 × $24 labor + 30 × ($6,000 ÷ 200) overhead = $2,820. Ten equivalent units cost $282 each. Revenue $3,000 leaves $180, or 6%, before excluded selling, administration, financing and tax items. Applied overhead can differ from actual overhead. Reconcile the period’s total applied cost to actual overhead separately. This is not a general ledger, inventory valuation certification, contribution-margin result or proof of avoidable cost. Output above planned activity does not automatically change the budgeted rate; review the relevant range. Illustrative editorial scene. All numerical business examples use fictional USD assumptions. Job order costing accumulates costs for an identifiable order, project or batch. It suits work where the job's materials, labor and support effort can be distinguished. A custom sign, installation project or client engagement can have its own cost sheet instead of receiving the average cost of every order. For an owner, the sheet should explain what the job consumed and which overhead was assigned. It should also preserve the difference between an estimate used for a quotation and costs recorded as work happens. A quoted price alone does not show whether the job used more labor than expected. What goes on a job cost sheet? Identify the job, customer, scope, dates and output unit first. Record direct materials from issue records, direct labor from approved time records and overhead using a documented allocation rule. Separate traced amounts from estimates. A job sheet can be operationally useful without pretending that every assigned cost is individually avoidable. Job cost sheet: records and boundaries Element Evidence Common mistake Direct materials Net materials issued to the identified job Ignoring returns or charging the same supply through overhead Direct labor Job hours × appropriate labor cost rate Using billed hours instead of worked hours Applied overhead Documented rate × job base usage Treating the assigned amount as the actual overhead invoice Output and revenue Comparable completed units and recognized net revenue Comparing an unfinished job with a completed sale Separate period costs Selling, administration and other excluded costs Calling the job subtotal total business profit Job order costing formula and overhead rate Assigned job cost = direct materials + direct labor + applied overhead. Direct labor is job hours times the selected labor rate. A common predetermined overhead rate is budgeted period overhead divided by the budgeted allocation-base quantity. Applied overhead is that rate times the job's actual base usage. Keep the same unit in numerator interpretation and job usage: a dollars-per-machine-hour rate needs machine hours, not labor dollars. Choose the base because it represents the support activity, then document its limitations. The cost-driver guide shows how different pools can use different bases. A single overhead rate is a simplified policy, not proof that all support costs move with labor hours. Example: a custom order of ten units A fictional studio completes ten comparable custom display units for $3,000 net revenue. Direct materials are $1,200 after returns. Approved job labor is 30 hours at $24 per hour, so labor costs $720. The period's budgeted overhead is $6,000 over 200 direct labor hours, giving a $30-per-hour predetermined rate. The job uses 30 of those base hours, so applied overhead is $900. Original fictional job cost sheet Line Working USD Direct materials Net materials assigned 1,200 Direct labor 30 × 24 720 Applied overhead 30 × (6,000 ÷ 200) 900 Total assigned job cost 1,200 + 720 + 900 2,820 Assigned cost per equivalent unit 2,820 ÷ 10 282 Net job revenue Ten completed units 3,000 Revenue less assigned job cost 3,000 − 2,820 180 The assigned-cost margin is $180 ÷ $3,000 = 6% . That figure is before any selling, administration, financing or tax items excluded from the sheet. It is not the same as contribution margin because applied overhead can include fixed commitments. Do not enter the full $282 assigned unit cost as a variable cost in a break-even calculator and then add the same fixed pool again. For an estimate-versus-actual review, suppose the quote allowed 25 labor hours but approved records show 30. At unchanged $24 labor and $30 applied-overhead rates, five extra hours add $120 of direct labor and $150 of applied overhead, a $270 assigned-cost increase. The underlying $150 does not necessarily represent a new cash payment. Investigate rework, scope changes, travel and rate assumptions separately. Assigned job cost is not contribution margin In this example, $1,200 materials plus $720 traced labor equals $1,920 before assigned overhead. Revenue less those two traced amounts is $1,080. After applying $900 overhead, revenue less assigned job cost is $180. Neither subtotal automatically equals total business profit. If the $1,920 were entirely variable and the $900 represented only a share of unchanged fixed overhead, contribution under those additional assumptions would be $1,080. The sheet alone does not establish those behaviors: direct labor can be a commitment, and an overhead pool can contain variable costs. Classify the underlying bills before using either number in a break-even or make-or-buy decision. Keep selling and administration outside this production-cost sheet while including them in the business's operating result. Job order costing versus process costing Selecting a cost accumulation approach Question Job order Process Where are costs accumulated? Identifiable job, project or batch Process or production department What kind of output fits? Distinct work with traceable requirements Relatively homogeneous flow Typical internal record Job cost sheet Production cost report How is unit cost interpreted? Job total divided by comparable job units Process cost assigned across output, including relevant equivalent-unit treatment A custom batch can still be one job even when it contains multiple units. Conversely, a continuous standard process does not become job costing merely because invoices have order numbers. Some businesses combine approaches. Evaluate how production and services actually happen before selecting the record structure. This guide introduces the distinction; it does not calculate process equivalent units or provide a full process-cost ledger. Where the job appears in manufacturing accounts For a manufacturing business, production costs normally accumulate in work in process while the job is incomplete, move to finished goods when completed and enter cost of goods sold when the product is sold. A job-sheet total is therefore not automatically the current period's expense. Inventory, revenue recognition and overhead adjustments require accounting records beyond this small calculator. A practical control is to reconcile the supporting job sheets to the work-in-process control balance at a stated date. Do not include a closed job in both unfinished and completed lists. Keep selling and general administrative period costs outside production inventory unless the applicable accounting policy actually supports a different treatment; this guide is not a substitute for preparing compliant statements. Applied overhead versus actual overhead Predetermined rates permit costing before all actual overhead is known. At period end, compare total applied overhead with actual overhead. In an independent example, 190 base hours at the $30 rate apply $5,700. If actual overhead is $6,200, overhead is underapplied by $500. That is a period reconciliation, not a reason to retroactively call every job's initial assignment actual cash cost. If actual overhead were $5,400 at the same 190 hours, applied overhead would exceed it by $300. The appropriate adjustment or allocation depends on the accounting policy and materiality; the embedded tool does not post journal entries, distribute a variance among inventory accounts or certify year-end valuation. Retain both the original rate and the reconciliation. Controls that make the sheet useful Assign a unique job identifier before work begins and record approved scope changes. Reconcile materials issued and returned, and separate directly traced supplies from overhead. Capture actual approved time rather than copying the estimate into the actual column. Use one documented rate basis and avoid duplicating payroll burden in direct labor and the overhead pool. Check job status and equivalent output before calculating unit cost or comparing revenue. Review estimate variances, then reconcile total applied overhead to the period's actual pool. For a detailed service application, use the existing landscaping estimate-versus-actual guide . For the operating statement, use contribution margin presentation . These pages answer related questions while preserving their different cost boundaries. Download the editable job cost sheet Download the formula-based job cost sheet CSV . Import into Excel or Google Sheets, replace the labeled input rows and recalculate. Incomplete, nonnumeric or invalid inputs leave results blank. This file follows the same fictional example and stated scope as the calculator; a CSV cannot preserve spreadsheet styling. Check the imported sheet: retain the original row positions and column-B formulas. Defaults should produce $720 direct labor, $900 applied overhead, $2,820 assigned cost and $282 per completed unit. The margin result is a decimal fraction: format 0.06 as 6%. At zero revenue the margin remains blank; zero job output or a zero overhead-base denominator is invalid. Missing inputs must not be read as zero costs. Build an estimate-to-actual bridge without losing the original quote Extend the original ten-unit job with a clearly labeled estimate. The quotation assumed $1,100 materials, 25 labor hours at $24 and the same $30 per labor-hour overhead rate. Estimated assigned cost was $1,100 + $600 + $750 = $2,450. Actual records in the main example show $1,200 materials, 30 hours at $24 and $900 applied overhead, giving $2,820. The assigned-cost increase is $370. Original ten-unit job: estimate versus actual assigned cost, USD Cost line Estimate Actual Actual minus estimate Materials 1,100 1,200 +100 Direct labor 600 720 +120 Applied overhead 750 900 +150 Assigned total 2,450 2,820 +370 At unchanged $3,000 revenue, the estimated revenue-less-assigned-cost result was $550, or 18.3333% of revenue. The actual result is $180, or 6%. The $370 reduction reconciles exactly to the three cost changes. It is a comparison within this sheet's scope, before excluded selling and administrative items. The $150 extra applied overhead is an assignment from the rate, not automatically an additional cash bill. Separate customer changes, rework and estimating error Suppose approved time records classify the five extra hours as two hours for a documented customer change and three hours of internal rework. At the unchanged rates, the change accounts for $48 labor plus $60 applied overhead, or $108 assigned cost. Rework accounts for $72 labor plus $90 applied overhead, or $162. Together the $270 hours-related increase matches the labor and applied-overhead bridge above. The separate $100 material increase still needs its own price, usage or scope evidence. Do not assume a customer owes another $108 merely because that amount appears in a cost report. Additional billing requires the agreed scope and approval terms, and the selling price need not equal assigned cost. Keep the original estimate, approved change record, revised estimate and actual cost as separate versions. If a scope change raises revenue, show that revenue bridge as well rather than attributing the entire margin change to delivery efficiency. Record rework once. If the three hours are already on the job time sheet, adding a separate $72 rework charge to the job would duplicate labor. Likewise, materials returned to stock should reduce the job's net issues under the chosen policy rather than remain as both job usage and available inventory. Different treatment of abnormal losses requires an explicit accounting policy; the simple widget does not make that policy decision. Close the job before using its unit cost for the next quote Confirm accepted output, remaining unfinished work, credits, returned materials and approved time through the reporting cutoff. The original $282 cost per unit assumes ten comparable completed units. If the same $2,820 relates to only nine accepted comparable units and no work remains in process, the assigned cost per accepted unit is $313.3333. If the tenth unit is unfinished, allocating every cost to the nine accepted units may be wrong: reconcile work in process instead. The denominator is an accounting and operational boundary, not a convenient number to make the margin look better. Do not change revenue automatically when changing output quantity. The revenue field represents recognized net revenue under the example's stated scope. Partial acceptance, refunds and billing milestones require their own records. A completed cost sheet is useful evidence for the next estimate, but one unusual job is not a universal standard for materials or labor. Reconcile the period after reconciling individual jobs Retain the existing $30 predetermined rate for the job comparisons. Separately, the period example applies $5,700 overhead over 190 hours and incurs $6,200 actual overhead, leaving $500 underapplied. The difference can reflect the budgeted cost pool, the activity level or both. It is not necessarily $500 of operational waste, and it is not automatically an extra charge to this one ten-unit job. Follow the documented period-end treatment for the relevant accounts and materiality. This guide does not prescribe a journal entry or automate allocation of an overhead adjustment between work in process, finished goods and cost of goods sold. Use the cost-driver guide to examine the rate basis and flexible-budget analysis to investigate comparable activity and spending. For an industry application, retain the separate landscaping estimate-versus-actual workflow . The existing job-cost calculator and CSV reproduce the $2,820 actual assigned total. Enter the estimate inputs to obtain $2,450, then retain both versions outside the widget; it does not store an estimate-versus-actual history, approve change orders or post inventory entries. Keep those controls in the underlying job records. Method and sources OpenStax explains job order versus process costing and predetermined overhead and application . All job figures, comparisons and calculator defaults above are original fictional examples. Keep job cost, billing and settlement as separate records The supplier approval workflow helps trace purchased materials to receiving evidence and the correct job or stock record. The customer collection workflow traces an accepted invoice to credits and receipts. Paying a previously posted supplier bill does not add its cost to the job a second time, and collecting a recognized customer invoice does not earn the revenue again. Reconcile both workflows to the job evidence without replacing this page’s cost sheet or its overhead treatment. Frequently asked questions What is job order costing? A system that accumulates costs for an identifiable job, project or batch, commonly using direct materials, direct labor and applied overhead. Can service businesses use job order costing? Yes, when costs can be meaningfully traced to client engagements or projects. The records and accounting boundaries should fit the service. What is the job cost formula? Direct materials plus direct labor plus applied overhead. Any excluded selling, administration and other period costs need separate treatment. Is applied overhead the actual overhead incurred? No. A predetermined rate assigns overhead using a budgeted base; total applied overhead is reconciled with actual period overhead separately. Is revenue minus assigned job cost contribution margin? Not automatically. Assigned overhead may include fixed costs, whereas contribution deducts variable expenses under its stated boundary. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Flexible Budget: Formula, Variance Analysis and Worked Example Published October 21, 2026 Updated November 6, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a flexible budget at actual activity, compare original and actual results, and reconcile volume and performance effects with a checked service example. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business Flexible budget: compare the same activity at original rates Recalculate planned revenue and variable expenses at actual activity, retaining the original rates and appropriate fixed commitments. In this fictional example, the flexible budget produces $4,000 operating income at 180 visits; actual income is $2,080 . The $1,920 unfavorable same-activity difference is separate from the $2,000 activity effect. Together they reconcile to the $3,920 unfavorable original-to-actual change. Flexible budget variance calculator Separate activity changes from same-activity performance. All figures must use one period and a consistent equivalent unit. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Original budget activity Units or equivalent completed jobs planned for the period. Actual activity Completed activity for that same period. Budgeted selling price per unit Original planned price; do not replace it with actual price. Budgeted variable cost per unit Original rate, excluding the fixed commitment below. Budgeted fixed operating expenses Original same-period commitment within the relevant activity range. Actual net sales Actual same-period revenue after discounts/refunds on a consistent basis. Actual total variable expenses Actual period total, not cost per unit. Actual fixed operating expenses Actual same-period total, counted once. Reset fictional example Operating-profit bridge Original budget operating income USD 6,000.00 Flexible budget operating income USD 4,000.00 Actual operating income USD 2,080.00 Activity effect: -USD 2,000.00 ( Unfavorable ). Same-activity performance effect: -USD 1,920.00 ( Unfavorable ). Total actual-minus-original profit variance: -USD 3,920.00 ( Unfavorable ). Line Original Flexible Actual Actual minus flexible Net sales USD 36,000.00 USD 32,400.00 USD 31,500.00 -USD 900.00 ( Unfavorable ) Variable expenses USD 16,000.00 USD 14,400.00 USD 15,120.00 USD 720.00 ( Unfavorable ) Contribution USD 20,000.00 USD 18,000.00 USD 16,380.00 -USD 1,620.00 ( Unfavorable ) Fixed expenses USD 14,000.00 USD 14,000.00 USD 14,300.00 USD 300.00 ( Unfavorable ) Operating income USD 6,000.00 USD 4,000.00 USD 2,080.00 -USD 1,920.00 ( Unfavorable ) Fictional USD defaults: original profit $6,000; flexed profit $4,000; actual $2,080. The total $3,920 unfavorable variance is $2,000 activity plus $1,920 performance. This is not a cash forecast or an employee responsibility verdict. Fixed budget costs do not scale with activity here. Rebuild the budget for cost steps, changed mix or nonlinear rates. Capacity and demand are not assessed. Currency selection changes labels only. Illustrative editorial scene. Financial examples in this guide use fictional USD assumptions. A flexible budget recalculates planned revenue and variable expenses for a different activity level while retaining the original budgeted rates and appropriate fixed commitments. For performance review, use actual completed activity. Comparing actual results with that same-activity budget separates the effect of doing more or less work from the effect of prices and spending. This guide uses one fictional USD service-business month, shows the full profit reconciliation and provides the calculator above. Figures are invented planning inputs, not benchmarks. The tool is a simple equivalent-unit operating model, not a cash forecast, manufacturing inventory model or explanation of who caused a variance. Flexible budget formula and assumptions Flexible revenue = budgeted price × actual activity. Flexible variable expense = budgeted variable cost per unit × actual activity. Flexible total expense = flexible variable expense + budgeted fixed expense. Subtract total expense from flexible revenue to calculate flexible operating income. Keep the original selling price and variable-cost rate when flexing the budget. Substituting actual rates would hide the differences you need to investigate. Do not scale every expense by the volume change: rent can stay fixed within a relevant range, while a per-visit supply cost changes with completed visits. A further supervisor, minimum staffing requirement or additional vehicle can create a new fixed-cost step. Use the fixed, variable and mixed-cost guide to define cost behavior. If a pool mixes fixed and variable amounts, split it using defensible records. The high-low method gives only a preliminary two-observation estimate and still needs checks against other records. A complete flexible budget example The original monthly plan is 200 completed equivalent cleaning visits at $180 each, with $80 variable expense per visit and $14,000 fixed operating commitments. Actual activity is 180 visits. Actual net sales are $31,500, actual variable expenses $15,120 and actual fixed operating expenses $14,300. At 180 actual visits, the original $180 price produces flexible revenue of $32,400, and the original $80 variable rate produces flexible variable expense of $14,400. The fixed budget remains $14,000. Actual revenue implies $175 per visit and actual variable spending $84 per visit in this simplified case. Those implied averages diagnose differences; they do not establish why prices or costs changed. Same fictional month: original, flexible and actual results Line Original: 200 visits Flexible: 180 visits Actual: 180 visits Net sales $36,000 $32,400 $31,500 Variable expenses $16,000 $14,400 $15,120 Contribution margin $20,000 $18,000 $16,380 Fixed operating expenses $14,000 $14,000 $14,300 Operating income $6,000 $4,000 $2,080 The static comparison says actual variable spending of $15,120 is $880 below the original $16,000 budget. That is a lower bill, but not evidence of efficient delivery: the business completed 20 fewer visits. At 180 visits, the appropriate variable-cost comparison is $15,120 actual versus $14,400 flexible, a $720 unfavorable difference . Flexible budget variance formula: label the sign This guide defines flexible-budget variance = actual result − flexible budget . A positive revenue difference is favorable; a positive expense difference is unfavorable. For operating income, positive is favorable. A label must accompany the sign so a higher expense is not mistaken for good performance. Actual-minus-flexible differences at 180 visits Line Difference Interpretation Revenue $31,500 − $32,400 = −$900 $900 unfavorable Variable expenses $15,120 − $14,400 = +$720 $720 unfavorable Fixed expenses $14,300 − $14,000 = +$300 $300 unfavorable Operating income $2,080 − $4,000 = −$1,920 $1,920 unfavorable The $900 revenue shortfall, $720 variable-spending excess and $300 fixed-spending excess together reduce operating income by $1,920. Do not add the contribution-margin variance again: contribution already combines revenue and variable expenses. A variance directs investigation; it is not automatically an employee fault, waste finding or price recommendation. Reconcile the full original-to-actual profit change Activity effect = flexible operating income − original operating income. Here it is $4,000 − $6,000 = −$2,000 . At the unchanged $100 planned contribution per visit, completing 20 fewer visits loses $2,000 contribution toward fixed commitments. Performance effect = actual operating income − flexible operating income. Here it is $2,080 − $4,000 = −$1,920 . The full change is −$2,000 + −$1,920 = −$3,920 , exactly matching $2,080 actual minus $6,000 original. That reconciliation prevents an unexplained residual from disappearing into a general budget label. For a multiple-product business, the equivalent-unit assumption can fail when mix changes. A more complex analysis must separate volume, mix, price and cost effects using a consistent base. Start with the sales-mix and weighted-margin guide rather than treating every completed order as identical. How to prepare a useful flexible budget Retain the original approved plan, rates and reporting period. A revised forecast is useful, but should not overwrite the comparison baseline. Reconcile actual activity and recognized net sales. Returns, discounts and incomplete jobs need a stated convention. Flex each variable line with its real driver. Job count can suit consumables, while miles or machine-hours may better explain another pool. Keep fixed commitments at their budgeted amount only within the valid range. Separately identify actual changes, cost steps and scope changes. Compare actual and flexible lines, then reconcile the activity and performance effects to the total operating-income difference. Investigate the largest controllable drivers with invoices, work records and schedules. Record an owner, action and next review date. A favorable cost variance can arise from deferred maintenance or reduced service quality. An unfavorable labor variance can arise from training, changed customer requirements or incorrect standards. The budget identifies a question to investigate, not a complete operational diagnosis. Flexible budget in Excel or Google Sheets For a compact worksheet, place planned units in B2, actual units B3, budgeted price B4, variable rate B5 and fixed budget B6. Original operating income is =B2*(B4-B5)-B6 ; flexible operating income is =B3*(B4-B5)-B6 . Enter actual revenue B7, actual total variable expense B8 and actual fixed expense B9. Actual operating income is =B7-B8-B9 . Require complete numeric inputs and a consistent period before calculating. The activity effect is flexible minus original; the performance effect is actual minus flexible. All three operating-income calculations should use the same included cost boundary. Use the contribution statement template to reconcile the revenue, variable-expense, contribution and fixed-expense lines. Where the simple model stops The calculator does not validate productive capacity, forecast demand, model tax or loan payments, or reproduce an external financial statement. Inventory changes and production-versus-sales differences require additional schedules. At zero actual units, unit-price averages are undefined; any positive actual revenue needs a timing or unit reconciliation before interpretation. Use a separate cash budget and receipt/payment schedule for liquidity. A favorable operating variance cannot pay a bill before customer cash arrives. Keep operating results, future demand and payment timing distinct. Turn the variance table into a performance report A useful flexible budget performance report answers three separate questions: how much work happened, what that work should have earned and cost at the approved rates, and what actually happened. Give each line an activity driver, evidence reference and explanation. Keep the signed difference separate from its favorable or unfavorable label. The label describes the operating-income effect, not whether someone made a good decision. In the existing cleaning example, revenue is $900 below the same-activity budget. The implied actual price is $31,500 ÷ 180 = $175, versus the original $180. The arithmetic explanation is 180 × ($175 − $180) = −$900. That does not establish a price-cutting problem: inspect discounts, refunds, job scope and the mix of visits before calling this a pure selling-price variance. A different service mix can change the average even if no individual price changes. The $720 unfavorable variable-expense difference equals 180 × ($84 − $80). Calling this an efficiency variance would go beyond the data. The $84 average can reflect higher input prices, more input quantities, different work or incorrect classifications. A visit-level total cannot identify labor hours and wage-rate effects without a supporting hours schedule. Separate labor rate from hours with a supporting schedule Consider a separate fictional labor schedule, not a breakdown of the $720 above. For 180 comparable visits, the standard allows 1.5 delivery hours per visit at $24 per hour. Standard hours allowed are 270 and the flexible labor budget is $6,480. Actual approved hours are 288 at $25, costing $7,200. The actual-minus-standard cost difference is $720 unfavorable. Independent labor schedule: actual cost minus allowed standard cost Component Calculation Cost effect Rate 288 actual hours × ($25 − $24) $288 unfavorable Hours (288 actual − 270 allowed hours) × $24 $432 unfavorable Total $7,200 − $6,480 = $288 + $432 $720 unfavorable Use actual hours for the rate component and standard hours allowed for actual output for the hours comparison. Using the original 200-visit labor allowance would mix volume with performance again. Confirm whether the labor pool includes overtime, employer burden and paid non-delivery time; the standard and actual columns need the same scope. An hours variance can reflect training or authorized service changes, so investigate records before assigning responsibility. The embedded calculator reports aggregate revenue and expense differences; it does not calculate these labor subvariances. When one activity driver is not enough Suppose a separate monthly support pool includes $1,200 fixed dispatch, $2 per completed visit and $0.40 per delivery mile. At 180 visits and 2,100 miles, its flexible amount is $1,200 + $360 + $840 = $2,400. Multiplying the entire original pool by a visits percentage would incorrectly scale the fixed commitment and assume miles always move with visits. Keep the three components in a supporting schedule and reconcile the total back to the operating report. Where a contract creates a capacity step, such as a second vehicle above a documented mileage threshold, use the applicable budgeted step rather than pretending the original fixed amount covers unlimited activity. Preserve the approved baseline and show scope changes separately. The simple calculator uses one equivalent activity unit and one fixed pool; use it only when that simplification fits, or prepare a driver-level schedule outside the widget. Example of a variance action record For the original $900 revenue shortfall, assign the sales owner to reconcile the 180 completed visits to net invoice lines, approved discounts and credits. Record a due date and the resulting explanation. For the $720 variable-spending difference, the operations owner should reconcile purchase usage and approved delivery time. For the $300 fixed-expense excess, inspect the actual invoice and whether it belongs to this period. These are evidence requests, not conclusions that the business should raise prices or reduce staffing. Review absolute dollars and the operational context together. A small percentage of a large pool may deserve attention, while a large percentage on a tiny line may not. Do not invent a universal investigation threshold. Agree a review policy before the period closes and track repeated small differences that accumulate. Close the review by recording the evidence, action, owner and next check; retain the original standards so a revised forecast does not erase accountability. Download and verify the flexible budget worksheet Download the formula-based flexible budget review CSV . It follows this guide’s 200 planned and 180 actual visits, producing $6,000 original operating income, $4,000 flexible income and $2,080 actual income. The final reconciliation should be zero: activity effect plus performance effect minus total change. Import into Excel or Google Sheets with formula interpretation enabled, retain row positions and verify those defaults before replacing inputs. Blank or invalid inputs suppress calculations. CSV does not preserve formatting, validation menus or multiple sheets. Use the restaurant operating-budget guide for a restaurant-specific plan and the restaurant sales forecast for demand assumptions. This page owns the same-activity performance comparison; it does not replace those industry plans. For the labor decomposition method, see OpenStax’s labor variance lesson . All additional schedules here are original fictional illustrations. Method sources OpenStax explains preparing flexible budgets and using budgets to evaluate results . This guide's service-business data, classifications and reconciliation are original illustrative examples. Keep the master plan behind the flexible comparison The master budget guide and cash bridge connect sales, delivery costs and collections before the period starts. Preserve that approved plan. This page flexes operating results at actual activity; it does not rebuild the full cash budget or projected balance sheet. Download a static budget variance report Use the budget vs actual Excel template when you need a monthly or YTD comparison against the original approved totals. Its blank report and filled example keep actual revenue, expenses and the operating-result bridge together. The template owns the download task; this guide owns the same-activity flexible-budget analysis. For a small static illustration, budget revenue of $30,000 less $20,000 included expenses gives $10,000 operating result. Actual revenue of $28,000 less $21,000 expenses gives $7,000. Using actual minus budget, the revenue difference is −$2,000, expense difference is +$1,000 and result difference is −$3,000. The result bridge is revenue variance minus expense variance. It is not a new example of the calculator's activity-adjusted results. Before calling the $1,000 expense increase inefficient, inspect completed activity and the expense boundary. More jobs, a rate increase, overtime or a timing adjustment can produce different explanations. Apply the original rates to actual activity in this page's calculator, then compare actual results with that flexible benchmark. For monthly reporting, enter explicit zeros for genuinely closed zero-activity accounts and leave unknown actuals blank. Match the YTD cutoff on both sides; do not compare three actual months with a full-year budget. Keep expense reductions caused by fewer jobs separate from improvements at the same workload. The workbook leaves incomplete periods unreported and shows no percentage when the budget denominator is zero. Preserve the approved budget when expectations change. Update future drivers in the rolling forecast and its dated worksheet , keeping its current expectations separate from the original target. Neither the operating comparison nor the forecast proves that customers will pay on time; use a dated cash schedule for that question. Investigate timing before explaining a spending variance A lower cash payment is not necessarily a favorable expense variance: an unpaid supplier service can still belong to the current reporting period. Use the liability and accrual schedule to identify the reporting cutoff, then compare recognized actual expense with the flexible allowance for the same scope. Keep supplier payment dates in the cash forecast. Likewise, use invoice and collection records to distinguish earned activity from its later receipt. Neither a late payment nor a late collection changes the calculator’s activity standard automatically. Frequently asked questions What is a flexible budget? It recalculates planned revenue and variable costs at a selected activity level while keeping original rates and appropriate fixed commitments. For performance review, use actual activity. What is flexible budget variance? Using actual minus flexible, positive revenue variance is favorable while positive expense variance is unfavorable. For operating income, a positive difference is favorable. Should fixed costs change when the budget is flexed? Not simply because activity changes within the valid range. Separate a genuine cost step or scope change instead of multiplying every fixed expense by volume. Does a favorable variance prove good management? No. It can reflect deferred spending, changed scope or a poor standard. Investigate invoices, quality and operating records before attributing responsibility. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Make-or-Buy Decision: Relevant Costs, Calculator and Example Published October 21, 2026 Updated October 23, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare make-or-buy relevant costs with a checked example, avoidable fixed costs, opportunity contribution and a calculator that keeps common costs separate. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business Make or buy: compare the costs that change Compare avoidable internal costs and feasible opportunity contribution with the supplier price and buying-only costs. In this fictional example, relevant make cost is $19,000 and buy cost is $18,500 , so buying is lower by $500 . If the $2,000 opportunity contribution has no feasible alternative use, make cost becomes $17,000 and the result reverses. Common unavoidable commitments do not become savings merely because work is outsourced. Make-or-buy decision calculator Compare the incremental economic cost of making internally with buying a comparable deliverable. Enter the same period and quantity. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Required quantity for the period Use comparable acceptable units, with the same specifications and delivery date. Avoidable make cost per unit Materials, truly avoidable labor and other variable make costs. Fixed cost avoided if buying Period cost that actually disappears when work is outsourced. Supplier price per acceptable unit Use a comparable quote; add other buying-only period costs below. Other buying-only period costs Shipping, inspection, setup and other additional costs; count each once. Contribution lost by making internally Net contribution of the best feasible alternative use of capacity, not its revenue. Unavoidable cost common to both Shown in both totals and excluded from the decision difference. Reset fictional example Cost comparison under your assumptions Relevant make cost, including opportunity USD 19,000.00 Relevant buy cost USD 18,500.00 Absolute cost difference USD 500.00 Buying has the lower modeled economic cost by USD 500.00. Including common unavoidable costs: make USD 23,000.00 ; buy USD 22,500.00 . The decision difference stays the same. Opportunity cost is economic, not necessarily a cash payment. Mathematical crossover: 1,125 units, holding all period amounts and rates constant. Compare feasible quantities on either side; capacity or supplier minimums can invalidate this threshold. Fictional USD defaults: make $19,000 versus buy $18,500, including $2,000 net opportunity contribution in the make alternative. Remove that opportunity only if no feasible alternative use exists: make then becomes $17,000. The $4,000 common commitment is not a saving. Lower modeled cost does not establish supplier quality, reliability, cash affordability or spare capacity. Validate those separately. Currency labels do not convert amounts. Illustrative editorial scene. Financial examples in this guide use fictional USD assumptions. A make-or-buy decision compares the future costs and benefits that differ between doing work internally and purchasing the same acceptable deliverable from a supplier. It is a relevant-cost decision: a cost that continues unchanged under both alternatives cannot make one option cheaper than the other. Use the calculator above to compare a single period and a consistent quantity. Then assess quality, lead time, supply continuity, cash timing and realistic internal capacity. A mathematically cheaper quote is not automatically the better operating decision, and the tool does not certify that either option is feasible. Make-or-buy decision formula Relevant make cost = required quantity × avoidable make cost per unit + avoidable fixed make costs + contribution forgone by making. Relevant buy cost = required quantity × supplier unit price + additional buying-only period costs. The modeled cost advantage is the difference between those two amounts. Include material purchases that change with the decision, labor that is genuinely avoidable, variable processing and the fixed commitments that actually disappear if production is outsourced. For buying, include freight, inspection, onboarding, handling, expected rework and other incremental costs where supported by evidence. Keep a cost either in the unit quote or the additional period line; do not count it twice. An allocated share of rent is not avoidable merely because an accounting report charges it to the component. If the lease and payment remain unchanged, the amount is common to both alternatives. Likewise, the historical purchase price of existing equipment is a sunk cost. Future sale proceeds or actual cancellation costs can be relevant, but require their own evidenced cash flows and may need a more detailed model. A worked make-or-buy example with capacity A fictional small business needs 1,000 acceptable product components this month. Making costs $14 per component in truly avoidable materials, paid labor and running costs. It can avoid $3,000 of period setup/support expense if it buys. A supplier quotes $18 per acceptable component, with an additional $500 for delivery and inspection. A separate $4,000 commitment continues under either alternative. If the internal team makes the components, it cannot perform another feasible job that would earn $2,000 net contribution after that alternative job's own variable costs. That is an opportunity cost of making, not another supplier invoice. These USD figures are invented examples, not market quotations or verified supplier terms. Fictional one-month relevant-cost comparison Decision line Make internally Buy externally Avoidable unit cost × 1,000 $14,000 $18,000 Avoidable make fixed costs $3,000 $0 Buying-only delivery/inspection $0 $500 Contribution forgone by making $2,000 $0 Relevant economic cost $19,000 $18,500 Common unavoidable commitment $4,000 $4,000 Comparison including common commitment $23,000 $22,500 Buying has a $500 lower modeled economic cost . Including the unchanged $4,000 in both columns leaves exactly the same difference. Removing that common cost from only one alternative would manufacture a false saving. Economic comparison and cash comparison are different here. Relevant make cash outflows are $17,000, whereas buy cash outflows are $18,500. Buying uses $1,500 more direct cash under this boundary, but releases an opportunity worth $2,000 net contribution if it is genuinely feasible. Its modeled economic advantage is therefore $500. Actual collections, deposits and payment dates still require a cash forecast. Idle capacity can reverse the result If there is no feasible alternative use of the released resources, enter zero opportunity contribution. Relevant make cost becomes $14,000 + $3,000 = $17,000 ; buy remains $18,500. Making now has a $1,500 advantage . Do not claim a released employee hour earns revenue just because the hour becomes available. Conversely, if making requires overtime, additional equipment or delayed higher-contribution work, those consequences may change the comparison. A salaried employee who stays employed can be an unavoidable cash commitment even when their scarce time has an economic opportunity cost. Model the relevant distinction without charging the same salary twice. For service work, the equivalent decision can be internal delivery versus subcontracting. Use comparable scope, acceptance standards, customer obligations and rework responsibilities. See the employee-versus-freelancer guide and subcontractor job-cost guide for related operating contexts. Calculate the crossover quantity carefully With constant unit rates and period amounts, equate the relevant cost lines. Crossover quantity = (avoidable make fixed costs + contribution forgone − buying-only period costs) ÷ (buy unit cost − make variable cost per unit). Using the main example: ($3,000 + $2,000 − $500) ÷ ($18 − $14) = 1,125 components . Both alternatives have a relevant economic cost of $20,750 at that quantity. At 1,000, buying is cheaper; at 1,200, making costs $21,800 versus $22,100 buying, so making is cheaper by $300 under the same assumptions. The opportunity amount is held constant in that mathematical illustration. In reality it may depend on released hours, demand or the quantity made. Supplier price tiers, minimum orders, overtime and capacity steps can also invalidate the crossover. A negative threshold is not a useful positive production target; equal unit rates may produce no unique threshold or a tie at every quantity. Records to collect before deciding A comparable specification: quantity, usable yield, quality tolerance, packaging, warranty and required date. A verified internal cost list: mark each line as avoidable, unavoidable, sunk or opportunity-related. Confirm cancellation and reassignment possibilities. A complete supplier quote: price basis, freight, inspection, minimum order, payment terms, rework responsibility and validity period. A capacity record: usable hours, bottlenecks, required setup time and the best feasible alternative work. An opportunity calculation: expected retained revenue less the alternative job's incremental costs, supported by demand and delivery capacity. A cash schedule: deposit dates and outflows, expected collections, available funding and a realistic buffer. Keep the original comparison and record what happens after implementation: accepted quantities, delivery time, defects, rework, actual supplier charges and retained internal commitments. A decision that looked cheaper can deteriorate when the quoted scope differs from the work actually supplied. Check allocation before treating it as a saving A cost-driver allocation can assign a support pool to a job without making that amount avoidable. Keep the documented driver and cost pool for job reporting, then independently identify which commitments disappear under each make-or-buy alternative. Common mistakes and practical controls Comparing a full allocated make cost with a partial buy quote. Reconcile both columns to the same cost boundary. Treating all direct labor as avoidable. Review actual employment and scheduling commitments. Using alternative revenue as opportunity benefit. Use net contribution from a feasible alternative after its relevant costs. Ignoring the cost of failures. A low quote is not comparable if it shifts inspection, waste or warranty obligations back to you. Confusing lower economic cost with cash affordability. An early supplier deposit can create a funding gap despite an attractive comparison. Use the cash forecast separately. Confusing a make-or-buy crossover with business break-even. The crossover compares two cost alternatives. Business break-even compares revenue with all included operating costs. Review the break-even formula guide for that separate question. What is the maximum acceptable supplier price? The crossover quantity answers how volume changes the comparison. A different question is the supplier unit-price ceiling at a fixed quantity. With the original 1,000 components, $14 avoidable internal unit cost, $3,000 avoidable fixed cost, $2,000 feasible opportunity contribution and $500 buying-only cost, the economic ceiling is ($19,000 − $500) ÷ 1,000 = $18.50 per acceptable component . At that quote both options have the same modeled economic cost. Below it buying is lower; above it making is lower, within the stated assumptions. Without an alternative job, relevant make cost is $17,000 and the ceiling falls to ($17,000 − $500) ÷ 1,000 = $16.50 . The $2 difference is the $2,000 opportunity contribution spread over 1,000 components. A buyer should therefore not negotiate against an $18.50 ceiling unless that alternative contribution is evidenced. This is an economic ceiling, not a statement that a deposit or invoice is affordable. How much alternative contribution makes outsourcing worthwhile? At the original $18 supplier quote, buying costs $18,500 and avoidable make cash costs are $17,000. Buying needs at least $1,500 of feasible released-capacity contribution to reach an economic tie. At $1,000 contribution, making remains lower by $500. At $2,000, buying becomes lower by $500. Use net contribution after the alternative job’s incremental costs, not its invoice value or gross revenue. Original 1,000-component case: sensitivity to feasible alternative contribution Contribution forgone by making Relevant make cost Relevant buy cost Comparison $0 $17,000 $18,500 Make lower by $1,500 $1,000 $18,000 $18,500 Make lower by $500 $1,500 $18,500 $18,500 Tie $2,000 $19,000 $18,500 Buy lower by $500 Confirm that outsourcing releases the actual bottleneck. If inspection still requires the same scarce technician, purchased components may free machine time without enabling the alternative job. Check setup, transfer time, delivery dates and customer demand together. A scenario table makes the assumption visible; it does not establish the probability of earning the contribution. Convert a quote into cost per acceptable component A quoted purchased unit and an acceptable delivered unit are not necessarily the same denominator. In a separate fictional case, the supplier charges $10 per purchased unit, expected usable yield is 95%, and the business needs 1,000 acceptable units. Before considering minimum order sizes, it must purchase at least ceiling(1,000 ÷ 0.95) = 1,053 units . Purchase cost is $10,530; with $300 incremental inspection and delivery, the modeled cost is $10,830, or $10.83 per required acceptable unit. The extra 53 purchased units are a planning allowance, not a guarantee that exactly 1,000 will pass. A yield estimate needs evidence and a contingency for variability. If the contract bills only accepted units or provides replacements, use those terms instead. Do not apply both a yield adjustment and the same defect allowance again as rework cost. Minimum orders, freight tiers and surplus inventory can invalidate a smooth unit-cost crossover, so compare actual order-sized alternatives. Check when an internal cost can actually disappear Attach a date and evidence to each claimed saving. Materials not yet ordered may be avoidable immediately. A cancellable machine rental may disappear only after its notice period. A supervisor salary that continues for the next three months is not an immediate saving merely because the production line stops. A reassigned employee can remain a cash commitment while released hours have a separate opportunity value. For a one-month decision, include only the costs and benefits relevant to that month. For a longer decision, show the transition months, cancellation payments, severance where applicable, continuing commitments, working capital and eventual equipment proceeds separately. Do not divide a first-year saving by monthly volume and present it as a permanent unit advantage. The embedded single-period calculator cannot discount a multi-year project or recognize staged cash flows; build a dated schedule where the decision requires one. Write a decision note someone else can verify A defensible note states the required quantity and acceptance specification; the quote validity date; make and buy cost boundaries; avoidable commitments and supporting cancellation terms; evidence for alternative contribution; and the owner responsible for delivery and quality. Include the base comparison plus a scenario with no opportunity contribution. In the original case, the note must state both the $500 economic buying advantage and the $1,500 higher direct cash outflow before the alternative work is collected. Set operational conditions before committing: agreed sample approval, inspection responsibility, acceptable delivery timing, escalation contacts and treatment of rejected units. Record which costs remain after outsourcing and compare actual accepted output with the assumptions after implementation. If the $2,000 alternative job is cancelled, revisit the decision rather than preserving a saving that no longer exists. Download the make-or-buy decision worksheet Download the formula-based make-or-buy review CSV . The original defaults calculate $19,000 relevant make cost, $18,500 relevant buy cost, a $500 buying advantage, an $18.50 supplier-price ceiling and a $1,500 opportunity-contribution tie threshold. The positive crossover is 1,125 components when period amounts stay constant. Retain the input and formula rows, enable formulas on import and check those results before editing. A blank crossover means no positive unique crossing under the entered assumptions; it does not mean zero units. Use contribution margin to define the net contribution released capacity can earn. Keep business break-even separate: it asks how sales cover operating costs, rather than which supplier or production alternative is lower. The evidence principles follow OpenStax’s relevant-information framework ; the thresholds and sensitivity figures above are original worked examples. Method source OpenStax's make-or-buy lesson discusses relevant costs and quantitative and qualitative considerations. This guide's figures and the capacity sensitivity are original fictional examples; they do not establish actual supplier savings. Frequently asked questions Which costs matter in a make-or-buy decision? Future costs and benefits that differ between alternatives matter. Common unavoidable commitments and sunk historical costs do not create an incremental saving. How does idle capacity change the choice? If there is no feasible alternative use, opportunity contribution can be zero. If internal work displaces a feasible profitable alternative, the contribution forgone belongs in the comparison. Should allocated fixed overhead be included? Include only the portion that changes with the decision. An allocated commitment that remains unchanged is common to both alternatives and must not be presented as a saving. Is the lower modeled cost always the right choice? No. Quality, delivery reliability, capacity, cash timing and contractual responsibilities also need evaluation. The calculator compares the entered economic cost assumptions.
