documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Contribution Margin Income Statement: Format, Template and Example Published October 19, 2026 Updated November 6, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Prepare a contribution margin income statement with a checked service-business example, editable CSV template and clear fixed-versus-variable cost boundaries. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business Illustrative editorial scene; the fictional business figures are explained in the article. A contribution margin income statement separates costs by how they behave: sales minus all variable expenses equals contribution margin; contribution margin minus fixed expenses equals operating income. It is an internal planning view, not a replacement for your statutory income statement or a cash-flow forecast. Use it when a busy month produces disappointing profit, when a discount changes the work needed to cover rent, or when you want to see whether additional completed jobs contribute enough. The key is not a new spreadsheet label: it is classifying the same period's costs consistently. Contribution margin income statement format The format has five essential lines. Start with net sales after sales discounts and refunds. Subtract variable delivery and selling expenses, including applicable processing fees, to find contribution. Deduct fixed operating commitments once to reach operating income. Contribution format: purpose of each line Line Calculation or meaning Net sales Completed sales recognized for the period, on a consistent basis Variable expenses Costs that change with those sales or the selected activity Contribution margin Net sales minus variable expenses Fixed operating expenses Period commitments that remain fixed within the stated range Operating income Contribution margin minus fixed operating expenses Operating income = (selling price − variable cost per unit) × units sold − fixed expenses. For mixed offers, sum actual contribution dollars across products or services. A simple average of percentages can misstate the result. Use the contribution margin per-unit and ratio guide for that input calculation. A complete small-business example This fictional cleaning business completes 200 equivalent visits in one month at $180 each. For each visit, supplies cost $12, labor paid only for that visit costs $63 and processing costs $5. Those variable costs total $80 a visit. Monthly fixed operating expenses total $14,000: $8,000 guaranteed salaries, $2,000 premises, $500 software, $500 insurance and $3,000 administration. These are illustrative USD inputs, not market rates. The guaranteed salaries are for different commitments from the $63 job-paid labor. Include no wage in both lines. If a cleaner receives a guaranteed salary regardless of visits, classify that commitment according to the actual arrangement rather than assuming all cleaning labor is variable. Fictional month: 200 visits at $180 Statement line Calculation Amount Net sales 200 × $180 $36,000 Variable supplies 200 × $12 $2,400 Variable job labor 200 × $63 $12,600 Variable processing 200 × $5 $1,000 Total variable expenses $2,400 + $12,600 + $1,000 $16,000 Contribution margin $36,000 − $16,000 $20,000 Fixed operating expenses Stated monthly commitments $14,000 Operating income $20,000 − $14,000 $6,000 The contribution margin ratio is $20,000 ÷ $36,000 = 55.56% , rounded for display. The operating margin is $6,000 ÷ $36,000 = 16.67% . Contribution is not profit: the fixed expenses consume $14,000 of the $20,000 contribution. At the same price and variable cost, unit contribution is $100 and operating break-even is $14,000 ÷ $100 = 140 visits . If you add a separate $2,000 owner-income planning goal, required visits become 160. That owner goal is a planning adjustment, not automatically an accounting expense. If owner salary is already included in the $14,000, do not add it again. Download the editable statement template Download the contribution margin income statement CSV template . Open it in Excel or Google Sheets. Replace the seven input amounts in column B: completed units, price, variable supplies, variable job labor, fees per unit, other variable cost per unit and total fixed operating expenses. The remaining rows contain spreadsheet formulas. Input status must show Ready: incomplete, nonnumeric or negative inputs leave the output formulas blank. The contribution ratio also stays blank at zero revenue. The file reproduces this article's 200-visit example. Use one reporting period and one equivalent sale unit. For different offers, prepare separate unit records and combine total sales and variable expenses; do not enter a misleading unweighted unit average. The file is an operating statement template, not an inventory valuation schedule or cash budget. What happens when sales volume changes? Keep price at $180, variable cost at $80 per visit and fixed expenses at $14,000. The following comparison isolates volume. It assumes staffing, service mix, prices and the fixed-cost range remain unchanged. Volume scenarios under the same cost boundary Visits Sales Variable costs Contribution Operating income 150 $27,000 $12,000 $15,000 $1,000 200 $36,000 $16,000 $20,000 $6,000 300 $54,000 $24,000 $30,000 $16,000 Each extra visit adds $100 toward operating profit while the assumptions hold. The 300-visit case is not a demand forecast or proof that the team can deliver 300 visits. Another supervisor, overtime or vehicle may create a step cost. Check available hours before treating the financial comparison as a workable schedule. Contribution format vs a traditional income statement A traditional income statement usually organizes expenses by function, with cost of goods sold deducted to show gross profit and selling/administrative expenses shown separately. The contribution format instead reorganizes expenses by behavior. A variable selling commission sits above contribution even if it appears below gross profit in a traditional presentation. Fixed production overhead can be inside inventory/COGS under absorption costing, so contribution and gross profit are not interchangeable. For a simple service-period example with no inventory timing differences and the same included expenses, changing presentation does not create extra profit. Manufacturing inventory changes can produce differences between absorption and variable-costing income. Do not force the two results to match by dropping an expense. See contribution margin vs gross margin for the boundary distinction. How to prepare your own contribution statement Choose a month and reconcile recognized net sales to your sales records. Sales tax collected for a tax authority is not sales revenue in this model. List all relevant expenses, including payment fees, delivery commissions, refunds and job-paid labor. Match them to the same activity and period. Separate fixed, variable and mixed costs. A monthly vehicle lease plus per-mile running cost needs two components. Use the high-low method guide only as a rough estimate when its assumptions fit. Calculate contribution and deduct fixed operating expenses once. Retain a reconciliation to the original ledger so no expense disappears. Compare actual and planned results. If units or mix changed, a sales-mix review is more informative than blaming every difference on price. Mistakes that overstate the answer Calling contribution take-home pay. Rent and other fixed commitments remain to be covered. Interest, income tax and owner distributions may also sit outside the stated operating result. Loan principal and equipment purchases belong in a separate cash plan rather than being casually treated as variable operating expenses. Using payment timing as expense classification. An annual insurance bill can be fixed even though cash leaves once a year. Recognizing a monthly share for an operating statement and forecasting the actual payment date answer different questions. Forgetting variable selling expenses. Materials alone are not the complete variable cost if every sale also causes a commission, fulfillment cost or payment fee. Double-counting payroll is equally damaging: include a fixed base and a variable component separately only when they represent different costs. Extrapolating beyond capacity. The fixed-cost assumption is conditional on the relevant range. For a monthly target, use the cleaning break-even planner with your own costs and capacity, without promising that template inputs transfer automatically. Method and source OpenStax's contribution margin lesson explains the internal contribution format and its unit, total and ratio measures. All business figures and scenarios above are MyBreakeven's fictional examples. Reconcile to a functional operating-margin view The operating margin calculator can use reported operating income or compatible revenue, COGS and OPEX subtotals. It does not infer variable costs from those accounts. Use the OPEX classification example to see why moving a cost between COGS and OPEX changes gross margin while leaving operating income unchanged. Use the contribution format for a defined CVP decision A contribution format income statement supplies sales, variable expense and fixed operating expense for a stated period. Use the complete cost-volume-profit method to test the resulting price, volume, mix and capacity assumptions rather than interpreting the statement as a forecast. The accounting-equation example separately shows why a loan receipt or customer collection is not additional operating profit. Preserve this page’s original statement and reconcile any planning adjustment to its included costs. Frequently asked questions What is the formula for a contribution margin income statement? Net sales minus variable expenses equals contribution margin. Deduct fixed operating expenses from contribution to find operating income for the stated period. Is contribution margin the same as net income? No. Contribution has not yet deducted fixed operating expenses. Net income can also include financing, tax and other items outside the stated operating result. Can a service business use a contribution statement? Yes. Define a consistent completed service unit, separate costs by behavior and reconcile the statement to period records. Guaranteed labor and job-paid labor must not be counted twice. Does the download include formulas? Yes. The CSV contains seven editable numeric inputs and spreadsheet formulas for revenue, variable expenses, contribution, ratio and operating income. It is not a cash forecast. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE High-Low Method: Calculator, Formula and Worked Example Published October 19, 2026 Updated November 23, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Split a mixed cost into fixed and variable components with a high-low calculator, six-month example, Excel formulas and checks for outliers and activity range. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business High-low method: formula and a checked example Estimate the variable rate by dividing the change in total cost by the change in activity, using the highest and lowest activity observations. With fictional costs of $1,640 at 80 units and $2,440 at 280 units, the variable rate is ($2,440 − $1,640) ÷ (280 − 80) = $4 per unit . The estimated fixed cost is $1,320 . This two-point estimate needs a consistent period and relevant operating range; it does not prove a causal relationship. High-low method calculator Estimate a mixed cost from two observations. First select the highest and lowest activity from your full records. This tool does not select those records for you. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Lowest activity Activity units in the lowest-activity observation. Cost at lowest activity Total cost paired with that activity, for the same period and cost pool. Highest activity Must exceed lowest activity; do not select by the highest bill. Cost at highest activity Total cost paired with the highest activity. Target activity Activity to estimate under the same cost model. Reset fictional example Your estimated cost equation Variable cost per activity unit USD 4.00 Fixed cost per period USD 1,320.00 Estimated total cost at target activity USD 2,200.00 Estimated cost = USD 1,320.00 + ( USD 4.00 × 220 activity units). Fictional USD defaults: 80 visits cost $1,640 and 280 visits cost $2,440. The fit is $1,320 fixed plus $4 per visit; 220 visits estimate $2,200. Replace every input. Currency selection changes labels only. Same cost pool, time period and activity unit required. Calculations retain precision before display rounding. Validate intermediate observations and unusual bills; this is a two-point estimate, not a forecast guarantee. See the six-month example and outlier check Illustrative editorial scene; the fictional business figures are explained in the article. The high-low method estimates the fixed and variable components of a mixed cost from two observations: the highest activity level and the lowest activity level, together with each observation's total cost. It is a quick preliminary estimate, not proof of a causal relationship or a substitute for reviewing all your records. For an owner planning costs, the useful output is an explicit equation: estimated total cost = fixed component + variable rate × activity . That can help prepare a budget or improve the cost inputs used in break-even analysis. The estimate is only as useful as the activity measure and observations behind it. High-low method formula Variable cost per activity unit = (cost at highest activity − cost at lowest activity) ÷ (highest activity − lowest activity). Then calculate fixed component = either selected total cost − variable rate × that observation's activity . Both selected observations should yield the same fixed component before rounding. Choose the extremes by activity, not by total cost. A month with a repair bill can have the highest cost without the highest activity. The rate's units matter: dollars per visit, dollars per machine-hour and dollars per mile are different inputs. Keep the cost scope and time period consistent. A six-month worked example A fictional service business reviews one monthly mixed vehicle-and-logistics cost pool against completed equivalent visits. The invented USD observations below illustrate the method; they are not expected industry costs. The business must first decide whether visits are a reasonable driver, or whether measured mileage would explain this pool better. Illustrative monthly cost observations Month Completed visits Total cost Interpretation A 80 $1,640 Lowest activity B 120 $1,800 Intermediate observation C 160 $1,980 Intermediate observation D 200 $2,120 Intermediate observation E 240 $3,000 Highest cost; investigate abnormal item F 280 $2,440 Highest activity Use month F and month A: ($2,440 − $1,640) ÷ (280 − 80) = $800 ÷ 200 = $4 per visit . The fixed component is $2,440 − ($4 × 280) = $1,320 per month . Check the low point: $1,640 − ($4 × 80) also equals $1,320. The resulting model is estimated monthly cost = $1,320 + $4 × visits . At 220 equivalent visits, the estimate is $1,320 + $880 = $2,200 . A target of 220 lies inside the observed 80–280 activity range, but that alone does not prove the estimate is reliable. Test the model against observations you did not select Check the high-low equation against all six fictional months, USD Month Visits Recorded cost Estimated cost Actual minus estimate A: low activity 80 $1,640 $1,640 $0 B 120 $1,800 $1,800 $0 C 160 $1,980 $1,960 +$20 D 200 $2,120 $2,120 $0 E: highest bill, not highest activity 240 $3,000 $2,280 +$720 F: high activity 280 $2,440 $2,440 $0 Residual = recorded cost − estimated cost. The two selected endpoints fit exactly by construction; the +$720 residual in month E is a reason to investigate the records, not evidence that month E belongs in the endpoint pair. The calculator uses the two observations you select; this table checks the full six-month example. At 240 visits the equation predicts $2,280, whereas month E records $3,000: an unexplained $720 difference. Do not silently discard it. Check repairs, fuel prices, route distances, recording errors, overtime or a different mix of jobs. The example does not establish which explanation is correct. At 160 visits it predicts $1,960 versus $1,980 actual, a $20 difference. A model that exactly fits its two chosen observations can still fit the business poorly. Plot all months and inspect the residuals before using the estimate for an important decision. If the relationship is not approximately linear, use a better driver, a separated cost schedule or an appropriate multi-observation regression rather than claiming the two-point line is accurate. Use the calculator above with your own records Collect comparable activity and total-cost records for the same monthly cost pool. Keep annual and monthly amounts separate. Identify the minimum and maximum activity observations from the full dataset. Enter the cost paired with each observation, even when another month has a higher total bill. Check the variable rate, fixed component and target-period estimate. Investigate a negative rate or negative fixed component rather than assuming it is a real saving. Compare the equation with intermediate observations. Rebuild it when contracts, prices, staffing or the service mix changes. The calculator accepts the two observations you have already selected. It does not inspect your full dataset or identify its extremes automatically. Its default entries reproduce this guide: low activity 80, low cost 1,640, high activity 280, high cost 2,440 and target 220. Currency labels do not convert exchange rates. High-low method in Excel or Google Sheets Put low activity in B2, its cost in C2, high activity in B3, its cost in C3 and target activity in B4. Calculate the rate with =(C3-C2)/(B3-B2) in B6, fixed cost with =C2-B6*B2 in B7 and the estimate with =B7+B6*B4 in B8. Require complete numeric inputs and B3 greater than B2 before evaluating these formulas. Do not use MAX on the cost column to choose the high observation. For a full dataset, select the row with maximum activity and the row with minimum activity, preserving the corresponding costs. If several months tie at the same extreme activity but have different costs, investigate the differences and document a defensible treatment; the two-point method does not decide it for you. How this changes your break-even inputs If the selected cost pool truly consists of $1,320 monthly fixed cost plus $4 per completed visit, include $1,320 in fixed overhead and $4 in variable cost per visit. Do not also add the full vehicle cost as another monthly expense. The remaining business costs still need to be included. For an independent fictional example, assume $100 price, $56 other variable costs, and $6,680 other monthly fixed costs. Adding this pool gives variable cost $60, contribution $40 and fixed costs $8,000. Operating break-even is 200 visits . This calculation assumes the entire combined cost model remains valid at 200 visits and does not forecast demand. See fixed, variable and mixed costs , the contribution income statement and the break-even calculation guide . When not to rely on high-low Abnormal endpoints: a shutdown, unusual repair or promotion can distort either selected point. Changing prices or methods: inflation, supplier changes, a new route or new equipment can mean observations no longer describe the same relationship. Step costs: another vehicle or supervisor changes the fixed component. One straight line is then misleading. Mixed activity: a short visit and a complex installation are not equivalent just because both are recorded as one job. Extrapolation: a target outside the observed activity interval has no endpoint support. Even an inside-range estimate needs the other checks. For high-stakes pricing or staffing, reconcile actual records and compare more observations. A negative fixed component can be a symptom of a poor driver or changing cost behavior; it is not negative rent. A zero rate is mathematically possible, but means the selected points provide no evidence of a positive variable component. Method and source OpenStax's fixed and variable cost equation lesson explains selecting the highest and lowest activity levels and using the associated costs. This article's six-month records and business scenarios are original fictional examples. Choose the next cost-planning step Review the activity driver before applying this equation to another service mix. Carry a defensible fixed/variable split into a flexible budget to compare actual cost at actual activity, or into contribution margin to test what each sale leaves. Do not subtract both the original mixed-cost bill and its estimated components. Frequently asked questions Which observations does the high-low method use? Use the highest and lowest activity levels and their corresponding total costs, not the highest and lowest cost amounts. What is the high-low cost formula? Variable rate equals the change in selected costs divided by the change in activity. Fixed cost equals selected total cost minus rate times that activity. Estimated total cost equals fixed cost plus rate times target activity. Can high-low produce a negative fixed cost? Yes mathematically, but a negative intercept needs investigation. It can indicate a poor driver, abnormal endpoint, changing prices or a nonlinear relationship. Is high-low more reliable than regression? It uses only two observations and ignores the remaining observations when fitting the line. Appropriate regression can use more data, but still requires checking assumptions, outliers and the cost driver. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Restaurant Cash Flow Forecast: A 13-Week Worked Example Published October 18, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a restaurant cash flow forecast with a 13-week example. Check payroll, supplier dates, card payouts and minimum cash before a shortfall arrives. Restaurant cash flow Cash flow projection Payroll timing 13-week forecast How to forecast restaurant cash flow Start with reconciled opening cash, add deposits when they are expected in the bank, and subtract payments when they must be funded. Carry that balance forward each week; compare the lowest balance with a minimum you have chosen from your obligations. In this fictional example, week 4 ends with $3,500 against an $8,000 planning floor: $4,500 below the target. A positive quarter-end balance does not resolve that earlier gap. Inspect the 13-week schedule , check the daily payroll low point , or build your own dated forecast in the existing tool . The tool does not automatically load this example. AI-generated editorial illustration of restaurant cash planning; not a real customer or financial record. A restaurant cash flow forecast maps when money is expected to reach and leave the bank. A restaurant cash flow projection is the same forward-looking schedule here; a cash flow statement reports a completed period. It connects service sales to card settlements, supplier due dates, payroll funding and other commitments. Use actual payment dates: a profitable month can still contain a day when the bank balance is too low to fund payroll. This guide builds one fictional US-dollar counter-service restaurant forecast over 13 weeks. The amounts, payment calendar and $8,000 minimum balance are invented planning assumptions, not restaurant benchmarks or a recommended reserve. The method can be adapted to another currency; US payment-provider examples are identified separately. The restaurant cash flow forecast formula Closing cash = opening cash + cash receipts − cash payments. Carry the closing balance into the following week. Then calculate headroom = closing cash − your chosen minimum cash balance . A negative headroom means the forecast falls below that planning floor, even when the bank balance is positive. A negative closing balance is an unfunded requirement, not permission to overdraw. For a restaurant, forecast receipts from cash deposits, card settlements, delivery-platform payouts, catering collections and other confirmed inflows. Forecast payments from the supplier ledger, payroll funding calendar, lease, utilities, loan schedule and other commitments. Depreciation is not a cash payment. An inventory payment or loan-principal payment can use cash even though it is not the same period's operating expense. Start with six records you can reconcile Opening bank position: reconcile the included accounts, outstanding payments and any genuinely restricted cash. Record which accounts are included; transfers between them are not new income. POS sales and tender split: separate physical cash, cards, delivery platforms and credit catering invoices. Keep food sales, sales tax, tips, refunds and discounts distinguishable. Processor settlement reports: match gross transactions, deductions, refunds, disputes and the deposits expected in the bank. Check the current payout settings rather than assuming sales settle immediately. Supplier payment schedule: list invoice amounts and agreed due dates, including opening unpaid bills. A food-cost percentage can estimate purchasing needs, but it does not establish when a supplier is paid. Payroll funding calendar: include wages and employer costs on the dates cash is needed. If net wages, withheld amounts and remittances are listed separately, reconcile them to the gross payroll so they are counted once. Nonweekly commitments: add rent, insurance renewals, equipment, loan principal and interest, tax remittances and owner withdrawals in the appropriate periods. Choose a consistent gross or net cash convention. For example, if card deposits enter the forecast after processing fees, do not subtract those fees again. If receipts include collected sales tax and tips, include the associated payments once. If you exclude a ring-fenced balance from opening cash, do not treat the same amount as a new reserve deduction. These are reconciliation rules; actual payroll and tax obligations depend on the business. Turn restaurant sales into bank receipts The restaurant sales forecast estimates orders, average checks and service days. A cash projection asks a different question: which week's bank deposits will those sales generate? Build a settlement bridge by channel before adding receipts to the cash schedule. Suppose $10,000 of card transactions is expected to generate $9,700 after hypothetical $300 deductions. If $7,700 arrives this week and $2,000 next week, enter those deposits in their respective weeks. Do not also enter the $10,000 as immediate cash. Reconcile the unsettled $2,000 and the deductions to the processor report. These invented figures are not a payment-provider fee quote. Square's US transfer-options documentation , checked October 18, 2026, explains that transfer timing varies with the selected option, cutoff, weekends and holidays. Use the schedule shown in your own account and bank records. Another processor or delivery marketplace may use a different cycle; an assumed faster payout is not available cash. Catering deposits and gift-card sales also require care. A receipt today can fund a future service obligation without representing earned revenue today. When an earlier deposit is applied to an event or a gift card is redeemed, do not enter the same cash again. Retain a separate liability and fulfillment record instead of treating every receipt as free-to-spend profit. A complete 13-week restaurant cash flow example Opening cash is $18,000 . Payroll funding is $18,000 every second week , including the employer costs assumed for this example. Supplier payments vary by week. Other payments include $4,000 operating payments and $1,500 owner drawings each week, plus $6,000 rent in weeks 1, 5, 9 and 13. Week 4 also contains a $6,500 sales-tax remittance and an $8,500 equipment purchase. Owner drawings are separate from employee payroll. The fictional receipt estimates are bank/cash deposits after processor deductions and include the collected sales tax relevant to the scheduled remittance. The example assumes no tips and no additional financing, tax, refunds or other flows beyond those stated. An actual forecast must add every applicable line, including opening liabilities and remittances beyond this horizon. Week numbers are relative planning periods; the invented four-week rent pattern is not a calendar-month schedule. Replace it with the dates in your lease. A zero row means none is assumed here, not that the cost is unnecessary. Hypothetical restaurant cash forecast; minimum planning balance $8,000 Week Opening Receipts Suppliers Payroll Other payments Closing Headroom 1 $18,000 $22,000 $7,000 $0 $11,500 $21,500 $13,500 2 $21,500 $24,500 $7,500 $18,000 $5,500 $15,000 $7,000 3 $15,000 $20,500 $7,000 $0 $5,500 $23,000 $15,000 4 $23,000 $27,000 $8,000 $18,000 $20,500 $3,500 -$4,500 5 $3,500 $26,500 $8,000 $0 $11,500 $10,500 $2,500 6 $10,500 $28,500 $8,500 $18,000 $5,500 $7,000 -$1,000 7 $7,000 $27,000 $8,000 $0 $5,500 $20,500 $12,500 8 $20,500 $29,000 $9,000 $18,000 $5,500 $17,000 $9,000 9 $17,000 $28,000 $8,500 $0 $11,500 $25,000 $17,000 10 $25,000 $30,000 $9,000 $18,000 $5,500 $22,500 $14,500 11 $22,500 $29,500 $9,000 $0 $5,500 $37,500 $29,500 12 $37,500 $31,000 $9,500 $18,000 $5,500 $35,500 $27,500 13 $35,500 $32,000 $9,500 $0 $11,500 $46,500 $38,500 Week 4 demonstrates the issue: $23,000 + $27,000 − $8,000 − $18,000 − $20,500 = $3,500 . Its $20,500 other-payments total is $5,500 regular payments + $6,500 tax + $8,500 equipment. Against the chosen $8,000 floor, the shortfall is $4,500 . The quarter ends at $46,500, but that later balance does not fund an earlier payment. Weekly closing balances can hide a midweek funding failure. If Friday deposits are needed for Tuesday's payroll, add a daily schedule around that week. Thirteen weeks is the selected near-term planning window, not a universal rule. A longer lease, seasonal closure or later obligation may require a longer view. Why a positive week can still miss payroll Allocate the same base-case week 4 across five illustrative business days. Start Monday with $23,000. The weekly receipts remain $27,000 and weekly payments remain $46,500; only their order is now visible. Assume no further weekend cash movements in this extract. This is an invented allocation, separate from the later $6,000 payout-delay stress test. Week 4 daily supplement, before any financing Day Receipts Payments Closing cash Monday $0 $8,000 suppliers $15,000 Tuesday $0 $18,000 payroll funding -$3,000 Wednesday $12,000 $6,500 sales-tax remittance $2,500 Thursday $5,000 $8,500 equipment -$1,000 Friday $10,000 $5,500 regular payments $3,500 The weekly closing balance is still $3,500, but Tuesday's payroll funding produces a $3,000 unfunded gap . Reaching the chosen $8,000 floor at that daily low point would instead require $11,000. These are alternative targets, not two amounts to add together. A negative cell is a warning that the plan is not funded; the table does not assume an authorized overdraft or say that payroll can be delayed. A confirmed available funding source or an actually adjustable commitment must be evaluated before that date. When the bank posts several transactions on one day, check their order and cleared availability as well; an end-of-day forecast can still miss an intraday shortfall. Test a payout delay before choosing a response Delay $6,000 from week 4 to week 5. Change only those two receipt cells: week 4 becomes $21,000 and week 5 becomes $32,500. Week 4 closing cash falls from $3,500 to negative $2,500 . Week 5 returns to the original $10,500 because the delayed amount is then received. The amount needed to reach the $8,000 planning floor at the low point is $10,500. Reaching zero instead would require $2,500. Do not add both as separate funding needs. Separately, move an uncommitted equipment purchase. In the original base case, moving the $8,500 purchase from week 4 to week 7 raises week 4 closing cash to $12,000. The lowest weekly closing balance becomes $12,000; week 7 and later closing balances return to their original values after the purchase is paid. The total purchase cost has not disappeared. This is a separate scenario, not combined with the delayed-receipt scenario. Only change a payment date if it can actually change. Confirm supplier terms, service continuity and any cancellation cost before moving a commitment. Do not model delayed wages or statutory payments as an automatic solution. A funding option is not cash until its availability, timing, cost and conditions are confirmed. If a shortfall cannot be resolved, escalate the decision before the affected service week. Reproduce this restaurant cash flow forecast in Excel Create eight columns matching the worked table: A Week, B Opening cash, C Receipts, D Suppliers, E Payroll, F Other payments, G Closing cash, H Headroom . Use row 1 for headings and rows 2–14 for the 13 weeks. Enter the chosen $8,000 minimum in K2 . Enter $18,000 in B2 and the example's receipts and payment amounts as numeric values in C2:F14. G2 = B2+C2-SUM(D2:F2) H2 = G2-$K$2 B3 = G2 Fill G2:H2 down through row 14. Fill B3 down through B14 so each opening cash value references the prior closing balance. Keep negative cash values visible. These English-language formulas may need the separator convention used by your spreadsheet locale. Summary cells for the base-case weekly forecast Cell Meaning Formula / input Example result K2 Chosen minimum cash 8000 $8,000 K3 Lowest weekly closing cash =MIN(G2:G14) $3,500 K4 Gap to the chosen minimum =MAX(0,$K$2-K3) $4,500 K5 Gap to zero cash =MAX(0,-K3) $0 Do not add K4 and K5: they answer different questions. Label the summaries weekly , because they do not include the daily supplement's lower balance. Before changing a scenario, preserve the base case and change only the intended receipt or payment cells. Keep a source reference and due date in a supporting ledger for every grouped payment. The existing cash flow forecast tool and downloadable template offers another way to enter dated cash movements. Its layout is separate from the A:H worksheet above; do not assume that its cells or categories use these exact addresses. Keep cash, the monthly budget and break-even connected A monthly restaurant budget compares planned sales and operating costs with actual results. A cash forecast schedules receipts and payments. The restaurant break-even calculator estimates the service volume needed to cover the entered contribution and monthly funding target; it does not produce this bank-date forecast. Use all three views. Loan proceeds increase cash without becoming restaurant sales. Loan principal and equipment purchases reduce cash without automatically becoming current operating expenses. Depreciation affects an accounting profit measure without creating the same cash payment that week. Owner drawings use cash but are different from paying a wage for work. Define these boundaries before comparing results. Improving menu contribution can help future cash generation, but it cannot bring a later settlement into an earlier week by itself. For service economics, continue with restaurant prime cost and delivery-app contribution per order . Keep channel fees consistent between the profit model and the bank receipt bridge. Run a weekly forecast-to-actual review Replace the completed week's estimates with reconciled deposits and payments. Explain material differences as volume, price, cost, missing entry or timing. A late collection is different from a permanently lost sale. Update unsettled card balances, unpaid supplier invoices and payroll funding dates. Recalculate the lowest closing balance and the minimum headroom across every remaining week. Assign an owner and decision date to each action. Keep a dated record of changed assumptions. Add one week at the end so the forecast remains rolling; carry forward later obligations instead of letting them vanish. For a worksheet, use the existing 13-week cash flow forecast tool and template . Opening that tool does not load the restaurant example. Enter your own receipts and payment categories, reconcile any grouped costs, and keep the detailed restaurant ledger as support. Use a daily supplement when weekly totals are too coarse. Sources, method and limits Sources reviewed October 18, 2026. OpenStax's short-term planning chapter explains a cash budget's opening balance, collections, disbursements and rolling periods. The SBA's forecasting explanation emphasizes monitoring business drivers and comparing forecasts with actual results. Square's transfer guidance above supplies a specific payout-timing example, not a promise for every restaurant. The 13-week amounts, planning floor and stress tests are original hypothetical examples constructed for this guide; they are not sourced industry averages or customer results. This is a management planning explanation, not a financial statement, lending offer or tax filing instruction. Replace the assumptions with reconciled business records and review material accounting or funding decisions with the appropriate adviser. Roll the forecast from actual cash and explain each variance A rolling forecast should start its next version from reconciled actual cash, rather than carrying forward last week’s estimate after reality changed. In a separate fictional restaurant week, opening usable cash is $10,000, forecast receipts are $12,000 and forecast payments $11,000, giving forecast closing cash of $11,000. Actual receipts are $10,500 and actual payments $11,400, so actual closing cash is $9,100 . Independent weekly variance bridge; USD Bridge line Effect on closing cash Running balance Original forecast closing — 11,000 Receipts: 10,500 instead of 12,000 −1,500 9,500 Payments: 11,400 instead of 11,000 −400 9,100 Next week opening actual Carry reconciled amount 9,100 Suppose $1,000 of the receipt difference is a documented settlement delay and $500 is genuinely lower receipts; the extra $400 payment is a one-off repair. Move only the $1,000 to its supported later settlement date. Do not add all $1,500 back next week or repeat the repair automatically. A lower sales level may affect later receipts too, so reassess the drivers instead of applying an unexplained plug. Keep thirteen forward weeks after each review Archive the completed week, reconcile its receipts and payments, set the new opening usable balance to actual, update remaining dated events and add a new final week. Exclude unavailable or restricted money consistently at the opening reconciliation; do not subtract the same reserved amount again in every weekly closing formula. Keep deposits that fund future obligations visible with those obligations. Check settlement batches, supplier invoices, payroll dates and the lowest individual day near large payments. An improved weekly close can still hide a morning shortfall. Connect the roll-forward with the recovery-action controls and the restaurant contribution and capacity checks . Higher contribution helps economics, while actual deposit dates determine whether this week’s obligations can be funded. Frequently asked questions How do you forecast cash flow for a restaurant? Start with a reconciled opening bank balance, schedule receipts by settlement date and payments by funding or due date, then roll closing cash forward. Compare every week with a chosen planning floor and check individual days around major payments. Is a restaurant cash flow forecast the same as a sales forecast? No. A sales forecast estimates revenue from orders, average checks and service days. A cash forecast schedules when the related deposits and payments occur, including commitments that are not current operating expenses. Why use a 13-week restaurant cash flow forecast? Thirteen weeks gives this example a near-term weekly planning window. Roll it forward each week, use daily detail for tight payment dates and extend the horizon for obligations or seasonal changes beyond the quarter. How much cash reserve should a restaurant keep? There is no universal amount established by this guide. Its $8,000 floor is fictional. Choose a minimum from actual payment obligations, uncertainty, seasonality and available funding, then test the lowest balance rather than only the quarter-end total. Do you deduct card processing fees twice in a cash forecast? No. If receipts are already net of processing deductions, do not deduct the same fees again. Reconcile gross transactions, deductions, unsettled balances and bank deposits so each cash movement appears once. Can a profitable restaurant run out of cash? Yes. A profitable operating period can still contain an earlier payment-date shortfall. Equipment purchases, loan principal, owner withdrawals, slow settlements and inventory payments can change cash differently from reported operating profit. How do I build a restaurant cash flow forecast in Excel? Use separate columns for opening cash, receipts and cash payments. Closing cash equals opening cash plus receipts minus payments; next week opens with the previous closing balance. Track headroom against a chosen minimum and use a daily supplement when weekly totals hide a funding gap. Which balance opens the next version of a rolling forecast? Use reconciled actual usable cash at the new start date. Explain the difference from the old forecast, update dated events and append a new final week to preserve the forward horizon. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: E-commerce BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How to Calculate Cost of Goods Sold: Inventory to Profit Published October 13, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate COGS from opening inventory, net additions and closing stock. Check a $30,000 example, supplier credits, freight, losses and the gross-profit bridge. Calculate COGS from your stock records Use inventory at cost from the same reporting period. Beginning inventory plus net inventory additions gives cost available for sale. Subtract ending inventory to estimate COGS. Enter net additions after supplier credits, with eligible inbound costs included once. Beginning inventory at cost (USD) Net inventory additions at cost (USD) Ending inventory at cost (USD) Cost available for sale $16,000.00 · Estimated COGS $10,000.00 Convert COGS to gross profit and gross margin E-commerce Inventory costing Working capital Worked examples Quick answer For the simplified periodic reseller case, COGS = beginning inventory + net inventory additions − ending inventory. Here, $12,000 + $29,000 − $11,000 = $30,000 COGS. Net additions already include the stated purchase credits and inbound freight. Separate losses or other inventory movements need their own reconciliation, and stock must be valued at cost under a consistent method. Illustrative editorial scene for this guide; use your own business records. Start with stock ownership, the period cutoff and a consistent inventory-cost policy. Reconcile opening stock to the prior closing record and counted ending stock to the ledger. Cash paid to suppliers and selling prices are not substitutes for those cost records. This guide builds a periodic inventory calculation for a small retailer or ecommerce seller. It then connects that calculation to gross profit, order contribution and inventory cash. All USD figures are hypothetical examples. Manufacturing, tax inventory rules and service cost reporting can require different treatments; this worksheet is a management explanation rather than a filing method. Quick answer: the cost of goods sold formula Cost of goods sold = beginning inventory + net inventory additions − ending inventory , provided there are no separately recorded losses or other inventory movements to reconcile. For a simple reseller, net additions can include purchases and inbound freight, less supplier returns, allowances and discounts under the stated costing policy. If beginning inventory is $12,000, net additions are $29,000 and ending inventory is $11,000, the simplified result is $30,000 COGS . Value both inventory balances at cost using a consistent method. Selling prices are not inventory cost. If stock was lost or written down separately, reconcile that adjustment rather than assuming every missing item was sold. Gather the records before calculating Choose the period first: one completed month, quarter or year. Use its opening and closing dates on every inventory report. Beginning inventory should reconcile to the previous period's ending inventory after any documented adjustment. Keep the same locations and ownership boundary in both counts. Records for a periodic reseller worksheet Input Record Check Beginning inventory Opening stock ledger at cost Same costing method and locations as closing stock Purchases received Supplier invoices and receiving records Receipt/ownership cutoff, not simply the bank payment date Supplier credits Returns, allowances and discount records Deduct each adjustment once Inbound freight Carrier and landed-cost records Do not add freight already inside the purchase/stock cost Ending inventory Counted units and unit costs Investigate damaged, missing and returned stock Other movements Write-offs, transfers and owner withdrawals Explain movements outside ordinary sales A purchase order alone is not proof stock belongs in the period. Goods in transit, consigned stock and returns awaiting inspection need a consistent ownership and cutoff policy. If stock is kept by a fulfillment provider, reconcile its units with your own ledger; do not omit it just because it is outside your building. Transfers between your own included locations should not become new purchases twice. Worked example: purchases are not the same as COGS Assume the period begins with $12,000 inventory at cost. Supplier purchases are $30,000, supplier returns are $1,500, recognized purchase discounts are $500 and additional inbound freight is $1,000. None of those adjustments is already included in another line. There are no separately recorded losses, manufacturing costs or owner withdrawals in this first example. Illustrative inventory reconciliation Line Calculation Amount Beginning inventory Opening stock at cost $12,000 Net additions $30,000 − $1,500 − $500 + $1,000 $29,000 Goods available $12,000 + $29,000 $41,000 Ending inventory Counted remaining stock at cost $11,000 COGS $41,000 − $11,000 $30,000 The business purchased $30,000 of merchandise, but that coincidence does not make purchases a substitute for the calculation. Change closing inventory to $14,000 while holding the other inputs unchanged and COGS becomes $27,000. Change it to $8,000 and the simplified inventory outflow becomes $33,000. Investigate why the stock balance changed before describing all of that difference as additional sales. Now suppose sales before customer discounts and refunds were $50,000. Customer refunds reduce sales by $3,000 and discounts by $2,000, leaving $45,000 net sales. With the first $30,000 COGS result, gross profit is $15,000 and gross margin is $15,000 ÷ $45,000 × 100 = 33.33% . That is not net profit or available cash. Separate supplier returns, customer refunds and shipping costs Supplier returns and customer returns are different transactions. A supplier credit reduces the purchase cost or other relevant inventory amount under your records. A customer refund reduces sales revenue. A customer-returned item may also return to inventory at an appropriate recoverable cost after inspection; a refund by itself does not prove the product is saleable again. If inspected customer-returned stock is already included in the $11,000 ending balance, do not deduct its recovered inventory cost a second time from the worksheet. If the product is destroyed, retain evidence of the loss and apply your reporting policy consistently. Return labels, inspection work and unrecovered payment charges are additional costs with their own boundaries. In this reseller worksheet, inbound freight brings goods into inventory. Shipping the completed order to a customer is tracked separately for the contribution comparison. A company's financial-statement classification may differ, so name the boundary on the report. The return-cost guide explains how refunded sales, recovered stock and unrecovered operating costs interact. Do not automatically put every warehouse, advertising or payment expense into the purchase line. Equally, do not assume COGS is always variable: a manufacturer can assign production labor and overhead to goods. Its work-in-process and finished-goods reconciliation needs more than the basic reseller formula. The gross-versus-contribution guide shows why the classifications can cross. Handle missing stock without counting the loss twice Suppose the first example's records identify $500 inventory cost lost through damage, and the reporting policy presents that loss separately from sold-goods cost. The inventory movement becomes $41,000 − $29,500 sold-goods cost − $500 loss = $11,000 ending stock . Sold-goods cost is $29,500 in that presentation, not $30,000 plus another $500 loss. If the $500 is instead already included within a $30,000 COGS line, do not subtract another $500 expense when reconciling the same inventory movement. The combined cost remains $30,000 in these two simplified presentations. This is an arithmetic boundary check, not a recommendation for where a particular loss must appear on a tax return or financial statement. Separate physical count discrepancies from unit-cost discrepancies. Ten missing units and an outdated cost assigned to ten present units are different problems. Recount expensive items, check unit packs, review transfers and compare the receiving cutoff before changing a margin target. Keep adjustments documented so the next opening balance is traceable. FIFO and weighted-average costing can change the result Consider an independent example with 100 opening units costing $8 each and 100 new units costing $10 each. There are 200 units and $1,800 cost available. The business sells 150 units and retains 50; there are no returns or losses. Same physical units, different stated cost-flow assumptions Method Cost assigned to 150 sold units Ending inventory FIFO 100 × $8 + 50 × $10 = $1,300 50 × $10 = $500 Periodic weighted average 150 × ($1,800 ÷ 200) = $1,350 50 × $9 = $450 Each route reconciles to the same $1,800 total cost. The $50 COGS difference changes reported gross profit by $50 when sales are identical. A perpetual moving average can differ when purchase and sale dates interleave; this table specifically uses a periodic average over all units available. Do not switch methods just to make a weak month look better or assign different cost bases to opening and closing stock. Method selection and changes have reporting and tax implications. Use the policy appropriate to your records and get qualified guidance for a filing decision. This article does not choose a tax inventory method for your business. Copy a COGS worksheet into Excel or Google Sheets Put beginning inventory in B2, purchases in B3, supplier returns/allowances in B4, recognized purchase discounts in B5, additional inbound freight in B6 and ending inventory in B7. For the simple reseller case with no other movements: Net additions in B8: =B3-B4-B5+B6 . Goods available in B9: =B2+B8 . COGS in B10: =B9-B7 . Net sales in B11; gross profit in B12: =B11-B10 . Gross margin in B13: =IF(B11>0,B12/B11,NA()) , formatted as a percentage. These are copyable instructions, not a downloadable file or a new calculator. Add a separate reconciliation for other inventory movements instead of silently forcing them into purchases. A negative COGS result needs investigation of credits, cutoff, valuation and adjustments; it should not be accepted as proof that selling products creates negative cost. Keep source references beside the cells and preserve the completed month's version. If you later correct a count, explain the change and reconcile the following opening balance. Rounding displayed currency to cents should not mean rounding every unit cost before multiplying a large quantity. Connect COGS to contribution and the inventory cash requirement Continue the first example: $45,000 net sales minus $30,000 COGS leaves $15,000 gross profit. Assume this reseller's $30,000 COGS varies with sold volume and contains no fixed production allocation. Suppose $4,000 variable selling costs are not already included in COGS, and monthly fixed operating expenses are $8,000. Contribution is $11,000 and operating profit under these assumptions is $3,000. Interest, taxes and any unentered owner-compensation requirement still need an explicit reconciliation. At a stable $11,000 ÷ $45,000 = 24.4444% contribution ratio, the $8,000 fixed-cost operating threshold is $8,000 ÷ (11,000 ÷ 45,000) = $32,727.27 , rounded for display. This requires the same cost mix and realistic demand. Enter consistent order-level costs in the existing ecommerce break-even calculator ; it does not import this inventory ledger. Inventory cash follows payment dates, while COGS follows the cost assigned to goods sold. Paying a supplier today for stock that remains unsold uses cash without creating the same immediate sold-goods expense. Selling stock bought in a prior month can create COGS without a new purchase payment that month. Use the reorder-point cash guide for the replenishment decision and the working-capital guide for the balance-sheet position. Finish the month with a reconciliation you can repeat Match the opening balance to the prior close. Reconcile units received, sold, returned, transferred and lost. Check supplier credits and landed costs for duplicate entries. Value closing stock under the stated method and document count corrections. Reconcile gross profit to contribution and operating profit with each cost counted once. Review stock aging and payment dates alongside the margin result. The result is useful when another person can follow each input back to a record. For the complete store reconciliation, continue with ecommerce profit margins after fees and overhead . For the cost of stock that remains unsold, use inventory holding cost per SKU . Sources and calculation scope The examples and spreadsheet layout were constructed for this guide. Pearson's COGS reference describes inventory reconciliation and cost-flow approaches. OpenStax explains inventory costing . For US filing rules rather than this management worksheet, consult the applicable IRS Publication 334 and a qualified adviser. Source methods do not supply our hypothetical amounts. Can you calculate COGS from a balance sheet or without opening inventory? A closing balance sheet alone does not normally provide purchases and all movements needed to calculate a period’s cost of goods sold. Nor does it establish a missing opening inventory amount. Use the opening stock record, purchase ledger, returns, freight-in policy and closing count for the same goods and period. Independent fictional stock bridge, USD; no other adjustments Known amounts Calculation Result Opening stock 10,000; purchases 42,000; closing stock 12,000 10,000 + 42,000 − 12,000 COGS 40,000 COGS 40,000; closing stock 12,000; opening stock 10,000 40,000 + 12,000 − 10,000 Purchases 42,000 The reverse purchases formula works only when the cost scope has no omitted returns, transfers, freight or other adjustments. If opening stock is unknown, the answer remains unverified. Enter zero only when evidence establishes that there was no opening stock, as can happen at the start of a genuinely new operation. “Unadjusted COGS” and “variable COGS” refer to specific costing conventions, not alternative spellings of the simple reseller roll-forward. A manufacturer’s applied-overhead adjustment needs its own schedule. A service business may have delivery costs without merchandise inventory. Keep those scopes separate rather than putting selling-price inventory, advertising or the same loss into the formula twice. See restaurant food consumption for a sector-specific inventory-to-sales example. Reconcile the inventory cost record to the ledger Preserve the opening inventory, supported purchases and closing inventory evidence behind this calculation. A monthly bookkeeping close helps identify missing supplier documents; the general ledger working record traces the related postings. Production equipment depreciation may form part of inventory cost under the applicable policy, while other depreciation may be a period expense. Document that classification before comparing costs, and avoid adding an amount already included in inventory or overhead a second time. Apply this result to the next decision Check the inventory valuation method before comparing periods. Reconcile returns against net revenue and the order-level return allowance . A customer refund reverses revenue, while a resellable return may also restore inventory; record the two effects once in the correct period. Frequently asked questions What is the basic cost of goods sold formula? For a simple reseller with no separately recorded inventory movements, COGS equals beginning inventory plus net additions minus ending inventory. Reconcile losses, transfers and other adjustments before treating the full stock outflow as sold-goods cost. Are purchases the same as cost of goods sold? No. Purchases add stock, while COGS measures cost assigned to goods sold. Unsold inventory remains in the closing balance, and supplier credits or landed costs can change net additions. Should inventory be valued at selling price? No. Use the appropriate consistent cost valuation for this worksheet. Selling prices belong in the sales calculation; mixing retail value with purchase cost produces a misleading COGS result. How do customer returns affect COGS? A refund reduces sales revenue, while inspected recoverable goods may return to inventory at an appropriate cost. If the returned stock is already included in closing inventory, do not deduct its recovered cost again. Does COGS include delivery and advertising? This reseller example tracks outbound fulfillment and advertising separately for contribution. Financial-statement classifications can differ; state your policy, and include each cost once rather than assuming every business uses the same boundary. Can I estimate COGS without a stock count? An estimate based on a cost ledger or historical gross margin can be useful provisionally, but it is not a verified physical count. Identify the estimate, its assumptions and the later reconciliation instead of treating an old margin percentage as proof. Does a lower COGS percentage mean more available cash? Not necessarily. Gross margin can improve while cash is tied up in unsold stock or receivables. Review purchase payments, collection dates and inventory movements alongside the margin. Can service businesses use this inventory formula? Only for a relevant inventory component with matching records. A pure service cost-of-sales calculation usually needs its own labor and delivery-cost boundary rather than pretending all service expenses flow through merchandise stock. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
