documents.text: Break-Even Concepts BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How to Calculate Working Capital: Formula and Examples Published October 13, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate working capital as current assets minus current liabilities. Check the $24,000 example, operating capital differences and the free Excel worksheet. Working capital Financial statements Cash planning Worked examples Quick answer Working capital = current assets − current liabilities at the same reporting date. The fictional balance sheet below has $62,000 current assets and $38,000 current liabilities, giving $24,000 working capital. Only $8,000 of the assets is cash. Operating working capital and days working capital use different account and period definitions; do not substitute either for this balance-sheet subtraction. Choose the working-capital calculation Term Definition to establish Avoid Net working capital Current assets minus current liabilities Using all assets and all liabilities Operating working capital Specified operating current assets minus specified operating current liabilities Silently including cash or financing debt in an operating-only definition Days working capital Defined average working capital divided by matching-period revenue, multiplied by days Mixing a closing snapshot with an unexplained annual denominator Total operating capital Definition can include long-term operating assets Treating it as a synonym for current working capital Illustrative editorial scene for this guide; use your own business records. Working capital formula: current assets minus current liabilities Working capital = current assets − current liabilities. At the same balance-sheet date, $62,000 of current assets less $38,000 of current liabilities gives $24,000 net working capital . Use current balances, not total assets or total liabilities. The amount is a liquidity snapshot, not profit or immediately spendable cash. Follow the three calculation steps , inspect the complete balance sheet , or download the free Excel worksheet . All example amounts are fictional USD planning assumptions, not industry benchmarks. Download the editable working-capital worksheet Download the free Excel working-capital worksheet . It starts with this guide’s fictional $62,000 current assets and $38,000 current liabilities. The result is $24,000 working capital, a 1.63 current ratio and a 0.79 quick ratio, rounded for display. The workbook calculates one balance-sheet snapshot. It does not connect to a bank or prove that payroll and supplier dates are funded. Every amount needs a numeric value, including an explicit zero when a category is absent. Blank or negative required inputs make the affected results unavailable instead of silently treating them as zero. See the worksheet cell map and instructions · Review the worked example · Check payment timing How to calculate working capital in 3 steps Add current assets. In the fictional snapshot, $8,000 cash + $22,000 net customer receivables + $30,000 inventory + $2,000 prepayments = $62,000. Use the balance-sheet classifications appropriate to the business and report date. Add current liabilities. $18,000 supplier payables + $6,000 accrued wages + $4,000 taxes payable + $10,000 current debt = $38,000. Include the current portion of longer-term debt when applicable; do not include its entire noncurrent balance. Subtract and label the result. $62,000 − $38,000 = $24,000 net working capital . Record the reporting date and currency, then check which assets can fund the payments as they become due. These figures come from the same balance-sheet example below . Do not substitute total assets or total liabilities: buildings and noncurrent debt do not belong in these current-account totals. Current classification follows the applicable reporting rules, including the normal operating cycle where relevant. What does a positive, zero or negative result mean? Independent scenarios using the same $38,000 current liabilities, USD Current assets Current liabilities Working capital Interpretation 62,000 38,000 24,000 Positive net current assets; still check realization and payment dates 38,000 38,000 0 Equal totals; no net balance-sheet cushion under this definition 30,000 38,000 −8,000 Current liabilities exceed current assets; investigate timing, funding and asset quality Zero working capital is different from zero liabilities. If liabilities are zero and current assets are $62,000, working capital is $62,000; the current ratio has a zero denominator and is unavailable. A negative working-capital result is mathematically valid and does not by itself establish insolvency. Start with a balance sheet and reconciled detail Use the same reporting date for assets and liabilities. A quarter-end inventory value combined with today's payable balance is not a consistent snapshot. Reconcile cash to the bank, receivables to the customer ledger, stock to counted inventory and obligations to the payable, payroll, tax and debt records. Records behind the working-capital calculation Balance Record to check Question to resolve Cash Reconciled bank balances Is any balance restricted or already earmarked? Trade receivables Invoice ledger and allowance records Which amounts are collectible, disputed or overdue? Inventory Units and consistent cost valuation Which stock is saleable and how soon might it sell? Prepaid/other current assets Supporting schedule Will this create cash, or merely reduce a future expense? Current obligations Supplier, payroll, tax and financing schedules What is due and on which date? For the usual simplified classification, current items relate to the next year or operating cycle. Use your applicable accounting classification when the operating cycle or financing arrangements are different. Long-term equipment is not made a current asset because you hope to sell it quickly. Conversely, the current portion of a long-term borrowing belongs among current obligations when your reporting rules classify it that way. Do not net every balance informally. A tax refund expected later and a tax payment due tomorrow can have different cash timing even when they seem to offset. Keep restrictions and currency differences visible; translate currencies consistently for the financial snapshot and schedule cash in the currency in which it must be paid. Worked example: $24,000 working capital and only $8,000 cash Assume the following reconciled balance sheet. Receivables and inventory are already stated at the values appropriate to this illustrative report; there are no other current items. One reporting-date snapshot Current assets Amount Current liabilities Amount Cash $8,000 Supplier payables $18,000 Customer receivables $22,000 Accrued wages $6,000 Inventory $30,000 Taxes payable $4,000 Prepaid expenses $2,000 Current debt $10,000 Total $62,000 Total $38,000 Working capital is $62,000 − $38,000 = $24,000 . The business has more current assets than current liabilities at this date. However, $54,000 of current assets is outside cash. Receivables require collection, inventory requires sale or another realization, and the prepaid amount is a benefit already purchased rather than a bank balance. This is why a healthy-looking difference cannot replace a cash forecast. The quality and timing of the current assets matter as much as the headline total. Compare the position with the actual due dates and the reliability of expected receipts. Compare working capital with the current and quick ratios The current ratio uses the same totals but a different operation: current assets ÷ current liabilities . Here it is $62,000 ÷ $38,000 = 1.63 , rounded. Working capital is a dollar difference; the current ratio is a ratio. They should not share the same cell label. For a stricter liquidity check in this guide, quick assets include cash and collectible trade receivables, and would include eligible short-term liquid investments if present. We exclude inventory and prepaid expenses. Quick assets here are $30,000, and the quick ratio is $30,000 ÷ $38,000 = 0.79 , rounded. Other published quick-ratio variants use different exclusions, so preserve the definition when comparing results. No single ratio guarantees that every bill can be paid. A mostly cash business with fast stock turnover differs from a slow project business with long credit terms. A ratio improvement created by doubtful receivables is different from an improvement created by cleared cash. If current liabilities are zero, these division-based ratios are undefined; working capital itself still equals current assets. Use a dated cash test before spending the reported cushion Return to the $8,000 bank balance. Suppose $6,000 payroll is due on day one, a $7,000 supplier payment on day two and $4,000 taxes on day three. A $12,000 customer receipt clears on day five. Assume no other transactions and that the receipt is not available early. Illustrative payment calendar despite positive working capital Event Receipt Payment Closing cash Opening — — $8,000 Day 1: payroll $0 $6,000 $2,000 Day 2: supplier $0 $7,000 −$5,000 Day 3: tax $0 $4,000 −$9,000 Day 5: collection $12,000 $0 $3,000 The negative balances identify an unfunded requirement; the table does not assume an overdraft is available. The lowest modeled balance is −$9,000. If the owner separately chooses a $3,000 reserve, the schedule requires $12,000 additional available cash or a verified change in receipt/payment timing to preserve it. That reserve is an illustrative choice. Ending with $3,000 does not erase the earlier shortage. Confirm timing with the relevant parties before moving a payment or treating an expected collection as certain. The weekly cash forecast guide provides a rolling layout; expand tight weeks into individual dates. The cash runway calculator models constant monthly flows and is not a substitute for this event calendar. Why better cash availability may leave working capital unchanged Consider each following transaction independently from the original $62,000/$38,000 snapshot. Assume no new profit, fee or valuation adjustment. Separate the cash movement from the net working-capital movement Transaction Cash effect Working-capital effect Collect $12,000 receivable Cash rises; receivables fall equally Stays $24,000 Buy $6,000 inventory for cash Cash falls; inventory rises equally Stays $24,000 Pay $7,000 current supplier payable Cash falls by $7,000 Assets and liabilities both fall; stays $24,000 Receive $5,000 short-term borrowing Cash rises by $5,000 Current assets and liabilities both rise; stays $24,000 Collecting an invoice can make payroll easier without increasing the net balance-sheet amount. Buying stock for cash can make payroll harder without reducing it. Financing can change payment timing and liquidity while also creating an obligation. These are classification illustrations, not financing recommendations. If instead a $6,000 inventory write-down is recognized with no offsetting current item, working capital falls to $18,000 while cash remains $8,000 at that moment. A loss of asset value and a cash payment are different events. Check required allowance or valuation adjustments before relying on an old balance. Operating working capital formula and worked example Operating working capital = operating current assets − operating current liabilities. The important step is defining the included accounts. A narrow trade measure and a broader operating measure can both be useful, but their amounts cannot be compared without a bridge. Three definitions from the same fictional balance sheet, USD Measure Included calculation Result Net working capital All current assets 62,000 − all current liabilities 38,000 24,000 Trade working capital Receivables 22,000 + inventory 30,000 − trade payables 18,000 34,000 Operating working capital: selected broader scope Receivables 22,000 + inventory 30,000 + operating prepayments 2,000 − trade payables 18,000 − accrued operating wages 6,000 30,000 For this broader operating illustration, assume the existing $4,000 taxes-payable balance is entirely income tax and is excluded from the selected operating measure. Cash and interest-bearing current debt are also excluded. Other reports may include different operating balances, customer advances or tax items. Document the policy and use it consistently; this example does not make those classifications universal. The bridge is $24,000 net working capital − $8,000 cash + $10,000 current debt + $4,000 excluded income tax payable = $30,000 operating working capital . Starting from the trade measure instead gives $34,000 + $2,000 operating prepayments − $6,000 operating wage accruals = $30,000. No cash was created by changing the definition. Original comparison. Different account boundaries explain the different totals. The Wall Street Prep operating working capital guide describes the operating-account formula. Our account bridge and amounts above are original fictional examples. The existing Excel worksheet calculates the net balance, current ratio and quick ratio; it does not automatically calculate this broader operating subtotal. Is total operating capital the same as operating working capital? Not necessarily. In some investment and valuation models, total operating capital also includes net long-term operating assets. Read the model's definition rather than treating “operating capital” as a synonym for the current-account measure. This guide's $30,000 is the explicitly scoped operating working capital amount, not a valuation or total-capital calculation. For inventory and invoice timing, continue to COGS and stock valuation and days sales outstanding . Use the operating cash flow sign rules when reconciling period changes rather than comparing one balance-sheet snapshot. Days working capital equation: use an average and a matching period Days working capital = average working capital ÷ net revenue for the period × days in that period. A simple two-date average is (opening working capital + closing working capital) ÷ 2. State whether the numerator uses net or operating working capital. For seasonal or volatile balances, more frequent observations can be more representative than two endpoints. Separate full-year example using 365 days and $440,000 net revenue, USD Measure Opening balance Closing balance Average Days calculation Net working capital 20,000 24,000 22,000 22,000 ÷ 440,000 × 365 = 18.25 days Selected operating working capital 26,000 30,000 28,000 28,000 ÷ 440,000 × 365 = 23.23 days The opening balances and full-year revenue are additional fictional assumptions, not amounts implied by the one-date worksheet. The same period and account policy must apply throughout. A 90-day analysis uses that period's revenue and 90 days, rather than combining quarterly revenue with 365. At zero revenue the ratio is unavailable. Negative working capital can produce negative days; it is not evidence that customers literally pay a negative number of days later. This is a balance-to-sales measure, not the time available before cash runs out and not a prediction of an individual receipt date. The cash conversion cycle uses inventory days + receivable days − payable days , with its own denominators. It is a different calculation. A lower working-capital-days result can reflect changed financing, customer advances or seasonality as well as operating efficiency. The days working capital reference sets out the average-balance formula. Our calculations use a declared definition and explicit periods. Use the dated cash forecast to test actual payment coverage. Change in working capital: separate the balance from the cash-flow adjustment Change in working capital = closing balance − opening balance , using the same account scope. In the full-year net example, $24,000 − $20,000 = a $4,000 increase. In the selected operating example, $30,000 − $26,000 = a $4,000 increase. These examples happen to have equal changes; differently defined balances do not always move together. In a clean operating cash reconciliation, an increase in the selected net operating assets generally absorbs cash; a decrease releases cash. Do not automatically subtract the change in all net working capital: that amount includes cash and may include financing debt or accounts needing different treatment. Remove acquisitions, exchange effects, write-offs, reclassifications and other noncash changes where applicable. If receivables fall by $5,000 because a customer actually pays, cash rises by $5,000 and standard net working capital stays unchanged. The narrow trade and selected operating balances fall by $5,000. A $5,000 receivable write-off would not produce the same cash receipt. The direct and indirect OCF example shows a complete period reconciliation; the cash flow statement guide connects operating cash with investing and financing. Test the working-capital effect of faster growth In an independent steady-sales scenario, a service business makes $60,000 net credit sales over 30 days, or $2,000 per day. At a modeled 30-day receivable cycle, the associated balance is $60,000. At 45 days it is $90,000: $30,000 more sales value remains in receivables under unchanged daily sales. This is an exposure estimate, not automatically $30,000 of extra payroll cost or a guaranteed financing need. A cash forecast must include actual margins, payroll, supplier dates, deposits, tax payments and existing cash. Growth can create more receivables before collections catch up even when each job has positive contribution. For ecommerce, larger purchase batches may tie up cash before stock sells. A discount that moves stock can also reduce contribution or increase fulfillment cost. Check replenishment cash and holding-cost economics together rather than optimizing one balance alone. Working capital analysis: turn the number into a decision Questions to ask after calculating the balance Check Evidence to review Decision supported Asset quality Receivable aging, disputes, inventory condition and valuation Which balances are likely to convert to cash? Payment timing Supplier, payroll, tax and principal due dates Can available cash cover the next obligations? Comparable trend Same definitions and comparable seasonal dates Did operations change, or did classification change? Operating investment Receivables, inventory, prepayments and operating liabilities Where is additional sales activity tying up resources? Actual cash conversion Bank receipts and reconciled operating roll-forwards Was cash genuinely released, or was an asset written down? The working-capital balance is not automatically a reserve requirement, a loan limit or a working-capital budget. Estimate future needs from purchasing, customer collections, payroll and payment dates. For an uncovered future payment, use the cash-flow shortfall and recovery example . For the budgeting narrative, connect the verified schedules to your business plan . Download the definition bridge and days examples (CSV) . This additional download contains the three scoped balances, independent result scenarios and average/days calculations as values. It has no formulas and does not recalculate after editing. The separate existing Excel worksheet remains the editable net-working-capital snapshot. Use the editable worksheet and preserve the account definitions Open the working-capital XLSX worksheet and replace the amber cells. The file contains one worksheet, so the inputs, subtotals and main results remain together. The fictional reporting date is September 30, 2026; replace it with your balance-sheet date. Cell map for the downloadable workbook Cells What to enter or review C3 and C4 Reporting date and currency label. The label does not convert amounts. C13:C18 Cash, net trade receivables, inventory, prepaids, eligible liquid investments and other current assets. C22:C27 Supplier payables, accrued wages, tax, current debt, customer advances and other current liabilities. C19 and C28 Calculated current-asset and current-liability totals. Do not overwrite these formulas. C6:C8 Calculated working capital, current ratio and quick ratio. Use one consistent reporting date and currency. Check the supporting ledgers and classifications before copying balances. Replace all twelve balance inputs, including the sample zero amounts. Enter each item once and add it to the matching category only. Use net collectible receivables and appropriately valued inventory. Keep restricted or otherwise unavailable cash identifiable in your supporting records. Review the quick-asset definition: cash plus net trade receivables plus eligible liquid investments. Inventory, prepaids and other current assets are excluded in this file. Check that totals match your source balance sheet. A complete-input status indicates numeric inputs, not independent verification of the records. Keep a dated copy before starting the next period. Add a separate cash schedule for realization and payment dates. With zero current liabilities, working capital remains equal to current assets while division-based ratios show n.a. . Clearing a required balance produces unavailable affected results. Negative working capital is a valid calculated result when current liabilities exceed current assets; it is not rejected as an input error. The formulas use familiar Excel functions and were recalculated and tested in the workbook authoring engine. If importing into Google Sheets or another application, check that the date stays a date and the formulas, blank handling and ratios behave correctly after conversion. Native Excel and Google Sheets application recalculation have not been independently verified in this review. Actual worksheet preview. Open the XLSX for editable inputs and formula results. For a concise business narrative, use the one-page business plan template . Keep the balance-sheet snapshot and dated cash schedule as supporting work rather than crowding all figures onto the plan. Stress-test the quality of the assets behind the result A correct subtraction can still hide a collection problem. Start with the reported $24,000 net working capital, then keep a separate risk schedule for overdue invoices, damaged stock and restricted cash. Do not assume every dollar classified as current will become available before the next payment. Independent sensitivity using the existing fictional balance sheet, USD Planning check Calculation Result Reported starting position $62,000 current assets − $38,000 current liabilities $24,000 net working capital Potential receivable shortfall 20% × $22,000 net receivables $4,400 less recoverable value Potential inventory shortfall 20% × $30,000 inventory $6,000 less recoverable value Combined downside sensitivity $62,000 − $4,400 − $6,000 − $38,000 $13,600 adjusted planning cushion This is a sensitivity, not an automatic accounting entry or a change to the workbook’s base example. Existing receivables are already net of recorded allowances; apply the assumed additional shortfall once. Actual impairment recognition and current classification follow the reporting framework used for the accounts. The standard reported balance remains $24,000 until the underlying reported amounts change. The bank balance is still $8,000 in this sensitivity. No cash is released by lowering an estimated asset value. Build a dated cash-receipts and payments forecast to test payroll and suppliers, and use the receivable/payable reconciliation to identify which invoices and payment dates drive the gap. Read the three-statement walkthrough to reconcile balances, then compare the liquidity-ratio definitions using the same account scope; a cash-runway estimate answers a different question. A liability balance is not automatically this month’s expense: use the fixed and variable cost guide when modeling the cost of future activity. Turn the result into a specific review Identify the assets that will become usable cash before the next major payments. Review overdue or disputed invoices individually rather than applying an optimistic average date. Check stock aging and upcoming purchase commitments before assuming inventory is liquid. Map payroll, tax, debt and supplier dates against realistic collections. Test the downside case with a delayed receipt and preserve the forecast you compared it with. Positive working capital is a starting position, not spending permission. Negative working capital deserves a close look at timing, turnover, customer advances and current obligations; it does not by itself prove insolvency or establish a financing solution. Use the cash-versus-profit guide to reconcile the different questions. Sources and definition boundaries The scenarios and worksheet are original illustrations. OpenStax's working-capital chapter explains current assets, obligations and liquidity limitations. CFI describes the working-capital formula . BDC's cash-flow planning guidance supports a dated forecast alongside balance-sheet analysis. Keep your applicable reporting classifications and agreement dates separate from these fictional amounts. Apply the next planning step A balance-sheet working-capital total does not tell you whether payroll is due before a customer pays. Enter expected bank dates to inspect the reserve gap. Build a dated 13-week cash flow forecast . Check the investment and its funding need separately Working capital is a balance-sheet measure, not the return on a proposed project. Use incremental receipts and avoidable payments in the business ROI calculator with monthly cash recovery . Opening the calculator does not transfer this guide’s figures; enter your own consistent assumptions. Connect working capital with earnings and cash Read the EBITDA versus operating-cash example to see how receivables, inventory and supplier credit can change cash without the same movement in earnings. Apply this result to the next decision Use financial ratios for a consistently defined current or quick ratio, and the 13-week cash forecast for dated funding needs. Review cash-flow analysis when reconciling movements; a change in a balance-sheet working-capital total is not automatically the operating cash-flow adjustment. Manage working capital and interpret turnover carefully Managing working capital means matching customer collections, stock commitments and supplier payments to the dates cash is available. A positive current-assets-minus-current-liabilities balance does not show whether inventory sells or customers pay before payroll. Review receivable aging, reorder commitments and supplier due dates beside the dated cash forecast . Working-capital turnover = net sales ÷ average net working capital , with average based on consistent opening and closing balances for the sales period. In a separate fictional USD year, opening working capital is $40,000 and closing is $60,000. Average is $50,000; $600,000 net sales ÷ $50,000 = 12 times. That describes sales relative to the average balance, not a collection speed or proof of liquidity. A zero average makes the ratio undefined. A negative or very small average can produce a negative or extremely large ratio that is hard to interpret as efficiency. Compare components and seasonality first; use more frequent averages when two endpoints are unrepresentative. Do not confuse this with inventory turnover or the cash conversion cycle. The financial-ratios calculator uses its stated statement scope; verify which average inputs its selected ratio requires. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate working capital from a balance sheet? Use current assets and current liabilities at the same date, then subtract liabilities from assets. Reconcile their supporting schedules and state the definition used before comparing periods. Is working capital the same as cash? No. It can include receivables, inventory and prepaid expenses as well as cash. A positive balance does not establish that those resources can fund a payment before its due date. What is the difference between working capital and the current ratio? Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities, expressed in money. The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities and expresses a ratio. They use the same snapshot but answer different questions. Is negative working capital always a sign of failure? No. Interpret it with turnover, cash receipts, customer advances and current obligations. It warrants a timing and asset-quality review, but the balance alone neither proves insolvency nor identifies a financing solution. Does collecting an invoice increase working capital? In the simple case, cash rises and receivables fall by the same amount, leaving working capital unchanged. Collection can still improve the ability to pay bills because the asset is now available cash. Does short-term borrowing improve working capital? If it adds cash and an equal current liability with no other changes, the net amount is unchanged. It changes liquidity and creates an obligation; the payment schedule still needs review. How much working capital should a small business keep? There is no universal amount in this guide. Model the operating cycle, asset quality, payment dates and chosen reserve, then test downside receipts and purchasing commitments. Is operating working capital calculated differently? Yes. Standard net working capital is all current assets minus all current liabilities. Operating working capital uses selected operating accounts. The fictional example gives $24,000 net, $34,000 narrow trade and $30,000 under the stated broader operating scope. Reconcile the included accounts before comparing them. Is there a free working-capital Excel worksheet? Yes. Download the editable XLSX from this guide. It includes current-asset and current-liability inputs, working capital, current and quick ratios, and the same fictional example used here. No signup is required. What happens if a worksheet input is blank or current liabilities are zero? Every balance input needs a number, including explicit zeros. Blank or negative required balances make the affected results unavailable. Zero liabilities still allow working capital to be calculated, while current and quick ratios show n.a. What is the formula for calculating current capital? If current capital means net working capital in the report you are reading, subtract current liabilities from current assets at the same reporting date. The standard label in this guide is working capital. Confirm the definition rather than treating every use of capital as the same measure. How do you calculate days working capital? Divide average working capital by net revenue for the same period and multiply by the days in that period. With $22,000 average net working capital, $440,000 annual net revenue and 365 days, the result is 18.25 days. State the account scope and use a representative average. Is total operating capital the same as working capital? Not necessarily. Some models include net long-term operating assets in total operating capital. Working capital concerns the stated current-account scope. Read the definition before using either formula. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How to Calculate Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) Published October 13, 2026 Updated November 7, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate DSO using matched receivables, credit sales and period days. Compare averaging methods and translate late payment into a payroll cash scenario. Agency Cash planning Receivables Worked examples Forecast accounts receivable using DSO: state the closing-balance convention Historical DSO measures receivables relative to credit sales and the matching day count. A forecast can use a chosen receivable-days assumption to estimate a balance, but that does not determine which specific invoices will be collected. Read the worked decision and its assumptions . Illustrative editorial scene for this guide; use your own business records. A client can accept an invoice and still pay after your crew's wages are due. Days sales outstanding helps monitor how much credit sales value remains in receivables, expressed as days of sales. To use it well, match the receivable balance, credit-sales period and day count, then look at the actual invoices behind the result. This guide uses an average-receivables method, explains where other DSO conventions differ, and connects a collection-delay scenario to payroll cash. It is useful for agencies, cleaning contractors and other invoice-based services. The examples are hypothetical USD amounts; they do not set an industry benchmark, predict collections or recommend a credit policy. Quick answer: the days sales outstanding formula DSO = average trade accounts receivable ÷ net credit sales for the same period × days in that period. For a simple two-point average, average receivables = (opening receivables + closing receivables) ÷ 2. With $18,000 opening receivables, $30,000 closing receivables and $90,000 net credit sales over 90 days, average receivables are $24,000. DSO is $24,000 ÷ $90,000 × 90 = 24 days . It is a ratio-based collection indicator, not proof that every customer pays in 24 days. Some reports use closing receivables instead of an average, total revenue instead of credit sales, or a fixed 360/365-day convention. Those can produce different results. This article states a matched-period average method; label a different convention and preserve it across comparisons. Use the receivable and sales records that belong together DSO input register Input Record Check Opening and closing receivables Reconciled trade invoice ledger Same customers, currency and reporting boundary Net credit sales Credit invoices less relevant credits/discounts Exclude cash sales that never create receivables Day count Defined reporting-period dates Monthly sales use monthly days, not an unexplained annual multiplier Due dates and disputes Agreement, approval record and invoice aging Separate contractual due date from expected cleared receipt Adjustments Write-offs, allowances and reclassifications A lower receivable balance may not represent cash collected Exclude balances unrelated to customer credit sales, such as an employee advance or a tax refund, from the trade receivable numerator. Keep customer credits and disputed balances visible. If net credit sales exclude sales tax, align the receivable measure rather than dividing a tax-inclusive balance by a tax-exclusive revenue flow without explaining it. State whether the receivable figure is gross or net of an allowance. A change in allowance can change a net-balance ratio even when no customer payment arrives. Use a consistent reporting definition and examine gross invoice aging alongside any adjusted balance. Do not silently mix a gross opening amount with a net closing amount. Worked example: quarterly DSO with a matched day count Take the 90-day example from the quick answer. All $90,000 sales used in the denominator were made on credit. Opening and closing receivables cover the same trade ledger. There are no unrelated advances or unrecorded adjustments in the numerator. Average-receivables calculation Measure Calculation Result Average receivables ($18,000 + $30,000) ÷ 2 $24,000 Credit sales per day $90,000 ÷ 90 $1,000 DSO $24,000 ÷ $1,000 24 days Period receivable turnover $90,000 ÷ $24,000 3.75 times Equivalent days check 90 ÷ 3.75 24 days The turnover calculation is for this 90-day period. Multiplying it into an annual figure requires a stated annualization assumption; do not label 3.75 as observed annual turnover. The actual calendar quarter might contain a different number of days. This illustration deliberately uses a defined 90-day window. If the business also had $30,000 cash sales, total sales would be $120,000. Dividing by that larger total would produce $24,000 ÷ $120,000 × 90 = 18 days . That lower number mixes sales that did not create these receivables into this credit-collection measure. It does not prove the credit customers paid faster. Calculate monthly and annual DSO without mixing periods For an independent 30-day month, suppose average trade receivables are $12,000 and net credit sales are $30,000. DSO is $12,000 ÷ $30,000 × 30 = 12 days . Use 31 for a defined 31-day month or the actual day count under your documented convention. For an independent 365-day year, $50,000 average receivables and $600,000 net credit sales produce $50,000 ÷ $600,000 × 365 = 30.42 days , rounded. A leap-year or standardized-day convention should be stated. Annual sales should be matched with a representative annual receivable average rather than an unexplained balance from a peak week. Do not take quarter sales and automatically multiply by 365. In the quarterly example, that would show $24,000 ÷ $90,000 × 365 = 97.33 days , a different scaling rather than the stated 90-day-period result. If a report annualizes sales first, reconcile its annualized denominator and day convention explicitly. Check average versus closing receivables and seasonal distortion Using the same quarterly sales but $30,000 closing receivables gives $30,000 ÷ $90,000 × 90 = 30 days . The two-point average gave 24 days. Neither number should be compared with the other as though the balance definition did not change. A two-point average can also miss a billing peak between the endpoints. If a more representative daily average were $25,000 under the same $1,000 daily sales measure, the ratio would be 25 days. Choose a consistent averaging method that fits the available data and show when the method changes. Rapid growth can reduce the ratio before collection habits improve. In a separate monthly example, $24,000 average receivables against $30,000 credit sales over 30 days gives 24 days. If credit sales double to $60,000 while average receivables remain $24,000, the ratio falls to 12 days. New invoices may simply not have reached their collection dates yet. Likewise, a calculation balance falling from $24,000 to $18,000 because of write-offs or a changed allowance would reduce the original 90-day ratio from 24 to 18 days without necessarily adding cash. Explain the balance movement before crediting the collection process. Compare mature cohorts, aging, disputes and actual cleared payments alongside the trend. Separate DSO, overdue days and invoice aging DSO scales receivables by sales. Overdue days measure how long an individual unpaid invoice has passed its due date. Payment duration measures the interval from a defined starting event to an actual receipt. These are related but different measures. In an independent ledger on day 30, invoice A for $6,000 was issued on day zero, due on day 10 and paid on day 20. It is now outside outstanding receivables. Its payment duration was 20 days and its lateness against the stated due date was 10 days. Invoice B for $8,000 is unpaid and was due on day 25: it is five days overdue. Invoice C for $4,000 is unpaid but due on day 40: it is not yet overdue. Outstanding receivables total $12,000, but overdue receivables total $8,000. Calling all $12,000 overdue would misstate the collection problem. For each invoice, retain the service date, allowed submission date, actual issue/approval date, contractual due date and expected clearance date. An approval delay before invoicing can create a payroll cash gap without appearing as overdue invoiced receivables. Work completed but not yet billable requires a separate schedule; DSO alone does not describe that earlier delay. Estimate the cash exposure from a collection-delay change At the quarterly example's stable $1,000 net credit sales per day, a ten-day increase in the modeled collection cycle corresponds to $10,000 additional receivables exposure . A reduction from 24 to 14 days corresponds to the same $10,000 lower balance under the steady-flow assumption. This is a balance estimate, not $10,000 new profit, a recurring monthly saving or cash already collected. It assumes comparable sales and collection behavior. Actual funding needs depend on when invoices clear and when payroll, suppliers, taxes and other obligations are paid. If the lower DSO occurs because credit sales grew, balances were written off or the period changed, do not claim a $10,000 collection release. Reconcile the actual customer receipts and record movements. Use working-capital analysis to view the wider current-asset and obligation position. Translate a late payment into a payroll cash calendar Use an independent service-contract scenario with $4,000 opening available cash. Payroll payments of $3,000 occur on days seven, 14 and 21. One $8,000 customer receipt clears on day 21, before that day's payroll. The owner chooses a $1,000 reserve. There are no other transactions in this simplified schedule. Receipt after the second payroll creates an earlier shortfall Event Receipt Payment Closing cash Opening — — $4,000 Day 7 $0 $3,000 $1,000 Day 14 $0 $3,000 −$2,000 Day 21 $8,000 $3,000 $3,000 The low point is −$2,000, so preserving the chosen $1,000 reserve requires $3,000 additional available cash or a verified scheduling change. The negative balance signals an unfunded requirement; it does not assume borrowing is available. If an agreed change instead makes the same receipt clear on day 12, the day-seven balance remains $1,000, day-12 cash rises to $9,000, day-14 cash falls to $6,000 and day-21 cash ends at $3,000. The reserve is preserved in this alternative. Earlier collection changes the timing, not the contract's total revenue or final cash in this simplified example. Do not assume the client will accept an earlier date or that a revised promise equals cleared funds. The cleaning payroll cash-gap guide develops a fuller event ledger, and the cash forecast guide provides the rolling monthly/weekly context. DSO monitors the collection pattern; those schedules locate the payment-day shortage. Copy the DSO formula into a spreadsheet Put opening trade receivables in B2, closing trade receivables in B3, net credit sales in B4 and period days in B5. Use: Average receivables, B6: =(B2+B3)/2 . DSO, B7: =IF(AND(B4>0,B5>0),B6/B4*B5,NA()) . Period turnover, B8: =IF(B6>0,B4/B6,NA()) . Steady-sales exposure for a proposed days change in B9, B10: =IF(B5>0,B4/B5*B9,NA()) . Enter a positive days change for added receivables exposure or a negative change for a lower modeled balance. The last cell is a scenario, not actual collected money. Keep currency formatting separate from days formatting and label the average method beside the inputs. With zero credit sales, ratio-based DSO is undefined even if old receivables remain outstanding. Report the balance, aging and collection plan instead of showing zero days. Negative sales or credit balances need reconciliation before interpreting this simple formula. These are copyable worksheet instructions; this release does not add a DSO calculator or an account-connected collection system. Review the specific collection bottleneck Confirm work has been accepted and invoices can be issued on time. Separate disputes, missing purchase-order references, approval waits and genuinely overdue amounts. Compare customers under their actual agreed terms rather than applying one universal “good DSO” number. Reconcile cleared receipts and write-offs before interpreting the trend. Update the cash calendar when the expected clearance date changes. For agency work, inspect client concentration alongside payment timing. One large late customer can dominate a small ledger. The agency break-even calculator tests monthly contribution and delivery capacity, while cash runway tests a constant-flow cash scenario. Neither calculates DSO or verifies client payment promises. Sources and measurement convention The examples, cash calendar and worksheet are original illustrations. AccountingTools discusses collection-period calculations and seasonality . OpenStax explains receivable turnover and collection measures . The Association for Financial Professionals defines DSO ; published report conventions vary, so our examples explicitly match sales, average balance and period days. Apply the next planning step DSO is an aggregate measure. Enter realistic dates for individual receipts and test a collection delay without treating the average as a promised payment date. Test collection dates in the cash flow forecast template . Forecast accounts receivable using DSO: state the closing-balance convention For a simplified steady-sales forecast, estimated closing receivables = forecast credit sales ÷ days in the period × assumed closing-receivable days. With fictional monthly credit sales of $90,000, a 30-day month and 20 receivable days, forecast closing AR is $60,000. This uses a closing-balance convention; do not silently substitute it for the historical average-AR method explained above. If opening AR is $50,000 and the model has no write-offs, returns, tax differences, foreign exchange or other adjustments, collections reconcile as $50,000 + $90,000 − $60,000 = $80,000. Forecasting 25 days instead raises closing AR to $75,000 and lowers modeled collections to $65,000. The five-day change ties up another $15,000 under these assumptions. Use only credit sales in this receivables schedule, keep the actual calendar-day count and reconcile any adjustments explicitly. For seasonal sales or a few large late invoices, an invoice-level collection schedule is more informative than a single DSO assumption. Keep forecast days separate from measured historical DSO. Carry collections into the cash forecast Method reference , reviewed October 22, 2026. The worked figures in this section are separate fictional assumptions. Rolling twelve-month DSO is not an unweighted average of monthly DSO For an independent 365-day reporting window, average eligible trade receivables of $100,000 and net credit sales of $1,200,000 give DSO = $100,000 ÷ $1,200,000 × 365 = 30.42 days. State how the average receivables were measured. More frequent observations can represent a seasonal business better than just the opening and closing balance. A separate 30-day month with $100,000 average receivables and $80,000 net credit sales gives 37.5 days. Averaging twelve monthly DSO percentages or day counts without their underlying sales and balance weights does not recreate the twelve-month calculation. Use the actual day count of the declared window; a leap-year window may differ from 365. Do not mix total cash and credit sales in the denominator unless the stated metric intentionally uses that definition. Days overdue concerns invoice terms and aging; DSO concerns the chosen receivables-to-sales measure. Neither a lower DSO nor a forecast receivable balance guarantees that a particular customer will pay before payroll. Link the result to the dated cash forecast and preserve disputed invoices separately. Keep the receivable basis consistent when reviewing collection days Reconcile customer invoices, credits and collections through the accounts receivable process before interpreting a change in days. The allowance rollforward separately explains the difference between gross receivables and their net carrying amount. Keep the receivable basis and credit-sales scope consistent with the stated DSO method and comparable periods. An increase in the allowance does not collect an invoice; investigate credit risk separately from payment speed. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate monthly DSO? Divide average trade receivables by net credit sales for the month and multiply by the stated month days. Keep the average method, sales boundary and day convention consistent. Should I use total sales or credit sales? For this matched credit-collection measure, use net credit sales because cash sales do not create the measured receivables. If another report uses total revenue, label that convention and explain the difference. Should DSO use average or ending receivables? This guide uses average receivables. A closing-balance version is another stated convention and can produce a different result. Preserve the method across trend comparisons and use a representative average when billing is seasonal. What is a good DSO for an agency or cleaning business? Compare your consistent trend with actual agreed payment terms, invoice approval timing and customer mix. This guide does not supply a universal industry target or assume that every invoice has the same terms. Is DSO the same as days overdue? No. DSO expresses a receivable balance in days of sales. Days overdue measure lateness against an individual invoice due date; outstanding invoices can include amounts not yet due. What happens when credit sales are zero? Ratio-based DSO is undefined. Report outstanding balances, aging and collection expectations rather than displaying zero days or assuming the old invoices disappeared. Does a lower DSO always mean faster collection? No. Sales growth, write-offs, allowance changes or a different balance/period convention can lower the ratio without a corresponding cash receipt. Reconcile the movement with actual collections. How do I estimate cash tied up by ten extra collection days? Under stable matched credit sales, multiply daily credit sales by ten. This estimates additional receivables exposure, not profit or cash already collected; a dated payment forecast is needed for the actual funding gap. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Cleaning BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cleaning Contract Cash Gap: Payroll Before Payment Published October 9, 2026 Updated November 3, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Plan cleaning contract cash needs with dated payroll and collection scenarios. Compare delayed payment, early receipts and a reserve before starting work. Cleaning Cash timing Payroll Contract collections AI-generated editorial illustration of this planning topic; not a real customer or business. A cleaning account can leave enough contribution on paper and still create a cash shortage before its first payment arrives. Your crew’s pay dates do not automatically follow the customer’s invoice schedule. Supplies and mobilisation purchases may also fall due before any receipt. This guide builds a dated cash schedule for that gap. It does not set a market price or recommend a loan. Every USD amount below is hypothetical; replace it with your contract, payroll schedule and available cash. Quick answer List the cash available at the start, then place each receipt and payment on its expected date. Carry the balance forward after every event. The lowest balance tells you whether the schedule breaches your chosen reserve. A positive monthly contribution does not establish that payroll can be funded on its actual due date. Choose a funding action from the dated cash forecast A profitable contract can still need cash before the first receipt. Use the dated ledger below to find the lowest balance, then compare the actions that change that date or amount. An invoice due date is not the same as a confirmed collection date. Record the invoice approver, submission requirements, dispute status and expected cleared receipt beside each forecast. Under the existing hypothetical example, $3,000 opening cash and a $1,000 reserve leave a $1,800 funding gap before the week-four receipt. The reserve is a minimum balance you want to preserve, not another expense. Run the following alternatives on the same ledger; they are planning scenarios rather than promises that a customer will accept changed terms. Actions against the existing payroll gap Option Cash effect to test Trade-off Keep original collection timing Opening cash needs $4,800 to retain the $1,000 reserve An extra $1,800 must be available before the low point Receive $2,400 before week two and $2,400 before week four The original ledger stays at or above $1,200 Requires agreed milestone billing and actual cleared receipts Week-four receipt arrives after payroll Required opening cash rises to $5,800 Same sale, another $1,000 of peak funding need Does an early-payment discount improve this specific gap? In a separate test, the client pays the entire $4,800 before week two in exchange for a hypothetical 2% discount. Cash collected is $4,704 and the discount costs $96 of revenue. Starting from $3,000, cash after mobilization is $2,200 and after week-one spending is $1,200. Adding $4,704 before week-two spending then funds the remaining three $1,000 outflows; the lowest balance remains $1,200. This avoids the example's reserve shortfall, but sacrifices $96 before any fee differences. The timing is what changes the gap; the discount itself does not create cash. Compare that $96 with the actual cost and feasibility of other available funding or collection arrangements. Do not accept a discount solely because the contract shows positive contribution. If the customer pays early without a discount, the economics differ again. Keep any funding repayment or cost in its proper cash dates rather than adding borrowed money to sales. Combine contracts before setting the company reserve Put every contract's dated receipts and payroll on one company calendar. Two accounts using the same bank balance cannot each claim all of it. Equally, adding two standalone peak gaps can overstate the company peak if their low points fall on different dates. Choose the company reserve once, then test the combined balance. Reconcile forecast against cleared cash at each payroll run and move late or disputed receipts immediately. Use completed-job cost reconciliation to update payroll assumptions. Keep the existing 13-week forecast and collection guides below for the wider cash plan. Start with payment dates, not invoice totals An invoice is a request for payment. For this schedule, the useful date is when cleared funds are expected to become available. Record when the work is completed, when the invoice can be submitted, whether approval is required and the expected receipt date. A payment term beginning at invoice approval can produce a different gap from one beginning on the service date. Use the agreement and the customer’s actual payment history where available. When either is missing, label the date as an assumption. Keep the contractual due date and a later-payment scenario in separate columns. A promise, an invoice sent and money available in the bank are three different events for this exercise. The Australian government’s cash-flow guidance uses opening cash, incoming payments, outgoing payments and closing cash to help identify shortages. We adapt that structure to weekly and dated cleaning payments; the government source does not supply the fictional cleaning figures used here. Start with cash you can actually use. Exclude money already committed to another payroll, tax payment or supplier bill. Decide whether the schedule covers only this contract or the whole business. A contract-only view helps reveal its funding requirement, but it cannot establish that the entire business has spare cash. Build a small event ledger Use these columns: Date or event Opening cash Cleared receipts Payments Closing cash Assumption Mobilisation Your usable balance Any agreed advance Equipment and setup paid now Opening + receipts − payments Receipt timing verified? Payroll date Previous closing Money available before payroll Payroll and other due items Carry forward Include employer costs? Customer receipt Previous closing Actual expected collection Other payments due Carry forward Due date or historical date? Split events occurring on the same day if their order matters. A customer payment received after payroll cannot fund a debit that already occurred. The event ledger is more useful than a monthly total when timing is tight. List cash payroll payments consistently. Include employer costs on their actual payment dates rather than assuming that the hourly wage represents every cash obligation. Record supplies when paid, not merely when consumed. If you buy a machine at the start, its purchase payment belongs here even if your profitability model treats it differently over time. Use one currency and state whether sales tax is included. Do not treat taxes collected for later remittance as unrestricted surplus without including the corresponding payment in the wider schedule. This is a planning ledger rather than a replacement for your accounting records. Worked example: enough contribution, insufficient early cash Assume a new account brings a $4,800 collection in week four. Mobilisation costs $800 at the start. Cash payroll is $900 each week and supplies paid are $100 each week. Opening usable cash is $3,000. The owner chooses a $1,000 minimum reserve. There are no other receipts or payments in this simplified contract-only example. The week-four receipt is assumed to clear before that week’s $1,000 payment. Event Receipts Payments Closing balance Opening cash — — $3,000 Mobilisation $0 $800 $2,200 Week 1 $0 $1,000 $1,200 Week 2 $0 $1,000 $200 Week 3 $0 $1,000 −$800 Week 4 $4,800 $1,000 $3,000 The reserve is breached in week two. Week three shows a funding shortfall even though the balance returns to $3,000 after collection. The final balance cannot erase the earlier shortage. The table assumes the payments can occur; the negative figure signals that an actual funding or scheduling solution would be needed. To preserve a $1,000 reserve until the week-four receipt, opening cash must cover $800 mobilisation plus three $1,000 payments plus the reserve: $4,800 . Relative to the assumed $3,000 opening balance, the additional requirement is $1,800 . If the customer pays after week-four payroll instead, four payments occur before collection. The opening requirement becomes $1,000 + $800 + $4,000 = $5,800 . That one change adds $1,000 to the required opening cash. Weekly totals alone can hide it. Test an earlier collection without assuming agreement Now assume the customer agrees to two $2,400 collections, one before week-two payments and one before week-four payments. With the original $3,000 opening cash, the balances become $2,200 after mobilisation, $1,200 after week one, $2,600 after week two, $1,600 after week three and $3,000 after week four. The lowest balance is now $1,200, above the chosen reserve. Total receipts and payments have not changed; timing has. This is a scenario to discuss and verify, not a claim that the customer will accept earlier billing. Do not schedule an unagreed advance as certain cash. Also run a downside case in which the second receipt slips by one payroll cycle. Carry all real payments forward while moving only that receipt. If the forecast fails, identify the specific event causing the breach rather than writing “cash flow risk” beside a monthly total. How to run your own numbers First use the cleaning business break-even calculator to assess whether visit contribution and expected volume support your monthly costs. Then build the dated ledger separately. The calculator’s monthly result does not forecast invoice clearance or payroll dates. For the contract price and service-cost assumptions, use the existing commercial cleaning contract bid guide . For shared payments outside this account, consult cleaning business monthly expenses . Keep those amounts in the business-wide schedule without counting the same payment twice. Review the schedule before accepting more work Check the first collection, the largest payroll and any upfront purchases. Ask which dates are verified and which are estimated. Replace estimates after the first actual cycle and compare forecast receipts with cleared receipts. If the customer pays late, update the next cycle instead of leaving the original assumption in place. A separate account may appear fundable in isolation while several accounts share the same payroll week. Combine their dated cash movements before deciding how much cash is available for another contract. Avoid allocating the same opening reserve to multiple accounts independently. For a repeatable collection indicator across invoice cohorts, see how to calculate days sales outstanding . DSO describes the receivable pattern; this contract ledger still determines whether cash arrives before a specific payroll. Common mistakes Counting invoiced revenue as cleared cash. Looking only at month-end balances and missing an earlier payroll breach. Omitting setup purchases because they are not recurring operating costs. Treating the chosen reserve as an expense, then subtracting it twice. Assuming an agreed due date guarantees receipt on that day. Using unrestricted opening cash when part of it is already committed. Frequently asked questions Is a cash gap the same as a loss? No. This schedule measures when money is available and when payments occur. Profitability asks a different question. A loss can also worsen cash, but payment timing alone can create a temporary shortfall. How much reserve should every cleaning company hold? There is no universal amount in this guide. Set a reserve using your actual obligations and uncertainty, then test it against dated events. The $1,000 figure is an illustrative owner choice. Should I forecast weekly or daily? Use daily events around tight payroll and receipt dates. A weekly view can be sufficient elsewhere, provided same-week ordering cannot change whether payments are covered. Can I include an expected deposit? Yes, as an assumption with its agreement and expected clearance date. Also test the schedule without it when receipt is uncertain. Do not count it again when the balance invoice is paid. Does the contract profit calculator calculate this timing gap? No. It helps assess service economics. A dated cash ledger is needed to model the gap between collections and cash payments. When should I update the forecast? Update it when work scope, payroll, billing approval or expected collection changes. Reconcile it with actual bank movements after each cycle. Should I add the cash gap from every contract together? Combine dated receipts and payments first and apply the company reserve once. Standalone peaks can overlap, offset or occur on different dates; the combined lowest balance determines the modeled funding need. Closing takeaways Place receipts and payments on their actual expected dates. Check the lowest balance, including same-day payment order. Test late collection before committing usable cash to more work. Use completed-job cost reconciliation to replace estimated service payments with observed job costs before updating the next schedule. Explore the Cleaning planning hub and all business guides . Sources and assumptions business.gov.au: Set up a cash flow statement . General cash-ledger structure; checked 9 October 2026. The weekly cleaning scenarios and reserve choices are hypothetical examples created for this guide. Replace the fictional example with your own records and review the stated assumptions before acting. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Cleaning BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cleaning Job Cost: Compare Your Estimate With Actuals Published October 9, 2026 Updated November 3, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Reconcile cleaning estimates with actual worker-hours, supplies, travel and callbacks. Use a variance bridge to separate changed scope from delivery overruns. Cleaning Job costing Cost variance Worker hours AI-generated editorial illustration of this planning topic; not a real customer or business. Compare a completed cleaning job with its accepted estimate by reconciling revenue, worker hours and each variable cost. The difference shows how much contribution changed and which items caused the change. A quote can look sensible before service yet leave less contribution after extra worker hours, additional travel or a return visit. This guide reconciles one completed job against its estimate. It does not repeat a house-cleaning price list. The example uses fictional USD costs so you can follow the method without treating them as local market rates. Quick answer Compare estimated and actual revenue and each cost category using the same basis. Calculate contribution as service revenue less the job’s variable costs. Explain the difference with worker-hour, supply, travel and fee variances. Keep shared overhead separate so a change in allocation does not look like a change in how the job was performed. Explain the variance before changing the next estimate A useful job close answers two questions: what changed, and which action follows? Preserve the accepted estimate and compare the same service boundary with the completed work. Then separate authorized scope additions, time used on the original scope, wage-rate changes, supply use, travel and customer credits. A single unfavorable total does not establish that the crew worked inefficiently. The existing $300 cleaning example loses $54 of expected contribution: labor rises $44, supplies $6 and vehicle cost $4. Price and the $9 payment fee are unchanged. That bridge explains the amount; a task record explains its cause. Close the existing $54 unfavorable variance Cost movement Amount Evidence and next action Two additional worker-hours at $22 $44 Separate approved extra tasks, access delay and original-scope time Additional supplies $6 Check quantity, unit price, waste and work scope Additional vehicle cost $4 Check route or collection trips against the estimate Total contribution reduction $54 Expected $127 becomes actual $73 Separate scope growth from original-scope performance Suppose the time record shows one of the two extra worker-hours was an approved added task and the other was needed to finish the original work. The original estimate remains six hours; an adjusted comparison allows seven hours for the agreed delivered scope. Actual time is eight. The $44 labor difference then splits into $22 scope growth and $22 above the adjusted time budget. It is not accurate to call all $44 crew inefficiency. If the extra task was approved without an added charge, its cost still reduces contribution. If a price change was agreed, add that actual revenue and its associated fee separately; do not erase the cost variance by rewriting the original quote. Record who approved the change and when, together with the tasks performed. Compare the full worker-hour result The original $127 contribution over six worker-hours is $21.17 per worker-hour. The completed $73 over eight hours is $9.13. Those values are before shared overhead and use the same whole-job boundary. Dividing actual contribution by estimated hours would hide part of the loss of capacity. If some payroll is committed regardless of jobs, keep a separate cash-avoidability view; an allocated hourly wage does not prove a saving is available next week. Close each job with estimate version, agreed scope changes, each worker's task hours, materials, route cost, callbacks, credits, final fee and collection status. Review recurring causes across comparable jobs before changing a standard time allowance. One obstructed property should not silently reset every estimate. Carry actual service contribution into client acquisition payback and paid outflow dates into the payroll cash plan . A pricing correction, an access agreement and a training need are different responses to different evidence. Preserve the original estimate Save the accepted scope, quoted amount, expected worker hours, rate assumptions and supplies allowance before replacing anything with actual figures. Otherwise the estimate becomes a moving target: after a difficult job, it is tempting to adjust expected hours and lose the comparison that would explain the miss. Attach a job identifier to time records, purchases, travel notes, credits and any return visit. Keep agreed scope changes separate from unplanned overruns. An extra room requested and paid for by the customer is different from an extra hour needed to finish the original scope. Start with the amount earned for the service, consistently excluding taxes collected for remittance if that is how your estimate was prepared. A payment fee belongs among costs; subtracting it from revenue and again from costs would count it twice. Record refunds or credits against the same job, even if issued after the initial payment. Use worker hours rather than elapsed hours Two cleaners working for three hours use six worker hours. If both work for four hours, the actual is eight. Comparing a six-hour labour estimate with four hours of elapsed time understates labour use. Decide whether the job’s time includes preparation, loading, travel and a return visit. Then use that boundary in both columns. Paid travel can be included in the labour figure or shown separately as paid time, but it should not appear in both. Vehicle running costs are a different item from the cleaner’s paid travel time. Use the same labour-cost basis in the estimate and actual. If your estimate includes employer costs, do not compare it with a wage-only actual. If employer costs are not yet final, mark the actual as provisional rather than presenting a false level of precision. An owner doing the work should record their time too; the chosen owner-labour allowance must be clear and applied consistently. Worked example: where $54 disappeared Assume a completed job has $300 service revenue. There is no scope change or refund. A payment fee is 3% of that revenue. The estimated labour cost is six worker hours at $22 per hour. Actual time is eight worker hours at the same rate. The rate is an illustrative cost assumption, not a wage recommendation. Item Estimate Actual Actual minus estimate Service revenue $300 $300 $0 Worker hours 6 8 +2 hours Labour cost $132 $176 +$44 Supplies $12 $18 +$6 Vehicle/travel cost, excluding paid labour $20 $24 +$4 Payment fee $9 $9 $0 Total job variable cost $173 $227 +$54 Contribution before shared overhead $127 $73 −$54 Estimated contribution is $300 − $173 = $127 . Actual contribution is $300 − $227 = $73 . The $54 reduction is fully explained by $44 additional labour, $6 additional supplies and $4 additional vehicle/travel cost. No unexplained “miscellaneous loss” is needed. The actual contribution ratio is $73 ÷ $300, or about 24.3% . That is this fictional job’s result before shared overhead. It is not a typical cleaning-company margin, take-home income or a recommended target. If you separately assign $30 of shared overhead to this job, the remainder becomes $43. The estimate’s remainder would have been $97 under the same allocation. The operational difference is still $54. Show the allocation separately; do not add $30 into variable cost and then subtract it again. Separate time changes from rate changes When both hours and labour rate change, break the difference into components. For a simple two-part comparison: Time variance = (actual hours − estimated hours) × estimated rate. Rate variance = actual hours × (actual rate − estimated rate). Together these reconcile actual labour cost against estimated labour cost. With eight actual hours at $24 instead of six hours at $22, the time component is 2 × $22 = $44. The rate component is 8 × $2 = $16. Total labour variance is $60, matching $192 actual less $132 estimated. This is an arithmetic decomposition, not proof of who caused the overrun. A higher rate may reflect a different crew assignment. Additional time might come from incorrect scope, access delays, training, equipment failure or a return visit. Add a short factual note to each material difference rather than blaming staff from the number alone. Distinguish a scope change from an execution miss Suppose the customer approved an extra $60 task. Record the additional revenue and its extra cost separately, then show the full job total. Comparing the larger actual job with the original smaller scope without explanation can make good additional work look like an overrun. For an uncharged extra, record what happened and why no additional revenue was collected. A discretionary goodwill action, an omitted quote item and a service correction call for different follow-up decisions. Do not rewrite the original quote to pretend the work was included all along. A return visit should remain attached to the original job where that is the work it corrects. Recording it as a new zero-revenue job may hide the cost from the original quote review. Include its time, transport and consumables in the reconciliation, with an explanation of the agreed accounting treatment where needed. Callback and credit: a separate worksheet example The free cleaning job cost worksheet uses a different fictional $240 job from the $300 example above. Estimated contribution is $110.80; first-visit actual contribution is $78.80. A callback costs $37 (one crew-hour at $25, $4 supplies and $8 travel). A $20 customer credit reduces retained revenue to $220. With actual payment fees still $7.20, total variable costs are $198.20 and final contribution is $21.80 , or 9.9% of retained revenue, before overhead. The $89 change from the quote reconciles to $25 of extra first-visit labour, $3 supplies, $4 travel, the $37 callback and the $20 credit. Enter callback costs only when absent from first-visit actuals, and deduct the credit from revenue once. Use the actual-fee override when your processor retains fees after a refund; a credit does not automatically reduce fees. Download includes a blank Job tab and the worked Example tab. Complete both columns, including zero for unused costs. Add extra-work revenue and costs separately, counting any extra processing fee once. A missing required input remains incomplete; a zero retained-revenue percentage displays “n.a.”. Final contribution still needs to cover fixed overhead. How to run your own numbers Use the cleaning business break-even calculator to test what your observed contribution per visit means for monthly volume. Enter representative completed-job economics rather than copying one unusually easy or difficult visit across the whole schedule. The cleaning contract profit calculator can help compare the next account’s service assumptions. It does not import time records or reconcile a completed job automatically. For quoting the next visit, return to house-cleaning pricing . For scope-specific work, use move-out cleaning job costs . Use the findings in the next estimate Review similar jobs together. Separate first visits from maintenance visits and small jobs from larger properties. If repeated overruns occur in the same scope category, update the relevant estimating assumption. One exceptional access problem is a reason to record a risk or condition, not automatically a reason to change every quote. Keep the estimate, actual result and next action in the job record. A useful action is specific: allow another worker hour for a documented task, verify access before scheduling or obtain approval for additional scope. “Charge more” does not identify which assumption failed. Reconcile the records soon after completion while crew notes are still useful. If costs arrive later, mark the review provisional and set a date to finish it. The goal is a repeatable feedback loop, not an attractive margin figure based on incomplete records. Common mistakes Comparing elapsed time with worker hours. Using different cost boundaries in the two columns. Counting a payment fee or paid travel twice. Omitting refunds, owner labour or correction visits. Treating allocated overhead as directly observed job spending. Replacing the original estimate before calculating the variance. Frequently asked questions Does positive contribution mean the job covered all business costs? No. Contribution is available to cover shared overhead and other obligations. It is not automatically final business profit. Should every supply purchase be charged to one job? Only if it belongs to that job under your chosen method. A bulk purchase used across visits needs a consistent usage allocation. Do not assign the full purchase to each visit. What if the customer has not paid yet? Keep service economics and collection status visible separately. A completed-job revenue comparison does not establish that cash has arrived; use a dated cash schedule for payment timing. Should I change every quote after one overrun? Review the cause and comparable jobs first. Repeated evidence can support a revised assumption. A one-off event may instead require a scope condition or operational correction. Can I compare jobs of different sizes? Yes, with context. Worker hours, contribution and scope notes can help, but a simple ranking without service mix can mislead. Compare like work where possible. Is this a new pricing calculator? No. It is a completed-job reconciliation method that feeds better assumptions into existing quoting and break-even tools. How do I separate added scope from a cleaning time overrun? Keep the original estimate, add a documented time allowance for agreed new tasks, then compare actual hours with that adjusted scope. Record any agreed price change separately rather than overwriting the original quote. Closing takeaways Preserve the original accepted estimate. Compare the same scope and cost boundary in both columns. Explain material variances before changing the next quote. If the job is complete but collection is still pending, use the cleaning contract payroll cash-gap guide for the separate payment-timing question. Explore the Cleaning planning hub and all business guides . Assumptions All job figures are hypothetical USD examples. The variance formulas reconcile the stated inputs; they are a management comparison rather than a tax-accounting rule. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
