documents.text: Agency BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Agency Client Concentration: Revenue, Contribution and Cash Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Measure agency client concentration using revenue and contribution. Stress a major-client loss, replacement sales and payment timing before adding commitments. Agency Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. Client concentration measures how much your agency depends on a small number of clients. Calculate revenue share, but also inspect the contribution, delivery hours and unpaid invoices attached to those clients. Losing a client that supplies 30% of revenue does not automatically remove 30% of profit or release 30% of usable capacity. The fictional USD examples here are operating scenarios, not universal safe thresholds or forecasts of client loss. Quick answer Divide each client's revenue by total agency revenue for the same period. Then model what disappears and what remains if that client leaves: avoidable costs, committed payroll, overhead, receivables and delivery hours. Compare the remaining contribution with monthly commitments. Use concentration as a scenario trigger rather than declaring a particular percentage safe for every agency. The direct answer: a five-client month Suppose five clients produce monthly revenue of $12,000, $8,000, $5,000, $3,000 and $2,000. Total revenue is $30,000. The largest client's share is $12,000 ÷ $30,000 = 40%. The two largest together account for $20,000 ÷ $30,000 = 66.67%. Now assume the largest client has $4,800 of genuinely avoidable delivery costs and fees. It leaves $7,200 contribution. The other clients leave contributions of $4,800, $3,000, $1,800 and $1,200. Total agency contribution is $18,000, and the largest client supplies 40% of that contribution in this deliberately simple example. Monthly committed overhead and a separately modeled owner-pay target total $14,000. The current scenario leaves $4,000 before taxes and unmodeled expenses. If the largest client leaves and only its $4,800 avoidable costs disappear, remaining contribution is $10,800. The agency falls $3,200 short of its $14,000 commitments. The $12,000 revenue loss and the $3,200 operating shortfall are different measures. The gap is not solved simply by winning any new $3,200 invoice; replacement work also has costs. If new work leaves 60% contribution, revenue needed to fill the $3,200 gap is $5,333.3333, or $5,333.34 rounded upward. These figures assume the remaining client's contributions and commitments stay unchanged. In reality, staffing, delivery dependencies and collection can change. The agency client-profitability guide provides the engagement-level cost view needed before making a loss scenario. What changes the answer Revenue concentration and contribution concentration can diverge. A large low-margin account might supply much of the revenue but little contribution. A smaller account with low direct cost can be more important to covering fixed commitments. Committed payroll is often the biggest boundary. If employees remain paid after a client leaves, those salaries are not immediately avoidable. Do not remove allocated engagement labor from the scenario and also assume the team continues to be paid elsewhere without reconciliation. Receivables create a separate exposure. A client can leave future work and also delay paying completed invoices. Track unpaid balances, due dates and actual collection assumptions. Revenue share alone cannot describe the cash at risk. Contracted notice and scope matter, but their enforceability is a legal question beyond this worksheet. Use the actual commercial arrangements to establish the planning timeline, with appropriate review where needed. Do not assume every client will continue paying for a forecast notice period. Freed delivery hours may not become paid work immediately. Sales lead time, specialist skills and client onboarding can delay replacement. Compare the work the team can actually deliver with the pipeline you can actually support. Several clients can share one source of risk. Accounts from one sector, referral partner or parent organization may behave similarly. A five-client portfolio can still be concentrated operationally even when no single invoice share appears dominant. The agency utilization guide helps distinguish available staff time from productive client-delivery capacity. Three worked scenarios A smaller high-contribution client leaves Suppose the $5,000 client leaves $4,000 contribution rather than the $3,000 assumed earlier. If total agency contribution is therefore $19,000, its contribution share is $4,000 ÷ $19,000 = 21.05%, while revenue share remains 16.67%. Losing it would reduce the $19,000 contribution to $15,000. Against $14,000 commitments, only $1,000 remains. Revenue share understated this client's importance to the operating cushion. A delayed invoice and a future cancellation Suppose the largest client has $6,000 unpaid completed invoices and then cancels future work. The $6,000 collection exposure is separate from the modeled $7,200 monthly contribution loss. If unrestricted cash is $10,000 and immediate committed payments are $8,000, the agency has a $2,000 cash cushion before collecting that invoice. Assuming collection before the payments would create a $8,000 cushion instead. The timing assumption materially changes the cash plan; neither amount is guaranteed by issuing an invoice. Build replacement contribution Assume the $3,200 monthly contribution gap from the original loss scenario. A new $2,000 retainer leaves $1,100 contribution and requires 20 delivery hours. Three such retainers leave $3,300 and use 60 hours. The portfolio would cover the modeled gap by $100, provided the retainers actually sell, pay and fit capacity. If only 40 suitable delivery hours are available, the proposed replacement plan is infeasible without changes. Counting prospects as signed clients would hide that uncertainty. How to run your own numbers Create a client table with revenue, direct avoidable costs, contribution, hours, unpaid balance and commitment dates. Use the agency break-even calculator to test the remaining portfolio and the replacement-engagement assumptions after a loss scenario. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Keep one currency and one period across clients. Annual contract values should not be mixed with one-month invoice revenue without a clear conversion and timing model. Model at least three situations: current portfolio, loss of the largest contribution client and delayed payment from the largest debtor. Keep them separate before testing a combined downside. That separation makes the cause of each shortfall visible. Write the action assumptions beside the numbers. Reducing committed spending, changing scope and selling replacement work happen on different timelines. A spreadsheet that removes all costs immediately after cancellation is an optimistic scenario unless those costs are truly avoidable at that time. The agency profit-margin guide connects these portfolio scenarios with the agency's overall operating result. Common mistakes Declaring a fixed client-share percentage safe treats unlike agencies as identical. Use the share to trigger an explicit loss scenario. Looking only at revenue misses contribution and unpaid cash. Record all three with clear definitions. Removing committed salaries immediately after a client leaves overstates cost flexibility. Use actual staffing commitments and timing. Assuming freed hours are instantly resold ignores lead generation and onboarding. Keep forecast replacements distinct from signed work. Counting several related accounts as fully independent can hide sector or parent-company dependence. Record shared exposure where it is material. Mixing annual contracts and monthly invoices produces misleading percentages. Use one observation period before dividing. Stress contribution loss separately from revenue concentration Independent hypothetical USD case: an agency earns $50,000 monthly revenue and $28,000 contribution before $22,000 of committed overhead and payroll. One client supplies $20,000 revenue and requires $8,000 of costs that would genuinely disappear if the engagement ended. Its revenue share is 40%, but its $12,000 contribution represents 42.86% of total contribution. A major-client exit with committed costs unchanged Monthly measure Before exit After exit Revenue $50,000 $30,000 Contribution $28,000 $16,000 Committed costs $22,000 $22,000 Operating surplus / shortfall $6,000 −$6,000 If replacement work contributes 50% of revenue, covering the $6,000 shortfall needs $12,000 replacement sales; restoring the original $6,000 surplus needs $24,000. These are different recovery goals. Signed revenue is still not cash collected, and new work can require onboarding and delivery spending before payment. Build a client-loss response with actual cost release dates Mark which contractor, software and travel costs stop immediately and which remain committed through notice periods. Do not call salaried delivery time an avoidable expense merely because hours become free. If an employee cost remains, it stays with committed costs in this stress model. Replacing a major client with ten small accounts can also add sales and account-management workload. Keep unpaid invoices separate. A $14,000 collectible receivable is a collection-timing exposure, not another $14,000 monthly revenue loss. Model a delayed or uncollectible balance explicitly, without deducting it twice. Record payment dates, cash reserves and committed outflows before describing a runway. Review the top client and top three clients over the same trailing period, then assess contribution, delivery hours, common ownership and renewal dates. Two brands with one purchasing decision can represent one commercial dependency. Use the client profitability guide for delivery economics and project-versus-retainer analysis for replacement workload. Diversification is useful only when the replacement portfolio can be sold, delivered and collected. Further reading and method: Industry source . Molinari Oswald explains why revenue share alone does not describe customer dependency. The loss and replacement-sales calculations here use our own assumptions rather than a universal risk threshold. FAQs What concentration percentage is too high? There is no universal safe percentage in this guide. The practical test is what the loss or delay does to contribution, cash and delivery capacity. A smaller share can still be material when the operating cushion is thin. Should I measure revenue or profit share? Measure revenue and contribution with clearly defined costs. Final profit allocation can be sensitive to shared-cost assumptions. Client contribution helps identify what remains available to cover commitments. Does a long contract remove the risk? No planning model can guarantee continued payment or demand. Use actual terms and appropriate review to establish assumptions. Also examine unpaid invoices and operational dependence. Are many small clients always better? More clients can diversify revenue but create coordination and acquisition costs. Compare the complete portfolio workload and contribution. Client count alone does not establish a stronger agency. Should I reject a large new client? The worksheet helps assess exposure, price and capacity; it does not decide the commercial relationship. Model the resulting portfolio and the loss scenario. Record any staffing or cash commitments that the new account creates. How often should I review concentration? Review when a material account starts, leaves, changes scope or delays payment. Use consistent monthly or rolling-period figures. A regular review is useful only if the cost and receipt assumptions are kept current. How much new revenue replaces a lost client? Choose the recovery goal first. Divide the lost contribution or the remaining monthly shortfall by the expected contribution ratio of replacement work; these can produce different sales targets. Does losing a client automatically eliminate its delivery payroll? No. Include only costs that can actually stop within the planning period as avoidable costs. Committed payroll remains a cash and operating obligation even if delivery hours become available. Closing takeaways Measure contribution and receivables alongside revenue share. Remove only costs that are truly avoidable in the scenario. Test replacement work against hours and realistic timing. Record shared sector or parent-account exposure. Browse the business guide library for related planning methods. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency PROFITABILITY GUIDE Agency Employee vs Freelancer: Find the Workload Threshold Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare employee and freelancer costs against productive capacity and uncertain demand. Test monthly commitments, overflow and onboarding before hiring. Agency Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. Compare an employee and a freelancer by the cost of delivering the same work at the same quality and time requirement. A committed employee can be cheaper at a sustained workload, while a freelancer can avoid some idle-capacity cost when work is uncertain. The choice also involves availability, supervision and continuity. The fictional USD examples below explain a cost threshold; they are not wage benchmarks, employment-law advice or worker-classification guidance. Quick answer Estimate the employee's complete committed monthly cost and productive delivery hours. Compare that with the freelancer's actual rate, minimum commitments and coordination costs for the same output. Divide the relevant fixed-cost difference by the variable-cost difference to find a workload threshold. Then test expected utilization and capacity rather than assuming every paid employee hour becomes billable work. The direct answer: a simple monthly threshold Suppose an employee creates $5,000 of committed monthly cost, including the salary and the employer costs you have actually identified for this hypothetical role. The employee has 120 productive delivery hours available after leave, internal work and other non-delivery time. A freelancer charges $60 per delivery hour with no minimum commitment in this illustration. Additional coordination costs $200 monthly for the freelancer arrangement. At 80 hours, the freelancer costs 80 × $60 + $200 = $5,000, equal to the employee's committed cost. Below 80 hours, the freelancer arrangement is cheaper under these assumptions. Above 80 hours and up to the employee's 120-hour productive capacity, the employee's $5,000 cost is lower than the freelancer's variable bill. This is a cost threshold, not proof that either arrangement produces equivalent work. At 100 hours, the freelancer costs $6,200, compared with $5,000 for the employee. At 50 hours, the freelancer costs $3,200, while the employee still costs $5,000. The employee's effective cost per used hour is $50 at 100 hours and $100 at 50 hours. Do not substitute nominal paid hours for productive delivery capacity. A person paid for a full month still needs leave, internal coordination and other work. The agency billable-utilization guide explains how that distinction affects a delivery plan. For US arrangements, the IRS worker-status guidance explains why the actual relationship matters. Worker status and applicable obligations must be resolved appropriately before a real engagement. This article does not determine whether someone may legally be treated as a contractor. The numbers are only a management comparison after the arrangements and costs are correctly established. What changes the answer Output quality and delivery time must be comparable. If the freelancer takes fewer hours or the employee requires more review, a rate-only comparison is misleading. Cost the agreed output and include the people who supervise or correct it. Employee costs extend beyond a quoted salary where actual obligations apply. Use the costs relevant to your jurisdiction and arrangement, verified through suitable sources or advisers. Do not invent a universal payroll multiplier or omit costs simply because they are not on the wage quote. Freelancer terms can include minimum days, retainers or rush charges. A pure hourly formula does not apply when you must reserve a block of capacity. Include the minimum even when actual work uses fewer hours. Recruiting and onboarding are separate initial costs. You can show a first-period result and a steady-state result, but spreading initial cost across a long assumed tenure needs an explicit assumption. Do not hide the upfront cash requirement. Coordination can be fixed or proportional to work. If a manager spends more time as volume increases, model that extra time rather than holding it at a flat $200. The same applies to software seats, equipment and secure access arrangements. Demand uncertainty changes idle capacity. A signed workload and an optimistic pipeline are different. Compare a low, expected and high workload scenario, keeping the forecast's evidence visible. The agency retainer-pricing guide connects staffing cost with a defined client scope. Engagement pricing complements this staffing choice without replacing worker-specific cost and availability checks. Calculate employee cost per productive hour before comparing rates The $5,000 monthly commitment in the threshold example needs a cost breakdown. Here is one possible fictional composition; use actual employer costs rather than applying a universal salary multiplier. Build the existing $5,000 monthly assumption Input Monthly amount Salary $4,000 Employer payroll costs $600 Benefits $300 Role-specific software and equipment allowance $100 Total committed employee cost $5,000 Suppose paid availability is 160 hours, of which 16 are leave and 24 are internal work and training. Productive capacity is 120 hours. Salary divided by paid hours is $25; complete committed cost divided by productive capacity is $41.67. At only 80 hours of actual client delivery, cost per used hour is $62.50. Those are three different ratios, not three competing wage quotes. Do not subtract the same leave twice through both reduced hours and a second utilization factor. If equipment cost is allocated here, reconcile it with the agency overhead budget. Keep upfront equipment cash separately from the monthly allocation. Compare contractor output, revisions and supervision on the same basis, then use client-level profitability to see whether the engagements support the staffing decision. This calculation does not classify a worker or prescribe payroll rates. Three worked scenarios Freelancer with a minimum Suppose the freelancer requires a 60-hour monthly minimum at $60, plus $200 coordination. Minimum cost is $3,800 even if only 40 hours are used. Effective cost per used hour is $95 at 40 hours. At 80 hours, total cost remains $5,000, equal to the employee in the original example. Below 60 hours, the pure hourly formula understates the freelancer bill. The actual agreement's minimum creates a different low-demand result. Employee plus overflow work Demand reaches 150 delivery hours, above the employee's 120-hour productive capacity. If a freelancer supplies the remaining 30 hours at $60 and incremental coordination costs $100, the mixed arrangement costs $5,000 + $1,800 + $100 = $6,900. Using the freelancer for all 150 hours under the original $200 coordination assumption costs $9,200. The mixed scenario is cheaper by $2,300, provided output, schedule and review requirements remain comparable. The employee alone cannot deliver 150 hours merely because the financial result looks attractive. Initial onboarding cost Suppose hiring the employee adds a one-time $1,500 recruiting and onboarding cost. First-month employee cost becomes $6,500. With freelancer cost $60 per hour plus $200, first-month equality occurs at ($6,500 − $200) ÷ $60 = 105 hours. The steady-state threshold remains 80 hours if later committed employee costs are $5,000. Showing both periods prevents a first-month cost from being silently ignored or repeatedly charged forever. Use the actual timing when planning cash. How to run your own numbers Build a staffing worksheet with committed employee cost, productive hours, freelancer rate, minimums, review time and initial costs. Use the agency break-even calculator to test whether the client revenue and contribution can support the selected staffing arrangement and workload. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Keep the same currency and month across options. A daily contractor quote must be converted using the actual paid day length and minimum terms, not an assumed eight productive hours. Separate the engagement-cost view from the agency cash budget. Allocating an employee cost to client jobs helps compare delivery economics, but the committed payroll still has to be paid during quiet periods. Reconcile allocations to the one total payroll cost. Test workload at 50, 80, 100 and 120 hours under the original assumptions, then replace those values with your forecast range. Record output requirements and supervision alongside cost. The cheaper spreadsheet option is not necessarily available or capable of delivering the work. The agency profit-margin guide and client-profitability guide connect staffing with the wider agency budget and engagement scope. Common mistakes Comparing salary with an hourly rate omits productive hours, minimums and coordination. Compare total cost for the same output. Assuming every paid hour is client delivery overstates capacity. Allow for actual non-delivery commitments. Treating salaries as avoidable per job in the cash plan hides idle-period payroll. Keep committed and incremental costs distinct. Ignoring recruiting and onboarding understates the first-period cash need. Show the initial and continuing results separately. Using cost calculations to decide worker classification reaches beyond the worksheet. Resolve the actual arrangement through appropriate review. Counting the same manager time in both overhead and contractor coordination duplicates it. Document the boundary and reconcile it. Test automation alongside the staffing decision If automation is an alternative to hiring or outsourcing, count human review and rework. Saved salaried time is capacity unless paid hours actually change. Test those separate assumptions with the AI automation ROI and payback calculator . Opening the calculator does not transfer this guide’s figures; enter your own consistent assumptions. Test the whole demand period before relying on one crossover A single workload threshold does not prove that a permanent commitment is economical. Compare the complete hiring period and verify that the employee can deliver the hours used in the comparison. Paid hours include leave, training, management and other work that may not be available for client delivery. Independent hypothetical USD model: the employee costs $4,800 per month across all included employment costs. Of 160 paid hours, 70% are available for the modeled delivery work: 112 productive hours. A freelancer charges $55 per comparable delivery hour plus $200 monthly coordination. Below capacity, the crossover is ($4,800 − $200) ÷ $55 = 83.64 hours approximately . A three-month demand sequence below employee capacity Month / required hours Employee commitment Freelancer + coordination Month 1: 40 $4,800 $2,400 Month 2: 90 $4,800 $5,150 Month 3: 110 $4,800 $6,250 Total: 240 $14,400 $13,800 Although two months exceed the crossover, the freelancer is $600 less expensive over this assumed three-month sequence. At 140 delivery hours in one month, an employee with 112-hour capacity needs 28 overflow hours. Adding $55 × 28 plus $200 coordination produces $6,540, compared with $7,900 for all-freelancer delivery. Availability, equivalent skill and actual minimum terms still need checking. Keep startup and supervision costs visible Include recruiting, onboarding, equipment, management and ramp-up where relevant. Do not divide committed salary by an unrealistic fully billable calendar or assume a new employee starts at experienced-team productivity. Compare the same quality, turnaround and rework boundary for both options. This cost model does not determine worker classification or employment obligations. Use applicable professional guidance for those decisions. For the business case, record a base, low-demand and high-demand month, then compare total commitments and delivered contribution. Check agency utilization and client dependency before using one uncertain account to justify a long commitment. Further reading and method: Industry source . Teamwork describes availability, skills and demand as workforce-capacity constraints. The employee cost, utilization and freelancer rates here are hypothetical, not wage or classification guidance. FAQs Is the 80-hour threshold universal? No. It comes only from the fictional $5,000, $60 and $200 assumptions. Your threshold changes with actual costs, minimums and comparable output. It is not an industry hiring rule. Should I divide salary by paid hours? That gives one wage-related ratio, but not necessarily delivery cost per productive hour. Use realistic productive capacity when comparing client work. Keep the complete committed cost and idle-period exposure visible. Can freelancers cost less even with a higher rate? Yes, when less capacity is needed and the arrangement avoids committed idle cost. Minimums and coordination can reduce that advantage. Compare the actual workload rather than the rate alone. Does this determine legal worker status? No. Classification and obligations depend on the actual arrangement and applicable rules. Obtain appropriate review for the real situation. The management model starts after the costs and status are correctly established. What if workload exceeds the employee's capacity? Model overflow staffing, changed scope or scheduling explicitly. A fixed monthly salary does not create unlimited hours. Compare the total cost and feasible delivery plan. Should I include the owner's supervision? Record it if the arrangement requires that work. Choose a consistent valuation and compensation boundary. Do not describe owner time as free or count the same compensation twice. Does a workload above the crossover make hiring the cheaper option? Not by itself. Compare all committed months, productive capacity, ramp-up, overflow and the same output-quality boundary. A temporary peak can coexist with a higher total employee cost. What happens above employee productive capacity? Cost the actual overflow or extra capacity rather than assigning unlimited work to the same salary. Include coordination, availability and any other costs needed to deliver the excess work. Closing takeaways Compare complete cost for equivalent output. Use productive hours and actual minimum commitments. Show first-period cash and steady-state cost separately. Keep classification decisions outside the arithmetic worksheet. Find related methods in the business guide library . Test your own cost and payment assumptions Calculate recurring employee cost, first-year hiring cost and cost per productive hour . Replace the fictional example with your own records and review the stated assumptions before acting. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency PROFITABILITY GUIDE Agency Project vs Retainer Profitability: Count the Hours Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare agency project and retainer contribution over the same period. Calculate scope-hour ceilings, revision costs and fee-aware price floors before renewing. Agency Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. A retainer is not automatically more profitable than a project. Compare the contribution each engagement leaves after direct delivery costs, then inspect the hours, scope and recurring commitments behind that contribution. A predictable invoice can hide open-ended work. A large project can hide weeks of revisions and unpaid coordination. All figures here are fictional USD planning assumptions, not agency rates or claims about typical margins. Quick answer Calculate engagement revenue minus delivery labor, contractors, sale-dependent tools, fees and acquisition costs. Compare contribution per delivery hour and total contribution over the same period. Keep shared overhead and owner pay separate. For a retainer, define included work and track actual hours; recurring revenue without a scope limit can become recurring underpricing. The direct answer: two ways to sell the same month Suppose a project sells for $6,000. It requires 80 delivery hours at a loaded direct cost of $35 per hour, or $2,800. Sale-dependent tools cost $200, acquisition cost assigned to this project is $300 and a 3% payment fee costs $180. Project contribution is $6,000 − $2,800 − $200 − $300 − $180 = $2,520. Contribution margin is 42%, and contribution per delivery hour is $2,520 ÷ 80 = $31.50. This still needs to cover shared commitments and owner income not already included in the labor boundary. A monthly retainer sells for $3,000 and uses 35 delivery hours at $35, or $1,225. Sale-dependent tools cost $100 and a 3% fee costs $90. There is no new acquisition charge in this month's example. Contribution is $1,585, or 52.83%, and $45.29 per delivery hour. The retainer leaves fewer total dollars but more contribution per hour under these assumptions. Two identical retainers would leave $3,170 from 70 hours, compared with $2,520 from the project's 80 hours. That comparison assumes you can actually sell and deliver the two retainers; it does not predict demand. If delivery wages are committed salaries rather than genuinely variable costs, use a consistent alternative view. You can allocate loaded labor for engagement comparison while keeping the cash payroll in the monthly budget. Do not subtract the same salary again when combining the two views. The agency retainer-pricing guide covers how to build a retainer price. This comparison tests which engagement structure fits contribution and capacity after scope is defined. What changes the answer Actual hours matter more than the proposal estimate. Include meetings, revisions, project management, quality checks and handover. Record owner delivery time as well as employee and contractor time so the comparison does not reward unrecorded labor. Scope determines the denominator. A retainer with unlimited requests can consume many more hours than its original plan. Define deliverables, revision limits, turnaround expectations and how additional work is handled. Pricing cannot solve scope that remains unspecified. Acquisition timing changes comparisons. A project may incur a new selling cost each time, while a retained client may not. You can examine acquisition payback across observed renewals, but do not assume an unverified lifetime. Keep the initial and continuing-month views separate. Payment timing affects cash. A project deposit and staged payments can fund work differently from a monthly invoice paid after delivery. Profitability and cash availability require separate schedules; neither billing structure guarantees prompt payment. Capacity affects what you can sell. A retainer reserves recurring hours, potentially crowding out a larger project. A project can create short peaks followed by idle periods. Compare engagement hours with productive team capacity in each relevant month. Client-specific tools belong with the client when they are avoidable. Shared software remains in overhead unless adding the engagement changes its cost. Avoid allocating an entire subscription to every client as though each pays it separately. The agency client-profitability guide explains how to track engagement cost without confusing invoice value with contribution. Three worked scenarios The retainer expands beyond scope Keep the $3,000 retainer, $100 tools and $90 fee, but actual delivery rises from 35 to 55 hours. Labor becomes $1,925. Contribution falls to $885, or 29.50%, and $16.09 per delivery hour. The revenue has not changed, but the economic result has. To preserve the original $1,585 contribution at 55 hours, required price solves price × 0.97 − $1,925 − $100 = $1,585. The result is $3,721.6495, or $3,721.65 rounded upward. The project takes longer Suppose the project grows from 80 to 100 hours while the price stays $6,000. Direct labor becomes $3,500. With the same $200 tools, $300 acquisition and $180 fee, contribution is $1,820. That is $18.20 per hour, down from $31.50. If the extra work is billable, model the additional agreed price and its fees. If it is included in the original scope, the quote estimate was insufficient; future proposals need a corrected workload assumption. A mixed month One original project and two original retainers generate $12,000 revenue. Their contributions total $2,520 + $1,585 + $1,585 = $5,690. Delivery hours total 80 + 35 + 35 = 150. If shared overhead and a separately modeled owner-pay target total $4,000, the month leaves $1,690 before taxes and unmodeled costs. If productive capacity is only 130 hours, the month cannot be delivered as planned without changes. Financial contribution alone has not made the workload feasible. How to run your own numbers Use the agency break-even calculator to model a representative engagement and monthly commitments. Compare project and retainer configurations separately, using their actual price, direct delivery costs, fees and hours. For a mixed portfolio, calculate a weighted engagement model with a consistent unit. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Use the same currency and time period when comparing options. A one-off project's full value should not be compared with a retainer's monthly value without accounting for the project's delivery period. Keep an engagement ledger with quoted hours, actual hours, invoiced revenue and direct costs. Review open scope requests before the end of the month, when there is still time to agree a change. A retrospective margin report cannot recover hours already delivered without an agreed charge. Use the billable-utilization guide to turn staff availability into a realistic delivery plan. Sales work, leave and internal administration reduce the hours available for paid client delivery. Common mistakes Treating recurring invoices as guaranteed retained revenue ignores cancellation and renewal. Model signed commitments and uncertainty separately. Comparing an entire project with one retainer month mixes periods. Use the same delivery window before comparing totals. Ignoring revisions and meetings understates actual work. Track complete delivery activities rather than only production tasks. Assuming unobserved lifetime value makes a weak initial engagement look stronger than the evidence supports. Separate initial acquisition payback from measured renewals. Counting committed salaries both as allocated direct labor and full overhead duplicates payroll. State the management and cash boundaries. Choosing the highest per-hour contribution without checking demand and capacity assumes you can sell any mix. Test the actual pipeline and schedule. Convert a retainer contribution goal into a delivery-hour ceiling A recurring invoice is easier to forecast than a sequence of unsigned projects, but predictability does not protect the margin on open-ended work. Compare the same output and period, including revisions, coordination and handoff. Keep committed salary in the monthly model if you do not treat delivery labor as variable; never charge the same payroll twice. Separate hypothetical USD costing view: a $6,000 monthly retainer has a 3% fee, $1,000 other engagement-linked costs and $45 delivery cost per hour. Contribution before shared overhead is $6,000 × 0.97 − $1,000 − ($45 × hours). Same retainer price; expanding paid delivery workload Delivery hours Delivery cost Engagement contribution 80 $3,600 $1,220 100 $4,500 $320 120 $5,400 −$580 To leave $1,500 contribution, the paid-hour ceiling is ($6,000 × 0.97 − $1,000 − $1,500) ÷ $45 = 73.78 hours approximately . If your planning system uses whole hours, 73 fits that floor and 74 does not. An 80-hour scope with the same contribution goal needs ($3,600 + $1,000 + $1,500) ÷ 0.97 = $6,288.66 rounded upward . Neither number is a recommended market rate. Define what renewal actually buys Record deliverables, revision rounds, meetings, response windows, unused-capacity treatment and the approval point for added scope. Track actual hours by engagement, not just billable time reported to the client. A fixed-price project must include its complete delivery life: a $12,000 two-month project is not directly comparable with one $6,000 retainer month. Reconcile the original estimate with actual delivery and collections before renewing. Do not count an advance payment as an additional sale or assume an unpaid invoice funds payroll. Use scope-creep costing for the change request and client concentration analysis before relying on one retainer to fund permanent commitments. Further reading and method: Industry source . Teamwork discusses profitability leakage through delivery and scope visibility. The retainer-hour ceiling and price-floor examples above are independently calculated assumptions. FAQs Are retainers better for cash flow? They can make billing more regular, but payment terms and collection still matter. A retainer paid late can strain cash. Build a dated receipt schedule rather than treating invoice frequency as cash certainty. Should project management count as delivery? Include client-specific coordination in engagement hours when it is required to deliver the work. Shared internal management can remain in overhead according to your boundary. Document the classification so projects and retainers are comparable. Can I spread acquisition cost across retainer months? You can analyze payback over observed or explicitly assumed months. Label the assumption and also show the first-month result. Do not use a long unverified relationship to hide a weak price. What if the owner does the work? Record the hours and choose a consistent compensation treatment. Owner delivery labor and owner income are related but not automatically the same field. Avoid counting the same compensation twice or treating all owner time as free. Should I offer unlimited work? Only a clearly defined service and capacity model can show what the offer costs. Unlimited scope creates uncertain hours. A fixed invoice alone does not protect contribution. Can a lower-margin engagement still be useful? Yes, if it adds contribution during spare capacity and fits the strategy. At full capacity, compare what it displaces. The decision needs both engagement economics and a realistic workload view. How do I set a retainer delivery-hour limit? Subtract percentage fees, non-hourly engagement costs and the contribution goal from revenue, then divide by the relevant hourly delivery cost. Keep the chosen labor boundary consistent. Can I compare a project invoice with one retainer month? Only after aligning the delivery period, scope, labor treatment and payment timing. A multi-month project fee cannot be treated as a single month of repeatable contribution. Closing takeaways Compare the same period and complete delivery hours. Track contribution dollars and contribution per hour. Define recurring scope before promising capacity. Keep acquisition assumptions and cash timing visible. Explore the business guide library for related methods. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Amazon vs Your Own Store: Compare Contribution per Order
documents.summary: Compare Amazon FBA and your own store after marketplace fees, fulfillment, product costs, advertising and expected returns.
documents.headings: Turn an Amazon FBA fee estimate into profit per order Quick answer The direct answer: a $40 product What changes the answer Three worked scenarios Lower own-store acquisition cost Different marketplace advertising cost Fixed costs and unequal volume How to run your own numbers Common mistakes Calculate the acquisition-cost ceiling at which the channels tie Reconcile channel overhead and settlement cash separately FAQs Are the example marketplace fees current Amazon rates? Is an own store always cheaper? Should I sell on both channels? How do I count organic orders? Should marketplace storage be a per-order cost? Does the higher contribution channel always win? How much own-store CAC can I afford compared with Amazon? Closing takeaways Continue with e-commerce business
documents.text: E-commerce PROFITABILITY GUIDE Amazon vs Your Own Store: Compare Contribution per Order Published October 7, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare marketplace and own-store contribution after product, fulfillment, fees and acquisition. Test channel volume and fixed costs with clear examples. Turn an Amazon FBA fee estimate into profit per order In Amazon’s Revenue Calculator, match your product category, dimensions, weight and selling price. In a fictional $40 sale, an $11 estimate for selling and fulfillment fees leaves $29. Deduct $12 landed product cost, $5 advertising and a $2 expected unrecovered return cost to get $10 contribution. Use separate costs for inbound shipping or storage only if they are absent from the estimate. Compare the store scenario using the same sale price, cost window and tax treatment. Use Amazon’s official fee estimator Carry order contribution into your ecommerce profit model E-commerce Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. Compare an Amazon marketplace order with an own-store order using the actual revenue and costs of each channel. Marketplace fees, fulfillment, advertising and refunds can differ from your store's payment fees, pick-and-pack and customer acquisition. Neither channel wins from its fee percentage alone. The fictional USD examples below illustrate the worksheet; they are not Amazon fee quotes, current rate estimates or a recommendation to choose one channel. Quick answer Subtract landed product cost, fulfillment, shipping subsidy, channel fees, expected order losses and acquisition cost from paid revenue. Compare contribution per order, total monthly contribution and the fixed commitments each channel adds. Use current statements and the fee calculator for your actual marketplace category and fulfillment method. Keep traffic forecasts separate from measured sales. The direct answer: a $40 product Suppose a marketplace order produces $40 revenue. Landed product cost is $12. A hypothetical marketplace selling fee is 15% of revenue, or $6. Fulfillment costs $5, attributed advertising $4 and the expected net returns-and-loss allowance $1. Contribution is $40 − $12 − $6 − $5 − $4 − $1 = $12, or 30% of revenue. The 15% assumption is purely illustrative. Actual Amazon referral and other fees depend on the product, program, category, dimensions, price and current terms. Use Amazon’s official selling-fee page and its product-specific fee tools for the actual configuration. Obtain the exact values rather than treating this example as a current fee schedule. Now model the same product through an own store at $40. Landed cost stays $12. Payment processing is hypothetically 3% plus $0.30, or $1.50. Pick-and-pack costs $2, seller-funded shipping $4, attributed acquisition $8 and expected net returns-and-loss allowance $1. Own-store contribution is $40 − $12 − $1.50 − $2 − $4 − $8 − $1 = $11.50, or 28.75%. Despite the lower selling fee, the own store leaves $0.50 less per order because acquisition and fulfillment differ. At 100 orders each, contributions are $1,200 and $1,150 before the channels' fixed commitments. This comparison cannot establish which channel will generate 100 orders. Keep observed orders and forecast orders clearly separated. The ecommerce contribution guide explains why these remaining dollars are not final profit. Platform subscriptions, software and committed staff still need coverage. What changes the answer Fulfillment method changes the costs. Marketplace-managed fulfillment and seller fulfillment use different fee and workload structures. Own-store fulfillment can also be outsourced or performed by committed staff. Compare a complete actual configuration, not a mixture of favorable parts from several options. Acquisition is often the deciding variable. Organic demand can reduce the incremental cash acquisition cost of some orders, but producing content, managing listings and running campaigns still consumes resources. Do not automatically call all organic sales free or charge the full monthly marketing budget to each order. Returns need a net cost boundary. Product recovery, unrecovered shipping, processing deductions and refund adjustments can all matter. Do not subtract the refunded revenue again if the revenue figure is already net of refunds. Model the expected loss consistently. Settlement timing affects cash. A channel may pay after the supplier or carrier must be paid. Contribution can be positive while cash is temporarily tied up. Use actual settlement terms rather than assuming both channels fund inventory on the same day. Storage and product dimensions affect fulfillment. A bulky low-price item can have a very different cost structure from a small high-price item. Use the SKU's actual size and weight when consulting a fee tool. Channel fixed commitments need a separate comparison. If one channel adds $200 monthly software and administration costs, its per-order contribution must cover that expense. Shared costs should not be allocated as though removing one channel would eliminate them all. The ecommerce return-cost guide helps you separate returned units, refunded revenue and the costs that remain after recovery. Three worked scenarios Lower own-store acquisition cost Keep the own-store example but reduce attributed acquisition from $8 to $5. Contribution rises from $11.50 to $14.50. At 100 orders, that is $1,450 before fixed commitments, or $250 more than the marketplace example. Under the remaining original own-store costs, contribution before acquisition is $19.50. To match the marketplace's $12, own-store acquisition can be no more than $7.50 per order. This is a contribution threshold, not a target return on advertising based on unknown traffic. Different marketplace advertising cost Increase attributed marketplace advertising from $4 to $7. Marketplace contribution falls to $9. At 100 orders it leaves $900. The selling-fee assumption has not changed; acquisition has. If own-store contribution remains $11.50, the own store leaves $250 more at equal 100-order volume. Actual order volumes, customer repeat behavior and fixed costs can reverse the monthly comparison, so keep them visible. Fixed costs and unequal volume Suppose marketplace contribution is $12 and the channel adds $150 monthly fixed commitments. At 200 orders, net channel contribution after those commitments is $2,400 − $150 = $2,250. Own-store contribution is $14.50, with $300 channel-specific fixed commitments and 150 orders. The comparable result is $2,175 − $300 = $1,875. Higher contribution per order has not produced the higher monthly result because volume and fixed costs differ. How to run your own numbers Create one consistent worksheet per SKU and channel, then use the ecommerce break-even calculator for each configuration. Enter the channel's paid price, product cost, fulfillment, shipping subsidy, fees and acquisition, with fixed commitments counted once. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Avoid comparing one channel's gross collected amount with another's net paid revenue. Taxes and money belonging to third parties require their own correct treatment outside this simplified contribution example. Use actual order statements to check the worksheet. Match each deduction to the field where it belongs. If a fee combines several services, do not add those same services again as separate guessed costs. Compare repeat orders separately when the data supports it. An initial acquisition cost may not recur on every repeat sale, but repeat customers still create payment, fulfillment and product costs. Do not assume a future lifetime value that has not been observed. The shipping-cost guide helps you distinguish carrier cost from the amount customers pay for shipping. Common mistakes Copying a general marketplace fee percentage into every SKU ignores product-specific terms. Verify the actual category and fulfillment configuration. Assuming own-store orders have zero acquisition cost overlooks paid campaigns and the resources used to build demand. Separate measured cash acquisition from committed marketing work. Comparing gross marketplace sales with net own-store revenue uses different definitions. Reconcile paid revenue first. Counting a returns allowance and the same net refund loss twice understates contribution. State the basis and recovery assumptions. Choosing solely by margin percentage ignores volume and channel-specific fixed costs. Calculate total monthly dollars as well. Using contribution to promise traffic confuses economics with demand. A mathematically attractive channel still needs customers. Calculate the acquisition-cost ceiling at which the channels tie Compare the same product, net revenue definition and fulfillment scope. In a separate fictional $50 order, product cost is $18 and fulfillment/shipping cost is $7 in either channel. Assume marketplace selling fees of $8 and advertising cost of $4 per order; own-store transaction fees are $2 before acquisition cost. These are teaching inputs, not current Amazon or processor rates. Independent matched-order contribution comparison; USD Line Marketplace Own store Net revenue 50 50 Product plus fulfillment −25 −25 Assumed channel transaction/selling fees −8 −2 Acquisition or advertising −4 −CAC Contribution before other differences 13 23 − CAC Own-store contribution ties the marketplace at $23 − CAC = $13, so CAC = $10 . At $12 CAC it is $11, or $2 lower; at $6 it is $17, or $4 higher. This ceiling changes when return burden, discounts, fulfillment, agency costs or net selling price differ. Include a cost once on the matching cohort and do not treat all repeat orders as acquisition-free. Reconcile channel overhead and settlement cash separately At a hypothetical $4 contribution advantage and $300 additional monthly store overhead, 75 comparable orders cover that extra overhead: $300 ÷ $4. This assumes the advantage applies to those orders and the marketplace overhead baseline is already matched. It does not prove the store can acquire that volume at the assumed CAC. Use actual customer cohorts and avoid allocating all paid acquisition only to the orders that happen to convert on one day. Check Amazon’s official fee and revenue-calculator information for the relevant category, plan and fulfillment method; do not apply one referral percentage universally. Then reconcile return costs and settlement timing . A reserve or delayed payout changes usable cash timing, while the related fee or loss needs its own profit treatment. FAQs Are the example marketplace fees current Amazon rates? No. They are explicit hypothetical assumptions for arithmetic. Use Amazon's current official fee tools and your actual product configuration before quoting or purchasing inventory. Is an own store always cheaper? No. Its payment fee may be smaller, while acquisition and fulfillment can be larger. Compare the complete paid order and monthly commitments under your actual costs. Should I sell on both channels? The worksheet can compare economics, but capacity, stock allocation and customer demand also matter. Test the channel-specific workload and cash timing. Positive contribution alone does not prove two channels fit the operation. How do I count organic orders? Record their actual order costs and any attributable acquisition spending. Keep committed content and marketing work in the appropriate monthly budget. Avoid calling every resource used to win organic demand free. Should marketplace storage be a per-order cost? It can be allocated for a management comparison, but label the period and denominator. If the same storage cost is already in overhead, do not enter it twice. Slow stock may need a separate holding-cost view. Does the higher contribution channel always win? Only at comparable volume and other relevant conditions. Fixed commitments, cash timing and actual sales can change the monthly result. Use a complete scenario instead of one isolated number. How much own-store CAC can I afford compared with Amazon? Calculate own-store contribution before CAC minus matched marketplace contribution. That difference is the tie-point CAC under the stated scope; revise it for different returns, fulfillment, overhead and customer cohorts. Closing takeaways Use actual product-specific fees and statements. Compare acquisition and fulfillment alongside selling fees. Calculate monthly contribution after channel-specific commitments. Keep sales forecasts separate from verified order economics. Explore more methods in the business guide library . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Salon PRICING GUIDE Bridal Hair and Makeup Pricing: Cost the Whole Booking Published October 7, 2026 Updated November 2, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build bridal hair and makeup packages from trials, artists, travel and service time. Use a scope worksheet and finish-time check before confirming a quote. Salon Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. Price a bridal hair and makeup package from all appointment work, travel, supplies, extra staff and the contribution the booking needs to leave. The wedding-day chair time is only part of the job. Trials, preparation, messages and cleanup also use paid or owner hours. In the fictional example below, a $650 package leaves $285.50 before monthly commitments. The figures are USD planning assumptions, not recommended local wedding rates. Quick answer Define the package before pricing it: people served, trials, services, location, travel, included changes and staff hours. Add the direct booking costs and required contribution, then divide by one minus the percentage fee. Check whether the available schedule can deliver the work. A headline package price is misleading when its scope is unclear. Turn the bridal quote into a service and timing worksheet A useful package shows exactly what the customer receives. Separate trials from wedding-day delivery and separate shared booking costs from per-person services. A provider's advertised bridal price cannot be copied safely without matching its included work. Define each bridal offer before costing it Offer Record in the quote Capacity check Bride with trial Hair/makeup scope, trial count, finish and changes Trial date plus wedding-day artist hours Bride and attendants Named services, counts, durations and artist minimums Each artist’s service sequence and finish deadline On-site booking Location, travel, parking, setup and early access Paid travel, available workspace and ready-by time A profitable package must still finish on time Separate hypothetical schedule: a bride needs two hours with one artist and four attendants each need one hour. One artist needs six service hours, before setup or breaks. In a three-hour service window, two suitably skilled artists could deliver six hours: Artist A serves the bride for two hours and one attendant for one; Artist B serves three attendants for one hour each. This only works if services can run independently and the venue supports both workstations. Add setup, cleanup and a realistic buffer outside that service-only allocation. Do not use this simplified sequence when hair and makeup require separate specialists or the bride cannot receive the planned services in parallel. Build a person-by-person sequence with your actual durations. Include minimum contractor commitments even when an artist's scheduled service time is shorter. Keep the quote and cash schedule together Use fields for person, service, trial inclusion, assigned artist, duration, products, travel allocation, extra requests, price and ready-by time. State who confirms changes and when the remaining balance is due under the actual agreement. A $1,200 booking paid $600 in advance and $600 later is still $1,200 total revenue; the advance is not another sale. As a scope example, Lyndsay Simon Beauty's published bridal packages itemize trials, attendants, travel and extra artists. Those are one provider's terms, not national rates or recommended rules. Use your own costs in the worked cases below. If a separate color service is included, cost it using the color appointment worksheet rather than absorbing it without revising the quote. The direct answer: one bride and one trial Assume a package covers one trial and wedding-day hair and makeup for one bride. Trial work takes two worker-hours, wedding-day services three, and preparation, messages and cleanup one. Total delivery work is six worker-hours at $35 per hour, or $210. Products and disposables cost $65. Travel and parking cost $70. The booking's incremental acquisition cost is $0 in this example because committed marketing sits in monthly overhead. Direct costs before a percentage fee total $345. At $650, a 3% processing fee costs $19.50. Contribution is $650 − $345 − $19.50 = $285.50, or 43.92% of package revenue. That contribution still needs to cover the salon's fixed commitments and owner income. Suppose the booking needs to leave $300 contribution. Required price is ($345 + $300) ÷ 0.97 = $664.9485, rounded upward to $664.95. A $665 package incurs a $19.95 fee and leaves $300.05 under the stated assumptions. The $35 labor rate is a fictional loaded delivery cost, not an industry wage estimate. If the owner performs the work, distinguish compensation for delivering the service from the separate owner-pay target. Model the chosen boundary consistently; do not quietly treat owner hours as free or duplicate owner pay. The salon service-pricing guide covers ordinary appointment economics. Bridal packages require a separate scope sheet because trials, travel and event timing can materially change the workload. What changes the answer Trials consume service time even if they happen weeks before the wedding. Include the agreed number and duration. A second trial or a changed look can add product and worker-hours; define whether that work is included or separately quoted. Location changes travel, parking and setup. Count the team's total travel time according to your labor boundary. Two artists traveling for one hour each consume two worker-hours, even though the journey lasts one hour on the calendar. Party size changes the staff needed to meet the finish time. Six guests requiring one hour each cannot be served by one artist in a three-hour window. Price the extra artists and setup before accepting a tightly timed package. Early starts or split-location work can create costs beyond normal appointments. Use actual staffing arrangements and transport costs rather than adding an unexplained premium. The quote should explain the service scope the extra charge supports. Product hygiene and disposables belong in direct costs where they change with the booking. Do not divide every new kit purchase by one wedding. Separate reusable stock, replacement assumptions and sale-dependent consumption. Cancellation and rescheduling affect cash and availability. A payment collected before service is not automatically additional revenue. Final booking terms need clear customer communication and appropriate review; this planning worksheet does not prescribe enforceable cancellation rules. Review the salon booked-hour capacity guide before selling a package that occupies the busiest part of the week. A profitable-looking wedding can displace several regular appointments. Three worked scenarios Add a bridesmaid service Suppose an added service sells for $120 and requires 1.5 worker-hours at $35, plus $12 products. Direct cost before fees is $64.50. A 3% payment fee costs $3.60. Added contribution is $120 − $64.50 − $3.60 = $51.90. That service looks positive in isolation. It is useful only if the agreed schedule can fit the extra work or if additional staffing has already been costed. If another artist must be booked for a minimum period, include that commitment before calling $51.90 the true gain. A package with two artists Consider a $1,200 booking with ten total worker-hours at $35, or $350 labor. Products cost $120, transport $100 and event-only equipment $50. Direct costs total $620 before a 3% fee of $36. Contribution is $544, or 45.33%. If two artists share the work evenly, each performs five hours, but scheduling still needs to match the individual service sequence. Total worker-hours alone do not prove every guest can finish before the ceremony. A longer trial If the original six-hour booking becomes seven hours, direct labor rises by $35 and total non-fee cost becomes $380. At the original $650 price, contribution falls to $250.50. To preserve the $300 target, price becomes ($380 + $300) ÷ 0.97 = $701.0309, or $701.04 rounded upward. The extra work has a visible cost. Whether the change is billable depends on the scope actually agreed with the customer. How to run your own numbers Use the salon break-even calculator with one package as the job unit. Enter the whole-package price, products, direct labor, travel and fees. Set delivery hours to total package worker-hours and compare the required monthly volume with available productive hours. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Use one currency and one unit throughout. A bridal-party package price paired with one person's product costs will overstate contribution. Keep a package worksheet listing each person, service, artist, duration and finish deadline. Put trials on the schedule as well as the wedding day. Compare available staffing by date, because a monthly capacity total cannot show two weddings booked at the same time. Record actual work after each completed booking. Compare quote hours with delivery hours, including communication and preparation. If trials consistently run longer than planned, revise future package scope rather than treating the extra hours as an unexplained profit loss. The salon profit-margin guide connects package contribution with fixed commitments and owner pay. A positive booking does not establish that the salon's entire month will be profitable. Common mistakes Pricing only wedding-day chair time leaves trials and preparation unfunded. Include the complete booking workload. Counting elapsed event time instead of total worker-hours understates labor for multiple artists. Multiply time by the people doing the work. Bundling unlimited changes into a fixed quote creates uncertain scope. Define the included services and trials before costing them. Charging the whole kit purchase to each booking overstates direct consumption. Separate reusable equipment from products actually used. Treating owner labor as free inflates contribution, while adding owner delivery pay and the same owner-pay target twice understates it. State your chosen boundary. Calling deposits extra revenue duplicates the completed package price. Reconcile advance and final payments against the one agreed booking value. FAQs Should a trial be included in the package? That is a commercial scope choice. If it is included, cost its time and products explicitly. If it is separate, explain its price and whether any amount is later credited to the wedding booking. How do I price a larger bridal party? Cost each service and the total staffing needed to meet the deadline. Some expenses are per person, while others are per booking. Recalculate artist minimum commitments and travel rather than simply multiplying the bride's package price. Is owner time a direct cost? It can be for a delivery-cost model, provided owner compensation is handled consistently. Keep the owner's service work distinct from the wider income target. Do not count the same payment twice. Can I use local competitors' package prices? They can help you understand the market, but their included scope and costs may differ. Build your own price floor first. The calculation cannot establish what customers will pay for your specific service. What if the venue changes? Recalculate travel, setup and staff time from the revised location. Check whether the agreed quote allows a change. A planning model helps explain cost differences but does not replace clear booking terms. Does a high package price mean high profit? No. A larger package may include more people, artists and travel. Compare the contribution after the complete direct workload, then test the salon's monthly commitments and capacity. How do I check whether a bridal party fits the available time? Assign each service to a suitably skilled artist and build the sequence backward from the ready-by deadline. Include setup, travel and buffers separately; total worker-hours alone do not prove the schedule fits. Closing takeaways Define people, trials, location and included services first. Cost all worker-hours, including preparation and travel where relevant. Check the finish-time schedule alongside monthly capacity. Separate advance payments from the total booking revenue. Explore related articles in the business guide library . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant PROFITABILITY GUIDE Coffee Shop Drink Contribution Margin: Cost Each Cup Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate coffee drink contribution after ingredients, cups and fees. Compare bottleneck minutes, remake losses and add-ons before changing the menu. Restaurant Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. A drink's contribution margin is the selling price left after the costs that change when you sell that drink. A coffee shop needs those remaining dollars to cover rent, scheduled staff, owner pay and profit. In the fictional example below, a $5 latte leaves $3.20 before those monthly commitments. That is a 64% contribution margin, not a 64% final profit margin. Every figure is a USD planning assumption rather than a market average. Quick answer Subtract coffee, milk, syrup, cup, lid, other sale-dependent costs and the payment fee from the actual selling price. Divide the remaining dollars by that price for the percentage. Then multiply contribution by realistic sales volume. A drink with a high margin percentage can still leave too little money if few customers order it. The direct answer: what a $5 latte leaves Assume coffee costs $0.45, milk $0.55, syrup $0.10 and the takeaway cup and lid $0.35. These ingredients and packaging total $1.45. Add $0.20 of genuinely incremental labor and a 3% processing fee, or $0.15 on a $5 sale. The sale-dependent cost is $1.80. Contribution is $5 − $1.80 = $3.20. Contribution margin is $3.20 ÷ $5 = 64%. Selling 100 identical drinks contributes $320 before fixed monthly costs. Selling 1,000 contributes $3,200, provided prices, portions and costs stay the same. Labor needs a deliberate boundary. If baristas are already scheduled for the shift and payroll will be paid whether you sell 100 or 110 drinks, that payroll belongs in the fixed-cost plan for this decision. If another order creates overtime or a separately paid production task, include the extra cost in contribution. Never count the same wages in both places. The $0.20 incremental labor assumption above is deliberately explicit. A shop with entirely scheduled labor would instead calculate $5 − $1.45 − $0.15 = $3.40 contribution and put the relevant wages in overhead. Neither convention lets you ignore payroll; it changes where payroll is counted. Use the actual sales price after discounts. Sales tax collected for an authority is outside the revenue in this example. If a processor charges fees on a larger collected amount or adds a fixed transaction fee, replace the simplified fee with the actual charge allocated to the order. The contribution margin guide explains why these sale-dependent costs differ from a monthly operating budget. Keep a written cost classification beside the drink worksheet so staff can reproduce your numbers. What changes the answer Recipe size moves both cost and selling price. A large drink might use another espresso shot and more milk, while its price premium is smaller than you expect. Cost each size separately rather than applying the small drink's percentage to the whole menu. Waste changes the usable cost. If a purchased bottle contains 100 theoretical servings but spills and leftover product reduce usable servings to 90, divide the bottle cost by 90. Record actual consumption over a reasonable period before assuming every purchased unit becomes a paid drink. Channel fees can overwhelm a small ingredient bill. A delivery drink may require different packaging and a percentage platform charge. An in-store margin cannot be copied to that order. Refunds and remakes also consume ingredients without creating a new paid sale. Sales mix changes monthly contribution. A customer buying an espresso and a customer buying a discounted flavored latte do not leave the same dollars. Calculate units by drink type, then total contribution. The weighted average should follow the shop's actual sales mix, not the owner's favorite product. Peak-time capacity matters. A drink that takes twice as much preparation time can displace other profitable sales during a queue. Compare contribution per production minute as a separate operational measure. That measure does not replace contribution per cup, and it is less useful when there is spare capacity. Review the coffee shop opening-cost guide for commitments that remain outside an individual cup calculation. Equipment purchases and deposits require cash even when they do not belong in ingredients per drink. Three worked scenarios A simpler drink with a stronger percentage An espresso sells for $3. Coffee and sale-dependent supplies cost $0.50, and a 3% fee costs $0.09. Contribution is $2.41, or 80.33% of price. That percentage exceeds the latte's 64%, but each espresso leaves $0.79 fewer dollars than the latte. At 200 espresso sales, contribution is $482. At 200 latte sales under the first assumptions, it is $640. Demand, preparation time and basket composition decide which mix works; the highest percentage alone does not answer the question. A promotion that needs more volume Discount the original latte from $5 to $4.50. Non-percentage variable costs remain $1.65, and the 3% fee falls to $0.135. Contribution becomes $2.715 per drink, a 60.33% margin. To replace the $320 contribution from 100 full-price drinks, you need $320 ÷ $2.715 = 117.8637 discounted drinks. Round upward to 118 whole drinks. Those contribute $320.37. A promotion that adds only ten sales would leave $298.65 from 110 drinks, below the original contribution. A delivery order with a different fee Suppose the same drink sells for $6 through a channel charging 20% of price. Assume ingredients and packaging total $1.70, incremental labor $0.20 and no additional processor fee in this illustration. Contribution is $6 − $1.70 − $0.20 − $1.20 = $2.90, or 48.33%. At 100 orders, that is $290. The higher sticker price still leaves fewer dollars than 100 in-store $5 lattes. Use the real platform agreement; do not stack a second fee if it is already included in the platform deduction. How to run your own numbers Choose a representative drink or a carefully weighted average order. Enter the actual price, ingredients, packaging, incremental labor and fees in the restaurant break-even calculator . Put scheduled payroll and other monthly commitments in overhead, then add owner pay and the profit goal separately. MyBreakeven supports currencies beyond USD. Use one currency consistently and replace all illustrative costs with your invoices, recipe portions and payment terms. Average order value is appropriate when customers buy several drinks together; do not mix an order price with a per-cup cost. Keep four columns for each menu item: paid units, net revenue, sale-dependent cost and contribution. Reconcile totals to the till and purchasing records. A cost card is a forecast until actual portioning, waste and sales results support it. If the monthly contribution requirement is $9,600 and your verified average contribution is $3.20 per sale, the plan needs 3,000 sales. Check whether opening hours, staffing and expected visits can support that quantity. Your calculator result does not predict that those customers will arrive. Common mistakes Counting every barista minute as variable labor while also entering the whole rota in overhead duplicates payroll. Choose one treatment for each cost and document it. Using menu prices instead of paid prices overstates revenue after promotions. Allocate a bundle discount consistently before comparing drinks. Costing theoretical portions ignores unusable milk, spills and remakes. Use realistic usable yield rather than adding an unexplained blanket percentage. Ignoring fixed transaction fees understates the cost of small orders. A $0.20 fee on one drink matters more than the same fee spread over four drinks. Calling contribution final profit skips the shop's monthly commitments. The coffee shop business-plan guide connects product economics to the wider cash and operating plan. Check peak-hour contribution, not just margin per cup A drink can leave more dollars per sale and still be the weaker choice during a queue. Compare the time it uses at the station that actually limits output. The example below is hypothetical USD planning, separate from the earlier latte example. Assume prices are net of sales tax and discounts; variable costs include ingredients, packaging and sale-dependent fees. Two drinks competing for the same limiting station Measure Simple drink Specialty drink Price / variable cost $4.50 / $1.50 $6.00 / $2.40 Contribution per paid drink $3.00 $3.60 Limiting-station minutes 1.0 2.0 Contribution per limiting minute $3.00 $1.80 At full demand, 30 available station minutes could support 30 simple drinks contributing $90, or 15 specialty drinks contributing $54. These are isolated capacity ceilings, not a sales forecast: concurrent equipment, order mix, demand and customer choice can change the result. When the station is idle, there may be no displaced order, and the specialty drink's additional $0.60 can still be useful. Include remake losses without charging for them twice If 100 paid simple drinks require five additional remakes using $1.20 of ingredients and packaging each, paid sales produce $450 revenue against $156 cost ($150 for paid drinks plus $6 for remakes). Realized contribution is $294, or $2.94 per paid drink before monthly commitments. If actual ingredient usage already includes those remakes, do not add the $6 again. No additional payment-processing fee is assumed on an unpaid remake. Record comps and refunds separately; not every replacement loses a full selling price. For an add-on, compare the incremental price with incremental ingredients, fees and preparation time. A $0.75 milk upgrade with $0.35 added variable cost leaves $0.40, not $0.75. Validate the standard recipe and milk yield before changing the menu. Review your menu contribution worksheet and recipe cost calculations together. Further reading and method: Industry source . Barista Underground discusses workstation layout and repeatable preparation. The monetary and station-time examples above are our own assumptions, not its performance figures. FAQs Is drink contribution the same as gross profit? Not necessarily. Contribution follows costs that change with the sale, while an accounting gross-profit definition may include a different cost boundary. Label the measure and list included costs so you can compare like with like. Should rent be divided across every cup? You can allocate rent to estimate a full-cost price, but it stays a monthly commitment in a contribution model. Include it once in the monthly amount to cover. Selling one more cup does not normally create another rent payment. How should I treat a milk upgrade? Calculate the extra paid price minus the extra usable milk cost and any extra percentage fee. Check the actual portion size. An upgrade can increase revenue while contributing very little if the premium barely covers the additional cost. Which drink should I promote? Compare contribution dollars, demand and preparation capacity. A percentage alone is insufficient. A promotion also needs an estimate of displaced full-price sales and the extra volume it realistically creates. Can I use the same margin for every size? Only if the prices and sale-dependent costs support it. Extra shots, larger packaging and different recipes change the calculation. Cost each size before averaging the menu. What if a customer buys several drinks? Use order-level fees and allocate them consistently across the basket, or model the whole order. Do not charge the full fixed transaction fee to every cup. Keep the unit definition consistent with your price and volume fields. Should I promote the drink with the highest contribution per minute? Only when that specific station is constrained and customers will buy the alternative. During spare capacity, contribution per sale, demand and guest experience can matter more. How should I include complimentary remakes? Use the actual incremental replacement cost and distinguish paid drinks from drinks prepared. Do not add a separate remake allowance if the same loss is already included in actual ingredient usage. Closing takeaways Cost the recipe, usable yield, packaging and actual payment terms. Compare contribution dollars alongside the percentage. Count scheduled and incremental labor once, in their appropriate places. Test sales mix and production capacity before committing to a promotion. Find related planning methods in the small-business guide library . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
