Should I price each guest or the whole event? Can I count expected drinks toward the minimum? What if the guest count falls? Does a profitable event fix a weak month? How do I estimate displaced regular service? Should the minimum equal the sales lost from normal service? Does a deposit count as extra event revenue? Closing takeaways
documents.text: Restaurant PRICING GUIDE Restaurant Private-Event Minimum Spend: Price the Space Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Set a restaurant event minimum using displaced contribution, setup costs and fees. Check guest guarantees, room charges and the final customer bill. Restaurant Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. A private-event minimum spend should cover the event's sale-dependent costs, extra setup costs and the contribution you give up by reserving the space. Start with what the event must leave the restaurant, then work backward to a customer-facing minimum. A busy Saturday closure deserves a different calculation from an otherwise quiet weekday room booking. All numbers below are fictional USD planning assumptions, not local rates or contract advice. Quick answer Estimate the regular-service contribution displaced by the booking. Add event-only fixed costs and any extra contribution target. Divide that requirement by the event's expected contribution margin to find the revenue floor. Then check staff hours, service duration and menu mix. Deposits, cancellations and taxes need their own clear treatment rather than being hidden in the minimum. The direct answer: a room reserved for an evening Suppose ordinary service in a room would generate $3,000 sales. Ingredients, payment fees and other genuinely sale-dependent costs equal 35% of those sales, leaving 65%, or $1,950 contribution. This is the contribution you expect to lose if the room is closed to regular diners. A private booking also creates $300 of extra setup, cleanup and equipment costs that do not vary with each guest. You want another $250 contribution for the disruption and event workload. The private event must therefore leave $1,950 + $300 + $250 = $2,500 before the restaurant's usual monthly commitments. Assume the event menu leaves 60% contribution after its sale-dependent costs. The revenue floor is $2,500 ÷ 0.60 = $4,166.6667. Rounded upward to cents, the minimum is $4,166.67. A $4,200 event contributes $2,520; after the $300 event-only fixed cost, $2,220 remains. That exceeds displaced contribution by $270. For 40 guests, $4,200 is $105 per guest as an explanatory average. It is not automatically a per-person contract price. A minimum spend often applies to an agreed group or space, and the actual menu selection determines revenue and costs. Do not add the ordinary rent allocation to this opportunity-cost comparison if it is already covered by the displaced-service contribution framework. The wider monthly budget still needs rent, but the event decision should count each commitment once. The restaurant contribution and menu-pricing guide helps define the money left after sale-dependent costs. Gross sales displaced by a closure are not the same as contribution displaced. What changes the answer The service period matters. Compare the booking with realistic regular service for that day, space and time. A Saturday dinner forecast should not be substituted for Tuesday lunch. Use comparable observations and explain the uncertainty rather than promising a full room of diners. Duration changes the opportunity cost. A booking that occupies a room for setup, reception and cleanup may block two selling windows. Count the actual closure period, not just the advertised guest event time. Menu mix changes contribution. Beverage-heavy and food-heavy bookings can leave different amounts after ingredients, staff and fees. Do not assume every dollar of minimum spend has the same cost. If guests can choose freely, test an unfavorable but plausible mix. Additional staffing can be fixed per event, variable per guest or committed in the ordinary rota. Decide which applies. A separately booked bartender for a flat amount belongs in event-only fixed costs; incremental per-guest service labor belongs in the contribution calculation. Equipment, security, cleaning and outside vendors need clear ownership. A supplier cost paid directly by the client is different from one the restaurant collects and pays. Pass-through arrangements should not inflate the revenue used to claim restaurant profit. Deposits affect cash timing, not the total value of a completed event. A deposit applied to the final invoice is part of payment, not extra revenue on top of the bill. Cancellation treatment depends on the agreed terms and relevant rules; this worksheet does not establish what you may legally retain. Review restaurant budgeting to keep event decisions connected with monthly cash and operating commitments. Three worked scenarios A weekday room with spare capacity Suppose regular weekday service would leave only $600 contribution in the reserved room. Event-only setup costs $200, and the additional target is $200. With a 60% event contribution margin, the minimum is ($600 + $200 + $200) ÷ 0.60 = $1,666.6667, or $1,666.67 rounded upward. A $1,800 booking contributes $1,080 before the $200 event setup cost, leaving $880. That is $280 above the displaced $600 contribution. The same booking would fail the busier Saturday plan, showing why a single minimum for every slot can misprice the space. A lower-margin menu Keep the original $2,500 contribution requirement, but suppose the selected menu leaves only 50% after sale-dependent costs. Required revenue becomes $5,000. At a $4,200 minimum, contribution is $2,100, below the $2,500 need by $400. You could change menu scope, raise the minimum or choose another date. The worksheet identifies the gap; it does not tell you that customers will accept the higher price. A longer closure Assume a longer event displaces $2,600 regular contribution and creates $450 event-only fixed costs. Add a $250 extra target. The requirement is $3,300. At 60% margin, the minimum is $5,500. If the customer pays $5,700, the event contributes $3,420 before those fixed costs. After $450, $2,970 remains, which is $370 above the displaced $2,600. The extra selling time has been priced rather than silently given away. How to run your own numbers Use the restaurant break-even calculator to model the event as one order or job. Put sale-dependent event costs in the direct-cost fields and enter the period's contribution requirement consistently. Use the calculator alongside the event worksheet; a monthly model does not automatically estimate displaced regular bookings. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Keep price, costs and overhead in the same currency, and identify whether the unit is a guest or a whole event. A whole-event price paired with per-guest costs produces an invalid model. Write a separate quote worksheet showing guest count, menu, included hours, space, equipment and service staffing. Cost setup and cleanup before comparing the minimum with another venue. Two offers can advertise the same minimum while including different workloads. Confirm whether taxes, service charges and gratuities count toward the agreed spend. Do not invent the customer's interpretation. Put your proposed commercial scope in writing and obtain appropriate review for the final terms. Common mistakes Using lost regular revenue instead of lost contribution exaggerates opportunity cost. The ingredient costs of displaced meals are not incurred when those meals are not sold. Setting the same floor for quiet and busy periods ignores alternative demand. Compare the actual space and selling window. Treating a deposit as extra income duplicates revenue when it is applied to the final invoice. Reconcile payment timing separately. Forgetting setup and cleanup understates the occupied period and labor. Count all event hours and all workers involved. Using a favorable menu margin for unrestricted guest choices can overstate contribution. Test the agreed mix and realistic substitutions. Calling the remaining contribution profit skips monthly commitments. The restaurant break-even guide covers that wider operating step. Turn an internal event floor into a clear customer quote A minimum spend is a revenue commitment; the business decision depends on what remains after delivering the event. Separate three layers: event contribution, any displaced regular-service contribution, and customer-facing bill terms . Do not add lost regular revenue as though every dollar would have been profit. In this independent hypothetical USD case, reserving a room displaces $900 of regular-service contribution. Event-only setup costs $300, and you want $200 additional contribution. If the event retains 60% of sales after all percentage variable costs, the floor is ($900 + $300 + $200) ÷ 0.60 = approximately $2,333.33 . A $2,334 minimum leaves $1,400.40 before setup, or $1,100.40 after setup: $200.40 above the displaced $900. Include each cost in either the percentage or the fixed event allowance, never both. The same $2,334 floor at different guaranteed guest counts Guests Minimum spend per guest Planning consequence 30 $77.80 Menu and beverage plan must support a higher spend per guest. 40 $58.35 Check staffing and the full reserved service window. 50 $46.68 The room still needs enough production and service capacity. Specify which payments count toward the minimum State whether eligible food and beverages count, whether room hire is additional, and how any shortfall is billed. Make taxes, gratuity, service charges, discounts, deposits and overtime treatment explicit in the written quote. This is a billing checklist, not a statement that every venue handles those items alike. A deposit applied to the final invoice is part of payment, not an extra sale. Calculate the quiet-day case again rather than applying a blanket discount. With no displaced contribution and the same $300 setup and $200 goal, a 60% contribution ratio produces an $833.33 mathematical floor. That difference comes from different opportunity cost, not an assumption that all weekdays are cheap. Protect the service duration and final guaranteed count in the booking process. Use event-level catering costing if staffing, transport or rentals change with the event. Further reading and method: Industry source . Maisie’s explains food-and-beverage minimums from a restaurant operator’s perspective, including reserved-space opportunity cost. Our dollar assumptions and formulas are independent examples. FAQs Is minimum spend the same as a room-hire fee? No. A spend minimum usually refers to an agreed amount of purchases, while a room fee may be a separate charge. Define what the proposed quote includes. Do not assume a customer's food bill and a space fee are interchangeable. Should I price each guest or the whole event? Either can be modeled, but keep units consistent. A whole-event model is useful for room closures and fixed setup costs. A per-guest view helps explain menu cost and headcount changes. Can I count expected drinks toward the minimum? Only according to the proposed commercial scope, and model their costs and fees. Forecast drinks conservatively when they are optional. Expected purchases are uncertain until actual orders occur. What if the guest count falls? Recalculate recoverable and committed costs. Fewer guests may reduce food but leave room occupancy, staffing and equipment unchanged. Any binding minimum or cancellation treatment requires clear agreed terms and suitable review. Does a profitable event fix a weak month? It helps only by the contribution it adds after its own costs and displaced sales. The restaurant still needs to cover monthly commitments. One attractive booking cannot prove the whole month is profitable. How do I estimate displaced regular service? Use comparable periods for the same room and time, adjusting for opening hours and known events. Keep a range where demand is uncertain. Record the assumptions rather than presenting the forecast as guaranteed sales. Should the minimum equal the sales lost from normal service? Not automatically. Compare the contribution displaced after avoidable normal-service costs, then fund event-only costs and the event contribution goal. Does a deposit count as extra event revenue? A deposit credited against the final bill is a payment toward that bill, not additional sales revenue. Cancellation and forfeiture terms need separate written treatment. Closing takeaways Price the occupied selling window and the alternative contribution. Separate event-only fixed costs from per-guest costs. Test the menu mix before setting the minimum. Reconcile deposits and final payments without duplicating revenue. Browse the small-business guide library for related planning methods. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Takeout vs Dine-In Profit: Compare the Whole Order
documents.summary: Compare dine-in, pickup and delivery using contribution, packaging, fees and kitchen time. Reconcile platform settlements without counting fees twice.
documents.headings: Quick answer The direct answer: one meal through three channels What changes the answer Three worked scenarios Quiet-night direct pickup A peak-hour platform trade-off A different platform price How to run your own numbers Common mistakes Reconcile channel economics before judging the winner Price parity does not mean contribution parity FAQs Is direct pickup always more profitable than delivery? Should takeout include rent? What if dine-in customers buy more drinks? Can I increase a platform menu price? How should I treat delivery tips? When should I pause a channel? Should I use the platform payout as sales? When can a lower-contribution takeout order still help? Closing takeaways
documents.text: Restaurant PROFITABILITY GUIDE Takeout vs Dine-In Profit: Compare the Whole Order Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare dine-in, pickup and delivery using contribution, packaging, fees and kitchen time. Reconcile platform settlements without counting fees twice. Restaurant Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. Takeout and dine-in should be compared by the contribution left after each channel's sale-dependent costs, then by the volume and capacity they consume. A takeout order can save table-service work but add packaging, platform fees and packing time. A dine-in order can include profitable extras but occupy a table longer. The fictional USD examples below separate those effects instead of assuming one channel is always more profitable. Quick answer Use actual paid order revenue, ingredients, packaging, incremental labor and channel fees. Subtract those costs to find contribution per order. Compare order volume, kitchen minutes and any displaced sales. Keep scheduled staff and rent in the monthly budget once. A channel's higher sales total or lower food-cost percentage does not by itself establish higher profit. The direct answer: one meal through three channels Suppose a dine-in order produces $25 revenue. Ingredients cost $8, genuinely incremental service labor $2 and a 3% payment fee $0.75. Contribution is $25 − $8 − $2 − $0.75 = $14.25, or 57% of revenue. An equivalent direct takeout order sells for $23. Ingredients cost $8, packaging $1, incremental packing labor $0.75 and a 3% fee $0.69. Contribution is $12.56, or 54.61%. Takeout leaves $1.69 less contribution per order under these assumptions, but that is not the complete capacity decision. Now sell the $23 order through a platform taking 20% of revenue, with no separate processing charge in this illustration. Ingredient, packaging and packing costs remain $9.75. The platform charge is $4.60. Contribution is $23 − $9.75 − $4.60 = $8.65, or 37.61%. The same meal therefore leaves three different contribution amounts. Actual contracts can define different fee bases, fixed charges or promotions. Replace these simplified assumptions with your statements. Never assume the platform deduction includes payment processing unless the agreement says it does. Scheduled labor belongs outside these figures when it is committed for the period. If the restaurant pays the same shift wages with or without the next order, those wages stay in the fixed-cost plan. The illustrative labor above is explicitly sale-dependent; count it once. The delivery commission guide explores platform deductions. This comparison includes direct pickup and dine-in as alternatives, making the operational choice wider than a fee calculation. What changes the answer Basket size matters. Dine-in customers may buy drinks, sides or desserts, while pickup customers may order several meals together. Compare observed order revenue and order cost, not an individual dish from one channel against a complete basket from another. Packaging changes with food and journey. A hot meal, liquid dish and dessert can require different containers. Count bags, seals, cutlery and remake costs where they apply. Packaging bought in bulk still has a cost per usable order. Capacity can make incremental takeout valuable during quiet service. If the kitchen and staff have room, a positive-contribution order can help cover existing commitments. During a full service, the same order might delay or displace a more valuable dine-in sale. Table occupancy has a separate limit. A dine-in order uses a seat and service time; takeout normally does not. Compare contribution per occupied table period only after keeping kitchen constraints in view. A freed table is worth money only if another customer is likely to use it. Refunds and remakes reduce realized contribution. Record who pays a refund, whether the platform returns its commission and whether replacement food creates another cost. A refunded order can leave more costs than the original worksheet predicts. Promotions alter the actual paid price and sometimes the fee base. A discount funded by the restaurant is different from one paid by the platform. Reconcile the settlement rather than assuming the listed discount describes your revenue loss. Use restaurant food-cost percentage for ingredient measurement, and keep the channel comparison tied to paid sales. Three worked scenarios Quiet-night direct pickup An extra 30 direct takeout orders at $12.56 contribution leave $376.80. Suppose they create a $100 extra fixed packing shift that was not included in the per-order labor. Incremental contribution after that shift is $276.80. If those orders use spare kitchen capacity and displace no other sales, that money helps cover monthly commitments. It is not final business profit. If the $100 shift was already included in direct labor, subtracting it again would be a mistake. A peak-hour platform trade-off Twenty platform orders at $8.65 contribution leave $173. Suppose accepting them means turning away 15 dine-in orders at $14.25 contribution, a loss of $213.75. The net change is $173 − $213.75 = −$40.75 before any other effects. Platform volume has increased gross sales but reduced the expected contribution from this constrained period. The displacement assumption is the key uncertainty. Measure actual kitchen delays and lost orders rather than treating the fictional trade-off as universal. A different platform price Raise the platform price to $26 while keeping $9.75 non-percentage variable cost and a 20% platform charge. Contribution becomes $26 × 0.80 − $9.75 = $11.05. To equal the direct takeout contribution of $12.56 under these same costs, required platform price is ($12.56 + $9.75) ÷ 0.80 = $27.8875, or $27.89 rounded upward. That solves the contribution equation; it does not establish demand, permitted pricing terms or customer acceptance. How to run your own numbers Model each channel separately in the restaurant break-even calculator . Enter a consistent order unit, channel-specific paid price, ingredients, packaging, incremental labor and fees. Keep monthly rent, scheduled payroll and owner pay in their appropriate fields. The calculator supports other currencies. Compare channels in one currency and one observation period. When modeling an average basket, use average basket costs and delivery hours as well; do not combine an order price with one dish's ingredients. Build a settlement worksheet with gross paid orders, discounts, refunds, platform deductions and payouts. Contribution is a planning measure based on sales and costs, while the payout also reflects settlement timing and adjustments. Reconcile them without assuming they must be identical on every day. Record peak and off-peak performance separately. An average can hide a channel that helps at lunch but causes delays at dinner. The restaurant sales-forecast guide connects expected orders to staffing and capacity. Common mistakes Comparing listed prices instead of paid revenue overlooks restaurant-funded discounts. Use the amount that belongs to the sale after the relevant adjustments. Counting an inclusive platform fee and a separate assumed processor fee duplicates costs. Verify the actual fee structure first. Ignoring packaging treats pickup as the same cost as plated service. Cost the usable packaging set for each order type. Calling every positive-contribution order beneficial ignores displaced orders at a bottleneck. Check what else could have used the same kitchen time. Charging the whole scheduled rota as both fixed payroll and variable labor double-counts wages. Identify incremental work separately. Using one average order for all channels hides different basket sizes. Keep the calculation's unit consistent before comparing results. Reconcile channel economics before judging the winner Use a channel worksheet that separates sales from cash settlement. A marketplace payout may already have commission, refunds and promotions deducted; treating it as sales and subtracting those amounts again understates contribution. Conversely, gross app sales are not the amount available to pay kitchen costs. Hypothetical USD example: an order has $24 sales after discounts, $7.20 ingredients, $2 incremental labor, $1.20 packaging, a 20% combined channel charge ($4.80) and a $0.50 restaurant-funded promotion. Contribution is $24 − $7.20 − $2 − $1.20 − $4.80 − $0.50 = $8.30 . The illustrative settlement before other adjustments is $18.70; subtracting the $10.40 delivery costs from that gives the same $8.30. The 20% is an assumption, not a quoted platform tariff. Do not add card processing if your combined charge already includes it. Price parity does not mean contribution parity If those non-fee costs total $10.90, a $10 target contribution and a 20% percentage fee require price = ($10.90 + $10) ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $26.125. Rounding up to $26.13 leaves $10.004 contribution. This is a cost-based planning floor, not evidence customers will pay it or that a platform contract permits different prices. Check these boundaries for each sales channel Boundary Record to use Sales and promotions POS sales after discounts; identify who funds each offer. Fees and refunds Settlement statement and contract fee base; distinguish refunded revenue from fees. Packaging and labor Actual containers, paid packing work and other incremental costs. Peak capacity Tickets at the limiting kitchen station, not app order volume alone. When capacity is full, compare the contribution and limiting-station time of the order you would otherwise serve. A delivery order leaving $8.30 is attractive during idle time; it may be a poor trade if it displaces a $12 contribution order using the same constrained slot. When time requirements differ, use contribution per limiting minute and realistic demand. Rent and already scheduled payroll still belong in the monthly plan. For fee-specific sensitivity, use the delivery commission guide ; this page owns the wider channel comparison. Further reading and method: Industry source . Lane Equipment discusses takeout packaging and third-party fees. The settlement bridge and target-price example here are independently constructed; actual platform terms control your inputs. FAQs Is direct pickup always more profitable than delivery? Not always. Direct pickup may have lower fees, but price, basket size, packaging and volume can differ. Compare contribution under your actual channel terms and include the operational effects of accepting each order. Should takeout include rent? Rent remains in the monthly operating plan unless the channel creates an additional space cost. You may allocate it for a full-cost view, but do not deduct it twice. Contribution explains what orders leave to cover such commitments. What if dine-in customers buy more drinks? Use the observed full basket rather than a meal-only comparison. Include the drink revenue and its sale-dependent costs. A channel comparison should represent what customers actually buy. Can I increase a platform menu price? The worksheet can calculate a required price, but permitted pricing and commercial terms come from your actual agreement. Customer demand also needs testing. A mathematically sufficient price is not a guarantee of accepted orders. How should I treat delivery tips? Keep money that belongs to another party outside the restaurant revenue used in this model. Treatment depends on the arrangement and applicable rules. Do not count all collected money as restaurant contribution. When should I pause a channel? Examine contribution, delays, refunds and displaced sales in the relevant period. A temporary capacity decision differs from abandoning the channel. Test the operational problem and track the resulting service performance. Should I use the platform payout as sales? Use a reconciliation that starts from sales and identifies every withheld item. If you start from a payout already net of commission, do not subtract that commission again. When can a lower-contribution takeout order still help? When it adds positive contribution without displacing more valuable constrained work or creating extra fixed commitments that exceed the benefit. Recheck kitchen and packing capacity. Closing takeaways Compare full paid baskets and actual channel costs. Separate quiet-period additions from peak-period displacement. Reconcile platform fees and discounts to statements. Keep monthly commitments outside contribution, counted once. Find more methods in the business guide library . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

Is 5% churn a normal rate? Should I include acquisition in every box? Are pauses the same as cancellations? Can growth create a cash shortage? How should I plan packing capacity? Closing takeaways Related planning decisions
documents.text: E-commerce PROFITABILITY GUIDE Subscription Box Churn and Break-Even: Count Active Orders Published October 7, 2026 Updated October 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate subscription box break-even from paid shipments, costs and churn. Test replacement spending, growth acquisition and the contribution needed. E-commerce Contribution Cost planning Worked examples AI-generated editorial illustration of this business topic; not a real customer or business. A subscription box needs enough paid active orders to cover product, packing, shipping, acquisition and monthly commitments. Churn reduces the active subscriber base, while new subscriptions consume acquisition cash before their future orders are certain. Calculate the current month's contribution first, then show retention and replacement assumptions separately. The fictional USD numbers below explain the mechanics. They are not retention benchmarks, forecasts of future renewals or a claim that the same costs apply to every subscription business. Quick answer Find contribution per paid shipped box, then divide monthly commitments by that amount for the required active orders. Model churn as lost subscribers from a defined starting base and add actual or explicitly forecast new subscribers. Keep acquisition cost, cancellations, refunds and payment timing visible. A subscriber count does not equal shipped paid boxes when pauses and failed payments occur. The direct answer: contribution from a $40 box Suppose a monthly box sells for $40. Products cost $14, packaging $2, pick-and-pack $3, seller-funded shipping $6 and payment processing 3%, or $1.20. Contribution before acquisition is $40 − $14 − $2 − $3 − $6 − $1.20 = $13.80. Monthly overhead and a separately modeled owner-pay target total $4,140. Without new acquisition cost in the month, the business needs $4,140 ÷ $13.80 = 300 paid boxes to cover those commitments. Three hundred orders produce $12,000 revenue and $4,140 contribution under the assumptions. Now start the month with 300 active subscribers. If 5% cancel before the next paid shipment, 15 leave and 285 remain. The 5% is a fictional scenario, not a benchmark or prediction. Assume every remaining subscriber pays and receives exactly one box; pauses and failed payments would require further adjustments. The remaining 285 boxes contribute $3,933. That is $207 below the $4,140 commitments before any new acquisition spending. Replacing the 15 lost subscribers can restore active quantity, but the replacement cost has to be funded too. If each replacement costs $20 to acquire, 15 new subscribers cost $300. A restored 300-box month contributes $4,140 before acquisition and $3,840 after it. The operation is still $300 short of the original monthly commitments. Subscriber replacement has preserved order volume, not necessarily profit. The ecommerce profit-margin guide explains order contribution. A subscription model adds recurring customer movement, which must be calculated rather than assumed. What changes the answer Define churn precisely. Customer churn, revenue churn, cancellations before billing and cancellations after shipment are different measures. Use the same starting base and period when comparing months. Do not apply a customer percentage directly to revenue if plans have different prices. Paid shipments need their own count. Paused accounts, failed collections and skipped months can reduce boxes below the active-profile count. Record the operational state that actually creates revenue and shipping cost. Acquisition cost belongs to new customers under the stated boundary. Do not charge the full acquisition amount to every continuing box and then subtract the same advertising budget again. Show the current-month cash spend and any separate payback analysis. Shipping and packing can change with volume. Supplier discounts, carrier commitments and labor shifts may have steps rather than a smooth per-box cost. Model the threshold where another packing shift or minimum purchase becomes necessary. Prepaid subscriptions change cash timing. Receiving several months of payment does not remove the cost of later fulfillment. Keep future box obligations in the planning schedule, and obtain appropriate accounting treatment for the actual arrangement. Product recovery and refunds matter. A cancellation before assembly may avoid more cost than a refund after delivery. Use a net loss assumption that does not duplicate refunded revenue already removed from the sales figure. Review the ecommerce return-cost guide to define which product, delivery and payment costs remain when an order is refunded. Three worked scenarios Churn falls in the next scenario At a fictional 2% churn on the same 300 starting subscribers, six leave and 294 remain. Those boxes contribute 294 × $13.80 = $4,057.20 before acquisition, a shortfall of $82.80. Replacing six subscribers at $20 each costs $120. With 300 paid boxes restored, contribution after acquisition is $4,020, or $120 below commitments. Lower churn has reduced replacement cost but has not made the original 300-box price-and-cost model sufficient for growth spending. Increase contribution per box Raise price to $42 with the same $25 non-percentage costs and a 3% payment fee. The fee is $1.26, and contribution before acquisition is $15.74. Without acquisition, required boxes become $4,140 ÷ $15.74 = 263.0241, rounded upward to 264. At 264 paid boxes, contribution is $4,155.36. If the month also spends $300 on acquisition, the contribution requirement becomes $4,440 and needs $4,440 ÷ $15.74 = 282.0839 boxes, or 283. Those contribute $4,454.42 before acquisition. The price calculation does not establish customer acceptance or future retention. Add customers while preserving a reserve Keep the original $40 price and $13.80 contribution. Starting after churn with 285 continuing subscribers, suppose 30 new subscribers pay for the current shipment. Total paid boxes are 315, contributing $4,347 before acquisition. At $20 per new subscriber, acquisition costs $600. Contribution after acquisition is $3,747, leaving a $393 shortfall against $4,140 commitments. The subscriber base has grown, while the modeled month's operating result has weakened. Future renewals might improve payback, but they must not be reported as already earned. How to run your own numbers Use the ecommerce break-even calculator for a paid box as the order unit. Enter product, packaging, fulfillment, shipping subsidy and fees consistently. Model acquisition using the month's actual subscriber movement, keeping continuing-order and new-order views distinguishable. MyBreakeven supports other currencies. Use one currency and one period across box price, monthly commitments and customer movement. An annual subscription receipt is not the same unit as one monthly shipment's contribution. Keep a movement table with opening paid-active base, cancellations, pauses, failed collections, reactivations, new subscribers and paid shipments. Reconcile those categories to the actual billing and dispatch records. A single churn percentage cannot explain all differences. Maintain a separate acquisition-payback table for observed customer cohorts. Record actual repeat paid boxes and actual loss costs. Do not assume infinite recurring revenue or use an unverified lifetime-value multiple to justify the current month's deficit. The free-shipping threshold guide offers a related order-cost lesson: promotional benefits still need funding from contribution. Common mistakes Counting registered subscribers instead of paid fulfilled boxes overstates revenue. Reconcile collection and dispatch first. Applying a churn percentage without a defined base makes month-to-month comparison unreliable. State whether it measures customers or revenue and when cancellation is counted. Assuming replacement restores profit ignores acquisition spending. Calculate the replacement month's contribution after that cost. Treating prepaid cash as free money ignores future fulfillment obligations. Keep the cash schedule and shipment commitments separate. Charging acquisition to continuing boxes and subtracting the same advertising budget again duplicates costs. Use a consistent boundary. Forecasting long retention as an established fact hides uncertainty. Show observed cohorts and assumptions separately. FAQs Does churn change contribution per box? Not directly if the price and per-box costs stay the same. It changes the number of boxes and often acquisition needed to replace customers. Volume-related supplier or labor changes can also alter the unit economics. Is 5% churn a normal rate? This example does not establish an industry benchmark. Five percent is an explicit fictional scenario. Use your own defined customer movement and comparable periods instead of treating an example as a benchmark. Should I include acquisition in every box? Show the chosen boundary clearly. Current-month cash acquisition applies to newly acquired customers, while a separate payback analysis follows their later orders. Avoid charging the same spend twice. Are pauses the same as cancellations? Not operationally. Both can reduce current paid shipments, but their future states differ. Keep them separate in the subscriber movement table before calculating contribution. Can growth create a cash shortage? Yes, when acquisition and inventory payments precede collected contribution. More subscribers do not guarantee enough current cash. Model supplier, campaign and settlement dates explicitly. How should I plan packing capacity? Use paid boxes and complete packing worker-hours, including preparation and dispatch. A higher subscriber count can require another shift or supplier commitment. Test those step costs before treating every additional box as identical contribution. Closing takeaways Use paid shipped boxes as the operating unit. Define churn and customer movement before forecasting orders. Calculate replacement and growth acquisition explicitly. Keep future renewals separate from earned current contribution. documents.text: Cleaning BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Cleaning Minimum Booking Charge: Cost, Time and Route Published October 6, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Set a cleaning minimum from paid staff time, travel, supplies and fees. Compare short bookings, repeat-route savings and contribution per staff hour. Cleaning Cleaning Minimum Booking Charge Generated editorial image illustrating this guide; not a photograph of a real customer or business. A cleaning minimum booking charge should cover the costs of turning up plus the contribution you need from that slot. In this example, a short visit costs $58 before card fees; a $125 minimum leaves $63.25 toward monthly overhead and owner pay. Charging by cleaning time alone misses travel, access and setup. All amounts below are fictional USD assumptions, not local market rates or a promise that customers will accept the price. Quick answer Add paid cleaning labor, paid travel and setup, supplies, vehicle expense and acquisition cost for the smallest visit you accept. Add the contribution required from that booking, then divide by one minus your payment fee rate. Check the resulting minimum against the number of short visits your route can actually deliver. Build the minimum from a complete visit A customer asks for a one-hour kitchen and bathroom clean. You pay one cleaner $24 per worker-hour, including the employment costs included in your own estimate. The cleaner spends one hour cleaning and another half-hour traveling, gaining access, unloading and packing away. Paid job labor is therefore 1.5 × $24 = $36. Consumables cost $4, vehicle expense and parking cost $8, and acquisition costs average $10 per completed first visit. Total non-percentage variable cost is $36 + $4 + $8 + $10 = $58. Travel labor and vehicle expense are separate costs: one pays the worker's time, the other pays for operating the vehicle. The owner plans $1,200 of monthly overhead, $2,400 of owner pay and $600 of additional profit. The funding requirement is $4,200. Suppose the route can support 70 completed visits with this scope and customers can be found for those visits. Required contribution is $4,200 ÷ 70 = $60 per visit. With a 3% fee on the collected service price, the minimum that meets this plan is ($58 + $60) ÷ 0.97 = $121.6495 before rounding. Round upward to $121.65, or choose a simple quoted minimum such as $125. At $125, the fee is $3.75 and contribution is $125 − $58 − $3.75 = $63.25. Seventy visits produce $4,427.50 of contribution. After $1,200 overhead and $2,400 owner pay, $827.50 remains before taxes and other unmodeled expenses. The $600 goal is met under these assumptions. It is still necessary to test demand: a mathematically sufficient price does not fill the route. This is a booking minimum, not an hourly wage multiplied by the time inside the property. Describe what the minimum includes, such as one cleaner, defined rooms and a normal-condition visit. An unusually dirty property or extra work needs a revised scope before confirmation. The house-cleaning pricing guide covers a broader quote. Four variables that change the floor Travel and access time. A small job on an existing route differs from a standalone visit across town. Record departure, arrival, entry and departure from the property. If parking or key collection routinely adds time, include it in the standard scope rather than calling every occurrence an exception. Visit frequency. A returning customer may not require another $10 acquisition cost at every appointment. Use a cost per completed visit derived from the chosen customer period. Do not remove acquisition because the booking came through a referral if you paid a referral reward or spent staff time following it up. Paid labor commitments. This example treats labor as varying with completed visits. If you guarantee a weekly wage regardless of bookings, put the committed amount in fixed costs and only incremental labor in the visit costs. You still count the full worker-hours for capacity. Mixing both methods overstates cost. What occupies the slot. One hour cleaning plus half an hour outside the property consumes 1.5 worker-hours. Two cleaners working together for one hour consume two cleaning worker-hours before travel. A customer-facing duration is not interchangeable with paid team time. A minimum can also depend on condition and equipment needs. Carrying a carpet machine into an upstairs apartment differs from wiping a small kitchen. Keep scope categories few enough for customers to understand, but different enough that the cost estimate describes the promised work. Three practical booking scenarios A repeat visit on the same route Assume travel and setup fall to 0.25 hours and acquisition falls to $2 per completed visit. Labor becomes 1.25 × $24 = $30. With $4 supplies and $4 vehicle expense, total variable cost before percentage fees is $40. To leave the same $60 contribution, the price floor is ($40 + $60) ÷ 0.97 = $103.0928, rounded upward to $103.10. A $105 repeat-visit minimum leaves $105 × 0.97 − $40 = $61.85. The lower minimum comes from a defined cost saving. Confirm that the shorter travel assumption describes the route before offering it. An isolated visit priced at $95 Retain the original $58 cost. At $95, contribution is $95 × 0.97 − $58 = $34.15. Covering $4,200 now needs 123 visits, because 122 × $34.15 = $4,166.30 and 123 × $34.15 = $4,200.45. One worker with 35 available hours per week has 35 × 52 ÷ 12 = 151.67 monthly hours. At 70% utilization, usable job time is 106.17 hours. Dividing by 1.5 hours allows only 70 whole visits. Even a full route of these visits cannot fund the plan. Seventy contribute $2,390.50, leaving a $1,209.50 shortfall after overhead and owner pay. A two-hour visit under the same minimum policy The longer visit uses 2.5 paid hours including travel and setup, or $60 of labor. Assume $6 supplies, $8 vehicle expense and $10 acquisition. Cost is $84. Charging the same $125 leaves only $37.25 after the fee. To retain $60 contribution, the floor is ($84 + $60) ÷ 0.97 = $148.4536, so round upward to $148.46. A $150 quote leaves $61.50. That price still earns less contribution per worker-hour than the short visit: $61.50 ÷ 2.5 = $24.60 compared with $63.25 ÷ 1.5 = $42.17. Compare the full monthly service mix before using the minimum as a universal price. Check the route before publishing the policy Use a recent week's completed visits to build a route sheet. Keep cleaning time, travel time, access delay and billable extras in separate columns. A single average can hide several isolated jobs that make the rest of the route look slow. Recalculate after removing those jobs or quoting them differently. The recurring versus one-time cleaning guide helps distinguish appointment economics. The monthly cleaning expenses guide helps check the overhead total. Neither replaces actual visit records. Write the minimum into the quote before the customer books. Explain included work and how added rooms or condition changes are approved. Do not promise a one-hour finish when the minimum describes a service scope rather than a stopwatch limit. Clear scope gives the crew a usable delivery instruction and reduces disputes over what was bought. How to run your own numbers In the cleaning business break-even calculator , enter $125 price, $4 materials, $36 labor, $8 other variable expense and $10 acquisition, with a 3% fee. Add $1,200 overhead, $2,400 owner pay and $600 target profit. For capacity use one worker, 35 weekly hours, 70% utilization and 1.5 worker-hours per visit. Other currencies are supported. The model requires 67 visits and permits 70; it does not predict bookings or optimize your route. Common mistakes Multiplying one hour inside the home by the wage while leaving paid travel out. Entering guaranteed payroll in overhead and again in every visit's labor cost. Offering the first-visit minimum on repeat jobs without checking acquisition and route differences. Applying the short-visit minimum to longer work with more supplies and labor. Treating the 70-visit capacity estimate as evidence of customer demand. Calculate the booking floor from the whole paid slot A one-hour clean is not necessarily one paid staff hour. Include travel, access, loading and reset time that the booking causes. When two cleaners spend one clock hour together, count two staff hours. Keep vehicle running costs separate from paid travel labor because they represent different costs. Independent hypothetical USD example: two cleaners require one cleaning hour and 0.25 travel/setup hour each. That is 2.5 staff hours at a $24 loaded hourly cost, or $60. Supplies add $6, vehicle expense $8 and attributable acquisition cost $10, giving $84 before card fees. To leave $60 contribution with a 3% percentage fee, charge ($84 + $60) ÷ 0.97 = $148.46 rounded upward . This is an internal planning floor, not a local rate recommendation. Same team and clean; different travel and selling burden Visit type Cost before fee Price leaving $60 contribution at 3% New isolated visit $84 $148.46 Repeat stop with travel/setup halved, vehicle $4 and no new acquisition cost $64 $127.84 The repeat visit uses 2.25 staff hours ($54), $6 supplies and $4 vehicle cost. There is no new $10 acquisition charge in this illustrative incremental view. If your monthly acquisition spending still serves repeat customers, allocate it consistently rather than assuming all selling cost disappears. A lower per-visit price can be rational only if the full slot economics support it. Turn the floor into a usable policy Define the included scope, service zone, minimum bill, add-ons and approval process before arrival. Do not promise unlimited work because the customer paid a minimum. Route a recurring nearby stop differently from a remote one-off visit only when the costs justify it and the quote explains the scope. Finally, compare contribution per paid staff hour and total route contribution. A minimum does not create bookings or guarantee enough work to fund monthly overhead. Track quoted price, booked price, total staff time, travel, rework and actual contribution for the next ten short visits. Use the recurring-versus-one-time comparison to check whether the discount produces a stronger schedule. Further reading and method: Industry source . TIDY identifies service scope, frequency and add-ons as pricing factors. The staff-hour and minimum-floor calculations here are hypothetical owner-side planning examples, not its consumer price ranges. FAQs Can I charge a minimum even for a tiny job? You can use a minimum to describe the smallest service your business offers. Explain it in the quote before booking and state the included scope. Customer acceptance still needs to be tested in your own market. Should the minimum include owner pay? Include owner pay once in the funding requirement if the business must support that income. This example shows it separately from operating overhead and extra profit. Do not also charge the same owner labor through per-visit wages. What if I work alone? Use a consistent labor boundary for your own time. You may put your income goal in owner pay and set direct owner labor to zero for cash planning. Keep all delivery hours in capacity even when no employee wage is paid. Is travel labor the same as mileage expense? No, paid travel time and vehicle operating expense are different items. Include each actual cost once. Do not add a mileage allowance and the same fuel expense again without checking what the allowance covers. Should every customer receive the same minimum? Use clear scope or route categories when costs differ materially. A close repeat visit and an isolated first visit need not have identical economics. Avoid changing the price after acceptance without agreeing on changed work. Does a higher minimum guarantee more profit? No, completed bookings may fall when the price changes. Compare contribution at the actual booking volume, not only at the previous volume. Also measure time freed for other work. Does a one-hour minimum pay for a two-person crew? Not necessarily. Two people cleaning for one clock hour consume two staff hours before travel, access or setup. Price the full staff workload and vehicle costs. Can a recurring nearby visit have a lower minimum? It can when measured travel, acquisition or setup costs are lower and the resulting contribution still funds the plan. Do not apply an automatic discount without checking the full paid slot. Takeaways Cost the whole visit, including paid travel and access. Connect the minimum to a realistic completed-booking count. Keep committed payroll and variable labor separate. Quote longer work from its own scope and worker-hours. Browse the business planning guides for other worked examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Salon BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Salon No-Show Cost: Missed Slots, Fees and Contribution Published October 6, 2026 Updated October 14, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate salon no-show cost from avoided expenses, sunk acquisition and collected fees. Compare replacements, owner pay and completed appointments. Salon Salon No-Show Cost and Contribution Generated editorial image illustrating this guide; not a photograph of a real customer or business. An empty salon appointment costs the contribution you would have earned, less any costs you avoid and any fee you actually keep. An unfilled $80 appointment in this example creates a $64.60 contribution gap when its acquisition cost is already spent. No-shows also waste capacity when the slot cannot be refilled. The calculation below separates completed visits, unreplaced missed slots and collected cancellation fees. All figures are fictional USD assumptions, not salon benchmarks or suggested legal terms. Quick answer Calculate contribution from a completed service after products, variable labor, acquisition and payment fees. For an unfilled no-show, subtract only avoidable costs and add only collected fees net of their costs. Multiply the contribution gap by unreplaced missed slots. Check remaining completed appointments against monthly overhead, owner pay and stylist hours. Measure the loss on the correct cost boundary Consider a salon with $2,000 monthly overhead, $2,500 owner pay and a $500 additional profit goal. The owner is the only stylist. Owner income is in the monthly requirement, so there is no separate owner wage charged per appointment. That prevents paying the same owner labor twice in this model. A service sells for $80. Products cost $10, laundry and disposables cost $3, and acquisition averages $10 per scheduled booking. Card processing is 3% of the collected ticket, or $2.40. A completed service therefore contributes $80 − $10 − $3 − $10 − $2.40 = $54.60. Suppose 100 appointments are scheduled and eight are missed without being refilled. Acquisition was already incurred for all 100 bookings. For the missed appointments, products, disposables and the service payment fee are avoided. With no collected cancellation fee, each missed booking has a contribution of negative $10 because acquisition is still spent. The gap between a completed appointment and a missed one is $54.60 − (−$10) = $64.60. Eight missed slots reduce the month's contribution by $516.80 compared with 100 completed appointments. This is different from simply saying that eight $80 tickets caused $640 of lost profit. With 92 completed visits, contribution after their allocated acquisition is 92 × $54.60 = $5,023.20. The eight missed bookings cost another $80 acquisition. Total contribution is $4,943.20. After $2,000 overhead and $2,500 owner pay, the result is $443.20, below the $500 target by $56.80. If acquisition genuinely occurs only on completion, a missed appointment could instead contribute zero and the gap would be $54.60. Your records decide the boundary. The completed-service contribution and the missed-booking cost must both be included when comparing the two outcomes. Four inputs that change the no-show result Whether the slot is replaced. A same-scope replacement can recover service contribution, although extra acquisition or discounting may change it. Track no-shows and unreplaced no-shows separately. Counting a refilled slot as a complete lost appointment overstates the effect on the month's result. When costs are incurred. Products may be avoidable before arrival, while a paid stylist's scheduled wage might remain payable. Enter committed wages in overhead if they do not change with completions. The salon profit margin guide explains why the chosen labor treatment matters. How much of the fee is retained. A policy saying $25 is not the same as $25 collected. Failed collections, waived charges and processing costs reduce retained cash. Track actual collected fees rather than multiplying a published fee by every missed booking. The service time being blocked. Missing a short trim and missing a long color appointment do not free identical hours. Record planned worker-hours and the service contribution attached to those hours. An average appointment model is useful only if the missed mix resembles the completed mix. For color appointments, prepared or wasted product can remain a cost even when the service is not completed. Use the hair-color appointment cost guide to build the service estimate, then identify which lines can actually be avoided at the cancellation time. Three worked responses to missed appointments Eight missed bookings with a collected $25 fee Assume all eight missed bookings pay a $25 charge and the same 3% processing assumption applies to that charge. Net fee proceeds are $25 × 0.97 = $24.25. After the already-spent $10 acquisition, a missed booking contributes $14.25. The month now contributes 92 × $54.60 + 8 × $14.25 = $5,137.20. After $4,500 overhead and owner pay, $637.20 remains. That exceeds the $500 goal. It assumes actual collection of every charge; it is not a claim about enforceability or permission to charge a customer's card. Half the missed slots are refilled Keep 100 original scheduled bookings and eight original no-shows. Four replacement customers complete services at the same price. Assume each replacement requires another $10 acquisition cost. There are 96 completed services in total and eight acquisition costs attached to the original missed customers. Contribution is 96 × $54.60 − 8 × $10 = $5,161.60. After $4,500, the result is $661.60. This preserves the original missed-booking acquisition rather than erasing it when a replacement arrives. If replacement customers cost less to acquire, enter that saving separately. Fifteen missed bookings and only ten paid fees Of 100 scheduled appointments, 85 complete. Ten of the fifteen missed appointments pay $25; five pay nothing. Completed contribution is 85 × $54.60 = $4,641. Ten paid missed bookings contribute $142.50; five unpaid missed bookings cost $50. Total contribution is $4,733.50, leaving $233.50 after overhead and owner pay. The published fee did not protect the $500 target because collection was incomplete and more appointments were missed. A reminder or waiting-list process should be evaluated through completed slots, collected cash and its own costs. Check hours as well as appointment counts One stylist with 35 weekly hours has 151.67 hours in an average month using 52 ÷ 12 weeks. At 75% utilization, 113.75 hours are available for the appointment workload. If each scheduled service blocks one worker-hour, 100 scheduled slots fit inside this illustrative ceiling. No-shows do not automatically create usable production time. A missed customer might be recognized too late to sell the slot, or the next service may require preparation. Track how much time is actually recovered. Capacity is a ceiling under the hours entered; it is not a forecast of demand. At $54.60 contribution, $5,000 needs 92 completed services if there are no additional missed-booking costs. With eight missed bookings whose acquisition has already cost $80, completed services need to fund $5,080: 94 × $54.60 = $5,132.40, while 93 leaves $5,077.80. Add a separate scheduled-slot count to your planning sheet rather than treating completions and bookings as the same number. The salon clients-per-day guide translates a monthly service target into the days you actually open. Use the same working calendar for both the appointment plan and the no-show record. Record the slot outcome, not only the no-show count Use a stated original booking cohort and cutoff. The same empty slot can lead to different outcomes if the cancellation happened early enough to avoid costs or to book an equivalent replacement. Missed appointment reconciliation Record Review question Original slot Service, price, duration and cancellation/no-show timing. Replacement Was the slot actually refilled with equivalent contribution? A lower-value replacement needs its own comparison. Avoided versus sunk costs Which products or variable compensation were avoided? Which preparation and acquisition costs were already incurred? Retained payment Was a fee actually retained, and what net processing cost applied? Keep refundable deposits separate. Recovery assumption Which reduction is a tested scenario rather than an observed improvement? Compare periods with the same definitions. The no-show calculator treats refills as equivalent completed services. If your refill differs, reconcile its actual contribution separately rather than entering a count that overstates recovery. The salon hub connects missed-slot results with completed visits and monthly capacity. How to run your own numbers Use the salon break-even calculator for the completed-service baseline: $80 price, $10 materials, zero direct owner labor, $3 other variable cost, $10 acquisition and a 3% fee. Enter $2,000 overhead, $2,500 owner pay and $500 target profit; use one stylist, 35 weekly hours, 75% utilization and one worker-hour per service. Other currencies are supported. It requires 92 completed services and shows 113 whole-service capacity. Keep missed-booking acquisition, fee collection and replacement slots in a separate reconciliation because the calculator does not model cancellations. Common mistakes Calling the entire missed ticket lost profit without subtracting avoidable service costs. Removing acquisition already paid when a customer misses the appointment. Treating every stated cancellation fee as successfully collected revenue. Counting both a no-show and its replacement as two lost slots. Using completed appointments for workload while ignoring unrecovered blocked time. FAQs Is the ticket value the cost of a no-show? It measures lost service revenue, not the contribution gap. Products, payment fees and some labor may be avoided. Costs already incurred and collected cancellation fees change the final loss. Should I add deposits to service revenue? A deposit applied to the eventual service price is part of that price. Do not count it again when the balance is paid. Track money retained after a missed booking separately using the actual agreed treatment. Can a waiting list recover the full loss? Only if a suitable customer completes the replacement service with comparable contribution. Extra discounting or acquisition can reduce the recovery. Record the original sunk costs even when the slot is refilled. What if my stylists are employees? Use the wage costs you actually owe under your staffing arrangement. If wages remain payable without appointments, they belong in committed overhead for this planning method. Count their available worker-hours separately. Does the calculator include a no-show rate? This guide uses the calculator for a completed-service baseline. It does not automate missed slots or fee collection. Reconcile those items outside the calculator to avoid disguising them as completed services. How should I assess a reminder service? Compare additional contribution from recovered completions with the reminder service's cost. Use before-and-after records for similar periods and service mixes. A lower missed-booking percentage alone does not prove the monthly profit improved. Takeaways Compare contribution, avoidable costs and collected fees. Keep scheduled slots and completed services separate. Preserve acquisition costs already spent on missed bookings. Measure actual replacement services and usable hours. Explore the small-business planning guides for related examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant PROFITABILITY GUIDE Catering Quote Profit: Guest Count, Labor and Event Scope Published October 6, 2026 Updated October 31, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Cost catering from guaranteed guests, service labor, transport and fees. Test guest-count changes and compare estimated contribution with actual results. Restaurant Catering Quote Profit: Costs and Capacity Generated editorial image illustrating this guide; not a photograph of a real customer or business. Quote catering from the full event workload, not just food cost multiplied by a markup. For the fictional 50-guest lunch below, a $1,500 quote leaves $505 after ingredients, event labor, transport, packaging and payment fees. That contribution must still pay monthly overhead and owner income. The decision is whether the event earns enough for the money and time it consumes. All figures are USD planning assumptions, not catering market rates or a recommended customer price. Quick answer Cost the confirmed guest count, usable food portions, event worker-hours, transport, rentals and packaging. Add the contribution the event must leave, then divide by one minus the percentage payment fee. Keep overhead and owner pay in the monthly plan. Compare event contribution per worker-hour and the kitchen calendar before accepting the quote. Work through a 50-guest lunch quote Suppose you offer a delivered lunch for 50 guests. Ingredients and planned preparation waste cost $450. The job requires 12 total paid worker-hours across preparation, packing, transport and cleanup at $25 per hour, or $300. Disposable packaging costs $100, transport costs $50 and equipment rental costs $50. Total direct cost before a percentage fee is $450 + $300 + $100 + $50 + $50 = $950. There is no separate event acquisition cost in this example; committed marketing belongs in overhead. Any actual per-event referral or sales fee would need to be added once. At a $1,500 quote, payment processing at 3% is $45. Event contribution is $1,500 − $950 − $45 = $505, or 33.67% of the selling price. The customer sees $30 per guest. Your business needs the $505 contribution figure as well as the per-guest selling price. Assume $1,200 monthly catering overhead and $2,400 owner pay, plus a $400 additional profit goal. The total contribution requirement is $4,000. Eight identical events contribute 8 × $505 = $4,040. Subtracting $1,200 overhead and $2,400 owner pay leaves $440 before taxes and unmodeled expenses. The exact price floor for eight events is ($950 + $4,000 ÷ 8) ÷ 0.97 = $1,494.8454, rounded upward to $1,494.85. A $1,500 quote meets that selected plan. It does not establish that eight events will book or that customers will buy the menu at $30 per person. The restaurant food-cost guide helps separate usable ingredients from purchase quantities. Do not use food cost alone to call the catering event profitable. A delivery that requires staff, rented equipment and cleanup has costs beyond the plated portions. Define the quote before scaling the guest count Write down confirmed portions, menu, dietary alternatives, delivery window, location access and who provides serving equipment. Specify whether the service is drop-off, staffed buffet or plated service. Those are different workloads, even when the food is identical. Use a job sheet with ingredient quantities and worker-hours by activity. Two workers preparing food for three hours consume six worker-hours. A four-hour event attended by two workers consumes eight worker-hours before travel or setup. Count the team, not just elapsed time on the customer's schedule. Keep sales tax and any pass-through amount outside the service revenue used here. If the payment processor charges on a larger collected amount, calculate that fee from the actual fee base rather than assuming 3% of net service revenue. This guide's fee assumptions are intentionally simple and must be replaced by your payment terms. Guest-count deadlines matter because purchases and preparation can become committed before the event. A late reduction from 50 to 40 guests may not save ten portions' full cost. Record what has already been bought or prepared. Price the revised scope using recoverable and unrecoverable costs rather than automatically multiplying the original per-person figure. Four variables that move catering contribution Portion yield. Purchase weight and usable portion weight are different. If a $24 ingredient batch yields 16 usable portions, cost is $1.50 per portion. A lower yield of 14 portions raises it to about $1.71. Use the portion count you can actually serve, including the waste already allowed in your recipe sheet. Staffing and service duration. A staffed buffet might need extra setup, attendance and cleanup. Count the actual loaded hourly cost and all worker-hours. If existing restaurant wages remain payable anyway, distinguish incremental labor from committed payroll rather than assigning the same wage to both catering and the restaurant plan. Delivery and equipment. Parking, stairs, repeated trips and return collection can make a nearby venue expensive to serve. Record rental charges, breakage exposure and the time required to collect equipment. A transport line of $50 is not enough when the job actually requires two vans and a second visit. Mix and calendar. A small event with a high percentage margin can still leave too few dollars to fund the month. A large event can leave more dollars while blocking multiple smaller bookings. Compare contribution and worker-hours for the actual events you expect to accept. The restaurant labor-cost guide offers a broader staffing view. For quote decisions, keep the marginal event cost boundary explicit so shared payroll is not deducted twice. Three event scenarios A smaller 30-guest version Assume ingredients fall to $270 and packaging to $60. Preparation still needs nine worker-hours, or $225, while transport and rental remain $50 each. Direct cost is $270 + $60 + $225 + $50 + $50 = $655. At the original $30 per guest, revenue is $900. Contribution is $900 × 0.97 − $655 = $218. Leaving the original $500 contribution requirement needs ($655 + $500) ÷ 0.97 = $1,190.7216, rounded upward to $1,190.73. You could quote $1,200 for this scope, which leaves $509. A minimum event charge reflects fixed event work; it is not evidence of customer willingness to pay. An 80-guest version Ingredients cost $720, packaging $160 and 18 worker-hours cost $450. Transport increases to $75 and equipment rental to $100. Direct cost is $1,505. At $30 per guest, revenue is $2,400 and contribution is $2,400 × 0.97 − $1,505 = $823. The larger event contributes more dollars, but needs six more worker-hours than the 50-guest event. Contribution per worker-hour rises from $505 ÷ 12 = $42.08 to $823 ÷ 18 = $45.72 before overhead. Confirm food storage, dispatch timing and venue capacity separately; worker-hour arithmetic does not establish food-production feasibility. Extra service added to the 50-guest event The customer asks for eight additional worker-hours on site and $50 of extra supplies. Direct cost increases by $250 to $1,200. Holding the quote at $1,500 leaves $255 contribution, about half the original $505. To preserve $505 contribution, quote ($1,200 + $505) ÷ 0.97 = $1,757.7319, rounded upward to $1,757.74. A $1,760 revised quote leaves $507.20. Confirm the added scope before doing the extra work; changing only the internal estimate does not change what the customer has agreed to pay. Check the monthly workload Two workers with 20 hours each per week supply 173.33 worker-hours in an average month. At 70% utilization, 121.33 hours are available for modeled event work. Dividing by 12 hours allows ten whole baseline events. Eight events require 96 worker-hours, so the financial plan fits this simplified workload ceiling. The date calendar still matters. Eight events requested for the same Saturday may be impossible even when monthly hours appear sufficient. Shared kitchen work, cold storage, dispatch windows and committed restaurant service require a separate scheduling review. The restaurant break-even guide covers the restaurant's own order-based model. How to run your own numbers The restaurant break-even calculator can approximate a consistent event-based quote: treat one modeled order as one event. Enter $1,500 price, $450 ingredients, $300 labor and $200 other variable costs, zero acquisition and a 3% fee; add $1,200 overhead, $2,400 owner pay and $400 target profit. Use two workers, 20 weekly hours, 70% utilization and 12 worker-hours per event. It requires eight events and allows ten. Other currencies are supported. This approximation does not model guest counts, concurrent events or food-safety requirements. Common mistakes Multiplying food cost by a markup while omitting event labor and rental. Counting two workers' elapsed service time as one worker's hours. Reducing a quote per guest after ingredients are already committed. Taking shared committed restaurant payroll as both overhead and event labor. Treating spare monthly hours as proof that overlapping event dates fit. Protect the quote when guest counts and service scope change Do not assume every catering cost falls in proportion to guest count. Ingredients and some disposables may scale by person, while delivery, setup and a booked service team may remain committed. Build a quote with a guest-linked cost and an event-level cost before adding percentage fees and the contribution goal. Independent hypothetical USD quote: 60 guaranteed guests require $9 food and disposables per guest, $420 event labor and logistics, a $600 contribution goal and a 3% fee on revenue. Required price is (60 × $9 + $420 + $600) ÷ 0.97 = $1,608.2474, rounded up to $1,608.25 . The $960 pre-fee cost is not the whole-business break-even requirement; the $600 contribution must still fund the relevant monthly commitments. Holding the per-person sales price fixed while committed event costs remain Measure 60 guests 45 guests Revenue at approximately $26.8042 per guest $1,608.25 $1,206.19 Guest-linked costs $540 $405 Committed labor and logistics $420 $420 Contribution after 3% fee About $600 About $345 At 45 guests, keeping the same $600 contribution goal needs (45 × $9 + $420 + $600) ÷ 0.97 = $1,469.08 rounded up . The unchanged event commitment is why a guaranteed minimum and a final-count deadline matter to planning. The client-facing terms must separately explain reductions, extra guests, extensions, rentals and approved changes; this article does not determine legal enforceability. Close the loop after the event Compare paid preparation, loading, travel, setup, service and cleanup hours with the estimate. Two people working four hours consume eight staff hours before travel or setup. Separate food purchased for this event from usable inventory carried forward. Reconcile discounts, refunds, settlement fees and the deposit credited to the invoice. Use the difference to correct the next estimate rather than hiding overruns inside a standard food-cost percentage. Where an event takes a dining room away from regular customers, add the private-event opportunity-cost check . A bigger guest count alone does not prove better contribution per scarce kitchen or staff hour. Further reading and method: Industry source . Katalyst discusses catering-specific costs and guest guarantees. Our 60-versus-45-guest calculation is hypothetical and does not use its market-price or staffing benchmarks. FAQs Should I quote per person or per event? You can show a per-person price while calculating the full event underneath. Transport, setup and rentals do not necessarily fall in proportion to the guest count. A stated minimum event charge can make that boundary clearer. Is $505 event contribution my profit? It is the amount left after the listed variable event costs. Monthly overhead and owner pay still need funding. The final result depends on the month's event mix and all costs included. What if ingredients are already purchased? Separate costs that can still be avoided from committed purchases. Some ingredients may be usable elsewhere, while prepared portions may have little recovery value. Update the quote decision using that actual recovery rather than assuming all food cost disappears. Can I use the restaurant calculator for catering? Use one event as the unit only for a consistent simplified scenario. Match price, costs and worker-hours to that event. A guest-count quote sheet and date calendar remain necessary outside the calculator. How do I compare two catering jobs? Compare contribution dollars, contribution per worker-hour and the hours each blocks on its actual date. Check cash commitments and equipment needs as well. A higher margin percentage alone is not enough to choose the job. Should deposits increase event revenue? A deposit applied to the agreed event price is part of that revenue. Count the total contract value once. Keep receipt dates and any changed cancellation treatment in a separate cash record. Why does a lower guest count reduce contribution so sharply? Some costs scale with guests, but committed setup, transport and staffing may not. Reducing sales per person while retaining those costs can consume the planned contribution. What should I compare after the catering event? Reconcile net sales, actual food used, event staff hours, transport, rentals and percentage fees against the quote. Credit deposits once and separate reusable inventory from event consumption. Takeaways Build the event cost before displaying a per-guest price. Count setup, attendance, delivery and cleanup worker-hours. Requote changed scope using the costs still committed. Check actual event dates as well as monthly capacity. Browse the business planning guides for more cost examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
