documents.text: Photography BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Photography Cost per Session: Include Editing and Delivery Time Published September 27, 2026 Updated November 21, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate photography cost per session including editing and delivery. Compare a $650 booking, longer edits and outsourcing against contribution and hours. Photography Editing Time Session Pricing Photography cost per session: cash costs and editing hours Record session-specific expenses separately from your own working time and monthly overhead. In the fictional $650 booking, $180 of session expenses leaves $470 contribution. Preparation, shooting, editing and delivery take eight hours. Ten completed sessions cover the $4,700 monthly overhead-and-owner-pay target, use 80 hours and generate $6,500 sales. The $470 is not take-home profit. Independent planning scenarios using the same $4,700 monthly target Scenario Contribution per booking Owner hours per booking Whole bookings needed Required owner hours Base: $650 price, $180 expenses $470 8 10 80 Editing rises from four to six hours; cash costs unchanged $470 10 10 100 Price falls to $500; $180 expenses $320 8 15 120 Outsource for $120; retain one hour of edit review $350 5 14 70 Choose the next practical step . Illustrative scene. Replace the figures in this guide with your own records. A two-hour shoot can occupy most of a workday after planning, travel, culling, editing and delivery. If you divide your session fee only by camera time, you can overestimate the number of clients your calendar will support. Measure the whole block and its job-specific costs. The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes photo editing and postproduction as part of photographers' work; count those hours in your own service model. Quick answer: Add shoot, preparation, travel, editing, delivery and communication hours per booking. Subtract print or gallery, assistant, travel and payment expenses from the collected session fee to find contribution. In an illustrative $650 booking with $180 job-specific expenses, contribution is $470; if overhead and an owner-pay target total $4,700, you need ten completed bookings and enough working hours to deliver them. Define a session from inquiry to delivery Record consultation, planning, location scouting, packing, travel, setup, shooting, backup, culling, retouching, proofing, revisions, gallery delivery, invoicing and follow-up. Some steps are shared across bookings, others are specific. A studio portrait and a wedding should not share a single editing-hour assumption. If you outsource editing, count the vendor invoice as a variable cost and keep your brief and review time in your own capacity plan. Separate job-specific cash costs from fixed monthly bills. Assistant fees, prints, online gallery fees charged per session, location or permit fees and payment processing may vary with each booking. Rent, subscriptions, insurance and owned-equipment replacement planning often persist in a month with few bookings. Decide how your own shooting and editing labor enters the plan. An owner-pay target in fixed monthly need can stand in for owner labor; do not then subtract the same owner's hourly pay from each job unless that is a deliberate separate wage. A complete $650 booking Assume a session fee of $650. This illustrative job costs $50 for prints or gallery delivery, $80 for an assistant, $30 for travel and $20 for fees. Variable cash expense is $50 + $80 + $30 + $20 = $180 . Contribution is $650 − $180 = $470 . If fixed costs plus planned owner pay total $4,700 a month, ten completed sessions supply $4,700 contribution. Ten bookings generate $6,500 sales and $1,800 session-specific cash expenses before fixed bills. Now count time. A typical booking might use one hour of planning, two hours of shooting, four hours of culling and editing, and one hour of delivery, revisions and admin: eight hours . Ten sessions use eighty working hours. If your realistic monthly client-delivery time after marketing, bookkeeping and time off is 100 hours, the plan fits with twenty hours of headroom. That is a capacity example, not a claim about how long all sessions take. Three changes that alter the plan Editing takes longer than quoted If editing takes six hours rather than four, a booking uses ten total hours. Ten sessions need all 100 available hours; the financial break-even number stays ten if cash expenses and price stay unchanged, but no delivery buffer remains. If revisions extend editing further, either scope or capacity must change. Track actual culling and retouching by package rather than inferring editing effort from gallery size. Lower price, unchanged cash cost At a $500 fee and $180 variable cash cost, contribution is $320. A $4,700 monthly target now requires 15 whole sessions because 14 × $320 = $4,480 while 15 × $320 = $4,800. At eight hours each, 15 sessions need 120 hours, above the 100-hour capacity. Lowering the headline price may increase inquiries, but it does not create twenty extra hours to deliver the work. Outsourcing edits Suppose an editor charges $120 per booking, and your own edit time drops from four hours to one hour of selecting, briefing and quality review. Variable cash expense rises to $300, so contribution at a $650 fee becomes $350. Monthly $4,700 target requires 14 sessions, since 13 × $350 = $4,550. Your own block is now five hours per booking, so fourteen sessions use seventy hours; that could fit if demand, editor availability, quality and revision turnaround hold. Paying an editor changes both capacity and contribution. Price scope, not just your shooting hour Put deliverables in writing: shoot duration, selected image count, editing level, turnaround, revision rounds, prints, travel boundary and licensing terms where relevant. A package with basic color correction has different hours from detailed retouching. Build prices from expected total work and costs, then test whether enough bookings exist at that price. The point is to make a promise you can deliver profitably, not to assign an unsupported industry rate to every image. Late gallery delivery can also shift collections into the next month. A deposit helps schedule cash but is not an additional sale on top of the total package fee. Keep booking, earned revenue and cash collection on separate lines if you use deposits. Equipment replacement belongs in your planning even if the camera was paid for years ago; decide how you will fund its future replacement without counting the same expense twice. Bookings also need a demand check. If ten completed sessions are required and only one in four qualified inquiries becomes a completed, paid booking under your own records, you need about forty qualified inquiries. That is ten ÷ 0.25, before accounting for reschedules or seasonal demand. Do not use a generic inquiry conversion rate from another photographer; track inquiries by service, source and month. A cheaper package might increase inquiry volume and still reduce contribution per available editing hour. Close the assignment time record after delivery The delivered gallery is a better cutoff than the final shutter press. Keep the accepted package intact and reconcile work from enquiry to delivery against it. Complete assignment review Record Review question Preparation and travel Include planning, setup, loadout, access delays and the complete trip on a stated paid-time basis. Post-production Record selection, editing, retouching, export, upload and revision rounds. Do not assume every delivered image needs equal time. Support and delivery Include client communication, gallery setup, product handling and fulfilment. Labour boundary State whether owner delivery hours carry an allowance. Do not count the same allowance twice alongside an owner-pay target. Scope versus estimate miss Separate agreed extra deliverables from time needed to complete the original package. The photography workflow gives a separate fictional $650 example: two extra hours at a $30 allowance reduce contribution by $60. Replace total assignment hours in the monthly planner ; a short shoot can still consume substantial editing capacity. How to run your own numbers Review your last ten to twenty completed bookings by package. Time each phase, record actual collected fees, assistants, travel, printing, platform fees and revisions. Use the average for a comparable package, not one unusually easy job. Enter package revenue, variable cost, overhead, monthly owner-pay target, leads and available time into the photography business break-even calculator . Compare required sessions with editing and delivery hours before making a sales target. The calculator supports other currencies where relevant. For broader packages, see the photography pricing guide ; for bookings required by an income goal, use the monthly photography client-count guide ; and for overhead and owner pay, read the photography profitability analysis . Common mistakes Billing the two-hour shoot and giving away editing: the client buys a finished deliverable, and your calendar must hold all its work. Calling deposits new revenue twice: a deposit is part of the package price, not an added booking. Ignoring assistant and gallery fees: those costs reduce contribution on each relevant session. Quoting unlimited revisions: unbounded editing can consume capacity even when cash expenses do not change. Using one average for unlike sessions: weddings, headshots and commercial product work have different scopes. Key takeaways Record every phase from inquiry through delivered gallery. Separate session-specific cash expenses from monthly costs and owner-pay target. Calculate whole bookings needed from contribution, then compare with available hours. Price editing and revisions into the scope before accepting another client. FAQs Should editing time be included in photography session pricing? Yes. Culling, retouching and revisions consume working hours even when the client only sees the finished photographs. Measure actual hours for the package you sell. How many $650 sessions cover $4,700 a month? With $180 variable cash expense per booking, each session contributes $470, so ten completed bookings cover a $4,700 contribution target. You must also confirm there is time and demand to complete them. Does hiring an editor always increase profit? No. It releases your time but adds a per-booking expense. Compare the new contribution, your remaining review time, quality control and the extra bookings you can actually sell. Is my deposit additional revenue? No. A deposit is an early payment toward the agreed package total. Record when cash arrives separately from the total sale to avoid counting the fee twice. What if editing time varies by client? Group completed bookings by comparable package and scope, then use a realistic range rather than one storewide average. Define revision rounds and update your estimate when actual time changes. Browse the MyBreakeven guide library for more planning guides. Check the next planning steps: Corporate Headshot Pricing: Setup, People and Delivery . For a different service scope, compare Photography Business Break-Even Calculator: Sessions, Pricing and Capacity and Product Photography Pricing per Image: Cost the Assignment . Recalculate contribution and delivery time for that scope. Choose the editing plan your calendar can support Against 100 available client-delivery hours, the base case leaves 20 hours, longer editing leaves none, and the lower-price case exceeds capacity by 20 hours. Outsourcing releases owner time but requires four more paid bookings than the base case. Check demand, editor availability, review time and revision scope before treating that capacity as usable. The table counts owner time as capacity; owner compensation is already included in the $4,700 monthly requirement. Do not subtract the same owner wage again from each booking. Compare package scope and pricing , check monthly client requirements , then enter your own inputs in the photography break-even calculator . These examples do not set market photography or editing rates. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: How Much Does It Cost to Open a Café or Coffee Shop?
documents.summary: Plan café opening costs, working cash, and daily break-even orders with three clear coffee shop budget examples and a capacity check.

documents.text: Restaurant STARTUP COST GUIDE How Much Does It Cost to Open a Café or Coffee Shop? Published September 26, 2026 Updated October 22, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Plan café or coffee shop opening costs, working cash, and the daily orders needed to break even with three transparent worked examples. Restaurant Café Startup Costs Coffee Shop Break-Even Planning Illustrative editorial scene for this guide; use your own business records. Opening a café can cost very different amounts depending on the lease, existing plumbing, espresso equipment, and whether you prepare food. To estimate your own cost, add one-time opening purchases, pre-opening deposits, and enough working cash to cover the early months. Then calculate the separate monthly sales target that pays rent, labor, supplies, and owner compensation. A coffee kiosk and a seated café need different budgets; a single national average cannot price your location. Quick answer: List build-out, equipment, deposits, permits, initial inventory, and launch costs to find opening cash. Add a reserve for early operating shortfalls. Then divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution left from each sale to find the orders needed to break even. The $40,000 opening budget below is an example for arithmetic, not a US market estimate or a quote. What goes into a café or coffee shop opening budget? Begin with the actual service format: a small takeout counter, a coffee kiosk, or a seated café with an in-house kitchen. Count the espresso machine and grinder, brewing equipment, refrigeration, water filtration, sinks, point-of-sale equipment, furniture, signage, and initial stock. Food preparation can add ventilation, storage, and equipment needs. Before signing a lease, check with the local health and building authorities whether the space and your proposed menu require alterations or permits. The US Small Business Administration recommends separating one-time expenses from monthly expenses . Its license and permit guide also explains that requirements vary with activity and location. Get written estimates for the actual unit, equipment, inspections, and insurance before treating a draft budget as a funding request. Here is an illustrative opening budget for a compact counter-service café. Every dollar is a modeling assumption, not a published average: One-time cash item Example amount Lease deposit and prepaid occupancy $6,000 Minor fit-out, plumbing, and electrical work $12,000 Espresso and brewing equipment $10,000 Refrigeration, point-of-sale, and smallwares $5,000 Permits, professional help, and opening insurance $2,000 Initial stock, signage, and launch $3,000 Fit-out contingency $2,000 Total opening cash before operating reserve $40,000 A deposit is cash tied up at opening, but it is not automatically an operating expense. Likewise, the full purchase price of an espresso machine belongs in the opening-cash calculation; a loan payment or lease charge belongs in monthly cash planning. Avoid counting the same equipment purchase twice. If you finance equipment, count the down payment at opening and the scheduled payments later. Ask an accountant how to record equipment and startup spending for tax purposes. The $2,000 contingency above is only a placeholder. In a space needing major plumbing, electrical upgrades, accessibility work, or a commercial kitchen, the cost can change substantially. Record vendor quotes and who is responsible for tenant improvements in the lease. A cheap empty shell can require more cash than a more expensive space already approved for your intended use. How much cash do you need beyond opening costs? Startup cost and funding need are different. The doors might open after spending $40,000, yet the business still needs money for payroll, rent, replenishment, and slow early sales. Create a month-by-month cash forecast beginning before the first sale. List cash paid, expected cash received, and the lowest balance reached; add a cushion for delays and repairs. A financing application should reflect that funding gap, not just the equipment list. For example, suppose the café loses $3,000 cash in month one and $1,000 in month two, then generates enough cash in month three to cover normal payments. The minimum extra cash to cover those two illustrative shortfalls is $4,000 ; with an additional $6,000 reserve for timing and surprises, the initial funding target is $50,000 ($40,000 opening cash + $4,000 forecast shortfall + $6,000 reserve). The reserve is a planning choice, not an industry benchmark. Do not multiply all fixed costs by an arbitrary number of months without modeling sales and payment dates. If the owner expects to draw wages before sales cover them, put those payments in the cash forecast. Also budget sales tax remittances, refundable deposits, loan principal, and supplier payment timing where relevant. Break-even operating profit and cash balance answer different questions; a profitable month can still have a cash squeeze when inventory or debt payments come due. What changes the cost of opening a coffee shop? Space and approvals. An existing food-service location may already have some suitable utilities, while a new fit-out can require permits and inspections. Confirm what the lease allows, the handover date, and who pays for improvements before accepting an estimate. Menu scope. Espresso drinks, brewed coffee, pastries bought from a supplier, and cooked-to-order meals use different equipment, staff time, spoilage assumptions, and food-safety processes. Model each menu category separately rather than using one ingredient percentage for everything. Equipment terms. Compare buying, leasing, and financing on total cash outlay, maintenance, warranty, and service downtime. A low initial payment can increase monthly fixed costs. Include water filtration and repairs in the plan, not just the machine. Hours and staffing. Longer opening hours can raise sales capacity, but also require more shift coverage. The Bureau of Labor Statistics food-service wage page can help benchmark a starting labor assumption; use local job listings and actual payroll burdens for your staffing plan. Owner shifts should have a fair wage even if the owner does not draw it immediately. Sales mix and location. A commuter kiosk may sell many drinks in a short rush. A seated café may make more from food and longer stays while paying for more space. Estimate foot traffic, conversion, average ticket, peak-hour throughput, and days open; then test whether the required orders are feasible at that location. Three café models: opening cash and monthly orders The cases below demonstrate the calculation, not typical café costs. Each uses different assumptions for fixed costs, average ticket, and variable costs. Variable costs include ingredients, cups or packaging, payment fees, and any sale-dependent labor; a guaranteed minimum shift belongs in fixed costs. Illustrative model Opening cash Monthly fixed cost Average ticket Variable cost per order Break-even orders per month Takeout kiosk $25,000 $8,000 $8 $3 1,600 Counter-service café $40,000 $15,000 $12 $4.50 2,000 Seated café with food $90,000 $30,000 $20 $8 2,500 For the counter-service case, contribution per order is $12 - $4.50 = $7.50 . Required monthly orders are $15,000 ÷ $7.50 = 2,000 . At 26 trading days, that is about 77 orders per day , rounded up. This is a useful capacity test: can the counter, baristas, and neighborhood support that volume across slow weekdays as well as weekends? If the same café wants $3,000 monthly operating profit, required orders become ($15,000 + $3,000) ÷ $7.50 = 2,400 per month , about 93 per trading day. With only 65 orders a day over 26 days, the model produces 1,690 orders and $12,675 of contribution, which is $2,325 short of its $15,000 fixed costs. The gap is a signal to revisit rent, staffing, average ticket, the menu mix, or demand rather than assume opening cash fixes monthly losses. A coffee-only kiosk may sell a lower average ticket at higher throughput. A seated café may sell food with a higher ticket and higher spoilage and labor. Compare each model's contribution per order and daily feasible orders, not its opening price alone. For more general restaurant setup decisions, read the restaurant startup cost guide . Turn the café budget into a quote and payment register For each opening item, record the supplier, quote date, expiration, included scope, excluded work, tax, delivery, installation, deposit, remaining balance and due date. Note whether equipment requires electrical, plumbing, ventilation or counter work. A machine price without the work needed to use it is not a complete installed cost. Separate refundable deposits from expenses and keep prepaid rent attached to the months it covers. A deposit is still an opening cash requirement even when it is not an immediate expense. Mark every estimate as quoted, contracted or paid so a preliminary allowance is not mistaken for a firm commitment. Test an opening delay using incremental costs only. If an additional delay creates $1,800 rent, $600 insurance/software and $1,200 committed training payroll not already in the budget, the added requirement is $3,600. If you fund it from the existing reserve, reduce the remaining reserve by $3,600; do not count both the reserve use and an extra funding amount for the same payment. Recheck the sales ramp from the revised opening date and preserve sufficient cash for the obligations that remain. A quote register will not remove construction uncertainty, but it makes missing scope and payment timing visible before you commit. How to run your own numbers Write down your quoted opening purchases and a separate operating cash reserve. For the monthly target, use your realistic blended ticket, variable cost per sale, monthly rent and minimum labor, owner pay, and target profit. Divide fixed costs plus desired profit by contribution per sale, then divide by trading days. If food and drinks have very different margins, calculate a weighted mix or model them in separate scenarios. Enter those assumptions in the restaurant break-even calculator ; it is the closest industry model for a café. Check its customer and capacity outputs against peak service hours and your likely foot traffic. The estimate depends on your inputs and does not include every lease term, financing cash flow, or permitting delay. For price decisions, use the restaurant menu pricing guide to test what remains after ingredients and fees. The restaurant covers guide explains how to convert a monthly target into service volume; adapt “covers” to café orders and trading hours. Common café budgeting mistakes Calling opening cash a monthly expense. A $10,000 machine purchase affects launch funding, while its financing, maintenance, and replacement reserve affect later months. Put each in the correct schedule. Forgetting the rush constraint. A target of 77 orders per day may look small averaged over 12 hours. If half arrive in two morning hours, equipment and staffing must handle roughly 19 to 20 orders per hour during that rush. Using beverage gross margin as café profit. Cups, card fees, food waste, rent, salaries, utilities, and owner pay still need covering. Use contribution after sale-dependent costs and include guaranteed shifts in fixed costs. Signing before checking the use. An affordable lease does not prove that your desired food preparation, seating, signage, or equipment will be permitted. Price the actual approved scope. FAQs How much does it cost to open a small café? There is no dependable single US price because the lease, existing utilities, menu, and equipment terms vary. Build a quote-backed list of one-time items, then add forecast early losses and a cash reserve. The $40,000 illustration above shows the method and is not a typical-cost claim. Is a coffee kiosk cheaper to open than a café? It can need less seating and fewer fixtures, but its rent, equipment, permits, and location fees still need checking. A lower upfront bill does not guarantee that the smaller average ticket will support monthly fixed costs. How many coffees do I need to sell to break even? Divide monthly fixed costs by contribution per sale, not the full sale price. At $8 per order with $3 variable cost and $8,000 fixed costs, the illustrative kiosk needs 1,600 orders monthly. If some orders contain food, use the actual blended contribution. Should I include my own pay in the café budget? Yes. If you cover shifts yourself, assign a realistic owner wage to those hours. Otherwise the model may show a profit that partly reflects unpaid labor. Does the opening budget include a working-capital reserve? List it separately so you can see the difference between launch purchases and funding for slow months. Base the reserve on a monthly cash forecast and the uncertainty of your lease, payroll timing, and demand. Can I use a restaurant calculator for a coffee shop? Yes, if you enter café-specific average ticket, sale-dependent costs, fixed expenses, owner pay, and practical service capacity. Interpret its results as a planning scenario, then check food and beverage mix, lease terms, and working cash outside the calculator. Takeaways Quote the actual site and equipment before treating any startup budget as reliable. Keep opening cash, monthly operating costs, and early cash shortfalls in separate schedules. Translate the monthly break-even target into daily orders and peak-hour capacity. Test coffee, food, and takeaway sales mix with their real variable costs. Browse more practical business models in the MyBreakeven blog library . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Restaurant Budget Template: Monthly Plan & Example Published September 26, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Download an editable restaurant budget template for Excel. Build a monthly sales and expense plan, compare actuals, and connect annual and cash forecasts. Compare 20 fictional restaurant scenarios and download their inputs . Restaurant Financial Planning Break-Even Download the restaurant monthly budget A restaurant operating budget starts with completed orders or covers × a matching average check, then deducts food cost, loaded labor and the other expenses included in the plan. Use the monthly Excel template below for budget-versus-actual review. An annual budget adds seasonal monthly plans; a cash forecast places receipts and payments on their actual dates. These are related schedules, not interchangeable templates. Download the editable restaurant budget for Excel (.xlsx) . Use it to compare one month’s planned sales and operating costs with actual results. Read the labelled example below before replacing its assumptions. This is an operating budget, not a dated cash forecast. For receipts, payroll dates, equipment purchases and debt principal, use the 13-week cash flow forecast . For the order volume needed to fund your entered monthly commitments, use the restaurant break-even calculator . Choose the restaurant planning schedule Question Use Keep separate What should this month earn? Monthly operating budget and actual comparison Inventory purchases versus food consumed How does seasonality change the year? Twelve-month operating budget A repeated average month versus supported seasonal inputs Can each payment date be funded? Dated cash forecast Profit, customer collection dates and debt principal Illustrative scene; use your own records for the calculations in this guide. New: Download the free editable 12-month restaurant budget workbook (Excel) . It provides monthly budget inputs, actual-vs-budget columns, an annual dashboard and an operating break-even estimate. The original one-month template remains available below. Choose the restaurant budgeting resource for your task Your planning question Use this existing resource Scope I need an editable restaurant budget template Download the monthly Excel workbook One monthly budget versus actual; editable inputs and calculated differences, not a 12-month forecast I need an annual budget example Download editable 12-month Excel workbook or view the illustrative calculation Separate 12-month editable workbook with monthly budgets, actuals and an annual dashboard; the article also includes a worked annual example I need payment-date cash planning Use the 13-week cash-flow calculator Separate dated receipts and payments, not operating profit This restaurant budget template pairs an editable Excel workbook with a monthly planning example. Use it to budget sales, food costs, loaded payroll and recurring overhead, then compare actual results with your original plan. A restaurant budget should tell you how many sales must arrive this month and what remains after food, labor, occupancy and owner pay. Start with orders or covers and an average check, then budget costs on the same monthly basis. Compare actual results with that plan as the month progresses. A lease budget written only as percentages cannot tell you whether Tuesday service will pay for a guaranteed shift. Quick answer: Forecast monthly orders and average check, subtract variable food and transaction costs, then subtract the costs due even when orders are slow. For example, 2,000 orders at $25 bring $50,000 sales; at $9 variable cost each, contribution is $32,000. With $27,000 fixed costs, the example leaves $5,000 modeled remainder after the included owner allocation. Make your own budget using quoted costs. Verified restaurant cost data for your budget Reviewed November 13, 2026. The National Restaurant Association’s 2025 Restaurant Operations Data Abstract reports 2024 operating data from more than 900 U.S. restaurants. These are segment-specific survey medians, not 2026 supplier quotes, forecasts or prescribed targets. 2024 U.S. restaurant survey medians, reported in 2025 Measure Fullservice Limited-service Food and nonalcoholic beverage costs / sales 32.0% 32.4% Income before taxes / sales 2.8% 4.0% Sources: National Restaurant Association food-cost findings, September 10, 2025 , and profitability findings, August 20, 2025 . The Association cautions that these ratios are not individual restaurant standards or goals. Compare account definitions, service type and sales mix before judging a difference. Separate medians do not form a single restaurant income statement. Our fictional workbook’s $11,800 remainder on $60,000 sales (19.67%) is not an industry net-margin claim: its cost scope and owner-pay treatment differ. Build your own budget from current inventory, recipes, payroll schedules, contracts and channel statements. How to budget a restaurant in five steps Choose the calendar month or accounting period, then forecast orders or covers by daypart and channel. Multiply each by the expected average check. Use inventory records for food and beverage cost, and record channel-dependent fees and packaging separately. Build paid hours by role, including employer costs. Separate guaranteed shifts from hours added for incremental orders. Add occupancy and other recurring commitments, counting owner compensation once. Keep equipment, deposits and financing payments in a separate cash schedule. Save the original budget. Compare actual results each week, explain the largest dollar variances, and update a separate forecast. The workbook example below follows its stated simplified cost boundary. Add any missing channel costs before using it as your own break-even model. A target percentage cannot replace the minimum staffing and payments your operation actually needs. The monthly restaurant budget, line by line Start with food and beverage revenue separately. Estimate covers by daypart, open days and average spend, not a single hopeful annual growth rate. Then enter food and beverage cost of goods sold (COGS), guaranteed payroll including employer costs, rent, utilities, marketing, owner pay and other fixed charges. Put opening equipment and deposits in a cash schedule; they are not the same as this month's cost of serving a meal. The OpenStax break-even guide explains why fixed and variable costs need separate treatment for break-even. A simple test uses 2,000 orders at $25 average spend: sales are $50,000. Ingredients, packaging and payment fees of $9 an order total $18,000, leaving $32,000 contribution. Assume rent, guaranteed labor, insurance, owner pay and other fixed costs total $27,000. The modeled remainder after the included owner allocation is $5,000; this is not after-tax net income or bank cash. Required orders to cover those fixed costs are $27,000 ÷ ($25 − $9), rounded up to 1,688 orders . At 26 open days, that is about 65 orders daily. Compare the required volume with your actual service capacity. Restaurant budget template for Excel: read the example first The editable sheet below uses a separate illustrative month from the $50,000 sales example above. Its budget is $45,000 food sales plus $15,000 beverage sales. Food and beverage cost of goods sold total $18,000. The committed expense lines total $30,200: $15,000 guaranteed payroll, $1,500 employer payroll costs, $4,000 owner compensation, $6,000 occupancy, $1,200 utilities, $800 marketing and $1,700 other fixed costs. Owner compensation is included once. Illustrative monthly restaurant budget and actual results in USD Line Budget Actual Actual less budget Food sales $45,000 $42,000 −$3,000 Beverage sales $15,000 $15,000 $0 Total sales $60,000 $57,000 −$3,000 Food and beverage COGS $18,000 $18,700 +$700 Sales less COGS $42,000 $38,300 −$3,700 Committed expense lines including owner compensation $30,200 $31,100 +$900 Modeled remainder after owner allocation $11,800 $7,200 −$4,600 Reconcile the change: $3,000 less sales, $700 more COGS and $900 more committed expenses reduce the modeled remainder by $4,600. A positive expense variance means actual spending exceeded the budget; it is not automatically a favorable result. Keep the original budget so you can explain each difference before revising the forecast. The sheet's simplified break-even calculation treats COGS as its only variable cost and the listed recurring expenses as committed. Budget contribution is $42,000 ÷ $60,000 = 70%, giving $30,200 ÷ 0.70 = $43,142.86 break-even sales. Actual contribution is $38,300 ÷ $57,000 = 67.19% when displayed to two decimals; using the unrounded ratio gives $46,284.60 break-even sales. Payment fees, delivery commissions and volume-dependent labor need separate treatment if they apply to your business. Include each cost once in a consistent category, and adapt the sheet or use a model that includes those costs before treating its result as your own threshold. This operating budget does not show bank cash, tax liabilities, debt principal or equipment payments. The loaded restaurant labor guide helps reconcile wages and employer costs with these payroll lines; keep opening purchases and payment timing in a separate cash schedule. When the workbook cannot report a break-even threshold The contribution calculation requires positive sales. If sales are zero, the workbook shows No sales ; if sales less COGS is zero or negative, it shows No positive contribution instead of a zero or negative break-even target. Adding volume at that contribution does not fund positive monthly commitments. Complete inputs means a required amount is blank or nonnumeric, while Check inputs identifies a negative entered amount. Enter a genuine zero explicitly. The break-even variance is Not comparable unless both columns have numeric thresholds. A valid zero threshold is possible when all committed costs are explicitly zero and contribution is positive. These checks do not validate demand or add omitted costs. The workbook remains a simplified operating model; use a dated cash forecast for payment timing and check service capacity separately. Use a budget that changes when the month changes Your monthly budget is the original target. Update a rolling forecast when bookings, sales mix, staff hours or ingredient invoices change; keep the original target to measure the difference. A $3,000 favorable sales variance may still leave you behind if a delivery channel carries $2,000 extra commissions. Separate the variance in sales volume from the variance in average ticket. Include payroll taxes and employer insurance in labor, and split minimum scheduled hours from extra hours needed for a busy service. Treat fixed rent and software differently from per-order processing fees. If your supplier prices rise, adjust the cost per plate rather than multiplying the entire restaurant's expenses by the same inflation number. The budget is only useful when its expense categories match invoices and the owner can update it each week. Three budget outcomes from the same dining room Base case: 2,000 orders × $25 = $50,000 sales. Variable cost is 2,000 × $9 = $18,000. Contribution is $32,000; less $27,000 fixed costs leaves $5,000. Slow month: 1,600 orders at the same ticket give $40,000 sales. Variable cost is $14,400, leaving $25,600 contribution. With the same guaranteed shifts and rent, the restaurant loses $1,400. Changing the order count alone changes the answer; copying last month's percentage profit would hide that loss. Discounted delivery mix: 2,200 orders at an average $23 ticket give $50,600 sales. If packaging, commissions and food raise blended variable cost to $11 per order, contribution is $26,400 and the business loses $600 after fixed costs. Higher order count did not repair the weaker contribution. Check channel mix before praising a sales increase. Explain the $4,600 shortfall with a flexible comparison This uses the same monthly workbook example, not a new restaurant dataset. Original COGS is $18,000 ÷ $60,000 = 30% of sales. Applied to $57,000 actual sales, the allowance is $17,100 . Holding $30,200 commitments constant gives a flexible comparison of $9,700 . This is a manual analysis; no additional workbook tab is claimed. Original budget, flexed comparison and actual: illustrative USD Line Original budget Flexed to actual sales Actual Net sales $60,000 $57,000 $57,000 Food and beverage COGS $18,000 $17,100 $18,700 Commitments including owner allocation $30,200 $30,200 $31,100 Modeled remainder $11,800 $9,700 $7,200 Lower-sales effect: −$2,100. ($57,000 − $60,000) × 70% budget contribution margin. COGS above flexed allowance: −$1,600. $17,100 allowed − $18,700 actual. Additional commitments: −$900. $30,200 budget − $31,100 actual. Check: −$2,100 − $1,600 − $900 = −$4,600; $11,800 − $4,600 = $7,200. The static COGS variance is only $700, but COGS is $1,600 above the sales-adjusted allowance. Investigate inventory usage, prices, waste and menu mix before cutting an unrelated expense. This revenue-based flex assumes stable prices, mix and cost behavior within the modeled range. Without covers, quantities and realized prices, the $2,100 cannot be attributed solely to fewer guests. Flex recipes and staffing to actual activity by channel for a real diagnosis. OpenStax explains the activity-based flexible-budget principle . Calculate budget inputs from source records These independent USD illustrations explain individual input lines; do not add them again to totals already entered. Use net sales after discounts and refunds, excluding sales tax collected for remittance. A cover is one guest; an order can include several guests. Match the unit to the average check. Illustrative calculations and supporting records Input Exact calculation Check against Net sales 2,000 orders × $25 = $50,000 POS net sales, refunds and channel totals Inventory-based COGS $6,000 opening inventory + $19,000 net purchases − $6,300 closing inventory = $18,700 Same-period counts, valuations, transfers and adjustments Loaded labor 600 paid hours × $20 + $1,200 employer costs = $13,200 Roster and payroll; the assumed 10% burden is not a statutory rate Delivery commission $10,000 commissionable sales × assumed 25% = $2,500 Contract and settlement statement; charging bases differ Prime cost percentage ($18,700 COGS + $13,200 loaded labor) ÷ $57,000 net sales = 55.96% Consistent period and sales denominator; include all applicable labor once Add separate delivery commission once if it is absent from entered costs. Do not both net it out of revenue and subtract it again. Split guaranteed staffing from incremental hours before calculating contribution; payroll is not automatically entirely fixed or entirely variable. Check rounding, capacity and owner compensation For the $50,000 quick example, contribution is $25 − $9 = $16 per order. The exact threshold is $27,000 ÷ $16 = 1,687.5 orders: 1,688 whole orders . The fractional daily average over 26 open days is 64.9038; a uniform whole-order target is 65 orders daily . That gives 1,690 monthly orders and a $40 remainder; 1,688 monthly orders leave $8. Check kitchen and seating capacity separately. The $27,000 quick-example commitments and $30,200 monthly workbook commitments include owner compensation once. The result is a planning remainder after the stated owner allocation , not automatically accounting operating profit, withdrawable cash or after-tax net income. Salary, drawings and distributions have different treatment depending on entity structure. Keep drawings, debt principal, capital purchases and payment timing in a separate cash schedule. The one-month workbook treats COGS as its only variable cost: its budget contribution margin is 70%. The separate annual workbook also includes packaging/delivery/fees. Its sample monthly base is $60,000 sales − $18,000 COGS − $1,800 variable fees = $40,200 contribution (67%). Less $30,200 commitments leaves $10,000; break-even is $45,074.63 . Do not transfer a margin between files without reconciling included costs. Enter every actual input, including genuine zeros, before interpreting an annual workbook month. Operating budget: original target, flexible comparison and cash plan An operating budget estimates same-period revenue and operating expenses. An annual operating budget can be built from monthly sales drivers, expense behavior and seasonal schedules rather than spreading every line equally across twelve months. Keep the original approved target unchanged so the comparison remains auditable. At month end, compare actual results with a budget flexed to actual activity using original rates. This distinguishes fewer orders from unfavorable ingredients or staffing costs. The operating-budget result is not the bank balance: equipment purchases, loan principal and collection/payment timing require a separate cash budget . Connect the restaurant budget to its supporting schedules A restaurant operating budget is part of a wider master budget . Keep the sales plan, purchasing and staffing needs, payment dates, equipment spending and financing connected. The service example in that guide is a simplified bridge; add inventory, unpaid bills, deposits and other restaurant-specific timing rather than copying its assumptions unchanged. How to run your own numbers Download the budget and replace the yellow sales and expense inputs with your own month. The example has budget and actual columns and shows the difference for each line. It is an operating model, so prepare a separate cash forecast for debt principal, equipment purchases and sales-tax remittances. Use the editable restaurant monthly budget template . Replace the yellow sample inputs; its figures are illustrations, not benchmarks. Enter your own average ticket, variable cost, monthly fixed costs, owner pay and operating capacity in the free restaurant break-even calculator . It is a planning model, not a forecast of customer demand. Common budgeting mistakes Using purchases as food cost. Inventory bought in the last week may not be used until next month; reconcile opening inventory, purchases and closing inventory. Ignoring owner hours. Profit improves on paper when the owner works a full schedule without a wage, even if that arrangement is unsustainable. Changing the target when results disappoint. Keep budget and revised forecast side by side. Budgeting labor as a flat percentage. A two-person minimum shift costs money even when no one walks in. Mixing sales tax with revenue. Remitted tax is not operating sales; keep your accounting basis consistent. Restaurant monthly expenses: reconcile before judging the variance Use the same month and accounting boundary in both workbook columns. Keep the approved budget, collect actual records, then explain differences before changing next month’s forecast. This checklist supports the existing one-month file; it does not add automated imports or a twelve-month dashboard. Monthly budget review: evidence and next decision Line to review Evidence and action Food and beverage sales Reconcile net sales by channel and daypart. Separate fewer covers from a lower average check; do not include tax collected for another party as sales. Food and beverage COGS Reconcile beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory. Investigate quantities, purchase prices and waste rather than treating every higher invoice as higher consumption. Payroll and employer costs Match paid hours, pay rates and employer charges to the period. Count owner compensation once and separate minimum shifts from additional hours. Other recurring expenses Check rent, utilities, subscriptions and invoice timing. Identify delivery commissions, payment fees and packaging before relying on the sheet’s simplified contribution ratio. Cash commitments outside this result Schedule deposits, equipment and debt principal in the cash forecast. A favorable operating variance does not establish that cash is available. In the existing workbook example, the $4,600 unfavorable operating-result variance consists of $3,000 less sales, $700 more COGS and $900 more committed expenses. It identifies the dollar bridge; it does not prove that food waste or staff inefficiency caused the change. Compare actual activity with original rates using flexible budget and variance analysis before making that decision. Download the restaurant monthly budget , retain a dated original for the period and record the explanation beside each material variance. Keep opening costs in the restaurant startup budget . Diagnose a restaurant budget variance before cutting costs Keep the original budget intact. Then ask three separate questions: did you serve the planned number of orders, did each order leave the planned contribution, and did monthly committed costs change? A lower food bill can simply mean fewer customers; it does not prove purchasing improved. Independent USD example: a volume and cost bridge, not the downloadable workbook's default inputs Measure Original budget Actual month Completed orders × net average check 2,000 × $25 = $50,000 1,800 × $25 = $45,000 Order-driven costs per order $9 $10 Contribution before monthly costs $32,000 $27,000 Committed monthly operating costs $27,000 $27,500 Operating result in this stated scope $5,000 −$500 The $5,500 deterioration reconciles exactly: 200 missing orders × $16 budget contribution = $3,200; $1 extra order-driven cost × 1,800 actual orders = $1,800; and $500 more monthly costs. The flexible comparison at actual volume would be 1,800 × $16 − $27,000 = $1,800. Actual performance is $2,300 below that comparison. This separates volume from cost changes without claiming a cause. At the new $15 contribution, covering $27,500 needs 1,834 whole orders; recovering the original $5,000 operating result needs 2,167. Check staffing, service hours and demand before treating either number as an achievable plan. This example excludes separate owner compensation, tax, financing and any unentered items. Match each budget line to a source record Sales: reconcile POS net sales by channel and service period. Keep customer taxes, tips and marketplace settlements distinct from the restaurant's sales. Ingredients used: reconcile opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock, with a consistent scope for transfers, credits and waste. Buying a month's stock is different from using it that month. Labor: reconcile the roster, paid hours and employer costs. Keep committed staffing in monthly costs and genuinely additional order-driven labor in direct costs; do not count the same shift in both. Delivery and payment fees: reconcile each channel's merchant statement. Do not add a second processing charge when the contracted fee already includes it. Overhead and cash: compare bills with the reporting period, then separately schedule their payment dates. Equipment purchases, loan principal and owner drawings need a cash plan even when outside the operating result. Investigate the largest dollar movement first, record its evidence and assign one action with a review date. For example, inspect portion and waste records before calling the $1 direct-cost increase supplier inflation. Keep the budget versus actual report for period review and the 13-week cash forecast for payment timing. What to do after the first month Compare budget with actual by food, beverages, labor and fixed categories. If food cost ran high, identify whether portions, purchase prices, waste or theft changed; do not assume the menu price is wrong. If sales fell, compare order counts by daypart and channel with what you expected. Use those observations to forecast the next month, then test whether the revised daily order target can actually be served. Build sales from orders and average checks. Keep guaranteed labor and per-sale costs distinct. Compare actuals with the original budget before updating the forecast. Maintain a separate cash schedule for opening and financing payments. Build an annual restaurant budget from seasonal monthly plans A restaurant annual budget should add twelve dated monthly plans rather than multiply its busiest month by twelve. Keep covers or completed orders, net average sale, food usage, loaded payroll and other commitments visible in each month. Use the same reporting scope when comparing a monthly restaurant budget example with actual results. Independent fictional annual illustration, USD; not the workbook default Line Calculation Annual amount Net sales January 80,000 + February 90,000 + ten months at 100,000 1,170,000 Food COGS 35% of each month’s net sales 409,500 Loaded payroll 30,000 each month × 12 360,000 Other included operating costs 20,000 each month × 12 240,000 Operating result 1,170,000 − 409,500 − 360,000 − 240,000 160,500 The modeled operating margin is 13.72%, rounded. January contributes only $2,000 under this scope: $80,000 less $28,000 food, $30,000 payroll and $20,000 other costs. An annual positive result therefore does not establish that every monthly payment date is funded. The example holds staffing and other monthly costs constant solely to isolate seasonality; test actual shifts, maintenance and contracts separately. For a bar, diner or fast-food operating budget, change the revenue mix and account definitions before using the same structure. Keep beverage and food denominators consistent, and separate launch spending from ongoing costs. Preserve the original budget, revise the forecast with evidence and use the dated cash schedule for deposits, supplier payments and tax dates. FAQs What belongs in a restaurant monthly budget? Sales by channel, cost of goods sold, loaded labor, occupancy, owner pay, utilities, marketing and other recurring expenses. Add notes for costs that are one-time or paid on a different schedule. How do I calculate restaurant break-even from the budget? Divide monthly fixed costs by contribution per order. In the worked example, $27,000 divided by $16 requires 1,688 whole orders, before a profit target. Should restaurant payroll be budgeted as a percentage of sales? Use the actual minimum schedule and employer burden first. A percentage can help compare periods, but it does not tell you what a slow Tuesday shift costs. What is the difference between budget and forecast? The budget is the approved target for the period. A forecast is your best current expectation after you learn more; preserving both lets you explain variances. Can I use last month’s food invoices as COGS? Not without checking inventory. Beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory is the period cost of goods sold under a consistent inventory method. Is the downloadable sheet a cash-flow forecast? No. It compares operating revenue and costs in one month. Plan deposits, debt principal, equipment purchases and timing of collections separately. Are the restaurant cost percentages recommended budget targets? No. The cited 2025 National Restaurant Association report describes 2024 survey medians. Use current local costs for your budget; the survey is comparison context, not prescribed targets. Why does the COGS variance change after adjusting for sales? At the original 30% rate, $57,000 actual sales allows $17,100 COGS. Actual COGS of $18,700 exceeds that allowance by $1,600, although it is only $700 above the original $18,000 budget. This flex assumes stable prices and mix. Apply this result to the next decision Reconcile food consumed with the food cost percentage calculator . Cost a particular dish using recipe costing , then test menu price contribution . Put supplier, payroll and collection dates into the cash forecast instead of assuming a positive operating budget funds every week. 20 restaurant budget scenarios: average ticket and food cost Controlled fictional analysis, not a market benchmark or demand forecast. These 20 cases isolate two assumptions while holding the rest constant. The ranges are deliberately chosen sensitivity tests around this guide’s worked example; they were not estimated from business accounts, a survey or US market rates. Use your own records before making a decision. Download the Excel workbook (.xlsx) or download the raw data (CSV) . Both contain the same 20 fixed scenarios and full calculator inputs; saved outputs do not recalculate when inputs are edited. Use the website calculator for a new plan. Assumptions and cost boundary Four average tickets ($20, $25, $30, $35) × five food costs ($4, $6, $8, $10, $12 per order). Every case adds $2 packaging and a 4% payment fee on its own ticket. Required orders = $27,000 ÷ contribution, rounded up. Daily planning target = whole monthly orders ÷ 26, rounded up; selling that same daily target every open day may exceed the monthly minimum. Revenue at the whole-order target = whole orders × ticket. For reproducibility, capacity inputs are six workers × 40 hours/week × (52 ÷ 12) weeks × 75% productive utilization ÷ 0.15 total worker-hours/order = 5,200 whole orders/month. These time assumptions stay fixed; they do not prove kitchen throughput, customer demand or available bookings. documents.text: Restaurant BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How to Calculate Restaurant Food Cost Percentage Published September 26, 2026 Updated November 26, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate restaurant food cost percentage from inventory and net food sales. Reconcile actual vs theoretical costs, credits and waste without double counting. Restaurant Financial Planning Break-Even Restaurant food cost percentage: inventory formula Food cost percentage = (beginning food inventory + net food purchases − ending food inventory) ÷ food sales × 100. Match the inventory counts, purchases and food sales to the same period and use consistent inventory values. In the fictional USD example below, $8,000 beginning inventory + $18,000 purchases − $6,000 ending inventory = $20,000 food used . Divide by $60,000 food sales: 33.33% actual food cost . Food sales must be positive; a food-only numerator should not be divided by food-plus-beverage sales. This period-level actual food cost differs from the theoretical ingredient cost of one recipe. Neither includes payroll or every operating expense. Follow the inventory example and recipe-cost comparison . Net purchases means received food purchases less supplier credits counted once. If your scope has transfers or documented meal reclassifications, use the adjusted inventory bridge . Waste already included in inventory usage is not an extra cost to add again. Open the food-cost reconciliation calculator for the same method; opening it does not import figures from this article. Illustrative scene; use your own records for the calculations in this guide. Food cost percentage formula: actual vs ideal food cost Actual food cost percentage = (beginning food inventory + net food purchases − ending food inventory) ÷ food-only sales × 100. Use a matched inventory and sales period. A restaurant's ideal (theoretical) food cost instead uses the recipes for the dishes actually sold, at the ingredient prices and portions assumed by those recipes. Both ratios use the same food-sales denominator when comparing the same period and sold mix. Fictional restaurant example: same $60,000 food sales period Measure Calculation Result Actual food used $8,000 opening + $18,000 purchases − $6,000 closing $20,000 Actual food cost percentage $20,000 ÷ $60,000 × 100 33.33% Ideal food cost percentage $18,200 recipe-standard cost of food sold ÷ $60,000 × 100 30.33% Variance to investigate $20,000 − $18,200; 33.33% − 30.33% $1,800; 3.00 percentage points The difference is not automatically waste or theft : check counts, purchase credits, recipe yields, staff meals, promotions, menu mix and ingredient-price changes before assigning a cause. This comparison is not a recommended food-cost benchmark. Calculate actual food cost from inventory , or calculate ideal cost by ingredient and usable yield . For an external method comparison, see US Foods' actual-versus-ideal food cost explanation . Reconcile the food-cost variance before changing menu prices The fictional example above has $1,800 more actual ingredient use than recipe-standard cost. This is a variance to explain , not proof that $1,800 was wasted. Compare like-for-like food sales, count dates, transfers, invoice credits and dish quantities before concluding what caused the gap. Worked diagnostic: allocate the $1,800 gap only after records support each amount Check Record to compare Action Inventory timing and adjustments Opening and closing physical counts, transfers, staff meals and spoilage Reconcile the same accounting period; explain unrecorded usage Supplier prices and credits Invoice unit costs, credited returns and contracted prices Update recipe ingredient costs when prices change Portion yields and substitutions Recipe weights, usable yield and actual portions Check whether standard ingredient quantities reflect service Sales mix and promotions POS item counts, discounts and food-only net sales Reweight theoretical cost to the actual dishes sold Reconciliation rule: actual ingredient usage minus theoretical usage equals the unexplained dollar gap until supported adjustments are recorded. Do not treat the difference as cash missing or as a prime-cost percentage. For food plus labor together, use the restaurant prime-cost guide ; for monthly planning rather than inventory variance, use the restaurant budget workbook . Food cost percentage compares the cost of food used during a period with food sales from that same period. It is useful for checking waste, portion control and purchasing after the fact. It differs from the recipe cost of one dish, which helps set a menu price before the sale. Mixing those two measures can make a menu seem healthy while inventory is disappearing faster than planned. Match the inventory bridge to the calculator fields The simple $20,000 example assumes no credits, transfers or reclassified meals. This separate fictional USD case shows each adjustment once. Keep opening and closing stock at cost and use the same period, locations and food-only sales category. Adjusted food-cost example: one matched period, USD Line Calculation Running amount Opening plus gross purchases $8,000 + $18,000 $26,000 Supplier credits − $500; purchases were gross $25,500 Transfers in and out + $300 − $200 $25,600 Closing stock − $6,000 $19,600 food used Documented meal reclassifications − $400 staff meals − $200 comps $19,000 adjusted food cost Adjusted food-cost percentage $19,000 ÷ $60,000 net food sales × 100 31.67% Theoretical cost of the same sold mix $19,000 − $18,200 $800 variance Recorded waste already within usage $800 gap − $600 recorded waste $200 remaining gap Reclassified meals remain business expenses elsewhere; they have not disappeared or created a saving. Leave these adjustments at zero if they remain in your food-cost scope. If purchases are already net of the $500 credit, leave the separate credit field at zero. Waste stays within the $19,000, so adding $600 again would overstate food cost; the $200 remainder still needs records before assigning a cause. Use the period food-cost calculator for this reconciliation, the recipe calculator for portions and yield, and the loaded-labor guide for payroll. Food cost alone is not prime cost or profit. The restaurant planning collection connects these distinct steps. The inventory formula and a complete example Count the food inventory at the start and end of the same accounting period. Add purchases received during that period to starting inventory, then subtract closing inventory. If you start with $8,000, receive $18,000 of food and close with $6,000, the cost of food used is $20,000. Against $60,000 in food sales, that is $20,000 ÷ $60,000 = 33.33%. Do not divide by all sales if beverages have a separate cost structure. If $12,000 of drinks are included in $72,000 total sales, a food-only numerator divided by total sales would misleadingly show 27.8%. The US Foods food-cost guidance discusses tracking food costs and price decisions; use local invoices and an actual inventory count for your number. Why recipe cost and actual food cost differ A recipe card can list $5 of ingredients for a $20 dish, suggesting a 25% theoretical food cost for that item. That is not the restaurant's period result. Trim, over-portioning, spoiled ingredients, staff meals and price changes can make actual consumption higher. Count beginning and ending stock the same way, keep units consistent and record waste separately so you can investigate the difference. For example, 1,000 bowls at $5 theoretical ingredients imply $5,000 usage. If matched inventory records show $5,700 food used for those bowls and no other meals in that category, the $700 gap needs explanation. At $20 each, sales of those bowls are $20,000; theoretical food cost is 25% and actual is 28.5%. A $0.70 per-bowl difference can be material even when the headline percentages look close. Three inventory situations that change the percentage Stable operation: $8,000 beginning stock + $18,000 purchases − $6,000 ending stock = $20,000 used. With $60,000 food sales, the result is 33.3%. More waste, same food sales: suppose closing stock falls to $4,000 because usable food is gone, while beginning stock and purchases remain the same. Food used rises to $22,000. At $60,000 food sales, food cost becomes 36.7%. Check records before assuming that loss was all waste; count errors, staff meals and theft also affect the reconciliation. Price rise without better purchasing: food used remains $20,000, but food sales reach $66,000 after a price change with the same mix. Cost percentage falls to 30.3%. The ratio improved even though the dollars of food used did not. Compare volume, menu mix and margin alongside the percentage. Turn the food cost formula into a variance check The month-end percentage answers what the restaurant used . Your recipe cards estimate what the dishes you sold should have used. Compare both on the same period and the same sold mix. In the example above, inventory says $20,000 of food was used against $60,000 of food sales: 33.33% . Now suppose the recipe quantities for the actual dishes sold add to an illustrative $18,200 at the relevant ingredient prices. The theoretical cost rate is $18,200 ÷ $60,000 = 30.33% . The dollar difference is $1,800 , or three percentage points of food sales. That $1,800 is a question to investigate, not automatically a theft or waste figure. First check the opening and closing count sheets for the expensive ingredients and confirm that received invoices and supplier credits are in the correct period. Then compare portion sizes, prep yield, spoilage, staff meals and promotions against the recipe model. A purchase price increase may make an old recipe card understate theoretical cost without any change in kitchen practice. Record each cause once: inventory used already captures food that was discarded, so adding the same recorded waste again to the numerator would double-count it. Same-period check Illustrative amount Percent of $60,000 food sales Recipe cost of food actually sold $18,200 30.33% Food used from opening stock + net purchases − closing stock $20,000 33.33% Gap to explain $1,800 3.00 percentage points Small count errors can change the conclusion. If closing inventory was entered as $5,500 when a corrected count is $6,000, the incorrect calculation would show ($8,000 + $18,000 − $5,500) ÷ $60,000 = 34.17% , rather than 33.33%. Correct the underlying units and values before changing menu prices. If you decide the ingredient cost has genuinely changed, the restaurant menu-pricing method deals with a specific dish; restaurant prime cost adds labor to the period-level picture. What changes the answer Consistent inventory valuation matters: counting one period at purchase cost and another at retail value produces a false trend. Returns and supplier credits must be assigned to the right period. Food supplied to employees, promotions and complimentary dishes use inventory without adding normal food sales, so record them rather than burying them in an unexplained variance. Track packaged takeaway costs separately if the purpose is ingredient food cost; include those costs in per-order contribution when checking break-even. Check recipe yields and portion weights on best-selling dishes first. An ingredient may look cheap by the case but lose a large share to trimming or spoilage. The restaurant can have a sound food-cost percentage yet still lose money if guaranteed labor and rent exceed the remaining contribution. Use the food-cost percentage calculator to reconcile the period inventory figures, or the recipe cost calculator to build ingredient cost from packs and usable yield. They answer different questions; compare the recipe model for the actual sold mix with period usage. Close the period before interpreting a food-cost variance A recipe standard and an inventory total can disagree because they describe different dates, sales mixes or valuation bases. Keep a short reconciliation beside the percentage so the next person can reproduce it. Food-cost reconciliation record Record or situation What to check Count cutoff Use opening and closing counts at the period boundaries; identify deliveries and sales around the cutoff. Purchases and credits Match received stock and supplier credits consistently. Check whether a credit has already reduced the purchase figure. Sold-mix standard Multiply each current recipe standard by its actual portions sold. Include the agreed treatment of modifiers and meal bundles. Unbilled consumption Record waste, staff meals, complimentary items and production trials separately. They can consume stock without corresponding menu sales. Unexplained remainder Recheck quantity, unit conversions and valuation before assigning a cause. The number alone does not establish theft or poor performance. Use the recipe calculator to establish portion costs, then the period food-cost calculator for the inventory comparison. The restaurant workflow shows the sequence and a separate $1,800 variance example. Keep actual food cost distinct from payroll, packaging and overhead when you move to menu contribution. How to run your own numbers Reconcile inventory and food sales for the same month; for each menu category calculate contribution after ingredients, packaging and sale-dependent fees. Then check whether the resulting sales mix covers fixed costs and realistic owner compensation. Enter your own average ticket, variable cost, monthly fixed costs, owner pay and operating capacity in the free restaurant break-even calculator . It is a planning model, not a forecast of customer demand. Common mistakes Dividing food used by beverage-inclusive sales. Keep numerator and denominator on the same basis. Counting a delivery on the wrong date. A purchase received after month-end belongs in the next period unless your accounting method properly records it as received before closing. Comparing actual COGS to one recipe. Compare the theoretical cost of the entire sold mix. Ignoring inventory units. A case of 24 bottles is not one bottle. Using a benchmark as a pricing command. A concept with more prep labor and less ingredient cost has different economics than a simple beverage counter. Turn the percentage into an operating decision If food used is $22,000 on $60,000 of food sales after it was $20,000 the prior month, locate the $2,000 movement: count variances by item, supplier price changes and menu mix. A better recipe card will not recover missing stock if portion practice is the issue. Once food cost is reliable, update prices and required order volume using current ingredient costs. Use beginning stock + purchases − ending stock for food used. Divide food cost by food sales from the same period. Compare actual and theoretical costs on the same mix. Use per-order contribution for the break-even decision. Build a recipe cost worksheet from the purchase pack Use one row per ingredient: purchase-pack cost, quantity purchased, usable yield, quantity used in the batch and batch servings. Keep the purchase and recipe quantities in compatible units. The following independent USD example costs one ingredient, not the whole dish. From purchased weight to one served portion Step Calculation Result Purchase 5 lb for $24 $4.80 per purchased lb Usable quantity 5 lb × 80% yield 4 lb Usable unit cost $24 ÷ 4 lb $6 per usable lb Ingredient used in batch 1.5 lb × $6 $9 Ingredient cost per serving $9 ÷ 12 servings $0.75 Repeat for every ingredient, including garnish and sauces, and sum the serving costs. If a sauce has its own recipe, cost that sub-recipe first and enter only the quantity used. Weight ounces and fluid ounces are different measures; a volume-to-weight conversion needs an ingredient-specific density. Do not deduct the same trim loss twice when yield already captures it. This worksheet estimates recipe ingredients. The RestoMetrics recipe calculator also explicitly separates ingredient costing from labor, packaging and overhead. Move those other costs into the full menu-price calculation , then reconcile the sold recipe mix with period inventory usage above. If ingredient prices change, retain the old recipe version so you can distinguish price changes from portion changes. Reconcile food cost before comparing a restaurant percentage A food cost percentage needs a cost numerator and the net food-sales denominator for the same period. Purchases alone omit the change in stock. Supplier returns, transfers and customer refunds also need different treatment; a refunded sale does not automatically put ingredients back into usable inventory. Independent fictional inventory reconciliation, USD Line Amount / effect Opening food inventory 8,000 Food purchases before the listed supplier return 32,000 Food transferred in 2,000 Supplier return credit on those purchases −1,000 Closing food inventory −9,000 Food cost consumed 32,000 Matching net food sales 100,000 Food cost percentage 32% This teaching reconciliation assumes no other inventory adjustments. Waste already reducing the counted closing stock is reflected in the consumption calculation; adding the same loss again would double-count it. Investigate the cause using portion, spoilage and transfer records rather than rewriting the count to hit a desired percentage. If opening inventory is unknown, entering zero is not a verified calculation. A new operation with documented zero opening stock is different from a missing count. A ±$2,000 error in the opening value alone changes this example’s percentage by ±2 percentage points. Compare food and beverage percentages separately when their sales mix and cost records differ. Follow the COGS record checks before relying on a food-cost benchmark. FAQs What is a good food cost percentage for a restaurant? There is no single percentage that tells you whether the restaurant makes money. Compare food cost with menu mix, labor, occupancy and the contribution you need from each order. Can I calculate food cost without inventory counts? You can estimate from recipes, but that is theoretical cost. You need reliable beginning and ending inventory to calculate actual food used for a period. Do beverage sales go in the food cost denominator? No, if your numerator includes food inventory only. Track beverages separately or combine both numerator and denominator when analyzing total cost of goods sold. Why did food cost rise when prices did not change? Possible causes include waste, larger portions, supplier increases, more sales of expensive dishes or an inaccurate inventory count. Reconcile units before acting. How is food cost percentage different from menu markup? Food cost percentage looks at ingredients relative to sales; markup compares a selling price with its cost. Neither includes all overhead or guarantees profit. Should packaging count as food cost? Keep the definition consistent. For ingredient food cost, show packaging separately; for per-order contribution, include packaging and other costs that rise with each order. Does a low food-cost percentage prove a dish is profitable? No. The dish still has other sale-dependent costs and contributes toward monthly commitments. Calculate contribution dollars and examine actual paid volume as well.
