documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Contribution Margin per Unit Calculator and Guide Published September 23, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate contribution margin per unit with variable costs and selling fees. Check the ratio, worked examples and costs that belong in your monthly plan. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business How do you calculate contribution margin? Contribution margin = net sales − variable costs. Calculate per-unit contribution for one product, order or job; divide it by that unit's selling price for the ratio. Multiply by a matching quantity for total contribution. In the calculator's fictional example, a $50 order with $25 other variable costs, a 3% fee and one $0.30 transaction fee leaves $23.20 contribution, or 46.4% . One hundred identical orders contribute $2,320 before monthly fixed costs. The unchanged calculator example: USD; 100 matching orders Measure Calculation Result Other variable cost plus fees per order $25 + ($50 × 3%) + $0.30 $26.80 Contribution per order $50 − $26.80 $23.20 Contribution margin ratio $23.20 ÷ $50 × 100 46.4% Contribution from 100 identical orders 100 × $23.20 $2,320 Use the calculator or check which costs belong in the formula . A flat checkout fee belongs once per transaction: allocate it when the chosen unit is an item in a multi-item order. Contribution is not net profit. Calculate contribution margin per unit and as a percentage An $80 sale with $44 of variable cost contributes $36 per unit. The contribution margin ratio is $36 ÷ $80 = 45%. At 100 identical sales, total contribution is $3,600 before fixed costs. Include any fee or shipping cost that changes with each sale. Recover fixed monthly costs from total contribution. Calculate your contribution margin Turn contribution into a target sales figure Contribution margin per unit calculator Calculate what one product, order or completed job leaves toward fixed costs and profit. Use the same sale unit for every input. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Selling price per unit After discounts; exclude sales tax collected for a tax authority. The percentage fee below is applied to this price. Other variable costs per unit Materials, variable labour, shipping, commissions and expected returns. Exclude fees entered separately below. Payment / platform fee (%) Enter your own combined rate, or 0. Do not also include this fee in other variable costs. Fixed transaction fee per unit A flat fee allocated to the chosen unit, not monthly overhead. For one $0.30 checkout containing two identical items, use $0.15 per item or define the whole order as one unit. Matching sold quantity Whole sold units of the same scope, from 0 to 1,000,000. The quantity check does not infer customers or change the unit formula. Reset fictional example What each sale contributes Contribution per unit USD 23.20 Contribution margin 46.4% Total variable cost per unit USD 26.80 Percentage fee per unit USD 1.50 Variable cost = USD 25.00 other costs + USD 1.50 percentage fee + USD 0.30 transaction fee. This sale leaves USD 23.20 toward fixed costs. It becomes profit only after those commitments are covered. Reconcile the matching sold quantity Revenue from sold units USD 5,000.00 Variable cost of sold units USD 2,680.00 Total contribution USD 2,320.00 Period contribution margin 46.4% Revenue minus variable cost equals contribution, before fixed commitments. These totals assume the entered price, fees and unit cost apply to every sold unit; no volume discount, changing mix or capacity step is added automatically. The starting values are a fictional USD example: $50 price, $25 other variable costs, 3% fee and $0.30 transaction fee produce $23.20 contribution and 46.4%. Replace every value with your records. Displayed amounts are rounded; calculations use unrounded inputs. Cost boundary: include labour here only when its cost changes with the sale. Keep salaried commitments, rent and other fixed overhead in the monthly plan. Enter each cost once. Contribution is not net profit. Fees are modelled on the entered selling price only. Providers may charge on tax or customer shipping too; reconcile the fee basis with your statement. For batches, allocate fixed transaction fees to the chosen unit. Refund and return allowances belong in your stated variable costs; this is not a separate refund model. Plan monthly break-even for products or orders , or choose a service-business planner to add fixed costs and capacity. Include the transaction fee above once in the planner's other variable costs. Read the formula, cost boundaries and examples . Service business owner calculating contribution margin from invoices and variable costs Per-unit formula and cost boundaries Contribution per unit = selling price − other variable costs − (selling price × percentage fee ÷ 100) − fixed transaction fee per unit. Contribution margin percentage = contribution per unit ÷ selling price × 100. Price must be positive for this percentage. Fixed overhead is deducted later when you evaluate the monthly operating result. Choose one consistent unit: a product, an order or a completed job. If an order contains several products, do not subtract a whole order's transaction fee from each product. Allocate the fee or calculate the complete order. Use retained selling revenue after discounts and match every cost to that same sale. Include materials, shipping and labour that changes with that sale. A guaranteed salary may remain fixed over your planning range; extra paid worker hours for a job may be variable. Check the actual arrangement. The calculator's other-cost field excludes the two separate fee fields. A processor's monthly subscription belongs in fixed overhead, not the fixed transaction fee. Checked fictional example with both fee types A $50 order has $25 of other variable costs, a 3% selling fee and a $0.30 transaction fee. The percentage fee is $1.50. Total variable cost is $25 + $1.50 + $0.30 = $26.80 ; contribution is $50 − $26.80 = $23.20 per order ; its contribution ratio is $23.20 ÷ $50 × 100 = 46.4% . These are illustrative inputs, not suggested fee rates. This differs from the Product A example below, whose specified costs do not include a $0.30 fixed fee. Keep each example's cost boundary intact. When taking this widget's example into the larger ecommerce planner, include the $0.30 once in other variable costs and keep the 3% fee in its percentage field. Read zero and negative contribution correctly Zero contribution means the sale pays its entered variable costs and leaves nothing for fixed costs. Negative contribution means it loses money before fixed costs; more identical sales increase that loss. A positive contribution is still not net profit. To assess monthly viability, add sales volume, fixed commitments and capacity in the ecommerce break-even planner or select your service-business model . The direct answer Contribution margin shows how much of your selling revenue is available to cover fixed costs such as rent, insurance, salaried labor, software subscriptions, and equipment payments. After fixed costs are covered, the amount left becomes operating profit, before items such as interest and taxes that your accounting method may treat separately. The basic formula is: Contribution margin = Total sales revenue − Total variable costs You can calculate it for a whole business, a product, a service, an order, or one unit. The calculation is useful because it focuses on what changes when sales change. A cost is variable when it increases or decreases with the quantity you sell or produce. Examples can include ingredients, packaging, payment-processing charges, sales commissions, delivery fees tied to an order, and hourly labor scheduled only for that work. Contribution margin ratio formula and percentage Contribution margin ratio expresses the amount left as a share of sales. The percentage uses sales revenue as its denominator, not variable cost. For the percentage, use: Contribution margin percentage = Contribution margin ÷ Sales revenue × 100 For an illustrative month with $10,000 sales and $6,000 variable costs, contribution is $4,000. The ratio is $4,000 ÷ $10,000 = 0.40; multiplying by 100 gives 40% . Each $1 of sales leaves $0.40 toward fixed costs and profit. This is not a 40% net profit margin. Contribution dollars, ratio and percentage answer different questions Measure Calculation Result Contribution amount $10,000 − $6,000 $4,000 Contribution margin ratio $4,000 ÷ $10,000 0.40 Contribution margin percentage 0.40 × 100 40% In Excel or Google Sheets, put same-period revenue in A2 and total variable costs in B2. Use =(A2-B2)/A2 and format the result as a percentage. Do not also multiply by 100 when using percentage formatting. Leave the result undefined when revenue is zero; zero sales cannot supply a meaningful ratio. The OpenStax contribution-margin lesson distinguishes unit contribution, total contribution and the sales-based ratio. The example here uses our own illustrative figures. A per-unit version is also useful: Unit contribution margin = Selling price per unit − Variable cost per unit For example, if you sell a service for $80 and the variable cost of delivering that service is $32, the unit contribution margin is $48. The contribution margin percentage is $48 ÷ $80 × 100, which equals 60%. What changes the answer Your result changes when revenue or variable cost changes. A higher price generally increases contribution margin if variable cost stays the same. If a $100 job costs $35, the contribution margin is $65. At a $90 promotional price, it falls to $55. Product mix can change your overall margin even when total sales stay constant. Imagine two products with the same $1,000 in revenue. Product A has a 70% contribution margin, while Product B has a 30% margin. A month that shifts customers toward Product B produces less money to cover fixed costs, even though the sales total looks unchanged. Volume matters because fixed costs are spread across more or fewer units, but volume does not change unit contribution margin by itself. If a product sells for $25 and has a $10 variable cost, each unit contributes $15 until price or variable cost changes. More units create more total contribution margin, while rent remains the same in the short term. Your cost definitions matter, too. Include costs that are truly attached to the sale. For a delivery order, that might include a per-order delivery charge and packaging. Do not automatically include the full monthly rent or a manager’s fixed salary just because the business needs them. Those are usually fixed costs for this analysis. Some costs are mixed. A delivery van may have a fixed lease plus fuel that rises with miles. A worker may receive a fixed weekly amount plus a commission. Split mixed costs into fixed and variable portions when you can. If you cannot do that precisely, state your assumption and use the same method each time so comparisons remain meaningful. Contribution margin is not a complete cash-flow measure. It does not account for payment timing, loan principal, owner draws, taxes, or every overhead cost. Use a broader budget for the full picture. Contribution in three different selling models Scenario 1: A cleaning service A cleaning business charges $180 for a standard visit. Supplies cost $12, credit-card processing costs $5, and a helper is paid $63 specifically for that visit. The total variable cost is $12 + $5 + $63 = $80. The unit contribution margin is $180 − $80 = $100 per visit . The contribution margin ratio is $100 ÷ $180 × 100 = 55.56% , rounded to two decimal places. If the business completes 25 similar visits, total contribution margin is 25 × $100 = $2,500 . That $2,500 can cover fixed expenses before any remainder becomes operating profit. The result depends on the cost boundary. If the helper is paid a fixed weekly salary that does not change with this visit, the salary may belong in fixed costs instead. The business should use the classification that matches how the work is actually scheduled and paid. For more pricing context, see this guide on contribution margin and gross margin . Scenario 2: A restaurant menu item A restaurant sells a pasta entrée for $22. Ingredients cost $6.40, the takeout container and utensils cost $0.60, and a delivery-platform fee tied to the order is $3.30. The variable cost per order is $6.40 + $0.60 + $3.30 = $10.30 . The contribution margin is $22 − $10.30 = $11.70 per entrée . The contribution margin ratio is $11.70 ÷ $22 × 100 = 53.18% . If 300 orders are sold, total contribution margin is 300 × $11.70 = $3,510 . If the same entrée is sold for dine-in without the container and platform fee, the variable cost is lower and the margin changes. That is why a single menu item can have different economics across sales channels. Compare like with like when setting prices. This fixed and variable costs explains the related pricing calculation. Scenario 3: A digital workshop An instructor sells 40 workshop seats at $75 each, producing $3,000 in revenue. The payment fee is $90, an attendee workbook costs $4 per person, and a guest instructor receives $400 only when the workshop runs. Variable costs are $90 + (40 × $4) + $400 = $650 . The total contribution margin is $3,000 − $650 = $2,350 . The contribution margin ratio is $2,350 ÷ $3,000 × 100 = 78.33% . If the instructor’s video software subscription is $120 per month regardless of attendance, keep it out of variable costs and treat it as a fixed cost for this analysis. The percentage alone is not enough. A high-margin sale may have a small dollar contribution, while a lower-margin sale may contribute more. Use both amount and ratio. Which record should supply each input? Evidence to collect before calculating Input Starting record Avoid Retained sales Sales and refund reconciliation Combining list-price revenue with already-refunded orders. Product or job cost Supplier invoices and delivery records Using costs from a different basket or service. Fees and acquisition Processor and campaign statements Counting the same fee in dollars and percentages. Reconcile contribution for a mixed-product month Use net retained sales and the costs connected to those sales. A separate fictional ecommerce example has two products sold one per order. Product A sells for $50 and has $20 product cost, $4 packaging and shipping, a 3% processing fee of $1.50, and a $1 expected returns allowance. Product B sells for $30 and has $12 product cost, $3 packaging and shipping, a $0.90 fee, and a $0.60 returns allowance. Product Net order revenue Modeled variable cost Unit contribution Contribution ratio A $50 $26.50 $23.50 47% B $30 $16.50 $13.50 45% These are illustrative USD assumptions. The returns allowance is a planning estimate, not a second deduction on top of the same actual refund. For historical reporting, reconcile actual net revenue, reimbursed fees, returned inventory and fulfillment losses instead. Keep the same cost boundary when comparing the two products. To reproduce Product A in the ecommerce calculator, enter price $50, materials $20, direct labor $0, shipping/returns $5, acquisition $0 and payment/platform fees 3%. The $5 combines $4 fulfillment and $1 expected returns; the calculator adds the $1.50 fee itself. The result should show $23.50 contribution. Replace all preset costs before comparing results. Suppose the month contains 100 A orders and 200 B orders. Revenue is 100 × $50 + 200 × $30 = $11,000 . Variable costs are 100 × $26.50 + 200 × $16.50 = $5,950 . Total contribution is $11,000 − $5,950 = $5,050 . The overall contribution ratio is $5,050 ÷ $11,000 × 100 = 45.91% . Do not take a simple average of 47% and 45%; the products generate different revenue totals. Average contribution per order is $5,050 ÷ 300 = $16.83 , rounded for display. Read that result in plain dollars: every $100 of this month's modeled sales leaves about $45.91 toward fixed bills and operating profit. It does not mean $45.91 is available for personal spending. Fixed expenses still come out of that amount. With $4,000 fixed monthly overhead, modeled operating profit is $5,050 − $4,000 = $1,050 before any costs excluded from the stated boundary. Contribution and operating profit answer different questions: the first shows what sales supply toward overhead, while the second deducts that overhead. Stress-test a change in the sales mix Now hold the total at 300 orders but reverse the mix to 200 A and 100 B. Revenue becomes $13,000. Variable costs become $6,950 and contribution becomes $6,050. The same order count contributes $1,000 more because the dollar contribution per A order is larger. The overall ratio is $6,050 ÷ $13,000 = 46.54% . Capacity can still limit the more attractive mix. Suppose an A order uses 12 fulfillment minutes and B uses six. The original 100-A/200-B mix uses 2,400 minutes, or 40 hours . The revised 200-A/100-B mix uses 3,000 minutes, or 50 hours . If only 45 usable fulfillment hours are available, the revised mix does not fit without a change in scheduling or resources. For a break-even comparison under the original one-A-to-two-B ratio, treat three orders as a repeatable basket. Revenue per basket is $110 and contribution is $23.50 + 2 × $13.50 = $50.50 . Covering $4,000 requires 79.21 baskets , rounded up to 80 whole baskets, or 240 orders . Those baskets contribute $4,040. Using a rounded $16.83 average too early can alter a boundary result; preserve full precision until the final operational rounding. This basket method assumes the mix can be repeated. If actual demand changes, recalculate with the new counts instead of forcing orders into the old ratio. For more detail, use the multiple-product break-even guide and compare contribution margin with profit margin . Contribution margin per bundle: choose the correct unit An actual product bundle is one offer sold at a combined price. Its contribution is the net bundle price minus all costs that change when that bundle is delivered. A sales-mix composite bundle is an accounting unit representing a fixed ratio of separately sold items; it need not be sold to one customer. Two meanings of bundle; figures are illustrative USD assumptions Unit Formula Checked example Actual offer bundle Net bundle price − total variable costs $70 − $25 product costs − $5 fulfillment − $2.10 fees = $37.90 Sales-mix composite bundle Sum of item quantities × item contribution Two A items at $12 contribution + one B at $8 = $32 For a product promotion, use the ecommerce bundle pricing guide to check displaced full-price orders and the required volume. For a fixed sales mix, use the multiple-product break-even guide to turn a composite contribution into individual product targets. Do not sum standalone selling prices after applying a real bundle discount, or add an order fee once for every component when it applies only once. Compare contribution per constrained hour Contribution per unit can rank offers differently from contribution per scarce hour. In an independent example, product A leaves $23.50 per unit and uses 12 minutes of the bottleneck process. Product B leaves $13.50 and uses six minutes. A yields $23.50 ÷ 12 × 60 = $117.50 per bottleneck hour; B yields $13.50 ÷ 6 × 60 = $135 . B has lower contribution per item but higher contribution per constrained hour. That does not mean making only B is optimal: demand, setup time, waste, contractual commitments and other capacity limits still matter. Use measured occupied minutes, including necessary changeovers, and check whether either option creates additional staffing or equipment costs. If the resource has spare capacity and no alternative sale is displaced, the hour ranking may be less relevant than the incremental contribution from an additional order. For a menu application, compare the dish contribution and kitchen-time guide . Contribution per pound: define the scarce resource When material supply is the bottleneck, contribution per finished item can rank offers differently from contribution per pound of scarce material. In an independent fictional example, offer A leaves $18 contribution and uses three pounds, so it yields $6 per scarce pound. Offer B leaves $20 but uses five pounds, yielding $4 per pound. B has more contribution per item; A uses the constrained material more efficiently. This calculation is contribution dollars divided by actual scarce-resource consumption, including relevant waste. It is not the contribution margin percentage, whose denominator is revenue. Before reallocating production, check demand, alternative bottlenecks and setup requirements. Use the make-or-buy comparison when an outside supplier can release that resource, and the flexible-budget bridge when comparing a completed month with its original plan. How to run your own numbers Choose one sale unit and one reporting period. Match its retained revenue to the costs of delivering those same sales. Use invoices, fee statements and job records to separate variable costs from fixed commitments. Mark allowances as estimates. Use the ecommerce break-even calculator for one product or a representative order. Enter each cost once, including percentage fees in their own field. For several products, use the mixed-product calculation above. Total contribution dollars before calculating the weighted ratio; keep full precision until final rounding. Compare monthly contribution with overhead and the owner-pay or profit requirement you actually want to cover. The OpenStax accounting glossary defines unit contribution and sales mix. It does not verify the fictional business inputs used here. Common mistakes Treating every cost as variable. Rent, business insurance, and a fixed software subscription do not normally rise with one additional sale. Including them in per-sale variable cost makes the unit contribution margin look too low. Leaving out small sale-linked costs. Packaging, transaction fees, commissions, and order-specific delivery can add up. If they occur because a sale occurs, include them or explain why you exclude them. Using gross sales when discounts are substantial. A margin based on a list price can overstate what the business receives. Use the revenue basis consistently and document discounts, refunds, and taxes. Mixing channels or products. A dine-in sale and a delivery sale may have different fees. A premium service and a basic service may require different labor. Calculate each meaningful offer separately before combining totals. Confusing contribution margin with profit. Contribution margin still has to cover fixed costs. A positive margin on every sale does not guarantee a profitable month if total contribution margin is below fixed expenses. Rounding too early. Keep cents through the calculation and round the final displayed result. If you round every input first, totals can differ from your accounting records. Allocate an order-level transaction fee before calculating an item margin A fixed fee per checkout is variable with transactions, but not automatically payable on every item inside the order. Keep the selling unit consistent. In a separate fictional order containing two identical $25 items, other variable cost is $12 per item. The processor charges 3% of the $50 order plus one $0.30 transaction fee. The order contributes $50 − $24 − $1.50 − $0.30 = $24.20 . One two-item checkout; illustrative USD; equal-item allocation only Calculation basis Net revenue Other variable cost Percentage fee Allocated flat fee Contribution Whole order 50.00 24.00 1.50 0.30 24.20 Each identical item 25.00 12.00 0.75 0.15 12.10 Two allocated item amounts 50.00 24.00 1.50 0.30 24.20 For this equal-item case, enter $0.15 in the widget’s flat transaction fee per unit when the unit is one item. Entering the full $0.30 against each item would deduct $0.60 per order and understate contribution by $0.30. Alternatively, define the entire $50 order as one unit and enter its complete $24 cost and $0.30 flat fee. Unequal items need a documented allocation basis; do not assume equal allocation always represents their economics. Reconcile unit contribution to a matching quantity The calculator’s quantity control multiplies the same unrounded unit economics by a whole number of matching sold units. At its original $50 price, $25 other variable cost, 3% fee and $0.30 flat fee, 100 sales produce $5,000 revenue, $2,680 variable cost and $2,320 contribution. Revenue minus variable cost must equal total contribution. Zero sold units give zero totals; the calculated margin for the defined offer remains 46.4%, but there is no observed period margin when revenue is zero. If the transaction or product mix changes, rebuild the average from matching records rather than multiplying an obsolete rate. A positive $2,320 contribution still has to fund fixed commitments. Use the contribution income statement for that next reconciliation, and the break-even formula reference for the volume that covers a stated fixed-cost requirement. OpenStax distinguishes unit, total and ratio contribution ; the checkout allocation above is an original example. FAQs Is contribution margin the same as profit? No. Contribution margin subtracts variable costs from revenue. Profit also reflects fixed operating costs and may include other expenses such as interest and taxes, depending on the profit measure you use. Can contribution margin be negative? Yes. If variable costs exceed revenue, contribution margin is negative. Each additional sale then adds to the shortfall before fixed costs are considered. Review the price, variable costs, product mix, or sales channel before increasing volume. Should labor be included in variable costs? Include labor when it changes with the sale, order, or production volume, such as per-job contractors or hourly shifts added for demand. A fixed salary generally belongs in fixed costs for contribution-margin analysis. Mixed pay may need to be split. What is a good contribution margin percentage? There is no universal target. A suitable percentage depends on your fixed costs, operating model, industry, sales channel, and desired profit. Compare your margin with your own break-even point and with consistent historical results rather than relying on one benchmark. Should payment-processing fees be variable costs? Usually, yes, when the fee is charged as a percentage or amount per transaction. Include the fee in the same channel’s calculation. If a processor charges a fixed monthly subscription instead, that portion may be fixed. How often should I calculate contribution margin? Calculate it whenever price, materials, commissions, fees, or labor terms change. Many businesses also review it monthly by product or service. Frequent review helps you spot a margin decline before it affects the entire business. Can I use contribution margin for pricing? Yes. Start with the variable cost of delivering the offer, then test prices against the contribution margin needed to cover fixed costs and provide profit. Also consider demand, capacity, customer value, and the difference between channels. How do I calculate contribution margin ratio from total sales? Subtract same-period total variable costs from revenue, then divide the contribution by that revenue. With $10,000 sales and $6,000 variable costs, the ratio is 0.40, or 40%. Fixed overhead is deducted afterward when calculating the modeled operating result. What is the contribution margin per bundle formula? For a sold offer, subtract all bundle-dependent variable costs from its net selling price. For an accounting sales-mix bundle, add each item’s contribution multiplied by its quantity in the composite unit. State which meaning you use; the composite unit is not necessarily a customer package. Should I charge a flat transaction fee to every item in a multi-item order? Not if the fee is charged once per checkout. Calculate the whole order or allocate that fee across the chosen item units on a documented basis. In a two-identical-item order with one $0.30 fee, the equal allocation is $0.15 per item, not $0.30 each. Publishing notes Turn contribution into a complete monthly statement A unit margin or ratio does not yet deduct monthly fixed expenses. In a fictional service month, 200 visits at $180 yield $36,000 sales; $80 variable cost per visit totals $16,000, leaving $20,000 contribution. Deduct $14,000 fixed operating commitments once to get $6,000 operating income. The contribution ratio is 55.56%, while the operating margin is 16.67%. Use the contribution margin income statement format and downloadable template to reconcile each line rather than treating contribution as take-home profit. Use the result without changing its meaning Use the contribution income statement to deduct monthly fixed operating costs once. Use the break-even formula reference to solve the sales threshold, or contribution versus profit margin to compare their different cost boundaries. Keep the weighted sales-mix calculation when products differ; multiplying one item's ratio across a different basket is not a valid shortcut. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Contribution Margin vs Gross Margin: Which One Should You Use? Published September 23, 2026 Updated October 22, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare contribution margin vs gross margin with clear formulas, worked examples, and guidance on choosing the right metric for break-even decisions. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business Ecommerce operator comparing contribution margin and gross margin on a packing table Contribution margin vs gross margin is not a choice between two competing versions of the same metric. Gross margin shows what remains after cost of goods sold, which can include allocated fixed production overhead, while contribution margin shows what remains after all costs that change with a sale. Use gross margin to understand product-level profitability and contribution margin to decide whether an additional sale, price, or order helps cover fixed costs. Quick answer: Gross margin is sales minus cost of goods sold, divided by sales. Contribution margin is sales minus variable costs, divided by sales. Gross margin is useful for reporting and comparing product economics. Contribution margin is more useful for break-even analysis, pricing decisions, sales mix, and short-term choices because it shows how much each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit. The direct answer The difference starts with the costs included in the calculation. Gross margin usually subtracts cost of goods sold (COGS) from revenue. COGS includes the costs assigned to the goods or services sold, such as purchased inventory, materials and, where applicable, allocated fixed production overhead. Direct-versus-indirect and fixed-versus-variable are different classifications. The exact accounting treatment can vary by business, so you should apply one consistent definition. The gross margin formula: > Gross margin = (Revenue − COGS) ÷ Revenue × 100 Contribution margin subtracts variable costs from revenue. A variable cost rises or falls with the number of units, jobs, orders, or customers you serve. Depending on your business, this can include payment processing fees, sales commissions, packaging, delivery charges, hourly labor tied directly to a job, and consumable supplies. The contribution margin formula: > Contribution margin = (Revenue − Variable costs) ÷ Revenue × 100 What changes the answer The right metric depends on the decision. If you are reviewing financial statements, comparing product economics, or checking whether purchase costs are under control, gross margin is often the clearer starting point. It keeps attention on the cost of what you deliver. If you are asking whether to accept one more order, run a promotion, add a delivery option, or calculate break-even sales, contribution margin is usually more useful. Those decisions depend on every cost that changes because the sale happens. A sale that looks attractive under gross margin can create little cash toward fixed costs if fulfillment, commissions, or transaction fees are high. Your business model also changes the practical answer. A retailer may focus on product purchase cost, shrinkage, and freight. A house-cleaning business may need to include cleaner wages, travel mileage, and job supplies as variable costs. A restaurant may include ingredients, packaging for takeout, and order fees that vary by channel. Read the explanation of fixed and variable costs if you are separating job-level costs from overhead. Finally, margin percentage and margin dollars answer different questions. A product with a 60% contribution margin may contribute $6 on a $10 sale. A product with a 30% contribution margin may contribute $30 on a $100 sale. Percentage helps compare offers at different prices; dollars help determine how many sales are needed to cover fixed costs. Worked pricing and operating scenarios The following are illustrative planning examples. They show the arithmetic rather than describe specific businesses or actual results. Scenario 1: A packaged product You sell a product for $40. The wholesale item costs $18, packaging costs $2, and a payment fee of $1.20 applies to each sale. Assume the wholesale item is COGS and packaging and the payment fee are variable selling costs. Gross profit is $40 − $18 = $22. Gross margin is $22 ÷ $40 = 55% . Contribution margin dollars are $40 − $18 − $2 − $1.20 = $18.80. Contribution margin is $18.80 ÷ $40 = 47% . The gross margin tells you how much remains after acquiring the product. The contribution margin tells you how much of each sale is available for rent, payroll that does not vary with this sale, software, and profit. If fixed costs are $1,880 per month, you would need $1,880 ÷ $18.80 = 100 sales to cover them, assuming the same price and costs. Scenario 2: A house-cleaning job You charge $180 for a cleaning job. Cleaner pay attributable to the job is $72, supplies are $8, and travel reimbursement is $10. Treat all three as variable costs for this planning decision. The business also has $2,000 of monthly fixed overhead. Contribution margin dollars are $180 − $72 − $8 − $10 = $90. Contribution margin is $90 ÷ $180 = 50% . At $90 per job, the break-even job count is $2,000 ÷ $90 = 22.22, so you need 23 whole jobs to cover the fixed overhead. At 23 jobs, contribution is 23 × $90 = $2,070, leaving $70 after the stated fixed costs. If you omitted travel and supplies, you would overstate the amount each job contributes. For this type of service, the price must cover the direct time and materials first. Then the contribution margin must be large enough to support scheduling, administration, insurance, and other overhead. A price can be higher than direct labor cost and still be too low for the business to sustain. Scenario 3: A restaurant menu item A menu item sells for $16. Ingredients cost $5.20, a takeout container costs $0.80, and a delivery-channel fee is $2.40 when the item is sold through that channel. Compare the economics of the same item by channel. For an in-house order, contribution margin is $16 − $5.20 = $10.80, or $10.80 ÷ $16 = 67.5% . This margin and markup can help you extend the calculation. For the delivery-channel order, contribution margin is $16 − $5.20 − $0.80 − $2.40 = $7.60, or $7.60 ÷ $16 = 47.5% . Why contribution margin can legitimately exceed gross margin COGS can contain fixed production overhead, while contribution deducts variable selling costs but excludes fixed production overhead. The two cost classifications cross; neither is simply a longer version of the other. AccountingCoach explains this manufacturing distinction . Consider a separate $20,000-sales month with $8,000 variable production cost, $3,000 fixed production cost, $1,000 variable selling cost and $4,000 fixed selling and administration costs. Assume all production is sold and inventory does not change. Gross profit: $20,000 − $8,000 − $3,000 = $9,000, or 45%. Contribution: $20,000 − $8,000 − $1,000 = $11,000, or 55%. Operating profit through either route: $4,000, or 20%. From gross profit, subtract variable selling costs and fixed selling/administration: $9,000 − $1,000 − $4,000. From contribution, subtract both fixed categories: $11,000 − $3,000 − $4,000. Each cost appears once. The higher contribution percentage is valid here, not evidence that someone necessarily omitted a cost by mistake. How to run your own numbers Start with a single unit of analysis. That unit might be one product, service call, customer order, table, or billable hour. Use the same unit for revenue and every variable cost. Mixing a per-order price with monthly costs produces a misleading margin. Next, record the selling price or average revenue per unit. If customers buy bundles, divide the bundle revenue and bundle costs consistently, or treat the bundle as the unit. Include discounts and refunds when they normally occur. A list price that customers rarely pay is not the right revenue input for planning. Then list costs in two groups. Put costs directly associated with making or acquiring the item in your COGS group. Put every cost that changes because this unit is sold in your variable-cost group. Now calculate both dollars and percentages. Use these four lines: Revenue per unit = your actual or planned selling price Gross profit = revenue per unit − COGS per unit Contribution margin dollars = revenue per unit − total variable costs per unit Contribution margin percentage = contribution margin dollars ÷ revenue per unit × 100 For a break-even estimate, add your fixed costs for the same period. Divide fixed costs by contribution margin dollars per unit. Round up to a whole unit when you are counting products, jobs, or orders. You can run the calculation in the MyBreakeven calculator , then compare the result with your own cost assumptions. Test changes one at a time. Try a higher price, a lower material cost, a different sales commission, or a different order mix. Common mistakes Using gross margin for a break-even calculation. Break-even depends on the amount available after variable costs. If transaction fees, commissions, shipping, or direct labor vary with each sale, leaving them out overstates the contribution from each unit. Treating every direct cost as variable. A direct cost may be fixed for a short period. For example, a salaried worker may support a product line without receiving more pay for the next order. Classify costs based on the decision period and document the choice. Mixing accounting definitions. One report may put packaging in COGS while another puts it in selling expense. The labels matter less than consistency and clarity. If you compare two margins, make sure the underlying cost groups match. Ignoring the sales channel. A direct website order, marketplace order, and delivery-platform order can have different fees and fulfillment costs. Calculate contribution by channel when those costs differ. Confusing margin with markup. Margin divides profit by selling price. Markup divides profit by cost. If an item costs $50 and sells for $75, profit is $25, margin is $25 ÷ $75 = 33.3%, and markup is $25 ÷ $50 = 50%. Rounding too early. Keep cents during the calculation and round the final result. Small per-unit costs can matter across many units, especially when break-even is near a whole-number threshold. Looking only at percentages. A percentage does not pay a bill by itself. Check contribution margin dollars, expected volume, capacity, and fixed costs together before making a pricing or promotion decision. For another angle, see calculate your break-even point . Browse the small business guide library for more planning examples. Closing takeaways Gross margin answers what remains after COGS; contribution margin answers what remains after all costs that vary with the sale. Use contribution margin dollars for break-even because those dollars pay fixed costs. Classify costs according to their behavior over the decision period, not only according to an accounting label. Calculate margins by product, service, and sales channel when variable costs differ. Review both percentages and dollars, then test price, volume, capacity, and cost assumptions together. Where the contribution income statement fits The contribution format reorganizes expenses by fixed versus variable behavior; a traditional gross-profit presentation groups them by function. A variable selling commission reduces contribution even when it appears below gross profit in the traditional view. Reorganizing a service-period statement does not itself create profit; manufacturing inventory valuation can introduce additional differences. The worked contribution income statement shows the full bridge from sales to operating income and provides a spreadsheet-ready template. Frequently asked questions Is contribution margin better than gross margin? Neither is always better. Gross margin is useful for understanding direct production or purchase economics. Contribution margin is usually better for break-even, pricing, promotion, sales mix, and incremental-order decisions because it includes variable costs beyond COGS. Can contribution margin be higher than gross margin? Yes. Gross margin can deduct fixed production overhead through COGS, while contribution excludes fixed costs and includes variable selling costs. Contribution can therefore be higher without either calculation being wrong. Reconcile both to operating profit using a consistent period and inventory treatment. Should labor be included in contribution margin? Include labor when the labor cost changes with the unit, job, order, or service level being analyzed. Exclude it from variable costs when it is fixed for the decision period. If labor has both parts, separate the variable and fixed portions. Does contribution margin include fixed costs? No. Contribution margin is revenue minus variable costs. The remaining contribution pays fixed costs first; whatever remains after fixed costs is profit under the scope of the analysis. How do I use contribution margin to set a price? List the variable cost per unit and choose a target contribution margin percentage. The basic price formula is variable cost per unit ÷ (1 − target contribution margin percentage). Then check whether the resulting price fits customer demand, competitors, capacity, and channel fees. Why does my gross margin look healthy while cash feels tight? Gross margin may exclude variable costs such as payment fees, commissions, shipping, and direct fulfillment labor. It also does not account for fixed overhead, timing of collections, inventory purchases, debt payments, or owner withdrawals. Review contribution dollars and cash timing together. Should I track both metrics? Usually, yes. Gross margin helps you monitor the direct cost of what you sell. Contribution margin helps you make operating decisions. Keeping both, with written definitions, gives you a clearer view than relying on either metric alone. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Break-Even Concepts PRACTICAL GUIDE Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs (With Examples) Published September 23, 2026 Updated November 20, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare fixed and variable costs in total and per unit. Use clear examples, identify mixed and step costs, and calculate contribution without double counting. Break-Even Concepts Financial Planning Small Business Quick answer Fixed costs stay constant in total within a stated period and operating range; variable costs change with activity. At $3,000 fixed cost and $8 variable cost per unit, 500 units cost $7,000 in total: $3,000 + 500 × $8. Average total cost is $14 per unit, but variable cost remains $8. The fictional example assumes no new capacity step or changing unit rate. Restaurant operator reviewing fixed and variable costs with receipts and calculator Fixed costs stay constant in total for a stated period and relevant activity range. Variable costs change with a specified driver: units produced, jobs completed or payments processed. Fixed cost per unit falls as activity rises; variable cost per unit is constant only under a linear-rate assumption. Split mixed bills and model capacity steps before calculating contribution or break-even. Quick answer: Fixed costs do not change in total when sales volume changes, such as rent or a software subscription. Variable costs change with each unit sold, such as ingredients, packaging, or sales commissions. Add fixed costs to find your operating base; subtract variable cost per sale from price to see what each sale contributes toward profit. Fixed vs variable costs: compare total cost and cost per unit Cost behavior within one stated period and relevant activity range Question Fixed cost Variable cost What happens to the total? Unchanged within the stated range Changes with the matching activity driver What happens per unit? Falls as the same commitment is spread over more units Constant only under a linear per-unit assumption At zero activity? The commitment can remain payable Zero for a purely volume-driven cost; check minimum commitments Typical conditional examples A monthly premises lease or guaranteed salary Material consumed, per-order packaging or a sales commission Choose the driver before assigning a label: units produced, jobs completed, miles driven and sales dollars are different measures. A percentage card fee varies with collected revenue, so a discount can change its dollar cost per order. Fixed does not mean permanent, and variable does not mean discretionary. Both labels describe behavior over a defined time and range. Total fixed cost formula and variable cost per unit Reconciled formulas using the existing 80-visit fictional example, USD Measure Formula Worked result Total variable cost Variable cost per visit × completed visits $81 × 80 = $6,480 Total cost Total fixed cost + total variable cost $3,200 + $6,480 = $9,680 Total fixed cost Total cost − total variable cost $9,680 − $6,480 = $3,200 Variable cost per unit Total variable cost ÷ matching units $6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 per visit Fixed cost per unit Total fixed cost ÷ matching units $3,200 ÷ 80 = $40 per visit Average total cost per unit Total cost ÷ matching units $9,680 ÷ 80 = $121 per visit The subtraction formula works only when total cost and variable cost cover the same costs, activity and period. It does not identify cost behavior from one unexplained bill. For total fixed cost = total cost − (variable cost per unit × units) , independently establish the per-unit rate first. At zero units, total fixed cost can still be measured, but per-unit divisions are undefined. To estimate a mixed bill from activity records, use the high-low method and its outlier checks . For the next calculation, follow the contribution-margin method and break-even formulas for units and sales dollars . Keep this page as the cost-classification reference rather than treating all four methods as interchangeable. The direct answer A fixed cost remains constant in total for a period, provided you stay within a normal operating range. If your shop sells 100 or 200 items this month, its monthly rent may still be $2,000. Other examples can include a basic insurance premium, a salaried office manager, accounting software, and a business license fee. A variable cost changes in total as activity changes. If you make twice as many products, you generally buy more materials. If you serve more customers, you may use more ingredients, disposable supplies, shipping materials, or transaction-based labor. A cost that is $4 per unit creates $400 of total cost at 100 units and $800 at 200 units. Use this basic structure: Total fixed costs: costs that do not change in total with short-term volume. Variable cost per unit: the activity-dependent cost for one defined unit, order, job or other driver, including applicable indirect variable costs. Contribution margin per unit: selling price minus variable cost per unit. Operating profit: total sales minus total variable costs minus total fixed costs. For example, if you charge $30 for a service and spend $12 on supplies and payment-related costs, your contribution margin is $18 per service. If monthly fixed costs are $1,800, you need 100 services to cover that fixed-cost base because $1,800 ÷ $18 = 100. Sales above that point can contribute to operating profit, assuming the cost assumptions remain accurate. What changes the answer The time period matters. Rent is usually fixed month to month. Over several years, a lease may renew at a higher amount. State the time frame for your analysis. The activity range matters. A small bakery may use its existing oven for 500 items a week. If demand reaches 1,000 items, it may need another oven or an extra shift. The original equipment cost behaves like a fixed cost within the first range, then the business takes a step up to a higher fixed-cost level. Some costs are mixed. A phone plan can include a fixed monthly charge plus usage fees. A delivery arrangement can include a base fee plus a per-mile charge. Separate the base and usage portions when you can. If you cannot separate them precisely, make a reasonable estimate and label it as an assumption. The unit must be clear. For a house cleaner, the unit might be one cleaning job. For a restaurant, it might be one meal, one order, or one cover. For a subscription business, a monthly subscriber may be the useful unit. Choose a unit that matches how you price and serve customers. Timing is not the same as behavior. An annual insurance bill can create a large cash payment in one month, but the underlying expense may cover twelve months. Pricing policies can change variable cost. A discount may lower your revenue per unit without lowering ingredients, labor, or fulfillment costs. Free shipping may turn a cost you normally pass to the customer into a variable cost you absorb. Review the actual offer, not only the standard price. Worked examples: Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs (With Examples) These are independent fictional USD illustrations, each limited to its stated scope. Their prices are not current market-rate claims. Scenario 1: House cleaning service You charge $160 for a standard cleaning. Supplies cost $10 per job, payment processing averages $5 per job, and you pay a cleaner $85 per completed job. The variable cost per job is therefore $100: $10 + $5 + $85 = $100 The contribution margin is $60 per job: $160 - $100 = $60 Your monthly fixed costs are $2,400. They include insurance, scheduling software, phone service, storage, and a regular administrative wage. The break-even volume is: $2,400 ÷ $60 = 40 jobs At 40 jobs, revenue is $6,400 and variable costs are $4,000. The remaining $2,400 covers fixed costs, so operating profit is $0. At 45 jobs, revenue is $7,200 and variable costs are $4,500. After fixed costs, operating profit is $300: $7,200 - $4,500 - $2,400 = $300 That calculation also shows why a price increase should be tested against demand. An extra $10 per job would increase contribution margin if job volume and variable cost stayed the same, but the result changes if the higher price reduces bookings. For related pricing decisions, see margin and markup . Scenario 2: Small restaurant menu item A restaurant sells a bowl for $14. Ingredients cost $4.20, the disposable container costs $0.60 for takeout orders, and a per-order fee averages $0.40. For a takeout bowl, variable cost is $5.20: $4.20 + $0.60 + $0.40 = $5.20 The contribution margin is $8.80: $14.00 - $5.20 = $8.80 Suppose monthly fixed costs allocated to the restaurant operation are $17,600. This includes rent, core salaried labor, insurance, and recurring systems. The number of bowls needed to cover that amount, if the bowl were the only item analyzed, is 2,000: $17,600 ÷ $8.80 = 2,000 bowls At 2,300 bowls, sales are $32,200. Variable costs are $11,960, calculated as 2,300 × $5.20 . Operating profit after the stated fixed costs is $2,640: $32,200 - $11,960 - $17,600 = $2,640 ways to lower your break-even point for a related pricing framework. Scenario 3: Handmade product sold online You sell a candle for $28. Wax and fragrance cost $6.50, the jar and label cost $3.50, packaging costs $2, and average payment and marketplace fees are $2.80. Total variable cost is $14.80: $6.50 + $3.50 + $2.00 + $2.80 = $14.80 Contribution margin is $13.20 per candle: $28.00 - $14.80 = $13.20 Monthly fixed costs are $1,584 for design software, insurance, a small studio, and baseline marketing subscriptions. Break-even volume is 120 candles: $1,584 ÷ $13.20 = 120 candles If you sell 150 candles, revenue is $4,200 and variable cost is $2,220. Operating profit is $396 after fixed costs: $4,200 - $2,220 - $1,584 = $396 Four questions before classifying an expense Which period and activity? Materials follow production or consumption; merchant fees follow processed sales. Purchased stock, units produced and units sold can belong to different periods. What is payable at zero activity? Separate the lease, base fee, minimum purchase or guaranteed shift from usage charges. What changes at the next threshold? A new shift, overtime rate or all-units rebate requires its own cost schedule. Does the split reconcile to the bill? Fixed component + usage rate × matching activity must reproduce the included total. Keep invoice, quantity, contract and assumption together; count every amount once. Behavior and traceability are different: directly attributable labor can be fixed when guaranteed, while shared supplies can vary with activity. Whether a fixed cost is avoidable depends on the decision and commitment period. The make-or-buy guide explains avoidable costs; an allocated fixed amount is not automatically an incremental cash saving. Classify common expenses by the actual arrangement Cost behavior is conditional; these are examples, not universal accounting rules Expense What to check Wages and direct labor A guaranteed salary may remain fixed; job-paid hours can vary. An additional shift can create a step cost. Direct materials and shipping Materials used and per-order carriage commonly vary; a shipping subscription or minimum commitment can add a fixed component. Utilities and electricity Separate the standing charge from usage charges; a capacity tariff or threshold can change the relationship. Depreciation Straight-line depreciation is commonly a fixed period expense; units-of-production depreciation varies with usage. Depreciation is not the same as an equipment cash payment. Advertising A committed campaign budget can be fixed for a period; a fee per conversion or completed sale can vary. Use the actual contract and attribution boundary. Cost of goods sold COGS is a functional classification and can contain fixed production overhead. It is not automatically identical to all variable expenses. Variable cost per activity unit = the selected total variable cost ÷ its matching activity. For inspection work, divide by comparable inspections; for delivery, mileage may be the driver. A variable-cost diagram shows the selected pool rising with activity; a mixed-cost line starts above zero because it includes a fixed component. Rebuild the model outside its relevant range. Use flexible budgeting to separate changed activity from spending differences without scaling every cost as variable. How to run your own numbers Start with one period, such as one month, and one unit of activity. A job, order, meal, or product is usually easier to analyze than a vague “customer.” Write down the price you actually collect, after routine discounts, rather than the list price. Use the MyBreakeven calculator to test your assumptions. Next, list every cost that increases when you deliver one more unit. Include materials, packaging, per-order fees, shipping you pay, commissions, and labor that is paid per job or hour of production. Divide the total by expected units to estimate variable cost per unit. Keep a note beside each estimate so you can replace it with actual results later. Then total the costs that remain for the period even if you sell nothing. Include recurring rent, baseline payroll, insurance, subscriptions, licenses, and planned overhead. Do not count the same cost in both lists. Use these formulas: Contribution margin per unit = selling price per unit - variable cost per unit Break-even units = total fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit Operating profit = (units sold × contribution margin per unit) - total fixed costs How to calculate variable cost per unit from your own jobs For a service business, begin with completed jobs from one consistent period. Imagine a cleaning team delivered 80 standard visits last month. Supplies consumed on those visits cost an illustrative $640 , payment fees were $240 , and labor paid specifically to complete the visits was $5,600 . These costs total $6,480. Divide by the 80 completed visits: $6,480 ÷ 80 = $81 variable cost per visit . At a collected price of $145 per visit, each job contributes $145 − $81 = $64 before monthly fixed costs. One month of standard visits Illustrative total Per completed visit Supplies used $640 $8 Per-payment fees $240 $3 Paid job labor $5,600 $70 Variable cost $6,480 $81 Suppose the business also has $3,200 monthly fixed costs , including planned administration and owner pay not already counted as per-job labor. Break-even is $3,200 ÷ $64 = 50 completed standard visits . At 40 visits, contribution is $2,560 and the model is $640 short . At 60, contribution is $3,840 and the model leaves $640 after fixed costs. That holds only while the job mix, collected price, per-job cost and available staff remain close to the assumptions. These are fictional example numbers, not typical US cleaning prices. If a phone plan has a $95 base charge plus $0.30 for each booking, put the $95 in the period's fixed costs and $0.30 in cost per booking. A full $119 bill for 80 bookings is not $119 of variable cost; allocating the fixed base to every booking and also entering $95 as fixed would count it twice. If you run out of crew capacity at 50 visits and must pay a new guaranteed shift, calculate a second range with that added fixed or step cost instead of projecting the original $64 contribution indefinitely. Our contribution margin guide shows how this per-job amount flows into sales goals. Common mistakes Calling every recurring cost fixed. A monthly bill may contain a usage component. Separate the base charge from the amount that grows with activity. Ignoring labor that follows sales. If you pay someone per job, per item, or per hour worked, that labor belongs in the variable-cost calculation for the relevant decision. Otherwise, your contribution margin will look too high. Using revenue instead of contribution margin. Revenue does not show what remains after fulfilling an order. Break-even volume based only on price will understate the sales needed. Mixing cash timing with cost behavior. An annual renewal is not automatically a variable cost because cash leaves the bank once a year. Spread the expense for operating analysis while separately planning the cash payment. Forgetting discounts, refunds, and waste. Your real selling price may be lower than the advertised price. Your real material usage may be higher than the recipe or bill of materials. Use observed averages when possible. Rounding too early. Keep cents through the contribution-margin calculation. Round the final break-even unit target up because partial units do not cover a real sales target. Separate average cost from variable cost and step costs Average total cost per job changes when fixed costs are spread over a different number of jobs. In a separate illustration with $3,200 monthly fixed costs and $81 variable cost per job, 40 jobs cost $3,200 + 40 × $81 = $6,440 , averaging $161 each. At 80 jobs, total cost is $9,680, averaging $121 each. Variable cost remains $81 within the assumed operating range. Do not enter the $121 average as variable cost while also entering $3,200 fixed costs: that would count the fixed allocation twice. Nor should the declining average be used to promise that every additional job becomes cheaper. Now suppose exceeding 60 jobs requires an extra $800 monthly commitment. At 70 jobs, fixed costs become $4,000 and total cost is $4,000 + 70 × $81 = $9,670 . At a $145 price, revenue is $10,150 and the modeled surplus is $480. Ignoring the step would overstate that surplus by $800. Write down the capacity threshold, commitment duration and which charges apply to existing as well as new jobs. A subscription upgrade that changes the fee on every order needs a whole-period recalculation, not just a fee applied to the extra orders. Why one extra job can temporarily reduce the remainder Extend the existing $145-price, $81-variable-cost illustration with its separate capacity condition: an extra $800 monthly commitment is triggered above 60 visits . Assume this added commitment supports up to 100 visits without changing price or variable cost. The no-step 80-visit cost record above uses a different capacity assumption; do not silently add this charge to that record. 60 visits Included fixed costs $3,200 Variable costs $4,860 Sales $8,700 Planning remainder $640 61 visits Included fixed costs $4,000 Variable costs $4,941 Sales $8,845 Planning remainder -$96 62 visits Included fixed costs $4,000 Variable costs $5,022 Sales $8,990 Planning remainder -$32 63 visits Included fixed costs $4,000 Variable costs $5,103 Sales $9,135 Planning remainder $32 70 visits Included fixed costs $4,000 Variable costs $5,670 Sales $10,150 Planning remainder $480 At 60 visits: $8,700 − $4,860 − $3,200 = $640 . At 61: $8,845 − $4,941 − $4,000 = −$96 . One extra visit adds $64 contribution but triggers $800 of fixed cost, reducing the remainder by $736. In the new 61–100-visit range, $4,000 ÷ $64 = 62.5 visits: 63 whole visits leave $32; 62 still leave a $32 shortfall. The original 50-visit threshold remains valid in the earlier range. Expanding capacity can therefore create a temporary loss after a profitable lower range. The original $3,200 includes an owner compensation allocation. These results are planning remainders after that allocation, not automatically accounting operating profit, after-tax income or withdrawable cash. Check a new staffing commitment’s duration and reversibility before accepting additional work. The CVP guide covers the wider profit method; this example shows why cost classification comes first. Estimate mixed costs without double-counting A fixed monthly vehicle commitment plus usage-dependent running costs is a mixed cost. If comparable observations show $1,640 at 80 equivalent visits and $2,440 at 280, the two-point estimate is ($2,440 − $1,640) ÷ (280 − 80) = $4 per visit; its monthly fixed component is $1,320. Check both observations: $1,320 + $4 × 80 = $1,640, and $1,320 + $4 × 280 = $2,440. At 200 equivalent visits the estimate is $2,120, averaging $10.60 per visit; that includes the fixed allocation and is not the $4 variable rate. Select the high and low observations by activity, not cost, and inspect all intermediate records. The high-low method calculator and six-month example shows why a high repair bill can distort a model. Cost behavior and traceability are different classifications: a cost can be directly attributable to a service while remaining fixed for the month, or indirect yet variable with activity. State the cost object and relevant range. After splitting a mixed cost, enter its fixed component once in overhead and variable component once per activity unit; do not add the original total again. Fixed and variable cost curves: total cost versus cost per unit Use the axes before interpreting a curve. In this independent fictional period, total fixed cost is $2,000, total variable cost is $20 × activity and a separate mixed-cost example is $1,000 + $10 × activity. The fixed line is horizontal on a total-cost chart; it is not horizontal on a cost-per-unit chart. These are three separate cost examples, not three components to add together. Original linear examples within an assumed 0–200-unit range. Each line is a separate model. Cost curves in numbers, fictional USD per period Activity Fixed total Variable total Mixed total Fixed per unit 0 2,000 0 1,000 Undefined 50 2,000 1,000 1,500 40 100 2,000 2,000 2,000 20 200 2,000 4,000 3,000 10 At positive activity the variable cost per unit stays $20 under the assumption, while fixed cost per unit falls as the same $2,000 is spread across more units. At zero activity, a per-unit cost cannot be calculated. The mixed cost per unit falls from $30 at 50 units to $15 at 200, even though its total rises. A declining average therefore does not prove the total bill fell. A capacity step can invalidate the old line Suppose a separate staffing arrangement costs $2,000 through 100 jobs and requires a second $2,000 shift for 101–200 jobs. The fixed commitment is $2,000 at 100 jobs and $4,000 at 101. It is a step schedule, not the horizontal $2,000 assumption used in the chart. Review the contract and practical capacity; do not extend a line beyond its relevant range. Accounting function is a separate dimension. An expense may be selling OPEX and variable, or administrative OPEX and fixed; production costs can also contain fixed and variable elements. The operating-expense guide owns classification against COGS, while the operating-margin calculator subtracts compatible statement totals. Do not transfer every OPEX line into a variable-cost field merely because it is an operating expense. Compare a higher fixed commitment with a higher per-order charge Consider two independent fictional fulfillment arrangements for identical service quality and scope. Option A costs $4,800 a month plus $20 per order; option B costs $1,200 plus $50 per order. They have equal modeled total cost at ($4,800 − $1,200) ÷ ($50 − $20) = 120 orders : each costs $7,200. At 80 orders A costs $6,400 and B $5,200; at 160 orders A costs $8,000 and B $9,200. This is a cost-indifference point, not the business’s sales break-even point. It excludes selling price, financing, switching costs, capacity and contract minimums beyond those stated. Check those conditions before selecting an arrangement. The make-or-buy decision guide covers avoidable costs and capacity; the CVP guide shows how selling price and contribution change the profit calculation. Method references and example boundaries Primary references: OpenStax cost behavior, per-unit costs and relevant ranges (§2.2) ; mixed-cost equations and estimation limits (§2.3) ; and break-even formulas and CVP assumptions (§3.2) . Reviewed November 13, 2026. The cases are independently constructed illustrations; the sources are not providers of these business prices. Use compatible costs and activity for the same period. A linear model assumes stable selling price, variable rates and sales mix within its relevant range. Zero or negative contribution cannot fund positive fixed commitments through extra volume. Keep financing principal, equipment cash purchases and payment dates in a separate cash plan; a positive modeled remainder does not establish sufficient bank cash. Review working capital and asset quality when funding commitments. Distinguish incremental tiers from an all-units price change A lower rate above a threshold can mean two different contracts. In this fictional 0–200-order operating range, both arrangements have a $600 fixed monthly commitment. Contract A charges $8 for each of the first 100 orders, then $6 only for additional orders. Contract B charges $8 per order through 100; if qualifying monthly volume exceeds 100, its $6 rate applies to every order in that month. Assume identical scope and no other charges. Original contract comparison; illustrative USD per month Orders A: incremental tiers B: all-units rate Why they differ 80 600 + 80 × 8 = 1,240 600 + 80 × 8 = 1,240 No threshold crossed 100 600 + 100 × 8 = 1,400 600 + 100 × 8 = 1,400 Threshold not exceeded 101 600 + 100 × 8 + 1 × 6 = 1,406 600 + 101 × 6 = 1,206 B reprices all qualifying orders 150 600 + 100 × 8 + 50 × 6 = 1,700 600 + 150 × 6 = 1,500 A retains the first-tier charge For contract A, total cost is 600 + 8 × MIN(Q,100) + 6 × MAX(Q − 100,0) . For contract B it is 600 + IF(Q ≤ 100,8 × Q,6 × Q) . These spreadsheet-style expressions require nonnegative whole Q within the stated range. The $600 remains fixed; the usage charge follows the applicable piecewise schedule. At the 101st order, A’s total bill rises by $6. B’s modeled bill falls by $194 because the prior 100 orders also receive the $2 reduction: $6 for the extra order minus $200 of repricing. Do not generalize that result to a real supplier without verifying eligibility, minimum commitments, credits and the period when the rebate is earned. An annual purchasing rebate is not automatically available in a monthly cost model. A single $6 or $8 rate cannot describe every point in both contracts. Nor is total bill divided by orders the variable rate: it includes the $600 fixed allocation. Keep the schedule, driver and activity range in the input record. For inventory, distinguish purchased units from consumed or sold units before assigning a period expense. The high-low estimation guide does not turn a known tier schedule into one reliable straight line; the transaction-fee allocation example shows the parallel need to define the selling unit. OpenStax’s cost-behavior chapter explains why a relevant range and the activity driver matter. The two supplier arrangements here are original hypothetical cases, not claims about a named provider’s current prices. Apply this result to the next decision For a mixed-cost estimate, see the high-low method and its limits . Keep average cost per unit separate from variable cost. A service business can connect the classification to sellable-hour pricing and the cost of an employee without adding the same wages to two cost buckets. Frequently asked questions What is the variable cost per unit formula? Add the costs that increase when you deliver the units in a comparable period, then divide by the number of completed units. Check that each expense is included once and the units share a comparable scope. Is an hourly wage always a variable cost? Job-paid production time often changes with completed work, but a guaranteed shift may remain payable even if bookings fall. Model the actual pay arrangement and staffing range rather than assuming all labor behaves the same way. Can an annual payment be a fixed cost? Yes. Fixed and variable describe cost behavior as activity changes, not the date cash leaves the account. Plan the annual cash payment separately from the operating analysis. What if one job takes twice as long as another? Use job types or a weighted mix rather than one average across unlike services. A deep clean and a standard maintenance visit may need separate per-job labor and price assumptions. Are payment-processing fees fixed or variable? A per-transaction or percentage fee varies with the matching sales activity. A monthly account charge or minimum can add a fixed component. Separate the contract’s base and usage amounts without counting either twice. Can a cost be partly fixed and partly variable? Yes. A base subscription plus a per-order charge is a simple example. Enter the base in monthly commitments and the incremental charge in sale-dependent cost, each counted once. How do you calculate total fixed cost? Subtract total variable cost from total cost for the same period and scope. If the variable rate is independently known, total fixed cost equals total cost minus variable cost per unit multiplied by units. In this guide, $9,680 minus $81 times 80 visits equals $3,200. Does a lower tiered rate apply to all units or only extra units? The contract determines that. An incremental tier changes the charge only for units in that tier. An all-units arrangement can reprice every qualifying unit when a threshold is met. Record the applicable range and rebate timing before using either rate in a contribution calculation. Does fixed cost per unit stay constant? No. The total can stay fixed within a stated range while its allocation per unit changes. A $3,200 fixed cost spread over 80 visits is $40 per visit; over 40 it is $80. At zero visits, the per-visit allocation is undefined. Can extra sales create a loss after a capacity step? Yes. In the stated example, 60 visits leave $640. The 61st adds $64 contribution but triggers $800 extra monthly commitments, leaving a $96 shortfall. The new 61–100-visit range requires 63 whole visits to cover $4,000 of included fixed costs. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
