documents.text: Landscaping PROFITABILITY GUIDE Landscaping Profit Margin: Follow the Money Behind Each Job Published September 20, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate landscaping profit margin with direct costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Compare price changes, monthly job goals and delivery capacity. Landscaping Profitability Margin Planning Landscaping business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs The example crew invoices $18,000 for 40 jobs and has $3,260 left after the listed job costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Its planning profit margin is 18.11%, while the contribution margin before those monthly requirements is 57%. Keep those two percentages separate when reviewing the business. The first tells you what the month leaves after the chosen pay treatment; the second tells you what the jobs contribute toward it. This guide uses illustrative USD figures and follows the hours behind the revenue, including price cuts and higher job costs. Quick answer State whether you mean job contribution, operating profit or profit after a chosen owner-pay goal. Use consistent revenue and cost definitions, include the relevant crew and equipment costs, then divide the resulting profit by revenue. Check the same plan against worker-hours and actual completed jobs. A positive margin percentage alone does not show whether the monthly income goal is achievable. Put the cost list beside the margin percentage Start the review with completed jobs and the revenue they brought in. Then subtract the costs that follow those jobs: materials, paid crew labor, other job expenses, acquisition and payment fees. The amount left is contribution toward the month's bills and income goals. For this guide, monthly planning profit is total contribution minus fixed costs and the separately stated owner-pay goal. Write that definition beside the result. It gives you a repeatable comparison from month to month even when another report uses a different profit measure. Choose how to handle the owner’s field time. If the direct labor line already pays for those hours, leave the identical pay out of the owner-pay goal. A solo operator can instead use owner pay for that income and exclude the same personal wage from direct job labor. Changing the method between months can make profit appear to move when only the classification changed. Keep cash purchases and accounting items in their appropriate records. Buying a mower, paying loan principal and using equipment during a job are different events. This worksheet focuses on operating contribution and the chosen monthly pay goal; a separate cash plan should show when larger payments leave the bank. Once the definition is settled, compare services. You can see which job types bring in the contribution and which absorb the hours. That is more useful than an overall percentage with no record of the work behind it. Build the example monthly result The example completes 40 jobs at $450 each. Each job has the following costs before percentage payment fees: Per-job input Example amount Materials $30 Paid direct crew labor $100 Other variable costs, including allocated equipment and travel $35 Acquisition cost per completed job $15 Total direct job cost before fee $180 Payment fee at 3% of $450 $13.50 Job contribution $256.50 At 40 completed jobs, revenue is $18,000 and direct costs before fees are $7,200. Payment fees total $540. Contribution is $18,000 − $7,200 − $540 = $10,260 , or 57% of revenue. Monthly fixed costs are $4,000 and the remaining owner-pay goal is $3,000. Profit after these bills and owner pay is $10,260 − $4,000 − $3,000 = $3,260 . The planning profit margin is $3,260 ÷ $18,000 = 18.11% . If you stop at contribution and call the 57% figure net profit, you hide $7,000 of monthly requirements. If you compare the 18.11% figure with another business that handles owner compensation differently, the comparison can also mislead. Keep the costs and compensation treatment next to the percentage. Include equipment and route costs once Equipment use can enter the model as a job-level allocation, a monthly fixed cost, or a combination covering different items. State what each line includes. For instance, fuel and job-specific wear may sit in other variable costs while recurring insurance and storage remain fixed. Do not include the same replacement allowance in both lines. Use actual worker-hours for crew labor. Two workers on a two-hour site job use four worker-hours, before any additional paid route time. A $100 labor cost for four hours implies a $25 hourly cost. If paid preparation or travel adds time, increase the labor cost and capacity duration accordingly. Acquisition spending needs a relevant denominator. Suppose a campaign costs $300 and generates 20 inquiries but only ten paid jobs. The cost per completed job is $30, not $15. Estimating from inquiry count alone can overstate contribution when conversion is weaker than expected. Keep maintenance routes and installation jobs separate if their economics differ. A blended job average is suitable for a monthly scenario only when its price, cost and worker-hours all use the same completed-job mix. Averaging price across one mix and labor across another creates a job that never exists. Compare three ways the monthly margin changes Hold monthly volume at 40 jobs and fixed costs plus owner pay at $7,000. Scenario Job price Direct cost before fee Job contribution Monthly planning profit Profit margin Base completed-job plan $450 $180 $256.50 $3,260 18.11% Price falls to $420 $420 $180 $227.40 $2,096 12.48% Direct costs rise to $210 $450 $210 $226.50 $2,060 11.44% The lower-price case loses $29.10 contribution per job after the fee adjustment, or $1,164 over 40 jobs. The direct-cost increase loses $30 per job, or $1,200 for the month. Revenue in the third row remains $18,000, so watching revenue alone would miss the profit decline. A $480 quote with unchanged $180 direct costs would leave $285.60 contribution. At the same 40 jobs, planning profit becomes $4,424 and margin becomes 23.04%. The quote still needs customer acceptance. Include any extra work sold with it before comparing the result. Use completed-job records to identify which change is relevant. If overruns are the cause, raising a menu price without fixing the estimate can leave the same cost uncertainty. If a service is consistently outside scope, change the written scope and approval process as well as the price. Calculate jobs needed for the monthly goal Suppose you also want $1,000 of target profit beyond fixed costs and owner pay. The combined goal is $4,000 + $3,000 + $1,000 = $8,000. At $256.50 contribution, required volume is $8,000 ÷ $256.50 = 31.19, rounded up to 32 completed jobs . At the lower $420 price, the same goal requires 36 jobs. At $210 direct cost and the original price, it also requires 36. Round up because you need whole completed jobs. Planning on 31 jobs in the base case would leave the stated goal short. If conversion from qualified inquiries to paid jobs is assumed to be 40%, 32 completed jobs require 32 ÷ 40% = 80 qualified inquiries. This is another explicit planning assumption. It does not mean every channel produces equally valuable leads or that your actual conversion will reach 40%. Compare that goal with delivery capacity Two workers with 35 weekly hours each and 70% utilization provide 2 × 35 × 52 ÷ 12 × 70% = 212.33 monthly delivery worker-hours . At four worker-hours per job, whole-job capacity is 53 jobs. The 32-job goal and 40-job monthly example fit this simplified hour model. If difficult access and route travel raise duration to six worker-hours, capacity falls to 35 whole jobs. At the same time, paid labor may also rise; leaving the $180 direct-cost estimate unchanged would be inconsistent unless another cost decreases. Model both the cost and time change rather than adjusting only the capacity figure. Weather and seasonality can affect the available schedule. Use a utilization assumption that reflects the period you are planning, and compare a shorter working month. A monthly margin measured during a strong period should not automatically become the annual forecast. Sum the expected months with their own revenue and costs when building a yearly plan. Enter the base case in the calculator Open the landscaping break-even calculator . Enter price $450, material cost $30, labor cost $100, other variable cost $35, acquisition cost $15 and payment fee 3%. Set fixed costs $4,000, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $1,000. Use two workers, 35 hours per worker per week, four worker-hours per job and 70% utilization. The result should show $256.50 contribution, 32 required jobs and 53 whole-job capacity. The calculator tests the monthly goal; calculate the actual month's profit from completed jobs rather than assuming capacity equals sales. What can make the monthly margin misleading Calling contribution net profit. Monthly fixed costs and the remaining owner income still need coverage. Double-counting owner wages or equipment. Explain which cost line includes each item. Counting calendar hours as crew-hours. Include every worker's time and relevant travel. Mixing job averages from different service mixes. Weight price, costs and duration consistently. Using a profitable month as the entire annual forecast. Plan seasonality and actual availability separately. Show a hiring change in both the margin and the cash calendar For a separate fictional landscaping month, revenue is $10,000, materials $3,000, variable job labor $2,000 and fixed operating costs $2,500. Operating profit under this defined boundary is $2,500, or 25% of revenue. Suppose a new guaranteed staff arrangement adds $1,800 committed loaded payroll but replaces $1,000 of the original variable labor. Count the replacement once: costs become $3,000 + $1,000 + $2,500 + $1,800 = $8,300. Operating profit becomes $1,700, or 17% , before any new volume or productivity benefit. If recruiting also creates $600 of additional external expense in that month, the illustrative operating result falls to $1,100, or 11%, assuming that expense belongs in the period. If all revenue is collected and all those expenses are paid in the same month, cash after those items is also $1,100. A separate $500 loan-principal repayment reduces the stated cash remainder to $600 , while principal itself is not another operating expense. Interest, asset purchases, taxes and other timing differences are excluded from this teaching case. Review recruitment strategy and ramp-up capacity , the full compensation budget and payroll reconciliation before assuming a hire increases margin immediately. More capacity helps only if the supported work can be sold and delivered; the extra payroll remains a commitment within the modeled range. FAQs Which margin should I use to review completed jobs? Use contribution after the costs that follow each job, with a consistent list of included items. Then subtract monthly fixed costs and the remaining owner-pay goal to review what the whole month leaves. Should the owner salary be included when comparing months? Use the same owner-pay treatment in every comparison and show it beside the result. If the owner’s field wages are already in direct labor, count only the remaining income goal in owner pay. How do I stop counting equipment costs twice? Write down what the job-use allowance covers and what remains in monthly overhead. Remove any overlapping fuel, insurance, maintenance or replacement allocation before calculating profit. Why does the goal require 32 jobs rather than 31? The $8,000 combined goal divided by $256.50 contribution is 31.19. Since completed jobs are whole units, 31 falls short and 32 meets the stated target. What if maintenance and installation jobs have very different margins? Keep separate job sheets first, including worker-hours. Build the monthly average from the completed or expected mix, using the same proportions for revenue, costs and time. Can a good profit month hide a problem for the rest of the year? Yes, the number of working days, job mix and paid volume can change across seasons. Build the annual plan from the separate monthly results instead of multiplying one strong month by twelve. Takeaways Define which costs and owner pay the margin includes. Allocate equipment once, with its included items written down. Use the same service mix for price, costs and worker-hours. Review seasonal months separately before building the annual total. For closer job reviews, read the landscaping job-costing guide , route density guide and crew utilization guide . More examples are in the business guides . For a different service scope, compare Landscaping Equipment Cost per Hour: Build a Job Rate and Landscaping Maintenance Contract Pricing: Scope and Visits . Recalculate contribution and delivery time for that scope. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Photography PROFITABILITY GUIDE Photography business profit margin: formula and worked example Published September 20, 2026 Updated November 23, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate photography profit margin with a $5,000 monthly example. Separate session contribution, overhead and owner pay, then test editing capacity. Photography Profitability Margin Planning How do you calculate photography profit margin? Margin = the result after your stated costs ÷ net sales × 100. In this fictional portrait month, $5,000 sales minus $1,650 session costs and fees leave $3,350 contribution (67%). After $700 overhead, $2,650 remains (53%) before the owner-income target. After a separate $1,800 owner-income target, the planning remainder is $850, or 17% . These are three different cost boundaries, not three interchangeable net-profit margins. The 17% result is before taxes, debt principal and new equipment purchases. Owner income is a planning target here; business-specific accounting treatment may differ. See the complete reconciliation , then test sessions and delivery capacity . Photography business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs Your photography business profit margin is the month's profit divided by the month's net sales, using a clearly stated cost boundary. In the fictional portrait month below, $5,000 sales leave $850 after variable costs, overhead and the owner's income goal: a 17% planning margin. That is different from a session's contribution percentage. Measure the actual service mix and complete editing workload before comparing margins. These USD figures are examples, not industry averages or a forecast of bookings. Reconcile a complete portrait month Fictional portrait month: ten completed $500 sessions, USD Measure Calculation Amount Percentage of $5,000 sales Net sales 10 × $500 $5,000 100% Session costs and fees 10 × ($150 + $15) $1,650 33% Contribution $5,000 − $1,650 $3,350 67% After $700 overhead; before owner target $3,350 − $700 $2,650 53% After $1,800 owner-income target $2,650 − $1,800 $850 17% Assume ten completed sessions sell for $500 each, producing $5,000 net sales. Each session carries $80 of incremental contractor labor, $30 travel expense, $10 delivery expense and $30 acquisition. Cost before processing is $150 per session. At 3%, the payment fee is $15 per session. Contribution is $500 − $150 − $15 = $335 per session. Ten sessions contribute $3,350, or 67% of net sales. A high contribution percentage is useful, but the studio has not paid its monthly commitments yet. Monthly overhead is $700 for the software, insurance, equipment and administrative commitments included in this example. Owner pay is a separate $1,800 income target. After those amounts, the result is $3,350 − $700 − $1,800 = $850. Dividing $850 by $5,000 gives a 17% owner-paid planning margin. This result is before taxes, debt principal, new capital purchases and any expense not listed. Owner pay here is a planning income goal, not a statement about how a particular business structure reports distributions. Label the boundary rather than calling it audited net profit. The photographer's production time is not also charged through an owner wage per session. The $80 contractor labor is a different paid input. If you choose to value owner delivery time as a direct wage instead, adjust the separate owner-pay treatment consistently so the same compensation is not deducted twice. At $335 contribution, paying $700 overhead and $1,800 owner income requires eight sessions: seven contribute $2,345, while eight contribute $2,680. A $500 additional profit goal raises the funding requirement to $3,000 and needs nine sessions. Nine leave $515 after the $2,500 overhead and owner-pay requirement. The contribution versus profit margin guide explains the denominator and cost boundary. Keep both figures in the monthly report so a high session contribution is not mistaken for the studio's final margin. Count the photographer's full workload Suppose each portrait session needs one hour shooting, four hours editing, one hour travel and two hours for consultation, file handling and delivery. That is eight photographer worker-hours. Ten sessions require 80 hours before any general business work outside the modeled job tasks. One photographer with 30 weekly hours has 130 monthly hours using 52 ÷ 12 weeks. At 65% utilization, 84.5 hours remain for this modeled session workload. Dividing by eight permits ten whole sessions. The ten-session month fits this simplified ceiling but leaves little room for job overruns. Keep the $80 contractor's work separate from the photographer's eight-hour capacity estimate. If the contractor's paid labor is already removing some editing work, the eight hours must reflect the remaining internal tasks rather than the full pre-outsourcing workload. Cost and capacity inputs should describe the same delivery arrangement. The editing cost-per-session guide helps record production time. Use actual logs to update the estimate when gallery size, revisions or delivery requirements change. A photographer can have a financially attractive session that cannot be produced at the volume required. Four variables that move the month's margin Booking count. Fixed overhead is paid across fewer sessions in a quiet month. Do not calculate a per-session overhead allocation from your busiest calendar and use it all year. Work from completed sessions and state the period. Price and scope. More edited images, travel or revision rounds can raise both cost and time. A higher package price may leave more dollars while earning less contribution per worker-hour. The photography pricing guide connects those promises to a quote. Acquisition and delivery costs. Advertising, referral charges, gallery delivery and outsourced production change what each booking leaves. If marketing is a committed monthly budget, keep it in overhead; if you enter an acquisition cost per session, avoid deducting the same budget again. Owner compensation and capital. A business that covers software and lab invoices while leaving the owner unpaid has not met this example's income goal. At the same time, purchasing a camera affects cash differently from the planning allowance used for equipment expense. Keep the cash schedule and operating calculation separate. Do not treat a single target percentage as a universal quality standard. The useful comparison is whether your price, workload and completed volume support the income and resilience you need under a stated cost boundary. Product mix and business commitments can make two identical percentages represent different dollar outcomes. Three monthly scenarios Six sessions in a quiet month Six $500 sessions create $3,000 sales and 6 × $335 = $2,010 contribution. Subtracting $700 overhead and $1,800 owner pay leaves a $490 shortfall. The owner-paid planning margin is −$490 ÷ $3,000 = −16.33%. If you report only the result before owner income, you would show $1,310 after overhead. That figure answers a different question. Keep both labels explicit so a quiet month is not described as supporting the owner's target when it does not. A $550 price with the original scope Keep the $150 non-percentage variable cost and eight-hour workload. At $550, the 3% fee is $16.50 and contribution is $383.50. Eight sessions contribute $3,068 and leave $568 after overhead and owner pay. Sales are $4,400, so the margin is $568 ÷ $4,400 = 12.91%. The $500 goal is met with eight sessions instead of nine. This assumes the bookings occur at the higher price and the scope is unchanged; demand is not established by the cost calculation. Editing expands to 12 hours per session Keep the original $500 price and $335 contribution, but internal delivery now takes 12 hours rather than eight. The 84.5-hour workload budget allows seven whole sessions. Seven sessions generate $3,500 sales and $2,345 contribution, leaving a $155 shortfall after overhead and owner pay. If no paid expense changes, the per-session contribution remains $335, yet the monthly result deteriorates because fewer sessions fit. To meet the $3,000 funding requirement at seven sessions, price must be ($150 + $3,000 ÷ 7) ÷ 0.97 = $596.4654, rounded upward to $596.47. A $600 price leaves $432 contribution; seven sessions leave $524 after overhead and owner pay. Actual customer demand and delivery scope still decide whether that plan is workable. Keep cash and margin in separate records A deposit applied to a $500 session is part of the same $500 price. Do not count it as additional revenue when the session balance arrives. The dates of deposit, delivery, contractor payment and final balance matter for cash, but they do not create a second sale. Track equipment purchases and planned replacements outside the simple monthly margin shortcut. The example's $700 overhead includes only the stated equipment expense assumption, not a new camera bought in cash. A positive owner-paid planning result does not mean the full amount is available for distribution after every cash commitment. Review a quiet-month and an overrun scenario before spending the apparent surplus. Use actual booking history for seasonality rather than adding an unsupported industry percentage. Keep uncertainty visible through different completion counts and workloads. How to run your own numbers Use the photography business break-even calculator with $500 price, zero materials, $80 contractor labor, $40 other variable costs and $30 acquisition, plus a 3% fee. Add $700 overhead, $1,800 owner pay and $500 target profit. For internal capacity, use one photographer, 30 weekly hours, 65% utilization and eight worker-hours per session. It requires nine sessions and permits ten. Other currencies are supported. A dated cash schedule and mixed-service report remain separate tasks. Common mistakes Calling the 67% contribution percentage the studio's final profit margin. Presenting a result before owner pay as the owner's supported income. Counting deposits and final balances as separate session sales. Deducting the same acquisition budget in overhead and per-session cost. Leaving revisions and delivery out of internal session hours. FAQs What is a good photography profit margin? Choose a target that supports your actual overhead, income needs and workload. This guide does not claim an industry average. Compare dollar results under a consistent cost boundary as well as percentages. Should owner pay reduce the planning margin? Include it if the question is whether the business supports that income. State the amount separately from overhead. Avoid charging the same owner compensation through both direct labor and owner pay. Does a high contribution margin mean the business is healthy? It leaves more of each sale for monthly commitments. The completed volume and fixed requirements still determine the final result. Capacity and cash timing need separate checks. How do I handle several kinds of shoot? Calculate contribution and internal worker-hours for each service. Build the month from its actual mix rather than averaging only prices. A large commercial project and a short portrait session are different workloads. Are equipment purchases operating profit costs? This guide uses a stated monthly planning allowance and keeps purchase cash separate. Your accounting treatment depends on your records and business arrangements. Do not deduct the same purchase again in the simple contribution calculation. Can a higher price fix a capacity problem? It can reduce the volume required under unchanged costs and scope. The new price still needs customer demand. Recheck hours if the higher package also promises more deliverables. Takeaways Report contribution and the final monthly result separately. State owner pay and all included cost boundaries. Count shooting, editing, travel and delivery time. Test quiet volume and longer workloads before spending surplus cash. Browse the business planning guides for related examples. Keep the margin calculation connected to the work Use the session-cost and editing worksheet example for delivery inputs, the monthly client target for completed volume, and the photography planning collection for related decisions. This article owns the whole-business monthly margin; a session contribution is an input to that result. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Mobile Detailing PROFITABILITY GUIDE Is Mobile Detailing Profitable? A Practical Owner-Operator Analysis Published September 20, 2026 Updated October 7, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Learn if mobile detailing is profitable by testing pricing, margin, fuel, travel, utilization, owner pay, break-even jobs, and capacity. Mobile detailing Profitability Margin Planning Mobile detailing business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs Yes, mobile detailing can be profitable for a US owner-operator when your prices cover travel, labor, supplies, overhead, and the time you spend selling and moving between jobs. It becomes much less profitable when you underprice packages, drive too far, or confuse busy days and gross sales with actual net profit. Quick answer: Mobile detailing is often viable because you can start with lower fixed costs than a shop, but profitability depends on route density, pricing, utilization, and owner workload. Track revenue per booked hour, variable cost per job, fixed overhead, and owner pay separately. A realistic target is positive cash flow after paying yourself a defined wage—not simply a full calendar. The direct answer A mobile operator has an important advantage over a fixed-location shop: you may avoid rent for a customer-facing bay. You still pay for a vehicle, water or power solutions, equipment replacement, chemicals, insurance, licensing, software, marketing, fuel, payment processing, and unpaid administrative time. The costs are simply distributed differently. Start with four terms. Gross margin is the percentage of sales left after direct costs required to perform the service. If a $240 detail uses $42 of chemicals, towels, card fees, and job-specific fuel, gross profit is $198 and gross margin is 82.5%. Net profit margin is what remains after all operating expenses, including fixed overhead, advertising, insurance, software, vehicle costs, and any paid labor. If monthly sales are $12,000 and net profit is $2,400 after those expenses, net profit margin is 20%. Contribution margin is the amount each job contributes toward fixed overhead and profit after variable job costs. A $240 package with $42 in variable costs has a $198 contribution margin. If monthly fixed overhead is $3,960, you need 20 such jobs to cover it because $3,960 divided by $198 equals 20. That break-even view is more useful than asking whether the industry is profitable in general. A route with six well-priced jobs in a compact area can outperform a route with eight discounted jobs spread across a county. What changes the answer Price and package design come first. A full interior-and-exterior service should not be priced as though it were a quick wash. Define what is included, how long it normally takes, what conditions trigger an upcharge, and whether travel outside your core area costs extra. Use a clear car detailing prices list as a planning reference, then adjust for your market, positioning, and actual job times. Utilization determines how much of your day earns revenue. Capacity is the number of service hours you could sell in a period. Utilization is the share of that capacity that is actually booked and completed. If you have 160 available work hours in a month but only 96 are spent detailing, your service utilization is 60%. The other hours go to driving, estimates, messages, purchasing, setup, and bookkeeping. Do not assume every weekday is billable. If you can work 20 days for eight hours each but reserve two hours per day for non-service work, your practical capacity is closer to 120 service hours. Booking 90 hours means 75% utilization of practical capacity, not 56% of an imaginary 160-hour total. Your mix of services matters. Maintenance details may be quicker and easier to repeat, while paint correction or ceramic coating can produce higher ticket revenue but require more skill, equipment, and quality control. Measure contribution margin per service hour, not just the invoice total. Startup investment affects the first-year result. A basic setup may need a van or trailer, extractor, pressure washer, generator or battery system, water solution, vacuum, towels, chemicals, branding, insurance, and booking tools. A thoughtful mobile detailing business startup cost guide can help separate one-time purchases from recurring expenses. Browse the MyBreakeven blog library for related planning guides. Account for equipment replacement over time rather than assuming the first setup lasts forever. Worked examples: Is Mobile Detailing Profitable? A Practical Owner-Operator Analysis The following figures are illustrative planning examples, not industry statistics . Recalculate them with your own prices, hours, costs, and your own costs. Scenario 1: A focused solo operator Suppose you complete 48 jobs per month at an average ticket of $275. Monthly revenue is 48 × $275 = $13,200 . Each job has $48 of variable costs for chemicals, towels, payment fees, and job-related fuel, so variable costs are 48 × $48 = $2,304 . Contribution margin is $13,200 − $2,304 = $10,896 , or 82.5%. Now assign $4,100 to monthly fixed overhead, including insurance, vehicle payment and reserve, phone and software, advertising, storage, and maintenance. Before owner pay, the operating surplus is $10,896 − $4,100 = $6,796 . If you pay yourself $4,000 for 192 hours of total monthly work, the remaining business profit is $2,796 . Net profit margin after that owner wage is $2,796 ÷ $13,200 = 21.2% . Scenario 2: A lower-ticket route with stronger repeat business Assume 60 maintenance jobs per month at $185 each. Revenue is 60 × $185 = $11,100 . Variable cost is $34 per job, or 60 × $34 = $2,040 . Contribution margin is $11,100 − $2,040 = $9,060 , giving an 81.6% contribution margin. Fixed overhead is $3,600, leaving $5,460 before owner pay. If the owner assigns $3,800 for 176 hours of work, business profit is $1,660 . Net profit margin after owner pay is $1,660 ÷ $11,100 = 15.0% . This can still be a good business. Repeat customers may reduce advertising and sales time, while concentrated routes may reduce travel. However, this model has less room for cancellations or repairs. Raising the average ticket by $15 adds 60 × $15 = $900 in monthly revenue; if variable cost does not rise, most flows to contribution margin. Scenario 3: A busy but underpriced schedule Now assume 52 jobs at $210, producing 52 × $210 = $10,920 in revenue. Variable cost is $46 per job, totaling 52 × $46 = $2,392 . Contribution margin is $8,528 , or 78.1%. Suppose fixed overhead is $4,250 and the owner takes $3,500 for labor. The remaining profit is $8,528 − $4,250 − $3,500 = $778 . Net profit margin after owner pay is only $778 ÷ $10,920 = 7.1% . If two jobs cancel and are not replaced, revenue falls by $420 and contribution margin falls by $328, assuming $92 of variable costs are avoided. Profit then drops to $450 . How to run your own numbers Build a monthly model with one row for each service package. Record price, expected jobs, on-site hours, travel and setup time, and variable cost per job. Include chemicals, consumables, card fees, job-specific fuel, subcontractor payments, and sales commissions. Calculate monthly revenue as price multiplied by jobs. Calculate contribution margin as revenue minus variable costs. Then subtract fixed overhead, including insurance, permits, software, base phone costs, storage, vehicle payment, accounting, marketing retainers, and a repair or replacement reserve. Finally, subtract a planned owner wage so you can see profit after paying for your labor. Your break-even job count is fixed overhead divided by contribution margin per job. If fixed overhead is $3,600 and the typical job contributes $180, break-even is $3,600 ÷ $180 = 20 jobs . At 35 jobs, contribution after fixed overhead is (35 × $180) − $3,600 = $2,700 , before owner pay and taxes. For a more useful capacity check, divide booked service hours by practical available service hours. If you can sell 120 on-site hours in a month and have 84 booked, utilization is 84 ÷ 120 = 70% . Then calculate revenue per total work hour, including travel and admin. A $12,000 month over 210 total hours equals $57.14 per total hour before expenses; that is the number that protects you from celebrating a high ticket that consumes your entire day. You can test the assumptions in the mobile detailing break-even calculator . Run at least three cases: conservative demand with lower utilization, a base case using your current average ticket, and an upside case with better route density or package pricing. Replace its assumptions with your own records. Common mistakes Counting sales as profit is a common error. Track contribution margin and net profit separately. Ignoring owner labor creates an inflated result. Put an hourly wage in the model even if you do not transfer that money to a separate account. Forgetting cash reserves makes a good month look better than it is. Set aside money for taxes, slow periods, insurance, equipment failure, and vehicle maintenance before treating the remainder as take-home. FAQs Is mobile detailing profitable for one person? It can be, especially when the owner keeps fixed overhead controlled and sells enough service hours at a sustainable price. The deciding metric is profit after assigning a fair wage to the owner’s labor, not the amount deposited from customer invoices. What is a good profit margin for mobile detailing? There is no single margin that fits every market, vehicle, or service mix. Track gross margin to understand job economics and net profit margin after overhead and owner pay to understand the business; a higher gross margin can still produce weak net profit if utilization is low. How many cars do I need to detail to break even? Divide monthly fixed overhead by the contribution margin per job. For example, $3,600 of fixed overhead and $180 of contribution per job require 20 jobs before owner pay, taxes, and extra profit. Should I charge a travel fee? Charge for travel when distance materially increases your time or cost, or set a service radius and decline distant jobs. You can also use zone pricing so customers see a clear, predictable price instead of a surprise surcharge. Is mobile detailing more profitable than opening a shop? Mobile service can reduce rent and facility costs, but it adds vehicle, travel, weather, and route-management costs. Compare contribution margin per total work hour and the full fixed-overhead model for both options rather than comparing rent alone. How much should an owner-operator pay themselves? Include a wage that reflects the work you perform, even if your legal structure uses draws or distributions. After that wage, retain enough profit for taxes, repairs, replacement equipment, and working capital before deciding what is available for personal take-home. Can weather make mobile detailing unprofitable? Yes. Rain, extreme heat, cold, or unsafe conditions can reduce usable capacity and cause cancellations. Build a weather policy, indoor partner options, rescheduling rules, and a cash reserve into your model instead of assuming every booked day converts to revenue. Takeaways Mobile detailing can be profitable when price, route density, utilization, and cost control work together. Use contribution margin to test each service and net profit margin to evaluate the whole business. Pay yourself for labor in the model before calling the remaining cash profit. Recalculate break-even with actual job times, travel, variable costs, overhead, and reserves. Improve pricing and route efficiency before simply adding more appointments. --- Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Salon PROFITABILITY GUIDE Salon Profit Margin: Services, Owner Pay and Retail Published September 20, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate salon profit after appointment costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Compare price changes, longer services, retail sales and team capacity. Salon Profitability Margin Planning Salon business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs A salon's profit margin comes from what appointments leave after service costs, payment fees, monthly bills and the owner-pay allowance you choose. A busy diary can still leave little surplus. In the example below, 200 appointments at $80 produce $16,000 revenue but an $80 shortfall after overhead and owner pay. The same salon needs 232 appointments for a $1,000 profit goal, with capacity for 234 under its stated working hours. These fictional USD figures show how to separate service contribution, compensation and retail sales without claiming a universal salon margin. Quick answer Calculate appointment contribution after service materials, direct labor, other appointment costs, acquisition and payment fees. Multiply by completed appointments, then subtract monthly overhead and owner pay. Divide the remaining profit by modeled revenue to get the margin. Keep retail sales and compensation methods explicit, and compare required appointments with the team's actual delivery hours. Decide what your margin includes Write the profit definition beside the percentage. A gross product margin, service contribution margin and operating surplus after owner pay are different measures. A percentage without its cost boundary is difficult to compare with another salon's claim. This guide uses operating profit after the stated owner-pay allowance, before any tax or financing calculation. It is a planning measure under the listed inputs. It does not claim to reproduce every salon's formal accounting statements. Use net collected service revenue on a consistent basis, excluding taxes collected for another party. Handle refunds and service corrections once. If tips or another amount are passed through to workers, do not assume that they fund the salon's rent. A single average appointment is a shortcut. A haircut, color correction and blow-dry have different prices, product consumption and time. Build the average using the same service mix for revenue, cost and worker-hours, then test it when that mix changes. Follow one appointment through the calculation Input per completed appointment Amount Average service price $80 Products and consumables $10 Paid direct delivery labor $24 Other appointment-related costs $4 Acquisition allowance $5 Payment fee 3% The $24 labor represents 1.25 worker-hours at $19.20 per hour in this example. These workers are paid for the modeled delivery hours. Committed non-delivery staffing costs are in overhead; the owner-pay allowance covers separate owner work. Reconcile those categories if your payroll arrangement differs. The fee is $80 × 3% = $2.40. Contribution is $80 − $10 − $24 − $4 − $5 − $2.40 = $34.60 per appointment . This leaves 43.25% of the price for monthly expenses, owner pay and profit. Monthly overhead is $4,000 and owner pay is $3,000. At 200 completed appointments, contribution is $6,920. Subtracting the $7,000 monthly requirement leaves −$80 , or −0.50% of the $16,000 service revenue. That figure does not mean every appointment loses money. Each appointment has positive contribution, but the total volume is not enough for the monthly expense-and-pay budget. Reducing the owner's pay changes the modeled result; it does not demonstrate that the same owner-income goal has been met. Find the appointment goal and staffing limit The overhead-and-owner-pay threshold is $7,000 ÷ $34.60 = 202.31, rounded up to 203 appointments . Add $1,000 desired profit and the requirement becomes $8,000 ÷ $34.60 = 231.21, rounded up to 232 appointments . At 232 appointments, revenue is $18,560 and profit after owner pay is 232 × $34.60 − $7,000 = $1,027.20 . The resulting margin is 5.53% when rounded to two decimal places. Three workers at 30 weekly hours and 75% delivery utilization provide 292.5 monthly worker-hours using 52 ÷ 12 weeks. At 1.25 worker-hours per appointment, the model allows 234 whole appointments . The profit goal fits, but with only two appointments of monthly headroom. That ceiling is not a demand forecast or a booking promise. Peak-day scheduling, specialist availability and overlaps can make the practical diary tighter. Count combined worker-hours when two people serve one appointment, and include cleanup and customer handover in the time estimate. Compare changes to price and delivery time Service scenario Contribution Appointments for $1,000 profit Capacity Base: $80 price, 1.25 hours $34.60 232 234 Discount: $72 price, same costs $26.84 299 234 Higher price: $90, same costs $44.30 181 234 Overrun: $80 price, 1.75 hours at the same pay rate $25.00 320 167 The discount uses $72 × 0.97 − $43 = $26.84. It needs more appointments than the unchanged team can deliver. Any claim that the discount will pay for itself needs evidence of more completed sales and enough hours to serve them. The $90 case leaves $90 × 0.97 − $43 = $44.30. Its target is 181 appointments. Whether that price suits the service and customer base is a separate market question; the calculation only shows what it funds under unchanged costs. In the overrun case, paid direct labor rises from $24 to $33.60. Direct costs before percentage fees rise to $52.60, leaving $25 contribution. Available hours support only 167 appointments. More bookings of that unchanged service do not solve its capacity gap. Use records to find the cause: insufficient consultation, an underestimated process, extra customer requests or avoidable rework. A five-minute average improvement should come from a real workflow change, not simply from typing a smaller time value into the plan. Give retail its own line Suppose one in four service customers buys a $20 retail product. Product cost is $10, sale-related commission and loss allowance total $2, and the fee is $0.60. Each retail sale contributes $7.40 . Across 200 service appointments, 50 retail sales contribute $370 on $1,000 additional revenue. Combined profit after the same monthly expenses is $6,920 + $370 − $7,000 = $290 on $17,000 revenue, a 1.71% margin. This assumes the existing overhead can support retail, with no additional fixed expense. Add shelves, storage or software costs if the retail operation actually increases the budget. Unsold stock needs cash even when it has not entered cost of sales. For a weighted appointment model, retail adds $5 revenue, $2.50 product cost, $0.50 other cost and $0.15 fees per appointment. Contribution becomes $36.45 . If selling a product takes four worker-minutes, weighted time rises by one minute per appointment to 1.2667 hours. That mixed model needs 220 appointments for the profit goal and supports 230 under the same hours. It is valid only if the 25% retail attachment assumption and service mix hold. The salon retail margin guide handles retail in more detail without replacing the service-business calculation. Reconcile your compensation arrangement If stylists receive fixed monthly pay, model the committed part in overhead or use a deliberate allocation that you reconcile back to payroll. Do not add a variable hourly wage as if every appointment creates a new wage payment while retaining the same full salary expense. Commission-based pay moves with the relevant service revenue according to your actual arrangement. Enter it as a direct cost consistently and recalculate when price changes if the commission is a percentage. The price scenarios above hold direct costs constant because their labor is an hourly amount, not a revenue percentage. Booth rental is a different business model: the owner may receive rent rather than the customer's whole service ticket. See the booth rent versus commission guide before comparing those arrangements. Keep the revenue you actually retain at the center of the plan. How to run your own numbers Open the salon break-even calculator with price $80, materials $10, labor $24, other variable costs $4, acquisition $5 and fees 3%. Enter overhead $4,000, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $1,000. Set three workers, 30 weekly hours, 75% utilization and 1.25 hours per appointment. The example should need 232 appointments against 234 capacity. Cost Builder can show the hours × pay labor calculation before applying it. Keep percentage fees and acquisition separate. Other currencies are available. The salon service-pricing guide explains the price-setting step. Common mistakes Calling appointment contribution the owner's take-home profit. Comparing percentages without their included costs. Counting full payroll again as labor per appointment. Forgetting that revenue-based commission changes with a price increase. Adding retail revenue without retail product cost, fees and time. Using a full diary as proof that the chosen owner pay is covered. Salon rent percentage: use the revenue that belongs to the model In a separate fictional employee-service salon, $3,500 monthly premises rent divided by $25,000 net salon sales is 14%. If sales drop to $20,000 and rent stays unchanged, the ratio rises to 17.5%. The ratio increased without a rent increase; it does not establish a universal good or bad salon-rent benchmark. For a booth-rental owner, do not divide rent by all renters’ client receipts unless those receipts belong to the owner’s reported revenue. Compare the property obligation with rental income and the owner’s remaining costs. The booth-rent and commission comparison keeps those arrangements separate. Service payroll, owner delivery compensation, products, retail COGS and overhead need defined lines before interpreting a salon profit margin. A high retail markup is not the same as salon-wide net profit. Review actual cancellations, worker-hours, lease commitments and payment dates alongside the sales ratio. Keep any benchmark’s geography, service mix, period and owner-pay policy visible. FAQs What is a good salon profit margin? A useful target depends on your compensation, service mix, costs and required owner income. This guide does not use a universal benchmark. Start with a defined after-owner-pay result and test whether your appointment volume can deliver it. Why can a busy salon still have a shortfall? Appointments may leave too little contribution for monthly expenses. Delivery overruns can also limit the number you can finish. Check both contribution per appointment and contribution per worker-hour. Should the owner's service work count as labor? It can, but reconcile it with monthly owner pay. Do not compensate the same hours twice unless the additional owner-pay amount deliberately covers different work or income. State the method before comparing margins. How do I include retail sales? Calculate retail contribution separately, then add it to service contribution or build a consistent weighted appointment. Include product cost, fees, losses and selling time. Do not assume every appointment includes a retail purchase. Do cancelled appointments count in revenue? Count collected revenue under your actual cancellation arrangement and model the time it consumes consistently. An unfilled cancelled slot does not become a completed service. Do not invent cancellation income to fill the forecast. Does 234 capacity guarantee 234 bookings? No, it is the example's monthly worker-hour ceiling. Demand, specialist skills and peak scheduling can reduce actual completed appointments. Confirm your expected volume separately. Takeaways Define margin after the specific costs and owner pay you include. Match price, costs and time to the same service mix. Reconcile committed payroll and direct labor. Add retail contribution and time together. Browse the small-business planning guides for more worked examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant PROFITABILITY GUIDE Restaurant Profit Margins: Gross, Operating and Net Examples Published September 20, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare restaurant gross, operating and net profit margins with a worked statement. Check owner wages, draws, interest and tax before comparing averages. Restaurant Profitability Margin Planning Restaurant business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs A restaurant profit-margin benchmark is useful only when its period, service format and profit definition match your own accounts. Keep gross margin, contribution, operating profit and income after financing and taxes separate. The worked examples below explain cost effects; they are not national averages. Quick answer: Restaurant economics work in layers. Gross margin remains after food and beverage costs. Contribution margin shows what each sale contributes toward fixed costs. Net profit margin remains after all business expenses. Owner take-home can differ from net profit because it includes wages, distributions, debt payments, taxes, and cash left in the business. The direct answer The National Restaurant Association's August 2025 summary of its 2024 restaurant respondent data reports median income before taxes of 2.8% of sales for fullservice respondents and 4.0% for limited-service respondents. These are dated respondent medians, not an average for every restaurant or after-tax net margins. The Association explicitly says the figures are not individual standards or targets. The full paid report was not used here. Start by separating the margins owners often blend together. Gross margin is sales minus the direct cost of food and beverages sold, divided by sales. If you sell a $20 entrée and ingredients cost $6, gross margin is $14 divided by $20, or 70%. That is what remains for labor, rent, utilities, marketing, repairs, and profit. Net profit margin is the net-income amount in your accounts divided by sales after all expenses included in that definition, including financing costs and taxes where applicable. Operating profit deducts operating expenses and must be labelled separately. If monthly sales are $100,000 and the business keeps $5,000, net profit margin is 5%. This is more useful for judging earning power, but confirm whether the figure includes a market-rate wage for your work. Owner take-home is the cash or compensation you receive through wages, an owner draw, profit distributions, or a combination. It is not automatically equal to net profit. A restaurant can report $8,000 of accounting profit while you take home $4,000 because the rest funds inventory, repairs, loan principal, or a reserve. Ask two questions separately: “What does the business earn?” and “What do I earn for working in it?” A sound target is a restaurant that pays you a fair working wage and still produces positive net profit. What changes the answer Labor is usually the largest swing factor. Include hourly wages, management salaries, payroll taxes, benefits, overtime, training, and the value of your own work. A schedule that is too lean can damage service; one that is too generous can erase busy-period contribution. Review labor by daypart, not only monthly. Food and beverage mix changes gross margin. A beverage-heavy menu can contribute more dollars per sale than one dominated by expensive proteins. Portion drift, waste, spoilage, comps, discounts, commissions, and theft can make actual cost higher than recipe cost. Compare theoretical food cost with purchases and inventory changes. Occupancy sets a hard floor. Rent, common-area charges, property taxes, insurance, and required maintenance remain payable during a slow month. A costly location needs enough sales volume to spread those fixed costs. Before signing a lease, calculate the sales required to cover occupancy at a conservative margin. Capacity and utilization matter. Your dining room, kitchen, seats, pickup counter, and opening hours are capacity limits. Utilization measures how much of that capacity you use. A 60-seat restaurant with two dinner turns has more potential volume than one with a single turn, but only if throughput, staffing, demand, and guest experience support it. Underused seats create a fixed-cost problem; overloaded capacity creates a service problem. Sales channels can change the margin on the same item. Dine-in may avoid a third-party commission but require more front-of-house labor. Delivery can add volume while sacrificing ticket percentage to commissions, packaging, promotions, and refunds. Track contribution by channel, not revenue alone. Taxes, equipment replacement, repairs, and working capital determine how much you can withdraw. If you are still building your concept, use the restaurant menu pricing formula to connect item pricing with ingredient cost and desired margin. For startup planning, review how much it costs to open a restaurant before treating a projected monthly profit as available cash. 3 realistic worked scenarios The following are illustrative calculations, not statistics . Each scenario uses simple monthly figures so you can see how a percentage changes when the underlying dollars change. Scenario 1: Full-service neighborhood restaurant Suppose your restaurant produces $120,000 in monthly sales. Food and beverage cost is $36,000, so gross profit is $84,000 and gross margin is $84,000 divided by $120,000, or 70% . Now subtract $42,000 of labor, $13,000 of occupancy, and $23,000 of other operating costs. Modeled operating profit is $6,000. Recalculate the operating margin: $6,000 divided by $120,000 equals 5% . The restaurant looks strong at the gross-margin level, but only five cents of each sales dollar remains after the full operating structure. Assume you work as the operating manager and should receive $7,000 in market-rate monthly compensation. If that amount was not included in the $42,000 labor figure, the adjusted result is a $1,000 loss, or negative 0.8% operating margin. The original $6,000 was not necessarily your true business profit; it partly represented unpaid owner labor. Scenario 2: Limited-menu counter-service concept Assume monthly sales of $80,000. Ingredients and packaging total $24,000, giving gross profit of $56,000 and a 70% gross margin . Labor is $20,000, occupancy is $8,000, and other operating costs are $14,000. Modeled operating profit is $14,000, which recalculates to 17.5% : $14,000 divided by $80,000. That result reflects a small menu, fast production, lower labor, and modest occupancy. It is not a promise. If a delivery platform takes an extra $4,000, modeled operating profit falls to $10,000. The new margin is 12.5% . Scenario 3: Slow sales at a high-occupancy location Imagine a 60-seat restaurant with $90,000 in monthly sales. Food cost is $27,000, leaving $63,000 of gross profit and a 70% gross margin . Labor is $36,000, occupancy is $18,000, and other expenses total $15,000. Modeled operating profit is negative $6,000 , so operating margin is negative $6,000 divided by $90,000, or negative 6.7% . Now recalculate without changing the rent or other fixed costs. If sales rise to $110,000 and food cost stays at 30%, food cost becomes $33,000. Assume labor rises to $39,000 because you need more coverage, while occupancy remains $18,000 and other costs remain $15,000. Modeled operating profit becomes $5,000: $110,000 minus $33,000 minus $39,000 minus $18,000 minus $15,000. The margin is $5,000 divided by $110,000, or 4.5% . The improvement comes from spreading fixed costs across more sales. Overtime, waste, or discounting can reduce it. Average restaurant revenue does not tell you the profit Revenue is sales; a profit percentage is what remains after a named set of expenses. No representative national average annual sales per restaurant was established for this guide. Do not apply a profit-margin survey median to an assumed average sales figure and call the result an expected owner income. Build a location-specific estimate from covers or completed orders, average check and open days. For an illustrative 80 covers a day at $25 across 26 days, monthly sales are 80 × $25 × 26 = $52,000 before considering the cost plan. This is arithmetic, not a market benchmark. The restaurant sales forecast guide checks dayparts, service capacity and channel mix. How to run your own numbers Build a monthly model using conservative sales, not your best Saturday. Separate channels with different costs, then list variable and fixed costs. For each menu or channel, calculate contribution margin as sales minus costs that rise with the sale, including ingredients, packaging, payment fees, commissions, and incremental labor. A $25 ticket with $8 of direct costs has a $17 contribution and a 68% contribution margin. That contribution helps pay fixed costs and profit. Total monthly fixed costs: rent, common-area charges, management, insurance, software, licenses, bookkeeping, maintenance, interest, and a realistic owner wage. Add a repair and replacement reserve. Your break-even sales formula is: Break-even sales = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin For example, if fixed costs are $50,000 per month and your blended contribution margin is 65%, break-even sales are $50,000 divided by 0.65, or $76,923 . If you want $8,000 of monthly profit, use the same calculation with $58,000: $58,000 divided by 0.65 equals $89,231 in required sales. These are illustrative figures, not statistics. Run low, expected, and high sales cases. Recalculate labor as sales change, test food inflation and delivery mix, and compare required sales with seats, turns, average check, operating days, throughput, and staff. Check the result with the restaurant break-even calculator after assembling assumptions. Reconcile it with your schedule, menu mix, and cash needs. Common mistakes Confusing gross margin with profit. A 70% gross margin does not mean you keep 70%; labor and occupancy consume much of the balance. Leaving out owner labor. Unpaid hours overstate profit. Add a market-rate wage even if you initially take no paycheck. Using recipe cost instead of actual cost. Waste, portions, spoilage, and inventory errors can make realized cost higher. Compare theoretical and actual food cost. Treating all sales as equal. A $100 delivery order with a 25% commission contributes less than $100 of dine-in sales. Track each channel. Ignoring utilization. Low sales may reflect weak demand, few open hours, poor turns, or slow production. Find the constraint before cutting service-protecting costs. Withdrawing every apparent dollar of profit. Reserve cash for taxes, inventory, payroll timing, repairs, debt principal, and seasonal dips before distributions. For the next decision in this plan, compare Takeout vs Dine-In Profit: Compare the Whole Order ; Restaurant Private-Event Minimum Spend: Price the Space . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. Restaurant average profit margin: define the subtotal before comparing Restaurant revenue, gross profit, operating profit and net profit answer different questions. A quoted restaurant-industry average is not meaningful unless its sample, period, venue mix and treatment of owner labor match the comparison. The following is an independent fictional statement, not an industry benchmark. One illustrative month, USD Line Amount Margin on 100,000 net sales Net sales after stated credits 100,000 100% Food COGS 32,000 32% Gross profit 68,000 68% Loaded payroll, including stated owner salary 30,000 30% Other operating costs, including any included depreciation 25,000 25% Operating profit 13,000 13% Interest 2,000 2% Income tax expense 3,000 3% Net profit 8,000 8% An owner drawing $4,000 from this business does not create a second wage expense in this example. The draw changes cash and equity; the owner salary already appears within payroll. Debt principal and equipment cash can also reduce available cash without being this month’s operating expenses. Keep their payment dates outside the margin calculation. Use actual records to determine whether a diner, franchise, delivery-led kitchen or full-service venue is comparable. A food gross margin of 68% cannot be reported as 68% restaurant net profit. Reconcile the budget , loaded labor and cash-flow statement before deciding what can be taken home. Reconcile EBITDA before comparing margins The EBITDA calculator bridges net income to a separately defined earnings measure. Do not relabel the operating margin or assume EBITDA represents collected cash. FAQs What is a good net profit margin for a restaurant? A low single-digit net margin may be workable, while an efficient concept can do better. Judge it after fair owner pay, repairs, debt costs, and replacement reserves. Is a 20% restaurant profit margin realistic? It can occur in a very efficient limited-service model, but it is aggressive for many US restaurants. Test it after including labor, occupancy, delivery, maintenance, tax, and owner-compensation costs. Should my owner salary count as an expense? Yes. A market-rate wage tests whether the restaurant works without unpaid labor; take-home can then include that wage plus a safe distribution. What is the difference between contribution margin and gross margin? Gross margin subtracts direct food and beverage cost. Contribution margin also subtracts variable packaging, payment fees, commissions, and incremental labor, making it more useful for channel and break-even decisions. How many sales do I need to break even? Divide monthly fixed costs by blended contribution margin. At $50,000 of fixed costs and 65% margin, illustrative break-even sales are $76,923; update both inputs as mix and costs change. Can higher sales reduce my profit margin? Yes. Overtime, waste, discounts, commissions, or extra management can absorb added revenue. Measure incremental contribution. How much cash can I safely take home? Do not base distributions on accounting profit alone. Reserve for payroll, taxes, inventory, debt principal, repairs, seasonal weakness, and working capital; then pay a wage and distribute supported surplus. Takeaways Gross margin is not operating or net profit: subtract the other costs included in the measure before describing what remains. Count your own labor: owner take-home combines compensation and distributions, but unpaid work can make profit look better than it is. Use contribution margin for decisions: it reveals which sales actually help cover fixed costs. Model capacity and cash: sales growth helps only when you can serve it without giving the gain back to labor, commissions, waste, or debt.
