documents.text: E-commerce PROFITABILITY GUIDE Ecommerce Profit Margins After All Fees: A US Owner-Operator Guide Published September 20, 2026 Updated November 28, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate ecommerce contribution and operating profit from net sales, fees, returns and overhead. Reconcile a monthly example before judging your margin. From profit per order to monthly operating margin Suppose each order averages $75 in net revenue after refunds, and $50 in variable costs after inventory recoveries. At 400 orders, net revenue is $30,000 and contribution is $10,000. With $7,000 in operating overhead, operating profit is $3,000 and operating margin is 10%. Keep the order count and cost basis consistent. Deduct any refund or recovered inventory only once. If your variable-cost total already includes payment processing, use the PayPal estimate to reconcile that cost rather than deducting the fee again. Estimate PayPal fees for a seller payment Model return costs per order Test the monthly ecommerce break-even order count E-commerce Profitability Margin Planning E-commerce business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs Your ecommerce profit margin benchmark should be based on what remains after product cost, shipping, payment processing, marketplace charges, advertising, returns, software, and overhead—not on the margin shown in your product catalog. For many owner-operators, a healthy business is one that produces a dependable net profit margin and pays a reasonable owner take-home after every cash cost is counted. Quick answer There is no universal ecommerce margin target supported by this guide. Separate gross margin, contribution margin, operating margin and net margin, then set a target from your actual costs, owner-compensation needs and risk allowance. A product-level percentage alone cannot show whether the whole store is profitable. The direct answer Start with four different measures instead of asking for one “good” margin. Gross margin measures what is left after the cost of goods sold. If you sell an item for $100 and the product, inbound freight, and packaging assigned to that order cost $45, gross profit is $55 and gross margin is 55%. Contribution margin goes one step further. It subtracts costs that rise with each sale, such as payment processing, marketplace fees, pick-and-pack labor, shipping subsidies, returns allowance, and order-level advertising. Contribution margin tells you how much each order contributes toward fixed overhead and owner pay. Operating profit margin is operating profit divided by net revenue, after variable and fixed operating expenses. Net profit margin uses the final profit after interest, taxes and other applicable non-operating items. These are different reporting boundaries. Owner take-home is the cash or compensation you actually receive. It is not automatically equal to net profit. You may leave profit in the business to buy inventory, repay a loan, build a tax reserve, or cover a slow season. Conversely, an owner-operator who performs fulfillment or customer service may be receiving labor value that the income statement does not show as a wage. First establish positive contribution per order, then check whether the realistic order volume covers fixed operating expenses and the stated owner-compensation requirement. A 60% gross margin can still lead to a loss after acquisition, shipping and overhead. State which costs each percentage includes. What changes the answer Average order value changes fee pressure. A $5 payment fee is a large percentage of a $35 order but a small percentage of a $150 order. Bundles and sensible add-ons can improve contribution margin per shipment, provided they do not increase returns or fulfillment complexity. Acquisition cost can dominate product margin. Suppose your gross profit is $40 per order. If paid advertising costs $18 to generate that order, the ad consumes 45% of gross profit before shipping, payment fees, or overhead. Track acquisition cost by channel against contribution profit. Shipping and returns can reverse the result. Free shipping is a pricing decision, not a free benefit. Include outbound postage, packaging, address corrections, replacement shipments, return labels, inspection time, refunds, and inventory that cannot be resold. A return rate that looks manageable in percentage terms can be material when average shipping cost is high. Channel fees differ. Your own storefront, a marketplace, social commerce, and wholesale account may each have different payment, referral, fulfillment, and advertising charges. Maintain a separate contribution margin view for each channel. Utilization and capacity matter. Capacity is the number of orders your current people, storage space, equipment, and systems can handle in a period. Utilization is how much of that capacity you are using. When utilization is low, an extra order may have little incremental labor cost. When you are near capacity, overtime, temporary help, a larger warehouse, or a 3PL can lower your margin. Three illustrative worked scenarios The following figures are illustrative, not statistics . Each scenario recalculates the result from revenue through owner take-home so you can see which assumption drives the answer. Scenario 1: A $60 direct-to-consumer order Assume one order sells for $60. Product and inbound freight cost $24, so gross profit is $36 and gross margin is 60%. Now subtract a $6.50 shipping subsidy, $2.10 packaging and fulfillment labor, $2.04 payment processing, a $1.80 returns allowance, and $12 of advertising. Contribution profit is: $60 - $24 - $6.50 - $2.10 - $2.04 - $1.80 - $12 = $11.56 Contribution margin is $11.56 divided by $60, or 19.3% . If monthly fixed overhead is $4,624, the store needs 400 similar orders to cover that overhead because 400 × $11.56 = $4,624 . At 500 orders, revenue is $30,000 and contribution profit is $5,780. After fixed overhead, operating profit is $1,156, or 3.9% operating profit margin . The order looked like a 60% gross-margin sale, but its after-fee economics are much thinner. Scenario 2: A $120 bundle with lower acquisition cost Assume a bundle sells for $120. Product and inbound freight are $48, producing $72 of gross profit, or 60% gross margin. Shipping subsidy is $8, fulfillment and packaging are $3.50, payment processing is $3.78, returns allowance is $3, and advertising is $16. The recalculation is: $120 - $48 - $8 - $3.50 - $3.78 - $3 - $16 = $37.72 Contribution margin is $37.72 divided by $120, or 31.4% . If fixed overhead is $6,000 per month and you complete 300 orders, revenue is $36,000. Contribution profit is $11,316, leaving $5,316 after overhead. Operating profit margin is 14.8% . If the bundle raises return shipping and inspection cost by $4 per order, contribution profit falls to $33.72. At 300 orders, operating profit becomes $4,116 and operating margin becomes 11.4% . That second recalculation shows why a returns allowance must be based on actual behavior rather than a convenient assumption. Scenario 3: A marketplace order near capacity Assume a marketplace order sells for $80. Product and inbound freight cost $32. Marketplace and payment fees total $12, fulfillment is $7, outbound shipping is $9, returns allowance is $2.40, and marketplace advertising is $4. $80 - $32 - $12 - $7 - $9 - $2.40 - $4 = $13.60 Contribution margin is 17.0% . At 600 orders, revenue is $48,000 and contribution profit is $8,160. With $6,500 of fixed overhead, operating profit is $1,660, or 3.5% operating profit margin . If capacity pressure adds $4 per order for overtime or outside fulfillment, contribution profit falls to $9.60 and operating profit becomes 600 × $9.60 - $6,500 = -$740 . The store is busy but unprofitable. Reconcile order contribution with the month's operating margin Start with net sales after customer discounts and refunds. Then subtract the variable costs associated with those sales, and finally deduct fixed operating expenses. A per-order contribution figure cannot be labeled net profit while monthly costs remain unpaid. The following is an invented USD month, not a benchmark for ecommerce stores. An online store records $30,000 of sales before $1,500 of discounts and $1,000 of refunded sales. Net sales are $30,000 − $1,500 − $1,000 = $27,500 . Assume the following costs are already reconciled to those orders: $10,500 product cost, $4,000 shipping and packing, $825 processing fees, $3,500 acquisition cost and $675 of unrecovered return handling. Total variable cost is $10,500 + $4,000 + $825 + $3,500 + $675 = $19,500 . Contribution is $27,500 − $19,500 = $8,000 ; contribution margin is $8,000 ÷ $27,500 = 29.09% . With $5,000 fixed operating expenses, operating profit is $3,000 and operating margin is $3,000 ÷ $27,500 = 10.91% . Owner compensation must be stated as included in those expenses or added once; this example does not claim net profit after every possible expense. The $1,000 refunded sales amount is already removed from revenue. The $675 return handling line represents separate unrecovered costs, not a second deduction of the same refunded revenue. Reconcile recovered stock value and fee refunds using actual records before constructing the variable-cost total. See the return cost per order guide for that boundary. Under an unchanged 29.09% contribution ratio, operating break-even sales are $5,000 ÷ (8,000 ÷ 27,500) = $17,187.50 . This is a scenario using the same cost mix, not a forecast. If acquisition cost rises by $1,500 while sales stay $27,500, contribution falls to $6,500 and operating profit falls to $1,500, a 5.45% operating margin. Assuming the new ratio persists, break-even sales rise to about $21,153.85. Record net sales, contribution dollars and operating profit dollars together. The contribution versus profit margin guide explains why all three are needed, while break-even ROAS isolates the advertising threshold for a defined order. Neither order-level view replaces the month's expense reconciliation. How to run your own numbers Use one recent month or a three-month average. Start with sales recognized for the chosen period, net of discounts and refunds, excluding sales tax and other amounts that are not your revenue. Match costs to the same sales; use collections separately in the cash forecast. Keep sales tax separate from profit because it generally belongs to the taxing authority. Next, calculate gross profit. Add product cost, inbound freight, duties, and packaging that is consumed per unit. Use the same costing method each month so your margin does not jump merely because purchase timing changed. Then build a contribution-cost list for each channel. Include payment processing, marketplace fees, shipping paid by you, fulfillment labor, pick-and-pack fees, returns, replacements, chargebacks, affiliate commissions, and advertising. Allocate software or subscriptions to an order only when the cost genuinely varies with volume; otherwise keep it in fixed overhead. After that, subtract monthly fixed costs. Include ecommerce software, email and customer-service tools, insurance, accounting, storage, rent, phone service, payroll, contractor retainers, vehicle costs used for the business, as operating expenses. Show loan interest separately when reconciling operating profit to net profit. If you do the work yourself, add a planning wage for the hours you would need to replace. Finally, test owner take-home. From projected operating profit, reserve money for income taxes, inventory purchases, debt principal, and a cash buffer. Reconcile the result with dated cash obligations and available cash before deciding on a distribution; operating profit alone does not establish spendable cash. You can run the revenue, fixed-cost, and unit-economics calculation with the ecommerce break-even calculator for your store . Enter conservative assumptions first, then run a second version with your best current numbers. Compare the required order volume with your actual capacity, because a mathematically profitable target may be operationally impossible. Common mistakes Spreading fixed costs across the wrong volume. If you divide overhead by an optimistic order forecast, each order appears cheaper than it really is. Ignoring owner labor. An owner can appear highly profitable while working nights on fulfillment and support. Add a replacement wage when comparing the business with another use of your time. Counting revenue before refunds. Refunds, discounts, chargebacks, and failed deliveries reduce what you keep. Measure net sales consistently. Treating ad spend as optional. If paid acquisition is required to sustain sales, it belongs in the contribution calculation. Scaling a weak order. More orders do not fix negative contribution margin. First improve price, product cost, shipping, conversion, return rate, or acquisition efficiency. Then confirm that added volume will not push you into expensive capacity costs. Reconcile Shopify product reports with the full business result A product report can be useful without representing the full business profit. Shopify's profit-report documentation explains the importance of product cost recorded at the time of sale and differences between report types. Products or variants missing relevant cost data can be absent from product-profit reporting; check report coverage before interpreting a blended percentage. Export the same period's net sales and identify which orders and variants are represented. Reconcile product costs, discounts and refunds first. Then list shipping, fulfillment, processing, marketplace charges, advertising, return handling and fixed operating expenses. Mark each as already included, separately deducted or not yet available. Report definitions differ, so do not assume every Shopify profit view contains the same costs. If refunded revenue has already reduced net sales, do not deduct the refund again as an expense. Include the remaining unrecovered handling or inventory loss once. A payout after fees is also not the original sales figure: using that payout as revenue and subtracting the same fees again understates contribution. Keep the completed reconciliation beside the month's operating margin. Reconcile interest, taxes and other non-operating items before labeling the final result net profit. This approach uses your own records and does not depend on a universal store-margin benchmark. For channel-specific decisions, compare marketplace and own-store profit per order . For recurring boxes, include subscription churn and acquisition recovery before projecting repeat-order contribution. FAQs What is a good ecommerce profit margin for a small business? There is no single margin that is good for every store. Calculate contribution and operating profit using complete, consistent costs, include owner compensation once, and test realistic demand and a downside case. Report net profit separately after applicable interest, taxes and other non-operating items. Is a 20% gross margin enough for ecommerce? A 20% gross margin alone does not establish viability. Deduct variable selling costs, then test whether the remaining contribution at realistic sales volume covers fixed expenses and the stated owner-compensation requirement. Should owner pay be included in ecommerce expenses? Include a replacement wage for your labor when evaluating whether the business is economically worthwhile. Then show owner distributions separately so you can distinguish compensation for work from profit earned by the business. Do marketplace fees belong in gross margin? They normally do not belong in traditional gross margin because gross margin is based on cost of goods sold. Put marketplace fees in contribution costs, then report an after-fee contribution margin for each channel. How much should I reserve for returns? Estimate returns from your own order history by product and channel. Multiply the expected return rate by refund exposure and add shipping, inspection, restocking, replacement, and unsellable-inventory costs; revisit the allowance when your mix changes. Why can a good product margin still leave weak profit? Acquisition, delivery, payment and return costs can reduce the order contribution. The remaining contribution must also cover fixed commitments. Product cost alone does not describe the complete result. Takeaways Benchmark after all fees. Gross margin is a starting point; contribution margin and net profit margin show whether the store actually works. Separate owner take-home from profit. Pay for your labor, reserve for taxes and inventory, and distribute only what the cash plan can support. Recalculate by channel and scenario. Advertising, returns, shipping, and marketplace fees can make identical products produce very different results. Respect capacity. A busy store can lose money when overtime, outside fulfillment, or added space raises the cost of each order. For more practical planning, browse the MyBreakeven blog hub . For the stock-cost reconciliation behind product margin, use how to calculate cost of goods sold . Keep purchase payments and the working-capital position visible alongside the month's profit. Calculate margin, markup and discount-adjusted price floors . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency PROFITABILITY GUIDE Agency Profit Margin: Gross, Contribution and Operating Profit Published September 20, 2026 Updated November 17, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate agency profit margin with a reconciled example. Separate gross profit, contribution, operating profit, owner pay and client delivery costs. Agency Profitability Margin Planning How to calculate an agency profit margin Operating profit margin = (revenue − all operating costs for the period) ÷ revenue × 100. Net profit margin instead uses net income after applicable interest, taxes and other nonoperating items. Name the measure before comparing agencies or months. In the fictional USD month below, $12,000 retainer revenue − $2,000 client-variable costs − $6,000 committed payroll − $2,000 other overhead = $2,000 operating profit, or 16.67% operating margin . This is before any additional owner-pay goal, interest or tax not already included. It is an example, not an industry average or a promised healthy margin. Reconcile salary and per-client labor so neither is counted twice. Test client contribution, monthly commitments and agency capacity after reviewing the cost boundary below; the example is not transferred automatically. Agency business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs Your agency profit margin improves when you price the work above its fully loaded cost and keep enough delivery capacity billable; utilization alone cannot rescue underpriced services. For most US owner-operators, the useful target is a healthy contribution margin at a sustainable utilization level, followed by enough operating profit to pay you fairly and fund the business. The direct answer Your agency profit margin is the percentage of revenue left after the costs required to deliver your work and run the business. The simplest formula is: Operating margin = (revenue − operating costs) ÷ revenue × 100 Gross margin measures what remains after direct delivery costs. Those costs may include subcontractors, freelance production, paid media that you resell or manage directly, project-specific tools, and the delivery portion of employee or owner labor. If you bill $20,000 and direct delivery costs are $8,000, gross profit is $12,000 and gross margin is 60%. Contribution margin is revenue minus variable or incremental costs. It shows how much a sale contributes toward fixed overhead and profit. A $5,000 retainer requiring $4,000 of extra labor and third-party costs contributes $1,000, or 20%, before fixed expenses. Operating profit margin comes after the operating costs in the stated income statement. With $5,000 monthly operating overhead, that $12,000 gross profit becomes $7,000 operating profit on $20,000 revenue, or 35% operating margin . It is not an established after-tax net margin. Net profit margin uses net income after the applicable nonoperating items, interest and income taxes, divided by revenue. OpenStax distinguishes operating income from net income ; classification and example checked October 17, 2026. Owner take-home is not the same as profit. It may include salary, guaranteed payment, owner draw, or distribution. In a one-person agency, assign delivery time a target market wage even if your tax treatment differs; otherwise, unpaid job wages can look like business profit. Utilization connects delivery hours with available capacity. If you divide by the whole paid schedule, reserve non-delivery time through the utilization assumption. If you first remove that time to create a smaller delivery-only pool, use a compatible rate for that pool. Do not remove the same hours twice. Close the monthly margin against committed payroll Gross margin, contribution margin and operating margin answer different questions. Direct delivery costs can include committed employee payroll. Contribution, however, depends on the costs that change under the decision you are modeling. A salary does not become avoidable because you allocate it across clients in a spreadsheet. Consider a separate fictional agency month with four $3,000 retainers. Revenue is $12,000. Contract-specific costs are $500 per client, including the variable contractors, tools and fees chosen for this example. Total variable costs are $2,000. Committed payroll is $6,000 and other monthly overhead is $2,000. Monthly line Amount Retainer revenue $12,000 Client-variable costs −$2,000 Contribution before committed costs $10,000 Committed payroll −$6,000 Other fixed overhead −$2,000 Operating remainder $2,000 Operating margin is $2,000 ÷ $12,000 = 16.67%. This result is before any owner-pay goal, tax or financing costs not already included in the stated boundary. It should not be presented as an after-tax net profit figure. If owner compensation is already part of committed payroll, keep it there instead of subtracting it again. Now lose one client while payroll and overhead remain committed. Revenue becomes $9,000 and variable costs fall to $1,500. Contribution is $7,500. Subtract the same $8,000 of committed costs and the result is a $500 loss, or −5.56% operating margin. The lost client’s short-term contribution was $2,500; allocating some salary to that client would not make the salary disappear. This is the practical reason to keep a cancellation case separate from a full-capacity job-costing case. Both can be useful, but they need different cost behavior assumptions. Reconcile every line to invoices, payroll and an explicit period before comparing the margins. Connect margin to monthly client capacity To reproduce that committed-payroll model, use the agency calculator with a $3,000 client price, $500 of total client-variable expense, zero other unused cost fields, and $8,000 monthly operating overhead. In this isolated example set additional owner pay and target profit to zero. The $500 already includes any fees assigned to it, so set the percentage fee field to zero rather than charging them twice. Contribution is $2,500 per client and operating break-even is 3.2 clients, rounded up to four. Three do not cover committed costs; four leave the $2,000 operating remainder shown above. Adding an unfunded $2,000 owner-pay goal raises financial need to $10,000, which four clients cover exactly. Adding a further $1,000 profit target requires five clients. Now check delivery. Two people at thirty-five scheduled hours weekly and 65% productive utilization supply 197.17 productive worker-hours per average model month. At forty total worker-hours per client, capacity is 4.93 clients, or four complete commitments. Four clients fit the aggregate check; the five-client goal does not. At the five-client financial goal, required contribution is $11,000. Four clients deliver $10,000, leaving a $1,000 gap. A plan can reach operating break-even and still fail to support the owner’s larger income goal. State which financial boundary a profitable-looking margin actually covers. For the same four-client capacity, suppose the total variable cost remains $500 per client and fee behavior stays inside that allowance. A $3,250 price contributes $2,750 per client; four then provide $11,000. That price solves the arithmetic under those fixed assumptions, but the offer still needs buyer acceptance and the same delivery scope. If fees rise with price, separate and recalculate them instead of retaining the flat allowance. Turn the review into one owner decision Read margins alongside client hours rather than making utilization the target by itself. Record collected revenue for the chosen operating period, costs actually incurred, estimated versus delivered scope, and compensation already funded by payroll or labor allowances. Keep deposits and unpaid invoices visible in a separate cash view. Then isolate the decision you are testing. If the issue is an underpriced retainer, compare a revised price or narrower scope. If the issue is committed payroll with too few clients, test qualified demand and fixed commitments. If the issue is full delivery capacity, adding leads does not create production hours. Each action should move a specific input you can verify. Keep this review connected to agency billable utilization and agency client profitability . The client guide shows which engagement earns its share; this monthly guide checks whether the combined portfolio supports the whole agency. How to run your own numbers Start with a monthly view, then extend it across 12 months so annual expenses and seasonal demand do not surprise you. List revenue by client or service. For fixed-fee work, divide each fee by all expected hours to find its effective rate. Calculate capacity by role. Begin with working hours, subtract time that cannot be sold, and divide expected billable hours by available delivery hours. Make a second calculation using total working hours to see how much of your whole job is delivery. Separate direct delivery costs from fixed overhead, including a target cost for your delivery labor. Include contractor-related costs tied to delivery. Then calculate: Gross margin: (revenue − direct delivery costs) ÷ revenue. Contribution margin: (revenue − variable costs) ÷ revenue. Operating margin: (revenue − direct costs − overhead) ÷ revenue. Break-even revenue: fixed overhead ÷ contribution margin percentage. For a faster check, enter your agency’s pricing, costs, and capacity into the agency break-even calculator . Reconcile its assumptions to your own spreadsheet, especially whether owner compensation is treated as a cost and whether contractor expenses are variable. Run conservative, expected, and strong-utilization cases. Test a lost client, delayed payment, contractor rate increase, and a project taking 20% longer. A margin that works only in the strong case is not reliable. Common mistakes Treating owner draws inconsistently makes periods incomparable. Give delivery labor a target cost, then keep distributions separate from operating performance. Using total clock hours as capacity exaggerates utilization. Sales and administration are necessary work, but they are not billable delivery unless a client pays for them. Ignoring scope creep makes a profitable proposal look good on paper while the effective rate declines. Track estimated and actual hours. Confusing gross margin with net margin hides overhead. A project can have excellent gross margin and still lose money when account management, software, insurance, and sales time are included. Planning for 100% utilization leaves no capacity for selling, learning, recovering, or fixing errors. A utilization target should support reliable delivery and future revenue. Agency margin should follow complete client delivery cost Suppose fictional monthly agency revenue is $20,000 and sale-dependent delivery, contractor, fee and client-tool costs total $9,000. Contribution is $11,000, or 55%. If shared commitments and separately modeled owner pay total $8,000, the remaining plan result is $3,000, or 15% of revenue, before taxes and unmodeled expenses. Compare client scope before comparing percentages. A contractor-heavy engagement can have a lower margin but require less internal delivery time. An internally delivered retainer may look strong while consuming many unrecorded owner hours. Record those hours and the chosen compensation boundary. Shared software and administration should not be charged in full to every client. Use allocations for management comparison where useful, then reconcile to the actual total. A high margin does not establish enough customer demand, and a busy team does not establish healthy pricing. Review contribution, utilization and monthly commitments together. For the next decision in this plan, compare Agency Client Concentration: Revenue, Contribution and Cash ; Agency Project vs Retainer Profitability: Count the Hours ; Agency Employee vs Freelancer: Find the Workload Threshold . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. Agency margins: reconcile gross, contribution and operating profit Agency operating profit margin = operating profit ÷ net revenue × 100. Agency profitability reports often use “margin” for different subtotals. State which costs move with a client and which costs are committed. In this independent fictional month, $100,000 net revenue supports $20,000 client-variable subcontracting, $50,000 committed delivery payroll, $5,000 tools and $10,000 other operating costs. Owner delivery compensation is already included in payroll. Three margins on the same invented agency revenue, USD Measure Cost definition Result Gross profit Revenue less 20,000 subcontracting and 50,000 delivery payroll 30,000 / 30% Contribution under stated behavior scope Revenue less only the 20,000 variable subcontracting 80,000 / 80% Operating result Contribution less 50,000 payroll, 5,000 tools and 10,000 overhead 15,000 / 15% The 80% contribution rate does not mean the agency has an 80% net profit margin. Committed delivery payroll still needs funding and is deducted once when reaching the operating result. Interest, tax, capital spending and collection timing are separate from these stated operating subtotals. A client-level report can allocate payroll for comparison, but the client allocations must reconcile to the actual payroll total. Do not deduct the full $50,000 against every account and then deduct it again at agency level. Review profitability by client with actual delivery hours and utilization . An agency’s affordable margin follows its complete cost and capacity plan, not a universal agency-average percentage. Compare the earnings subtotal on a consistent basis Use the EBITDA and margin calculator only with the same reporting period and entity. Keep D&A, interest and income-tax add-backs distinct from the operating and net margins discussed here. Separate an invoice advance from agency revenue and delivery margin For a separate fictional cash example, an agency has a valid $12,000 client invoice. A hypothetical factor advances 85%, or $10,200, holds $1,800 as reserve and charges 2% of invoice face value for the agreed period, or $240. If the client pays in full under those assumptions, the later release is $1,800 − $240 = $1,560 . Total agency cash from the arrangement is $10,200 + $1,560 = $11,760 . The advance is not a second $10,200 of retainer sales, and the held reserve is not all a fee. Keep the revenue period, delivery costs, financing charge and cash dates visible separately. Accounting classification and recourse depend on the actual agreement; do not infer a sale or complete transfer of risk from the product name alone. A profitable invoice can need a bridge before payroll, while a recurring loss needs a different operating decision. Compare invoice financing and factoring , the working-capital repayment test and complete borrowing-cost comparison . The updated agency calculator separates committed payroll, owner allocation and new-client acquisition. Use payroll records to reconcile the cash dates rather than putting guaranteed salary into both monthly overhead and per-client delivery cost. FAQs What is a good agency profit margin? There is no universal target because service mix, owner compensation, geography, and growth investment differ. Use a margin that pays a market-based owner wage, covers overhead, builds cash reserves, and leaves a deliberate profit after those costs. Is utilization the same as profitability? No. Utilization measures how much capacity is sold, while profitability measures what remains after costs. You can be highly utilized at an underpriced rate and earn little, or have moderate utilization with strong pricing and a better margin. Should I include my own labor in agency costs? Yes, for management decisions, especially when you perform client delivery. Assign your delivery time a reasonable target cost so that profit does not simply represent unpaid wages. Keep the management calculation distinct from your tax or bookkeeping presentation when needed. What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin? Gross margin usually subtracts direct delivery costs, including the cost of producing the work. Contribution margin focuses on costs that change with a specific sale or client and shows how much revenue is available to cover fixed overhead and profit. Your accounting policy should define which costs go into each measure. How do retainers affect utilization? Retainers can stabilize revenue, but they can also hide unused or unlimited scope. Record the hours each retainer consumes, including meetings and revisions, then compare the effective hourly rate and contribution margin with your capacity plan. What happens if my utilization is too low? Verify your available-hour denominator and consistent time records. Then improve qualified lead flow, tighten the offer, adjust pricing, or reduce fixed costs instead of automatically adding services. What happens to margin when a client leaves but payroll stays fixed? Lost revenue is reduced only by costs that actually disappear. In the separate example, losing one $3,000 client avoids $500 variable cost while $8,000 committed costs remain, changing a $2,000 operating remainder into a $500 loss. Should contractor expenses be deducted before contribution? Include client-specific costs that change with the engagement under the chosen boundary. Committed arrangements may need a different cash treatment. Count each cost once and explain the classification. Takeaways Price every engagement against total delivery time , not only the visible production hours. Track gross margin, contribution margin, operating margin, and owner take-home separately so one number does not hide another. Use sustainable utilization , leaving capacity for sales, administration, quality control, and recovery. Recalculate scenarios before changing your offer ; a higher price, narrower scope, or better capacity mix can improve profit without simply working more hours. Treat the figures as a management model , and update the assumptions when your team, service mix, or overhead changes. Apply the next planning step Compare the two denominators before interpreting a pricing percentage. The widget only includes its entered cost; a price margin is not automatically agency net profit. Check margin versus markup on your defined cost basis . Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Cleaning STARTUP COST GUIDE How Much Does It Cost to Start a Cleaning Business? Published September 18, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a cleaning startup budget from local quotes, setup purchases and payment timing. Separate launch cash from monthly costs, owner pay and job targets. Cleaning Startup Costs Break-Even Planning Cleaning owner reviewing startup costs and opening budget To budget for a cleaning business, add the purchases and deposits needed to launch, then map when ongoing bills and customer payments fall due. Keep that funding plan separate from the jobs needed to cover monthly costs. The USD examples below show the method; they are not current US market prices or required spending for every cleaner. Quick answer: An illustrative solo cleaning business might need $4,850 in one-time startup cash and $2,650 in monthly fixed costs, before variable supplies and job-level labor. The staffed examples below use different equipment, wages and payment assumptions. Treat startup cash as a funding question; treat monthly fixed costs, owner pay, and target profit as the break-even question. The direct answer: separate startup cash from monthly break-even There are two different numbers behind this question. Mixing them produces a budget that does not help you decide how many jobs to sell. One-time startup costs are purchases or setup payments made before, or around, launch: registration, equipment, a website, uniforms, insurance deposits, and a vehicle down payment. They are not automatically monthly break-even expenses. Recurring monthly fixed costs continue whether you clean five homes or fifty. Examples include a phone plan, software, vehicle payment, insurance, storage, and owner pay. Break-even asks whether job contribution covers these costs; a target profit can be added to find the sales level you want. Here is an illustrative solo residential cleaning budget. These are planning figures, not market statistics: Illustrative startup budget (USD) One-time item Illustrative cost Business registration and local permits $250 General liability insurance deposit $450 Vacuum, mop, buckets, and durable tools $1,200 Initial chemicals, cloths, and paper products $350 Basic website, domain, and printed materials $400 Uniforms and protective equipment $200 Used vehicle down payment or launch transport reserve $1,500 Contingency for small setup purchases $500 Total one-time startup cash $4,850 Now list the monthly fixed costs separately: Illustrative monthly budget (USD) Monthly fixed item Illustrative monthly cost Vehicle payment $450 Commercial auto and general liability insurance $300 Phone and scheduling software $120 Storage or small workspace $180 Advertising budget $350 Bookkeeping and software subscriptions $100 Owner pay $1,150 Total monthly fixed costs $2,650 In this example, the owner needs $4,850 for setup plus working cash for the first months . The monthly break-even target is not $4,850; it starts with the $2,650 fixed-cost total, then accounts for variable costs and desired profit. Suppose the average cleaning job is priced at $180. Assume $30 of each job goes to variable supplies, payment processing, and mileage. The contribution per job is: $180 price - $30 variable cost = $150 contribution per job To cover monthly fixed costs: $2,650 ÷ $150 = 17.67 Because you cannot sell a fraction of a job, the owner needs 18 jobs per month to cover the listed fixed costs. If the target is $800 of monthly profit, the calculation becomes: ($2,650 fixed costs + $800 target profit) ÷ $150 contribution = 23 jobs, rounded up The 23-job result is the target in this illustration; it does not repay the initial $4,850 or promise results. For a closer look at customer pricing and job-level costs, see house-cleaning pricing guide . Build the launch budget from dated quotes The US Small Business Administration startup-cost guidance separates one-time spending from recurring expenses. Apply that distinction to your own quotes rather than treating the examples here as local prices. A quote register for a US cleaning launch Budget line Evidence to collect Timing Tools and opening supplies Supplier quote, quantities and service scope Purchase date; then replenishment as supplies are used. Insurance and recurring services Written quote with deposit and monthly charge separated Deposit at launch; renewals on their actual dates. Vehicle or storage Existing resources plus any new scoped commitment Upfront payment and subsequent bills recorded separately. Working cash Customer receipt dates against wages and supplier payments Largest projected cumulative cash shortfall. Do not assume every month needs the same reserve. Prepare a dated cash schedule through the planned ramp-up and test delayed receipts. Keep personal household reserves separate from business cash. For an invoice-paid contract, the cleaning payroll cash-gap example shows why contribution and collection timing answer different questions. Outside the US, use quotes and applicable local requirements in one currency throughout. Changing USD to GBP, CAD or AUD does not convert prices or establish a local registration or insurance cost. What changes the answer Your service area changes the launch bill. Registration, insurance, storage, parking, and travel costs vary by location. A home-based solo operator may avoid storage rent, while a wider territory can require more fuel and vehicle capacity. Your staffing plan changes cash needs and the math. A solo owner needs one equipment set and may avoid payroll while building demand. Hiring before the schedule is full adds wages, payroll taxes, workers’ compensation, recruiting time, and possibly another vehicle. Guaranteed hours are usually fixed; job-based labor is often variable. The service mix changes equipment and contribution. Standard home cleaning may need basic tools. Post-construction work can require heavier machines, safety gear, disposal fees, and more labor. A higher price does not mean a higher contribution if the job consumes proportionally more inputs. Payment terms affect working cash. A residential customer may pay at the appointment, while a property manager may pay after an invoice cycle. If wages and supplies are paid first, your startup reserve must cover the gap even when the contract is profitable on paper. Your owner-pay decision changes the break-even target. Leaving it out can produce a low break-even number while the business cannot support your household. Add planned owner compensation to monthly fixed costs, separate from personal spending the business does not pay. Separate one-time setup and deposits from recurring insurance premiums. Obtain actual policy quotes for your location, services and staffing arrangements; a pricing example does not establish insurance costs. Three realistic worked scenarios The following are illustrative planning examples, not market statistics. Scenario 1: Solo operator using an existing car A solo owner already has a car and starts with residential recurring cleans. One-time costs are: $200 registration + $600 equipment + $250 initial supplies + $300 website and print + $250 insurance deposit + $300 reserve = $1,900 Monthly fixed costs are: $280 insurance + $90 phone and software + $250 advertising + $80 bookkeeping + $1,400 owner pay = $2,100 Each $150 job has $25 of variable supplies, card fees, and mileage, so contribution is: $150 - $25 = $125 Break-even for the month is: $2,100 ÷ $125 = 16.8 The owner needs 17 jobs per month to cover the listed fixed costs. With a $600 profit target: ($2,100 + $600) ÷ $125 = 21.6 That means 22 jobs per month . The $1,900 launch amount remains separate. Scenario 2: Two-person residential team This business hires one cleaner and buys a second equipment set. Its illustrative startup cash is: $500 registration and permits + $2,400 equipment + $600 initial supplies + $1,500 insurance deposits + $3,000 vehicle down payment + $900 website, uniforms, and setup = $8,900 Monthly fixed costs, including guaranteed wages, are: $650 vehicle payment + $500 insurance + $180 phones and software + $400 storage + $350 advertising + $2,400 guaranteed cleaner wages + $1,800 owner pay = $6,280 Assume the team completes jobs priced at $260. Variable cost per job is $50, including additional supplies, processing, and job-related travel. Contribution is: $260 - $50 = $210 The monthly break-even job count is: $6,280 ÷ $210 = 29.9047... Round up to 30 jobs per month . With a $1,500 profit target: ($6,280 + $1,500) ÷ $210 = 37.0476... The target is 38 jobs per month . Check whether two people can complete that volume in available working hours; a sales target above capacity is a scheduling problem, not a pricing solution. Scenario 3: Small commercial-cleaning launch This owner targets offices and small facilities, so the budget includes more equipment and a cash buffer: $600 registration and permits + $5,000 equipment + $1,200 initial supplies + $2,000 insurance deposits + $4,000 van down payment + $1,200 website, uniforms, and sales materials + $2,000 working-cash reserve = $16,000 Monthly fixed costs are: $900 van payment + $700 insurance + $250 storage + $200 phone and software + $700 sales and advertising + $4,200 scheduled labor + $2,500 owner pay = $9,450 Each $1,200 contract has $300 of supplies, travel, and transaction costs. Contribution is: $1,200 - $300 = $900 Break-even contracts are: $9,450 ÷ $900 = 10.5 The business needs 11 contracts per month for fixed costs. Add a $2,000 target profit: ($9,450 + $2,000) ÷ $900 = 12.7222... The target becomes 13 contracts per month . If clients pay on 30-day terms, model collection dates against wages, supplies, and vehicle bills before deciding whether the funding left after setup purchases covers that payment gap. See cleaning client-count and lead-demand example for lead assumptions. How to run your own numbers List one-time purchases separately from monthly fixed costs. Estimate the price and variable cost of one job or contract, add owner pay and a target profit if needed, then check the result against hours, crew, vehicles, and leads. MyBreakeven’s free cleaning business break-even calculator lets you test those assumptions, include owner salary and target profit, and use other currencies besides USD. Browse the MyBreakeven blogs for related planning topics. The calculator uses your assumptions; it is not a forecast or guarantee. Common mistakes Counting equipment twice. An initial $1,000 supply purchase belongs in startup cash; supplies used on jobs belong in variable cost. Treating both as fixed costs distorts break-even. Leaving owner pay out. Add planned owner compensation to the monthly amount the business must cover; otherwise “break-even” may mean you work for free. Using revenue instead of contribution. Subtract supplies, payment fees, mileage, subcontractor pay, and other job-level costs before dividing fixed costs by the result. Forgetting collection timing. A profitable contract can create a cash squeeze when payroll is weekly but the client pays 30 days after invoicing. Add that reserve to startup funding. Assuming every booked hour is sellable. Travel, estimates, supply runs, cancellations, and invoicing consume time. Check jobs against real team capacity. Treating target profit as earned cash. It is an added sales requirement, not money you can count before customers pay. Add a first-contract cash bridge to the startup purchase list A commercial contract can require payroll before the first customer payment. In a separate fictional launch test, wages and other cash payments are $700 at the end of each of four weeks; the first $3,600 customer payment arrives after week four. The maximum gap immediately before collection is $2,800. That amount is additional funding if it is not already covered by the reserve in your startup budget. First collection test, USD; no opening cash allocated Point in time Cumulative payments Customer collections Cumulative net cash End of week 1 700 0 −700 End of week 2 1,400 0 −1,400 End of week 3 2,100 0 −2,100 Week 4, before collection 2,800 0 −2,800 After first collection 2,800 3,600 800 The final $800 is not proof of net profit: this short bridge excludes other opening and overhead payments. Replace the terms and timing with the agreed contract and real payroll dates. Do not add $2,800 twice if your existing opening reserve already funds these exact payments. Pair the SBA startup-cost planning guidance expense split with the cleaning break-even guide for the separate recurring job target. Frequently asked questions Can I start a cleaning business with $1,000? Possibly, if you already own a vehicle and equipment, begin alone, and serve a narrow area. You still need registration, insurance, supplies, customer acquisition, and cash for slow weeks; $1,000 leaves little repair or payment-delay cushion. Is a cleaning business startup cost the same as the break-even point? No. Startup cost funds setup and the early gap. Break-even is the recurring sales level that covers monthly fixed costs after variable job costs are removed. Should cleaning supplies be a startup cost or a monthly expense? The first stock is a startup purchase. Supplies consumed on jobs are variable cost; a fixed restock can be split between a baseline amount and a per-job amount. Should I include my salary in cleaning-business break-even? Yes, if the business is expected to pay you. List planned owner pay as monthly fixed cost so the result does not assume you work for free. How many months of cash should I hold before opening? It depends on payment timing, personal runway, launch speed, and fixed costs. Build a monthly cash plan for purchases, collections, bills, payroll, taxes, repairs, and cancellations. Can a higher price lower the number of jobs I need? Yes, if customers accept it and extra labor, supplies, travel, and discounts do not consume the increase. A $180 job less $30 variable cost contributes $150; a $210 job less $35 contributes $175. Does the calculator work if I do not use dollars? Yes. It supports other currencies. Enter every price and cost in the same currency. ## Takeaways - Separate one-time startup cash from recurring monthly fixed costs before calculating sales needs. - Include owner pay in the monthly amount the business must cover. - Subtract variable job costs before using contribution to calculate break-even jobs. - Add a target profit only after you know the monthly fixed-cost requirement. - Check the required jobs or contracts against real hours, vehicles, crew capacity, and payment timing. Do I need to buy a vehicle before starting? Budget from the service area and equipment you actually need. An existing suitable vehicle and a new financed vehicle create different upfront and recurring costs. Check practical transport needs and obtain relevant quotes before adding a purchase to the plan. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Landscaping STARTUP COST GUIDE What Does It Cost to Start a Landscaping Business? Published September 18, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a landscaping startup budget from opening purchases, monthly costs and ramp cash needs. Compare slower sales, payment timing and worker capacity. Landscaping Startup Costs Break-Even Planning Landscaping owner reviewing startup costs and opening budget The maintenance business in this example needs $23,401 to open and cover its initial cash shortfall. That includes $19,000 of opening outlays, a $1,900 contingency and $2,501 to fund the assumed sales ramp. Your purchase list will change with the equipment you own and the services you offer. The more useful number is what remains in the bank after buying the tools, paying deposits and meeting bills before enough customer cash arrives. The USD amounts here are illustrative; replace each with a quote or your own payment schedule. Quick answer List each opening purchase, deposit and setup cost, then separate recurring monthly bills and job-level expenses. Estimate paid job contribution and the sales ramp. Calculate the deepest cumulative cash deficit during that ramp, add it to opening outlays and an explicit contingency, and check that the required jobs fit crew capacity. Replace every placeholder with scoped quotes and records. Choose the launch service before buying the equipment Write the first service list on one page. If you are starting with mowing and routine maintenance, separate the tools needed for those jobs from equipment you might want for installation work later. Buy for the booked service plan rather than letting a discounted equipment bundle expand the scope. Next, list what you already have and what is available to use reliably. An owned vehicle avoids a purchase payment today, but still needs fuel, maintenance and eventual replacement. A borrowed trailer may save opening cash while limiting which days you can work. Put that restriction into the schedule. For each new item, keep the quoted price, delivery cost, payment date and included accessories together. A mower price without the transport or preparation needed to put it to work is an incomplete cash estimate. Replace allowances with quoted amounts as you obtain them. The SBA startup-cost guide separates one-time and monthly expenses. Use those two groups for the first budget, then add a cash timeline. The landscaping figures below are an example of that process, not prices from the SBA. Avoid spending the reserve because the tools came in under budget. Check the ramp and payment dates first. A smaller opening purchase bill does not remove payroll, storage or the owner’s draw during a slow first month. Build the opening cash list The example business starts a maintenance service using an already owned towing vehicle. It needs the following additional cash before the first paid job: Opening item Fictional cash amount Mower $6,000 Trailer $3,000 Handheld tools $2,000 Safety equipment and work supplies $500 Setup, registration and local approvals allowance $500 Initial insurance and storage deposits $1,000 Website, branding and launch materials $1,000 Opening consumables $1,000 Other scoped transport and equipment preparation $4,000 Total opening cash outlay $19,000 The approval allowance is a placeholder, not a statement of local requirements or fees. Obtain the applicable information for your location and service scope. Deposits are shown because they use cash even when they are refundable or not an immediate accounting expense. Add a chosen 10% contingency on this opening list: $19,000 × 10% = $1,900. Ten percent is an illustrative choice, not a universal reserve rule. The contingency should address specified uncertainties and should not be confused with the operating cash required during the sales ramp. Keep monthly and job costs separate The example monthly fixed costs are $1,500, including the recurring items in the chosen plan. Owner pay is a separate $2,500 goal. The operating cash target before growth profit is therefore $4,000 per month. Any loan payment, tax cash reserve or additional commitment would need its own explicit cash-plan line; none is included in this simplified example. Each completed maintenance job sells for $180 and uses $10 materials, $50 paid direct labor, $20 other variable costs and $10 acquisition cost. A 3% payment fee adds $5.40. Contribution is $180 − $90 − $5.40 = $84.60 per completed job . This contribution is available for the monthly fixed-cost and owner-pay goal. It does not repay the $19,000 opening outlay automatically. If you want to recover that investment over a chosen period, model the additional monthly recovery goal separately and make clear that it is a planning target rather than an accounting expense. Opening consumables also need consistent treatment. In a cash plan, show when supplies are purchased. In the job model, show the cost of supplies used. Do not charge the entire opening stock again to the first month while also charging each job its consumed share in the same cash forecast. Calculate the sales-ramp cash requirement For this example, assume customer cash is collected in the month the job is completed and variable costs are paid in that same month. The first three months complete 25, 40 and 55 jobs respectively. Month Completed jobs Contribution Fixed costs plus owner pay Monthly cash change Cumulative cash change 1 25 $2,115 $4,000 −$1,885 −$1,885 2 40 $3,384 $4,000 −$616 −$2,501 3 55 $4,653 $4,000 $653 −$1,848 The deepest cumulative deficit is $2,501 , at the end of month two. That is the operating shortfall for this base ramp under same-month payment assumptions. Do not add the positive third month's cash change as another loss. A slower ramp of 20, 35 and 45 jobs gives contributions of $1,692, $2,961 and $3,807. Monthly changes are −$2,308, −$1,039 and −$193, creating a deepest cumulative deficit of $3,540 . The launch budget would then be $19,000 + $1,900 + $3,540 = $24,440 . For a third controlled case, keep the 25, 40 and 55 job ramp but use $75 contribution because job costs are higher. Monthly changes become −$2,125, −$1,000 and $125. The deepest cumulative deficit is $3,125, so the opening-plus-reserve total becomes $24,025. These scenarios show why the same equipment list can require different launch cash. Check payment timing before trusting the reserve The base ramp assumes prompt collection. If month-one customers pay in month two, the cash balance can fall further even though the completed-job contribution has not changed. Build a cash timeline with actual expected receipts and payment dates when work is invoiced after completion or suppliers require advance payment. The base launch total is therefore $19,000 opening cash + $1,900 contingency + $2,501 operating shortfall = $23,401 . That amount covers the stated base scenario, not every possible delayed receipt or interruption. Extend the monthly timeline and test actual payment delays before using it as a funding target. Any extra reserve should be shown as a chosen buffer with its purpose stated, rather than hidden inside the equipment estimate. Compare the required jobs with capacity At $84.60 contribution and a $4,000 monthly goal, required volume is $4,000 ÷ $84.60 = 47.28, rounded up to 48 jobs . One worker at 35 weekly hours and 70% utilization provides 106.17 delivery hours per month. At 1.5 worker-hours per completed job, capacity is 70 whole jobs. The base monthly goal fits this hour model, and the month-three 55-job ramp fits too. A fit does not establish demand. Travel, weather interruptions, access and scheduling must already be represented in the chosen job duration and utilization. If the service takes two hours instead, capacity falls to 53 whole jobs and the 55-job ramp becomes infeasible under the same hours. If you add $500 monthly target profit, the goal becomes $4,500 and requires 54 jobs. That result matters before buying equipment on the assumption that the business can recover its opening spending quickly. Check both the operating target and the additional goal you actually intend to pursue. Use the calculator for the operating plan Open the landscaping break-even calculator . Enter price $180, material cost $10, labor cost $50, other variable cost $20, acquisition cost $10 and payment fee 3%. Use fixed costs $1,500, owner pay $2,500 and target profit $0, with one worker, 35 weekly hours, 1.5 hours per job and 70% utilization. The result should show $84.60 contribution, 48 required jobs and 70 whole-job capacity. This tests ongoing operations. Keep the opening purchase list and cumulative cash timeline alongside it; the break-even result does not calculate deposits, equipment purchases or collection delays for you. Budget gaps to settle before launch Using equipment cost as the entire budget. Opening deposits and operating shortfalls also use cash. Treating existing assets as costless forever. Record their operating and replacement needs. Adding every monthly loss without a cumulative timeline. Use the deepest cumulative deficit and actual payment dates. Double-counting opening stock. Separate purchase cash from job-level consumption. Assuming profitable jobs guarantee a workable ramp. Check demand, collection timing and delivery hours together. Landscaping launch cash includes equipment and the wait for payment A fictional launch needs $9,000 equipment, $1,000 initial materials, $2,000 deposits and $3,000 working cash, totaling $15,000. This is an illustrative category exercise, not a typical industry startup budget. Truck ownership, hired equipment and supplier terms can materially change the actual amount. If a job leaves $250 contribution and monthly commitments total $5,000, operating break-even is 20 jobs. Customers paying after job completion can still create a funding gap before fuel, labor and materials are due. Put those payment dates in the cash schedule rather than assuming the twenty-job target pays every bill on time. Separate reusable equipment from materials consumed on each job. A rental cost for one assignment can be direct; a committed monthly lease may be overhead under the chosen boundary. Test crew worker-hours and seasonality alongside volume. The initial funding and operating target answer different questions and should not be merged into one unexplained cost-per-job number. Separate cash purchases from the value of equipment you own A launch budget should show what must actually be paid before customers pay you. In a separate fictional purchase list, required equipment and setup total $12,000 at quoted cash prices. Suitable equipment you already own accounts for $4,000 of that list, leaving $8,000 of new payments. Add an assumed $1,000 for immediate repairs and $3,000 for separately modeled launch cash needs: funding required is $12,000, not $16,000. Do not subtract equipment you own unless it meets the planned service and capacity requirements. Keep the asset inventory and replacement allowance alongside this cash view. Owned equipment still needs maintenance; its historical purchase price is not a new launch payment. Conversely, a loan approval does not pay a supplier until the funds are available. Record cash due dates before accepting work that needs rented machinery or materials bought ahead of customer payment. The SBA startup-cost planning guidance distinguishes one-time and monthly expenses; use the cash forecast to schedule your actual collections and payments. FAQs Can I start with equipment I already own? Yes, put any new cash needed to prepare it in the opening list. Then include its operating costs and a separate replacement plan rather than treating it as free to use indefinitely. Do deposits belong in the budget if I can get them back? Include them in opening cash because you have to pay them before using that money elsewhere. Keep refundable deposits separate from immediate operating expenses in the records. Why is the reserve $2,501 when month three makes money? The cumulative operating balance reaches its lowest point at the end of month two. The $653 increase in month three replenishes part of that deficit; it does not remove the need to fund the earlier low point. What if customers pay a month after the job? Move the expected receipt to its payment month while keeping payroll and supplier payments on their due dates. The cash low point can deepen even though each completed job still has the same contribution. How do I allow for recovering the opening investment? Choose a recovery period and show the resulting amount as an additional monthly planning goal. Keep it separate from the recurring bills so the operating break-even calculation remains understandable. Which purchase should I delay if the budget is tight? Review whether the item is needed to deliver the launch services and confirmed workload. Compare deferring, hiring or using existing equipment with the full cost and scheduling limits of each option. Does a profitable job eliminate the need for working cash? No. Supplier and labor payments can precede collection from the customer. Model dates and payment terms separately from the job's contribution. Takeaways Price the equipment needed for the launch services you actually plan to sell. Put deposits and payment dates in the opening cash list. Fund the lowest cumulative cash balance during the ramp. Check that the completed-job target fits worker-hours before adding a recovery goal. Continue with the landscaping equipment cost guide , landscaping seasonal break-even guide and landscaping break-even guide . Browse the business guides for more examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
