documents.text: E-commerce STARTUP COST GUIDE Ecommerce Startup Costs: New Store or Online Extension? Published September 18, 2026 Updated November 21, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build an online store startup budget for setup, stock and cash reserves. Compare an existing shop with a new store, platform billing and inventory payments. E-commerce Startup Costs Break-Even Planning How much does it cost to start an online store? Choose the launch model before comparing totals. Our fictional existing-shop extension needs $750 new setup spending plus a $765 modeled ramp shortfall: $1,515 before added contingency and changed payment timing. The separate new-store purchase list is $1,600 setup + $3,000 stock = $4,600 before its cash reserve. The second figure is an opening subtotal, not a fully funded alternative to the first. Ecommerce startup cost checklist: keep the cost and payment views separate Cost group Existing shop adding online sales New stock-holding store Website and setup Quote genuinely additional work; reuse suitable assets Quote platform setup, content, photography and equipment Opening inventory Already-owned stock is not new purchase cash; goods sold still have a cost Record the supplier payment and usable opening stock separately Monthly commitments Incremental $400 overhead + $500 separate owner-work target in the example Build an independent recurring budget; do not inherit a shop’s existing resources Cash reserve The $765 low point depends on the stated replenishment and collection timing Reconcile prepaid stock and actual payment dates before adding a reserve All dollars here are fictional assumptions. Check current platform billing and costs outside the subscription , then follow the stock and launch-cash reconciliation below. Choose the next practical step . E-commerce owner reviewing startup costs and opening budget Starting an ecommerce store needs a budget for setup purchases, the extra cost of fulfilling orders and cash for the first slow months. An existing physical shop can have a smaller additional cash requirement than a brand-new business because some stock, equipment and overhead are already in place. Our lean online-extension example needs $750 of one-time setup spending plus $765 to cover the deepest modeled operating shortfall: $1,515 before an additional chosen contingency. These are fictional USD assumptions, not a typical launch price or a complete quote for your store. Quick answer Separate one-time launch spending from recurring overhead and costs per completed order. For an existing shop, identify which resources are already paid for and which online costs are genuinely additional. Forecast the early sales ramp and cumulative shortfall. Keep stock purchases and payment dates in a cash schedule rather than treating operating break-even as the entire startup budget. What does the platform price leave out? Pricing rechecked November 21, 2026: Shopify’s US pricing page lists Basic at $39 USD per month on monthly billing, or a $29 monthly equivalent with yearly billing. The annual equivalent is not a promise of a $29 month-to-month payment. Check billing commitment, taxes, location and current checkout terms. That subscription is not a complete startup budget. Quote the domain and renewal, optional theme or development work, product photos, apps, opening inventory, inbound freight, packing equipment and launch marketing. Then list recurring subscriptions and order-linked payment, fulfillment, shipping and returns costs separately. The $400 monthly overhead in our example is a fictional combined allowance, not a Shopify fee. For each item record supplier, scope, amount, payment date, renewal basis and whether it is already owned . Compare a stock-holding launch with made-to-order or dropshipping by collection and supplier-payment dates, not by assuming that no inventory means no cash need. The return-cost guide and cash forecast cover two commitments that a website setup quote can miss. Make two budgets before buying anything The first budget asks what cash the launch needs. It includes actual new purchases, deposits, setup work and payment dates. The second asks whether completed orders can cover recurring expenses and your chosen owner compensation. You need both. A cheap platform setup can lead to an expensive fulfillment operation. Conversely, a business can have positive contribution on every order while needing cash to pay for stock long before customers buy it. The SBA startup-cost guidance recommends identifying startup expenses and distinguishing one-time and ongoing costs. The numbers below are independent illustrative budgets. Replace each amount with your own quote, account record or explicit assumption. Keep a note beside every line showing when it is paid and what it covers. “Marketing $500” is ambiguous: does that buy setup work, monthly advertising or acquisition across a defined number of orders? Assign it to one treatment so the same spending is not entered three times. An existing shop adding online orders Suppose a shop already owns $2,000 of suitable stock and has a computer and packing bench. The following launch budget includes only its genuinely new online setup purchases: New one-time purchase Cash amount Store setup work $300 Product photography for the launch range $250 Small shipping-label printer $200 Total new setup spending $750 The existing stock is not another $2,000 launch cash payment. However, products sold online still have a cost and must eventually be replenished. Being already owned does not make that stock free in the order-profit calculation. The example assumes replacement stock and packing materials are paid for as orders ship. That makes the operating shortfall an approximate cash requirement under these stated dates. If you instead buy a large stock batch or packing supply upfront, build the actual cash schedule and remove duplicated payments from the ramp calculation. Monthly additional overhead is $400 for the online extension. Existing shop costs stay in the original shop budget for this incremental view. A separate whole-business check should include the full rent, committed payroll and other obligations when you judge overall viability. The owner assigns another $500 monthly pay to the additional online work. That is a budgeting choice. Do not add it if the same work is already fully compensated in an unchanged owner-pay plan; instead explain how the added workload will be handled. What one completed order contributes Online order input Amount Average modeled order revenue $50 Product cost $20 Packing materials $2 Paid direct fulfillment labor $4 Shipping paid by the store $6 Acquisition per completed order $5 Payment fee 3% Here the $4 labor pays a helper, while monthly owner pay covers separate owner work. The fee is $1.50, so contribution is $50 − $20 − $2 − $4 − $6 − $5 − $1.50 = $11.50 per order . The modeled revenue is consistent with shipping: any amount charged to the customer for shipping must be included if it is part of the price on which these costs and fees are calculated. Taxes collected for another party are excluded from this simplified revenue figure. The $900 combined overhead-and-owner-pay requirement needs $900 ÷ $11.50 = 78.26, rounded up to 79 orders . Adding a $200 profit goal raises the requirement to $1,100 ÷ $11.50 = 95.65, rounded up to 96 orders . At 96 orders, contribution is $1,104 and profit after the additional owner pay is $204. This is the online extension's modeled operating surplus. It does not automatically pay back launch purchases or establish that the entire physical shop is profitable. Budget for the sales ramp Assume orders gradually increase while monthly overhead and additional owner pay remain $900. The reserve calculation uses operating shortfalls without the optional $200 profit goal, because that goal is a desired surplus rather than a required payment. Month Orders Contribution Operating balance Cumulative balance 1 30 $345 −$555 −$555 2 60 $690 −$210 −$765 3 100 $1,150 $250 −$515 The deepest cumulative shortfall is $765 after month two. New setup spending of $750 plus that modeled reserve gives $1,515 . The month-three surplus starts rebuilding cash; it does not remove the need to fund the earlier low point. This is a lower-bound planning example under its payment assumptions. A contingency, stock purchase, processor payout delay or supplier deposit can raise the cash need. Identify those items rather than presenting $1,515 as a universal startup cost. If the ramp is slower at 20, 40 and 70 orders, operating balances become −$670, −$440 and −$95. The cumulative low point is $1,205, so setup plus modeled reserve becomes $1,955 . None of those volumes is a demand forecast; they are scenarios to replace with your own evidence. Compare another launch model A new business cannot assume it already owns the shop's resources. Suppose it spends $1,600 on setup and equipment and commits $3,000 to an opening stock purchase. That is $4,600 before any operating reserve, but the stock payment must be handled correctly. If you use an accrual contribution model that deducts product cost as sales occur, the separate cash schedule must recognize when the inventory was paid for. Do not add the full stock purchase and then assume every product-cost expense is another identical cash payment during the same period. A preorder or made-to-order model has different collection and supplier timing. It may reduce inventory held, but it does not eliminate customer-service work, supplier risk or fulfillment costs. Write those dates and commitments before comparing it with an in-stock launch. For a small test, launch a narrow range you can cost and fulfill consistently. Keep a real record of order revenue, payment fees, packing time, shipping and unrecovered return losses. Expand the budget after the test rather than spreading an assumed average across products you have not shipped. Check whether your team can fulfill the target For the incremental online work, one worker provides ten hours per week at 75% delivery utilization. That gives 32.5 monthly worker-hours using 52 ÷ 12 weeks. At 0.3 worker-hours per order, capacity is 108 whole orders , so the 96-order goal fits the assumption. If order handling rises to 0.4 hours, capacity falls to 81. The $200 profit goal then does not fit. Packing, customer messages and dispatch preparation must be included in your time definition, with the same team-hours counted once. The ecommerce shipping guide helps identify the full parcel cost. Use the return-cost guide for losses that remain after refunds and recovered stock, and the product-pricing guide for the selling-price decision. Complete the online-store launch checklist before spending Keep one dated record for each launch assumption. Mark it quoted, paid or still estimated; a tick alone does not prove the cost or demand. The same stock purchase, owner wage or marketing payment must appear only once in its cash category. Evidence and cash treatment for a small ecommerce launch Check Evidence to retain Where it belongs Product and supplier Sample approval, unit quote, minimum order, delivery and payment dates Product cost in contribution; actual stock payment in dated cash Existing stock Counted usable units and their cost, separate from new purchases Opening inventory; not a second new cash purchase Platform and setup Current plan quote, setup scope, renewal date and transaction terms One-time setup versus recurring overhead, with percentage fees separate Fulfillment and returns Packaging, carrier, paid handling time, returns policy and recovery assumptions Order-driven costs, with returns deducted once on the stated revenue basis Customer test Paid test orders, actual checkout amount, completed shipments and attributable ad spend Evidence for a volume assumption; abandoned carts are not completed sales Collections Processor settlement dates, reserves, refund deductions and bank receipts Dated customer cash, separate from earned sales Owner and team Paid hours, delivery time, owner-compensation boundary and capacity Labor and owner pay counted once; completed orders must fit available hours Launch funding Opening purchases, the deepest dated shortfall, chosen reserve and confirmed funding source Funding requirement; a loan application is not confirmed cash Calculate the launch funding gap Use the business startup cost calculator to separate launch payments, already-paid amounts, early trading shortfalls, a chosen reserve and cash available now. The online-store preset uses its own fictional $4,600 launch budget; it does not import this guide's figures. Replace the preset with your quoted costs and settlement assumptions, then use the dated forecast to test actual due dates. Run the dated launch cash check Carry the actual payment and collection dates into the 13-week cash forecast . Enter the operating shortfalls and purchase dates without duplicating stock payments. Check a completed period with the net cash flow calculator . For the full narrative and inventory/settlement model, use the ecommerce business plan template . Opening these tools does not transfer this guide's inputs. For the existing extension example, $750 new setup spending plus a $765 deepest modeled ramp deficit gives $1,515 before additional contingency, upfront stock or payout delays. Keep that limited example separate from a new store with $4,600 opening purchases. Rebuild the dated forecast whenever supplier or processor timing changes. How to run your own numbers Open the ecommerce break-even calculator and enter price $50, materials $20, labor $4, other variable costs $8 for packing and shipping, acquisition $5 and fees 3%. Set fixed costs $400, owner pay $500 and target profit $200. Use one worker, ten weekly hours, 75% utilization and 0.3 hours per order. The calculator should show 96 required orders and 108 whole-order capacity. Keep the $750 setup spending and dated cash ramp outside recurring overhead. Cost Builder can help separate packing, labor and other order costs before applying them. Other currencies are supported. Common mistakes Treating existing stock as another new purchase, or as free goods sold. Counting setup marketing and acquisition spending twice. Paying the same owner hours through direct labor and owner pay. Adding a whole stock purchase to a cash reserve that already pays for those goods again. Treating a profit goal as an unavoidable reserve payment. Assuming platform setup is the complete online-launch cost. FAQs Is an online extension cheaper than a new store? It can need less additional cash when stock and equipment already exist. Include all genuinely new expenses and check the whole business separately. Resources you already own still have operating and replacement costs. Should I include my existing rent? Include it in a whole-business viability model. For an incremental online-extension budget, include the rent increase or additional space cost caused by the launch. State which view you are using so rent is not silently omitted from the business as a whole. Where does the opening stock purchase belong? It belongs in the cash schedule on its payment date. Goods sold still need a cost in the contribution model. Reconcile the two views so you do not count the same purchase twice as cash leaving the business. Why is the operating reserve $765? That is the deepest cumulative deficit in the 30, 60 and 100-order ramp. Month three adds $250 back after the earlier shortfalls. Payment delays and a chosen contingency would need additional modeling. Does the calculator include launch purchases? Its monthly model covers contribution, recurring expenses, owner pay, profit goals and capacity. Keep one-time purchases and cash timing in a separate launch schedule. Do not paste every opening purchase into monthly overhead. Can I use another currency? Yes, the calculator supports other currencies. Keep revenue and costs in the same currency and use your own current supplier and shipping amounts. The USD examples here are illustrations rather than local price quotes. Takeaways Separate launch cash from monthly operating viability. Define whether you are modeling an extension or the whole business. Count existing stock cost when sold without duplicating its cash payment. Fund the deepest ramp shortfall and check fulfillment hours. Explore the business planning guides for more startup examples. New online-store example: reconcile prepaid inventory and reserve This independent fictional case extends the $4,600 purchase list. Its $3,000 stock payment buys 150 units at $20 each before launch; setup is $1,600. Assume one unit per $50 order, $18.50 other cash cost per order, and $900 combined monthly commitments ($400 overhead + $500 for the separately defined owner work). The $18.50 is $2 packing + $4 helper labor + $6 shipping + $5 acquisition + $1.50 payment fee. None includes another stock purchase. Test a slower launch with zero, 30 and 60 completed orders. Assume receipts and the specified operating payments occur in the same month, no additional inventory is bought in these three months, no refunds and no other cash movements. These are monthly scenarios, not an intramonth payment calendar or demand forecast. Independent new-store cash reconciliation, USD; opening stock already paid Month Orders / receipts Non-stock order cash Monthly commitments Cash movement after opening purchases 1 0 / $0 $0 $900 −$900 2 30 / $1,500 $555 $900 +$45 3 60 / $3,000 $1,110 $900 +$990 Cumulative operating cash is −$900, −$855 and +$135. The month-end low point is $900, so $4,600 purchases + $900 modeled operating buffer = $5,500 before contingency, minimum cash balance, intramonth gaps or excluded payments. The opening purchase and later product expense are different views: 90 units sold use $1,800 stock, leaving 60 units costing $1,200. That $1,800 is not a second cash payment in this case. The matching operating contribution view is $0, $345 and $690; after $900 monthly commitments, results are −$900, −$555 and −$210. Its $1,665 cumulative operating deficit differs from the $900 cash low point because inventory was prepaid. Do not add the whole $1,665 as new stock cash on top of a budget that already paid for those goods. Replace the timing assumptions with your real supplier, processor and refund dates before relying on a funding figure. Use the startup cost calculator for funding categories, the dated cash forecast for timing, and the ecommerce business-plan resource for the complete launch plan. Keep the ecommerce break-even calculator focused on monthly order economics. For choosing between sales channels, use marketplace versus own-store contribution rather than turning this startup budget into a channel comparison. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency STARTUP COST GUIDE How Much Does It Cost to Start a Marketing Agency? Published September 18, 2026 Updated November 21, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a marketing agency startup budget from setup purchases, monthly costs and a cash reserve. Compare solo and team examples, owner pay and client targets. Agency Startup Costs Break-Even Planning Marketing agency startup costs: separate three budgets There is no single startup price for every marketing agency. The fictional solo launch list below totals $3,200 before operating reserve. Its separate monthly commitments, including $4,000 owner pay, total $5,450. At a 90% contribution margin, required monthly sales are approximately $6,055.56, displayed as $6,056 in whole dollars. Setup cash does not include that month’s costs or prove that clients will arrive. Existing fictional USD examples; launch purchases exclude a cash reserve Operating model One-time launch list Monthly commitments including owner pay Contribution ratio Whole-dollar monthly sales requirement Solo specialist $2,500 $3,820 95% $4,022 One employee and workspace $6,300 $14,150 80% $17,688 Remote full-service $4,500 $6,120 85% $7,200 Choose the next practical step . Agency owner reviewing startup costs and opening budget Build two itemized cost lists and a dated launch cash forecast. The worked budgets below show different service and staffing assumptions; none establishes a typical market startup price. Quote purchases and recurring commitments for your own location and scope. The direct answer, expanded There are two numbers to plan. Startup cash pays for launch items. Break-even revenue pays the bills every month. Mixing them does not tell you whether the agency can support you after launch. Here is an illustrative solo-agency budget in USD. These figures are examples, not market statistics. One-time startup costs Illustrative startup budget (USD) Item Cost Business registration and basic legal setup $250 Brand, website setup, and copy $900 Laptop and monitor $1,400 Initial templates, stock assets, and onboarding materials $350 Launch sales materials and sample campaigns $300 Total one-time startup cost $3,200 That $3,200 is the cash needed for this launch list. It does not include an emergency fund or operating reserve. Those are funding needs, not recurring break-even expenses. Recurring monthly fixed costs Illustrative monthly budget (USD) Item Monthly cost Software subscriptions $220 Phone and internet $140 Insurance $110 Coworking desk $300 Bookkeeping $180 Owner pay $4,000 Ongoing sales and marketing $500 Monthly fixed-cost total $5,450 Assume this agency keeps 90% of sales after variable delivery costs. Its contribution margin is 0.90. The break-even calculation is: $5,450 ÷ 0.90 = $6,055.56 Rounded up, the agency needs $6,056 in monthly revenue to cover the listed fixed costs and owner pay. If the owner also wants a $1,000 monthly profit target, the calculation becomes: ($5,450 + $1,000) ÷ 0.90 = $7,166.67 The target is then $7,167 per month . That is a planning target, not a promise. It depends on the assumptions holding and on having enough capacity and qualified leads. For owner-pay planning, see agency profit and owner-pay guide . A lower draw reduces the target. Unpaid owner labor can make a business appear to break even when your work is missing from the cost base. What changes the answer Your delivery model changes variable costs. An agency that buys media or hires specialists on every project may keep less of each sales dollar than a strategy-and-reporting agency. A 90% margin and a 70% margin produce different targets even when fixed costs match. Owner pay changes the monthly number directly. If you need $5,000 per month, include $5,000. If you can draw $2,500 while building a client base, use that figure and label it. Do not hide pay under “profit.” Team size changes cash needs and capacity. A two-person agency may need payroll, contractor deposits, more software seats, and enough work to keep both people productive. Salaries may be fixed, while project-based contractors can be variable. Location and workspace affect fixed overhead. A home office may remove a desk payment but not insurance, equipment, or internet. An office adds rent, utilities, deposits, furniture, and commuting time. Treat the deposit as one-time cash and rent as recurring. Sales timing affects startup funding. An agency can sign a project and still face a cash gap if the client pays in 30 days while payroll is due sooner. That gap is separate from break-even. See cash-flow forecasting and payment timing . Capacity sets a ceiling on the target. If your target requires eight retainers but you can service only five, the arithmetic is not a plan. Count strategy, meetings, revisions, reporting, and sales hours first. Three realistic worked scenarios All figures below are illustrative USD examples. Each scenario separates one-time launch cash from the monthly revenue target. 1. Lean solo specialist A solo paid-search specialist works from home and uses contractors only when needed. One-time costs are registration ($150), a simple website and portfolio ($700), a laptop ($1,200), templates and training materials ($250), and launch outreach ($200): $150 + $700 + $1,200 + $250 + $200 = $2,500 Monthly fixed costs are software ($180), phone and internet ($100), insurance ($90), bookkeeping ($150), owner pay ($3,000), and sales activity ($300): $180 + $100 + $90 + $150 + $3,000 + $300 = $3,820 Suppose variable costs leave a 95% contribution margin. Break-even sales are: $3,820 ÷ 0.95 = $4,021.05 The owner needs $4,022 per month to cover the listed costs. For an $800 profit target: ($3,820 + $800) ÷ 0.95 = $4,863.16 The target becomes $4,864 per month . At a $1,200 retainer, that means four clients for break-even and five for the profit target. 2. Small agency with an employee This agency has an owner, one full-time employee, a workspace, and more software seats. One-time costs are legal setup ($600), website and brand ($1,800), two computers ($2,800), furniture ($600), and launch advertising ($500): $600 + $1,800 + $2,800 + $600 + $500 = $6,300 Monthly fixed costs are software ($420), phone and internet ($200), insurance ($180), workspace ($900), bookkeeping ($250), owner pay ($5,000), employee salary ($6,000), and sales ($1,200): $420 + $200 + $180 + $900 + $250 + $5,000 + $6,000 + $1,200 = $14,150 If contractor and payment costs leave an 80% contribution margin, monthly break-even sales are: $14,150 ÷ 0.80 = $17,687.50 Rounded up, the agency needs $17,688 per month . Add a $2,500 profit target: ($14,150 + $2,500) ÷ 0.80 = $20,812.50 The target becomes $20,813 per month . Five $3,500 retainers produce $17,500: $187.50 below the exact $17,687.50 sales threshold. At 80% contribution, they leave $14,000 against $14,150 commitments, a $150 shortfall. Six whole retainers are needed under these assumptions. 3. Remote full-service agency This remote agency avoids office rent but carries a larger owner draw and software stack. One-time costs are legal setup ($400), site work ($1,200), a laptop ($1,800), portfolio production ($400), and launch ads ($700): $400 + $1,200 + $1,800 + $400 + $700 = $4,500 Monthly fixed costs are software ($350), phone and internet ($120), insurance ($150), owner pay ($4,500), sales ($800), and bookkeeping ($200): $350 + $120 + $150 + $4,500 + $800 + $200 = $6,120 At an 85% contribution margin: $6,120 ÷ 0.85 = $7,200 Break-even is $7,200 per month . With a $1,500 profit target: ($6,120 + $1,500) ÷ 0.85 = $8,964.71 Rounded up, the revenue target is $8,965 per month . Its sales target still depends on the owner's $4,500 pay and available delivery capacity. How to run your own numbers Start with two lists. Put registration, equipment, deposits, branding, and launch materials in the one-time list. Put monthly software, insurance, rent, payroll, owner pay, and sales costs in the recurring list. Estimate contribution margin after costs that rise with each sale, then add target profit. Enter those assumptions in the agency break-even calculator . It supports other currencies and lets you test owner salary, target profit, sales volume, and team capacity without treating the result as a forecast. For related planning topics, the MyBreakeven blog has more articles on pricing, capacity, and break-even planning. Common mistakes Counting the laptop twice. A laptop bought before launch belongs in one-time startup costs. Use a monthly replacement or financing cost only if one actually applies. Calling client ad spend fixed when it is not. If you pass through $2,000 of media spend and collect $2,000, that revenue does not create $2,000 of contribution. Put the spend in variable costs or model the fee separately. Leaving owner labor at zero. A business that covers subscriptions while the owner works unpaid has not shown that it can support the owner. Add the draw you need, even if you phase it in over time. Using listed package prices as revenue. A $2,000 package may produce less after fees, subcontractors, refunds, or discounts. Calculate from the amount retained, not the headline price. Ignoring payment timing. Break-even can say a month works while the bank account is short because invoices are collected later. Keep a separate cash cushion for deposits, tax payments, payroll timing, and slow-paying clients. Assuming more clients fit automatically. If each retainer requires 15 hours and you have 100 service hours, six retainers use 90 hours. A seventh may push deadlines past your capacity. Turn the purchase list into a funded launch Mark each purchase as already owned, needed before the first client, or deferrable. Removing an already-owned $1,400 computer from the separate $3,200 worked launch list reduces new purchase cash to $1,800; it does not remove future replacement needs. These examples are selected budgets, not minimum investment figures or market averages. Replace every line with your own quote and document the included scope. Next map payment dates and realistic client receipts in a cash forecast . Add funding for the deepest modeled cash deficit and a separately chosen contingency; do not count the same payroll or owner withdrawal twice. Test recurring client requirements with the agency calculator , price the scope with retainer pricing , and check billable delivery capacity . A sales threshold is not a bookings forecast. Frequently asked questions Is $5,000 enough to start a marketing agency? It can cover a lean, home-based solo agency with existing equipment and a narrow offer. It may not cover a team, office deposit, or operating reserve. Build the one-time list first, then set a separate reserve. Should owner salary count as a startup cost? Owner salary is normally a recurring monthly fixed cost, not a one-time setup purchase. Include it in break-even if the business must pay you. If you need cash to live before clients pay, that is an additional funding requirement during the startup period. What if I have no clients yet? Calculate a required sales target from planned costs and margin. Translate it into clients, projects, or leads using price and close rate. It shows what must happen, not whether sales will arrive. Are freelancers fixed or variable costs? Classify the cost by its behavior. A contractor paid only for a particular project is usually variable; a monthly retainer is closer to fixed. Split the two when you use both. Do I need to include taxes in break-even? Include business taxes or provisions in your plan, but label the assumption. Personal tax treatment varies by structure and location, so ask an accountant how to model it. How much cash should I keep after paying startup costs? There is no single correct reserve. List payment dates, expected client receipts, and your minimum draw. The gap, plus a delay buffer, is a cash-funding question rather than part of monthly break-even. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Cleaning BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE How Much to Charge for House Cleaning Published September 17, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Price house cleaning from cleaner-hours, scope, fees and overhead. Compare hourly and flat quotes, then verify your monthly job target in the calculator. Cleaning Pricing Profit Planning House cleaning professional reviewing service costs and pricing assumptions A workable house-cleaning price starts with your cost per job, not a competitor’s menu. Add loaded labor, supplies, travel, payment fees, and a share of monthly overhead, then leave room for profit and the owner’s pay. The example below is for planning, not a market quote; your city, service level, crew speed, and customers will change the answer. Before publishing a rate, test it against a slower month because a full calendar can hide a price that fails when bookings soften. Quick answer: For a standard recurring clean, calculate the job’s labor and other variable costs, add an allocation for monthly overhead, and divide by one minus your target margin. For example, $156 of total cost at a 30% target margin produces a price of about $223. Charge more when the home takes longer, carries extra risk, or requires add-on work. The direct answer, expanded There is no single correct house-cleaning rate. A useful starting price pays for the job’s hours and contributes toward costs that continue when no cleaner is at a property. Use this calculation: Price = (direct job costs + overhead allocated to the job) ÷ (1 − target operating margin) Direct job costs include cleaner wages and payroll burden, products, mileage, disposal, and any fixed per-job fee. Treat a percentage card fee separately because it changes with the final quote. Overhead includes insurance, software, phone service, storage, advertising, and your administrative time. If you clean personally, include the pay you need for those hours; otherwise, a low price can look profitable only because your labor is free. Here is a full example for a recurring three-bedroom clean. Two cleaners spend two hours at the home, so the job uses four labor-hours. Assume the loaded labor cost is $24 per labor-hour, supplies cost $12, and travel costs $8. Labor: 4 hours × $24 = $96 Supplies: $12 Travel: $8 Direct job cost: $96 + $12 + $8 = $116 Monthly fixed overhead: $1,200 Planned jobs this month: 30 Overhead per job: $1,200 ÷ 30 = $40 Total cost before profit: $116 + $40 = $156 This first example assumes no additional percentage payment fee. If the target operating margin is 30%, divide $156 by 0.70. The result is $222.86 , so a practical posted price is $223 . At that price, the contribution after direct costs is $223 − $116 = $107 . After the $40 overhead allocation, about $67 remains for operating profit or additional owner compensation. That method is safer than copying a local rate. A competitor may have a faster crew, lower rent, different insurance, or a price that excludes supplies and travel. Their number does not tell you whether the job works for your business. For hourly billing, estimate labor-hours, multiply by your loaded rate, and state what is included. For a flat rate, convert that estimate into a clear scope: rooms, bathrooms, appliances, pet hair, and home condition. Turn a walkthrough into a flat quote The base guide shows how a standard clean should cover costs. For a home you have not cleaned before, write the scope before you choose a flat fee: rooms, bathrooms, condition, floor types, access, pets, equipment you bring and requested extras. Then estimate paid cleaner-hours , not just the time on a wall clock. Two cleaners on-site for three hours each consume six paid hours. These example amounts are assumptions for one inspected recurring clean, not a rate for any US city. Quote input Illustrative cost Two cleaners × three hours each × $28 fully loaded per paid hour $168 Supplies and laundry $18 Job-specific travel $22 Share of monthly overhead and owner administration $60 Cost before percentage payment fee $268 Suppose payment fees are 3% of the final collected price and the business wants a 25% operating margin on that price after all the listed costs. Let the price be P. The equation is P − 0.03P − $268 = 0.25P , so 0.72P = $268 and P = $372.22. A $373 quote yields about $11.19 in fees and $93.81 after the stated costs, or a 25.15% margin. At $370, the result is $90.90 / $370 = 24.57%. This calculation shows why adding 25% to $268 would miss a 25% margin target. Confirm the quoted scope and any change triggers in writing. If a home needs extra degreasing, heavy buildup removal or a second visit, price those as approved additions rather than silently stretching a standard clean. Compare the estimated six cleaner-hours with actual time after the first visit and update future quotes. For a one-off renovation cleanup with dust stages and punch-list returns, use the post-construction estimate guide ; it answers a different scope question. The cleaning monthly-expenses guide helps verify the $60 allocation against a realistic booking count. Hourly or flat-rate: choose from the job scope Choose a quote method before publishing a price Method Useful situation What the quote must explain Hourly Uncertain first-clean condition Rate per cleaner-hour, expected range and approval for extra time. Flat per visit Inspected recurring scope with measured time Included tasks, exclusions and changes that trigger a new quote. Room or area basis Comparable properties with consistent condition Size alone does not capture bathrooms, buildup or travel. Jobber's cleaning pricing guide discusses these billing structures. It does not determine what your crew should charge. Check your own labor-hours and costs before using any advertised range. For US customers, describe the home size and scope in the quote. In other markets, labels such as domestic cleaning, fortnightly service or end-of-tenancy cleaning may describe similar work with different inclusions. Confirm those inclusions and use local costs; USD, GBP, CAD and AUD are currency labels, not exchange-rate conversions. Percentage-fee pricing: price = cost before the percentage fee ÷ (1 − fee rate − target margin). The denominator must be positive. This is a cost-based quote check, not evidence that customers will accept the price. The margin-versus-markup guide explains why adding a percentage to cost gives a different result. What changes the answer Labor time and crew size move the price fastest. Two cleaners working for two hours consume four labor-hours, not two. Track actual time. If a “two-hour clean” routinely takes 2.75 hours, your original price is missing 37.5% more labor than planned. The condition and scope of the home matter. A recurring clean after a customer has maintained the home is different from a first-time deep clean. Heavy buildup, oven work, blinds, pet hair, and move-out disposal add time or supplies. Put those items on an add-on list instead of quietly absorbing them. Location changes travel cost and usable capacity. A distant job may add only $6 in fuel but consume an hour that could have been spent cleaning. Group nearby appointments, set a service radius, or charge a travel fee when the route makes the job uneconomic. Team structure changes both cost and throughput. A two-person crew may finish a home sooner on the clock, but it still uses the combined labor-hours. Check whether the team can complete the jobs assumed in your overhead allocation. Payment fees and taxes can reduce the money left over. Include processor fees before judging margin. Keep sales tax separate when collected for a government authority; it is not operating revenue. Frequency and cancellation risk affect the price. Weekly or biweekly service may require less reset time than a one-off clean. A recurring customer can still cancel, so do not rely on every appointment repeating forever. For related planning, use the cleaning business startup costs and cleaning business profit calculations . Those topics help separate the cash needed to open from the monthly costs your pricing must cover. Worked pricing and operating scenarios These invented figures show the arithmetic; they are not claims about prevailing prices. Scenario 1: Solo cleaner with recurring clients You work alone and expect 20 jobs in a month. A recurring job takes three hours. Loaded labor is $26 per hour, supplies cost $10, and travel costs $7. Monthly fixed overhead is $900. Labor: 3 × $26 = $78 Supplies and travel: $10 + $7 = $17 Direct cost: $78 + $17 = $95 Overhead allocation: $900 ÷ 20 = $45 Total cost: $95 + $45 = $140 For a 25% target margin, calculate $140 ÷ 0.75 = $186.67 . Quote $187 and review it after tracking real job time. At $187, the amount left after direct costs and allocated overhead is $187 − $95 − $45 = $47 , which is close to 25% of the rounded price. Scenario 2: Two-person team doing a deep clean A two-person team spends 3.5 hours at a first-time home, or seven labor-hours. Loaded labor is $25 per hour, supplies are $20, travel is $15, and overhead allocation is $60. Assume card processing is 3% of the selling price and the target margin is 30%. Before the percentage fee, cost is $175 labor + $20 supplies + $15 travel + $60 overhead = $270 . Because the fee and target margin are both percentages of price, solve the price as $270 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.30), or $270 ÷ 0.67 = $402.99 . Quote $403 . The card fee is $403 × 0.03 = $12.09 ; total cost is $270 + $12.09 = $282.09 , leaving $403 − $282.09 = $120.91 , or about 30% of the price. Scenario 3: Move-out clean with disposal Three cleaners spend four hours on a move-out job, using 12 labor-hours. Loaded labor is $25 per hour. Supplies cost $28, travel costs $18, disposal costs $12, and overhead allocation is $60. With a 3% card fee and a 28% target margin, the pre-fee cost is: $300 labor + $28 supplies + $18 travel + $12 disposal + $60 overhead = $418. The price is $418 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.28) = $418 ÷ 0.69 = $605.80 . Quote $606 . The card fee is $606 × 0.03 = $18.18 , so total cost is $418 + $18.18 = $436.18 . The remaining $169.82 is approximately 28% of $606. If the property is unusually dirty, revise the labor estimate before accepting it. How to run your own numbers List one representative job, then enter labor-hours, loaded labor cost, supplies, travel, fees, monthly fixed costs, expected jobs, owner salary, and desired profit. Test your expected volume and a slower month; capacity matters if your price assumes more work than your team can deliver. MyBreakeven supports USD and other currencies and runs privately in your browser. Use the cleaning business break-even calculator to run your assumptions. Your number is different because your route, crew, scope, and overhead are different. The calculator is a planning tool based on those inputs, not a prediction or a guarantee. Reproduce the cleaning calculator example This is an actual MyBreakeven calculator demonstration captured on October 12, 2026, using illustrative USD inputs. It is not a customer case study, an industry average or a prediction. Open the calculator linked under “How to run your own numbers”, choose Reset example , and compare every input with the table. If presets change later, enter these values manually. Inputs used for the captured demonstration (USD amounts; other units are in the field labels) Calculator field Value Average price per job ($) 180 Materials / product cost per job ($) 18 Direct labor per job ($) 58 Travel + equipment use per job ($) 12 Lead generation cost per booked job ($) 10 Monthly operating overhead ($) 3,200 Monthly owner pay ($) 4,500 Target monthly profit ($) 1,000 Payment and platform fees (%) 2.9 Active team members 3 Hours per team member / week (hrs) 35 Delivery hours per job (hrs) 3.5 Productive utilization (%) 75 Inquiry-to-job conversion (%) 30 The percentage fee is calculated from price. $180 × 2.9% = $5.22; contribution is $180 − $18 − $58 − $12 − $10 − $5.22 = $76.78. Verified output from the same inputs Result Value Monthly amount to cover $8,700.00 Exact required volume 113.31 jobs Whole-unit target 114 jobs Sales at whole-unit target $20,520.00 Whole-unit delivery capacity 97 jobs Inquiries for whole-unit target 380 Actual calculator screen, October 12, 2026. The displayed amounts come from the illustrative inputs above. The monthly target requires 114 jobs, but the modeled team can deliver only 97 whole jobs. The 17-job gap means this plan needs a change in price, scope, costs or productive hours. Adding hours can also add wages; update both fields together. A full booking calendar cannot close a workload gap by itself. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 ÷ 12 × productive utilization ÷ worker-hours per job. Required volume rounds up; deliverable volume rounds down. Owner pay and the extra profit goal are included in this target. Set both to zero only when checking overhead-only operating break-even. Common mistakes Quoting from the clock instead of labor-hours. A two-person crew working two hours has four labor-hours. Multiplying only the elapsed time by one cleaner’s rate cuts the labor cost in half. Using wage instead of loaded labor cost. Payroll taxes, workers’ compensation, paid training, and non-cleaning paid time can sit outside the wage number. If those costs are real, include them in the hourly cost used in the quote. Treating the first clean as a recurring clean. Initial buildup often takes longer. Write a separate first-clean or deep-clean scope so the recurring price is not forced to subsidize it. Forgetting payment fees before comparing prices. A $200 card sale at a 3% fee leaves $194 before other costs. Comparing that net amount with a competitor’s advertised cash price creates a false margin comparison. Dividing overhead by an optimistic job count. If $1,200 of monthly overhead is divided by 30 jobs but you usually complete 20, the allocation is understated by $20 per job ($60 versus $40). Price from a realistic schedule, then test what happens if bookings fall. Leaving owner work out of the model. Scheduling, quoting, supply runs, and cleaning are all time. Decide whether the price is meant to pay you for those hours, produce profit after your pay, or both, and label the result clearly. Check the first completed clean against the quote Return to the $373 walkthrough quote above. It includes six worker-hours at $28, $40 supplies and travel, $60 allocated overhead and a 3% fee. The expected remainder after those costs is $93.81. What if the crew records 7.5 worker-hours for the same agreed scope? Same $373 price; illustrative time variance Measure Estimate Actual Worker-hours 6 7.5 Loaded labor at $28/hour $168 $210 Supplies and travel $40 $40 Fee at 3% $11.19 $11.19 Allocated overhead $60 $60 Remainder after stated costs $93.81 $51.81 The extra 1.5 worker-hours cost $42, reducing the modeled margin from 25.15% to 13.89%. Do not bill the customer retroactively for an estimating error. Record whether the extra time came from condition, omitted tasks, access delays or a service failure. Revise the next quote or agree a scope change in advance. Keep an accepted scope, estimated worker-hours, actual worker-hours and explanation beside each first clean. The existing job-cost worksheet and estimate-versus-actual guide support that review. A return visit uses additional labor and travel too; recording only the original visit can hide the true cost of retaining the account. Price a cleaning visit using worker-hours and the fee basis Two cleaners spending 2.5 hours on site use five worker-hours, not 2.5. In this independent fictional quote, loaded labor is $24 per paid worker-hour. Five on-site hours cost $120; one additional paid travel worker-hour costs $24. Add $12 supplies, $8 acquisition and a $20 overhead allowance: defined dollar costs are $184 before the percentage card fee. If the card fee is 3% of the final customer price and the desired quote margin after these stated costs is 15%, price = $184 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.15) = $224.39, rounded. A $225 quote leaves $34.25 after the $6.75 fee and $184 defined costs, a 15.22% quote margin. These assumptions are not local cleaning prices or a guaranteed accounting net margin. The $20 overhead allowance is an allocation for quoting. Reconcile all job allocations back to actual monthly overhead rather than treating each allocation as a separate cash bill. If owner delivery labor is within the loaded rate, do not charge the same hours a second time as owner wages. Record bedrooms, bathrooms, access, condition, extras and exclusions before converting the estimate to a flat price. Compare actual worker-hours after the first visit. A recurring discount needs a verified change in time or cost; square footage alone cannot establish the cleaning scope. Use the quote-versus-actual worksheet and the monthly budget together. Quote an extra hour without confusing crew time and worker-hours In a separate fictional quote, two cleaners each need one extra hour. That adds two worker-hours. At $24 loaded cost per worker-hour plus $4 extra supplies and travel, incremental cost is $52. With an assumed 3% payment fee and a 20% target operating margin on the added charge, quote $52 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.20) = $67.53 rounded to cents. At $67.53, the assumed fee is about $2.03, leaving about $13.50 after the $52 incremental cost. The job’s original quote must still cover its assigned overhead and original work. This is an additional-scope calculation, not a replacement for the full-job budget or a local market rate. Agree the rooms, tasks and extra time before accepting the change, then compare actual worker-hours with the quote. Use the monthly cleaning break-even model to check whether the combined booking mix supports the whole business. FAQs Should I charge by the hour or by the job? Hourly pricing is easy to explain while you are learning how long different homes take. Flat pricing is often easier for customers to budget, but it requires a defined scope and reliable time estimates. You can use hourly calculations internally while presenting a flat quote externally. How do I price a house I have never seen? Ask about square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, occupants, pets, flooring, last professional clean, and requested add-ons. Give a range or a provisional quote with assumptions, then confirm the price after a walkthrough or photos. Write down what would trigger a change. Should supplies be included in the cleaning price? Usually, yes, because supplies are part of the cost of delivering the service. Track them by job or use a reasonable per-job estimate that you update from receipts. Do not assume a small bottle-level cost is immaterial when multiplied across many appointments. Do I need a separate price for recurring cleaning? Often, yes. Recurring visits may have a narrower scope and more predictable labor time, while a first-time or one-off clean may require extra work. State the frequency, included tasks, and cancellation or rescheduling terms rather than offering a vague discount. How much profit should I add? Choose a target that reflects your overhead, risk, owner-pay plan, and reinvestment needs. The examples use 25% to 30% only to demonstrate the formula; they are not a universal benchmark. Run a lower-volume month as well as your expected month before settling on a price. What if my calculated price is higher than local competitors? First check whether you measured labor-hours, payroll burden, travel, fees, and scope consistently. If the arithmetic is sound, narrow the service area, reduce wasted route time, change the scope, or explain the value of the included work. Cutting the price without changing the cost simply removes the money available for overhead and profit. Does price per square foot replace a job estimate? No. It can summarize a quote, but condition, tasks and access can change the workload at the same floor area. Cost the defined scope and total worker-hours before using an area-based price. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.summary: Learn lawn care pricing per acre with cost-based formulas, real examples, minimum charges, and a capacity check for profitable quotes and profit goals.

documents.text: Landscaping PRICING GUIDE Lawn Care Pricing: How to Set Your Rates Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 22, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Learn lawn care pricing per acre with cost-based formulas, real examples, minimum charges, and a capacity check for profitable quotes and profit goals. Landscaping Pricing Profit Planning WORKED PRICING REVIEW · FICTIONAL USD INPUTS Build the service quote before dividing by acreage Acreage alone does not determine delivery effort. Count each person’s paid work once, including travel labor if it is included in these hours. Monetary travel cost below excludes labor already counted. Acres in this service quote Current price per acre Total worker-hours per visit Loaded cost per worker-hour Materials per visit Other travel cost per visit Other variable cost per visit Percentage payment fee Chosen contribution target per visit Quoted revenue $320.00 Entered variable cost before fee $205.00 Fee on quoted revenue $9.60 Contribution at current quote $105.40 Minimum quote for chosen contribution $335.06 Contribution at minimum rounded quote $120.01 Minimum quote divided by service acres: $167.53 per acre. Use the whole-visit quote for the financial check; a rounded per-acre display can leave a different total. Required quote = (entered variable cost + chosen contribution) ÷ (1 − fee rate). The minimum quote rounds upward to cents and is checked again after the fee. Contribution funds overhead and owner pay; it is not accounting net profit or a market rate. Reset pricing example The default 2-acre visit collects $320 and costs $205 before fees. Contribution is $105.40. A $120 target needs a $335.06 whole-visit quote. Compare crew-hour capacity and equipment allowances without counting the same cost twice. Use capacity planning to test delivery limits and controlled product/service records to preserve the assumptions behind a price. This widget does not change the original guide examples or save entries. Pricing example and links reviewed November 20, 2026. Existing publication dates and original content preserved. Lawn care operator reviewing acreage, route and pricing details If you price lawn care per acre, start with the cost of delivering one visit, then add the contribution needed for overhead and profit. A useful starting point is direct job cost ÷ (1 − target contribution margin) , with a minimum charge for small or awkward properties. A per-acre figure is only a unit. A flat, open acre on a regular route is not the same job as a sloped, overgrown lot with gates and obstacles. Your rate must pay for crew time, equipment, travel, overhead, owner pay, and planned profit. Quick answer: For a routine one-acre mowing visit, add labor, fuel, equipment wear, and job supplies to find direct cost. If that total is $110 and you need a 45% contribution margin, divide $110 by 0.55: $200. Round for a clean quote, then adjust for access, terrain, frequency, and a minimum service charge. The direct answer, expanded There is no single correct lawn care pricing per acre number. The practical answer is the price that leaves enough money after the job’s direct costs to pay your monthly fixed costs and the return you expect from the business. For each service, estimate full-visit crew hours, multiply by loaded labor cost, then add fuel, equipment wear, disposal, materials and fixed-per-transaction fees. For a separate percentage-of-price fee, divide the non-percentage cost by one minus the fee rate minus your target contribution margin; otherwise divide by one minus the target margin. Round upward when setting a cost-based floor, and check it against a minimum charge and the requested frequency. The contribution margin is the part of the sale left after variable, job-level costs. It is not the same as net profit. For example, suppose a two-person crew spends 1.5 hours on a flat one-acre mowing visit. At a loaded labor cost of $28 per crew member per hour, labor is 2 × 1.5 × $28 = $84 . Fuel and equipment wear add $18, and bags, trimmer line, and other visit supplies add $8. The direct cost is therefore $84 + $18 + $8 = $110 . If your target contribution margin is 45%, the portion available for overhead and profit is 0.45 of the price. The remaining 0.55 must cover the $110 direct cost: $110 ÷ (1 − 0.45) = $110 ÷ 0.55 = $200 A $200 quote leaves $90 after direct costs, because $200 − $110 = $90 . That $90 is not automatically profit. If monthly fixed overhead is $4,200 and planned owner pay or profit is $1,800, you need $4,200 + $1,800 = $6,000 of monthly contribution. At $90 per visit, that is $6,000 ÷ $90 = 66.67 , or 67 comparable visits. That check matters. A $200 price may be sound per visit, yet 67 visits may not fit your mowing days, route density, or crew capacity. If one visit takes three total crew-hours, 67 visits require 67 × 3 = 201 crew-hours before loading, breakdowns, weather delays, and estimates. Use competitor prices as a market check, not the formula. Their route, equipment, insurance, or service scope may differ. Your cost sheet tells you whether the rate supports your business. What changes the answer Property shape and access. Acreage is an area measurement, not a labor measurement. A rectangle with a wide gate can be quick; beds, fences, trees, ponds, and retaining walls may require more trimming and turning. Ask for a site visit or clear photos when the property is not plainly open and flat. Terrain and vegetation. Slopes slow a walk-behind crew and increase safety requirements. Wet grass, dense growth, leaves, and neglected edges add passes, cleanup, or disposal. Quote a first cut separately when it is harder than recurring service. Crew and equipment. A solo operator with a residential mower has a different cost per acre from a two-person crew using commercial equipment. Faster equipment can lower labor per visit. Separate usage-related wear and repairs from fixed commitments, account for depreciation consistently, and record equipment purchases and debt principal in the cash plan rather than treating them as ordinary monthly operating expenses. Travel and route density. A nearby acre can be profitable at a lower price than an isolated acre because drive time is not billable mowing time. Include windshield time in the estimate. Set a service-area minimum or charge more for a remote stop instead of hiding the difference in an acreage rate. Service frequency and season. Weekly mowing usually keeps growth manageable. A monthly visit may require more time and cleanup. Spring growth, fall leaves, irrigation, and weather can change labor, so avoid one fixed rate when the scope changes. Fees, taxes, and contract terms. Card processing, sales tax, late-payment risk, and cancellation rules affect what you collect and keep. State whether a quote is before or after tax, and do not treat collected sales tax as overhead revenue. If you publish a per-acre rate, state what it includes, such as mowing, trimming, edging, blowing, clippings, and routine cleanup. List extras such as bagging, leaf removal, hedge work, irrigation repair, steep-slope work, or storm debris. Worked pricing and operating scenarios Scenario 1: One-acre recurring mowing route A two-person crew spends 1.5 hours at the property. Loaded labor is 2 × 1.5 × $28 = $84 . Fuel and equipment wear total $18, and consumables total $8. Direct cost is $84 + $18 + $8 = $110 . With a 45% target contribution margin, the calculated price is $110 ÷ 0.55 = $200 . At four weekly visits in a four-week billing cycle, the customer’s monthly service charge is 4 × $200 = $800 . The monthly contribution from that account is 4 × ($200 − $110) = $360 , before fixed overhead and owner pay. Scenario 2: Two-acre open property with efficient access The crew can mow two open acres in 2.25 hours because the route has wide gates and few obstacles. Labor is 2 × 2.25 × $28 = $126 . Fuel and equipment wear are $32, while supplies and cleanup are $16. Direct cost is $126 + $32 + $16 = $174 . At the same 45% target margin, the floor calculated from cost is $174 ÷ 0.55 = $316.36 . Rounding to a customer-friendly quote of $320 gives an effective rate of $320 ÷ 2 = $160 per acre . The per-acre price is lower than Scenario 1 because the crew gets more acreage from one setup and travel stop. Do not use that $160 figure for every two-acre property; it depends on the measured production time. Scenario 3: One-time overgrown three-quarter-acre cleanup This is not a routine mowing visit. Two workers spend 3.5 hours cutting, trimming, and loading material. Labor is 2 × 3.5 × $28 = $196 . Fuel and equipment wear total $32, and green-waste disposal costs $42. Direct cost is $196 + $32 + $42 = $270 . Applying the 45% contribution target gives $270 ÷ 0.55 = $490.91 . A quote of $500 leaves $500 − $270 = $230 for fixed costs and profit. The apparent per-acre rate is $500 ÷ 0.75 = $666.67 , but that number should not be advertised as the recurring mowing rate. It reflects the extra labor and disposal in this particular scope. After the cleanup, quote recurring maintenance from the expected time for a maintained property. These are planning illustrations, not market promises. For related planning, use landscaping startup costs , landscaping profit margin , and lawn volume needed for $100,000 revenue . Check the minimum visit and percentage fee separately The $110-cost, $200-price example assumes no extra percentage fee outside that $110. If a processor separately takes 3% of selling price and you still require 45% contribution, solve price = $110 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.45) . Round the $211.5385 result upward to $211.54. At $200, that extra fee would leave $84 contribution, a 42% margin, not 45%. A minimum visit also explains why a quarter-acre is not necessarily one quarter of the one-acre price. In a separate illustrative model, mobilization costs $30 per visit and mowing costs $80 per acre, with no percentage fee in this example. Illustrative cost-based floor before monthly fixed costs Area Visit cost Price at 45% contribution 0.25 acre $30 + $80 × 0.25 = $50 $90.91, rounded up 1 acre $30 + $80 = $110 $200 Replace those costs with measured crew and route records; these are not local market rates. The Jobber lawn-pricing guide discusses pricing models and property conditions. Check your own equipment cost boundary and route economics before turning a quote into a public per-acre rate. How to run your own numbers Choose a representative property, measure crew time, and include travel, loaded labor, fuel, equipment use, supplies, disposal, card fees, and owner labor you want replaced. Set a target contribution margin, then test the price against fixed costs and available crew hours. For a private calculation of break-even revenue, required sales volume, contribution margin, and team capacity, use the landscaping break-even calculator . It is a planning tool based on your assumptions, not a guarantee or forecast. The calculator supports currencies other than USD if you price in another market. Common mistakes Dividing monthly overhead by acres without counting productive hours. Convert the target into visits and crew-hours, then compare it with realistic capacity. Using square footage or acreage as the only labor input. Two properties with the same measured area can require very different trimming, turning, and cleanup time. Time the whole visit, not just the mower’s engine hours. Forgetting non-wage labor. Loading, fueling, sharpening, route planning, and estimating consume time. If those hours never enter the model, your quote is lower than it appears. Quoting a recurring rate for a first cut. An overgrown lawn can require extra passes, bagging, or disposal. Separate the initial restoration price from the ongoing maintenance price so the recurring contract is not built on an unrealistic first-visit assumption. Copying a competitor’s per-acre price. Their service may exclude edging, carry less insurance, or be working a denser route. Use competitor quotes to understand the market conversation, then confirm that your own price covers your costs. Treating revenue as take-home pay. A $200 visit is not $200 of income. Direct costs, overhead, taxes, equipment replacement, and owner compensation all need a place in the model. Frequently asked questions Is pricing per acre better than pricing by the hour? Neither is automatically better. Customers may prefer a per-acre or per-visit quote, while your internal model should use hours and direct costs. Convert measured hours into a fixed quote so faster work improves productivity without making the customer watch the clock. What should I charge for a small residential lawn? Use a minimum service charge instead of multiplying a low per-acre rate by a tiny area. A quarter-acre visit still requires driving, unloading, trimming, edging, and payment administration. Should I charge more for hills? Charge for extra time, equipment, and risk rather than adding an arbitrary percentage. Estimate added crew minutes and specialized equipment, include them in direct cost, and recalculate. Decline an unsafe site or price a safer method. How do I price weekly versus biweekly mowing? Estimate the labor and cleanup for each frequency. Biweekly service may take longer per visit, so its per-visit price should not simply be half of a weekly visit. Present the customer with a per-visit price and a monthly or seasonal total that reflects the actual number of visits. Should owner labor be included in lawn care pricing? Yes, if you want the business to replace your work with a paid operator or to measure a real return for your time. Put your target owner pay in the fixed-cost or required-profit portion of the model, and record your hours separately so you can see whether the route is buying you a job or building a business. How often should I review my per-acre rate? Review it when fuel, wages, insurance, equipment payments, route density, or scope changes. A quarterly check and a fresh time study after seasonal changes can expose underpricing early. Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for related planning guides. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
