How much should I include in a photography package? Should owner salary be included in photography pricing? Do I need different prices for different photography services? What if my calculated price is higher than local photographers charge? How often should I review my package prices? Should I price a package only from shooting hours? Related planning decisions
documents.text: Photography PRICING GUIDE Photography Pricing Packages: Costs, Time & Profit Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Compare two photography packages using shoot time, editing, travel, gallery costs, processing fees and overhead. Keep each scope profitable. Photography Pricing Profit Planning Photographer reviewing package pricing and delivery scope Photography pricing packages should start with the amount each booking must contribute to your business, not with a competitor's rate card. Add the cost of delivering the shoot, payment fees, overhead, and the profit or owner pay you need; then turn that number into a package with a clear scope. This approach gives you a price you can explain and adjust. It also prevents a familiar problem: a calendar full of shoots that still does not cover editing time, equipment replacement, insurance, and your own pay. For more pricing topics, see the MyBreakeven blogs hub . Quick answer: Build a photography package by calculating the contribution needed from one booking. Subtract direct job costs from the price after payment fees, then use the result to cover monthly fixed costs and your target profit. Set the package scope, inclusions, and add-ons around that price. The direct answer, expanded A workable package has three parts: a promise to the client, a delivery limit for you, and a price that leaves enough contribution after direct costs. The promise might be a two-hour family session with 30 edited images, a wedding day with a second shooter, or a commercial shoot with licensed files. The delivery limit defines what is included and what costs extra. Start by separating fixed costs from per-booking costs . Fixed costs recur even when no one books you, including insurance, software, marketing, studio rent, equipment replacement, administration, and planned owner pay. Per-booking costs happen because a specific client booked: an assistant, travel, venue hire, albums, prints, outsourced retouching, and the payment-processing fee. The basic package equation is: Required contribution per booking = (monthly fixed costs + target monthly profit) ÷ planned bookings Price before rounding = (required contribution per booking + direct costs) ÷ (1 - payment fee rate) Suppose your monthly fixed costs are $2,700. That figure includes $1,500 for your planned owner pay, $350 for insurance and software, $400 for marketing and studio costs, and $450 for equipment replacement and administration. You want another $1,500 in monthly business profit, and you expect six paid bookings. Each booking must therefore contribute: ($2,700 + $1,500) ÷ 6 = $700 You estimate $150 of direct costs per booking. Payment processing is 3% of the sale, so the price calculation is: ($700 + $150) ÷ (1 - 0.03) = $850 ÷ 0.97 = $876.29 You could set the package at $880 . At that price, the processing fee is $26.40, and the contribution is $880 - $150 - $26.40 = $703.60 . Six bookings produce $4,221.60 of contribution. Subtract $2,700 of fixed costs and the result is $1,521.60 before tax, slightly above the $1,500 target. The price is only half of the package decision. Write down what the $880 buys: consultation, shoot length, gallery size, delivery deadline, and locations or outfit changes. Price rush delivery, extra retouching, prints, and additional shooting time separately. Otherwise an $880 package can quietly become an underpriced custom project. Check the workload as well. If the booking takes two hours on location, one hour of travel, four hours of editing, and one hour of communication, it consumes eight working hours. The $703.60 contribution is $87.95 per working hour before fixed costs, which may expose an oversized scope. Compare the hours behind two packages A package can look attractive on a price list while extra images and revision time consume the margin. Draft its deliverables first, then count the paid work. In this illustrative portrait example, the standard package sells for $650. It takes two shooting hours, four editing hours and one hour for consultation, file preparation and delivery: seven hours at a hypothetical $35 fully loaded cost per working hour, or $245. Travel costs $30 and gallery delivery costs $15. Allocate $100 of monthly overhead per booked package at a realistic booking count. Payment processing takes 3% of the collected price. Package Standard portrait Expanded portrait Collected price $650 $950 Paid production and delivery hours 7 × $35 = $245 11 × $35 = $385 Travel and digital gallery $45 $45 Additional album cost $0 $80 Allocated overhead $100 $100 Payment fees at 3% of price $19.50 $28.50 Profit after listed costs $240.50 $311.50 Standard profit checks: $650 − $245 − $45 − $100 − $19.50 = $240.50 , or 37% of collected price. The expanded package adds one shoot hour, three editing hours and an $80 album. That is four more paid hours × $35 = $140, so total hours cost $385. Its result is $950 − $385 − $45 − $80 − $100 − $28.50 = $311.50 , or 32.79%. The expanded package earns $71 more dollars but uses four additional hours and has a lower percentage margin. Capacity may make the smaller package more attractive in a busy month. For a 30% target margin on the standard scope, the price P must satisfy P − 0.03P − $390 = 0.30P , since $245 + $45 + $100 = $390 before fees. Thus 0.67P = $390 and P = $582.09; a $583 whole-dollar quote clears the target on these assumptions. That is a floor calculation, not a claim that customers will pay any given fee. Define coverage, edited-file count, revision rounds, travel radius, delivery date and usage rights so the modeled hours match the actual promise. The editing cost per session guide helps with time records; mini-session event economics handles a dated block of multiple small bookings. What changes the answer Your mix of services changes the required price. Portraits, weddings, product shoots, and real-estate assignments have different direct costs and editing burdens, so keep separate assumptions for each package. The number of bookings you can actually deliver changes the math. Six weddings may be impossible in a month even if six portrait sessions are feasible. Count editing, consultations, travel, album design, sales calls, and admin time. If you need 10 bookings but have room for seven, raise the price or reduce the scope. Location and travel can erase contribution. A nearby session may use $10 of fuel and parking; a destination wedding may require lodging, tolls, and a second day of travel. Decide whether travel is included within a radius, charged by distance, or quoted separately. Team and outsourcing choices move direct costs. Price the actual per-job amount for a second shooter, makeup artist, assistant, album designer, or retoucher, including taxes or fees you bear. Taxes, payment methods, and sales terms affect the amount left over. A card fee, installment-plan fee, gallery fee, print-lab charge, or collected sales tax should not be confused with profit. Decide whether the displayed price is tax-inclusive and model the payment fee against the amount you keep. Season and cancellation risk affect cash flow. A wedding package may look profitable on paper but leave a slow month empty. Deposits and cancellation terms help, but they do not turn an empty date into revenue. Price from the annual workload you can support, not your busiest weekend. Worked pricing and operating scenarios Scenario 1: Solo portrait photographer You run a portrait business with $1,800 of monthly fixed costs. A session uses $75 of direct costs for travel, a gallery, and small supplies. You want $900 of monthly profit and plan to deliver eight sessions. The required contribution is: ($1,800 + $900) ÷ 8 = $337.50 per session With a 3% payment fee, the unrounded price is: ($337.50 + $75) ÷ 0.97 = $425.26 Set the package at $430 . The fee is $12.90, so contribution is $430 - $75 - $12.90 = $342.10 . Eight sessions create $2,736.80 of contribution; after $1,800 of fixed costs, profit is $936.80 . The package should state whether the eight sessions include studio rental, extra images, and print products. If those costs are not in the $75 estimate, recalculate. Scenario 2: Wedding package with a second shooter Your wedding business has $4,200 of monthly fixed costs. One wedding carries $540 of direct costs: $350 for a second shooter, $120 for an album or lab order, and $70 for travel. You want $1,800 of monthly profit and can responsibly book three weddings. The required contribution is: ($4,200 + $1,800) ÷ 3 = $2,000 per wedding The price before rounding is: ($2,000 + $540) ÷ 0.97 = $2,618.56 A package price of $2,650 gives a $79.50 processing fee and $2,030.50 of contribution per wedding. Three weddings produce $6,091.50; less $4,200 of fixed costs leaves $1,891.50 . That result assumes the $540 includes every direct delivery cost. Add the cost of a large album, rush edits, or an engagement session before publishing the price. Scenario 3: Small commercial photography project You have $6,500 of fixed monthly costs, including a studio and paid marketing. A commercial project uses $400 of direct costs for a prop assistant, travel, and outsourced retouching. You want $2,500 of profit from five projects. The required contribution is: ($6,500 + $2,500) ÷ 5 = $1,800 per project At a 3% payment fee: ($1,800 + $400) ÷ 0.97 = $2,268.04 Quote $2,300 as the starting project price. The fee is $69, leaving $1,831 of contribution. Five projects yield $9,155; after $6,500 of fixed costs, profit is $2,655 . Define usage rights too. Paid advertising, national territory, or a longer license is a different commercial product from basic file delivery. These scenarios are planning examples, not market quotes. Your number will change with costs, capacity, tax treatment, and service mix. For comparisons, see photography business profit margins and photography business startup costs . For volume planning, see how many photography clients you need per month . How to run your own numbers List monthly fixed costs, owner salary, direct cost per package, payment rate, realistic bookings, and target profit. Run each package separately, then check whether the bookings fit your shooting, editing, travel, and sales capacity. MyBreakeven supports other currencies as well as USD and lets you test demand and capacity. Use the photography business break-even calculator to run your own numbers. Common mistakes Using the competitor's package as your cost model. A nearby photographer may have different rent, insurance, equipment debt, editing speed, or owner-pay needs. Competitor research cannot tell you whether your price covers your business. Treating the deposit as extra revenue. A deposit is usually part of the package price, not a bonus. Record the full contract value and model cash timing separately from delivery. Leaving editing out of the job cost. Two hours shooting plus eight hours of culling, retouching, exporting, and gallery support is a 10-hour booking. Counting only camera time overstates the hourly return. Forgetting fees before comparing prices. A competitor may take bank transfers while your installment plan takes a percentage of every payment. Subtract the actual processing cost before comparing margins. Bundling unlimited revisions or images. “Unlimited” can turn a defined package into an open-ended editing job. Set a gallery size, revision round, delivery window, and add-on rate. Pricing the best month and spending the average month. A full wedding season can hide quiet dates, equipment repairs, and late invoices. Use a booking count you can deliver across the period, with a separate reserve for uneven demand. Photography package cost includes editing and delivery A photography package consumes more than session time. Suppose a fictional package needs two hours shooting, three editing, one preparation and one delivery-and-administration hour. Seven worker-hours at a $30 loaded delivery cost total $210. Add $40 sale-dependent travel and products and a 3% fee on the $500 package, or $15. Contribution is $235. If editing grows from three to five hours, direct labor rises by $60 and contribution falls to $175 at the same price. The package's apparent shooting rate has not changed, but its complete economics have. Track actual turnaround and revision time before deciding a package is profitable. Define image quantity, retouching scope and included revisions. Reusable equipment belongs in the appropriate equipment or overhead plan, while a purchased print for this customer belongs with the package. Owner delivery hours and a separate owner-pay target require a stated boundary so compensation is not ignored or counted twice. For the next decision in this plan, compare Photography Print Package Profit: Albums, Time and Fees . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. FAQs Should I charge by the hour or sell photography packages? Use an hourly calculation internally so you know what the work must return. Sell a package when the client is buying a defined result; for unusual commercial work, quote a project fee with an hourly or day-rate basis behind it. How much should I include in a photography package? Include deliverables you can repeat at the calculated price: consultation, coverage, locations, edited files, gallery delivery, and turnaround. Keep albums, prints, rush work, extra images, extended travel, and expanded usage as priced additions. Should owner salary be included in photography pricing? Yes, if the business is expected to pay you. Put planned owner pay into fixed costs rather than waiting to see what remains after expenses. Do I need different prices for different photography services? Usually. Services have different assistant costs, editing times, travel patterns, sales cycles, and capacity limits. Calculate contribution for each major service separately. What if my calculated price is higher than local photographers charge? Check the scope and assumptions before cutting the price. You may have included a cost a competitor excludes, or promised more images, time, or licensing. If the costs are real, reduce deliverables or change the booking mix rather than pricing below required contribution. How often should I review my package prices? Review them when a major cost, fee, team arrangement, or deliverable changes, and on a regular schedule such as quarterly. Recalculate after a season if editing time or booking volume differs from the plan. Should I price a package only from shooting hours? No. Include preparation, editing, communication and delivery work needed for the agreed scope. A package with a short session can still require substantial production time afterward. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Mobile Detailing BUSINESS PLANNING GUIDE Car Detailing Price List: Scope, Costs and Worker-Hours Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 11, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Build a detailing price list from scope, supplies, labor, travel and fees. Compare repeat visits, larger services, extra work and route capacity. Mobile detailing Pricing Profit Planning Mobile detailing professional reviewing vehicle service pricing Build a car detailing price list from service scope, vehicle condition and complete delivery cost. In the fictional maintenance-detail example below, a $160 price leaves $54.20 after supplies, paid labor, travel, acquisition and card fees. That contribution must fund overhead and owner income. A public list should show what the price buys and when a condition-based quote is needed. These USD figures illustrate a cost model; they are not current local detailing prices or industry averages. Mobile detailing price list: include the trip and setup For mobile detailing pricing, state whether the listed service includes travel, water setup and pack-down. Count total paid worker-hours across the crew, then compare the contribution with the jobs your route can actually deliver. Keep a condition-based quote for vehicles outside the stated scope. The examples here illustrate costing; they are not a verified local market price list. Quick answer For each service, define vehicle size, included work and expected worker-hours. Add consumables, direct labor, travel, acquisition and payment fees, then calculate contribution at the proposed price. Check the monthly job target against route capacity. Use starting prices only where the included scope and conditions for a revised quote are clear. Build the maintenance-detail price first Assume a maintenance detail uses two worker-hours at a loaded $25 per hour, or $50. Consumables cost $12, vehicle expense and parking cost $14, and acquisition averages $25 per completed job. Cost before percentage fees is $12 + $50 + $14 + $25 = $101. At $160 with a 3% fee, processing costs $4.80. Contribution is $160 − $101 − $4.80 = $54.20. This is the amount available for monthly overhead and owner pay before any extra profit goal. It is not the owner's take-home from the appointment. Assume $1,000 monthly overhead, $2,500 owner pay and a $500 additional profit goal. The requirement is $4,000. At $54.20 contribution, 73 jobs produce $3,956.60 and miss that goal. Seventy-four produce $4,010.80, leaving $510.80 after overhead and owner pay. Suppose one technician has 35 weekly hours at 75% utilization. Using 52 ÷ 12 weeks, usable monthly time is 113.75 worker-hours. At two hours per job, only 56 whole jobs fit. The $160 list price does not support the selected income plan at this scope and time budget, even if every available appointment sells. With 56 jobs, required contribution is $4,000 ÷ 56 = $71.4286. The cost-based price floor is ($101 + $71.4286) ÷ 0.97 = $177.7614, rounded upward to $177.77. A $180 quote leaves $73.60 contribution and needs 55 jobs. Fifty-six jobs leave $621.60 after overhead and owner pay. Demand must be tested at the new price. You cannot assume the old booking volume remains unchanged. The mobile detailing break-even guide connects job contribution with the monthly route, while the price list communicates the service a customer can buy. Turn the estimate into a usable price list Use named service rows with explicit inclusions: vehicle size category, interior or exterior scope, expected condition, location coverage and quoted extras. A maintenance detail and restoration work should not share a cost assumption simply because both involve cleaning the same car. Keep the number of categories manageable. A customer needs to know whether the listed price applies to a compact car in normal condition, a larger vehicle or a heavily soiled interior. State when photographs or an inspection are needed before confirmation. Avoid a vague starting price that never describes the service available at that price. For an actual booking, carry the chosen list row into the job sheet. Record arrival, setup, work and pack-down time, plus any separately modeled travel. Compare the result with the estimate after completion. If a category repeatedly overruns, revise its scope or price rather than relying on the technician to rush. If you are the owner-technician, choose a consistent pay treatment. This example uses incremental paid technician labor and separate owner income for management or ownership. If the same owner performs all labor and puts their compensation in owner pay, do not also pay the same time through the direct wage line. Hours remain part of capacity regardless of the cash treatment. Four variables that move the service price Vehicle condition. Embedded pet hair, stains or residue can extend labor and product use. Estimate the added work before promising a fixed price. Use a defined extra or revised quote tied to scope rather than assuming every large car is equally dirty. Service duration. Worker-hours cover the entire modeled delivery process. A four-hour elapsed visit with two technicians can consume eight worker-hours. For mobile work, route time must either be included in job time or deducted from available time, consistently. Distance and access. Tolls, parking, travel labor and setup differ by location. The mobile travel-fee guide isolates that decision. Do not enter both a full travel allowance and the same vehicle expense again without checking what the allowance covers. Repeat bookings. A maintenance-plan visit may have lower acquisition and a narrower service scope. Those savings can justify a different price. The maintenance-plan pricing guide keeps the recurring commitment separate from a one-off full detail. Use actual supplier and booking records for these inputs. A competitor's price list can inform what customers see elsewhere, but it does not reveal their labor boundary, overhead or route. Your floor needs your own costs and delivery assumptions. Three service scenarios A repeat maintenance visit Keep the $160 price, $12 supplies, $50 labor and $14 vehicle expense, but acquisition falls to $5 per completed visit. Cost before processing becomes $81. Contribution is $160 × 0.97 − $81 = $74.20. Funding $4,000 requires 54 visits because 53 contribute $3,932.60 and 54 contribute $4,006.80. This fits the 56-job workload ceiling. The improvement relies on the lower acquisition being real and the service staying within two worker-hours; it is not a reason to silently expand the included scope. A full detail with longer delivery time Assume a full detail sells for $300 and takes four worker-hours. Paid labor is $100, supplies $25, vehicle expense $14 and acquisition $25. Cost before percentage fees is $164. Contribution is $300 × 0.97 − $164 = $127. The $4,000 requirement needs 32 jobs. At 113.75 usable hours, only 28 whole four-hour jobs fit. Twenty-eight contribute $3,556, leaving $56 after the example's $3,500 overhead and owner pay. The bigger ticket does not meet the additional $500 target at this workload. To fund $4,000 with 28 jobs, the price floor is ($164 + $4,000 ÷ 28) ÷ 0.97 = $316.3476, rounded upward to $316.35. A $320 quote leaves $146.40 and needs 28 jobs. Customer demand and actual route timing still need evidence. An extra hour of interior work A $180 maintenance quote requires one additional paid hour at $25 and $3 more supplies. Cost rises from $101 to $129. Holding the price leaves $180 × 0.97 − $129 = $45.60, down from $73.60. To preserve $73.60 contribution, quote ($129 + $73.60) ÷ 0.97 = $208.8660, rounded upward to $208.87. A $210 revised quote leaves $74.70. But three worker-hours per job reduce the capacity ceiling to 37 whole jobs. Repricing one appointment does not repair a monthly plan built on two-hour work if every appointment now takes three. How to run your own numbers Use the mobile detailing break-even calculator with $180 price, $12 supplies, $50 labor, $14 other variable cost and $25 acquisition, plus a 3% fee. Enter $1,000 overhead, $2,500 owner pay and $500 target profit; use one technician, 35 weekly hours, 75% utilization and two worker-hours per job. It requires 55 jobs and permits 56. Other currencies are supported. Run each service row separately before constructing a mixed monthly plan. Common mistakes Posting a maintenance price without describing vehicle size and normal condition. Omitting travel or pack-down from either costs or capacity. Charging the same owner labor in direct wages and the monthly owner-pay goal. Assuming a larger ticket automatically produces more contribution per hour. Applying lower repeat-visit acquisition to every first-time customer. FAQs Are these current detailing market prices? No, they are fictional USD worked examples. Replace them with your own costs and local demand evidence. The guide explains how to test a price rather than publishing a market survey. Should I show a starting price? Use one only when the customer can see the included vehicle category and service condition. Explain how additional work is quoted before acceptance. The price should describe an available scope rather than an undefined minimum. Is contribution the same as profit? Contribution is revenue after the listed variable job costs. Monthly overhead and owner income still need to be paid. The remaining result depends on completed jobs and the costs included. How do I handle a heavily soiled car? Estimate additional worker-hours and supplies before confirming the scope. Recalculate the contribution at the revised quote. Keep extra time in the capacity model as well as the cost model. Can a repeat customer have a lower price? Lower acquisition, tighter routing or a smaller maintenance scope can change the cost floor. Verify those savings and the appointment duration. A repeat booking does not remove all delivery costs. What if I offer several services each month? Use the actual mix of service contribution and worker-hours. Do not average prices alone while keeping the cheapest service cost. Confirm the mixed workload against the route and calendar. Takeaways Connect every price-list row to a defined scope. Calculate contribution after full job costs and fees. Check larger services against worker-hours, not ticket size alone. Update prices or scope when actual jobs repeatedly overrun. Explore the business planning guides for more examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.title: Salon Service Pricing: Setting Rates That Cover Costs
documents.summary: Learn salon service pricing with a cost-based formula, worked examples and break-even checks so your rates cover labor, products and overhead.
documents.headings: The direct answer, expanded What changes the answer Worked pricing and operating scenarios Scenario 1: solo stylist with a small studio Scenario 2: two-chair salon with a mixed average ticket Scenario 3: color-heavy menu with two service types How to run your own numbers Common mistakes Frequently asked questions Related planning decisions
documents.text: Salon PRICING GUIDE Salon Service Pricing: Setting Rates That Cover Costs Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 22, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Learn salon service pricing with a cost-based formula, worked examples and break-even checks so your rates cover labor, products and overhead. Salon Pricing Profit Planning Salon stylist reviewing service costs and pricing Salon service pricing should begin with your cost per appointment, then add enough contribution to pay overhead and owner income. Competitor prices are a reference, not proof that your costs are covered. A workable price leaves money after delivery and fits the appointments your team can complete. The examples use USD and illustrative figures. Quick answer: Add direct labor, product, booking and payment costs to find the variable cost of a service. Then divide monthly fixed costs and desired profit by the contribution from each appointment. Add that required contribution to the variable cost. The result is a cost-based starting price, not a guarantee of demand. The direct answer, expanded For salon pricing, use this basic calculation: Price = variable service cost + required contribution per appointment Variable costs rise with each appointment: service labor, product, laundry, card processing and booking commissions. Rent, insurance, software, utilities and planned owner salary are monthly fixed costs. Suppose a stylist offers a cut and blowout. The service takes 1.5 hours. You assign $24 to direct labor, $5 to product and consumables, and $0 for laundry because it is already included in the monthly overhead estimate. The salon pays a card fee of 2.9% plus $0.30 on a card transaction. If the menu price is $95, the processing fee is ($95 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $3.055 , or $3.06 when rounded to cents. The variable cost is therefore $24 + $5 + $3.06 = $32.06 . Each appointment contributes $95 - $32.06 = $62.94 toward fixed costs and profit. Assume monthly fixed costs, including a planned owner salary, total $6,000. The service must be booked $6,000 ÷ $62.94 = 95.33 , so you need 96 appointments to cover that amount. At 96 appointments, contribution is 96 × $62.94 = $6,042.24 , leaving $42.24 after the listed fixed costs. If you want another $1,000 of monthly profit, the target becomes $7,000. You would need $7,000 ÷ $62.94 = 111.22 , or 112 appointments. The same math tests capacity. One stylist working 22 days at four services per day can deliver 88 appointments. The $95 price needs a different service mix or more capacity to support the $7,000 target. Use the same method for color, extensions and treatments. A higher ticket can still be weak when it consumes costly product or several hours of labor. For a useful comparison, see the salon profit margin guide and salon chair clients per day guide . Those topics help you separate a profitable menu price from a sales target that your calendar cannot support. What changes the answer Location changes fixed cost. A high-rent salon needs more contribution per booking even when product costs match a lower-rent studio. Local wages and parking can change the cost base too, so a nearby menu is only a reference. The team model changes labor math. Include pay for owner labor and management time. Commission, hourly wages and booth rent place costs in different parts of the model, so use the arrangement you actually operate. Service duration affects the price floor. A $90 service taking 90 minutes is not equivalent to one taking 45. Track consultation, setup, cleanup and the gap before the next client, not just hands-on time. Product usage varies. A routine root touch-up and corrective color should not share one allowance. Measure product where possible and price recurring extras into the service or add-on. Fees, discounts and no-shows reduce collections. A $100 menu price is not $100 received after discounts, platform fees or unpaid cancellations. Model the amount actually collected and calculate processing on that transaction. Your service mix matters. A low-priced cut and a high-contribution color booking do not pay overhead at the same rate. Review contribution by service instead of relying on one average ticket. Worked pricing and operating scenarios Scenario 1: solo stylist with a small studio A solo stylist has monthly fixed costs of $3,500, including rent, insurance, software and a planned owner salary. A haircut is priced at $85. Direct labor and supplies total $24 before payment processing. The card fee is ($85 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $2.765 , or $2.77. Total variable cost is $24 + $2.77 = $26.77 , so contribution is $85 - $26.77 = $58.23 . Break-even volume is $3,500 ÷ $58.235 = 60.07 , which rounds up to 61 appointments. Those 61 bookings generate 61 × $58.235 = $3,553.34 , enough to cover $3,500. Keep full precision in your working sheet and round only the final appointment target. If the stylist wants $1,000 of profit, the required contribution is $4,500. The appointment target is $4,500 ÷ $58.235 = 77.27 , so 78 appointments. With 22 working days, that is about 3.55 haircuts per day. The number is feasible only if the stylist’s service time and admin work leave room for that pace. Scenario 2: two-chair salon with a mixed average ticket A two-chair salon has $10,500 in monthly fixed costs. Across its normal mix of cuts, blowouts and color services, the average collected ticket is $110. Direct labor and product average $42 per booking. Processing is ($110 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $3.49 , making total variable cost $42 + $3.49 = $45.49 . Contribution is $110 - $45.49 = $64.51 . The salon needs $10,500 ÷ $64.51 = 162.77 , or 163 appointments to break even. At 163 bookings, contribution is 163 × $64.51 = $10,515.13 . If both stylists work 22 days and complete four appointments each day, their combined capacity is 2 × 22 × 4 = 176 appointments . That leaves 13 appointment slots above break-even. A week of cancellations could use much of that buffer, so the owner should not treat all 176 slots as guaranteed sales. Scenario 3: color-heavy menu with two service types A small salon has $7,000 in monthly fixed costs. Its planned month contains 80 color services at $150 and 100 cuts at $70. Color labor and product total $48 before payment processing. Its processing fee is ($150 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $4.65 , so color contribution is $150 - ($48 + $4.65) = $97.35 . The 80 color appointments contribute 80 × $97.35 = $7,788 . Cuts have $20 of direct labor and supplies. Their processing fee is ($70 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $2.33 , so cut contribution is $70 - ($20 + $2.33) = $47.67 . The 100 cuts contribute 100 × $47.67 = $4,767 . Total contribution is $7,788 + $4,767 = $12,555 . After $7,000 of fixed costs, the planned mix leaves $5,555 before tax and any costs omitted from the assumptions. The mix looks strong because color contributes more per booking. If cuts replace color, 180 appointments can produce less contribution, so track the mix rather than count alone. How to run your own numbers List each service’s actual time, product and payment cost. Then enter monthly fixed costs, owner salary, target profit, expected service mix and available team hours. Your number is different, so run it in the salon break-even calculator , which supports other currencies as well as USD and checks whether the required demand fits your stated capacity. The calculator is a planning tool based on your assumptions, not a forecast or a promise that clients will accept the price. Compare the result with the salon booth rent versus commission guide before changing a rental arrangement. Common mistakes Pricing from a competitor’s menu alone. A nearby salon may have lower rent or a different commission plan. Its rate is a reference, not your cost calculation. Leaving owner pay out of fixed costs. If owner labor is free on paper, the break-even price is too low. Add a planned wage or draw. Using one product allowance for every color service. Corrective work can use more product than routine work. Separate services or add a surcharge where the cost changes. Treating a full calendar as full revenue. Cancellations, discounts and card fees reduce cash received. Use collected revenue and realistic gaps when testing capacity. Rounding too early. In the examples, fees were rounded for display but the break-even division used the unrounded contribution. Keep full precision in your working sheet and round only the final menu price or appointment target. Ignoring service mix. Count service types, not just appointments. Calculate contribution by service and weight it by expected mix. For the next decision in this plan, compare Bridal Hair and Makeup Pricing: Cost the Whole Booking . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. Frequently asked questions Should salon prices be based on an hourly rate? An hourly rate is a useful starting point because it exposes the cost of time. It is not the whole price, since product, processing fees, overhead and the value of a specialist service still need to be covered. Use the time-based cost to build a service price, then test the full menu against monthly costs. How much should I charge for a haircut? There is no responsible single haircut price without the service duration, labor cost, overhead and target volume. For example, an $85 haircut with $26.77 of variable cost contributes $58.23 before fixed costs. Put your own figures into the formula rather than copying a local menu. Should I include my salary in salon pricing? Yes, if the salon is expected to pay you for the work or management time. Put the planned owner salary in fixed costs when you are calculating the contribution needed from services. Otherwise, the result can show a profit that disappears when you pay yourself. How do I price color services when product use varies? Separate routine color from services that regularly use more product or time. Measure product for a sample of real appointments and add the average direct cost to labor and payment fees. For unusually complex work, quote after a consultation instead of forcing every client into the cheapest menu tier. Is a 30% markup enough for salon services? Markup is not the same as contribution margin. A 30% markup on direct cost may leave too little money for rent, software, owner pay, cancellations and taxes. Calculate the contribution left after variable costs and compare the total with your monthly fixed costs and desired profit. Should I raise prices if my salon is busy? A busy calendar can still be weak if the services take too long or the contribution per booking is low. First calculate contribution by service and check whether the required demand fits capacity. A price change, shorter service time or better mix may solve the problem, but the numbers should show which lever matters. How often should salon prices be reviewed? Review them whenever rent, wages, product costs, payment fees or service times change, and set a regular check at least a few times a year. You do not need to change every price at each review. The purpose is to catch a shrinking contribution before it becomes a cash problem. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Agency PRICING GUIDE Agency Retainer Pricing: How to Price Monthly Work Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 13, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Set agency retainer pricing from real delivery costs, owner pay, fees, and profit so each monthly client supports a workable business model. Agency Pricing Profit Planning Agency owner reviewing retainer scope, workload and pricing If you want agency retainer pricing that pays for delivery, owner time, overhead, and profit, start with your costs rather than a competitor’s menu. A workable monthly retainer is the revenue needed to cover fixed costs divided by the share of each dollar left after delivery costs and fees. Quick answer: Add monthly overhead, the owner salary you want to pay, and your target profit. Divide that total by your contribution margin, then divide the result by the number of clients you can serve. If delivery and payment costs consume 28% of revenue, your contribution margin is 72%. The direct answer, expanded Ask what monthly revenue your agency needs and how many retainers it can deliver without overloading the team. Competitor rates do not answer that question. Use four figures: fixed monthly costs, planned owner pay, target profit, and the variable cost rate for delivery labor, freelancers, media handling, and payment fees. Treating owner time as free makes the retainer look cheaper than it is. The basic calculation is: Required revenue = (fixed costs + owner pay + target profit) ÷ contribution margin Contribution margin is the part of revenue left after variable costs. If variable costs are 28%, the contribution margin is 72%, or 0.72. Suppose a solo marketing agency has $3,000 in monthly fixed costs. The owner wants $6,000 in pay and another $2,000 in profit. Delivery labor and payment fees average 28% of revenue. Required revenue = ($3,000 + $6,000 + $2,000) ÷ 0.72 Required revenue = $11,000 ÷ 0.72 = $15,277.78 If the owner wants four retainer clients, the mathematical minimum per client is: $15,277.78 ÷ 4 = $3,819.45 per month That is a floor, not necessarily the published price. At four clients paying $3,900, revenue is $15,600. Variable costs are 28% of $15,600, or $4,368. The contribution is therefore $11,232. After $11,000 of fixed costs, owner pay, and planned profit, only $232 remains as a cushion because the rounding has put the agency slightly above its target. If scope changes and the agency needs a freelancer, the variable rate may rise. Price from the delivery model you expect to run, not the leanest version you hope to maintain. What changes the answer Delivery hours per client are usually the biggest swing factor. A retainer with weekly strategy calls, daily messages, reporting, revisions, and implementation consumes more capacity than one with a monthly report and a short planning call. List the work included, estimate the hours, and assign a real labor cost to those hours. If you are the person doing the work, use the pay you would need to hire someone competent, not zero. Your fixed-cost base changes the required revenue. A home-based solo agency may have a few thousand dollars of overhead. An agency with employees, office rent, tools, sales support, and a project manager needs much more revenue before profit appears. Add recurring costs that are easy to forget, including annual subscriptions divided by twelve and employer-side payroll costs. Client mix affects the blended margin. Strategy, creative, media buying, web development, and white-label fulfillment do not consume the same resources. A $5,000 retainer with $2,000 of subcontractor work has a different contribution than one delivered mostly with your own billable hours. Price each package from its expected cost, then check the blended result across your client mix. Scope and revisions can turn a good price into a bad one. “Social media management” might mean eight scheduled posts or daily content production with community replies. Put a boundary around deliverables, response times, meetings, revision rounds, and out-of-scope work. If the client can add work without adding price, your variable cost rate is not the number in your spreadsheet. Capacity limits the number of retainers you can sell. Revenue math can say you need four clients while your available delivery time supports only three. A low price may require eight clients when your sales pipeline can support five. A price is feasible only when the required client count fits both team hours and realistic lead demand. The agency break-even planning guide covers the related cost and capacity questions, while agency utilization guide explains how to measure productive delivery hours. Worked pricing and operating scenarios Scenario 1: Solo content agency with four retainers A solo agency has $3,000 of fixed costs each month. The owner budgets $6,000 for pay and wants $2,000 in profit. Freelance editing, stock assets, and card fees consume 28% of revenue. $3,000 + $6,000 + $2,000 = $11,000 100% - 28% = 72% $11,000 ÷ 0.72 = $15,277.78 With four clients, the minimum average retainer is $3,819.45. A posted price of $3,900 produces $15,600 in revenue. Variable costs are $4,368, leaving $11,232 for the fixed-cost, owner-pay, and profit target. The excess is $232, so the price covers the stated plan but has little room for an unbilled revision cycle. Scenario 2: Small performance agency with six retainers A team agency carries $12,000 of monthly fixed costs, including base staff and software. The owner needs $7,000 in pay, and the business target is $5,000 in profit. Contractor fulfillment and payment fees average 35% of revenue. $12,000 + $7,000 + $5,000 = $24,000 $24,000 ÷ 0.65 = $36,923.08 If the agency wants six clients, the average retainer must be: $36,923.08 ÷ 6 = $6,153.85 Rounding to $6,200 gives $37,200 in revenue. Variable costs equal: $37,200 × 0.35 = $13,020 That leaves $24,180. After the $24,000 cost, owner-pay, and profit requirement, the cushion is $180. The arithmetic works, but check whether six clients fit team capacity. A higher price or narrower scope would create more room. Scenario 3: Specialist agency with a lighter delivery model A specialist consulting agency has $5,000 in fixed costs, $4,000 in planned owner pay, a $3,000 profit target, and 15% direct delivery costs and fees. $5,000 + $4,000 + $3,000 = $12,000 100% - 15% = 85% $12,000 ÷ 0.85 = $14,117.65 With five clients, the minimum average retainer is: $14,117.65 ÷ 5 = $2,823.53 At $2,900 per month, five clients produce $14,500. Variable costs are $2,175, leaving $12,325. That is $325 above the requirement. If each client takes 12 delivery hours per month, the five retainers require 60 hours. An owner with 80 genuinely available delivery hours has 20 hours left for sales, administration, and interruptions. If the “available” figure includes all working time, the capacity check is too optimistic. The same formula produces different prices because cost base, margin, client count, and delivery model differ. For more comparisons, use agency profit margin guide and agency client delivery-cost example . Browse the MyBreakeven blog hub for the planning series. How to run your own numbers Enter your fixed monthly costs, planned owner salary, target profit, expected variable delivery costs, number of clients, and capacity assumptions. Include payment processing fees and contractor costs before you compare the result with a competitor’s rate. Then run your assumptions through the agency break-even calculator . It is a planning tool based on your inputs, not a prediction or a guarantee; it also supports currencies other than USD. Common mistakes Copying a competitor’s retainer without copying the scope. Their price may cover fewer revisions, use a lower-cost fulfillment team, or exclude ad spend and production. Compare deliverables and direct hours before comparing dollars. Treating owner labor as free. If your monthly price covers software and freelancers but not the time you spend selling, managing, and delivering, the agency may generate cash without paying you fairly. Put owner pay into the target before dividing by clients. Using markup when you need margin. Adding 20% to a $1,000 delivery cost produces $1,200, but the resulting margin is $200 ÷ $1,200, or 16.67%, not 20%. Use the contribution-margin calculation when you are working backward from a required revenue number. Leaving payment fees outside the model. A 3% card fee on a $5,000 retainer is $150. If you compare the full $5,000 with delivery cost and ignore that fee, the contribution is overstated by $150 every month. Selling unlimited access inside a fixed retainer. A client who can add meetings, channels, revisions, and urgent work changes the labor cost. Define a service boundary and price overages or a higher tier. Ignoring utilization and sales time. Eighty paid client hours are not the same as 80 hours in the workweek. Reserve time for proposals, follow-up, bookkeeping, management, and rework before deciding how many retainers the team can carry. Apply the next planning step If staff deliver the retainer, budget recurring employer costs and productive hours before allocating that cost to client work. Keep payroll once in the combined monthly plan. Check employee cost per productive hour . Frequently asked questions Should an agency charge a percentage of ad spend or a fixed retainer? Either model can work when it matches the work and the client’s expectations. It can underpay you when budgets are small and overpay you when budgets rise without much extra work. Calculate the hours and direct costs first, then choose the structure that keeps the contribution margin healthy. Is a $3,000 monthly retainer too low for an agency? There is no universal minimum. It may work for a tightly scoped service with low delivery cost, but it can fail when the account requires frequent meetings, custom creative, or several specialists. Run the retainer through your own fixed costs, variable cost rate, and capacity. How much profit should I build into an agency retainer? Set a dollar target that reflects why you are operating the agency and the cash buffer you need. A percentage copied from another business is less useful than stating, for example, “I need $5,000 left after owner pay and operating costs.” Then divide the total requirement by your contribution margin. Should owner salary be a fixed cost? For pricing purposes, include planned owner pay in the monthly amount the business must cover. Whether you record it as payroll, a draw, or another accounting treatment depends on your structure, but excluding it makes a self-employed agency appear healthier than it is. What if every client has a different scope? Estimate delivery hours and direct costs for each package or client type. Use a blended contribution margin only after you know the expected mix. If one account is unusually demanding, price that account on its own rather than hiding its cost inside an average. Can I lower the retainer to win more clients? Only if the lower price still covers the required contribution and the added clients fit your delivery capacity. More clients also create more meetings, reporting, and coordination. Test the lower price with the revised client count and hours rather than assuming volume will make up the difference. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: E-commerce PRICING GUIDE How to Price Products for Your Online Store Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 7, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Price ecommerce products from order costs, fees and a contribution target. Compare a direct-cost floor with a sustainable price and fulfilment capacity. E-commerce Pricing Profit Planning WORKED PRICING REVIEW · FICTIONAL USD INPUTS Check the contribution a quoted ecommerce price leaves A price must leave enough after the costs that belong to that completed order. This separate teaching check does not include refunds, taxes or unentered overhead. Current selling price Product cost Fulfilment cost Seller-paid shipping Acquisition cost per order Percentage fee Chosen contribution target Quoted revenue $60.00 Entered variable cost before fee $35.00 Fee on quoted revenue $1.80 Contribution at current quote $23.20 Minimum quote for chosen contribution $61.86 Contribution at minimum rounded quote $25.00 Required quote = (entered variable cost + chosen contribution) ÷ (1 − fee rate). The minimum quote rounds upward to cents and is checked again after the fee. Contribution funds overhead and owner pay; it is not accounting net profit or a market rate. Reset pricing example The default $60 price leaves $23.20 contribution. A $25 target needs at least $61.86, leaving $25.0042 before overhead. Review sales deductions and acquisition scope before using real figures. Use capacity planning to test delivery limits and controlled product/service records to preserve the assumptions behind a price. This widget does not change the original guide examples or save entries. Pricing example and links reviewed November 20, 2026. Existing publication dates and original content preserved. Ecommerce owner reviewing product costs, shipping and pricing If you sell products online, start with your cost per order, not a competitor's sticker price. The right price covers product and fulfilment costs, payment fees, returns and marketing per order. Across a realistic number of orders, the remaining contribution must cover monthly overhead, owner pay and a profit target. A price that clears supplier cost alone can still fail this test. Quick answer: Add order-level costs and choose a contribution target. If non-payment variable costs are $30.75, the illustrative payment fee is 2.9% plus $0.30 and you want a 40% contribution margin, the price is about $54.38: ($30.75 + $0.30) ÷ (1 − 0.029 − 0.40). Check demand and the orders you can fulfil. How to price an ecommerce product from its order costs Use this sequence: add landed cost, packaging, pick-and-pack labour, shipping subsidy, returns, order-level marketing, and payment fees. Set a contribution margin target, then check the price against customer demand and the orders your store can fulfil. Percentage fees make a simple markup unreliable. All USD figures below are illustrative assumptions, not provider quotes or market averages. Check your own rates and order records. Suppose an order has these costs: Product landed cost: $18.00 Packaging: $1.25 Pick-and-pack labour: $2.00 Shipping subsidy: $3.50 Returns allowance: $1.00 Advertising cost per order: $5.00 Payment fee: 2.9% of the selling price plus $0.30 The costs other than payment processing total $18 + $1.25 + $2 + $3.50 + $1 + $5 = $30.75 . If the target contribution margin is 40%, let the selling price be P . The contribution is P − ($30.75 + 0.029P + $0.30) , or 0.971P − $31.05 . Set that equal to 40% of the price: 0.971P − $31.05 = 0.40P 0.571P = $31.05 P = $54.38 At $54.38, the payment fee is $1.88 after rounding, total variable cost is $32.63, and contribution is $21.75. Divide $21.75 by $54.38 and the contribution margin is 40.0% after rounding. The direct pricing formula is (non-percentage order costs + flat payment fee) ÷ (1 − percentage payment fee − target contribution margin) . Here it is ($30.75 + $0.30) ÷ (1 − 0.029 − 0.40) = $54.38 . That is a price for a 40% contribution target . If competitors charge $39, compare shipping, product cost and advertising before matching them. Next, calculate the orders needed. If monthly fixed costs are $6,000 and you want $2,000 for owner pay plus $1,000 in profit, the store needs $9,000 of contribution. At $21.75 per order, that is 9,000 ÷ 21.75 = 413.79 , so you need 414 orders . At $54.38 each, those orders produce $54.38 × 414 = $22,513.32 in revenue. Contribution, not revenue, covers fixed bills and target pay. What changes the answer Landed product cost: include supplier price, inbound freight, duties and preparation before sale. Shipping terms: include carrier cost even with free shipping. If buyers pay shipping, include both that revenue and the carrier cost. Fees and acquisition: include percentage and flat payment fees, marketplace commissions and advertising per acquired order. Returns and discounts: estimate unrecovered refund, return-shipping and replacement costs. Recalculate at the discounted price before a promotion. Order mix and capacity: a $20 accessory can use almost as much packing time as a $100 bundle. Compare contribution dollars and required order volume by product. Three worked ecommerce pricing examples Scenario 1: A low-priced accessory A phone accessory has a landed cost of $8.00. Packaging is $0.75, fulfilment is $1.50, the average shipping subsidy is $2.75, returns allowance is $0.50, and advertising costs $3.50 per order. The non-payment variable costs total $8 + 0.75 + 1.50 + 2.75 + 0.50 + 3.50 = $17.00 . At a selling price of $29.00, payment processing is ($29 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $1.14 after rounding. Total variable cost is $17.00 + $1.14 = $18.14 , so contribution is $29.00 − $18.14 = $10.86 . The contribution margin is $10.86 ÷ $29.00 = 37.4% . If monthly fixed costs are $3,000, owner pay is $2,000, and the profit target is $1,000, required contribution is $6,000. The store needs 6,000 ÷ 10.86 = 552.49 , or 553 orders . That means about 553 ÷ 26 = 21.3 orders per selling day on a 26-day month. Being above product cost is not enough; required daily volume is the test. If the price falls to $25 with the same order costs, the fee is $1.03 after rounding, contribution is $25 − $17 − $1.03 = $6.97 , and the same $6,000 target takes 6,000 ÷ 6.97 = 860.83 , or 861 orders . The $4 discount therefore requires 308 more orders than the $29 price, assuming demand and costs otherwise stay the same. Scenario 2: A higher-priced bundle A skincare bundle costs $42.00 landed. Packaging is $1.50, fulfilment is $3.00, shipping subsidy is $6.00, returns allowance is $2.00, and advertising is $8.00 per order. Those costs total $42 + $1.50 + $3 + $6 + $2 + $8 = $62.50 before payment processing. At $119.00, the payment fee is ($119 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $3.75 after rounding. Total variable cost is $62.50 + $3.75 = $66.25 ; contribution is $119 − $66.25 = $52.75 , and contribution margin is $52.75 ÷ $119 = 44.3% . With $9,000 in monthly fixed costs, $3,500 of owner pay, and a $2,500 profit target, required contribution is $15,000. The order requirement is 15,000 ÷ 52.75 = 284.36 , so it needs 285 orders . Revenue at that volume is $119 × 285 = $33,915 . If the bundle were priced at $99, the payment fee would be $3.17, contribution would be $99 − ($62.50 + $3.17) = $33.33 , and the same target would require 15,000 ÷ 33.33 = 450.05 , or 451 orders . The $20 cut adds 166 monthly orders. Scenario 3: A subscription-style replenishment product A replenishment box costs $16.00 landed. Packaging is $1.00, fulfilment is $2.25, shipping is $4.25, expected refunds and replacements are $1.25, and retention marketing allocated to each renewal is $2.00. The non-payment total is $16 + $1 + $2.25 + $4.25 + $1.25 + $2 = $26.75 . At $59.00, the payment fee is ($59 × 0.029) + $0.30 = $2.01 after rounding. Total variable cost is $28.76 ; contribution is $30.24 , and contribution margin is $30.24 ÷ $59 = 51.3% . If fixed costs and target owner pay together require $8,000 of monthly contribution, required renewals are 8,000 ÷ 30.24 = 264.55 , or 265 renewals . If 10% of billed subscriptions fail or cancel before renewal, 265 successful renewals require roughly 265 ÷ 0.90 = 294.45 , so plan for at least 295 renewal opportunities to obtain 265 successful renewals under that assumed 90% success rate. That does not tell you how many new customers to acquire: also measure cancellations, failed payments, and first-order conversions separately. A minimum price is different from a sustainable price A price that covers one order's variable costs creates no contribution for rent, software, owner pay or profit. Calculate that direct-cost floor separately from the contribution target. Every amount below is an invented USD input, including the fee assumption; it is not a payment-provider quote. Suppose non-payment order costs total $24 and payment processing is 3% of price plus $0.30. Contribution is 0.97 × price − $24.30 . Setting that amount to zero gives a direct-cost floor of $24.30 ÷ 0.97 = $25.0515 , or $25.06 rounded up. At that price, contribution is only about one cent. Calling it a sustainable retail price would ignore the monthly business costs. For a 35% contribution margin, price is $24.30 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.35) = $39.1935 , rounded up to $39.20. The fee is $1.476 before cent rounding, so contribution is $13.724, or 35.01% of price. With $3,000 monthly fixed costs and a separate $1,000 profit target, required contribution is $4,000. Using the unrounded $13.724 contribution, you need 292 orders: 291 produces $3,993.684, while 292 produces $4,007.408. If you round each transaction cost to cents in your accounts, use the resulting consistent per-order amount when planning. Price decision Price Contribution before cent rounding What it supports Direct-cost floor $25.06 $0.0082 Almost none of the fixed overhead 35% contribution candidate $39.20 $13.724 Overhead and target profit at sufficient volume Discounted candidate $35.00 $9.65 Requires more orders for the same target At $35, the same $4,000 requirement needs 4,000 ÷ 9.65 = 414.51 , rounded up to 415 orders. If packing takes 12 minutes per order and only 70 productive hours are available, capacity is 70 ÷ 0.2 = 350 orders . The discounted plan exceeds that capacity by 65 orders. Use the discount recovery guide to preserve a baseline result, and the contribution versus profit margin comparison to avoid calling the contribution target net profit. A markup on landed product cost cannot answer these questions without fees, delivery costs, monthly overhead and capacity. How to run your own numbers In the ecommerce quick model, enter the actual order price (including shipping charged to the buyer) and product cost. Put packing labour in direct labour; put shipping costs, expected returns and flat transaction fees in other variable costs. Enter acquisition cost per order and percentage fees in their own fields. Add monthly overhead, owner pay and profit target once each. For a promotion, change the order price. Compare required orders with demand and packing capacity. The quick model displays USD; the full calculator supports other currencies. Run your assumptions in the ecommerce break-even calculator . The SBA break-even guide explains the unit formula; Shopify’s pricing guide illustrates percentage and flat fees. Check your own fee schedule. For other topics, visit the MyBreakeven blogs hub . These are planning estimates, not forecasts. Common mistakes Using supplier cost as the whole variable cost. The missing lines are usually fulfilment, shipping, fees, returns, and advertising. Add them per order before you decide that a product has a healthy margin. Applying a markup to a price that includes percentage fees. A 50% markup on cost does not mean a 50% contribution margin. Percentage fees rise with the price, so solve for the price after including them. Treating free shipping as free. The customer may see $0 at checkout, but the carrier still invoices you. Put the average shipping subsidy in the order cost. Ignoring the discount version of the offer. A product can work at $60 and fail at $45 during a promotion. Recalculate contribution at the actual sale price, then check whether the extra volume would really cover the lost dollars per order. Blending first orders and repeat orders. Acquisition cost is often concentrated on the first purchase. If repeat buyers cost less to acquire, calculate first-order contribution separately and avoid using a blended average that hides an unprofitable entry offer. Pricing every product with one percentage markup. Bulky, fragile, low-priced, and high-return products consume different resources. Price by order economics instead. Key takeaways Build the price from landed cost and every cost that rises with an order, including shipping, returns and acquisition. Solve percentage fees and your contribution target together; a markup on supplier cost does not give the same margin. Test the required whole-order volume at full price and at every proposed promotion price. Use your own payment terms, order mix and capacity; the worked figures are illustrative assumptions. Related planning guides ecommerce startup cost budget ecommerce profit margin breakdown orders per day needed for profit Solve a contribution price rather than adding a margin to cost For a target dollar contribution with percentage fees, price equals non-percentage variable cost plus target contribution, divided by one minus the fee rate. With fictional $25 variable costs, a $15 contribution target and a 3% fee, price is $40 ÷ 0.97 = $41.2371, rounded upward to $41.24. The price leaves $15.0028 contribution under unrounded fee arithmetic. A percentage margin target uses a different equation. With the same $25 cost, a 3% fee and a 30% contribution-margin target, price is $25 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.30) = $37.3134, or $37.32 upward. Check that the denominator is positive before applying this formula. Discounts, shipping subsidies and marketplace deductions change the actual cost boundary. Test the paid price after the promotion rather than the list price. The computed floor is a planning result, not evidence that customers will buy at that price or that the product has verified demand. For the next decision in this plan, compare Inventory Holding Cost per SKU: Price the Stock You Keep ; Inventory Reorder Point: Protect Stock and Cash Together . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. FAQs Should I price from cost or from competitors? Start from cost so you know the minimum economics of the order. Then use competitor prices to test positioning, features, shipping terms, and customer expectations; a competitor's price is context, not proof that your costs are covered. What contribution margin should an ecommerce store target? There is no universal target because fulfilment, advertising, repeat purchase rate, and fixed costs differ. Choose a margin that covers your monthly contribution requirement at a plausible order volume, then test the result against demand and capacity. Do I include my own salary in product pricing? Yes, if the store is expected to pay you. Add the monthly owner salary to fixed costs when calculating required contribution; otherwise the model can show a profit while your labour remains unpaid. How should I price when customers pay shipping? Separate the shipping charge from the product price in your model. Include the shipping revenue and the carrier cost, plus any difference you absorb, so the order's contribution reflects what actually reaches your bank account. Should discounts come out of margin or marketing budget? Either treatment can be useful, but the arithmetic must be visible. Model the discounted selling price as the price the customer pays, then include the campaign's advertising and fulfilment costs; do not label the discount as marketing while leaving the lower revenue out of the calculation. How often should I recalculate prices? Recalculate when supplier costs, carrier rates, fees, ad costs, or return rates change. A monthly review is sensible for a growing store, while a promotion or supplier change deserves a fresh calculation before it goes live. Is markup interchangeable with margin? No. Markup uses cost as its denominator, while margin uses selling price. A target margin cannot be achieved simply by adding the same percentage to cost. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
