documents.text: Restaurant PRICING GUIDE Restaurant Menu Pricing: Ingredients to Order Contribution Published September 17, 2026 Updated October 22, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Price restaurant menu items from usable portions, waste, packaging and fees. Compare order contribution, monthly targets and kitchen worker-hour capacity. Restaurant Pricing Profit Planning Restaurant owner reviewing recipe costs and menu pricing Price a menu item from its usable ingredient portions, order-related costs and the contribution it needs to leave for the restaurant. Food-cost percentage is useful, but it does not include every cost of selling the order. In the example below, a $22 dish has $6 of ingredients and leaves $11.34 after all listed variable costs and fees. That restaurant needs 1,764 comparable orders for a $2,000 monthly profit goal. The following fictional USD examples separate recipe cost, waste, packaging and compensation so the same expense is not counted twice. Quick answer Calculate ingredient cost from usable yield and portion size, then add any separate waste allowance, packaging, truly variable labor, acquisition and fees. For a chosen contribution, divide those fixed-dollar order costs plus the contribution goal by one minus the fee rate. Check that customers, menu mix and kitchen capacity support the resulting price and order target. Cost the portion the kitchen serves Start with the recipe and actual portion. Record the purchased quantity, usable yield, unit cost and number of portions. A supplier's kilogram price is not the same as the cost of a kilogram after trimming, cooking loss or unusable pieces. Suppose an ingredient costs $8 per purchased kilogram. A three-kilogram purchase costs $24. With 80% usable yield, it supplies 2.4 usable kilograms. At 0.15 kilograms per portion, that is 16 portions, making this ingredient $1.50 per serving . Compare a lower 70% yield: the same purchase supplies 2.1 kilograms, or 14 portions, and costs about $1.71 per serving. The supplier price has not changed, but each usable portion costs more. Validate the yield with kitchen records rather than a rounded guess. Repeat that calculation for the other ingredients, including sauces, garnish and oil assigned to the dish. The example's full recipe totals $6 per serving. If measured yield already includes a particular preparation loss, do not add that same loss again in a separate waste allowance. Use invoices and actual serving records from comparable periods. A bulk purchase discount may lower unit cost but also increase spoilage or cash tied in stock. Keep those effects visible rather than treating the cheapest purchase price as the cheapest usable portion. Keep food cost and full order cost separate Input for one comparable order Amount Net modeled customer price $22 Usable ingredients from the recipe $6 Separate waste allowance, beyond measured recipe yield $0.50 Packaging $1 Truly variable additional order labor $2 Acquisition cost $0.50 Payment fee 3% The $6 ingredient amount is 27.27% of the $22 price. Ingredients plus the separate waste allowance are $6.50, or 29.55%. Those are explicitly defined food-cost ratios in this example. The $10 of total direct costs before fees includes packaging, labor and acquisition too. Calling $10 ÷ $22 a food-cost ratio would hide the distinction. The payment fee adds $0.66, making full variable costs $10.66 and leaving $11.34 contribution . The $2 labor represents genuinely additional order-linked labor under the illustrative staffing arrangement. Committed payroll is in monthly overhead. If your kitchen staff are paid the same committed wages regardless of this order count, do not add another variable wage for those same hours. This guide uses one average completed order containing the modeled dish and no extra revenue. If the actual bill includes drinks or several dishes, build a consistent weighted order with all associated costs and worker-hours. Do not put a whole table's bill against one plate's ingredients. Turn the cost into a contribution-based price Suppose you want the order to leave $12 after the listed variable costs and percentage fee. The required price is ($10 + $12) ÷ 0.97 = $22.6804, rounded upward to $22.69 . At that price, contribution is $22.69 × 0.97 − $10 = $12.0093. The denominator matters because the 3% fee applies to the selling price. Adding 3% to the dollar cost does not necessarily fund a 3% deduction from the final revenue. If a fixed processor charge also applies, include it in the fixed-dollar order costs before solving. An ingredient-only approach gives a different question. With a chosen 30% ingredient-cost ratio, $6 ÷ 0.30 = $20. That tells you the price associated with that recipe-cost ratio, but it says nothing by itself about packaging, fees, payroll, rent or your income. At $20, the full example leaves $20 × 0.97 − $10 = $9.40 contribution . The dish could meet that ingredient percentage while needing far more orders to cover the restaurant. Choose the ratio and contribution target consciously, then check customer value and alternatives before adopting the price. Check the monthly plan Monthly overhead is $15,000, including the committed payroll not already in direct costs. Owner pay is $3,000, and the additional profit goal is $2,000. The required monthly contribution is therefore $20,000 . At the $22 base price, $20,000 ÷ $11.34 = 1,763.67, rounded up to 1,764 comparable orders . Revenue is $38,808. Monthly profit after owner pay is 1,764 × $11.34 − $18,000 = $2,003.76 . The operating threshold without the additional profit goal is $18,000 ÷ $11.34 = 1,587.30, rounded up to 1,588 orders. Keep the two targets labeled. Covering the bills and chosen owner pay is different from also creating the desired surplus. Four workers with 35 weekly hours and 75% delivery utilization have 455 monthly worker-hours using 52 ÷ 12 weeks. At 0.2 combined worker-hours per comparable order, the capacity ceiling is 2,275 orders . An order served by several workers can use more worker-hours than its elapsed ticket time. The 0.2-hour input means their combined work, not twelve minutes for every person separately. Kitchen stations, seats and peak service periods may impose tighter limits than this monthly worker-hour model. Compare price, waste and delivery-platform scenarios Order scenario Contribution Orders for the profit goal Base: $22 price, 3% fees $11.34 1,764 $24 price, unchanged dollar costs and 3% fees $13.28 1,507 $22 price, separate waste allowance rises by $1 $10.34 1,935 $22 price, simplified 28% combined fee assumption $5.84 3,425 The $24 case uses $24 × 0.97 − $10 = $13.28. The waste case uses $22 × 0.97 − $11 = $10.34. Both change the required volume, even before any effect on demand. The last case assumes a 25% platform fee and 3% processor fee both apply separately to the same $22 revenue base. Under that explicit simplified assumption, contribution is $22 × 0.72 − $10 = $5.84. It needs 3,425 orders, beyond the 2,275-order worker-hour ceiling. Your actual platform statement may include processing, use another charge base or apply fixed fees. Reconcile it rather than automatically adding 25% and 3%. The delivery-app commission guide handles that separate channel decision. Review menu mix before changing every price An ingredient-heavy special can lower average contribution if it becomes a large share of orders. A drink or side may lift the basket, but include its preparation, ingredients and fees. Weighted revenue without weighted costs gives a misleading result. Review collected price, product mix, waste and completed orders together. If a promotion increases covers while reducing contribution per order, calculate whether the added contribution covers the same monthly budget and any new labor commitment. The restaurant food-cost guide explains ingredient reporting, while the prime-cost guide considers food and payroll at business level. Keep those measures separate from per-order contribution instead of giving several different totals the same label. Work backward from the number of orders you can serve A desired food-cost percentage is not a substitute for the monthly contribution requirement. Use the existing example's $20,000 requirement, $10 non-fee variable cost and 3% fee. Suppose a revised staffing plan can deliver only 1,500 comparable orders and the demand estimate also supports that volume. Each order must then contribute $20,000 ÷ 1,500 = $13.3333 before monthly commitments. Same costs, different pricing question Pricing method Price calculation What it covers 30% ingredient ratio $6 ÷ 0.30 = $20 Ingredients only; leaves $9.40 full contribution $12 contribution target ($10 + $12) ÷ 0.97; round up to $22.69 Leaves $12.0093 per order $20,000 requirement over 1,500 orders ($10 + $20,000 ÷ 1,500) ÷ 0.97; round up to $24.06 Leaves $20,007.30 across 1,500 orders The last price is a feasibility floor for these assumptions, not a recommendation that customers will pay it. If demand at that price falls below 1,500 orders, recalculate. If improving capacity adds payroll, revise the cost requirement too. Keep the same order scope in every row; a cake batch, individual serving and whole customer check cannot share one unit calculation. For several dishes, use menu engineering and kitchen-time comparisons . Test a limited menu change against paid volume, contribution and service speed before applying one percentage to every item. The menu pricing calculator compares ingredient-target pricing, contribution-target pricing and the funding floor at whole monthly capacity. Start with itemized costs from the recipe calculator , then review the entered monthly scope and demand assumption. Move recipe costs into menu pricing without duplicating fees Keep the selling unit intact when moving between tools. The recipe calculator's fictional eight-unit batch has $3.20 of ingredients, $12 of batch labour and $0.25 packaging per unit. That is $0.40 ingredients + $1.50 labour + $0.25 packaging = $2.15 variable cost per unit before fees . A $4 price and 3% fee leave $1.73 contribution . For the same unit in the menu pricing calculator , enter ingredient cost $0.40, variable labour $1.50, packaging $0.25, other cost $0, price $4 and fee 3%. Do not enter $2.15 as ingredients and also add the labour and packaging; do not include the $0.12 payment fee in other costs when the percentage field already calculates it. These inputs reproduce contribution, not a monthly viability verdict. Batch labour in this illustration is treated as variable. If the same paid shift is already in monthly fixed payroll, choose a consistent alternative boundary rather than charging it twice. Enter monthly commitments and a deliverable volume separately. Use the restaurant workflow and records checklist before interpreting the funding target. How to run your own numbers Use the restaurant break-even calculator with price $22, materials $6.50 for ingredients plus the distinct waste allowance, labor $2, other variable costs $1, acquisition $0.50 and fees 3%. Add overhead $15,000, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $2,000. Set four workers, 35 weekly hours, 75% utilization and 0.2 combined worker-hours per order. Check 1,764 required orders against 2,275 capacity. Cost Builder can separate ingredients, packaging and genuinely variable labor before applying them. Keep percentage fees and acquisition in their separate fields. Other currencies are supported. Common mistakes Using purchased weight instead of usable yield when costing portions. Calling ingredients, packaging and labor together a food-cost percentage. Adding a waste allowance for a loss already included in recipe yield. Entering committed payroll again as avoidable per-order labor. Counting a platform's included processing charge twice. Comparing a whole-table receipt with one dish's cost and time. FAQs Is food-cost percentage enough to price a dish? It describes the ingredient cost relative to the price under a defined basis. It does not include every order or monthly expense. Check full contribution and monthly sales requirements alongside it. Should packaging be counted as food cost? Keep it labeled separately so the ingredient ratio stays understandable. Packaging still belongs in full order-variable cost. The distinction helps you compare eat-in and takeaway channels. How should I estimate waste? Use preparation, spoilage and service records where available. Separate a loss already included in usable recipe yield from any additional waste allowance. Do not charge for the same loss twice. Where do fixed staff wages belong? Committed payroll belongs in monthly overhead or a reconciled allocation. Truly additional order-linked wages can belong in direct cost. Choose a consistent method that agrees with your actual compensation arrangement. Can I simply add platform and payment fee percentages? Only when they are separately charged on the same revenue base. Some arrangements include processing or use different bases. Check the statement and model the actual charges once. Does the calculated price predict customer demand? No, it shows what the stated costs and contribution goal require. Customer response, competing offers and perceived value remain separate questions. Test a price and menu mix before treating the assumed order volume as realistic. Takeaways Cost usable portions rather than purchased weight alone. Label ingredient cost and full order cost separately. Reconcile payroll, waste and channel fees once. Check price against contribution, demand and operational capacity. Explore the restaurant and business planning guides for more examples. For the next decision in this plan, compare Menu Engineering: Contribution, Popularity and Kitchen Time ; Coffee Shop Drink Contribution Margin: Cost Each Cup . Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Cleaning BREAK-EVEN GUIDE Cleaning Business Break-Even: Jobs, Costs and Crew Capacity Published September 10, 2026 Updated November 10, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate the monthly cleaning jobs and revenue needed to break even after labor, supplies, travel and marketing costs. Cleaning Business Job Pricing Profit Planning Capacity A cleaning business owner reviews job schedules, costs and revenue before setting a realistic monthly break-even target. What this number really tells you A full calendar can still lose money. The useful question is whether each completed cleaning job contributes enough to cover payroll, supplies, travel, overhead and the owner's income target. Operating break-even covers the included operating costs. Adding separately entered owner pay or a profit goal produces a higher monthly planning target; include each cost once. Contribution from completed jobs must cover the chosen monthly requirement. Use actual per- job costs and realistic productive capacity, then calculate your cleaning break-even point with your own figures. What the linked calculator checks Exact jobs and revenue targets without hiding fractional results A separate whole-job operating target for real-world planning Contribution margin after supplies, cleaner labor, travel, equipment use, card fees and lead generation Required customer inquiries based on your conversion rate Team-capacity and feasibility comparison using productive hours Price sensitivity, cost-drift scenarios and a transparent formula trace What the Cleaning business calculator calculates The calculator connects unit economics, monthly financial needs, customer demand and operating capacity. It first finds contribution per job, then calculates the exact jobs and revenue required to cover overhead, owner pay and optional target profit. It also shows the rounded-up operating target, required inquiries and whether the team has enough productive capacity. Inputs to gather before you start Use recent, representative figures instead of best-case estimates. Enter average job price, supplies, direct cleaner labor, travel and equipment use, marketing cost per booked job, monthly overhead and team capacity. Keep fixed monthly overhead separate from costs that rise with each job. If a cost applies to every sale, include it in the per-job fields. Average price per cleaning job Cleaning supplies and direct labor per job Travel, laundry or equipment use per job Lead-generation cost and card fees Rent, software, insurance, vehicles and other monthly overhead Cleaner count, weekly hours, job duration, utilization and booking conversion The break-even formula Contribution per job = average price − payment fees − direct materials − direct labor − other variable costs − acquisition cost. Required jobs = (monthly overhead + owner pay + target profit) ÷ contribution per job. Exact break-even revenue = required jobs × average price. MyBreakeven keeps the exact fractional result and displays the next whole job separately. How the cleaning business break-even calculation connects contribution, required jobs , revenue and capacity. How to use the calculator step by step Select Cleaning business from the industry list. Choose the currency used by your records; the tool labels values but does not convert exchange rates. Enter price and every direct cost per job. Add monthly overhead, owner pay and optional target profit. Enter team hours, delivery time, productive utilization and inquiry conversion rate. Review exact and whole-unit targets, contribution margin, required inquiries and the capacity gap. Compare conservative and optimized scenarios before making a pricing or spending decision. Worked cleaning business example Illustrative inputs: $180 per job; $18 supplies, $58 direct labor, $12 travel/equipment, $10 acquisition and $5.22 payment fees. Total variable cost is $103.22, leaving $76.78 contribution. Monthly overhead of $3,200, owner pay of $4,500 and target profit of $1,000 give a $8,700 monthly contribution target. The exact target is 113.31 jobs and $20,395.94 revenue; round up to 114 whole jobs and $20,520.00 sales. Three workers, 35 weekly hours each, 75% productive utilization and 3.5 team labor-hours per job yield 97.50 jobs of capacity (97 whole jobs), below the target. At 30% conversion, the exact fractional target corresponds to 377.70 inquiries. These inputs are examples, not benchmarks. Set target profit to zero for a target that covers only overhead and owner pay. How to interpret feasibility A break-even target can be mathematically correct but operationally impossible. Compare required jobs with realistic productive capacity after setup, travel, administration, gaps and rework. A negative capacity gap means the current team cannot deliver the target under the assumptions entered. Test price, service mix, variable costs, utilization or staffing one change at a time. A practical monthly decision table Original fictional USD example: whole sales, inquiries and capacity Measure Calculation Result Contribution per completed job $180 − $103.22 $76.78 Monthly amount to cover $3,200 overhead + $4,500 owner pay + $1,000 goal $8,700 Practical sales target Round 8,700 ÷ 76.78 upward 114 jobs Qualified inquiries at 30% Round 114 ÷ 0.30 upward 380 inquiries Available whole-job capacity Round 97.50 downward 97 jobs Contribution at available capacity 97 × $76.78 $7,447.66 Shortfall against the stated monthly goal $8,700 − $7,447.66 $1,252.34 Use a complete job cost without counting payroll twice The example variable cost is $103.22: $18 supplies, $58 job labor, $12 travel/equipment, $10 acquisition allowance and $5.22 payment fees. Subtracting it from $180 gives $76.78 contribution. A fixed vehicle commitment belongs in monthly overhead; a genuine extra-mile running cost can belong in job cost. Include each expense once. The $4,500 owner-pay amount is a separate planning requirement here. If that same compensation is already in overhead or direct labor, remove the duplicate before calculating. The $1,000 profit goal is additional to those commitments, so 114 jobs is a target including owner pay and that goal, rather than a claim of zero operating profit. Plan bookings from whole jobs, not a rounded fractional lead count The mathematical 113.31-job target corresponds to about 377.70 inquiries at 30% conversion. Operational planning instead begins with 114 complete jobs: 114 ÷ 0.30 = 380 qualified inquiries. This is an assumption about the sales funnel, not a prediction that 380 people will enquire or that every booking will be completed. Keep recurring and first-time work separate when acquisition spending differs. The $10 per-job allowance must represent the chosen mix and period; do not charge the full cost of acquiring one new customer again on every recurring visit. Reconcile the acquisition budget to actual new customers and repeat jobs. What to change when the crew can deliver only 97 jobs The stated capacity supports 97 whole jobs, leaving a 17-job gap to the 114-job target. At the original price and variable cost, 97 jobs contribute $7,447.66 and miss the $8,700 monthly goal by $1,252.34. That shortfall is against a requirement already containing owner pay and a profit goal; it should not automatically be called an accounting loss. Check route time, cleaning scope, cancellations and paid team-hours before assuming another worker solves the gap. Hiring may increase guaranteed payroll and therefore the target. Recalculate both the required jobs and capacity after changing staffing, price or scope. Two cleaners working 1.75 hours use 3.5 worker-hours per job. Compare estimated and actual cleaning job costs Review the minimum charge for a cleaning visit Common mistakes to avoid Treating all cleaner payroll as fixed when labor changes by job Omitting travel time, laundry, supplies or equipment wear Using total leads instead of qualified booking inquiries Assuming every paid hour is available for billable cleaning Ways to improve the result Focus on the assumptions with the largest verified effect rather than changing every input at once. Review route density, job minimums, recurring-client mix, cleaner utilization, supply control and quote-to-booking conversion. Recalculate after each change and preserve a conservative scenario so the plan does not depend on perfect conditions. Check the price change against the existing capacity limit The worked example needs $8,700 of monthly contribution and has capacity for 97.50 jobs. At the original $76.78 contribution per job, 97 whole jobs provide $7,447.66, leaving a $1,252.34 gap. The next question is which input can change without overloading the crew. In a separate sensitivity, raise price from $180 to $195 while holding the stated non-fee variable costs at $98 and the card fee at 2.9%. The fee becomes $5.655 and contribution $91.345. Required jobs are $8,700 ÷ $91.345 = 95.24, rounded up to 96. At 96 jobs contribution is $8,769.12, or $69.12 above the stated target. This fits the 97-whole-job capacity assumption, but does not prove customers will accept the price or that job duration will stay constant. Retain full precision until the final display. If supplies, crew time or acquisition costs rise with the higher-priced scope, revise them too. Setting the $1,000 target profit to zero answers a different question; it should not silently replace the original owner-pay-and-profit plan. Review the scope behind your house-cleaning quote Frequently asked questions What does the Cleaning business break-even calculator include? It includes price, direct costs, payment fees, acquisition cost, monthly overhead, owner pay, target profit, required jobs, inquiries and productive capacity. Why are exact and whole jobs different? The exact result preserves the mathematical fraction. The whole-unit target rounds up because selling only part of a job is usually not operationally possible. Does the calculator predict guaranteed profit? No. It produces an assumption-based planning estimate. Actual sales, costs, cancellations, taxes and timing can differ. How often should the calculation be updated? Update it whenever price, wages, supplier costs, advertising performance, overhead or team capacity changes materially, and review it at least monthly during active planning. documents.text: Landscaping BREAK-EVEN GUIDE How to Do Break-Even Analysis for a Landscaping Business Published September 10, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate landscaping break-even jobs from price, costs and crew capacity. Test a whole-job shortfall, price-sensitive fees and added staffing costs. Compare 20 fictional landscaping scenarios and download their inputs . Landscaping Lawn Care Crew Capacity Job Costing A landscaping team checks job profitability and route capacity before committing crew time and equipment. What this number really tells you To do break-even analysis for a landscaping business, subtract job-level costs from your average job price, then divide monthly fixed overhead by the contribution left per job. Round up to a whole job and check whether your crew can deliver that volume. Add owner pay and target profit separately when planning the income you want the business to support. Operating break-even covers the included operating costs. Adding separately entered owner pay or a profit goal produces a higher monthly planning target; include each cost once. Contribution from completed jobs must cover the chosen monthly requirement. Use actual per- job costs and realistic productive capacity, then calculate your landscaping break-even point with your own figures. What the linked calculator checks Separate fixed overhead from job-level costs Calculate contribution with a transparent worked example Distinguish operating break-even from owner pay and profit goals Check seasonal demand against crew labor-hour capacity How to do landscaping break-even analysis step by step Use completed-job records and a representative month. The figures below are illustrative USD assumptions, not market prices or industry benchmarks. Choose one service or calculate a weighted average using the mix of jobs you actually sell. List monthly fixed overhead, such as insurance, storage, software and fixed vehicle commitments. Calculate costs that change per job: materials, direct labor, fuel, equipment use, acquisition and payment fees. Subtract those variable costs from the average job price to find contribution per job. Divide monthly overhead by contribution, then round up the required jobs. Add owner pay and optional profit as separate planning goals, then compare the target with crew capacity and seasonal demand. Inputs to gather before you start Choose a completed visit, an installation project or a billable worker-hour as the unit before collecting costs. Use invoices and paid crew records from the same representative month. Fixed payroll remains monthly overhead when it does not change with the next job; job-dependent crew wages belong in direct cost. Do not count either amount twice. Match landscaping records to the calculation Record Input Check Completed visits and invoices Collected or consistently accrued price per completed unit Separate maintenance visits from larger installations. Crew time and loaded payroll Paid labor cost and total worker-hours per unit Two workers for 2.5 hours consume five worker-hours. Material, fuel and disposal records Job-dependent cost per unit Use quantities consumed; keep stock purchases and cash timing separate. Equipment and vehicle commitments Monthly overhead or usage-dependent job cost Follow the expense boundary; track loan principal separately in cash planning. Route and workable-day records Productive utilization and delivery hours Do not deduct the same travel or weather downtime twice. Average landscaping or lawn-care job price Plants, materials and direct field labor Fuel, disposal and equipment use per job Sales or lead cost per booked job Vehicles, rent, insurance, software and monthly equipment costs Crew size, weekly hours, job duration, utilization and close rate The formula: operating break-even versus your income target Contribution per job = average price − total variable cost per job. Operating break-even jobs = monthly fixed overhead ÷ contribution per job. An owner-pay and profit target uses (fixed overhead + owner pay + target profit) ÷ contribution instead. Round up only after calculating the full result. Count each expense once. If owner field labor is already included in direct labor per job, do not add that same labor again as owner pay. Include only additional compensation you want the business to support. Keep fixed advertising spend in overhead or allocate it per booked job, without counting the same spend twice. How the landscaping business break-even calculation connects contribution, required jobs , revenue and capacity. Worked example: a $320 landscaping job Assume a $320 average job price. Materials are $62, direct labor $96, fuel and equipment use $24, and acquisition $18 per completed job. A 2.9% payment fee adds $9.28. Total variable cost is $209.28, leaving $110.72 contribution per job. With $4,800 monthly overhead, operating break-even is $4,800 ÷ $110.72 = 43.35 jobs. Round up to 44 jobs, producing $14,080 in sales and $4,871.68 in contribution. That covers overhead under these assumptions; it does not also cover the separate owner-pay goal. Adding $5,000 in owner pay raises the monthly need to $9,800: $9,800 ÷ $110.72 = 88.51, rounded up to 89 jobs. Adding a further $1,500 profit goal raises the need to $11,300: 102.06 jobs, rounded up to 103 jobs and $32,960 in sales. The unrounded revenue target is $32,658.96. Four workers at 38 hours weekly, 52 ÷ 12 weeks per model month and 72% productive utilization supply 474.24 productive labor-hours. At five total worker-hours per job, capacity is 94.85 jobs, or 94 whole jobs. A two-person crew working 2.5 hours uses five worker-hours. The 103-job target exceeds this capacity; the 89-job owner-pay target fits the estimate but still needs demand and weather checks. Turn the capacity gap into a whole-job decision The worked example above requires 103 whole jobs but estimates capacity at 94.85 jobs. Under that job-duration assumption, only 94 complete jobs fit. The gap is nine whole jobs, not the rounded difference between two fractional figures. Do not round available capacity up simply because the decimal is close to the next job. At 94 jobs and $110.72 contribution per job, monthly contribution is 94 × $110.72 = $10,407.68. Against the $11,300 financial need, the shortfall is $892.32. This remains an illustrative USD model, not a revenue forecast or an industry benchmark. In practical terms, your current crew can complete the available jobs and still finish short of the monthly goal. Financial need means the overhead, owner pay and target profit included in this scenario. More inquiries alone do not close a gap caused by a full crew schedule. One response is to increase contribution enough for 94 jobs to cover the target. The required contribution is $11,300 ÷ 94 = $120.2128, so a two-decimal planning target of $120.22 provides a small rounding buffer. If the entire $209.28 variable cost stayed unchanged, a $329.50 price would leave $120.22 contribution. But that condition does not hold when a payment fee rises with the price. For a separate fee-sensitive scenario consistent with the same starting totals, suppose the $209.28 contains a 2.9% fee on the original $320 price. That fee is $9.28, leaving $200 of other variable costs. Keeping those other costs unchanged, solve (price × 0.971) − $200 = $120.22. The result is $329.7837, rounded up to $329.79. Contribution is approximately $120.23 after the fee, which is enough for the 94-job target. The 2.9% is a stated assumption, not a claim about your processor. Compare operational changes before adding a crew A higher-contribution scenario can close the financial gap without making more hours available. A route or scheduling change can instead raise deliverable jobs, but only if measured travel, setup or downtime actually falls. Keep these as separate scenarios so the model shows which change is responsible for the result. At the original $110.72 contribution, delivering 103 jobs produces $11,404.16, leaving $104.16 above the $11,300 target. That would require capacity to rise from 94.85 to at least 103 jobs under the original duration assumptions: about an 8.59% increase in modeled output. Check actual paid crew hours and route records before treating that improvement as available. If a schedule change only supports 100 whole jobs, contribution is $11,072 and the remaining gap is $228. It helps, but does not fully meet the target. A partial improvement should not be described as solving break-even merely because capacity increased. Now consider a separate staffing scenario that brings an additional $900 monthly fixed cost. The financial need becomes $12,200. If contribution remains $110.72, required output becomes $12,200 ÷ $110.72 = 110.19 jobs, rounded up to 111. The added staffing must support that revised target, with demand to match. Keeping the old 103-job target after adding the cost would understate the requirement. Weather also changes the schedule. Use the number of workable days for the month you are testing and avoid promising jobs that need unavailable conditions. If fixed payroll continues during downtime, put it in the monthly boundary consistently rather than assuming it disappears with a cancelled visit. Before adopting a scenario, compare price acceptance, sold workload, material costs, job duration and inquiries. The calculator can trace the arithmetic, but your completed-job records establish whether the inputs are credible. Preserve a conservative case alongside the improved case so the plan does not require perfect routing or every quote to close. How to interpret feasibility A break-even target can be mathematically correct but operationally impossible. Compare required jobs with realistic productive capacity after setup, travel, administration, gaps and rework. A negative capacity gap means the current team cannot deliver the target under the assumptions entered. Test price, service mix, variable costs, utilization or staffing one change at a time. Common mistakes to avoid Ignoring seasonal downtime and weather disruption Leaving fuel, disposal or equipment wear out of job cost Using crew clock hours as fully productive hours Mixing one-time installation jobs with recurring maintenance without a weighted average Ways to improve the result Focus on the assumptions with the largest verified effect rather than changing every input at once. Improve route density, minimum visit pricing, crew scheduling, maintenance-plan mix and material markups supported by actual costs. Recalculate after each change and preserve a conservative scenario so the plan does not depend on perfect conditions. Use the analysis for seasonal lawn care and mixed services For comparable maintenance visits, use a job-weighted price and cost. For unlike services, a revenue-weighted contribution ratio can be clearer. In a separate illustrative month, maintenance produces $18,000 sales and $10,800 variable costs; installations produce $12,000 sales and $8,400 variable costs. Contributions are $7,200 and $3,600: total $10,800 on $30,000 sales, or 36%. At $6,000 shared monthly fixed overhead, operating break-even revenue is $6,000 ÷ 0.36 = $16,666.67 when displayed to cents. This revenue threshold assumes the same service mix, prices and cost behavior. A simple average of the service ratios, 40% and 30%, would give 35% and represent a different mix. Do not add separate full-overhead break-even targets for each service. Test a slow-season month separately. If sales fall 20% to $24,000 at the same 36% contribution ratio, contribution becomes $8,640; after $6,000 overhead, the modeled result is $2,640. If mix, guaranteed payroll or job cost changes, update those inputs too. A yearly average can hide a month with too little cash or too few workable crew hours. Translate a landscaping sales target into crew hours For landscaping, a job target needs a compatible crew-hour model. Two workers delivering a four-hour visit consume eight worker-hours. If the team has 240 productive worker-hours for the month, capacity is 30 such visits before other constraints. Counting four hours per job would incorrectly double the apparent capacity. Suppose a visit leaves $180 contribution and monthly commitments total $5,400. The financial requirement is 30 visits. The hour model also allows 30, leaving no planned cushion for unexpected work. If average delivery rises to nine worker-hours, capacity falls to 26.6667 visits, or 26 whole visits. The price-and-cost plan still requires 30. Include paid travel according to the chosen delivery and labor boundary, and avoid counting it twice as both route time and an unexplained surcharge. Equipment, disposal and material costs should follow the job's actual scope. Quote assumptions are not proof that the crew can deliver the route or that customers will book the required volume. How to do break-even analysis for a landscaping business Use one complete job or a consistently weighted mix of maintenance visits and installation projects. Record net job price, materials, paid crew labor, travel, equipment use, fees and booked-job acquisition before calculating contribution. Check that the labor and editing amounts refer to different costs. If editing labor is already in the $140, do not charge it again inside the $45. The $9,100 monthly requirement includes $2,900 overhead, $5,000 owner pay and a $1,200 profit goal. A guaranteed assistant salary may remain a monthly commitment even when bookings fall; job-paid assistant time can vary by session. Your contract and actual cost behavior determine the classification. Do not use a simple average of a short portrait package and a multi-day commercial assignment. Model separate package scenarios or use a realistic weighted mix. A higher price can improve contribution but may change conversion; a faster editing workflow can release time but may add outsourcing cost. documents.text: Mobile Detailing PROFITABILITY GUIDE Mobile Detailing Break-Even: Jobs, Route Costs and Capacity Published September 10, 2026 Updated October 7, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate mobile detailing break-even from job contribution, route travel and worker-hours. Compare price changes, service scope and monthly capacity. Mobile Detailing Route Planning Service Pricing Technician Capacity A mobile detailing owner reviews bookings, route density and job profitability beside an equipped service van. Mobile detailing break-even is the number of completed jobs whose contribution covers the monthly costs and income goals you enter. Calculate contribution after supplies, direct labor, travel, acquisition and fees, then compare the required jobs with the route you can deliver. A revenue target alone cannot show whether there are enough working hours or suitable customer locations. This updated guide uses fictional USD examples and explicit route assumptions; the figures are not current market rates or a forecast of bookings. Quick answer: Subtract all job-variable costs and percentage fees from the average job price. Divide monthly overhead, additional owner pay and target profit by that contribution. With $220 price and $83.40 contribution, a $6,000 monthly need requires 71.94 jobs, rounded up to seventy-two. If the team can finish only fifty-three, the financial target is not operationally feasible under those assumptions. Calculate the job contribution first Start with one defined service. Record the vehicle scope, travel area, expected staff time and consumables. An interior-only appointment and a preparation-heavy coating package need different estimates. Use recorded completion time and invoices to replace the illustrative allowances below. Suppose a routine mobile job sells for $220. Supplies cost $25, direct labor $70, travel and equipment use $20, and customer acquisition allocation $15. Non-fee variable expense is $130. A 3% collection fee is $6.60. Contribution is $220 − $130 − $6.60 = $83.40, or 37.91% of revenue. Contribution is the amount available to fund the monthly business. It is not net profit on the invoice. If your technician wage remains payable even when a job is cancelled, classify that committed payroll in the monthly model instead of assuming it disappears with every unsold appointment. Monthly funding line Assumed amount Operating overhead $2,000 Additional owner compensation $3,000 Target profit $1,000 Total contribution need $6,000 Divide $6,000 by $83.40 to get 71.9424 jobs. Round up to seventy-two whole jobs. Seventy-one contribute $5,921.40 and leave a $78.60 gap. Seventy-two contribute $6,004.80 and cover the stated need by $4.80. Practical revenue at that target is $15,840. The break-even boundary matters. Overhead-only break-even in this example is $2,000 ÷ $83.40 = 23.9808 jobs, rounded up to twenty-four. That keeps the stated operating commitments funded but does not support the additional owner-income and profit goals. Say which target you mean when describing the business as breaking even. Put driving and setup into the same time boundary Assume two workers, thirty-five scheduled weekly hours each and 70% productive utilization. The calculator uses 52 ÷ 12 weeks per month, producing 212.3333 productive worker-hours. At four total delivery worker-hours per completed job, capacity is 53.0833 jobs, rounded down to fifty-three. Fifty-three jobs contribute $4,420.20, leaving a $1,579.80 gap against the $6,000 need. The seventy-two-job funding target does not fit. More inquiries cannot fix this unchanged delivery constraint. You need to test price, scope, cost or usable capacity rather than simply increase the sales target. Use worker-hours consistently. Two people spending ninety minutes on site use three worker-hours. If both also spend thirty minutes on the job's travel and setup, the total becomes four worker-hours. Do not enter two elapsed hours as the total labor requirement for a two-person crew. You can include route travel inside delivery hours, or reserve a separate allowance when estimating productive utilization. Choose one boundary and explain it. If you subtract travel from available hours and include it again in every delivery estimate, capacity will be understated. If neither boundary includes it, capacity will be overstated. What changes the result Route density changes driving expense and working time. Nearby appointments can share a route, while distant bookings may need a minimum travel charge or narrower service area. Compare actual grouped routes rather than assuming each appointment has the same drive. Service mix changes contribution and hours. A premium invoice can use disproportionately more time. The ceramic-coating margin guide checks preparation-heavy packages separately, and the car-detailing price-list guide helps distinguish routine service scopes. Acquisition changes with the customer relationship. A new one-time customer may require paid selling expense that a repeat booking does not. Keep initial acquisition and repeat-service costs identifiable, then test the supported mix rather than applying the new-customer amount blindly to every job. Fees also change the target. Use the actual fee basis and include fixed transaction charges where relevant. This example uses one simple 3% rate and no fixed component. The rate is a chosen assumption, not a claim about your payment provider. Compare three practical changes First, raise price to $260 while keeping the original $130 non-fee cost and four worker-hours. Fees become $7.80 and contribution $122.20. The $6,000 need requires 49.0998 jobs, rounded up to fifty. Fifty contribute $6,110 and fit the fifty-three-job aggregate capacity. Buyer acceptance and unchanged scope still need evidence. Second, keep the $220 price but improve the route so other variable expense falls from $20 to $15 and delivery time falls from four to three worker-hours. Contribution becomes $88.40. Required jobs are 67.8733, rounded up to sixty-eight. Capacity rises to 70.7778 jobs, rounded down to seventy. This case fits only if the claimed travel and time improvements are real. Third, keep the original price and cost but add a third worker who can perform the same delivery tasks and has compatible equipment. Three workers at thirty-five hours and 70% utilization create 318.5 productive hours, or 79.625 four-hour jobs. The capacity rises to seventy-nine complete jobs. Before accepting the result, add any new committed expense and confirm a suitable vehicle, tools and locations are available. These are isolated tests. Combining all favorable assumptions would create a different scenario and require recalculation. Do not add a worker without costing the commitment, or raise price while pretending no customer changes behavior. Check bookings and leads separately At an illustrative 30% inquiry-to-booking conversion, the original fractional financial target needs 239.81 inquiries, rounded up to 240. Seventy-two whole bookings divided by 30% is exactly 240. That does not mean every set of 240 inquiries will produce seventy-two completed jobs; cancellations and conversion variability remain outside this simple average. Use distinct records for inquiries, booked appointments and completed paid work. Revenue comes from the modeled completed jobs. If demand already exceeds the deliverable schedule, more leads may worsen delays instead of closing the funding gap. Review maintenance-plan pricing when repeat bookings share the route. How to run your own numbers Enter price $220, materials $25, direct labor $70, travel/water/equipment expense $20, acquisition $15 and payment fees 3%. Clear unused presets. Enter $2,000 overhead, $3,000 additional owner pay and $1,000 profit target. The labor line contains delivery wages only; it does not include the separate owner-income goal in this example. Set two active workers, thirty-five weekly hours each, 70% utilization, four total delivery worker-hours per job and 30% inquiry conversion. The mobile detailing break-even calculator reproduces $83.40 contribution, seventy-two required whole jobs and fifty-three whole-job capacity. It supports other currencies. Save the original assumptions before changing price or time. Then adjust one input and record what changed in funding and capacity. Keep a separate route calendar for actual locations and appointment times; the calculator's monthly aggregate does not prove a workable daily sequence. Common mistakes Comparing a whole-business income target with overhead-only break-even. Entering crew-clock time instead of total worker-hours. Omitting travel from both the job duration and the utilization boundary. Adding employees without adding equipment or their committed expense. Treating inquiries, bookings and completed jobs as the same count. FAQs Does positive contribution mean each job is profitable? It means the job adds money toward the stated fixed commitments. Monthly profit depends on completing enough jobs to cover those commitments and the other included goals. Why does the calculator show fractional jobs? The fractional value shows the exact financial threshold. You generally need to round required complete jobs up and available complete-job capacity down for the operating plan. Should travel time count as productive time? Use a clearly stated boundary. If delivery hours include travel, use a compatible utilization assumption; do not subtract the same travel hours a second time. What if I do the detailing myself? Assign a chosen direct delivery wage for management decisions, or explicitly place your compensation in the monthly model. Avoid both omitting your labor and paying the same wage twice in the example. Can I combine routine jobs and coating packages? Yes, but use the actual service mix and total worker-hours. A single average can conceal a few long jobs that fill the schedule, so check each service's scope before averaging. What should I change when the target exceeds capacity? Test supported changes in price, scope, job-variable cost or delivery resources. Adding demand alone does not create working hours, equipment or usable customer locations. Takeaways Calculate contribution before choosing a monthly job target. Include route time through one consistent boundary. Compare rounded required jobs with rounded capacity. Track qualified demand and completed bookings separately. Find related examples in the small-business guide library . Check the next planning steps: How to Price a Fleet Detailing Contract and How Many Detailing Jobs Per Week to Go Full Time? . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: E-commerce PROFITABILITY GUIDE Ecommerce Break-Even: Net Orders, Costs and Capacity Published September 10, 2026 Updated October 12, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate ecommerce break-even after product, shipping, returns and ad costs. Reproduce verified calculator inputs and check demand and packing capacity. Ecommerce COGS Customer Acquisition Fulfillment An e-commerce founder evaluates order economics, shipping and fulfillment performance at an active workspace. Ecommerce break-even starts with what one completed order leaves after product cost, fulfillment, shipping, acquisition, returns-related costs and fees. Divide the monthly funding requirement by that contribution and round up to whole orders. In this fictional store, a $60 order contributes $18.20; covering $1,000 overhead, $2,000 owner pay and $500 extra profit needs 193 orders. The next check is whether fulfillment hours and customer demand support them. All figures are USD assumptions, not ecommerce benchmarks or forecasts. Quick answer Use one consistent order unit and a net selling price after discounts. Subtract product and order-related costs, including acquisition and payment fees, to find contribution. Divide overhead plus owner pay plus target profit by that amount, rounding up. Then check fulfillment workload, traffic assumptions and inventory cash separately from the operating result. Cost the same order on both sides Assume one order sells for $60 before any pass-through tax. The product costs $22 including the inventory cost allocated to goods sold. Incremental paid fulfillment labor costs $3. Packaging and shipping paid by the store cost $7, unrecovered return-handling costs average an assumed $2, and acquisition costs $6 per completed order. Non-percentage variable cost is $22 + $3 + $7 + $2 + $6 = $40. Payment processing is modeled at 3% of the $60 service revenue, or $1.80. Contribution is $60 − $40 − $1.80 = $18.20 per order, a 30.33% contribution ratio. The $2 return line in this example covers separate unrecovered handling expense. The model assumes the $60 net selling value and the $22 product cost are already reconciled consistently to the order basis. It does not deduct the same refunded revenue or recoverable stock twice. If your order history includes refunds, build a reconciled average first rather than adding a refund percentage to an unreconciled gross ticket. Monthly overhead is $1,000, owner pay is $2,000 and the additional profit goal is $500. Total contribution required is $3,500. At $18.20 per order, 192 orders contribute $3,494.40 and miss the goal by $5.60. One hundred ninety-three orders contribute $3,512.60. Sales at that volume are 193 × $60 = $11,580. After $1,000 overhead and $2,000 owner pay, the result is $512.60 before taxes and unmodeled expenses. Its owner-paid planning margin is $512.60 ÷ $11,580 = 4.43%, much lower than the order contribution ratio of 30.33%. If you only want to cover operating overhead, the model needs 55 orders because 55 × $18.20 = $1,001. Including owner pay needs 165 orders, and adding the $500 target raises it to 193. Name the threshold you mean by break-even rather than switching between those three questions. Keep product, order and customer units separate This example is one average completed order, not one product sold or one new customer. A basket can contain multiple products, and a customer can place several orders. Put revenue and product cost on the same order basis before dividing the monthly requirement. An acquisition figure per new customer needs a stated conversion into the chosen order period. Do not spread it over an unlimited assumed customer lifetime. If you use $6 per completed order, explain which orders and marketing spend produced that figure. Keep a committed monthly marketing budget outside the same acquisition line when it is already included in overhead. Shipping charged to the customer should be handled consistently. Include the shipping revenue you retain and the actual shipping expense, or use a reconciled net shipping subsidy. Do not use both treatments on the same order. The shipping-cost guide explores that boundary. The return cost-per-order guide helps separate refunded revenue, recovered stock and unrecovered handling. Those records are needed before an average order can support a meaningful monthly estimate. Four variables that move the order requirement Net basket value. Discounts change what the customer actually pays. Keep product cost unchanged unless the basket itself changes. A percentage payment fee should be recalculated on the actual fee base rather than left at the original ticket amount. Acquisition. An order that costs more to obtain leaves less for the month. Track the chosen order and customer boundary. A return customer may have different acquisition economics, but those savings should be measured rather than assumed for every order. Fulfillment and shipping. Packing time, carrier expense and parcel size can vary with mix. An apparently better basket may require a more expensive parcel or additional labor. Count that change before treating higher sales as higher contribution. Monthly commitments and capacity. Rent, storage, software and committed payroll change the required contribution. A new fulfillment hire or larger storage contract can add a step in fixed cost. Test the new requirement, not only the previous per-order margin. Keep owner labor consistent. This example uses paid fulfillment labor distinct from the $2,000 owner income goal. If the owner performs that same packing work, choose a single compensation treatment and retain all packing hours in capacity. Three worked store scenarios A $6 discount on the same basket Price falls from $60 to $54 while the $40 non-percentage cost stays unchanged. The fee is $1.62. Contribution becomes $54 − $40 − $1.62 = $12.38. Funding $3,500 needs 283 orders, because 282 contribute $3,491.16 and 283 contribute $3,503.54. Required order volume rises by 90 compared with 193 at the original price. Whether the discount can create those extra orders needs demand evidence; the arithmetic alone cannot establish that outcome. Acquisition increases from $6 to $10 Non-percentage cost rises to $44. At the original $60 price, contribution becomes $60 × 0.97 − $44 = $14.20. Funding $3,500 requires 247 orders; 246 contribute $3,493.20 and 247 contribute $3,507.40. The extra $4 acquisition cost raises the order target by 54. The break-even ROAS guide isolates advertising economics for a defined basket. Use the complete store model as well so a campaign threshold is not mistaken for owner-paid monthly profit. Packing time rises from 0.25 to 0.4 hours Suppose paid packing labor is $12 per worker-hour. The baseline 0.25 hours cost $3. At 0.4 hours, paid labor costs $4.80, increasing non-percentage cost to $41.80. Contribution becomes $60 × 0.97 − $41.80 = $16.40. The funding target needs 214 orders, since 213 contribute $3,493.20 and 214 contribute $3,509.60. Capacity also changes. One fulfillment worker with 20 weekly hours at 75% utilization has 65 usable monthly worker-hours. At 0.25 hours, that supports 260 whole orders; at 0.4 hours, it supports only 162. Thus the 214-order financial requirement cannot fit the revised 162-order workload ceiling. At 162 orders, contribution is $2,656.80 and the result after $3,000 overhead and owner pay is a $343.20 shortfall. Faster work, additional hours, outsourcing or a different basket changes the model and its costs. Translate orders into demand without calling it a forecast If the original 193-order target is spread across 26 fulfillment days, it averages 7.42 completed orders per day. That average does not describe peak days or dispatch cutoffs. Review actual daily volume before relying on it as a staffing plan. With a hypothetical 2% purchase conversion from qualified site visits, 193 orders require 9,650 visits. This is a scenario using a chosen conversion assumption, not a benchmark or a prediction of traffic. The store still needs evidence for traffic source, conversion and repeated orders. Inventory cash is another separate check. The $22 product cost represents goods sold. Buying 300 units at $22 uses $6,600 cash before those units necessarily sell. Do not deduct the purchase again from the contribution of those same goods. Keep supplier payment dates, stock recovery and reorder timing in a cash schedule. Check the same order basis across channels Reconcile these records before comparing channels Record Use in the model Boundary Order and refund export Consistent retained revenue and completed order count Keep canceled and refunded orders identifiable. Payment or marketplace settlement Actual percentage and fixed fees Do not add processing again if already bundled. Carrier, fulfillment and return records Net merchant-paid costs for the same order mix Reconcile reimbursements and recovered stock. Campaign and acquisition records Acquisition cost assigned to the modeled orders Do not also include that same spend in overhead. Shopify's break-even explanation supplies the basic fixed-cost and unit-contribution relationship. The store examples here separately include shipping, acquisition and owner-pay assumptions. Replace USD inputs with consistent local figures when working in another country; the calculator does not supply exchange rates or local fee schedules. For an advertising decision, compare the break-even ROAS calculation . For damaged returns and unrecovered delivery costs, use the return-cost-per-order guide . Neither an ad-return ratio nor a positive unit contribution proves that monthly overhead is covered. How to run your own numbers Use the ecommerce break-even calculator with $60 price, $22 product cost, $3 labor, $9 other variable costs and $6 acquisition, plus a 3% fee. Enter $1,000 overhead, $2,000 owner pay and $500 target profit. For capacity use one worker, 20 weekly hours, 75% utilization and 0.25 worker-hours per order. It requires 193 orders and permits 260. Other currencies are supported. Use your own conversion assumption; the model does not forecast traffic, inventory balances or parcel-level queues. Reproduce the ecommerce calculator example This is an actual MyBreakeven calculator demonstration captured on October 12, 2026, using illustrative USD inputs. It is not a customer case study, an industry average or a prediction. Open the calculator linked under “How to run your own numbers”, choose Reset example , and compare every input with the table. If presets change later, enter these values manually. Inputs used for the captured demonstration (USD amounts; other units are in the field labels) Calculator field Value Average price per order ($) 86 Materials / product cost per order ($) 29 Direct labor per order ($) 7 Shipping subsidy + returns allowance ($) 9 Paid acquisition cost per order ($) 13 Monthly operating overhead ($) 7,800 Monthly owner pay ($) 5,000 Target monthly profit ($) 2,000 Payment and platform fees (%) 3.2 Active team members 3 Hours per team member / week (hrs) 35 Delivery hours per order (hrs) 0.28 Productive utilization (%) 78 Inquiry-to-order conversion (%) 2.8 The percentage fee is calculated from price. $86 × 3.2% = $2.752; contribution is $86 − $29 − $7 − $9 − $13 − $2.752 = $25.248. The screen rounds this to $25.25, but the calculation retains full precision. Verified output from the same inputs Result Value Monthly amount to cover $14,800.00 Exact required volume 586.19 orders Whole-unit target 587 orders Sales at whole-unit target $50,482.00 Whole-unit delivery capacity 1,267 orders Inquiries for whole-unit target 20,965 Actual calculator screen, October 12, 2026. The displayed amounts come from the illustrative inputs above. The model has room for 587 orders within its 1,267-order monthly capacity. That does not prove demand, inventory availability or sufficient dispatch capacity on peak days. At the assumed 2.8% conversion, the target requires 20,965 inquiries. Use measured qualified visits and conversion for your own store; this number is not a traffic forecast. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 ÷ 12 × productive utilization ÷ worker-hours per order. Required volume rounds up; deliverable volume rounds down. Owner pay and the extra profit goal are included in this target. Set both to zero only when checking overhead-only operating break-even. Common mistakes Using a product price with costs from a multi-product order. Calling contribution margin final profit before overhead and owner pay. Deducting refunded sales twice through revenue and a returns allowance. Spreading acquisition across an unsupported lifetime order count. Treating inventory purchases and the same goods sold as two operating costs. FAQs Should I use gross sales or net sales? Use a consistently reconciled selling value after customer discounts and refunded sales. Keep pass-through tax outside revenue available to fund the business. Match the product and return-cost treatment to the same basis. Does break-even include owner pay? Only if you include it in the requirement. This example shows overhead-only, owner-paid and additional-profit thresholds separately. State which target the order count supports. Can I use average order value? Yes, when the matching average costs describe the same order mix and period. Recalculate when baskets, channels or returns change materially. An average can hide a negative-contribution product or channel. What if contribution is zero or negative? Additional orders cannot fund positive monthly commitments under that unchanged model. Revise price, product cost, shipping, acquisition or scope before increasing volume. Check the resulting demand and workload again. Is fulfillment capacity a sales forecast? No, it is a ceiling under the entered hours and time assumptions. Demand, stock availability and peak dispatch timing need separate evidence. A monthly ceiling can still hide busy-day bottlenecks. Can a profitable store run short of cash? Yes, inventory purchases and other payments can precede customer receipts. Contribution does not show those dates. Keep a cash schedule alongside the order model. Takeaways Match net revenue and costs to one consistent order unit. Label overhead, owner pay and additional-profit thresholds. Recalculate fees, contribution and hours when the basket changes. Keep demand evidence and inventory cash beside the operating model. Browse the business planning guides for related examples. Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

documents.text: Restaurant PROFITABILITY GUIDE Restaurant Break-Even: Orders, Costs and Service Capacity Published September 10, 2026 Updated October 7, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate restaurant break-even orders from food, labor and channel costs. Separate owner pay from overhead, then check kitchen capacity and fees. Restaurant Finance Food Cost Order Volume Kitchen Capacity A restaurant owner reviews food costs, order volume and revenue before the next service period. Restaurant break-even is the order volume needed for contribution from sales to cover the costs you include in the monthly plan. Calculate what an average order leaves after food, relevant labor, packaging, commissions and fees, then divide the financial need by that contribution. Finally, check whether the kitchen and service team can deliver the required orders. A busy dining room alone cannot answer either question. The USD figures below are fictional examples, not restaurant-industry averages. Quick answer: At a $34 average order and $23.59 variable cost, contribution is $10.41. A $24,500 overhead-only target needs 2,354 whole orders. Adding $6,000 owner pay and $3,000 target profit raises the goal to 3,219 orders. The example team’s aggregate capacity supports only 2,852, so the larger goal does not fit the current assumptions. Separate operating break-even from the owner-pay target An order contributes the amount left after costs assigned to that order. It is not the same as the restaurant’s final profit. The SBA’s break-even framework divides fixed costs by contribution per unit; here the unit is one representative completed order. Start with a consistent monthly period and a sales mix you can support. Use revenue belonging to the restaurant under your chosen accounting boundary, rather than simply treating every dollar passing through a payment terminal as revenue. Keep the treatment of sales tax, gratuities, refunds and pass-through charges explicit in your source records. This example uses the following order economics: Item Per order Average order revenue $34.00 Ingredients $10.50 Direct order labor $8.50 Packaging and other order expenses $2.20 Promotion cost per completed order $1.20 Payment fee at an assumed 3.5% $1.19 Contribution $10.41 The $8.50 labor allowance must fit your payroll boundary. Include only the payroll assigned through this per-order model, then reconcile the remaining committed payroll in monthly overhead. If your entire payroll is fixed for the planned volume, a different fixed-payroll model may be more appropriate. Do not subtract the same kitchen wages per order and again as overhead. With $24,500 monthly overhead, operating break-even is $24,500 ÷ $10.41 = 2,353.51 orders, rounded up to 2,354. At that volume, contribution is $24,505.14. It covers the stated overhead with $5.14 left; it does not fund a separate owner-pay or profit goal. Adding $6,000 owner pay and $3,000 target profit creates a $33,500 financial need. Required orders are 3,218.06, rounded up to 3,219. Practical revenue at $34 is $109,446. Keep these two targets labeled so a reader does not mistake overhead coverage for adequate owner income. Check the schedule before accepting the target Assume ten team members each provide thirty-two hours weekly. At 72% productive utilization and 52 ÷ 12 weeks per model month, productive hours are 998.40. If each order consumes 0.35 total worker-hours across preparation and service, aggregate capacity is 2,852.57 orders, or 2,852 whole orders. The full financial goal exceeds that capacity by 367 whole orders. At 2,852 orders, contribution is $29,689.32, leaving a $3,810.68 shortfall against the $33,500 goal. More inquiries alone cannot fill a kitchen schedule that is already full under the model. Check actual operating days as well. Over twenty-six days, a 3,219-order target averages 123.81 orders daily. A restaurant might have enough aggregate monthly hours but still struggle with a concentrated dinner rush. Inspect daypart throughput, seats, equipment and role bottlenecks separately. Total labor-hours are a screening measure, not a guarantee of orders per service. What changes the answer Average order value changes contribution when the additional revenue does not require equivalent extra cost. But an extra menu item also uses ingredients and preparation time. Model the new order economics rather than increasing revenue while leaving every cost untouched. Channel mix changes costs. Dine-in, direct pickup and delivery can have different packaging, commission and labor patterns. Use actual completed-order proportions to build a weighted average. The delivery-app contribution guide focuses on one channel’s economics; this guide uses that information to build the whole-restaurant target. Waste and labor allocation can change without menu prices moving. Compare ingredients used against the sales period and inspect paid hours that remain when orders fall. The restaurant food-cost guide and labor-cost guide help establish those inputs before they enter break-even. Finally, capacity changes have costs. An additional shift, person or piece of equipment may increase both hours and financial need. Recalculate the target after adding the cost. Keeping the old break-even number after expanding the operation understates the new requirement. Three decisions to test Raising average order revenue under fixed cost assumptions Suppose average revenue rises to $36 while the $22.40 of non-percentage variable costs stays unchanged. At 3.5% fees, the fee becomes $1.26, leaving $12.34 contribution. The $33,500 goal requires 2,714.75 orders, rounded up to 2,715. That fits the 2,852-order aggregate capacity estimate. At 2,715 orders, contribution is $33,503.10. This scenario is valid only if the higher average order does not change the stated ingredient costs, labor, job duration or demand. If it requires a larger serving or additional preparation, update those lines too. Changing the delivery share Consider a separate channel-mix example in which direct orders contribute $12 each and delivery orders contribute $6. At 70% direct and 30% delivery, weighted contribution is $10.20. A $20,000 monthly financial need requires 1,960.78 orders, rounded up to 1,961. At 50% direct and 50% delivery, weighted contribution falls to $9 and required orders rise to 2,222.22, rounded up to 2,223. This is a 262-order increase in the whole-order target despite the same financial need. The channel contribution inputs here are independent fictional assumptions, not fee rates taken from any platform. Compare the mix with actual kitchen work. Delivery orders might consume a different duration or cause peaks. A weighted contribution without a compatible weighted worker-hour estimate can make the financial plan fit an unrealistic schedule. Staffing adds committed cost Return to the baseline $10.41 contribution. Suppose a staffing change adds $1,500 monthly fixed cost not already included in direct order labor. The financial need rises to $35,000. Required volume is $35,000 ÷ $10.41 = 3,362.15 orders, rounded up to 3,363. If the added capacity supports only 3,200 whole orders, contribution is $33,312 and the revised goal still has a $1,688 gap. Added staffing is not sufficient merely because it improves the original 2,852 capacity. It has to support the new target, and the orders have to be sold. How to run your own numbers Enter the baseline inputs below in the restaurant break-even calculator . Replace every preset and keep one consistent revenue, expense and worker-hour boundary. The tool supports currencies other than USD but does not convert exchange rates. Restaurant field Baseline input Average price per order $34 Materials / product cost per order $10.50 Direct labor per order $8.50 Packaging + delivery commission per order $2.20 Promotion cost per order $1.20 Payment and platform fees 3.5% Monthly operating overhead $24,500 Monthly owner pay $6,000 Target monthly profit $3,000 Active team members 10 Hours per team member / week 32 Delivery hours per order 0.35 total worker-hours Productive utilization 72% Inquiry-to-order conversion 45% In this baseline, the percentage field contains the payment fee only. Add a delivery commission in the other-cost field or in the percentage field using a compatible weighted rate, not in both. Clear unused allowances before testing a new channel case. Treat inquiry conversion cautiously. An order is not necessarily generated by a recorded inquiry in a restaurant. The field is useful only when you have defined a measurable opportunity-to-order boundary. Do not interpret the calculator’s inquiry output as required website visitors or unique diners without a compatible source definition. The example tests operating economics rather than cash collection timing. Supplier payments, deposits, loan principal and other cash movements need a separate cash schedule. Preserve a conservative scenario alongside an improved one so the business plan does not rely on every assumption improving together. Common mistakes Calling overhead coverage profit while owner compensation remains unfunded. Counting committed payroll as both per-order labor and overhead. Entering delivery fees in both dollar costs and a percentage field. Ignoring channel mix when calculating average contribution. Rounding deliverable capacity up instead of down. Adding staffing cost while retaining the old volume target. Separate restaurant commitments from costs that follow orders Rent, base software and committed service payroll can remain payable during a quiet month. Ingredients, packaging and some channel fees normally follow paid orders under the stated boundary. Step costs require a separate row when crossing a threshold creates another fixed commitment. Suppose average order contribution is $12 and monthly commitments including separately modeled owner pay total $12,000. The plan needs 1,000 orders. Adding a $1,200 fixed kitchen-service commitment raises the need to 1,100. If the new service also reduces direct cost by $1 per order, contribution becomes $13 and the requirement is $13,200 ÷ $13 = 1,015.3846, or 1,016 whole orders. Do not treat every operating expense as a percentage of revenue without checking how it behaves. Keep deposits, equipment purchases and timed supplier payments in the cash plan. The monthly contribution formula identifies an operating volume; it cannot determine when cash will arrive or whether service capacity can deliver that volume. FAQs Is break-even based on revenue or orders? Both can describe the same model. Orders make the required operating workload visible, while revenue expresses its financial size. Use the same average order and costs for both. Should owner pay be included? Include it as a separate planning goal if the business needs to support it. Do not add compensation already included in payroll a second time. Label the overhead-only and owner-pay targets separately. Can I use one average for dine-in and delivery? Yes, for a stable mix with correctly weighted costs and labor-hours. Keep channel-level checks so a change in mix does not quietly invalidate the average. What if capacity is below the target? Test contribution, service mix, workload and financial need one at a time. If you add capacity with extra cost, recompute the required orders. Demand must still support the plan. Does the example describe typical restaurant margins? No. These are fictional input values chosen to explain the model. Use your own completed-order and payroll records. Is cash break-even the same as this result? No. Operating economics and cash timing answer different questions. Keep a separate schedule for collection, payment commitments and financing cash flows. Are all restaurant labor costs fixed? No. The treatment depends on the actual scheduling commitment and decision period. Count committed wages and incremental hours in their appropriate places, then reconcile them without duplication. Takeaways Trace contribution from one representative completed order. Distinguish overhead coverage from the full owner-pay target. Reconcile payroll and commissions once. Compare whole orders with realistic capacity and demand. Find related examples in the MyBreakeven guide library . Check the next planning steps: How Much Does It Cost to Open a Restaurant? . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.
