documents.text: Salon PROFITABILITY GUIDE Salon Break-Even: Appointments, Service Mix and Stylist Capacity Published September 10, 2026 Updated October 8, 2026 Published by MyBreakeven . Editorial standards and corrections . Report a calculation or content issue to mybreakeven1@gmail.com . Calculate salon break-even from service contribution and stylist hours. Compare appointment mixes, owner pay and whole-job capacity before planning. Salon Business Service Mix Stylist Capacity Appointment Pricing A salon owner evaluates appointment capacity, service mix and revenue in a modern salon. Salon break-even is the appointment volume whose contribution covers the monthly commitments and income goals in your model. Calculate each service's contribution and delivery time before using an average ticket. A full calendar of low-contribution or time-heavy appointments may not support the owner's income target. This updated guide uses fictional USD figures to connect service mix, stylist worker-hours and monthly funding; it does not state current salon rates or predict customer demand. Quick answer: Subtract products, direct labor, job-specific expense, acquisition and percentage fees from appointment revenue. Divide the monthly need by that contribution, then test delivery capacity. A $100 appointment with $39 contribution needs 256.41 appointments to cover $10,000, rounded up to 257. At 1.5 worker-hours each, that target needs 385.5 productive hours, even before appointment-specific scheduling constraints. Calculate contribution without confusing it with take-home pay Start with a defined appointment. Record the agreed service, product usage, active stylist work and other committed time. A short cut and a color appointment do not necessarily use the same people, chairs or minutes. Build separate estimates before combining them into a service mix. For a fictional average appointment, assume price $100, product cost $12, direct labor $35, laundry and disposables $5, and acquisition allocation $6. Non-fee variable expense is $58. A 3% fee adds $3, leaving $39 contribution and a 39% contribution margin. Contribution remains available for the monthly business; it is not the final amount the owner can withdraw. Suppose overhead is $6,000, additional owner pay $3,000 and target profit $1,000. Total contribution need is $10,000. Required volume is $10,000 ÷ $39 = 256.4103 appointments, rounded up to 257. At 256 appointments, contribution is $9,984 and falls $16 short. At 257, it is $10,023. If direct labor includes a wage for the working owner, make the separate owner-pay goal additional compensation rather than the same wage repeated. If stylist payroll remains payable during empty hours, do not describe all of it as a cost that vanishes with an unbooked appointment. Classify committed payroll in overhead and use only genuinely appointment-variable labor in the contribution calculation. Check whole appointments against stylist capacity Assume three stylists with thirty scheduled weekly hours each and 75% productive utilization. Using 52 ÷ 12 weeks per model month gives 292.5 productive worker-hours. At 1.5 worker-hours per appointment, capacity is 195 appointments. The 257-appointment target exceeds it by sixty-two complete appointments. At 195 appointments, contribution is $7,605. Subtract the $10,000 need and the model shows a $2,395 gap. A positive per-appointment contribution does not close that gap when the team cannot deliver enough appointments. More bookings alone would increase the workload beyond the stated capacity. Keep active stylist time, processing time and chair occupancy distinct. If a stylist can safely perform another task during processing under the actual service setup, elapsed appointment time may differ from active worker-hours. Do not automatically assume all overlap is usable. Use the hair-color appointment-cost guide to build the service boundary. Skill availability can also constrain bookings. Three stylists do not create three interchangeable schedules if only one performs a certain service. The aggregate model is a screening check; keep a separate appointment calendar by role, chair and service. What changes the monthly requirement Price changes contribution, but the service scope and demand response matter. A higher ticket that includes more product and time cannot be modeled as a price-only increase. Keep the cost boundary explicit whenever the offer changes. Service mix changes contribution per worker-hour. Calculate the appointments you actually expect to sell and complete. Averaging a high-revenue service into the plan without its longer duration can create an unrealistic target. See salon service pricing for scope-based comparisons. Empty time changes usable capacity. Track gaps, cancellations, administration and cleanup under a consistent utilization definition. A 75% assumption is a chosen scenario here, not a universal target or a measured salon average. Use your records to replace it. Commission and booth arrangements change the business boundary. A salon collecting service revenue and paying commission has a different cost model from an owner receiving rent. Keep those business models separate rather than mixing all receipts into an average appointment. The booth-rent versus commission guide explains that distinction. Compare three service and pricing scenarios First, test price $115 while the original $58 non-fee cost and 1.5-hour delivery scope stay unchanged. Fees are $3.45 and contribution $53.55. The $10,000 need requires 186.7414 appointments, rounded up to 187. That fits the 195-appointment aggregate capacity, leaving eight complete-appointment slots under the assumptions. Second, compare a two-service mix. A fictional short service sells for $70 with $27 non-fee cost, 3% fees and 0.75 delivery worker-hours. Contribution is $40.90. A longer service sells for $180 with $85 non-fee cost, 3% fees and 2.5 worker-hours. Contribution is $89.60. The larger ticket produces more contribution per appointment but less per worker-hour: $35.84 compared with $54.5333 for the short service. At 120 short and sixty long appointments, revenue is $19,200. Contribution is 120 × $40.90 + 60 × $89.60 = $10,284. Worker-hours are ninety plus 150, or 240. This mixed scenario covers the $10,000 need and fits the 292.5-hour aggregate pool. It still requires compatible skills, chairs and actual demand for that mix. Third, keep 180 appointments but change the mix to sixty short and 120 long. Revenue rises to $25,800 and contribution rises to $13,206. Worker-hours rise to forty-five plus 300, or 345. The higher-revenue mix exceeds the same productive pool by 52.5 hours. It is financially attractive on paper but does not fit the stated schedule. These comparisons demonstrate why revenue per appointment is insufficient. Record contribution, worker-hours and role availability together. Keep each example's costs separate; the two-service scenarios are not derived by splitting the original $100 average appointment. Reproduce a mixed-service average carefully For the 120-short, sixty-long mix, weighted average price is $19,200 ÷ 180 = $106.6667. Weighted non-fee cost is (120 × $27 + 60 × $85) ÷ 180 = $46.3333. At a 3% fee, average contribution is $57.1333. Average delivery time is 240 ÷ 180 = 1.3333 worker-hours. At that exact mix, the $10,000 need requires 175.0292 average appointments, rounded up to 176. Aggregate capacity is 219.375 average appointments, rounded down to 219. The exact 180-appointment schedule above is clearer than the average because real short and long appointments are indivisible and need matching staff availability. Use averages only for a mix you can support. When the mix changes, recalculate both costs and hours. Otherwise, the calculator will accurately solve the wrong assumption set and make a difficult schedule appear deliverable. How to run your own numbers For the first example, enter price $100, materials $12, direct labor $35, laundry/disposables $5, acquisition $6 and fees 3%. Clear unused defaults. Use $6,000 overhead, $3,000 additional owner pay and $1,000 profit target. Set three workers, thirty weekly hours, 75% utilization and 1.5 delivery worker-hours per appointment. At an illustrative 40% inquiry conversion, the exact fractional financial target requires 641.03 inquiries, rounded up to 642. For the practical target of 257 whole appointments, calculate 257 ÷ 0.40 = 642.5 and round up to 643 inquiries . This is a planning assumption, not a guarantee that 643 inquiries produce 257 completed appointments. Record cancellations and completed services separately. Use the salon break-even calculator to compare the base case with the $115 price or a carefully weighted mix. Other currencies are supported. Keep a service-specific calendar alongside it to check chairs, stylist skills and peak booking times. Common mistakes Using average ticket price without weighting service costs and duration. Calling contribution owner take-home before overhead and compensation. Treating processing time, active worker time and chair occupancy as identical. Assuming every stylist can perform every booked service. Counting commission labor or owner delivery wages twice. FAQs Can a busy salon still miss break-even? Yes. If appointments leave too little contribution for the committed costs, a full calendar can still fall short of the monthly goal. Check the mix and time boundary before adding more bookings. Should I use one average appointment in the calculator? It can be a useful first screen when price, cost and hours come from the same evidenced mix. Keep separate service-level scenarios and a real schedule to verify the average does not hide bottlenecks. Does raising prices always solve a capacity gap? It can reduce the required volume under unchanged scope and costs. Demand, buyer acceptance and any extra service included at the higher price still need testing. How do I treat paid stylists during empty hours? Keep committed payroll in the monthly funding boundary when it remains payable. Only subtract genuinely appointment-variable labor when calculating short-term contribution. What if two services overlap during processing? Use an actual feasible schedule and the relevant service instructions. Overlap may save active worker time while still occupying a chair, so check both resources separately. Are the example prices industry averages? No. Every amount is a fictional planning assumption. Use your own product invoices, compensation arrangements and recorded service times. Takeaways Build contribution and hours for each service before averaging. Compare whole-appointment targets with productive worker capacity. Check skills and chair occupancy outside the aggregate model. Separate committed payroll from appointment-variable costs. Explore the business guide library for related planning examples. Check the next planning steps: How Many Clients Does a Salon Chair Need Per Day? . Planning estimates only—not accounting, tax, legal or lending advice.

Financial ratio formulas and their measurement bases Liquidity is a balance-sheet snapshot. Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities. Quick ratio = (cash + eligible liquid investments + eligible trade receivables)/current liabilities. Cash ratio excludes receivables. Working capital = current assets − current liabilities; it is money, not a percentage or times ratio. The quick formula excludes inventory and prepayments rather than assuming all current assets are immediately spendable. Gross margin = (revenue − COGS)/positive revenue × 100. Operating, net and EBITDA margins use their separately named profit numerator over the same revenue. Operating profit is not silently substituted for EBIT. EBITDA must be reconciled separately before entering it; it is not cash available for bills. Closing liabilities/assets expresses the percentage of assets funded by all liabilities. Interest-bearing debt/equity uses loans and similar financing, while liabilities/equity also includes non-interest obligations. Interest coverage = period EBIT/positive interest expense. Zero interest is not displayed as an ordinary infinite coverage score. Inventory turnover = period COGS/average inventory. Receivables turnover = period net credit sales/average net trade receivables. DSO = average trade receivables/net credit sales × actual period days. Asset turnover = period revenue/average assets. Average means (opening + closing)/2, not an assumed year-end balance. ROA = period net income/average assets × 100. ROE = period net income/average equity × 100. These are period returns. A 90-day return is not automatically multiplied by four, and a two-point average can still misrepresent seasonal balance swings. Use a more representative average outside this tool when needed. A high current ratio may include slow stock. High ROE can reflect a thin equity base. A positive accounting profit can coexist with cash collection problems. Understand all seven financial ratio categories Liquidity ratios measure resources against current obligations; high inventory or overdue receivables can make apparent liquidity misleading. Profitability ratios compare different profit definitions with revenue or invested capital. Do not confuse EBITDA with cash from operations, and match period flows to suitable balance averages. Leverage and solvency ratios distinguish all liabilities from interest-bearing debt and opening equity from closing equity. Negative equity makes some conventional comparisons inappropriate. Efficiency ratios use reported period sales, purchases and costs against opening/closing averages. The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivables days minus payables days; DPO here uses purchases, not assumed COGS. Cash-flow ratios use reported operating cash flow, not adjusted net profit. Free cash flow here subtracts capital expenditures, and a negative result may be meaningful. Coverage ratios test ability to cover obligations under stated definitions. Cash-based debt service coverage is not automatically the DSCR covenant defined by a lender. Market-value ratios need consistent valuation-date share prices, share counts or market capitalization. A private business without observable stock price should not invent a P/E or P/B. Required versus undefined financial ratio results Required means a source value is blank. Select that measure in the direct calculator and fill only its displayed input fields. Blank is unknown, not zero. Undefined means the denominator is zero, negative or economically non-comparable. Do not turn undefined results into zero or infinity. The starting example supplies just some statement balances. Optional share-market and cash-flow amounts are intentionally blank, so not all 55 results appear immediately. Currency choice changes labels without converting values. Interpret results without a universal good-ratio score Compare each result with the business model, seasonality, contract terms and the same measure over time. Inventory turnover differs between a grocer and an equipment distributor. Liquidity ratios do not reveal the exact dates on which customer receipts arrive and supplier payments fall due. A second period can help identify a change, but it does not explain the cause. Percentage ratios show a percentage-point difference; a change from 10% to 12% is +2 percentage points, not +2% relative growth. Different-length periods make turnover and return deltas especially easy to misread. Before concluding that leverage improved, reconcile the balance sheet and check whether liabilities were reclassified. Before concluding that margins improved, verify the revenue, expense recognition and one-off items. Use a cash-flow forecast for payment timing and a separate valuation method for business value. Common financial ratio mistakes to avoid Do not add liquid investments twice by entering the same balance in cash and investments. Do not replace missing net credit sales with total sales unless all sales are genuinely on credit. Do not divide annual revenue by an unrelated year-end asset value and call the result an average-assets turnover. Do not mix consolidated assets with a subsidiary’s profit or use liabilities from one date and equity from another. The tool can warn when entered totals fail assets = liabilities + equity, but it cannot verify statements or infer omitted obligations. Separate operating cash flow from EBITDA and working capital. The integrated leverage method selector changes the chosen definition, not your source balances. A denominator that is zero or economically non-comparable requires explanation rather than a fabricated zero result. Assumptions and limits Use one entity, currency and accounting policy for each dataset. Balance-sheet values are closing balances; profitability inputs are flows for the stated period. Average inventory, receivables, assets and equity use explicit opening and closing values. No opening value is inferred from a blank. Turnovers and returns describe the entered period, without automatic annualization. Equity multiplier and the two equity-based leverage measures use closing equity; return on equity uses average equity and is flagged when either endpoint is nonpositive. The ROE convention here is entered net income divided by average total equity; common-shareholder ROE needs an appropriately adjusted income/equity dataset. Liquid investments must be eligible short-term amounts not already in cash. Receivables must be collectible net trade balances. No accounting reconciliation, restatement, industry benchmark, valuation, forecast or credit eligibility decision is supplied automatically. A warning does not correct the source data. Results outside the supported range are withheld. Currency labels do not convert values. Frequently asked questions What financial ratios does this calculator calculate? It provides liquidity, margins, leverage, coverage, turnover, DSO and returns: 55 measures including working capital as a money amount. Every measure shows its formula and input requirements. Are financial ratios and equivalent ratios the same? No. Financial ratios analyze business statements. Equivalent ratios are mathematical proportions such as 2:3 and 8:12; they are a separate task. What is the financial leverage ratio formula? There is more than one convention. The integrated selector distinguishes total assets/equity, total liabilities/equity and interest-bearing debt/equity using the same closing date. Why are some results unavailable? A required value may be blank or invalid, or the denominator may be zero or non-comparable. The result explains the missing requirement instead of assuming zero. Does this annualize quarterly returns? No. The entered period is displayed. Returns and turnover remain for that period, and DSO uses the explicitly entered number of days. What is a good current ratio or debt ratio? It depends on the business, industry, timing and trend. This tool does not apply a universal healthy range or lending approval score. Can I compare two periods and export the results? Yes. Enable the independent comparison dataset, enter its values and check period lengths. The CSV includes results, units, formulas and missing-input status. documents.text: FREE · EXPLAINED FORMULAS · NO SIGNUP Equivalent Ratio Calculator Compare financial and operating proportions between two periods or businesses. Analyze cost efficiency, leverage, productivity and revenue mix, then check a target against your actual result. Enter my numbers Compare business ratios on the same basis Compare cost, debt, sales mix or operating productivity ratios between periods or businesses. Compare like-for-like periods and units. For margin, markup and named financial ratio calculations, use the dedicated calculators linked below. Financial ratios calculator · Margin versus markup guide Compare mode: enter two complete ratios in the same component order. The result checks all corresponding pairs exactly. Use integers, decimals or fractions (for example 1/2). In solve mode, leave exactly one value blank or enter x. Other blanks are unknown, not zero. Period A 30.00 % Period B 30.00 % Change 0.00 percentage points Direction: Unchanged . Lower cost-to-revenue generally leaves more revenue before other expenses, but this comparison alone is not net profit. These ratios are equivalent. First simplified ratio 3 : 10 Second simplified ratio 3 : 10 Common scaling factor 3/2 Step-by-step working First ratio: 30 : 100. Second ratio: 45 : 150. 30 × 150 = 4500; 100 × 45 = 4500. Every component pair agrees. Common scale factor: 3/2. Composition of each ratio normalized to 100%. Visual proportions are approximate; equivalence is determined using exact fractions. First ratio Second ratio Term 1 Term 2 Copy result & steps Download CSV Print / save PDF Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Quick answer Business ratios are meaningful only when the numerator, denominator, measurement units and time periods are consistent. Compare cost divided by revenue, debt divided by equity, labor hours per unit, or product revenue shares. Equal ratios can occur at different business scales and do not establish equal profits. What this calculator includes Compare cost-to-revenue percentage between periods. Review debt-to-equity exposure using consistent debt and equity definitions. Measure labor hours per finished unit and the change in operating intensity. Track three-product revenue mix and percentage-point share changes. Set your own cost, leverage or productivity target and see the gap. Export an exact comparison, review assumptions and access advanced proportion mathematics. How to compare business ratios between periods Choose Cost-to-revenue, Debt-to-equity, Labor productivity or Sales mix from the business scenario cards. Enter Period A and Period B values in the same units and consistent accounting or operating definitions. Read the normalized KPI values and the absolute difference. Percentage changes in revenue mix and cost share are shown in percentage points. For cost, debt or labor metrics, enter a target you chose for your business to see the target gap and investigation guidance. Use Copy or CSV to retain your report. Advanced ratio mathematics remains available for exact fractions, scaling and missing-value equations. Business ratio formulas and what they measure Cost-to-revenue ratio = eligible costs ÷ matching revenue × 100. If costs are $30,000 and revenue $100,000, the ratio is 30%. A second period with $45,000 costs and $150,000 revenue is also 30%, even though the business is larger. This is not the same as net profit margin. Debt-to-equity = interest-bearing debt ÷ equity when those are the selected consistent definitions. $40,000 debt divided by $60,000 equity equals 0.667×. Interpret the figure alongside cash flows, debt service, maturity dates and industry context; lower is not automatically better in every capital structure. Labor intensity = labor hours ÷ finished units. Twenty hours for 100 units equals 0.20 hours per unit; thirty hours for 100 units equals 0.30 hours per unit. The increase is 0.10 hour per unit and may warrant checking staffing, downtime, quality or product mix. Revenue mix share = product revenue ÷ total selected product revenue × 100. Track each product as a percentage of the same basket and compare percentage-point changes, not just absolute sales. Business ratio comparison examples with verified calculations Illustrative business scenarios, not industry benchmarks Business question Period A Period B and decision insight Did cost efficiency change? $30 cost ÷ $100 revenue = 30% $45 ÷ $150 = 30%; unchanged, despite higher sales Has debt-to-equity changed? $40 debt ÷ $60 equity = 0.667× $60 ÷ $90 = 0.667×; same debt/equity proportion Is production using more labor? 20 hours ÷ 100 units = 0.20 h/unit 30 hours ÷ 100 units = 0.30 h/unit; 0.10 more hour per unit Did product revenue mix shift? A/B/C = $20/$30/$50 → 20%/30%/50% A/B/C = $40/$60/$100 → 20%/30%/50%; same shares Is a 28% cost ratio target met? Target = 28% Actual = 30%; target not met by 2 percentage points What if sales grow but expenses grow faster? Cost $30 ÷ sales $100 = 30% Cost $54 ÷ sales $150 = 36%; cost share increases by 6 pp Equal ratios do not imply equal total sales, absolute expenses, cash balances or business value. Always examine monetary changes alongside normalized KPIs. A target is a planning threshold selected by the user. The tool offers areas to investigate, not a diagnosis that any one change caused the outcome. Business scaling, benchmarking and revenue-mix tables Proportional scaling is useful for comparing periods of different sizes. A $30 cost for $100 revenue and $45 cost for $150 revenue both represent 30 cents of cost per revenue dollar. This normalization does not identify cost categories or estimate future spending without assumptions. In a three-product revenue mix, calculate every product share against the same selected product total. A product can gain sales dollars while its share declines because other products grew faster. Review contribution margins before declaring a mix shift beneficial. Compare ratios only across compatible units, matching accounting policies, the same period length and the same business model where possible. A numeric threshold without those checks can create false benchmarks. Common mistakes in business ratio interpretation Do not interpret an unchanged ratio as unchanged financial performance. Absolute revenue, cost, cash flow, capital employed and risk can change substantially. Never confuse debt-to-equity with debt-to-assets, cost-to-revenue with gross margin, or labor hours per unit with units per labor hour. Their numerators and denominators differ. Treat targets as internal planning choices rather than universal industry standards. Check data quality, seasonality, product mix, capacity and definitions before deciding on operational changes. Use Advanced ratio mathematics only if you need exact proportional equations, missing-value solving or scaled ratios. Those mathematical outcomes do not substitute for a financial statement analysis. Assumptions and limits Business inputs should be nonnegative and use consistent reporting periods, units and numerator/denominator definitions. The denominator must be positive. For labor hours per unit, product quality and product mix must be comparable. Debt-to-equity here is debt divided by equity, not a credit recommendation. The target is user-defined, not an industry benchmark. The exact-ratio engine supports fractions, decimals, two- and three-term vectors and solving x in advanced mode, but mathematical equivalence alone does not measure profitability. Frequently asked questions What does this business ratio calculator compare? It compares cost-to-revenue, debt-to-equity, labor hours per output unit and three-product revenue mix between two periods or businesses. How is cost-to-revenue calculated? Divide selected costs by matching revenue and multiply by 100. A result of 30% means 30 cents of selected cost per dollar of revenue. What does an unchanged ratio mean? The normalized proportion is unchanged. Total revenue, expense, profit and risk can still change. What is a percentage-point difference? It is the direct subtraction of percentage values: moving from 30% to 36% is an increase of 6 percentage points. How does the target versus actual comparison work? Enter a business-chosen cost, debt or labor intensity target. The tool compares it with Period B and shows the numerical gap; it is not an industry benchmark. Can I compare product revenue mix? Yes. Enter three product revenue amounts for each period. The calculator shows each product share and its change in percentage points. Does a lower debt-to-equity ratio always mean a healthier company? No. Capital structure, cash flow, borrowing costs, maturity and equity quality also matter. Can I still solve equivalent ratios with fractions? Yes. P&I stops at payoff; final payment adjusts any rounding residual. Interest calculations keep precision internally and displayed cents may not sum exactly. No daily accrual, extra payments or prepayment penalty is modeled. Illustrative editorial scene. Exact quantities and calculations appear in the worked examples. Quick answer A simple fee-recovery threshold is net upfront fees ÷ positive monthly payment saving. For a fuller comparison, include cash paid and principal still owed at the same date. A lower payment does not automatically mean a lower borrowing cost. What this calculator includes Fixed-rate fully amortizing mortgage comparison using current balance and remaining months. Upfront fees, financed fees, lender credits and temporary closing liquidity entered separately. Same-date cumulative cash and remaining-principal comparison, including the first nonnegative economic break-even month. Independent schedules through both payoff dates, balance chart and complete CSV. Zero-rate support, explicit no-payment-savings states, reset, currency labels and print. How to use the mortgage refinance calculator Enter the current unpaid principal, current fixed annual note rate and months remaining. Do not restart the existing mortgage at its original term. Enter the new note rate and proposed term. Rates here are your assumptions or actual quote details; the calculator does not supply a current market offer. Separate transaction fees paid upfront from fees financed into the new balance. Enter lender credits only against the upfront fee bucket, and do not repeat any financed amount there. Choose the number of months until you expect to sell, repay or refinance again. Both options are compared at that same date, even if one loan has already been paid off. Optionally enter taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA, mortgage insurance and temporary closing liquidity. Review their timing assumptions, then compare payments, interest, cash and balances. Download both schedules and compare the modeled figures with a lender’s Loan Estimate. Check costs, payment timing and any unsupported loan features separately. Refinance payment formula and same-date cost comparison For principal P, monthly note rate i and n remaining payments, principal-and-interest payment M = P×i/[1−(1+i)^(−n)]. At zero interest, M = P/n. The current schedule uses today’s outstanding balance and remaining term. The new schedule starts with that balance plus financed transaction fees. Each month’s interest = opening principal × monthly rate. Principal reduction = actual P&I payment − interest. The final payment is capped or adjusted to remaining balance plus interest. This model rounds the regular payment to cents while retaining interest precision internally; lender daily-interest and rounding conventions can differ. At holding month h, keep-current cost = cumulative current cash payments through h + outstanding current principal at h. Refinance cost = net upfront transaction fees + cumulative new cash payments through h + outstanding new principal at h. Positive current-cost minus refinance-cost favors refinancing under the entered assumptions. Including outstanding principal matters when terms differ. A smaller payment can leave a larger balance at sale. Financing fees increases the new principal and associated interest; adding those fees again to upfront cash would double count them. The common starting mortgage principal cancels from the difference. The simple payment threshold rounds net upfront fees/positive initial monthly saving up to a whole month. It is shown only without financed fees. It assumes the initial saving persists, so a threshold beyond either payoff date is flagged. It does not establish that all later dates are cheaper: use the full schedule to see how the comparison changes. Refinance examples: fee recovery, term changes and zero interest Original fictional arithmetic cases; no lender offer or rate recommendation Scenario Calculation Meaning Simple fee recovery 6,000 net upfront fees / 250 positive monthly saving = 24 months Requires the assumed saving to continue; inspect balances too Zero-interest loan 12,000 principal / 12 months = 1,000 P&I No interest; payment is all principal Identical loans, no fees Same balance, note rate and term Zero payment and same-horizon cost difference Finance 5,000 of fees 250,000 current balance + 5,000 = 255,000 new principal Do not also add 5,000 to upfront fees Credits offset fees 6,000 upfront fees − 1,000 credits = 5,000 net upfront Credits can involve a different quoted note rate Shorter new term A higher payment can reduce principal faster No simple payment saving does not prove no total-cost benefit Default example: 250,000 unpaid balance, 6.5% current note rate, 300 months remaining, 5.5% new note rate, 300 new months, 6,000 upfront fees and a 60-month holding period. These assumptions are deliberately editable, not a statement of current market rates. Read the current and new schedule together rather than treating the lower-rate label as a conclusion. Extending the same principal into a longer term may reduce the monthly payment while increasing lifetime interest. A shorter term may raise monthly payments but leave substantially less debt at the same holding date. Those are distinct cash-flow and cost decisions. Classify closing costs before calculating break-even Enter irreversible transaction charges such as origination, appraisal and title charges in the correct upfront or financed bucket. Discount points can be entered as an actual currency amount included in fees; enter the corresponding quoted note rate separately. No fixed points-to-rate conversion is assumed. Lender credits reduce upfront transaction fees in this model. They do not automatically reduce financed fees or produce unrestricted cash back. The quoted rate may differ when taking credits, so compare complete offers rather than changing credits alone and assuming everything else stays equal. Escrow deposits, prepaid property taxes and insurance can affect cash needed at closing without being new irreversible transaction costs in the same way. This tool shows a separate temporary liquidity amount but does not model escrow refunds, prepaid timing or tax benefits. Reconcile the closing ledger with the lender if timing materially affects the decision. Decide which comparison answers your refinance question For monthly affordability, review P&I plus your entered housing costs. For an expected sale or another refinance, review cumulative cash plus debt remaining at that date. For the full loan lives, compare scheduled interest and fees while recognizing that the payoff dates differ. None of these is a guaranteed benefit or lender approval. A first fee-recovery point may not remain favorable forever if a new term runs much longer. The schedule therefore keeps both paths visible through the longer payoff date or holding horizon. Loan payments stop at payoff; ongoing property expenses do not disappear merely because mortgage principal reaches zero. Mortgage insurance is not assumed to cancel at an equity threshold. If cancellation would occur before payoff, this constant-cost model will not reproduce that changing path. Likewise, adjustable rates, cash-out borrowing, penalties and extra payments need a different schedule. Do not force those cases into this rate-and-term model. Common refinance calculation mistakes Do not enter APR as the note rate: APR incorporates certain financing charges, while interest accrues from the contractual note rate. Do not compare the original mortgage amount with today’s new refinance balance, or compare loans over different sale dates and call the result a same-horizon saving. Do not count financed fees both in principal and upfront. Do not treat all cash to close as an unrecoverable fee. Do not assume a lower monthly payment guarantees lower lifetime interest, especially when restarting a long term. The result is undiscounted. It does not calculate the return you could earn on freed cash, the time value of paying costs today, interest tax deductions, home appreciation or refinance eligibility. Those assumptions can change an actual decision and should be evaluated separately. Assumptions and limits This is a fixed-rate, fully amortizing, rate-and-term mortgage model. No cash-out/cash-in, ARM resets, balloon payments, extra principal, daily accrual, prepayment penalties, lender underwriting, live rates or tax deductions are modeled. Use note rate, not APR, for interest: monthly rate = annual note rate/12. Regular principal-and-interest payments round to cents; monthly interest keeps precision internally, and final payoff adjusts the rounding residual. Other housing costs stay constant through the horizon, including after payoff; entered mortgage insurance stays constant until modeled loan payoff, with no earlier cancellation inferred. Lender credits offset upfront fees only and cannot create a cash rebate. Financed fees increase new principal once. Escrow/prepaids are liquidity amounts excluded from irreversible transaction cost; their recovery timing is not modeled. Same-horizon comparison is undiscounted and excludes investment returns, tax effects and home-price changes. Both options retain the same home and start from the same outstanding mortgage debt. Currency labels do not convert values. Tiny balances whose rounded payment cannot amortize are outside support. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate refinance break-even? The simple fee-recovery threshold is net upfront transaction fees divided by positive monthly payment savings, rounded up. Compare remaining principal at the same holding date for a fuller cost assessment. Why can a lower monthly payment cost more overall? A longer new term can spread principal over more months and leave a larger balance at sale or create more lifetime interest. Check both schedules and the same-date comparison. Can I roll closing costs into the new mortgage? Yes, enter them in financed fees. They increase new principal and interest once; do not repeat the same fees as upfront charges. Does this calculator support cash-out or adjustable-rate refinancing? No. This release covers fixed-rate, fully amortizing rate-and-term mortgages. Cash-out, cash-in, ARM changes and balloon structures need a different model. Should I enter interest rate or APR? Enter the annual note interest rate. APR is a broader financing-cost disclosure and is not used as the monthly accrual rate here. What if there are no monthly payment savings? There is no simple payment-savings threshold. A shorter term can still reduce total cost; examine cash paid plus principal remaining at your selected date. Does cash to close equal refinance cost? Not always. Transaction fees, financed charges, lender credits and temporary escrow or prepaids have different roles. This tool separates them and does not model escrow refund timing. Are rates live and is this a lender offer? No. Defaults are fictional examples; enter your own quote or assumption. The tool does not make an eligibility decision or guarantee savings. How to use the FIRE retirement calculator Enter your current age and invested retirement assets, excluding amounts you cannot appropriately commit to this model. Estimate annual retirement spending the portfolio itself must fund, in today’s money. Include retirement taxes and healthcare you expect the portfolio to pay; do not subtract future benefits without checking dates and eligibility separately. Enter a fixed-real monthly contribution. This contribution maintains purchasing power, so the actual nominal deposit would rise with inflation. Choose nominal effective annual return, fee, inflation and withdrawal assumptions. The 4% example is a selectable scenario, not a guaranteed safe rate. Set a maximum projection age. Optionally enter a target age to calculate its required savings separately. Review slower/faster growth scenarios, then save the full schedule. FIRE number formula and inflation-adjusted growth F = annual portfolio-funded spending ÷ withdrawal fraction. With a 4% fraction, F is 25 times the entered annual spending. A different chosen withdrawal rate changes the target; the tool does not choose a suitable rate for your retirement horizon. Net nominal annual factor = (1 + return) × (1 − fee). Real annual factor = net nominal factor ÷ (1 + inflation). Effective monthly factor = real annual factor^(1/12). Monthly balance = prior balance × monthly factor + end-month contribution. All rate inputs are percentages converted to decimal fractions in these formulas. The engine checks each whole month until the target is first met or the chosen maximum projection age is reached. It does not interpolate a fractional month and label it a verified retirement date. A target not reached inside this horizon is not a claim that it can never be reached. Required monthly contribution = max(0, [F − current assets(1+i)^n] ÷ A). The displayed required amount rounds upward to cents so the minimum is not understated. The main table stops at first target attainment or the projection horizon. Neither schedule models retirement withdrawals after you stop contributing. FIRE versus Coast FIRE: two different milestones FIRE accumulation asks when ongoing assets and contributions could meet the full spending-based portfolio target. Coast FIRE asks whether assets already invested could grow to that future target without further retirement deposits. A Coast threshold can be met while current assets remain far below the full FIRE number. Use the separate Coast FIRE calculator when considering a no-more-contributions scenario. Retirement-account restrictions and future pension or Social Security dates are not inferred from your age. Do not treat all net worth, including a home you plan to occupy, as an automatically spendable portfolio. Compare assumptions and revisit records. The three rate scenarios change growth assumptions only; they are not confidence bands or probabilities. The separate withdrawal-rate table changes the target only; it does not validate the chosen rate. Assumptions and limits This is a deterministic accumulation model, not a drawdown simulation, market forecast, success probability or decision that you can retire. Fixed-real monthly contributions are paid at month-end; their nominal amounts would need to rise with inflation. Portfolio-funded annual spending must include applicable retirement taxes, healthcare and other expenses you intend the portfolio to cover. Benefits, pensions, access restrictions, individual tax rules, changing spending and market-return sequences are not calculated. Home equity and emergency cash are not automatically counted as invested retirement assets. Currency labels do not convert values. Current inputs are memory-only and reset on reload. Bounds are support limits, not recommended return/withdrawal ranges. Frequently asked questions What does FIRE stand for? Financial Independence, Retire Early. This calculator estimates a spending-based portfolio target and accumulation timing; it does not decide whether retiring is appropriate. How is my FIRE number calculated? Divide annual retirement spending that your portfolio must fund by your selected withdrawal fraction. At 40,000 and 4%, the number is 1,000,000 in today’s money. Does reaching the FIRE number guarantee my money lasts? No. This model does not simulate retirement drawdown, changing returns, taxes or lifespan. A threshold calculation cannot certify withdrawal sustainability. Are monthly contributions nominal or inflation-adjusted? They are fixed in today’s purchasing power. Maintaining them would require increasing nominal deposits with inflation; Future Value instead models fixed nominal deposits. Why is my target not reached? The chosen assets, contribution and real growth did not meet the threshold within your selected projection age. Review assumptions; a negative real rate can reduce progress. Can I leave target age blank? Yes. The main accumulation projection still runs. The separate required-monthly-savings result asks you to choose a target age. Is Coast FIRE the same calculation? No. Coast FIRE discounts a future full target back to the invested amount needed today with zero further contributions. This FIRE tool includes continued monthly saving. The rate is g = [(1+nominal return) × (1−annual fee) ÷ (1+inflation)] − 1. This divides growth factors rather than simply subtracting inflation. The fee is a disclosed annual asset-fee model; real product fee timing may differ. Do not deduct the same fee twice when your assumed return is already net. How to calculate EBITDA from your records Select one reporting period and one entity perimeter. Replace all fictional example amounts with matching income-statement records. Enter net income after interest and income taxes. Find the included interest, income-tax expense or benefit, depreciation and amortization; enter zero explicitly when absent. Enter matched net revenue only when you need a margin. Blank revenue keeps the earnings total but does not invent a denominator. Review the signed bridge. Open Adjusted EBITDA only for documented extra adjustments; keep the base subtotal visible. Reconcile the earnings result with cash flow and commitments before using it for a business decision. EBITDA formula and margin denominator EBITDA = net income + included interest expense + income-tax expense + included depreciation + included amortization. EBITDA margin = EBITDA ÷ positive net revenue × 100. A negative income-tax benefit reduces the add-back bridge. EBIT plus depreciation and amortization can be another route only when EBIT is correctly defined and reconciled. Operating profit does not always equal EBIT when non-operating items exist. Do not start with EBITDA and add D&A again. Identify the right income-statement inputs Keep accrual expense and cash movements distinct Input Use Do not substitute Net income Bottom-line earnings for the chosen period Revenue or bank balance Interest Included interest expense under the stated definition Loan principal or entire loan payment Income tax Included income-tax expense or signed benefit Every sales/payroll tax or cash payment Depreciation and amortization Included expense, including any portion in COGS Asset purchase cash or accumulated lifetime balance Net revenue Same-period revenue after relevant returns/discounts Gross customer receipts or unrelated group sales Reconcile an original business example Harbor Supply fictional annual USD statement; no additional non-operating items Line Amount Revenue 1,000,000 COGS 600,000 Operating expenses, including 20,000 D&A 290,000 Operating profit / EBIT in this example 110,000 Interest / income tax 10,000 / 20,000 Net income 80,000 Depreciation / amortization 15,000 / 5,000 EBITDA 130,000 EBITDA / operating / net margins 13% / 11% / 8% Check the bridge: 80,000 + 10,000 + 20,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = 130,000. The percentages are example arithmetic, not industry averages. All included D&A is counted once. Independent negative example: net loss of 30,000 plus 5,000 interest, zero tax, 10,000 depreciation and zero amortization gives negative 15,000 EBITDA. Removing selected expenses does not necessarily turn a loss into positive earnings. Keep Adjusted EBITDA separate and reviewable Adjusted EBITDA = base EBITDA + signed extra adjustments. In an independent scenario, base 130,000 plus an included 12,000 proposed expense adjustment less an included 5,000 nonrecurring gain gives 137,000. This is a different example ledger from Harbor Supply. Every adjustment needs an amount, unique description and rationale. An identical amount under a different description can still be a duplicate: the tool cannot inspect invoices or approve recurrence claims. Necessary owner work may require replacement pay; owner draws are not automatically an income-statement expense. Read the result without calling it cash The Harbor Supply cash bridge is 80,000 net income + 20,000 noncash D&A − 25,000 receivables increase − 10,000 inventory increase + 5,000 supplier-payable increase = 70,000 operating cash flow. This assumes a simplified US-style operating interest/tax policy, no changes in those payables and no other adjustments. Positive EBITDA does not prove all bills can be paid. Debt principal, capital purchases, working-capital changes and actual collection dates still matter. Compare matched businesses and periods rather than applying one universal good-margin threshold. Trace the complete earnings-to-cash example Review adjustment evidence and recurrence Assumptions and limits Use the same entity and completed reporting period. Only add back expenses already included in net income. Income-tax benefits retain their negative sign; debt principal is not interest. EBITDA is a non-GAAP earnings measure, not operating cash flow, a bank balance, a valuation or a lending decision. Adjusted items are user-proposed and not professionally approved by this tool. Revenue is optional; a missing or zero denominator has no defined margin. Money displays cents while the engine retains precision. Currency selection changes labels only; values are not converted. Frequently asked questions How do you calculate EBITDA? Add included interest, income-tax expense, depreciation and amortization back to net income for the same period. Preserve negative tax benefits and avoid adding expenses already excluded. Can EBITDA be negative? Yes. If the earnings bridge remains below zero, the calculator reports negative EBITDA rather than forcing a positive result. Is EBITDA the same as operating profit? Not necessarily. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortization, and an EBIT-based route also needs reconciliation of any non-operating items. Why is my EBITDA margin undefined? The margin needs a positive matched revenue denominator. Blank or zero revenue still allows the earnings total but does not produce a meaningful percentage. Does Adjusted EBITDA approve my add-backs? No. It applies your signed amounts separately. The records, recurrence, contract definition and professional acceptance must be reviewed independently. Can I change currency? Yes. Currency selection changes display labels only. Enter every amount in the same currency; no exchange-rate conversion occurs. How to use the Future Value calculator Enter current principal, fixed deposit per selected payment period and horizon in whole months. Zero is a deliberate absent amount; blank is incomplete. Choose annual, quarterly or monthly contributions. Annual payments require whole years, quarterly payments whole quarters. Select effective annual or nominal annual rate. With nominal rates, select the compounding frequency; the tool converts to a matching payment-period rate. Choose beginning or end deposits. Add an inflation assumption and compare the three editable annual-rate scenarios. Review the schedule, growth chart and assumptions; download the CSV or print the scenario. Future value formula with recurring contributions Let PV be starting principal, PMT each equal deposit, n the number of contribution periods and i the matching effective period rate. End-period FV = PV(1+i)^n + PMT[(1+i)^n − 1]/i. Beginning deposits multiply only the contribution term by (1+i). At i = 0 the expression becomes PV + PMT × n. For nominal annual rate j with m compounds/year and p contributions/year, i = (1+j/m)^(m/p) − 1. For effective annual R, i = (1+R)^(1/p) − 1. The displayed effective period rate and formula substitution show the selected basis. Nominal future money versus today’s purchasing power Inflation-adjusted ending value = nominal ending value ÷ (1+annual inflation)^years. A nominal balance can grow while its purchasing power grows less, stays flat or falls. The calculator keeps fixed nominal deposits; it does not automatically raise them with inflation. Do not subtract total nominal contributions from the real ending balance and call the result real investment profit: contributions occurred on different dates. A full real-cash-flow comparison would deflate each contribution separately. Fees and taxes require additional assumptions and are excluded here. Plan a reserve without confusing it with project ROI A business can use a future-value scenario to explore an equipment replacement reserve from current funds and affordable contributions. Keep the expected replacement price on the same nominal or today’s-money basis as the target comparison. This does not determine whether equipment improves operating profit or whether payroll can fund early contributions. Project ROI/payback and dated cash forecasts answer those separate questions. Compare a project’s costs, benefits and cash recovery Check actual short-term payment dates Common future-value calculation mistakes Using an annual rate as a monthly rate, treating nominal and effective annual rates as equal, adding an extra beginning payment, giving the final ordinary payment a full period of growth and rounding the engine after every display step can all change the result. A high return input is an assumption, not evidence it can be earned. Keep positive, zero and negative cases visible; compare like cash-flow dates. For product-specific posting or tax treatment, use the actual terms and an appropriately scoped model. Assumptions and limits Fixed entered rate and fixed nominal deposits at equal selected intervals; no withdrawals, fees, tax or variable returns. The equivalent-rate convention applies smooth exponential growth between stated compounding dates; actual product posting rules can differ. Whole contribution periods only, up to 1,200 months. Negative valid rates model losses, not negative deposits. Inflation deflates only the ending balance into today’s money. Today’s-money amounts of each historical contribution are not calculated. Rates are illustrative user assumptions, not market quotes, guaranteed returns or investment advice. Inputs remain in this tab; downloads occur only when requested. Currency selection relabels values without conversion. Frequently asked questions Can I include monthly contributions? Yes. Choose monthly contributions and enter the amount deposited each month. Contributions remain fixed in nominal money under this model. What is the difference between nominal and effective annual rates? A nominal rate needs a stated compounding frequency. An effective annual rate already represents the annual growth factor; the tool converts either to the selected payment interval. Do beginning contributions earn more? With a positive rate and the same number of deposits, they earn one extra period of growth. At zero rate they agree; negative rates can reverse the result. Does this include tax or fees? No. The calculator excludes tax, fees, withdrawals and changing returns. It does not model account-specific rules such as 401(k) limits. Why must my horizon match the contribution period? The schedule models equal whole payment periods. Annual contributions need whole years and quarterly contributions whole quarters; no fractional final payment is invented. Are the three scenarios probabilities? No. They are user-entered annual-rate assumptions with the other inputs unchanged, not confidence intervals, recommended returns or forecasts. Close the funding gap or revise costs and collections before committing. Download startup plan CSV Print / save PDF CSV is a current-values snapshot, including your cost lists and schedule. It contains no formulas. No inputs are transferred to other tools. Check actual payment dates in the 13-week forecast → Inspect the monthly cash path Trading cash starts at zero here so its deepest deficit can be measured separately from launch payments and funding. It is not the actual bank balance. Baseline cash payments are $2,800.00 per month. AI-generated editorial illustration of startup budgeting; not actual business records, supplier quotes or a financial forecast. Worked example: keep paid costs out of the new funding gap The service example budgets $2,500 launch cash, of which $500 is already paid. The $2,000 unpaid balance plus $200 chosen contingency, $2,600 deepest cumulative trading deficit and $1,000 cash floor requires $5,800 before available funds. With $3,000 usable cash left after paid costs, the additional funding gap is $2,800. Including the $500 historical payment, the full plan totals $6,300. These are planning assumptions, not surveyed prices. What this calculator includes Editable one-time launch and recurring cash lists, with already-paid launch amounts tracked separately. A 1–24 month schedule of customer cash collections and additional payments, with no assumed growth. Reserve based on the deepest cumulative trading deficit plus your chosen cash floor. Contingency on unpaid launch cash only, with available funds and the remaining gap shown separately. Service and online-store fictional examples, zero-receipts stress test, CSV snapshot and print option. Currency labels without exchange conversion; your inputs stay in this tab’s memory. How to calculate business startup costs and the cash needed now List the new cash payments needed to open: setup, deposits, equipment, initial stock, permits and other applicable items. Use supplier evidence from your own location. A category is a prompt, not a compulsory purchase. Enter the already-paid part beside each launch budget. Enter the unrestricted cash still available after those payments. An asset you already own with no new cash payment belongs in your asset record, not as a second purchase here. Build a monthly baseline from cash commitments you will actually pay: workplace, software, insurance, paid team and owner support. Include each commitment once. Annual premiums paid upfront should be scheduled when due rather than charged twice as an upfront and monthly payment. Choose the trading horizon. Enter usable customer cash collections and extra payments by month, including changing inventory purchases, delivery costs or debt payments that you decide to model. Do not enter projected invoices as bank receipts. Choose a minimum cash floor and a contingency percentage for unpaid launch costs. There is no universal percentage or horizon that makes a launch adequately funded. Review the full planning period as well as near-term dates. Review the deepest cumulative deficit, funding gap and individual months. Run the zero-receipts stress case. Replace estimates after quotes, paid pilots and settlement evidence improve, then carry the actual dates into the 13-week forecast. Startup funding formula: launch payments plus the cash shortfall Unpaid launch cash = sum of launch budgets − sum already paid. The launch contingency = unpaid launch cash × your contingency percentage ÷ 100. A refundable deposit is still cash unavailable for trading; this does not make it an accounting expense. For each month, net trading cash = customer cash collected − baseline monthly cash payments − additional payments. Cumulative trading cash starts at zero and adds each net month. The trading reserve is the largest cumulative shortage, not the sum of all negative months. Earlier trading surpluses can support later payments within this month-end model. Deepest deficit = max(0, −minimum cumulative trading cash). Required cash now = unpaid launch cash + launch contingency + deepest deficit + chosen minimum cash floor. Funding gap = max(0, required cash now − available cash now). Cash above the requirement = max(0, available cash − required cash). The historical launch payments are shown for the full plan but are not charged a second time against the cash available now. A zero funding gap means only that the entered monthly scenario is covered. It does not establish that customers will buy, a loan will arrive or a quote will hold. Worked startup-cost examples with a reconciled cash path Fictional USD cases; both have three trading months and a chosen $1,000 floor Measure Service example Online-store example Total launch budget / paid $2,500 / $500 $4,600 / $0 Unpaid launch / contingency $2,000 / $200 $4,600 / $460 Monthly baseline cash $2,800 $1,200 Monthly customer receipts $1,000; $2,000; $3,000 $1,000; $2,000; $3,000 Extra cash paid by month $0; $0; $0 $800; $1,000; $1,200 Cumulative trading cash −$1,800; −$2,600; −$2,400 −$1,000; −$1,200; −$600 Deepest deficit / required cash $2,600 / $5,800 $1,200 / $7,260 Available cash / funding gap $3,000 / $2,800 $4,000 / $3,260 In the service example, a $200 positive third month does not erase the earlier $2,600 funding need. Funding exactly $5,800, paying the $2,000 launch balance and leaving $200 contingency untouched produces a lowest uncommitted balance of $1,000 and a final balance of $1,200. The online-store example puts $3,000 opening stock inside the launch budget. Its monthly extra payments are new replenishment and other variable cash, not a repeat of that same opening purchase or a second cost-of-goods-sold deduction. The ecommerce startup guide has other examples; loading this preset does not import those examples or their timing. What belongs in a small-business startup budget? Classify cash once and retain the evidence Payment Where to enter it Evidence and boundary Equipment and fit-out Launch budget if paid before trading New payment only; record existing owned assets separately Opening stock Launch budget if paid before trading Count stock on hand and supplier payment date; avoid repeating the same purchase later Deposit and prepaid rent Launch budget if paid before trading Separate refundable cash tied up from recurring rent and expense recognition Permits and professional setup Launch or extra monthly payment when due Use the actual requirement and current quote; no jurisdictional fee is assumed Annual insurance or software prepayment Launch or extra monthly payment when due Do not also enter the same covered amount as a monthly cash payment Owner support and payroll Monthly baseline or dated extra cash Use one owner-compensation boundary; include additional employer payments if applicable Processor deductions, refunds and shipping Collections net of deductions, or extra payments State the chosen basis and never deduct the same item twice Loan proceeds and debt service Usable current funding / extra cash payments Promised proceeds are not current funds; future principal and interest must be included once if modeled What changes when customer receipts arrive late? Set the default service receipts to zero while leaving every cost unchanged. Three months of $2,800 baseline cash produces an $8,400 cumulative shortage. Add $2,000 unpaid launch, $200 contingency and $1,000 floor: required cash becomes $11,600. With $3,000 available, the gap is $8,600. This is a stress case, not a probability estimate. A late collection can move the lowest point even when total eventual sales are unchanged. Move a receipt to the month it can actually be used. If a processor settles after payroll is due within the same month, this tool’s monthly netting can still hide the shortage. Use the dated forecast for that decision. Shortening the horizon can make the displayed requirement smaller by excluding later commitments. It does not remove those commitments. Review the horizon, stock replacement, tax dates, debt service and owner needs before describing a plan as funded. Startup funding is different from break-even sales and cash runway This page answers how much cash covers launch payments and an entered early cash path. The monthly break-even calculator answers how much contribution is needed to fund recurring commitments and a profit goal. A startup can need substantial opening cash even if its later monthly break-even target is achievable. Cash runway starts with available cash and asks how long an ongoing cash gap can be sustained. A general startup budget also records payments needed before trading begins. Neither substitutes for a full financial model, a lender-requested business plan or a schedule of actual bank dates. Check cash runway for an ongoing monthly gap Use the ecommerce launch checklist and cost examples Assumptions and limits This is a monthly startup cash planning model, not a forecast of demand, profit, business valuation, loan approval or tax deductibility. All unpaid launch spending is assumed due before month one. Trading payments and receipts are netted at each month end; an earlier supplier payment or delayed settlement can require more cash than shown. The contingency percentage applies only to unpaid launch items and is held aside, not spent in the schedule. The cash floor is an additional chosen minimum. Baseline payments remain constant; add changing amounts in the monthly schedule. Available cash is unrestricted money usable now after historical payments, not expected loans or future customer collections. Costs and receipts outside the entered horizon are excluded. No tax, debt payment, owner pay, refund, fee or replacement cost is supplied unless you enter it. Input amounts are limited to 1 billion per field; monetary displays round to two decimals while the calculation retains greater precision. Frequently asked questions How much does it cost to start a small business? There is no universal amount in this calculator. The result comes from your launch payments, paid amounts, cash collections, ongoing payments and chosen reserve. The presets are fictional cases rather than typical prices. Why subtract already-paid startup costs? They remain in the full launch budget, but the same historical payment must not be deducted again from cash that is already measured after payment. Available cash must use that same cutoff. Does the reserve equal monthly overhead times a fixed number of months? Only if there are no customer receipts or changing payments. This tool calculates the deepest cumulative trading deficit in your entered schedule, then adds the cash floor you choose. What costs receive the contingency percentage? Only unpaid launch costs. The tool shows that amount separately and leaves it aside. It does not apply the percentage to historical paid items, monthly payments or the selected floor. Can I include inventory, deposits and owner pay? Yes, as cash payments with a clear timing boundary. Opening inventory and refundable deposits still tie up cash. Count owner support once and avoid duplicating a stock payment through both launch costs and monthly cost of goods sold. Can I download the startup budget? Download a CSV snapshot of the current cost lists, inputs, funding result and monthly schedule, or use browser print/save PDF. The CSV contains values and does not recalculate. No Excel formula workbook or Google Sheets compatibility is claimed. Does a zero gap mean I am ready to launch? It means your available cash covers the entered month-end scenario. Confirm quotes, practical capacity, actual payment dates, customer evidence and funding availability separately. Does changing currency convert the amounts? No. Currency selection changes labels only. Enter all amounts in one consistent currency.
