documents.text: COMPLETED-PERIOD CASH · FREE · NO SIGNUP Net Cash Flow Calculator Summarize actual operating, investing and financing cash for one completed period. Reconcile opening to closing cash, keep exchange effects separate, and inspect your observed balance and chosen reserve. Fictional example loaded. Currency labels do not convert amounts; enter explicit zeros for inactive categories. Calculate my cash movement → Summarize a completed period Use actual cash records for one consistent group of accounts. Dates label your totals; they do not filter or import bank transactions. Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Period start Period end Reset fictional example Try loan-funded cash growth Try FX and balance difference Opening balance Opening cash Reconciled cash immediately before the first date. This simplified scope excludes restricted cash and models overdraft borrowing separately. Operating cash Operating receipts Cash actually collected, not invoices issued. Include each operating receipt once. Operating payments Cash paid for suppliers, payroll, rent and other operating items; not accrued expenses or depreciation. Investing cash Investing receipts For example, cash proceeds from equipment or non-cash-equivalent investment sales. Investing payments Cash paid for long-term assets/investments. Exclude non-cash purchases and depreciation. Financing cash Financing receipts Loan proceeds or owner capital actually received; these are not customer sales. Financing payments Debt principal and owner distributions paid. Classify interest once under your reporting policy. Reconciliation and reserve Exchange-rate adjustment Signed effect on held foreign-currency cash, already translated into the selected currency. Use 0 if none. Not an operating/investing/financing receipt. Observed closing cash (optional) Reconciled closing cash with the same account scope. Blank = not checked; zero is an actual zero. Chosen closing-cash reserve (optional) Your nonnegative management threshold, not a cash payment or restricted balance deduction. Blank disables headroom. Inputs remain in this tab; no scenario is saved to an account. Your cash movement $2,500.00 Net cash flow from three activities 2026-09-01 through 2026-09-30 · 30 calendar days, inclusive · USD Total external receipts $24,000.00 Total external payments $21,500.00 Calculated closing cash $7,500.00 Total change, including FX $2,500.00 Where cash came from and went Operating cash flow $2,000.00 Receipts $20,000.00 Payments $18,000.00 Investing cash flow -$3,000.00 Receipts $0.00 Payments $3,000.00 Financing cash flow $3,500.00 Receipts $4,000.00 Payments $500.00 Opening-to-closing reconciliation Opening cash $5,000.00 + Operating cash flow $2,000.00 + Investing cash flow -$3,000.00 + Financing cash flow $3,500.00 + Separate exchange-rate effect $0.00 = Calculated closing cash $7,500.00 Closing balance check: not checked. Enter the observed balance to compare. Separate financing from the cash position Operating + investing movement -$1,000.00 Closing cash excluding net financing $4,000.00 Net financing included in actual closing $3,500.00 This removes both financing receipts and payments while holding operations, investing and FX unchanged. It is an arithmetic comparison, not an alternative funding plan, free cash flow or forecast. Chosen reserve check No reserve supplied; headroom is not calculated. Download cash summary CSV Print / save PDF CSV includes your currency label, dates, every amount, unrounded calculation values and assumptions. It contains no formulas and does not recalculate. Plan future cash dates in the 13-week forecast → See the separate cash movements Bars compare absolute amounts; labels retain each sign. FX remains outside the three-activity net cash-flow subtotal. Operating $2,000.00 Investing -$3,000.00 Financing $3,500.00 FX effect (separate) $0.00 RECONCILE THE RECORD Check a payment-processor settlement before entering totals A net bank deposit can already exclude the processor fee. This fictional check compares a documented gross collection, its fee and the matching net deposit. Keep refunds, taxes, held reserves, chargebacks and payouts across different periods outside this simple check until separately reconciled. Gross customer cash collected Processor fee withheld Matching net bank deposit Gross cash less fee $970.00 Observed deposit less expected net $0.00 The entered amounts agree to the displayed currency precision. This checks the entered figures, not the existence or completeness of transactions. For a fee-only settlement that reconciles, compare gross operating receipts of $1,000.00 plus a separate operating payment of $30.00 , or the expected net deposit of $970.00 without deducting that withheld fee again. Whether gross reconstruction is appropriate depends on the actual records and reporting scope. Using the net deposit and subtracting the fee again would leave $940.00 . Reset settlement example This check does not populate the cash-summary inputs or save values. Currency labels do not convert amounts. Settlement checks and planning links reviewed November 18, 2026. Example: more cash, with borrowing shown separately The loaded example collects $20,000 from operations and pays $18,000, producing $2,000 operating cash. A $3,000 equipment purchase uses investing cash. A $4,000 loan receipt less $500 principal repayment adds $3,500 financing cash. Total net cash flow is $2,500. Add $5,000 opening cash to reach $7,500 closing cash. The loan improves cash without becoming customer revenue. AI-generated editorial illustration of a cash-record review; not actual business records. What this calculator includes Gross external receipts and payments, three activity subtotals and a separate FX effect. Opening-to-closing bridge with a real zero distinguished from an unknown observed balance. Currency labels without conversion; valid reporting dates with an inclusive day count. Financing-excluded comparison and an optional period-end reserve threshold. Private tab-only inputs, precise CSV values, print and checked worked examples. Net cash flow formula: three activities, one cash bridge Net cash flow = operating cash flow + investing cash flow + financing cash flow. Within each activity, subtract cash payments from cash receipts. Calculated closing cash = opening cash + net cash flow + the separately entered exchange-rate effect. Opening cash is a balance carried into the period. Adding it to receipts would count money you already had as newly generated cash. The result labels keep the three-activity subtotal separate from the total change in cash when an exchange-rate adjustment exists. Fictional activity breakdown in USD: operating receipts $20,000 less payments $18,000 = +$2,000; investing receipts $0 less payments $3,000 = −$3,000; financing receipts $4,000 less payments $500 = +$3,500. Total receipts $24,000 less payments $21,500 = +$2,500. The same total can be checked as $24,000 total receipts minus $21,500 total payments = $2,500. Keeping the activity subtotals visible explains where that increase came from. With no exchange-rate effect, $5,000 opening cash plus $2,500 movement equals $7,500 closing cash. Prepare the cash records before entering totals Choose one completed period and one cash-account scope. For several included bank accounts, use their combined reconciled opening and closing balances. Match bank movements to the ledger and confirm cutoff dates. Enter amounts when cash moved, rather than the invoice, purchase-order or accounting expense date. Group each external receipt and payment once. Remove transfers between accounts inside the selected scope; they do not create cash for that combined group. Enter positive receipt and payment totals in all six activity fields, including an explicit 0 for an inactive category. Do not enter a negative payment to reverse the subtraction. Translate foreign-currency activity consistently before entry. Record any separate exchange-rate effect on held cash in its signed adjustment field. Enter the observed closing balance if available. Investigate any difference before using the calculated closing cash as the next forecast opening balance. The dates identify the period you summarized. Changing a date does not recalculate your underlying bank records. A September total labeled October is still a September total until you replace the amounts. Keep the source export or reconciliation beside the downloaded snapshot. Keep cash classification consistent without double counting Operating cash covers the cash side of ordinary business activity. Investing commonly includes cash paid for long-lived equipment and cash proceeds from its disposal. Financing commonly includes borrowing, principal repayments and owner capital movements. The SEC reference explains these three categories. This tool does not assign transactions automatically. Follow the classification policy used for your records, especially for interest, dividends, taxes and unusual transactions. A formal reporting framework can require treatments and disclosures beyond this summary. Customer invoice issued but unpaid: No cash receipt yet; keep it in the receivables records. Equipment bought with cash: Record the cash payment once; do not also enter depreciation as a payment. Loan received: Keep the receipt separate from customer collections. Loan installment: Split principal and interest from the lender statement; assign each once under your policy. Transfer between included accounts: Exclude both sides from combined external cash movement. Non-cash equipment financing: Do not invent a cash receipt and payment; retain it separately for accounting review. If you are summarizing only one account rather than the whole business, a transfer crosses that account boundary and requires separate identification in your supporting schedule. Do not silently mix an account-only statement with a business-wide cash total. Positive total cash can hide negative operating cash Consider a second fictional month: customer and other operating receipts are $15,000 against $18,000 operating payments. Operations use $3,000. Equipment payments use another $3,000. A $10,000 loan receipt less $500 principal repayment supplies $9,500 financing cash. Net cash flow is −$3,000 − $3,000 + $9,500 = +$3,500. Starting with $5,000 cash gives $8,500 closing cash. The bank balance increased while operating activity consumed cash. Treating all $25,000 of receipts as customer sales would conceal the funding source. The next useful question is whether the operating shortfall is temporary or recurring. Trace collections, supplier terms and payroll dates. Then put the confirmed loan proceeds and future repayments into a dated forecast. A cash increase by itself does not show that the business can keep funding operations. Why net cash flow does not equal net income or free cash flow Profit and cash answer different questions. The SEC guide explains how non-cash charges and operating balance changes can create a difference. This calculator starts from actual cash totals; it does not convert your income statement into cash automatically. For an arithmetic illustration only, suppose net income is $6,000. Add $2,000 depreciation, subtract a $4,000 increase in receivables, subtract a $3,000 increase in inventory and add a $1,000 increase in operating payables. Those specified adjustments produce $2,000 operating cash: $6,000 + $2,000 − $4,000 − $3,000 + $1,000. Assume no other reconciling items in this fictional example. Do not paste the $6,000 net income into operating receipts. That would bypass the cash records and could double count amounts already reflected in collections and payments. An indirect cash-flow reconciliation is a separate preparation method. Free cash flow also needs a stated definition. It often focuses on cash remaining after capital spending, whereas this page includes financing cash in its net total. The loaded example has $2,000 operating cash and $3,000 equipment spending, but its $2,500 net increase also includes borrowing and repayment. Use the displayed activity subtotals rather than relabeling the total as free cash flow, investment return or distributable profit. Reconcile closing cash without inserting a balancing plug In the loaded example, calculated closing cash is $7,500. If the comparable bank reconciliation shows $7,300, observed less calculated is −$200. That difference is a prompt to investigate; it is not proof of a particular missing expense. Check that the opening and closing balances include the same accounts. Then inspect uncleared items, duplicate entries, omitted charges, interaccount transfers and period cutoff. An invoice expense with no payment does not explain a bank outflow until cash actually moves. Correct the source records and the appropriate category, rather than inventing a $200 miscellaneous payment to force agreement. A zero difference verifies the arithmetic against the entered observed balance. It cannot establish that all records are complete or that every receipt was correctly classified. Leaving the optional observed field blank produces “not checked”; entering 0 performs a real comparison. If the exchange-rate adjustment is +$100 with all default cash activity unchanged, net cash flow stays $2,500 while total change in cash becomes $2,600 and calculated closing cash becomes $7,600. That exchange effect is not an additional customer collection. Use monthly or annual totals, then inspect payment timing The formula works for a week, month or year when all inputs share that period. For an annual calculation, total the actual yearly cash activity by category and use cash immediately before the year starts as opening cash. Do not multiply one month by twelve and describe it as an observed annual result. A positive period-end balance can still hide a shortage earlier in the period. For example, $1,000 opening cash followed by a $4,000 payroll payment on Monday reaches −$3,000 before a $6,000 Friday collection lifts cash to $3,000. The period totals alone do not display that sequence. The calculator has no minimum daily balance output because it accepts activity totals, not individual events. Use the 13-week forecast for future dated receipts and payments, and check daily sequencing separately when weekly cash is tight. A negative calculated balance here flags incomplete funding or records; it does not authorize an overdraft. Build the dated 13-week cash schedule Compare the cash schedule with the sales break-even target Keep a cash summary, then roll verified actuals into the forecast Download the CSV after checking the period, currency and closing difference. It preserves the entered category totals and calculated results as values. Editing the file does not update formulas because there are none. The download does not include bank transactions or independently verify your source records. When the period is closed, carry the reconciled closing cash into the next forecast opening balance on the same account basis. Remove cleared forecast events instead of keeping both the actual payment and its original expectation. Move a genuinely uncollected invoice to its revised expected date; do not invent a second receipt. Keep uncertain collections, planned financing and reserve assumptions visible in the forward plan. The actual-period summary explains what happened. The forecast tests whether the next payroll, supplier payment or equipment purchase can be funded on its payment date. Read financing support and reserve headroom without inventing a forecast Cash movement before financing = operating cash flow + investing cash flow. Closing cash excluding net financing = opening cash + operating cash flow + investing cash flow + FX. Both financing receipts and payments are removed; all other totals are held unchanged. This is not free cash flow, because investing cash may include asset sales and investments as well as capital spending. In the default fictional example, operating + investing = $2,000 − $3,000 = −$1,000. With $5,000 opening cash and zero FX, the financing-excluded closing comparison is $4,000. Adding the actual +$3,500 net financing gives $7,500 calculated closing cash. Do not interpret the $4,000 comparison as a prediction of what would happen without a loan. Chosen reserve headroom = calculated closing cash − your threshold. With $7,500 calculated cash and a chosen $8,000 threshold, headroom is −$500. The reserve is not subtracted when calculating closing cash. It is not a legal minimum or a recommended buffer, and the threshold is not a forecast of future bills. The second preset adds a +$100 FX effect to the default activity totals: activity net cash flow stays $2,500; total cash change becomes $2,600 and closing cash $7,600. Observed closing cash of $7,400 produces a −$200 difference. Against the chosen $8,000 reserve, calculated headroom is −$400. These are illustrative arithmetic checks, not observed business results. Check deposits, card settlements and reporting policy Use one basis throughout: cash receipts and payments from records reconciled to the same opening and observed closing scope. If a payment processor nets its fee from customer settlements, do not enter the net deposit as gross receipts and deduct that fee again. Reconstruct gross receipts plus the separately identified fee only when the supporting records and chosen scope reconcile. Pending card receipts need explicit treatment in that scope. For a multi-account cash summary, remove internal transfers between included accounts. A transfer to an excluded account crosses your boundary; identify it in the supporting schedule before assigning its activity. Transfers are not new customer revenue merely because they appear as bank credits. Non-cash depreciation, asset exchanges and equipment acquired entirely through non-cash financing do not become receipts or payments. An unpaid supplier invoice is not a cash payment. Classify actual cash interest, dividends and tax consistently under your applicable reporting framework; this calculator does not make that accounting-policy decision. As of this review, IFRS 18 applies to annual periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, with earlier application permitted. It also amends aspects of IAS 7, including interest/dividend classification and the indirect-method starting point. This tool is a direct cash summary and does not certify either pre- or post-adoption statutory presentation. Assumptions and limits Simplified direct cash summary for a completed period; not a statutory statement, bank reconciliation service, tax calculation or forecast. Choose a consistent cash-account scope and classification policy. This model excludes restricted cash and assumes nonnegative opening and observed cash; it does not determine formal overdraft or cash-equivalent presentation. Only FX can be signed as an input; enter receipts and payments as positive amounts. Required blanks are incomplete, not zero. Optional observed balance and reserve distinguish blank from stated zero. Amounts are capped at one trillion each. Calculations use decimal precision40; displayed money rounds to cents and small nonzero values use scientific notation. Currency changes labels only. A reserve is a chosen threshold, not an expense or deduction from cash. Intraperiod liquidity, automatic transaction classification and indirect-method preparation are outside this summary. Frequently asked questions How do I calculate net cash flow? Subtract payments from receipts within operating, investing and financing activity, then add those three net amounts. Add the result and any separate exchange-rate effect to opening cash to calculate closing cash. Can net cash flow be negative? Yes. Payments can exceed receipts. Whether closing cash is also negative depends on opening cash and the separate exchange-rate adjustment. Review the activity causing the outflow and its funding. Is opening cash included in cash inflows? No. Opening cash is the balance already held at the start. It belongs in the bridge to closing cash, not in newly received cash for the period. Where do loan proceeds and principal repayments go? In this simplified example, loan proceeds are financing receipts and principal repayments are financing payments. Keep interest separate and classify it once according to the policy used for your records. Can I calculate annual net cash flow? Yes. Enter one full year of actual cash receipts and payments and the matching opening balance. The dates are labels for your totals, not an automatic transaction filter or annualization feature. Why is my closing cash different from the bank balance? Check account scope, opening reconciliation, cutoff dates, missing or duplicated movements and exchange effects. Compare on a consistent basis and correct the records rather than adding a balancing plug. Can I import bank transactions or connect my bank? No. Enter summarized totals manually. The CSV download is a values-only record of the summary, not a bank integration or accounting ledger. Does this replace a 13-week forecast? No. This page summarizes a selected completed period. The separate forecast accepts dated future events and tests timing and reserve gaps. Does changing currency convert my amounts? No. Select one currency label and enter every activity, balance and FX effect already translated consistently to that currency. The tool does not retrieve exchange rates. Is the exchange-rate effect part of net cash flow? The three-activity net total excludes the separately entered FX effect. Total cash change includes it, so calculated closing cash can differ from opening cash plus activity flows alone. What does closing cash excluding financing mean? It removes net financing receipts less payments while holding operations, investing and FX unchanged. It is an arithmetic comparison, not free cash flow or a financing/demand forecast. Does reserve headroom show that I can pay every bill? No. It compares calculated period-end cash with your chosen threshold. A period can end above reserve after running short earlier; use the linked dated 13-week forecast for payment timing. documents.text: Financial performance calculator Operating Profit Margin Calculator Use a consistent reporting period to calculate operating margin. Choose reported operating income or build it from revenue and costs, with every subtotal visible. Connect revenue, gross profit and operating income Start with net revenue after returns and discounts. Subtract the adopted cost of sales once to find gross profit, then operating expenses once to find operating income. A positive operating margin alone does not fund expansion or recover customer acquisition costs. Navigation and planning connections reviewed November 17, 2026. Choose your input method Input method Build from revenue, COGS and OPEX Use reported operating income Choose one method for the same reporting period. Each method keeps its own values; the two sets are never combined. Amounts are labeled USD, with no currency conversion. Net revenue Same-period sales after returns and discounts. Cost of goods sold / cost of sales Include amounts already classified in cost of sales once. Operating expenses excluding COGS Include operating depreciation here only if it is not already in COGS. Reset fictional example Your result 24% Operating profit margin Same-period calculation reconciliation Line USD / percent Net revenue $50,000.00 Less COGS $20,000.00 Gross profit $30,000.00 Less operating expenses $18,000.00 Operating income / loss $12,000.00 Operating margin 24% OPEX / revenue, excluding COGS 36% Margin = operating income ÷ net revenue × 100. This result is neither net margin nor operating cash-flow margin. AI-generated editorial illustration of an operating-expense review; not actual business records. Read the worked example before changing costs Fictional baseline: 50,000 revenue − 20,000 COGS − 18,000 OPEX = 12,000 operating income. Margin = 12,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 24%. OPEX excludes COGS; operating depreciation is included once in the relevant subtotal. What this calculator includes Two exclusive input methods with independent values Visible income-statement reconciliation Operating losses allowed; zero-revenue ratio unavailable No signup; inputs remain in the page state Operating profit margin formula and the two input methods Operating profit margin = operating income ÷ net revenue × 100. In statement mode, operating income = net revenue − COGS − OPEX. OPEX excludes COGS in this presentation. Enter all three same-period amounts; include any operating depreciation in the appropriate cost subtotal once. Direct mode instead takes reported operating income and revenue, without deducting the hidden COGS or OPEX fields. Choose direct mode when an income statement already provides a reconciled operating-income subtotal. Choose statement mode when you have compatible COGS and OPEX totals. The modes keep independent inputs, so switching methods does not combine a reported profit with costs that were already deducted. A blank field requests input; explicit zero is accepted where meaningful. For the fictional baseline, net revenue 50,000 less COGS 20,000 gives gross profit 30,000; less OPEX 18,000 gives operating income 12,000. Dividing 12,000 by 50,000 gives 24%. The OPEX ratio excluding COGS is 36%. COGS 40% + OPEX 36% + operating margin 24% reconciles to 100%. Classify the example OPEX schedule before entering costs Gather matching records before calculating Use a closed reporting period and the same business or segment boundary. Reconcile net sales after the returns and discounts already recognized in the period. Do not add sales taxes collected for a third party into this example’s revenue. Keep customer deposits, loans and owner contributions distinct from earned sales. COGS should follow the goods or services recognized in that period, not simply the inventory purchased or supplier cash paid. Check whether production wages, depreciation, shipping and other costs are included there. Then define OPEX without those same amounts. The calculator does not decide accounting policies or infer cost classifications from a bank statement. Interest and income tax are excluded from operating income under this nonfinancial-business illustration. Specialized businesses and different presentations may differ. Use the actual reported subtotal and document the definition when comparing companies. Do not automatically remove restructuring, unusual operating losses or recurring charges to create an adjusted number. Compare profitable, loss-making and growth cases Each row below changes the stated inputs independently. A higher sales number does not guarantee a higher operating margin. The lower-cost case assumes no adverse effect on quality or sales solely to show the arithmetic; it is not evidence that a cut can be implemented without consequences. Original fictional same-period examples, USD Case Revenue COGS OPEX Operating income Operating margin Baseline 50,000 20,000 18,000 12,000 24% Higher sales, same 40% COGS rate 60,000 24,000 18,000 18,000 30% Growth with weaker costs 60,000 27,000 22,000 11,000 18.33% Lower OPEX with unchanged sales 50,000 20,000 16,000 14,000 28% Operating loss 30,000 15,000 18,000 −3,000 −10% No revenue 0 0 2,000 −2,000 Unavailable At zero revenue, the loss amount remains meaningful but dividing by zero does not give a meaningful margin. At positive revenue with zero operating income, the margin is exactly 0%. A negative margin is valid and should not be suppressed. The tool rejects amounts outside its supported numerical range instead of displaying infinity. Interpret the margin without inventing a good-margin benchmark A 24% operating margin means 24 cents of the stated revenue dollar remains as operating income under the entered boundary. It does not mean the business has collected 24 cents in cash or that owners can withdraw that amount. Receivables, inventory, capital spending, financing and tax require other schedules. For trend review, compare matching periods, similar product mix and the same cost classifications. A seasonal month can differ from a full year, and an acquisition or new site can change the scope. Do not use a universal good-margin threshold: the appropriate comparison depends on the business model and evidence from comparable operations. This calculator does not contain verified industry benchmarks. Look at operating income dollars alongside the percentage. A smaller high-margin business can earn fewer dollars than a larger lower-margin business. At 50,000 revenue and 12,000 operating income, margin is 24%; at 100,000 revenue and 18,000 operating income it is 18%. Income rises 6,000 while margin falls six percentage points. Neither metric should replace the other. Operating, gross, contribution, net and EBIT margins Gross margin uses revenue less COGS. Operating margin also deducts the defined operating-period expenses. Contribution margin instead subtracts variable costs, which can exist inside both COGS and selling expenses. A functional income statement does not by itself identify which bills vary with sales. Net margin uses net income after the relevant non-operating and tax items. Operating margin excludes those items under this example’s boundary. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortization under its definition and is outside this tool. Do not add those noncash charges back when the task is operating margin. Operating income and EBIT are not universally interchangeable. In a separate illustrative reconciliation, operating income is 12,000, non-operating income is 1,000, interest expense is 500 and income tax is 2,500. Pretax income is 12,500 and net income is 10,000. Defining EBIT as net income plus interest and income tax gives 13,000. Operating margin remains 24%, while that EBIT divided by 50,000 would be 26%. State the measure rather than silently swapping numerators. Operating cash-flow margin divides operating cash flow by revenue and answers a different question. It is deliberately excluded from this calculator and from the operating-margin keyword targets. Cash-flow classifications and timing need their own evidence. Contribution versus gross margin Contribution versus profit margin Build a contribution income statement Check whether a ratio change is only a reclassification In the baseline, move 2,000 of a legitimately reclassified expense from OPEX into COGS. COGS becomes 22,000, OPEX becomes 16,000 and operating income remains 12,000. Gross margin falls from 60% to 56%; the OPEX ratio falls from 36% to 32%; operating margin stays 24%. No cash has been saved by the relabeling alone. The example is a diagnostic, not permission to choose accounts to achieve a preferred result. Keep a record of the policy change and compatible comparison periods. Reconcile actual expense amounts and operating work before treating a lower ratio as improved performance. Use the result to choose the next investigation Reconcile sales, COGS and OPEX to the source records and preserve the original reporting boundary. Identify whether the change comes from selling prices, mix, cost of sales or operating commitments. Check capacity, service quality and customer retention before assuming a cost reduction preserves revenue. Review cash timing separately; a positive operating margin does not fund a supplier payment before collections arrive. Investigate activity and spending with a flexible budget Connect the operating result to a cash and resource plan Assumptions and limits One matching reporting period and business scope. Revenue and cost inputs are nonnegative; direct operating income may be negative. Input limit is 1 trillion per field. Displayed currency is USD without conversion. No tax, cash-flow, inventory or adjusted-earnings model is automated. Frequently asked questions What is the operating profit margin formula? Operating income divided by same-period net revenue, multiplied by 100. In build mode, income is revenue less COGS and OPEX excluding COGS. Can operating margin be negative? Yes. Revenue 30,000 less COGS 15,000 and OPEX 18,000 gives a 3,000 operating loss and −10% margin. What if revenue is zero? The calculator shows the income or loss amount but marks the ratio unavailable. Zero revenue cannot be used as a ratio denominator. Is operating margin the same as net margin? No. Net margin uses net income after the relevant non-operating and tax items; operating margin uses the operating subtotal. Is operating margin the same as EBIT margin? Not always. A separately defined EBIT figure may include non-operating income or expenses. Reconcile its definition before using it. Can I include depreciation separately? Include it once in the appropriate operating cost subtotal. Do not add a second charge if depreciation is already in COGS or OPEX. No fractional month, continuation beyond the last entered month or guaranteed future receipts are assumed. The example pays $6,000.00 initially and another $1,000.00 in month one. Quick formula check ROI = (total modeled benefits − total modeled costs) ÷ total modeled costs × 100. In the fictional AI example, $200 monthly cash savings less $100 running cost gives $100 net per active month. With $600 setup and 12 active months, total costs are $1,800, net benefit is $600 and total-cost ROI is 33.33%. Simple payback is six months. The other 30 saved hours are capacity, not cash. What this calculator includes Business investment and AI automation modes with independent inputs. Total-cost ROI, net modeled cash benefit, fractional payback and month-end recovery. AI task adoption, human review, paid-hours changes and remaining capacity kept separate. Lower, entered and higher workload comparisons with per-task AI cost scaling. Month-zero investment and monthly cumulative recovery table. Global currency labels with no exchange conversion; browser-only inputs. CSV snapshot and browser print / save PDF. How to use the business ROI calculator Choose Business investment or AI automation. Switching preserves each mode’s separate inputs. Choose one currency and a whole-month planning horizon. Enter all costs and benefits in that same currency. Enter incremental one-time cash investment and fixed monthly costs. Exclude costs already paid regardless of the decision. Business mode: enter additional collected contribution after incremental variable costs, plus genuinely avoidable cash payments. Do not enter gross sales as contribution. AI mode: enter eligible task volume, adoption, before/after time including checking, and the share of net hours that actually changes paid labor. Only monetize remaining released hours when there is capacity, sell-through and a defensible contribution per hour. Do not count the same hours as both payroll savings and new work. Compare lower workload, entered workload and higher workload. Review the month-by-month cash path and actual payment dates before acting. ROI and payback formulas: one explicit cost boundary Total modeled costs = one-time investment + all fixed monthly running costs + active-month per-task AI costs + any additional paid labor required. Total benefits = active-month incremental contribution + actual avoided cash payments. Net benefit = total benefits − total costs. ROI (%) = net benefit ÷ total costs × 100. Zero total cost makes ROI undefined, even if a benefit exists. With no delay and a positive stable monthly net benefit, fractional payback = setup cash ÷ monthly net benefit. With d months of benefit delay: payback = d + (setup + d × fixed monthly cost) ÷ active monthly net benefit. A zero or negative active net benefit has no finite payback in this model. A result beyond the chosen horizon is labeled as such. The table records the full setup outlay at month zero, then each month’s cash benefits less cash costs. It identifies the first recovered month-end within the chosen horizon. Fractional payback and the first recovered month-end can differ. ROI uses the selected horizon and a total-cost denominator. It is not the return divided only by setup cost, and it is not annualized CAGR. Comparing different horizons without that context can mislead. How the AI automation mode values saved time Adopted tasks = eligible monthly tasks × adoption rate. Net saved hours = adopted tasks × (manual minutes − AI minutes including human review and correction) ÷ 60. Paid-hours change = net saved hours × paid-hours conversion rate. Multiply that signed hours change by loaded hourly cost. A positive paid-hours change counts as avoided labor cash; a negative change creates an additional labor cost. A zero paid-hours share models fixed salary cash even when the workflow frees or consumes time. Remaining hours = net saved hours − paid-hours change. Assumed extra sold hours = max(remaining hours, 0) × sell-through rate. Extra contribution = sold hours × collected contribution per hour after incremental delivery costs. This partitions the time: paid hours are not available again for selling. A slower AI workflow may consume capacity. The model shows that instead of clamping all time savings to zero. No automatic performance improvement, hourly rate or tool price is promised. Per-task cost covers your own API/usage estimate; fixed subscription and maintenance belong in fixed monthly cost. Reproduce the fictional worked examples Business case: $6,000 setup, $200 monthly running cost and $1,200 monthly additional collected contribution. Net monthly benefit is $1,000; 12 months gives $14,400 benefit minus $8,400 total cost. AI case: 80 adopted tasks at 60 manual minutes versus 30 minutes with AI and human checking saves 40 hours. At $20/hour and 25% paid-hours conversion, 10 paid hours save $200. Thirty hours remain as capacity. With $100 monthly running cost, no per-task charge and $600 setup, net monthly cash benefit is $100. If payroll stays unchanged and none of the released capacity is sold, set paid-hours conversion and capacity sell-through to zero. Forty hours can still be released, but the tool reports no labor cash savings and no assumed sales. For a two-month benefit delay in the AI example, fixed cost still runs from month one. Ten active months produce $2,000 benefit; costs are $600 + 12 × $100 = $1,800. Net benefit is $200, ROI is 11.11%, and payback is 2 + ($600 + 2 × $100) ÷ $100 = 10 months. 12-month examples, USD, no benefit delay; not market benchmarks Case Benefits Total cost Net benefit Total-cost ROI Simple payback Business investment $14,400 $8,400 $6,000 71.43% 6 months AI: paid hours actually fall $2,400 $1,800 $600 33.33% 6 months AI: same fixed salary, no extra sales $0 $1,800 −$1,800 −100% No finite payback Compare scenarios without treating them as demand predictions The default comparison uses 75%, 100% and 125% of entered workload. These are editable what-if assumptions, not confidence intervals. Costs are not all scaled by the same percentage. Business mode scales additional contribution with workload, holds the separately entered avoidable monthly cash saving constant and holds fixed running cost constant. AI mode scales task volume, related time changes, extra-work contribution and per-task costs. Adoption and time per task stay as entered; other avoidable monthly cash saving stays constant. A smaller workload can have a different ROI even though the subscription is unchanged. More work is not automatically better if each AI task creates more cost than benefit. Check demand, staff availability and task quality separately. Look at net cash benefit and the lowest cumulative balance, not ROI alone. A high percentage on a small cost base may produce little money. For actual funding dates, continue to the dated cash-flow tool. Check these records before replacing the example The calculator does not connect to your payroll, AI provider or sales account. Inputs and scenario factors are assumptions you supply. Compare the result with actual results after a pilot and update the model when costs or adoption change. Use a matching workflow and period Input Evidence Avoid Task volume and time Task logs, sample timed runs, review and failure/rework time Assuming every task is suitable for AI Paid-hours share Overtime, contractor invoices, actual hours that will be added or removed Calling unchanged salary cash a saving Recurring and setup cost Supplier quote, implementation scope, API/usage report Counting a subscription twice Extra contribution Confirmed workload and contribution after added delivery costs Using gross sales or selling the same hours twice Assumptions and limits The business and AI modes use pre-tax, undiscounted incremental cash. A separate uneven schedule calculates simple and discounted month-end recovery. These are not accounting net profit, IRR or a demand forecast. Benefits start after the entered delay; fixed running cost starts in month one. There is no terminal asset/resale value, financing, depreciation or unentered tax/cost. Monthly benefits and costs are constant after launch. Fractional payback assumes smooth cash timing within a month; real dates and intramonth shortfalls require a cash forecast. Saved salary time is not a cash saving unless actual paid hours change. Extra contribution requires completed and collected extra work. Currency changes relabel amounts; they do not convert values. Frequently asked questions How do you calculate business ROI? This tool divides modeled net benefit by total modeled costs over your chosen horizon. Costs include setup and ongoing payments. Inputs must describe incremental cash benefits and costs on the same boundary. What does the AI automation mode do? It converts adopted task volume and net time change into actual paid-labor changes and remaining capacity. Optional extra sold hours produce contribution only from the remaining positive capacity and your sell-through assumptions. Are all saved hours cash savings? No. A salaried employee’s unused time can remain capacity while payroll is unchanged. Only the entered paid-hours conversion share changes cash labor cost. Why is ROI 33.33% when $600 setup produces $600 net benefit? The default AI case also incurs $1,200 recurring cost over 12 months. Total modeled cost is $1,800, so $600 net benefit divided by $1,800 is 33.33%. Dividing by setup alone is a different return measure. What if setup cost is zero? ROI can still be defined if there are recurring costs. If every modeled cost is zero, the percentage is undefined. With no initial outlay there is no setup cash to recover; inspect the running net benefit instead. What if benefits start late or never cover the running cost? Fixed monthly running cost starts immediately. Benefits and usage costs start only after the delay. Nonpositive active monthly net benefit has no finite payback; no automatic borrowing is added. Does ROI include taxes, financing or resale value? The business and AI modes are pre-tax and undiscounted. The separate uneven schedule discounts entered monthly net cash at your annual effective rate. Include any relevant tax, financing or resale cash consistently if using that schedule; neither mode supplies tax assumptions, IRR or a formal valuation. Are the workload scenarios forecasts? No. They are editable workload assumptions. No customer demand, adoption rate, time saving or sales conversion is independently verified. Does changing currency convert my values? No. It changes labels and formatting. Enter every amount in the chosen currency using your own consistent conversion if needed. Are my inputs saved or sent? The calculator itself keeps inputs in browser memory for the current tab and has no save or submission request. Reloading resets them. Downloaded CSV files contain the values you choose to export. Reset example What the discount must earn back Sales needed to preserve baseline profit 136 / month 36 additional completed sales (36% above baseline). 5 % off 10 % off 15 % off 20 % off Sale price USD 90.00 10% off · USD 10.00 saved per sale Contribution per sale USD 27.30 Previously USD 37.00 Expected completed sales 120 Profit change after campaign cost -USD 424.00 Contribution change -USD 424.00 less USD 0.00 campaign cost Expected volume leaves profit below the baseline. Existing overhead is assumed unchanged. This is profit change, not absolute net profit. Revenue-only recovery 112 sales This ignores fulfillment costs and campaign expense. Profit recovery 136 sales Includes variable costs, percentage fees and the campaign cost. The recovery target fits entered capacity. Profit change at full entered capacity: USD 395.00 . See the calculation Baseline: USD 37.00 contribution × 100 sales = USD 3,700.00 . Discounted contribution = USD 90.00 × (1 − 3% ) − USD 60.00 = USD 27.30 . Required sales = ceiling[( USD 3,700.00 + USD 0.00 ) ÷ USD 27.30 ] = 136 . Continuous sales lift before whole-sale rounding: 35.53% . Expected contribution: USD 3,276.00 . Profit change = USD 3,276.00 − USD 3,700.00 − USD 0.00 = -USD 424.00 . Contribution margin changes from 37% to 30.33% . This is not net profit margin. Calculations retain precision; displayed money and percentages round to two decimals. Required sales round up and expected completed sales round down. Compare the offer before you launch Discount supported by expected sales 6.35% limit Minimum price rounded upward to two decimals: USD 93.65 . The displayed percentage limit is rounded downward. Uses 120 completed sales, revised costs and the campaign expense. This is a mathematical limit, not a recommended promotion. Discount supported by capacity 12.71% limit Minimum price rounded upward to two decimals: USD 87.29 . The displayed percentage limit is rounded downward. A capacity limit describes what you can deliver, not what customers will buy. Each card keeps your expected sales at 120 and changes only the discount. Revised costs, fees and campaign expense stay the same. 0% off Sale price USD 100.00 Contribution per sale USD 37.00 Required sales 100 Profit change USD 740.00 Target fits capacity 5% off Sale price USD 95.00 Contribution per sale USD 32.15 Required sales 116 Profit change USD 158.00 Target fits capacity 10% off Sale price USD 90.00 Contribution per sale USD 27.30 Required sales 136 Profit change -USD 424.00 Target fits capacity 15% off Sale price USD 85.00 Contribution per sale USD 22.45 Required sales 165 Profit change -USD 1,006.00 Target exceeds capacity 20% off Sale price USD 80.00 Contribution per sale USD 17.60 Required sales 211 Profit change -USD 1,588.00 Target exceeds capacity 25% off Sale price USD 75.00 Contribution per sale USD 12.75 Required sales 291 Profit change -USD 2,170.00 Target exceeds capacity Download promotion CSV Print / save PDF Per-sale contribution reaches zero at 38.14% off using the promotion cost. This boundary funds no baseline contribution or campaign expense; stay below it to retain positive per-sale contribution. What this calculator includes Enter percentage off, amount off per sale or a proposed sale price. Include percentage fees and changed promotion delivery costs without counting them twice. Include additional fixed campaign expense once for the same modeled month. Separate revenue-only recovery from the whole-sales target preserving baseline profit. Check required and expected sales against optional monthly delivery capacity. Calculate discount limits at expected sales and at full capacity. Compare six discount scenarios with costs, fees and campaign expense held constant. Download inputs and results as CSV, or print / save PDF. Choose among 155 currency labels without converting amounts. How to use the discount break-even calculator Start with one product, service or comparable order type. Use a representative completed month rather than mixing several periods. This makes the extra sales target comparable with your actual workload. Enter the current net selling price and variable delivery cost for one consistent product, service or customer cohort. Exclude sales tax collected for others. Enter revised promotion cost if extra packaging, shipping or variable labor changes the per-sale cost. Blank keeps the old cost; zero sets revised cost to zero. Add the percentage selling fee separately. Put flat transaction charges in variable cost and avoid counting any cost twice. Choose percentage off, amount off per sale or the proposed sale price. These are alternative ways to enter one discount, not stacked discounts. Enter completed monthly sales before the offer and your expected sales increase. All modeled sales receive the promotion; unaffected customers belong in a separate group. Add fixed campaign spending for this same month, then enter deliverable monthly capacity if known. Compare required sales, expected profit change and the discount limits. Compare several discounts, download the scenario CSV or print the result. A mathematical threshold does not predict demand. Measure the promotion before applying it to every sale Gather a matched set of records before replacing the example inputs. These are input checks, not market averages. Records to check before calculating Input group Record to use Boundary to check Price and fee Paid invoice and processor statement Use the realized discounted price; flat charges belong in variable cost. Completed volume Fulfilled orders for the affected offer Exclude canceled orders and sales that never receive the promotion. Sales lift and capacity Prior offer results and delivery schedule Enter an assumption you can track; required sales are not forecast demand. Discount break-even formula after costs and payment fees Let P be the current price, f the percentage fee as a decimal, V0 the original variable cost, V1 the promotion variable cost, Q0 the baseline monthly sales and K the additional fixed campaign expense for that month. Current contribution per sale C0 = P × (1 − f) − V0. Discounted price P1 = P × (1 − d), or P − amount off. From a proposed sale price, d = 1 − P1 ÷ P. Discounted contribution per sale C1 = P1 × (1 − f) − V1. Whole sales needed for the same profit = ceiling[(Q0 × C0 + K) ÷ C1], when C1 is positive. Required extra sales = target − Q0. Whole-sale lift = (target ÷ Q0 − 1) × 100. Negative extra sales can occur when revised costs fall enough. Expected sales Q1 = floor[Q0 × (1 + assumed lift)]. Profit change = Q1 × C1 − Q0 × C0 − K. Existing fixed overhead is assumed unchanged and cancels from this comparison; this does not calculate absolute net profit. Revenue-only recovery = ceiling(P × Q0 ÷ P1), when the sale price is positive. It ignores variable costs and campaign spending, so it can materially understate the sales needed to preserve profit. At a chosen completed volume Q, the minimum price preserving baseline profit is [(Q0 × C0 + K) ÷ Q + V1] ÷ (1 − f). Maximum discount = 1 − minimum price ÷ P. If the minimum price exceeds P, no discount fits that volume. Apply this separately to expected volume and capacity. With unchanged cost, no percentage fee and no campaign expense, the simplified continuous formula is extra sales ratio = d ÷ (m − d), where m is the original contribution margin ratio. A 40% margin and 20% discount need 100% more sales, not 20%. If d is at least m, no positive contribution remains. How many extra sales does a 10% discount need? These are illustrative planning examples, not customer results or market averages. The starting service example contributes $100 × 0.97 − $60 = $37 per sale. At 100 sales, the baseline is $3,700. A 10% discount makes the selling price $90 and contribution $27.30. The exact recovery ratio is $3,700 ÷ $27.30 = 135.5311… sales. Round upward to 136 completed sales: 136 × $27.30 = $3,712.80. The whole-sale recovery target is therefore a 36% sales increase. At your assumed 20% lift, 120 sales contribute $3,276, which is $424 below the baseline. Illustrative scenarios using unrounded contribution values Scenario New contribution per sale Required whole sales Expected contribution change Service: $100 price, $60 cost, 3% fee; 100 sales; 10% off, 20% lift $27.30 136 (+36%) −$424 at 120 sales Retail: $50 price, $25 cost, 3% fee; 200 sales; 15% off, 40% lift $16.225 290 (+45%) −$157 at 280 sales Service: same baseline; 20% off, 20% lift $17.60 211 (+111%) −$1,588 at 120 sales The retail example starts with $23.50 contribution per sale and $4,700 monthly contribution. A $42.50 discounted price leaves $16.225 before display rounding. At 280 completed sales, contribution is $4,543. Required sales use the unrounded value: 290 sales contribute $4,705.25. If service capacity is 150 sales, the 10% discount recovery target of 136 fits. The 20% discount target of 211 does not. Capacity is a delivery ceiling, not evidence that customers will buy. What to check before acting on the result Save the baseline price, cost and contribution before the offer starts. Compare completed promotional sales with the recovery target; record extra staffing or campaign spending separately. If the promotion changes the basket or product mix, recalculate using that mix rather than counting every extra order as equivalent. Read the sales increase, margin impact and capacity results The default 10% discount needs 112 whole sales just to preserve $10,000 revenue, but 136 to preserve $3,700 contribution with unchanged overhead. At the entered 120 sales, revenue rises to $10,800 while contribution falls to $3,276, a $424 reduction. If the same offer adds $300 of fixed campaign spending, the unchanged-profit target becomes ceiling[($3,700 + $300) ÷ $27.30] = 147 sales. Expected profit falls $724 at 120 sales. Campaign spending is deducted once, not once per order. At 120 expected sales and no campaign expense, the exact price floor is approximately $93.64261168, allowing about 6.35738832% off. A final price of $93.65 or a discount no larger than the displayed conservative 6.35% limit preserves the baseline under these assumptions. The proposed 10% discount does not. At 150-sale capacity, the same default cost structure supports an exact discount of about 12.71477663%; the displayed conservative limit is 12.71%. This is not a recommended discount, and capacity is not evidence of demand. Zero or negative discounted contribution means more units cannot recover a positive baseline plus campaign expense. The zero-contribution boundary ignores existing overhead and campaign recovery. Promotion-specific cost can move this boundary below the full price. This model applies the promotion to every modeled completed sale. It does not estimate cannibalization, repeat purchase value, inventory liquidation value, refunds, tax, staggered redemptions or a changing product mix. Evaluate those separately instead of treating future benefits as guaranteed. Common mistakes when calculating discount profitability Recovering revenue instead of contribution. Revenue ignores the cost of fulfilling each extra sale. Entering profit margin as variable cost. Use actual per-sale delivery costs. Counting the payment fee inside cost and again in the fee field. Assuming additional sales need no staff time or capacity. Applying the discount to a few customers while entering the volume of the whole business. Model the affected group separately. Calling the recovery target a forecast. Validate demand with your own promotion records. Assumptions and limits This is a one-month comparison of the same product, service or affected customer cohort. Every modeled sale receives the discount; price and per-sale cost are constant within each scenario. Existing fixed overhead is unchanged. Additional campaign spending is incremental fixed expense for the same month, counted once. Profit change is contribution change less campaign expense, not absolute net profit or cash flow. Sales mix and the percentage fee remain unchanged. New per-sale costs can be entered separately. Whole expected sales round down; recovery targets round up. Capacity warnings do not cap projections or prove demand. Currency changes labels only. Discount limits round down to two percentage decimals and quoted price floors round up to two amount decimals; actual currency or platform pricing increments may differ. No automatic churn, demand, tax, lifetime value or redemption prediction is made. Frequently asked questions Is a 10% discount recovered by 10% more sales? Usually not. In the default example, 100 sales become a 136-sale recovery target after variable costs and a 3% fee, or 36% more completed sales. The discount percentage and the required sales lift use different bases. How do I enter a fixed amount off or a sale price? Select Amount off per sale or Sale price. A $10 reduction from $100 and a $90 sale price both describe a 10% discount. These modes are alternatives, not cumulative discounts. What is the discount break-even formula? Required whole sales = ceiling[(baseline monthly contribution + additional campaign expense) ÷ discounted contribution per sale]. Discounted contribution is sale price less percentage selling fees and promotion variable cost. It must be positive to recover the baseline. Does this calculate net profit after a discount? It calculates profit change when original fixed overhead stays unchanged, after deducting incremental campaign expense. Absolute net profit, owner tax and cash flow require a full business model. Contribution remains separately labeled. Why does revenue rise while profit falls? Extra sales still incur fulfillment costs. In the default example, 120 sales at $90 increase revenue to $10,800, but leave only $3,276 contribution versus $3,700 before the promotion. That is a $424 reduction before any campaign expense. How should I enter advertising and promotion costs? Enter a fixed campaign budget or setup expense for the modeled month as Additional campaign cost. Put a genuine variable cost per completed sale in promotion variable cost instead. Do not enter the same cost in both fields. What if the offer changes shipping, packaging or labor cost? Enter the promotion variable cost per sale. Blank keeps the current cost; zero deliberately removes that cost. Percentage selling fees stay separate and apply to the sale price. What happens when required sales exceed capacity? The recovery target is not deliverable within the entered limit. The calculator also reports profit change at full entered capacity and the discount supported by that volume. It does not reduce your expected-sales projection automatically. How is the maximum discount at expected sales calculated? It solves for the price that funds original monthly contribution plus campaign spending at your expected completed volume, after revised costs and fees. The displayed discount rounds down and the two-decimal price floor rounds up. This is a mathematical limit, not a recommendation or forecast. What if discounted contribution is zero or negative? No positive sales volume can recover the original positive baseline and campaign cost. The tool shows Not recoverable. A zero sale price also has no finite revenue-recovery target. Can I use this for multiple products or selective coupons? Use one consistent product or stable average order with comparable economics. Model only the cohort that receives the offer. Different product mixes, redemption rates and unaffected full-price buyers need separate scenarios. Are my figures saved or converted between currencies? Inputs and downloaded results are handled in your browser tab without an account. Currency selection changes labels, not exchange rates. The calculator does not save a promotion to your account. documents.text: FREE · NO SIGNUP · PRIVATE INPUTS Price Increase Calculator Test a percentage increase or enter your new price directly. See how many sales you can lose while preserving revenue or profit, including changing costs and extra monthly overhead. Calculate my pricing scenario → Read the step-by-step guide Illustrative starting scenario: $60 variable cost and a 3% payment fee. A 10% price increase can absorb a loss of 20 whole sales. Quick answer A price increase calculator compares contribution before and after raising prices, then finds the minimum sales needed to preserve your current monthly contribution. At $100 price, $60 variable cost and a 3% fee, a 10% increase needs 80 of the original 100 sales. Losing 20 whole sales still preserves contribution. Your pricing scenario Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Service price rise Product price rise Current price per sale Use net service/product revenue. Exclude sales tax collected for others. Variable cost per sale Include materials, direct labor, shipping and acquisition once. Exclude the percentage fee below and monthly overhead. Revised variable cost per sale (optional) Enter a changed delivery cost after the increase. Leave blank to keep current cost. Payment / selling fee (%) Percentage of the selling price. Include flat per-sale fees in variable cost. Current monthly sales Whole completed sales before the price change. Enter the proposed price as Percentage increase New selling price Proposed price increase (%) Applied to every modeled sale. Use revised cost if delivery costs also change. Expected customer / sales loss (%) Assumes each lost customer represents the same number of sales. Enter the percentage of sales lost. Additional monthly overhead (optional) New fixed monthly commitments caused by this change. Blank means zero; existing overhead is assumed unchanged. Available monthly capacity (optional) Maximum completed sales you can deliver. Leave blank if unknown. Reset example What this change needs Minimum sales to preserve current profit 80 / month You can lose up to 20 whole sales (20%) and still preserve the baseline profit. 5 % increase 10 % increase 15 % increase 20 % increase New selling price USD 110.00 Contribution per sale USD 46.70 Previously USD 37.00 Your expected monthly sales 90 Contribution change / month USD 503.00 Your expected sales preserve baseline profit after additional overhead. Profit change deducts additional overhead; this is not absolute net profit. Existing overhead is assumed unchanged. The required sales fit your entered capacity. Keep the same revenue 91 sales Up to 9 whole sales lost ( 9% ). Keep the same profit 80 sales Up to 20 whole sales lost (20%). Expected profit change USD 503.00 Contribution change less USD 0.00 additional monthly overhead. Current versus your expected scenario Measure Current Proposed Completed sales 100 90 Revenue USD 10,000.00 USD 9,900.00 Contribution USD 3,700.00 USD 4,203.00 What if sales fall? Each case uses your proposed price, revised cost, fees and additional overhead. These are assumptions, not demand predictions. 0% sales loss Completed sales 100 Revenue USD 11,000.00 Contribution USD 4,670.00 Profit change USD 970.00 5% sales loss Completed sales 95 Revenue USD 10,450.00 Contribution USD 4,436.50 Profit change USD 736.50 10% sales loss Completed sales 90 Revenue USD 9,900.00 Contribution USD 4,203.00 Profit change USD 503.00 15% sales loss Completed sales 85 Revenue USD 9,350.00 Contribution USD 3,969.50 Profit change USD 269.50 20% sales loss Completed sales 80 Revenue USD 8,800.00 Contribution USD 3,736.00 Profit change USD 36.00 25% sales loss Completed sales 75 Revenue USD 8,250.00 Contribution USD 3,502.50 Profit change -USD 197.50 Download scenario CSV See the calculation Contribution per sale = price × (1 − fee rate) − variable cost. Current contribution = USD 37.00 × 100 = USD 3,700.00 . New contribution = USD 110.00 × (1 − 3% ) − USD 60.00 = USD 46.70 . Required sales = round USD 3,700.00 ÷ USD 46.70 upward to 80 whole sales. Price increase = ( USD 110.00 ÷ USD 100.00 − 1) × 100 = 10% . Increase per sale: USD 10.00 . Contribution margin: 37% before → 42.45% after. This is after the entered selling fee, not net profit margin. Revenue-neutral continuous sales-loss threshold: 9.09% . Profit-neutral continuous threshold: 20.77%. Whole-sale limits above account for rounding. Expected sales are rounded down to whole completed sales. Calculations use unrounded values; displayed money rounds to two decimals. What this calculator includes Compare current and proposed revenue and contribution side by side. Include percentage payment fees and direct costs without counting them twice. Round required sales upward to whole completed sales. Check the required and expected sales against optional monthly capacity. Try preset scenarios or compare 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% changes. Search by country, currency name or code, then choose your currency. Currency selection does not convert amounts. Enter revised variable cost when materials, labor or fulfillment costs change. Find the maximum whole-sale loss that preserves the baseline, or the extra sales needed when costs rise too far. Enter either a percentage increase or an exact proposed selling price. Compare revenue-neutral and profit-neutral whole-sale limits separately. Deduct additional monthly overhead when measuring profit change. Compare sales-loss scenarios and download the calculations as CSV. How to use the price increase calculator for customer loss Choose one consistent product, service or customer group that will receive the increase. Use completed sales for the same monthly period in both scenarios. If customers buy different amounts, estimate lost sales rather than the percentage of customer names. Enter your current selling price, direct variable cost per sale and percentage selling fee. Enter revised variable cost only if delivery costs will change. Leave it blank to keep current cost; entering zero deliberately sets the revised cost to zero. Choose Percentage increase or New selling price. Both modes describe the same price change; the latter calculates the percentage for you. Enter current monthly completed sales and expected sales loss. Model only affected sales, not customers who remain on the old price. Enter any additional fixed monthly overhead caused by the change, and optional available capacity. Compare both thresholds, the expected profit change and the sales-loss scenarios. Download the CSV to retain your assumptions. Track the customers actually receiving the increase Gather a matched set of records before replacing the example inputs. These are input checks, not market averages. Records to check before calculating Input group Record to use Boundary to check Current price and cost Completed invoices and job/order costing Use a comparable selling unit and include percentage fees separately. Revised cost Current supplier quotes and delivery records Blank keeps the old cost; zero means a deliberate zero revised cost. Lost sales Renewals and completed purchases after the change Compare the affected cohort over matching periods; pending renewals are not confirmed losses. Price increase and allowable customer-loss formula Current contribution per sale = current price × (1 − fee rate) − current variable cost. New price = current price × (1 + increase rate). New contribution per sale = new price × (1 − fee rate) − revised variable cost. Minimum required whole sales = round upward (current contribution per sale × current monthly sales ÷ new contribution per sale). Allowable whole-sale loss = current monthly sales − minimum required whole sales, when that difference is positive. The tool calculates expected sales by rounding downward (current sales × (1 − expected loss rate)). Required sales are rounded upward because a partial completed sale cannot fund the baseline. If higher costs make required sales exceed the starting volume, the result shows additional sales needed instead of an allowable loss. Percentage increase = (new price − current price) ÷ current price × 100. Amount of increase = new price − current price. A rise from $80 to $100 is 25%, not 20%; the denominator is the original price. With additional monthly overhead H, profit-preserving sales = ceiling[(current monthly contribution + H) ÷ new contribution per sale]. Profit change = expected new contribution − current contribution − H. If new contribution is zero or negative, no positive sales volume can preserve this positive baseline. Revenue-preserving sales = ceiling(current price × current sales ÷ new price). With no whole-sale rounding, revenue-neutral loss = 1 − current price ÷ new price. Contribution-neutral loss = 1 − old contribution per sale ÷ new contribution per sale when overhead is unchanged. These are different limits. How many customers can you lose after a 10% price increase? All figures below are illustrative planning assumptions. The starting service sale contributes $100 × 0.97 − $60 = $37. At 100 sales, monthly contribution is $3,700. Raising price to $110 leaves $110 × 0.97 − $60 = $46.70 per sale. The exact target is $3,700 ÷ $46.70 = 79.2291… sales, so you need 80 completed sales. Losing 20 of the original 100 sales leaves $3,736 contribution, still $36 above the baseline. Losing 21 leaves 79 × $46.70 = $3,689.30, below the baseline. Illustrative scenarios using unrounded contribution values Scenario New contribution per sale Minimum whole sales Expected contribution change Service: $100 price, $60 cost, 3% fee; 100 sales; 10% increase, 10% loss $46.70 80 (up to 20 lost) +$503 at 90 sales Retail: $50 price, $25 cost, 3% fee; 200 sales; 15% increase, 15% loss $30.775 153 (up to 47 lost) +$531.75 at 170 sales Service: same baseline; 10% increase; revised cost $80, 10% loss $26.70 139 (+39 required) −$1,297 at 90 sales In the retail example, $57.50 price contributes $30.775 after fees and $25 direct cost. Baseline contribution is $4,700. At 170 expected sales, contribution becomes $5,231.75. The whole-sale recovery target is 153, allowing a loss of 47 sales, or 23.5% of the original 200. A higher price does not protect contribution if delivery costs rise too far. In the third example, revised $80 cost leaves $26.70 contribution per sale. You need 139 sales to preserve $3,700, even though the price increased. At 90 expected sales, contribution is $2,403. What to check before acting on the result Keep unaffected customers outside this comparison or run a separate group. Track contribution as well as revenue; fewer higher-priced sales can change them in different directions. Check whether the retained volume still covers the monthly business requirement, not just the prior contribution baseline. Understand revenue loss versus contribution after raising prices In the default service example, 90 sales at $110 produce $9,900 revenue, down from $10,000. Contribution rises from $3,700 to $4,203 because each sale leaves more money after direct cost and fees. This is why revenue retention and contribution retention answer different questions. The allowable loss applies to completed sales with comparable economics. It is a customer-loss threshold only when each customer represents the same number and type of sales. A high-value customer leaving can change the answer more than several small customers leaving. The capacity check compares required and expected sales with the entered limit. It does not cap projections or prove demand. Enter new fixed commitments as additional overhead; use the full break-even calculator for absolute monthly profit targets. The default scenario needs 91 whole sales to preserve $10,000 revenue ($10,010 at $110 each), but only 80 to preserve $3,700 contribution. Exact continuous loss thresholds are about 9.09% and 20.77%; whole-sale loss limits are 9% and 20%. Neither number predicts actual customer response. If the same price change also adds $600 monthly overhead, the unchanged-profit target rises to ceiling($4,300 ÷ $46.70) = 93 sales. At the expected 90 sales, contribution improves $503 but profit falls $97. This explains why contribution growth alone can be misleading. Common mistakes when testing a business price increase Using lost customer count when customers have different order values. Model affected sales or comparable groups. Leaving revised cost blank even though fulfillment costs are rising. Treating higher revenue as proof of higher profit without checking contribution. Applying a price rise to new customers but modeling all existing sales at the new rate. Ignoring flat transaction charges or counting percentage fees twice. Treating allowable loss as predicted churn. The calculator gives a threshold based on your inputs. Assumptions and limits Model only the product, service or customer group receiving the increase, with the same sales mix and percentage selling fee. Costs entered are variable per completed sale; added monthly overhead is a separate fixed commitment. Existing fixed overhead is unchanged and cancels out of the profit comparison. Profit change is contribution change minus additional overhead; it is not absolute net profit. Taxes, working capital, staged rollout, customer lifetime value and recurring churn over several months are not modeled. Customer loss equals sales-volume loss only for customers with comparable purchasing patterns. Required sales round up; expected sales round down. Currency selection changes labels, not exchange rates. Capacity warnings do not cap projections or prove demand. Frequently asked questions How much customer loss can a 10% price increase absorb? It depends on contribution before and after the increase, including fees and direct costs. In the worked service example, you can lose 20 of 100 completed sales. Use your own inputs; 20% is not a universal threshold. Why can revenue fall while contribution rises? Fewer higher-priced sales can leave more contribution per sale after delivery costs and fees. In the default example, revenue falls $100 while contribution rises $503. Monthly overhead still needs to be deducted. Can I use this when supplier or labor costs rise? Yes. Enter the changed cost in revised variable cost per sale. If revised contribution is lower than before, the tool may show that you need more sales despite the higher selling price. Is customer loss the same as sales loss? Only if customers represent comparable completed sales. For different order sizes or recurring frequencies, enter the percentage of sales lost or run separate customer-group scenarios. Does the calculator recommend a safe price increase? It shows the contribution threshold for the percentage you enter. It does not forecast churn, measure willingness to pay or recommend a guaranteed increase. Compare several scenarios with your actual retention evidence. Does it include taxes, overhead and owner pay? Enter any additional monthly overhead caused by the change. Existing overhead is assumed unchanged; owner pay, taxes and absolute net profit are not calculated. Enter selling prices excluding sales tax collected for others. Use the full business break-even calculator for a complete monthly target. Can I raise prices only for new customers? Yes, but model that affected group separately. The tool applies the new price to every proposed sale you enter; it does not automatically preserve legacy customer rates. How do I calculate the percentage increase from an old and new price? Subtract the old price from the new price, divide by the old price and multiply by 100. Moving from $80 to $100 is ($20 ÷ $80) × 100 = 25%. Choose New selling price to calculate this automatically. How much customer loss preserves revenue after a 10% increase? The continuous revenue threshold is 1 − 1 ÷ 1.10 = 9.0909…%. With 100 original completed sales, 91 whole sales are required, so at most 9 sales can be lost. The contribution or profit threshold depends on costs and overhead. Does this calculate net profit? It calculates the change in profit under unchanged existing fixed overhead, after deducting any additional overhead entered. It does not calculate absolute net profit, owner tax or cash flow. Contribution remains separately labeled. Can I use this for subscriptions or an increase that applies to only some customers? Use monthly paying accounts only when each account has comparable economics. Model the affected cohort separately. The tool is a one-period comparison; it does not compound churn over time, model downgrades or forecast customer lifetime value. Build a cost breakdown, check campaign performance and see how support costs or overhead change the revenue you need. Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin before ads 1. An $80 order with $44 direct cost and a 3% fee leaves $33.60, or 42% contribution. Its break-even ROAS is 2.38×. This is a campaign contribution threshold, not whole-business break-even. Break-even ROAS, target ROAS or profit: choose the right result Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin ratio before advertising. With the fictional default $80 order, $44 direct cost and 3% fee, pre-ad contribution is $33.60, or 42%. Break-even ROAS is 2.380952…×; its displayed 2.38× is rounded, so use the unrounded calculation when checking the boundary. How to calculate break-even ROAS after fees Use one campaign or a comparable group of orders over a consistent period. If you mix a low-margin product with a high-margin product, the average must represent the orders your advertising actually sells. Enter net average order value after discounts and refunds. Enter direct cost before advertising: products, fulfillment, shipping subsidies and flat fees. Enter the percentage selling fee separately. Do not count it again in direct cost.
