Refunds and fees Returns records and processor/marketplace statements Net refunded revenue once; avoid counting platform-inclusive fees again. Break-even ROAS and maximum CPA formulas Contribution per order = order value × (1 − fee rate) − direct cost. Contribution margin = contribution ÷ order value. Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin. Actual ROAS = attributed revenue ÷ ad spend. Contribution after ads = attributed revenue × contribution margin − ad spend. Maximum CPA before fixed overhead equals contribution per order. Target ROAS = 1 ÷ (contribution margin − target margin). Use decimals in this formula. If the target margin is at least the pre-ad contribution margin, there is no finite ROAS that reaches that target with positive ad spend. Does a 4× ROAS mean your ads are profitable? These examples are fictional planning assumptions, not advertising benchmarks. At $80 order value, $44 direct cost and 3% fees, contribution is $80 − $2.40 − $44 = $33.60. Margin before ads is 42%; break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.42 = 2.380952…×. With $1,000 spend and $4,000 attributed net revenue, actual ROAS is 4×. Estimated contribution after ads is $4,000 × 0.42 − $1,000 = $680. A target of 10% revenue left after ads requires 1 ÷ (0.42 − 0.10) = 3.125×. If direct cost rises to $60, contribution falls to $17.60, or 22%. Break-even ROAS rises to 4.54545…×. The same 4× return now leaves $4,000 × 0.22 − $1,000 = −$120. A fixed ROAS benchmark misses this cost change. What to check before acting on the result Read the campaign contribution threshold separately from whole-business profitability. At the default 42% pre-ad contribution rate, a 10% after-ad target leaves 32% for advertising: target ROAS is 3.125 times. Track returns that arrive after the reporting cutoff and revise the matched cohort. Attributed revenue does not prove advertising created incremental sales. Read campaign contribution before increasing spend A positive result covers the modeled direct costs, fees and ads. It still has to fund rent, salaries, software and owner pay. Use the ecommerce break-even calculator to add those monthly commitments. Maximum CPA is a per-order ceiling before overhead, not a recommended bid. Actual platform attribution can include sales that would have happened without the ads. Compare the model with refund-adjusted records and your own testing. Common ROAS calculation mistakes Using gross revenue before returns alongside net costs. Counting ads in direct order cost and again as ad spend. Comparing different attribution windows or currencies. Calling the contribution after ads net profit. Using one average margin when ads change the product mix. BE ROAS versus a product gross-margin shortcut BE ROAS, also written BEROAS, means break-even return on ad spend. Start with contribution before advertising when payment fees, shipping subsidy and other order-dependent costs must also be recovered. A product-only gross-margin shortcut can understate the required ad return. In a separate fictional $100 order, product cost is $40, so the product-only gross margin is 60% and its reciprocal is 1.67×. Add $15 fulfillment and shipping, a $5 expected unrecovered return allowance and a $3 payment fee. Full pre-ad contribution becomes $37, or 37%, requiring 2.702702…× ROAS before fixed overhead. At 2× ROAS, attributed revenue of $2,000 against $1,000 spend leaves $2,000 × 0.37 − $1,000 = −$260 contribution after ads. Use net revenue and a consistent return-cost definition so refunds or recovered inventory are not counted twice. This example assumes the stated $5 is additional unrecovered cost outside the already-defined net revenue. The calculator does not independently validate attribution, demand, repeat-customer value or your refund records. Review the full order-profit boundary Build a direct-cost ledger without counting refunds twice The calculator uses retained net revenue: subtract discounts and refunded sales, and exclude sales tax or VAT collected for someone else. Use the same definition for average order value and the campaign revenue. The total-cost and itemized-cost methods are alternatives; selecting itemized costs replaces the total. In the default fictional order, product cost 32, fulfillment and packaging 6, net merchant shipping 4, a flat transaction fee 0.50 and other unrecovered costs 1.50 sum to 44. A 3% selling fee on an 80 net order adds 2.40. Contribution before ads is 80 − 44 − 2.40 = 33.60. The numbers can represent any single currency; the selector does not convert them. Refunded sales already removed from net revenue must not appear again as another full refund expense. Include only additional unrecovered handling, delivery, dispute fees or inventory losses in direct costs. Reconcile recovered stock and fee reversals. If your processor charges fees on gross receipts, derive an effective percentage of retained net revenue or an average flat cost, and enter it once. Reconcile additional return costs per order Check return handling costs with the return-cost calculator Include agency costs and overhead at a stated ad budget The order contribution threshold excludes fixed period costs. Expand the campaign controls to add a fixed support budget and the share of overhead the campaign must fund. These amounts use the same reporting period as ad spend. Keep percentage agency charges out of this fixed-cost assumption unless you calculate their amount for the entered budget and update it whenever spend changes. With the default 42% contribution rate and 1,000 media spend, add 150 support cost and 250 allocated overhead. Total period outlay to recover is 1,400. Required net revenue = 1,400 ÷ 0.42 = 3,333.333…; required media ROAS = 3.333333…×. At 4,000 net revenue, the remaining amount is 4,000 × 0.42 − 1,000 − 150 − 250 = 280, or 7% of net revenue. To leave a 10% margin after those same costs, required revenue is 1,400 ÷ (0.42 − 0.10) = 4,375; media ROAS is 4.375×. This differs from the contribution-only 3.125× target. The general formula is period target ROAS = (ad spend + support + allocated overhead) ÷ [ad spend × (contribution rate − target margin)]. It requires positive ad spend and a positive remaining contribution rate. The 280 planning remainder is not automatically whole-store net profit. It excludes tax, unallocated commitments and unentered costs. Order counts inferred from revenue ÷ AOV are estimates, not measured new customers or evidence of incremental sales. Check the full store’s monthly break-even volume Separate ROAS from campaign ROI Translate ROAS into ACoS, a target CPA and a percentage ROAS is attributed net revenue ÷ media spend. ACoS is media spend ÷ attributed net revenue × 100, so a 4× ROAS corresponds to 25% ACoS. This reciprocal relationship only compares the same spend and revenue basis. A total marketing-efficiency ratio that includes organic or returning-customer revenue answers a different question. At the default 80 AOV and 33.60 contribution, the contribution-only CPA ceiling is 33.60. Keeping 10% of revenue means reserving 8 per order, leaving a target CPA of 25.60 and target ROAS of 80 ÷ 25.60 = 3.125×. That is 312.5% expressed as a ROAS percentage; it is not 3.125%. The CPA figure still excludes support and overhead unless those reserves are reflected in the chosen margin. Google Ads describes target ROAS as an average conversion-value return and expresses it as a percentage. An economic threshold here is a planning constraint, not an instruction to set a bid strategy to that number. Check your historical performance, conversion lag and conversion-value setup; an overly high target can restrict traffic. If platform conversion values include tax or unadjusted refunds, first reconcile the basis instead of directly comparing unlike ROAS figures. It is a sensitivity check, not a forecast of demand. A 4× ROAS is profitable on contribution at a 42% margin but loses 120 on 1,000 spend at a 22% margin. Before raising a budget, model the additional spend and additional retained revenue separately. For example, another 500 of spend that yields 1,000 net revenue is a 2× incremental ROAS. At 42% contribution it leaves 1,000 × 0.42 − 500 = −80 before any extra support cost, even if the earlier campaign average looked attractive. Recheck discounts, product mix, shipping, refunded sales and conversion delays at a stated cutoff. Do not add revenue claimed by Meta, Google and another platform without deduplicating order IDs. Repeat purchase value belongs in a separately evidenced retention model; this calculator does not assume it. Download the CSV to retain the exact inputs, revenue basis and unrounded scenario outputs for your review. Set a CPA ceiling that also funds overhead At the default $80 order value, $44 direct cost and 3% selling fee, pre-ad contribution is $33.60. The $33.60 contribution-only CPA ceiling leaves nothing for fixed overhead. In a separate planning case, reserve $8 per order for overhead and $4 for extra operating profit. This leaves $21.60 for acquisition and requires $80 ÷ $21.60 = 3.7037× ROAS, rounded. The $12 remaining contribution is 15% of the $80 order value. Entering a 15% after-ad target represents that entire reserve under this example, not a claim that the calculator separately deducts actual rent and payroll. The allocation depends on achieved order volume; reconcile the real monthly costs before calling it net profit. BE ROAS and break-even ROAS name the same contribution-threshold task here. Use retained net revenue, matching direct costs and one attribution window. A reported ROAS setting or a maximum CPA is not a guaranteed or recommended ad bid. Follow the CPA, overhead and net-revenue reconciliation Keep dispute rates and additional costs separate Assumptions and limits Use retained net revenue, a stable average order mix and matching order costs, fees and attribution windows. Refunds must already be netted from revenue; enter only additional unrecovered costs once. Order contribution thresholds exclude fixed period costs. Period thresholds include only the support costs and overhead allocation you enter at the stated media budget; update those amounts when spending changes. Remaining contribution is before tax, unallocated commitments and unentered costs. No lifetime value, future demand, attribution accuracy or incrementality is assumed. Currency labels do not convert amounts. Frequently asked questions What is a good break-even ROAS? There is no universal number. Your direct costs and fees determine the contribution margin. A 42% margin before ads needs about 2.38×; a 22% margin needs about 4.55×, both before overhead. Is ROAS the same as ROI? No. ROAS compares attributed revenue with ad spend. This tool also shows contribution after direct costs and ads, but does not calculate whole-business ROI. Can I use this for Meta or Google Ads? Yes, if you supply consistent net revenue and spend from the same reporting window. The tool does not connect to either platform or verify attribution. Why is target ROAS not attainable? Your requested post-ad margin leaves no positive allowance for ads. Lower the target or improve the order contribution before comparing returns. Does maximum CPA include overhead? No. It is the contribution available per order before advertising and fixed overhead. Set a lower operational ceiling if you need those orders to fund monthly commitments. Can a profitable ROAS still leave the store losing money? Yes. This calculator excludes monthly fixed overhead, owner pay and other unentered commitments. Campaign contribution must also cover those costs in the full store plan. Can I calculate break-even ROAS before launching ads? Yes. Enter a positive order value and the matching costs, then set ad spend and revenue to zero. The unit break-even ROAS and target CPA remain available. Actual ROAS and campaign ROAS including period costs need positive media spend. How do I include fixed agency fees and overhead? Expand the campaign controls and enter fixed support cost and allocated overhead for the same period. The period threshold includes these amounts at your stated media budget. Recalculate when the budget or fee amount changes; do not also include those costs in direct cost or media spend. What if contribution is zero or my target margin is too high? Zero or negative pre-ad contribution has no finite recovery ROAS for positive ad spend. If the target margin is at least the pre-ad contribution rate, no finite ROAS leaves that margin while paying for ads. Improve price or costs, or revise the target. How do ROAS and ACoS relate? With the same revenue and spend basis, ACoS percent equals 100 divided by ROAS. A 4× ROAS is 25% ACoS. Neither figure alone proves that fixed costs are covered. Should I enter 3.125 or 312.5% in a ROAS percentage field? A 3.125× multiple equals 312.5%. The calculator shows an economic threshold, not a recommended platform setting. Match conversion-value definitions and review historical performance before changing bidding targets. Quick answer Divide annual owner income, overhead and profit needs by annual billable hours, then gross up for percentage fees. A $4,000 monthly income goal, $600 overhead and $400 buffer need $60,000 a year. At 35 weekly hours, 46 weeks and 60% billable time, a 3% fee requires at least $64.04 per billed hour. A rate rounded upward to the next cent, with monthly and annual checks. How to calculate a freelance hourly rate Start with the income your business needs to fund before personal income tax. Add costs the business must pay regardless of which client buys your time. Enter your monthly owner income goal and overhead. Add a separate profit buffer if you want retained business profit. Enter total weekly work hours and the weeks you plan to work each year. Estimate billable share after admin, prospecting, meetings and revisions you cannot invoice. Add payment or platform fees. Check the resulting rate against the hours you can realistically sell. Build the rate from hours you can actually invoice Gather a matched set of records before replacing the example inputs. These are input checks, not market averages. Records to check before calculating Input group Record to use Boundary to check Monthly funding need Owner-income budget and overhead ledger Keep the additional profit buffer distinct from compensation for your work. Working weeks and weekly hours Annual availability calendar Remove planned leave and closures through working weeks, not a second duplicate deduction. Billable share Recorded invoiced hours divided by working hours Administration, sales and revisions can consume time without becoming extra invoices. Hourly rate formula with non-billable time and fees Annual billable hours = weekly working hours × working weeks × billable percentage. Annual funding need = (monthly owner income + monthly overhead + monthly profit target) × 12. Required rate = annual funding need ÷ annual billable hours ÷ (1 − percentage fee). Round upward to the next currency cent so the displayed rate does not underfund the target. Average monthly billable hours are annual billable hours ÷ 12. This average smooths time off across the year; it does not assume every month has the same invoicing pattern. Freelance hourly rate example with 60% billable time Illustrative example: owner income $4,000, overhead $600 and profit buffer $400 total $5,000 per month, or $60,000 a year. Weekly hours 35 × 46 working weeks × 60% billable time = 966 billable hours. The fee-adjusted rate is $60,000 ÷ 966 ÷ 0.97 = $64.0333… per hour. Rounded upward, charge at least $64.04 under these assumptions. Annual billed revenue is $64.04 × 966 = $61,862.64. After a 3% fee, $60,006.7608 remains to fund the annual need. If billable share falls to 40%, annual billable hours fall to 644. The same funding need requires $96.05 per billed hour. This is a capacity issue: more total working hours do not help if the additional hours cannot be invoiced. What to check before acting on the result Use a lower-billable-time case alongside your current estimate. A minimum rate assumes the entered hours sell. Compare the required rate with realized billings after discounts, write-offs and included revision time. For fixed-price work, divide realized job revenue by all occupied hours; compare the result with the hourly funding requirement. Understand minimum rate versus a market price The result is your funding threshold, not evidence that customers will accept the rate. Test it against the work scope, delivery skill, buyer demand and observed client budgets. A project quote can also price scope and outcomes rather than hours. The monthly amount after fees and overhead should cover owner income and the entered profit buffer. If a job needs materials, subcontractors or other project costs, charge them separately or use the agency calculator for that delivery model. Common hourly pricing mistakes Dividing income by every working hour instead of billable hours. Using 52 working weeks while planning several weeks away. Counting personal income tax as already included when it is not. Adding profit buffer but forgetting committed overhead. Assuming invoiced hours are collected when clients pay late or do not pay. Assumptions and limits The model assumes all planned billable hours are sold and collected at one rate. Monthly income, overhead and profit targets are annualized over 12 months. It excludes unentered per-project costs, unpaid invoices, tax calculations and changes in workload. The fee applies to all billed revenue. Currency selection changes labels only. Frequently asked questions Should I use 40 hours as billable time? Only if you actually invoice and collect for all 40 hours. Enter total working hours first, then reduce the billable share for admin, marketing and non-chargeable delivery time. Does the hourly rate include tax? It does not calculate personal income tax, sales tax or VAT. The owner income goal is before personal income tax. Adjust your own funding target with qualified advice where needed. Why are fees divided out instead of added? A percentage fee takes a share of the final billed amount. Dividing by the retained percentage funds the target exactly; adding the same percentage does not. Can I price projects with this? Use the rate as an internal labor funding reference and multiply by estimated billable project hours. Add direct project costs and check scope changes separately. Is this the best rate for my market? No. It is a minimum funding rate under your assumptions. Your market price also depends on demand, scope, value and how reliably you can sell the modeled hours. Does the rate include personal income tax? No. The owner-income amount is funded before personal income tax under this model. The calculator does not determine tax liability; enter a clearly defined income requirement and keep the tax/payment schedule separate. Monthly incoming cash Expected collection dates Use receipts, not invoices that remain unpaid. Monthly outgoing cash Payroll, supplier, tax and debt payment schedule Include actual cash payments; depreciation alone is not a cash payment. Cash runway formula using net burn Usable cash = current cash − protected reserve. Monthly net cash burn = monthly payments − monthly receipts. Runway to reserve = usable cash ÷ positive monthly burn. Ending cash at month N = current cash − net burn × N. Extra cash needed to protect reserve = the greater of zero and (net burn × N − usable cash). When receipts equal or exceed payments and cash is above reserve, the constant-flow model has no depletion horizon. If current cash already equals reserve, the tool reports zero room above reserve today even if future receipts would build cash. Cash runway example for a six-month planning horizon These are illustrative cash assumptions. Start with $30,000 accessible cash and protect $6,000. Usable cash is $24,000. With $10,000 monthly payments and $7,000 receipts, monthly net burn is $3,000. Runway to the reserve is $24,000 ÷ $3,000 = 8 months. Six-month ending cash is $30,000 − 6 × $3,000 = $12,000, so no additional cash is needed to keep the $6,000 reserve over that horizon. If receipts fall to $5,000 while payments remain $10,000, burn rises to $5,000. Runway becomes 4.8 months, or four full months above reserve. After six months, projected cash is zero; the reserve funding gap is $6,000. Negative later balances show a cash need, not money the business can actually spend. What to check before acting on the result Read the whole-month room above reserve as a constant-flow scenario. If equipment or a large tax payment occurs once, use a dated forecast rather than pretending it repeats every month. Check the earliest daily or weekly low point. Monthly closing cash can conceal a payment due before a customer receipt. Read cash runway without confusing it with profit A profitable business can still have a cash gap when customers pay late, inventory is purchased early or loans are repaid. Count money when you expect it to move. The result is a simple planning screen, not a forecast based on your transaction dates. A no-depletion result means only that the entered recurring receipts cover payments. Recheck when contracts end, tax payments arrive or large purchases are planned. The reserve is your assumption; the tool does not prescribe a universal safe buffer. Common cash runway mistakes Counting unpaid invoices as cash available today. Using revenue earned instead of cash received. Leaving owner withdrawals or debt payments outside monthly payments. Assuming a positive monthly ending balance means every earlier bill can be paid. Ignoring one-off purchases, seasonality or funding that has not been secured. Assumptions and limits Receipts and payments stay constant and are evenly spread for the fractional-month runway estimate. The model excludes unentered one-off purchases, new financing and seasonal changes. It reports time to your reserve, not a legal insolvency date. A monthly ending balance can miss an earlier payment shortfall within that month. Use a dated cash-flow forecast for actual payment scheduling. Frequently asked questions What is the difference between cash runway and profit? Runway measures available cash against cash moving in and out. Profit uses accounting revenue and costs. Timing differences mean a profitable business can still run out of spendable cash. Why protect a reserve? The reserve defines cash you do not want the plan to consume. Choose it for your own needs; there is no universal reserve amount built into this calculator. What if monthly cash burn is zero or negative? When cash is above reserve, the model shows no depletion at the entered pace. Receipts cover payments. This does not account for unentered seasonal or one-off expenses. Does 4.8 months mean I can pay every bill for that long? No. Fractional runway assumes the net flow is evenly spread. Actual payment dates may create a shortfall earlier. Use a dated cash-flow forecast for payment decisions. Can the projection show negative cash? Yes. A negative ending balance represents an unfunded cash requirement. The tool does not assume overdraft or borrowing is available. How should I include seasonal receipts or a one-off purchase? This tool assumes constant monthly flows. Use the linked cash forecast guide to schedule changing receipts and individual payments by date; do not rely on an averaged runway alone. A $18, 1,000 mL developer bottle contributes $1.08 for 60 mL. Product cost is $7.08 per service. Discarding 15% wastes $1.06 of that cost; it is already included, not an extra charge. Eighty services cost $566.40. Reducing mixed-product waste from 15% to 5% with unchanged mixed quantities lowers the identified wasted value from $1.062 to $0.354 per service. Total product cost remains $7.08 until you actually mix less. To model a 10% smaller bowl at the same recipe ratio, reduce color to 27 g and developer to 54 mL; product cost becomes $6.372 per service. What to check before acting on the result The default bowl costs $7.08 before service labor and other products. A 15% discarded share identifies $1.062 of that cost, not an extra purchase. If both mixed quantities are reduced by 20%, color falls to 24 g and developer to 48 mL. Cost becomes $5.664 per service, or $453.12 for 80 services. That smaller-bowl scenario assumes it still meets the actual service need; the calculator does not advise formulation, suitability or chemical handling. Avoid double counting and misleading averages Use the same discarded proportion for both products only when the mixture is uniform. Run separate recipes for toner, bleach or additional bowls and sum their service costs. Keep quantities and reporting periods consistent. Include a cost in only one field. Use a separate scenario when the cost mix changes. Assumptions and limits Each product has its own consistent quantity unit. Grams and mL are never converted between products. Mixed usage includes waste. The discarded share applies proportionally to a uniform mixture. Labor, foil, toner, rent and other service costs are excluded. Frequently asked questions Why does changing waste not change product cost? The quantities entered are already removed from stock. Discarding some identifies waste within that cost. To model a smaller bowl, reduce the mixed quantities themselves. Adding waste again would double count it. Are the example values industry averages? No. They are fictional inputs chosen to demonstrate and check the formula. Replace them with your records. Does this include all business expenses? Each product has its own consistent quantity unit. Grams and mL are never converted between products. Mixed usage includes waste. The discarded share applies proportionally to a uniform mixture. Labor, foil, toner, rent and other service costs are excluded. Can I change the currency? Yes. Search the currency selector by currency code, name or country. Carry the relevant per-service cost or contribution into the linked industry calculator and add monthly overhead and owner pay there. Avoid counting the same allowance twice. Ecommerce return allowance per order with inventory recovery. How to use the ecommerce return cost calculator Start with one consistent service, route, product recipe or order cohort. Use invoice costs and measured operating records rather than a generic industry rate. The reset figures are a fictional example for checking the method. Match fulfilled orders and returns from the same cohort; recent orders may not yet have completed the return window. Value recovered stock at retained cost after write-downs, not expected resale revenue. Enter only net unrecovered shipping and fee amounts. Use the allowance once in planning; do not add outbound costs again if already embedded in the same allowance. Build the allowance from reconciled returned orders Gather a matched set of records before replacing the example inputs. These are input checks, not market averages. Shipping, handling and retained fees Refund/carrier/processor records Enter net unrecovered costs and keep refunded sales revenue separate. Ecommerce return allowance per order with inventory recovery: formula Expected returns = orders × return rate. Inventory loss = product cost × (1 − recoverable cost share). Cost per return = inventory loss + unrecovered outbound shipping + return shipping + processing + retained fees. Monthly burden = expected returns × cost per return. Allowance per fulfilled order = return rate × cost per return. Calculations retain decimal precision. Displayed money rounds to two decimals. Refunded revenue and lost sales contribution are separate. At an 8% return rate with all per-return costs unchanged, monthly burden falls from $2,600 to $2,080, saving $520 in modeled operating costs. At 100% inventory-cost recovery and a 10% return rate, cost per return falls from $26 to $20 and monthly burden becomes $2,000. Refunds still reduce revenue separately. What to check before acting on the result At the default $26 per return, a 10% return rate creates $2.60 cost allowance per fulfilled order. A 15% rate creates $3.90, or $3,900 across 1,000 orders. Check which outbound costs already appear in your original order costing before adding the allowance. Include each cost once in the combined view. Reconcile refunded revenue separately and retain a dated refund-payment schedule. This allowance is not the complete lost contribution or a cash forecast. Avoid double counting and misleading averages Enter only net unrecovered shipping and fee amounts. Use the allowance once in planning; do not add outbound costs again if already embedded in the same allowance. Keep quantities and reporting periods consistent. Include a cost in only one field. Use a separate scenario when the cost mix changes. Assumptions and limits Full-order returns and refunds only. This is an operating-cost allowance, not total profit loss, lost contribution, cash-flow timing or an accounting journal. Refunds reduce revenue separately. Recovered inventory is valued at retained acquisition cost. Resale revenue is excluded. No monthly overhead or advertising is counted. Frequently asked questions Does this measure the total profit lost from a return? No. It measures the operating cost burden of fully returned orders. Revenue refunds and the original sale contribution are separate. If revenue is already net of refunds, do not subtract those refunds again. Are the example values industry averages? No. They are fictional inputs chosen to demonstrate and check the formula. Replace them with your records. Does this include all business expenses? Full-order returns and refunds only. This is an operating-cost allowance, not total profit loss, lost contribution, cash-flow timing or an accounting journal. Refunds reduce revenue separately. Recovered inventory is valued at retained acquisition cost. Resale revenue is excluded. No monthly overhead or advertising is counted. Can I change the currency? Yes. Search the currency selector by currency code, name or country. It changes display labels; enter all amounts in the same currency. How should I use this with break-even planning? Carry the relevant per-service cost or contribution into the linked industry calculator and add monthly overhead and owner pay there. Avoid counting the same allowance twice. Can I use the same allowance for partial returns? This model assumes full-order returns. For partial returns, calculate a separate consistent item-level scenario or reconcile the actual order costs; do not apply a full-order loss to every returned item. documents.text: SALON ATTENDANCE · FREE · NO SIGNUP Salon No-Show Profit Loss Calculator Separate missed service revenue from the contribution your salon actually loses. Use real refill values, retained payments and wasted costs, then test whether an intervention covers its monthly cost. Calculate my attendance gap → See the method Illustrative appointment diary. Replace the example with matched booking and payment records. Quick answer The example has 200 original bookings, 20 missed appointments and 5 refills. The monthly contribution gap is $645.75. A hypothetical 40% proportional reduction recovers $258.30; after a $100 intervention cost, net improvement is $158.30. Your monthly booking cohort Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Currency labels only; no conversion. All example amounts are hypothetical. Reset example Try lower-value refills Try no retained fees 1 · Appointments and empty-slot time Original bookings / month Original appointment cohort; exclude replacement bookings. No-shows Original guests who did not attend. Late cancellations Separate appointments; do not also count them as no-shows. Missed slots refilled Completed replacements using those missed slots, one per slot. Minutes per original slot Used only for unfilled-slot time, not a labor wage calculation. 2 · Original service and replacement economics Original service ticket Net service price excluding tips and tax collected for remittance. Variable cost per original service Full products and variable compensation cost if the original service had been completed. Service processing rate (%) Same effective percentage on original and replacement services. Processing cost per service Fixed payment component; assumes one transaction per completed service. Replacement service ticket Actual average for refills. A cheaper service does not replace the original ticket. Variable cost per replacement Actual products and variable compensation for the completed replacement, counted once. 3 · Actual wasted costs and money retained Extra wasted costs, monthly total Incremental unrecoverable preparation beyond completed-service costs; exclude unchanged rent/salaries. Fees/deposits actually retained, gross After refunds, before payment costs. Exclude refundable/future-service deposits; valid fees on refilled slots may be included. Costs of retained fees/refunds Actual payment/refund costs for this missed-booking cohort; include non-returned processing charges once. 4 · Test an intervention Assumed reduction in missed bookings (%) Scales misses, refills, waste and retained fees together. It is your scenario, not software efficacy. Monthly intervention cost Reminder/admin/program cost; remains payable even with zero modeled improvement. Months/year with this pattern 1–12 identical modeled months; not an annual demand forecast. Inputs stay in this tab. No scenario is saved to an account. Program cost stays fixed. This is a scenario, not an effectiveness forecast. Download scenario CSV Print / save PDF CSV includes every input, unrounded results and assumptions. Printing includes this scenario and its method. How much improvement would cover your cost? These hypothetical reductions use the same proportional assumptions and monthly intervention cost. No recovery rate is promised. 0 % fewer missed bookings Recovered before program cost USD 0.00 Net monthly improvement -USD 100.00 25 % fewer missed bookings Recovered before program cost USD 161.44 Net monthly improvement USD 61.44 50 % fewer missed bookings Recovered before program cost USD 322.88 Net monthly improvement USD 222.88 75 % fewer missed bookings Recovered before program cost USD 484.31 Net monthly improvement USD 384.31 100 % fewer missed bookings Recovered before program cost USD 645.75 Net monthly improvement USD 545.75 What this calculator includes Separate no-shows and late cancellations using one original booking cohort. Value replacement services at their actual ticket and variable cost. Reconcile wasted costs and net fees retained after payment/refund charges. Compare recovery with intervention cost, a break-even reduction and a chosen annual pattern. Exact decimal arithmetic; private tab-only inputs, CSV export and printing. How to use your appointment and payment records Choose one month and original booking cohort. Count no-shows and late cancellations as disjoint groups. Count replacement services actually completed in those missed slots. Enter their own ticket and variable cost. Use full variable cost if an original service had been completed. Enter actual wasted preparation separately, once. Reconcile fees actually retained after refunds and their payment/refund costs. A card on file or an unpaid policy fee is not collected money. Enter a hypothetical reduction and monthly program cost. Review whether the implied improvement funds that cost; do not assume software will achieve it. Match the records before calculating Use the appointment diary for the original denominator and final slot outcomes; payment settlements for tickets, refunds and retained fees; and service costing records for products and variable compensation. Keep tips and tax collected for remittance outside the ticket. Each refill is assumed to occupy one original slot without displacing another booking. Different-duration services or a replacement that would have booked anyway need a separate incremental comparison. Unfilled-slot hours measure only completely empty slots; they do not value every unused minute within a shorter refill. Normal salaried payroll and rent are unchanged in this counterfactual. Do not deduct them again. Products wasted on a missed appointment belong in wasted cost, and must not also be included in actual replacement costs. A future-service deposit or refundable amount is not a retained no-show fee. Formula: reconcile the original service and actual slot outcome M = no-shows + late cancellations; unfilled slots = M − completed refills. Each original and replacement contribution equals ticket × (1 − service processing rate) − per-service processing charge − its variable service cost. Monthly gap = M × original contribution − refills × replacement contribution + actual wasted costs − (gross fees retained − their payment/refund costs). Positive means a shortfall relative to delivering the original booked services; negative means the entered receipts/refill contribution exceed that comparison. Gross service revenue gap = M × original ticket − refills × replacement ticket. It excludes retained fees and is not the contribution gap. Different service prices and costs therefore matter even when a slot was refilled. For reduction d%, scenario gap = baseline gap × (1 − d/100). Modeled recovery = baseline gap × d/100; net improvement = recovery − intervention cost. This proportional scenario scales missed bookings, refills, retained fees, their costs and waste together. Tickets, variable rates, original booking denominator and refill share stay fixed. For a positive baseline gap, break-even reduction = intervention cost ÷ gap × 100. The displayed target rounds up to 0.01 percentage point. A target over 100% is not attainable under this model. Annual figures multiply by your chosen number of identical months, not an assumed four-week month. Checked examples: money retained is not the service ticket Default fictional USD example: 12 no-shows + 8 late cancellations = 20 misses out of 200 bookings (10% combined). Five refills leave 15 fully unfilled slots. At $80 ticket, $25 variable cost, 3% service processing and zero fixed processing charge, original and equivalent-refill contribution is $52.60 each. Potential contribution on the 20 original services is $1,052. Refill contribution is $263. Wasted costs are $75; $225 gross retained fees less $6.75 payment costs gives $218.25 net retained. Check: $1,052 − $263 + $75 − $218.25 = $645.75. The gross service revenue gap is $1,200. A 40% proportional scenario reduces the gap to $387.45 and recovers $258.30 before program cost. A $100 monthly intervention leaves $158.30 net improvement. Across 12 identical months, that is $1,899.60, not the $7,749 baseline annual gap. Lower-value refill example: at a $60 replacement ticket and $20 variable cost, replacement contribution is $38.20. Five refills contribute $191, so the gap is $717.75. A refilled count alone would overstate recovery if it assumed every refill matched the original service. These are hypothetical calculations, not observed salon prices, performance benchmarks or promised recovery. If you change collection policy or fee amounts independently of misses, rerun the baseline with those actual assumptions instead of interpreting the proportional scenario as a full policy forecast. Use industry figures as context, not your default inputs Zenoti’s May 13, 2026 calculator article lists a 2% no-show rate for its “Salons” segment and 4% for nail studios, citing its 2026 platform benchmark report. Those vendor-defined segment figures are not a national standard or a combined no-show-plus-late-cancellation target. This calculator’s 10% combined example is deliberately fictional. Use your own matched diary records. Keep the definitions and denominator consistent when comparing months; a cancellation rate and a no-show rate describe different appointment outcomes. Zenoti: 2026 segment context and no-show/cancellation distinction Assumptions and limits Counterfactual contribution gap, not accounting net profit, cash flow or customer lifetime value. Only one replacement per missed slot is modeled. Fees are amounts actually retained after refunds; their payment/refund costs are separate. Unchanged fixed overhead cancels out. The proportional recovery scenario does not predict demand, staff availability, policy legality or software effectiveness. Negative values remain visible. Use separate cohorts for substantially different services. Frequently asked questions Why is revenue lost different from contribution lost? A missed service can avoid variable costs, while actual waste and retained fees change the outcome. The model compares original-service contribution with replacement contribution and net fees; it does not equate the full ticket with profit. Can I enter both no-shows and late cancellations? Yes, as separate non-overlapping counts from the same original diary. Their sum cannot exceed original bookings. Do not count one appointment in both groups. Can a cheaper replacement recover the whole loss? Not necessarily. Enter its actual ticket and variable cost; a lower-contribution refill leaves a gap even though the slot was used. How are deposits and cancellation fees entered? Enter only amounts actually retained after refunds for this missed-booking cohort. Refundable and future-service deposits are excluded. Enter related processing/refund charges separately. Does a card on file mean the fee was collected? No. A policy amount or stored card is not a settled receipt. Use actual collection and refund records; a payment can fail or be waived. Should salaried staff and rent be entered as waste? Only incremental costs caused by these missed bookings belong in this comparison. Unchanged salaries and rent cancel out; deducting them again would double count fixed costs. What does a negative contribution gap mean? Entered refill contribution and retained fees exceed the original-service comparison and waste. It is not proof that cancellations are desirable, legal, sustainable or good for customer retention. Is the reduction scenario a forecast of reminder effectiveness? No. It is your proportional assumption. Misses, refills, fees and waste scale together while intervention cost stays fixed. Track actual results to evaluate any program. What if the break-even reduction exceeds 100%? The entered monthly program cost exceeds the baseline gap. Even eliminating the modeled exposure cannot cover that cost under these assumptions. Why can the scenario show fractional appointments? Baseline counts must be whole numbers. Scenario counts are expected values from a percentage reduction; they are not a claim that part of a real appointment can be served. How should I annualize a seasonal salon? Enter how many months share this pattern, from 1 to 12. For distinct seasons, calculate separate cohorts and add compatible results; do not repeat one unusually busy month automatically. Is the currency selector an exchange-rate converter? No. It changes currency labels only. Enter all tickets, costs and fees in one consistent currency. What this calculator includes Calculate privately in this tab without an account. Use one connected workflow for recipe cost, period food usage and selling-price decisions. Keep ingredients, variable contribution and monthly funding requirements distinct. Use explicit weight, volume and count units without assuming ingredient density. View worked examples, formulas and source references. How to cost a recipe from the purchase pack Enter the purchase-pack cost, quantity and unit for each ingredient. Enter usable quantity used in the batch and its matching measurement type. Enter measured edible yield: 80% means one fifth of purchased quantity is unavailable. Do not add that trim loss again. Choose how many selling units the batch produces. One whole cake is one unit if the quote is for the entire cake. Add variable batch labor, per-unit packaging and other batch costs once. Set price and percentage fees to inspect contribution. Carry the itemized costs into menu pricing and review the monthly assumptions there. Recipe cost, yield and contribution formulas Usable purchased quantity = purchase quantity × unit conversion × yield rate. Ingredient cost = pack cost × compatible usable recipe quantity ÷ usable purchased quantity. Sum all ingredient lines for batch ingredient cost. Ingredient cost per unit = batch ingredient cost ÷ selling units. Total variable cost per unit = ingredient cost + batch labor ÷ units + other batch costs ÷ units + per-unit packaging. Contribution = selling price × (1 − fee rate) − variable cost. A zero selling price leaves percentage results undefined but does not stop recipe costing. Zero servings, zero yield, negative amounts and mixed measurement dimensions are rejected. Checked recipe and whole-cake examples Flour: $12 for 5 kg, with 500 g used, costs $1.20. Sugar: $4 for 1 kg, with 200 g used, costs $0.80. Butter: $6 for 500 g, with 100 g used, costs $1.20. With full yield, ingredients total $3.20. The whole-cake preset uses $19.70 ingredients, $54 batch labor (three active hours at $18 per hour), $4 packaging and $5 other batch cost for one cake. Total variable cost is $82.70. At $130 and a 3% fee, contribution is $43.40; this is not net profit. For a separate yield check, $24 for 5 lb with 80% usable yield gives 4 usable lb. Using 1.5 usable lb costs $9, or $0.75 across 12 servings. Review portions and complete job costs Confirm recipe quantities describe usable ingredients rather than raw quantity that already includes trim. Check actual portions and ingredient price changes before quoting the same recipe again. For whole cakes, retain decoration time, packaging and delivery in the scope. Do not silently convert a whole-cake quote into slice revenue. Keep owner compensation once: either in variable labor or a separate monthly requirement for the same work. Assumptions and limits Recipe usage is usable edible quantity. Yield reduces the usable purchase quantity once. The cost equation can span multiple packs. Weight converts only to weight, volume only to volume, and count only to count. Ingredients must use compatible units; cups and mass-to-volume conversions are outside this model. Batch labor and other costs allocate once to selling units. Contribution excludes monthly fixed costs, unentered costs and taxes. Frequently asked questions Can I use pounds and grams together? Yes, both are weight units. The tool converts them to a consistent base before costing. It rejects a weight purchase paired with volume usage because no density is assumed. US fl oz means the US customary volume unit, not Imperial or a rounded nutrition-label measure; use the metric quantity when that is the pack measurement. Does recipe cost include labor and overhead? Ingredient cost is shown separately. Enter variable batch labor, packaging and other batch costs to see contribution. Monthly overhead belongs in the menu or whole-business funding plan. Can I price a custom cake? Use the whole-cake preset and one selling unit for a whole-cake quote. Replace ingredients, labor and delivery with the accepted scope, then test monthly funding and capacity in menu pricing. How does yield affect cost? Yield reduces purchased usable quantity. A lower yield makes each usable quantity more expensive. Do not add the same trim or waste again elsewhere. Are costs saved to my account? No. Inputs remain in this tab. The optional menu transfer stores only a one-time cost summary in session storage and does not submit it to an account. Does changing the unit dropdown change its quantity? No. Select the correct unit for the quantity you enter. The cost calculation converts the declared units; changing a label does not rewrite the input quantity. documents.text: FOOD INVENTORY · FREE · NO SIGNUP Food Cost Percentage Calculator Reconcile inventory, supplier credits and transfers with matching food sales. Separate documented meal reclassifications, compare actual with theoretical usage, and inspect your own target without counting waste twice. Calculate my food cost → Read the formula Quick answer The fictional example uses $8,000 opening stock + $18,000 purchases − $6,000 closing stock = $20,000 food used. With no meal adjustments and $60,000 net food sales, food cost is 33.33%. The $18,200 theoretical cost leaves a $1,800 gap; $600 recorded waste explains part, leaving $1,200 to reconcile. The example amounts are fictional; use your own records. What this calculator includes Reconcile inventory movements, supplier credits and documented meal reclassifications. Keep gross food usage visible alongside the adjusted food-sales percentage. Compare the actual sold mix with theoretical recipe cost and a separate waste log. Test your own target and inspect cost/sales sensitivity without promised savings. Export all inputs, unrounded results and assumptions to CSV; print the current scenario. How to calculate food cost percentage from your records Choose inventory-count boundaries for a week, month or other completed period. Match purchases, transfers and net food sales to those dates and locations. Value opening and closing stock consistently at cost. Use invoices for goods received, then subtract supplier credits only if purchases are gross. Enter transfers across the counted boundary at cost. A move between two included storerooms is not a transfer in or out of this scope. If your reporting policy moves staff meals or complimentary food to another expense, enter only their documented ingredient cost. Otherwise leave these adjustments zero. Enter the theoretical cost of the actual sold menu mix, including modifiers, if known. Match the ingredient prices and scope used for the actual comparison. Use a waste log to explain part of the variance. Enter your own optional target, then review the signed gaps and source records before acting. Food-cost formula: inventory bridge, adjustments and percentages Net purchases = received purchases − supplier credits. Food available = opening inventory + net purchases + transfers in − transfers out. Gross food used = food available − closing inventory. Adjusted food usage = gross food used − reclassified staff-meal cost − reclassified complimentary/promotional food cost. Adjusted food-cost percentage = adjusted usage ÷ net food sales × 100. Gross usage percentage is also shown so a reporting reclassification is not mistaken for reduced total consumption. Actual–theoretical gap = adjusted usage − matched theoretical recipe cost. Gap in percentage points = gap ÷ net food sales × 100. Recorded waste is already in usage: remainder after recorded waste = gap − waste log cost. This signed remainder can include offsetting count, yield, price, portion or mix differences. Target cost allowance = net food sales × your target percentage ÷ 100. Actual less allowance is a signed budget comparison, not a recoverable-savings promise. Sales at unchanged usage = adjusted usage ÷ (target ÷ 100), rounded up to cents. This holds total usage constant; it is an algebraic comparison, not a sales plan. Checked examples with the same inventory and sales boundary Default fictional period: $8,000 + $18,000 − $6,000 = $20,000 food used. Zero transfers and meal adjustments leave adjusted usage at $20,000. Divide by $60,000 net food sales for 33.3333…%, displayed as 33.33%. Food sales less adjusted ingredients is $40,000 before labor, other variable costs and overhead. At $18,200 theoretical cost, the theoretical rate is 30.3333…%; the actual gap is $1,800 or 3.00 percentage points. A $600 recorded waste log leaves $1,200 to reconcile. Waste is not added to usage and is not subtracted when calculating food-cost percentage. With a chosen 30% target, the allowance on $60,000 sales is $18,000. Actual usage is $2,000 above that allowance. Holding $20,000 usage constant requires $66,666.67 sales algebraically; additional sales normally change ingredient usage, so this is not a forecast. Adjustment example: keep the original inventory and sales, add $500 transfers in and $300 transfers out, and reclassify $400 staff meals plus $200 complimentary food. Gross usage becomes $20,200 (33.67% of sales); adjusted usage is $19,600 (32.67%). The $600 reclassified cost remains elsewhere in business expenses. Inventory check: if closing stock is $4,000 instead of $6,000 and other default inputs stay fixed, usage is $22,000 and food cost is 36.67%. An inaccurate closing count can therefore change the ratio without a real operating change. Match each input with a supporting record Inventory: dated physical counts, units and consistent valuation. Purchases/credits: receiving reports and supplier credit memos. Transfers: paired records at cost between locations or departments. Reclassified meals: authorized staff/comp logs and the receiving expense account. Sales: food-category POS net sales, with dates and discounts reconciled. Theoretical usage: dishes and modifiers actually sold multiplied by standard recipe ingredient costs on a comparable valuation basis. A planned menu mix or a partial set of recipes is not a complete period benchmark. Waste: measured quantities priced at cost for this same period, excluding the meals already reclassified. Supplier payment timing is separate from inventory receipt timing. Include food received on credit in purchases; exclude a deposit for food not yet received. Do not reduce net sales again for discounts already netted in the POS report. Investigate a high food-cost percentage before changing prices Recheck high-value item counts, units, receiving cutoff, credit memos and transfers. Confirm food-only costs and food-only sales share one boundary. Adding unrelated beverage sales can make the rate look better without reducing usage. Review recipe prices, edible yield, actual portions, substitutions, modifiers and recorded waste. A variance alone does not identify theft or prove avoidable loss. Evaluate recipe contribution and full restaurant commitments separately. A lower food percentage does not establish profitability, and a meal reclassification does not create savings. Assumptions and limits All examples are hypothetical USD, not market benchmarks. Use ingredient costs for one matched inventory and sales scope. Transfers cross that scope; credit memos are subtracted once. Staff/promotional costs are optional documented expense reclassifications, not eliminated expenses. Waste remains in adjusted food usage. Theoretical cost must exclude the same reclassified meals and reflect the actual paid mix. Labor, packaging, platform fees and overhead are excluded. No accounting profit, demand forecast, automatic POS connection or guaranteed saving is calculated. Frequently asked questions What is the food-cost percentage formula? For the adjusted scope, divide inventory-based food usage after documented transfers and meal reclassifications by matching net food sales, then multiply by 100. The inventory bridge stays visible alongside the adjusted ratio. Is this a recipe cost calculator? This page reconciles a completed inventory period. Use the separate recipe calculator for purchase packs, usable yield and cost per portion, then menu pricing to test complete variable costs. What is a good food-cost percentage? There is no universal target in this calculator. Choose a target from your menu mix, complete cost structure and budget. The illustrative 30% target is an assumption, not a national average or recommendation. Should I subtract staff meals or complimentary meals? Only when their ingredient cost is already in usage and your reporting policy reclassifies that cost to a separate expense. Enter cost, not menu price. Ordinary discounts do not justify subtracting ingredient cost; they already reduce net sales. Should recorded waste be added to food used? No. A physical closing count already reflects consumed, spoiled or discarded stock. The waste field explains part of the actual–theoretical gap; it does not change usage or the percentage. How do supplier credits and transfers work? Use gross received purchases and subtract credits once, or use net purchases with zero credits. Enter cross-boundary transfers at cost. Do not count a return both as a credit and as a transfer out. Can the actual–theoretical gap be negative? Yes. Actual usage can be below the recipe model, or logged waste can exceed the net gap because other favorable differences offset it. Check counts, valuation and portions; a negative amount is not automatically a verified saving. Why are theoretical usage, waste and target optional? Blank means unknown or unused; zero is a stated zero for theoretical usage and waste. A target must be positive. Missing optional fields leave the corresponding comparisons unavailable rather than inventing data. Why can food cost exceed 100%? Usage can exceed sales in a low-sales period or because of losses, timing, count errors or mismatched scopes. The tool keeps that result visible. Negative inventory usage is rejected for reconciliation. Does sales less food cost mean profit? No. It is the remainder before labor, packaging, payment/platform fees, occupancy and other expenses. Reclassified meals also remain a business expense. Use the linked restaurant plan for full costs. What does sales at unchanged usage mean? It divides the current total adjusted usage by your target rate. It assumes usage does not change; it is not a prediction of demand or a recommendation to raise prices. Are currency amounts converted or saved? Currency selection changes labels only. Enter every amount in the same currency. Inputs remain in this tab; CSV and print actions export the current scenario when you choose them. Targets based on food-cost percentage are not substituted for your tested price. Weekly item capacity cannot tell us team size or worker-hours. Enter those separately below; the full plan recalculates capacity and adds the promotion cost you enter here. Check that all monthly commitments cover the same modeled orders and compensation is counted once. Additional promotion cost per order Enter 0 only if none, or if already included above. Active team members Whole people delivering the modeled orders. Hours per team member / week Available working hours before productive utilization. Total worker-hours per order Two people working 15 minutes each use 0.5 worker-hours. Productive utilization (%) Share of working time available for these orders, 0–100%. Qualified visit or inquiry conversion (%) Use the same demand basis throughout, above 0% up to 100%. Each selling unit is one complete representative order. Its costs, monthly commitments and expected sales share the same scope; labor and owner compensation are counted once. Continue with this order in the full calculator → Only this explicit action carries a temporary plan in the same tab. It expires after five minutes and is removed when opened. No financial inputs enter the URL or analytics. Need several dish or channel scenarios instead? Review menu mix and kitchen time before combining them. Review or change your inputs ↑ Food costing engine 1.0.1 . Calculations retain precision; displayed money rounds to cents. Price floors round upward. Illustrative planning scene. The example amounts are fictional; use your own records. What this calculator includes Calculate privately in this tab without an account. Use one connected workflow for recipe cost, period food usage and selling-price decisions. Keep ingredients, variable contribution and monthly funding requirements distinct. Use explicit weight, volume and count units without assuming ingredient density. View worked examples, formulas and source references. How to test a menu price after fees Use ingredient cost per serving or whole item from the recipe calculator. Add sale-dependent labor, packaging and other non-percentage costs once. Enter fees, your chosen ingredient percentage and contribution percentage separately. Enter the selling price you actually want to test. The alternative price outputs do not automatically replace it. Define the monthly funding requirement and the comparable expected sales and capacity. Review fixed scope and owner compensation carefully. Compare the required whole units, capacity and contribution at expected volume before treating a price as feasible. Food-cost, contribution and capacity price formulas Ingredient-target price = ingredient cost ÷ target ingredient rate. It excludes the other variable costs when setting price. Contribution-target price = all non-percentage variable cost ÷ (1 − fee rate − target contribution rate). The denominator must be positive. At the tested price, contribution = price × (1 − fee rate) − non-percentage variable cost. Required units = ceiling(monthly funding requirement ÷ positive contribution). Whole monthly capacity = floor(weekly capacity × 52/12). Capacity funding price = (variable cost + monthly requirement ÷ whole monthly capacity) ÷ (1 − fee rate), rounded upward. Zero capacity has no capacity-based price. Checked pricing and capacity comparison The default costs total $10. A $20 ingredient-target price leaves $20 × 0.97 − $10 = $9.40 contribution. A 55% contribution target needs $10 ÷ 0.42 = $23.8095…, rounded upward to $23.81. At the entered $22 price, contribution is $11.34. A $20,000 monthly requirement needs 1,764 whole sales. Weekly capacity of 400 gives 1,733 whole monthly units; the target does not fit. Expected volume of 1,700 leaves $19,278 contribution and a $722 shortfall against the requirement. The capacity-based price floor is $22.21, assuming all 1,733 available monthly units sell. This is not evidence customers will pay that price. Check price, scope and deliverable demand together Keep a serving, a whole cake and a customer check as separate possible units; match every cost and capacity entry. For multiple items, use a stable representative mix or run separate scenarios. Do not assign the full overhead to every item. If expanding capacity adds payroll or equipment commitments, revise the monthly requirement before comparing the new result. After a price change, review paid volume, portion practice, contribution and kitchen time using actual records. Assumptions and limits One consistently defined selling unit and a stable cost/channel mix. Percentage fees stay constant. Required monthly units round up; capacity uses weekly units × 52/12 and rounds down. Price floors round up to cents. The funding requirement includes only entered fixed commitments, additional owner compensation and profit goal. Existing labor compensation must not be duplicated. No seating, kitchen bottleneck, demand prediction or accounting net-profit calculation is provided. Frequently asked questions Can I carry these numbers into a full restaurant plan? Yes. Review the result-panel handoff, confirm one selling unit represents a complete order with matching monthly scope, and enter promotion cost, team hours, utilization and conversion. The tested price and itemized costs carry in the same tab with your currency. Weekly item capacity is replaced by a workforce-based capacity calculation; expected sales remain an assumption. Is a 30% food-cost target a 70% profit margin? No. It leaves 70% of price before labor, packaging, selling fees and fixed costs. The contribution calculation deducts all entered variable costs and fees separately. Is contribution margin the same as markup? No. Contribution percentage divides contribution by selling price; markup divides a price uplift by cost. This target uses margin on revenue. Why is the capacity price different from the margin price? One funds a stated monthly requirement at the available whole-unit capacity; the other meets a chosen per-unit contribution ratio. Both depend on inputs, not customer demand predictions. How should I enter owner labor? If the same owner work is already costed as variable labor, do not also enter it as additional monthly owner pay. A separate profit goal is beyond that compensation. Can I price delivery orders separately? Yes. Run a separate consistent scenario with that channel’s fees, packaging and other costs. Do not apply a delivery commission to unrelated dine-in sales. Does a feasible capacity target guarantee sales? No. The tool checks your entered volume and capacity. Demand, willingness to pay and operational bottlenecks still need evidence. documents.text: ← All free business tools Staffing & service costs · Free, no signup Employee Cost Calculator Find the annual cost of a hire beyond salary, then divide it by realistic productive hours. Compare recurring cost with first-year hiring cost and check the work needed to fund it. Illustrative example: $60,000 salary plus $22,500 recurring employer costs gives $82,500 annually. With 1,380 productive hours, cost is $59.78 per productive hour. A $5,000 hiring cost raises the first-year requirement to $87,500. Your employee cost inputs Currency USD 155 currencies. Search and choose one; currency labels change, but amounts are not converted. Annual gross salary Before employee deductions. Leave pay already in salary is not added again. Annual bonus / additional cash pay Add only compensation outside the salary figure. Annual employer taxes / contributions Enter your employer-only amount from payroll records. No country tax rates are assumed. Annual employer-paid benefits Insurance, retirement contributions and other benefits, excluding amounts already entered. Annual allocated overhead Equipment, software, space and training allocation. Include each cost once. One-time hiring / onboarding cost Added to first-year cost only. Exclude amounts already in annual overhead. Annual paid hours Example 40 × 52 = 2,080. Adjust for the actual contract period. Paid leave / holiday hours Subtract from paid hours; unpaid hours should not be included in paid hours. Productive share of remaining hours (%) After leave. For recovery, use billable/deliverable hours; admin time remains outside. Collected revenue per productive hour Use the same delivery scope and net revenue after discounts and percentage fees. Other variable cost per productive hour Exclude this employee cost: it is the funding requirement, not subtracted twice. Reset example Calculations run in this browser tab. These tools do not save or submit the entered costs. Reloading clears your changes. Currency labels do not convert amounts. Annual employee cost and capacity Recurring annual cost $82,500.00 First-year cost including hiring $87,500.00 Cost per paid hour $39.66 Cost per productive hour $59.78 First-year cost per productive hour $63.41 Productive annual hours 1,380 First-year recovery hours 1,093.75 Contribution less first-year cost $22,900.00 Hours available after leave: 1,840 . Recurring cost ÷ salary: 1.38× . Entered productive capacity can fund the modeled first-year employee cost. Recovery hours use first-year cost ÷ (collected hourly revenue − other hourly variable cost), rounded upward to 0.01 hour. The contribution comparison excludes other unentered business commitments and is not accounting net profit. Review your inputs ↑ Connect loaded employee cost with usable capacity Employee take-home pay, employer loaded cost and collected billable contribution are different records. The existing calculator above keeps its original engine and assumptions. Its current results below show which question each amount answers. Recurring annual employer cost 82,500 First-year cost including hiring 87,500 Annual productive hours 1,380 First-year recovery hours 1,093.75 In the fictional default, $60,000 salary + $3,000 bonus + $6,300 employer costs + $9,000 benefits + $4,200 overhead = $82,500 recurring cost. Add $5,000 hiring for $87,500 first-year cost. Productive hours are (2,080 paid − 240 leave) × 75% = 1,380. At $90 collected revenue less $10 other variable cost per hour, 1,093.75 productive hours recover $87,500; using every planned 1,380 hours yields $22,900 after this employee cost, before other business commitments. Do not add paid leave again if its pay is already in salary. Do not treat employee tax withheld from gross pay as an additional employer cost. A chosen utilization rate is an assumption, not proof that hours will sell or that one employee removes a separate process bottleneck. Connected cost/capacity review November 20, 2026; original engine, defaults, cover and review date preserved. AI-generated editorial scene. All calculator and template example amounts are fictional. What this calculator includes Separate recurring annual employer cost from first-year hiring cost. Enter employer-only contributions as amounts without assumed country tax rates. Compare paid-hour and productive-hour costs on one annual basis. Check first-year recovery hours against entered productive capacity. Calculate in your browser without an account or sending input values. How to calculate the true cost of an employee Use one employee and one consistent twelve-month budget. For a partial-year hire, build a matching partial-year cost and hours scenario rather than mixing annual salary with three months of hours. Enter gross salary, additional bonus and employer-only payroll contributions from your records. Do not add employee tax withholding to gross salary again. Add employer-paid benefits and a documented overhead allocation. Review software, equipment, training and office costs so each appears once. Enter one-time recruiting and onboarding costs separately. Use actual expected spending rather than an arbitrary salary multiplier. Enter paid hours and paid leave. Apply productive share to the remaining hours to allow for admin, meetings and non-delivery time. For a hiring recovery test, enter collected revenue and other variable costs per productive hour. Compare required hours with productive capacity and realistic demand. Records to gather before budgeting a hire Keep cost and time boundaries consistent Input Record Check Salary and bonus Offer and compensation budget Gross annual cash pay; bonus outside salary only Employer contributions Payroll provider or current employer-cost schedule Employer share only; no employee withholding duplicated Benefits and overhead Provider quotes and allocation policy Include each annual cost once Paid hours and leave Contract, holiday calendar and leave policy Subtract paid leave once; keep unpaid time outside paid hours Productive share Observed billable or delivery hours Apply after leave; use comparable role and scope Annual employee cost and productive-hour formulas Recurring annual cost = salary + bonus + employer contributions + benefits + allocated overhead. First-year cost = recurring cost + one-time hiring cost. Available hours = paid hours − paid leave hours. Productive hours = available hours × productive share ÷ 100. Recurring cost per paid hour = recurring cost ÷ paid hours. Recurring cost per productive hour = recurring cost ÷ productive hours. First-year recovery hours = first-year cost ÷ (collected revenue per productive hour − other variable cost per productive hour). Other hourly cost excludes this same employee cost. A zero or negative contribution denominator has no finite recovery target. Zero productive hours leaves productive-hour rates undefined. Zero salary leaves the cost-to-salary multiplier undefined. Neither condition turns the remaining employee costs into zero. Employee cost example: paid hours versus billable hours The example adds $60,000 salary, $3,000 bonus, $6,300 employer contributions, $9,000 benefits and $4,200 overhead: $82,500 recurring cost. The contribution amount is fictional, not a U.S. or UK statutory tax rate. 2,080 paid hours minus 240 leave hours leaves 1,840 available hours. At 75% productive share, 1,380 hours remain. Recurring cost is $39.66 per paid hour and $59.78 per productive hour. Adding $5,000 hiring cost produces $63.41 per first-year productive hour. At $90 collected revenue and $10 other variable cost per productive hour, $80 is available to fund the hire. $87,500 ÷ $80 = 1,093.75 recovery hours. All 1,380 productive hours would leave $22,900 after the stated first-year cost, before other unentered commitments. If productive share falls to 50%, capacity falls to 920 hours. The same first-year requirement still needs 1,093.75 recovery hours; annual contribution is $73,600 and the funding gap is $13,900. Lower utilization increases hourly cost even when salary is unchanged. Use the result to decide whether the hire fits Compare the recurring result with next year’s budget and the first-year result with the hiring year. Recruiting costs should not silently repeat forever. Check whether forecast demand fills productive capacity. Available staff hours do not create customer work. Use the same cost boundary for a contractor comparison, including management time and delivery scope. This does not determine legal worker classification. Move payroll, employer contributions and benefit payments into the dated cash forecast. Annual affordability can still hide an earlier cash gap. Direct labor budget: required hours are not a full annual hire cost A direct labor cost budget starts with required activity times standard paid delivery hours times the relevant labor rate. For 200 fictional equivalent jobs, 1.5 paid delivery hours per job and a loaded rate of $32, the same-period labor budget is 300 hours and $9,600. A wage-only $24 rate would instead show $7,200 before the additional employer burden; do not call those two scopes the same cost. This employee calculator answers a different but connected question: full annual employment cost and productive-hour recovery. Reconcile the period, paid-versus-productive hours and cost inclusions before taking its hourly result into a job budget. Do not also charge the same guaranteed salary as extra per-job labor. Carry a consistent labor boundary into job costing Use traced job hours and the appropriate labor rate; keep any employer burden out of the overhead pool if already included directly. A full annual employment cost and a short-period job cost answer different questions. Job order cost sheet and worked example Assumptions and limits This is one annual employee budget, not a payroll tax return or legal employment classification tool. Salary, bonus, employer contributions, benefits and allocated overhead are recurring costs. One-time hiring cost belongs only to first year. Paid leave already included in salary changes available hours, not the salary amount. Productive share applies after leave. Recovery assumes every modeled productive hour is delivered and collected at the entered net rate; it does not predict demand. It excludes unentered commitments and accounting adjustments. Frequently asked questions Does this calculate USA or UK payroll taxes? No. Enter the employer-only annual amount from your current payroll records or adviser. Tax rates, thresholds and benefit rules vary by jurisdiction and date. Currency selection changes labels only. Should I add paid holidays to salary? Not when salary already pays those days. Subtract their hours from available time. Adding their salary cost again would double-count the same compensation. What does fully loaded employee cost include? Here it includes gross salary, extra bonus, employer contributions, benefits and allocated overhead. First-year cost also includes one-time hiring. The result only includes the amounts you enter. Are productive hours the same as paid hours? No. Paid hours include paid leave and may include administration. This tool removes paid leave, then applies your productive share to the remaining hours. For revenue recovery, use billable or deliverable hours. What happens at zero productive hours? Productive-hour costs are undefined. Annual employee cost remains and the contribution comparison shows the unfunded requirement. Is the displayed funding surplus net profit? No. It compares collected productive-hour contribution with this employee’s first-year cost. Other business commitments, interest, tax and accounting adjustments require a separate reconciliation. See your 13-week balances, test late customer collections and download a free editable template. Opening cash + cash receipts − cash payments = closing cash. The example starts with $12,000 and ends with $15,000. Delaying operating receipts 14 days creates a −$3,000 weekly balance even though total receipts are unchanged. Loan principal receipts and repayments are financing; interest follows the adopted reporting policy. Record asset purchases in the cash plan even when depreciation is the current-period expense.
