This is a planning requirement, not a demand forecast. At these assumptions, estimated delivery capacity is 97 whole jobs per month. The current capacity is below the required volume. These are planning estimates, not a sales forecast. Reset example Continue with these numbers in the full calculator Unit: one completed, comparable cleaning visit. Employee wages vary with visits in this model; committed payroll belongs in fixed costs. Owner compensation is counted once in the monthly owner allocation. Sample inputs are fictional USD, not local prices or wage benchmarks. Currency label USD CAD GBP EUR AUD PKR AED INR Formatting only; changing currency does not convert amounts. Reset detailed cleaning example Load the worked two-employee example (USD) 1. Visit price and employee labor Price / completed visit (USD) After discounts, excluding sales tax collected for others. Use a comparable visit, not an entire recurring contract. Employees on this visit Paid employees only. Enter owner time separately; use zero for owner-only delivery. On-site hours / employee (hours) Elapsed cleaning hours for each employee. Two employees × two hours means four worker-hours. Paid travel + setup hours / employee (hours) Attributable paid time per employee in addition to on-site time. Do not subtract it again from available hours. Variable employee wage / hour (USD) Visit-dependent wage only. Guaranteed payroll belongs in fixed costs; avoid counting it twice. Employer burden on variable wages (%) Your effective add-on for applicable employer costs. No statutory rate or wage benchmark is assumed. 2. Owner time and other visit costs Owner on-site hours / visit (hours) Owner time is a capacity constraint. Compensation is funded once through monthly owner allocation. Owner travel + setup hours / visit (hours) Owner delivery time beyond cleaning. Exclude it from employee count and wage costs. Supplies / visit (USD) Consumables used for this completed visit. Vehicle + parking cost / visit (USD) Job-linked fuel, vehicle use and parking; separate from worker travel wages. Acquisition allocation / completed visit (USD) Blended spend across this visit mix. Do not apply a one-time client acquisition cost to every repeat visit. Percentage processing fee (%) Rate on the visit price excluding collected tax. Extra fee on tax belongs in Other costs. Flat fee allocated / visit (USD) Allocate an invoice-level fee across visits once when several visits are billed together. Other variable cost / visit (USD) Only costs not entered elsewhere, such as a visit-linked equipment charge. 3. Monthly costs and completed visits Monthly fixed operating costs (USD) Include committed payroll and insurance here; exclude the same variable costs entered above. Monthly owner-pay allocation (USD) Owner compensation funded here, without another owner wage in per-visit costs. Extra monthly remainder target (USD) Goal beyond fixed costs and owner allocation; before unmodeled tax/financing items. Planned completed visits / month Whole comparable completed visits. Canceled or unpaid bookings are not automatically revenue. Capacity, recurring clients and demand 4. Delivery and scheduling assumptions Available employee delivery hours / month (hours) Total staff worker-hours after other downtime, but including cleaning and the travel/setup time entered above. Available owner delivery hours / month (hours) Owner hours usable for on-site and travel/setup work after other responsibilities. Completed visits / recurring client / month Use your actual schedule or a consistent average. Four visits and weekly service are not always identical. Service days / month Whole working days from 1 to 31. New inquiry-to-visit conversion (%) Measured comparable inquiries converting to completed new visits. Repeat visits need a separate pipeline check. Contribution / completed visit $76.78 42.66 % of visit revenue · before fixed costs and owner allocation Operating break-even 42 Visits covering fixed operating costs only. Including owner pay 101 Visits covering fixed costs and the owner allocation. For your profit target 114 Visits including the extra monthly remainder target. Employee worker-hours / visit 2.5 Owner worker-hours / visit 1 Loaded variable wage / hour $23.20 Variable employee labor / visit $58.00 Percentage processing fee / visit $5.22 All variable costs / visit $103.22 At 120 planned completed visits Planned volume exceeds entered capacity. The remainder below is hypothetical at that volume; revise staffing, owner availability, delivery time or planned visits. Visit revenue $21,600.00 Operating remainder before owner allocation $6,013.60 Remainder after owner allocation $1,513.60 Above / below extra target $513.60 Operating margin of safety: 65.27% . Uses the exact operating threshold of 41.68 visits . Capacity: 90 whole visits. Employee limit: 104 ; owner limit: 90 . A role with no visit time is not a constraint. The full target exceeds these entered hours. Scheduling, equipment and client demand still need checks. Full target: $20,520.00 visit revenue; average 5.18 visits across 22 service days, or 6 each day using a constant ceiling. About 29 recurring clients at 4 completed visits/client/month. Validate the actual calendar. Minimum price at planned volume: $128.39 for operating costs; $175.60 including owner pay and extra target. Rounded up to 0.01. Other costs, volume and fee terms are held constant. If every target visit were new: 380 inquiries at 30 % conversion. Existing repeat visits do not need reacquisition: apply conversion only to your remaining new-visit gap. Download cleaning scenario (CSV) Free local export of inputs and unrounded results. No figures are sent to MyBreakeven. This is not a cash forecast or payroll calculation. Cleaning revenue and operating cost by completed visits Operating break-even is 41.68 visits. Owner allocation and extra profit are excluded from the operating-cost line. $0.00 0 $14,256.00 72 $28,512.00 144 Completed cleaning visits / month Visit revenue Variable costs + fixed operating costs Owner allocation and extra profit remain separate goals. One-change cleaning scenarios Scenario Contribution / visit Visits for all targets Whole-visit capacity Target fits? Current inputs $76.78 114 90 No 10% lower visit price $59.30 147 90 No 30 more minutes on site per employee $65.18 134 86 No 25% fewer available staff hours $76.78 114 78 No Changes are isolated assumptions, not predictions. Longer employee on-site time changes both labor cost and staff capacity. Owner time stays as entered; update it separately if the scope changes. How the detailed cleaning break-even calculation works Choose one comparable completed visit: a standard home clean, a defined office visit, or another repeatable scope. A monthly contract containing twelve visits is twelve units, not one unit at a per-visit price. Exclude pass-through sales tax and reconcile discounts, unpaid work and cancellations before choosing your realized price. Mixed deep cleans, maintenance visits and specialist jobs need separate scenarios or a representative mix. Cost employee time and owner compensation once Employee worker-hours / visit = employees × (on-site elapsed hours + paid travel/setup hours per employee) Loaded variable wage = wage × (1 + employer burden fraction) Variable employee labor = employee worker-hours × loaded variable wage Contribution / visit = visit price × (1 − fee fraction) − labor − supplies − vehicle − acquisition − other costs − flat-fee allocation Use only visit-dependent employee wage cost in this equation. Put guaranteed payroll in monthly fixed costs and keep it there once; all employee hours still consume delivery capacity. A representative effective wage and burden may be needed when only part of payroll varies. This simple rate does not calculate overtime, wage-group differences or statutory payroll limits. Use records appropriate to your employment arrangement. Owner on-site and travel hours are separate capacity inputs. Owner compensation is funded once through the monthly owner-pay allocation, so operating break-even intentionally excludes that owner funding goal. Owner time is not free: inspect the owner-covered and full-target results before accepting a plan. Do not add the same owner compensation again to variable labor or Other. If you prefer replacement-cost economics, prepare a separate consistent model rather than mixing that cost with the same owner-pay allocation. Travel wages and vehicle cost are distinct. The U.S. Department of Labor’s hours-worked guidance distinguishes travel between job sites during the workday from ordinary commuting. Enter the attributable paid time required for your situation; this calculator does not determine legal pay obligations. No wage, employer-burden or mileage rate is presented as a current national benchmark. Three thresholds and two delivery constraints Operating visits = fixed operating cost ÷ contribution Owner-covered visits = (fixed operating cost + owner allocation) ÷ contribution Full target visits = (fixed operating cost + owner allocation + extra target) ÷ contribution Staff capacity = available staff worker-hours ÷ employee worker-hours / visit Owner capacity = available owner hours ÷ owner hours / visit Order targets round upward to whole visits. Each applicable capacity rounds downward; the smaller employee or owner limit controls. A role with zero delivery time is nonbinding, rather than dividing by zero. Available delivery hours already exclude unrelated downtime but must still include the travel/setup time charged to each visit. Do not remove that travel twice. A pooled hours model does not prove that routes, crew attendance, equipment and appointment windows align. A reconciled two-employee example All amounts below are fictional USD assumptions. Charge $250 per completed visit. Two employees each clean for two hours and use another 0.25 paid hour for travel/setup. At a $20 visit-dependent hourly wage and 20% entered burden, loaded pay is $24 and 4.5 worker-hours cost $108. Owner cleaning takes 0.5 hour plus 0.25 travel/setup hour and is funded through monthly owner allocation. Worked visit economics — illustrative USD Line Calculation Amount Employee labor 2 × (2 + 0.25) × 20 × 1.20 108.00 Supplies, vehicle and acquisition 12 + 10 + 5 27.00 Percentage and flat fee 250 × 3% + 0.30 7.80 All variable costs 108 + 27 + 7.80 142.80 Contribution 250 − 142.80 107.20 Monthly fixed costs of $2,500 need 24 whole visits. Adding $3,000 owner allocation requires 52; an additional $500 remainder goal raises the full target to 56. At 60 planned visits, the model gives $3,932 before owner allocation and $932 afterward. However, 260 available staff hours support only 57 visits, while 45 owner hours support 60. The 56-visit target fits, but the 60-visit plan exceeds staff capacity. Do not treat that 60-visit remainder as a deliverable forecast. Price, clients and margin of safety The operating price floor at a positive planned volume is (non-percentage variable cost + fixed cost / planned visits) / (1 − fee fraction). The full target price replaces fixed cost with fixed cost plus owner allocation plus extra target. The worked full price is $242.58 rounded upward to a cent at 60 planned visits, but that volume still needs a staffing or time change. Percentage fees rise with price, so adding the existing fee amount to a cost total is not a valid price solver. The Stripe break-even explanation covers the underlying fixed-cost/contribution relationship. Operating margin of safety uses the exact operating threshold, not a rounded visit count. It is unavailable with zero planned visits or nonpositive contribution. Recurring-client estimates use the exact target divided by your entered completed visits per client per month, rounded up; validate actual service dates. The all-new inquiry estimate is a separate extreme assumption, not a demand forecast or a need to reacquire every recurring visit. Schedule collections, wages, supplier payments and equipment spending separately in the cash-flow forecast . Use the cleaning contract profit calculator for a specific contract and the cleaning business budget workbook to reconcile monthly records. This model does not establish tax-adjusted net profit, cash availability or a market-acceptable cleaning price. Worker-hours and loaded labor Time sheets including setup and allocated paid travel Detailed mode multiplies employee count by elapsed hours and counts owner time separately. Quick mode takes total person-hours directly. Monthly commitments Insurance, admin, equipment and owner-pay budget Keep costs already charged per visit out of overhead. In the detailed plan, enter two employees and two elapsed on-site hours to calculate four employee worker-hours; enter owner time separately. In the quick estimate, enter four total worker-hours directly. Model one completed visit consistently and price multi-visit contracts in the linked tool. Use the cash runway calculator to compare available cash with expected receipts and payments. INDUSTRY-SPECIFIC UNIT ECONOMICS What this cleaning break-even analysis includes This model calculates contribution per job after cleaning supplies, direct labor, travel, equipment use, card fees and lead-generation cost . It then determines the exact volume and revenue required to cover monthly operating overhead, owner compensation and an optional target profit. Because a financial target is useful only when the business can deliver it, MyBreakeven also compares required volume with productive team hours and estimates the customer inquiries needed at your conversion rate. Exact financial target See fractional break-even volume, exact revenue and the minimum practical whole-unit target separately. Operational feasibility Compare required jobs with estimated monthly delivery capacity before committing to the plan. Private and transparent Inputs stay in your browser, while the formula trace explains how each result was calculated. Formula, assumptions and rounding — quick estimate Contribution per job = average price minus direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and percentage payment fees. Required monthly jobs = (operating overhead + owner pay + target profit) divided by contribution per job . For a traditional operating break-even calculation, set owner pay and target profit to zero. Keep owner pay if you want the business to cover your compensation, and add profit only when calculating a profit target. The example values are illustrative USD inputs, not industry averages. The example contribution is $76.78 per job . The exact target is 113.31 jobs ; rounding up gives 114 whole jobs and $20,520.00 in monthly sales. Costs entered per job must not also be included in monthly overhead. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 / 12 × productive utilization ÷ delivery hours per job . Delivery hours mean total team labor hours per job , including preparation and travel where relevant. Whole-unit capacity rounds down, while required sales round up. Inquiry estimates use your assumed conversion rate, not a prediction of demand. For recurring work, count existing customers separately from new customer acquisition. The full calculator supports other currency labels; it does not convert exchange rates. Read the cleaning break-even guide Read the calculation methodology · Browse business planning guides QUESTIONS THIS MODEL ANSWERS Cleaning break-even questions How many cleaning jobs do I need to break even? Quick-estimate illustration: At the example price of $180.00, each job contributes $76.78 after direct costs and fees. Covering $8,700.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 114 whole jobs, or $20,520.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. The detailed crew plan separately displays operating break-even, owner coverage and the full profit goal. Can my cleaners deliver the required monthly jobs? Quick-estimate illustration: The example requires 114 whole jobs and estimates capacity for 97 whole jobs per month, using 3 team members, 35 hours each per week and 75% productive time. Adjust those inputs to check your own delivery limit. The detailed crew plan separately displays operating break-even, owner coverage and the full profit goal. How many cleaning leads does my conversion rate require? Quick-estimate illustration: At the example 30% inquiry-to-job conversion rate, the model estimates 377.70 inquiries for the exact fractional financial target (378 rounded up). Use your measured conversion rate for a more useful demand estimate. The detailed crew plan separately displays operating break-even, owner coverage and the full profit goal. How are operating break-even and owner income different? Operating break-even covers entered fixed operating costs only. Owner-pay coverage also funds your separate monthly owner allocation. The third threshold adds your extra monthly profit target. Owner allocation is not automatically an accounting expense. How do I count a crew’s cleaning and travel hours? Employee worker-hours equal employee count multiplied by elapsed on-site plus paid travel/setup hours per employee. Two employees working two hours use four worker-hours. Owner time is entered separately. Vehicle cost and paid travel time are different costs. Does this calculate payroll taxes or overtime automatically? No. Enter an effective employer burden and wage from your own payroll records. Include applicable overtime or different wage groups in a representative blended rate, or run separate scenarios. This is not a payroll or labor-law compliance calculator. Can an owner-operated cleaning business use the detailed model? Yes. Set employee count to zero, enter the owner’s on-site and travel hours, and fund owner compensation through the monthly owner allocation. Owner hours still constrain capacity. Do not add the same owner wage again to Other costs. Should guaranteed employee wages be variable or fixed? Keep wages that remain payable regardless of visit volume in fixed costs. Enter only genuinely visit-dependent employee labor in the wage calculation. Use an appropriate blended variable wage if only part varies; do not repeat the same payroll in both. Capacity still uses all employee delivery hours. Are recurring clients the same as cleaning visits? No. Divide the exact target visits by expected completed visits per client per month and round up for a planning client count. Frequency is an average: weekly service is not exactly four visits in every calendar month. Match the actual schedule before quoting or hiring. Does the inquiry target include repeat customers? The displayed all-new inquiry requirement assumes every target visit needs a new comparable inquiry. Recurring visits normally do not. Subtract already secured repeat visits, then apply conversion to the remaining new-visit requirement separately. Can I download the detailed cleaning plan for free? Yes. Download this scenario exports detailed inputs and unrounded results as a local CSV without an account. Quick estimate retains the existing full-calculator continuation and its account-based saved-plan options. Can I use a monthly cleaning contract as one job? The detailed crew plan uses one completed visit; split a monthly contract into comparable visits and use visits per client for the client estimate. The quick estimate can represent a whole monthly contract only when price, costs and total worker-hours all use that same entire-contract unit. What if required sales exceed capacity? The target does not fit the productive hours you entered. Test price, costs, delivery time or a revised capacity plan. Recalculate any new monthly staffing or equipment commitment; more available hours do not prove customer demand. Is this a cash-flow forecast or net-profit statement? No. It models contribution, a monthly funding target and productive-hour capacity. Schedule collections, supplier payments, taxes, equipment cash and loan principal separately; reconcile any unentered items before interpreting accounting net profit. Review the target before changing your plan Record the entered unit, period and cost boundary alongside the result. Compare required whole sales with both capacity and evidence of demand. Run a downside case using a lower realized price or higher delivery cost. Add new commitments if the operating range changes. Check a dated cash forecast before treating a profitable target as available cash. Price a recurring contract Review quote versus actual cost Method and example inputs reviewed November 12, 2026 . Calculation methodology · Editorial standards and corrections . How to do break-even analysis for a landscaping business Define one completed landscaping job, calculate the contribution it leaves, then divide the commitments for the same period by that contribution. Separate the operating threshold from owner coverage and an extra profit goal. Finally check crew hours, owner hours and the active earning season. For a separate fictional USD teaching case, a $500 job with $300 of fully specified variable cost leaves $200 contribution. Monthly fixed operating costs of $4,000 need 20 jobs . If a separate $3,000 owner allocation and $1,000 extra target are not already included, the full goal needs ($4,000 + $3,000 + $1,000) ÷ $200 = 40 jobs . At 39 jobs, contribution is $7,800 and the full plan is $200 short. These teaching inputs are independent of the live form above. If each job needs six total crew-worker-hours and 180 crew-worker-hours are available, the crew can deliver only 30 jobs. The 40-job target therefore does not fit, even before checking owner time or equipment. Avoid adding payroll or equipment cost twice when moving figures between these records. Decision guide and arithmetic reviewed November 20, 2026 . Landscaping break-even: job costs, routes and seasonal recovery Define one completed, comparable job. A maintenance visit, a mulch installation and a complete design/build project do not share the same material, labor or equipment consumption. Use separate scenarios unless you have a measured stable mix. Enter realized service revenue after discounts, excluding sales tax collected for others. Canceled appointments and unpaid quotations are not completed revenue-producing jobs. Separate people, machines and route costs Employee hours = employee count × (elapsed on-site hours + paid travel/setup hours per employee) Loaded variable wage = wage × (1 + employer-burden fraction) Employee labor = employee hours × loaded variable wage Equipment cost = total machine-hours × use-related cost / machine-hour Job contribution = price × (1 − fee fraction) − employee labor − materials − route vehicle/disposal − equipment − acquisition − other direct costs − flat fee Only visit-dependent employee wages belong in variable labor. Put committed payroll in fixed operating costs once; capacity still uses those employees’ delivery hours. A blended wage and employer-burden percentage are inputs from your own records, not a statutory payroll calculation. Owner time is a separate capacity constraint and owner compensation is funded once through the monthly owner allocation. Do not add that same owner wage again in Other. Equipment hours are total running machine-hours. Two mowers each running one hour use two machine-hours even if four employees attend the job. Choose a consistent allowance for fuel, repairs and wear, and keep any cost already included there out of other lines. Fixed depreciation, rental or insurance may belong in fixed costs when not already allocated; a replacement allowance and depreciation for the same economic cost should not both be charged. Debt principal and buying a mower are cash movements that need their own schedule. Vehicle/disposal expense differs from paid travel time. The Department of Labor’s hours-worked guidance distinguishes workday travel between job sites from ordinary commuting. Use the attributable paid time appropriate to your employment arrangement; this tool does not calculate legal wages or overtime. No national wage, equipment rate, margin or acreage productivity benchmark is assumed. Calendar-month targets versus a shorter earning season The standard fixed-cost/contribution relationship gives operating jobs = fixed cost / contribution. Owner-covered jobs add the owner allocation; the full target also adds the extra monthly remainder goal. These first three results cover one calendar month only. Annual fixed requirement = monthly fixed cost × 12 Annual full requirement = (monthly fixed cost + monthly owner allocation + monthly extra goal) × 12 Seasonal full jobs / active month = annual full requirement ÷ (active months × job contribution) Annual planned contribution = planned jobs / active month × active months × contribution The seasonal comparison deliberately assumes zero off-season contribution and all twelve months of the entered costs and goals. It is a recovery budget, not a prediction of rainfall or demand. If you have snow work or other winter services, reconcile their contribution and hours in a separate combined annual plan. Do not use their gross sales as a contribution credit. If all twelve months earn the same job mix, seasonal monthly targets equal the calendar-month targets. Financial targets round upward to whole jobs; employee and owner capacity each round downward. The smaller applicable role limit controls. A role with zero job time does not constrain capacity. Available delivery hours must include the travel/setup time used in the denominator, after other downtime: subtracting the same travel twice understates capacity. Hours alone do not prove that routes, staff availability, equipment and appointment windows align. A worked landscaping scenario with an eight-month season These are fictional USD inputs, not quoted market rates. Price is $300 per job. Two employees each work 1.5 hours on site plus 0.5 paid hour for travel/setup. At $20 variable wage plus 20% entered burden, four worker-hours cost $96. Owner time is 0.75 hour on site plus 0.25 travel hour. Materials cost $35; vehicle/disposal $12; two machine-hours at $8 cost $16; acquisition allocation is $8. A 3% processing fee costs $9 plus a $0.50 flat allocation. Worked landscaping job — illustrative USD Line Calculation Amount Variable employee labor 2 × (1.5 + 0.5) × 20 × 1.20 96.00 Materials, route, equipment, acquisition 35 + 12 + (2 × 8) + 8 71.00 Processing fees 300 × 3% + 0.50 9.50 Contribution 300 − 96 − 71 − 9.50 123.50 Calendar-month fixed costs of $4,000 need 33 jobs; adding $3,000 owner allocation needs 57, and a $1,000 extra goal raises the target to 65. Recovering twelve months of those amounts over eight earning months instead requires 49 operating, 86 owner-covered and 98 full-goal jobs per active month. With 360 available employee worker-hours, staff capacity is 90 jobs. With 80 owner hours, owner capacity is 80, so overall capacity is 80. The calendar target of 65 fits, but the 98 seasonal goal and 90 planned jobs do not. At 90 jobs for eight months, annual contribution is $88,920; after $48,000 fixed costs and $36,000 owner allocation, $4,920 remains, which is $7,080 below the $12,000 extra goal. This arithmetic is conditional because planned volume exceeds entered capacity. Use price floors and recurring-client counts carefully At positive planned volume, the calendar operating price is (non-percentage variable cost + fixed cost / planned jobs) / (1 − fee fraction). Add owner allocation and extra goal to solve the calendar full price; use the annual full requirement divided by active months and planned jobs for the seasonal price. The worked seasonal full price is $310.14 rounded upward to a cent at 90 jobs per active month. That price does not resolve its staffing/owner-capacity gap or establish what customers will pay. Margin of safety uses the exact calendar operating threshold and is unavailable at zero planned volume or nonpositive contribution. Recurring-client counts on the main results relate to the calendar full target and your entered jobs per client; they are not the seasonal goal. Validate actual service dates. The all-new inquiry estimate assumes every target job needs acquisition; existing repeat work should instead reduce your new-job gap. The minimum annual full-goal job count and a constant rounded monthly pace can differ. In the worked case, 778 whole annual jobs are the financial minimum; 98 jobs in each of eight months gives 784. Plan uneven demand with a dated budget rather than calling those two numbers identical. Review lawn-route profit , the landscaping working-capital guide and the cash-flow forecast before treating a contribution target as bank cash. The existing price and capacity examples below use the quick model. The detailed seasonal comparison above uses its own entered costs and earning-month assumptions. How to do break-even analysis for a landscaping business Find contribution per completed job after materials, paid crew labor, fuel, equipment use, acquisition and percentage fees. Divide monthly overhead by positive job contribution for operating break-even and round jobs upward. Add owner pay and a profit goal once for the higher monthly funding target. Compare required whole jobs with productive crew worker-hours divided by complete worker-hours per job. Check job mix, seasonal demand and actual collection/payment dates before committing to expansion. Landscaping break-even example: price versus crew capacity These independent USD scenarios use the calculator's initial example, not your edited inputs. At $320 per completed job, subtract $62 materials, $96 direct labor, $24 fuel and equipment use, $18 acquisition and $9.28 payment fees. That leaves $110.72 contribution per job. Operating overhead alone is $4,800: 44 whole jobs cover that amount. Including $5,000 owner pay needs 89 jobs. Adding the $1,500 profit goal needs 103 jobs, producing $32,960 sales. Set owner pay and target profit to zero in the calculator when you want only operating break-even; a target including those amounts answers a broader funding question. Five worker-hours could be two people working 2.5 hours; it is not automatically five elapsed crew-hours. The initial 72% share gives 94 whole jobs, below the 103-job target. Improving price can close an arithmetic gap, but does not establish customer demand. Use a consistent mix of mowing visits and installation projects Do not average a weekly mowing visit with an installation project unless the planned mix is explicit. For a fictional ten-job mix of eight visits leaving $50 each and two projects leaving $300 each, weighted contribution is $100 per job. If visits require two worker-hours and projects 12, weighted time is four worker-hours. Both averages must use that same 8:2 mix. When the mix changes, revise contribution and time together, or plan separate service schedules. Plan seasonal months separately The 52 ÷ 12 conversion is an average month, not a promise of working days. Reduce available hours or productive share for weather, equipment downtime and seasonal work patterns. Count paid idle payroll once in the relevant cost schedule. Model each month separately when winter revenue or staffing differs; do not multiply a strong summer month by twelve and call it an annual forecast. Equipment replacement, debt principal and delayed customer payments also need a separate cash forecast . For route travel and repeated mowing stops, use the lawn route profit calculator . For a property quote, use the lawn care pricing per acre guide . Keep the monthly model focused on how many complete jobs the business must fund and can deliver. Crew-hours and vehicle/material cost Route log and job cost records Separate crew time from route elapsed hours and include allocated travel once. Fixed commitments Equipment, insurance and overhead ledger Separate usage-related wear from fixed costs; loan principal belongs in cash planning. Use measured crew-hours for the complete visit, including necessary setup and travel. A per-acre public price still needs the cost and delivery time of a complete job; small properties may require a minimum visit charge. It then determines the exact volume and revenue required to cover monthly operating overhead, owner compensation and an optional target profit. Because a financial target is useful only when the business can deliver it, MyBreakeven also compares required volume with productive team hours and estimates the customer inquiries needed at your conversion rate. Exact financial target See fractional break-even volume, exact revenue and the minimum practical whole-unit target separately. Operational feasibility Compare required jobs with estimated monthly delivery capacity before committing to the plan. Formula, assumptions and rounding — quick estimate Contribution per job = average price minus direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and percentage payment fees. Required monthly jobs = (operating overhead + owner pay + target profit) divided by contribution per job . For a traditional operating break-even calculation, set owner pay and target profit to zero. Keep owner pay if you want the business to cover your compensation, and add profit only when calculating a profit target. The example values are illustrative USD inputs, not industry averages. The example contribution is $110.72 per job . The exact target is 102.06 jobs ; rounding up gives 103 whole jobs and $32,960.00 in monthly sales. Costs entered per job must not also be included in monthly overhead. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 / 12 × productive utilization ÷ delivery hours per job . Delivery hours mean total team labor hours per job , including preparation and travel where relevant. Whole-unit capacity rounds down, while required sales round up. Inquiry estimates use your assumed conversion rate, not a prediction of demand. For recurring work, count existing customers separately from new customer acquisition. The full calculator supports other currency labels; it does not convert exchange rates. Quick-model illustration: At the example price of $320.00, each job contributes $110.72 after direct costs and fees. Covering $11,300.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 103 whole jobs, or $32,960.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. Detailed job costs and seasonal recovery use their separate inputs above. Is current crew capacity enough for the target? Quick-model illustration: The example requires 103 whole jobs and estimates capacity for 94 whole jobs per month, using 4 team members, 38 hours each per week and 72% productive time. Adjust those inputs to check your own delivery limit. Detailed job costs and seasonal recovery use their separate inputs above. How does average job price change break-even volume? Quick-model illustration: In this example, each job contributes $110.72 after direct costs and fees. Changing the price or a per-job cost changes that contribution and therefore the number of jobs needed. Enter your own assumptions to see the effect. Detailed job costs and seasonal recovery use their separate inputs above. What does the seasonal landscaping target recover? It assumes all entered monthly fixed costs, owner allocation and extra goal continue for twelve calendar months, but job contribution is earned only during your entered active months. Off-season contribution is zero in this comparison. The calendar-month targets remain separate. Are equipment machine-hours the same as crew-hours? No. Two employees working one hour use two worker-hours. One mower running for one hour uses one machine-hour. Enter the combined running time of all included equipment and a representative use-related cost per machine-hour. Do not multiply it by crew count again. How do I avoid counting equipment costs twice? Use the hourly equipment allowance for the usage-related costs you choose to include, and fixed overhead for separate fixed commitments. If depreciation, a replacement reserve or rental is already included in that hourly allowance, do not add the same amount again to fixed costs. Loan principal and capital purchases need a separate cash forecast. Does owner labor get counted twice? Employee labor is calculated only for employees. Owner on-site and travel time limit owner capacity, while owner compensation is funded once through monthly owner allocation. Operating break-even excludes that allocation, so inspect the owner-covered and full-goal targets too. What if I earn income from snow work or winter cleanups? The seasonal comparison assumes zero off-season contribution. If winter services contribute, build a dated combined plan with their own prices, costs and hours rather than subtracting their gross revenue from landscaping overhead. Twelve active months models the same representative job mix all year. Can I combine mowing visits and installation projects? Only with a stable, representative job mix and compatible price, material cost and hours. Otherwise run separate scenarios. Use the lawn route tool for route-specific economics and keep maintenance visit frequency separate from a complete installation project. Does available time guarantee enough jobs can be delivered? No. This is a pooled employee/owner hours screen. It does not optimize appointment windows, simultaneous crew availability, equipment sharing, routes or weather. Compare both planned volume and seasonal target with capacity, then check the actual schedule. Can I download the detailed landscaping plan? Yes. The free local CSV includes input assumptions and unrounded calendar and seasonal results. Detailed inputs remain separate from the original quick estimate, which retains full-calculator transfer and its existing saved-plan options. Does acreage belong in the job count? Only if one modeled unit consistently means one acre with matching price, costs and crew-hours. For complete visits, use visits as the unit and test property sizes separately. What if required sales exceed capacity? The target does not fit the productive hours you entered. Test price, costs, delivery time or a revised capacity plan. Recalculate any new monthly staffing or equipment commitment; more available hours do not prove customer demand. Is this a cash-flow forecast or net-profit statement? No. It models contribution, a monthly funding target and productive-hour capacity. Schedule collections, supplier payments, taxes, equipment cash and loan principal separately; reconcile any unentered items before interpreting accounting net profit. Review the target before changing your plan Record the entered unit, period and cost boundary alongside the result. Compare required whole sales with both capacity and evidence of demand. Run a downside case using a lower realized price or higher delivery cost. Add new commitments if the operating range changes. Check a dated cash forecast before treating a profitable target as available cash. Compare a complete lawn route Set a fee-aware per-acre quote Method and example inputs reviewed November 12, 2026 . Variable contractor cost / client-month Only contractor work that increases with this client. Do not repeat salaried staff here. Separate staff and owner capacity Available staff hours / month Aggregate paid staff worker-hours before productive utilization; exclude owner hours. Owner delivery hours / client-month Review and strategy time; zero if owner is not needed in delivery. Retained clients and new-client pipeline Planned active clients this month Whole client-months with comparable scope. This is your assumption, not a demand forecast. Active clients entering the month Whole clients before this month’s modeled churn. Monthly client churn assumption (%) Retained count rounds down conservatively; replace projections with actual renewals when known. Qualified inquiry-to-new-client conversion (%) Use matching qualified inquiries and completed wins. Zero cannot produce a finite lead estimate. Acquisition expense / new client One-time new-client cost in this month; not charged to every retained client. Do not repeat it in overhead. Your monthly agency plan Contribution / active client-month $2,160.00 Operating break-even clients 5 Clients covering owner allocation 7 Clients for full profit goal 9 Whole-client delivery capacity 12 Minimum retainer at planned volume $2,639.18 After modeled churn, the conservative retained-client count is 6 . The full target requires 3 new clients , 12 qualified inquiries , and $1,200.00 acquisition expense. A retained count is not a guaranteed renewal. The aggregate hours cover the full goal; check role-level bottlenecks and actual demand. Staff capacity: 12 clients; owner capacity: 12 clients. Productive hours are 240 staff and 60 owner hours. Reconcile your planned 10 active client-months Monthly item Amount Retainer revenue $30,000.00 Client-dependent costs $8,400.00 Contribution before commitments $21,600.00 Fixed overhead + committed payroll $10,500.00 New-client acquisition expense $1,600.00 Operating remainder $9,500.00 After owner allocation $5,500.00 Surplus / shortfall against extra profit goal $3,500.00 The planned volume needs 200 staff delivery hours and 50 owner hours. Both entered hour limits cover this planned volume. It needs 4 new clients and 16 qualified inquiries. The minimum retainer assumes those same costs and client counts, rounds upward to a cent, and does not establish willingness to pay. Compare one assumption at a time Independent alternatives; no automatic demand response Scenario Contribution / client Full target Capacity After-owner remainder at planned clients Current plan $2,160.00 9 12 $5,500.00 10% higher price $2,451.00 7 12 $8,410.00 25% more delivery hours $2,160.00 9 9 $5,500.00 One retained client lost $2,160.00 9 12 $5,100.00 Show the calculation trace Contribution = retainer × (1 − percentage fee ÷ 100) − contractor − client software − other variable cost − flat fee. Fixed commitment = overhead + committed payroll. Conservative retained clients = floor(existing clients × (1 − churn ÷ 100)). For each candidate total Q: new clients = max(0, Q − retained); acquisition = new clients × CAC. The smallest whole Q must satisfy Q × contribution − acquisition ≥ the selected funding requirement. Operating uses fixed commitments; owner coverage adds owner allocation; the full goal also adds extra profit. Staff capacity = floor(staff hours × utilization ÷ 100 ÷ staff hours per client); owner capacity uses its own inputs. The smaller applicable capacity controls. Zero hours per client removes that resource constraint. The model assumes every needed new client contributes a full client-month; prorated onboarding needs a separate scenario. At 9 clients the full-goal surplus is $1,740.00 ; at 8 it is -$20.00 . This checks the whole-client boundary without rounding contribution first. Download agency CSV Print / save PDF Reset agency example How to calculate agency break-even without counting payroll twice Define one unit as one active retainer client for a full month. Use the agency’s own service fee after discounts. Keep pure client ad budgets and reimbursed pass-through spending outside both sides of this planning model; a management fee belongs in agency revenue. One-off projects, different service tiers and onboarding months need separate scenarios unless their cost and hour mix is genuinely comparable. 1. Separate committed payroll from incremental delivery cost Guaranteed staff salaries remain a monthly commitment when a client leaves. Enter loaded delivery payroll once in the payroll field and shared software, administration and premises in overhead. Contractor hours purchased only for the client, incremental licences and sale-dependent charges belong in per-client costs. Staff hours still constrain delivery even though the salary is fixed. Owner time is another capacity constraint, with compensation funded once by the owner allocation. In the original retainer example, a $3,000 agency fee incurs $600 variable contractor work, $100 client software, $50 other variable cost and a 3% payment fee ($90). Contribution is $3,000 − $600 − $100 − $50 − $90 = $2,160 per client-month . Monthly commitments are $2,500 overhead plus $8,000 loaded payroll, totaling $10,500. Owner allocation is $4,000 and the extra profit goal is $2,000. These are illustrative USD inputs, not market rates or recommended salary levels. 2. Fund retained clients and new-client acquisition separately Seven clients enter the example month. With a 10% churn assumption, the projection is 6.3, rounded down to six retained clients as a conservative whole-client planning assumption. This does not mean a fraction of an actual client cancels; use actual renewals when available. Each needed new client costs $400 to acquire in this month. Do not also deduct that $400 from every retained client's contribution or repeat the same spending in overhead. Original retainer example: three distinct monthly targets Target Whole clients New clients Acquisition expense What is covered Operating break-even 5 0 $0 $10,500 commitments Owner coverage 7 1 $400 $14,500 including owner allocation Full profit goal 9 3 $1,200 $16,500 before acquisition The nine-client goal leaves 9 × $2,160 − $10,500 − $4,000 − $1,200 = $3,740 after owner allocation , above the $2,000 extra goal. Eight clients leave $1,980 after owner allocation and $800 acquisition, missing that goal by $20. Ignoring new-client acquisition would incorrectly report eight as sufficient. At a 25% qualified-inquiry conversion, three new wins need 12 inquiries , not a new lead for every retained client. When retained contribution cannot cover a requirement, an added client must contribute more than its one-time CAC to make a larger total solve the gap in this one-month view. Lifetime contribution from a new client can still be attractive, but this calculator does not project subsequent retention, acquisition timing, onboarding delays or customer lifetime value. It assumes new clients contribute a full month; use a separate prorated ramp-up forecast if they start mid-month. 3. Test staff and owner delivery capacity independently The default staff pool has 320 monthly hours at 75% productive utilization: 240 delivery hours. At 20 staff worker-hours per client, that supports 12 whole clients. The owner has 80 hours at 75%, or 60 delivery hours; five owner hours per client also supports 12. The lower applicable limit controls. Do not count owner hours in staff capacity too, or remove the same nonbillable time twice. The scope-creep preset raises staff hours to 32 per client, owner hours to eight and contractor cost to $900. Contribution falls to $1,860 and the full financial target becomes ten clients, but both resource limits fall to seven. A ten-client invoice target cannot fix that delivery gap. Additional hires, contractor substitution or less scope must change the corresponding costs and hours together. Aggregate capacity also does not prove that a specialist designer or account director is available when needed. 4. Compare a freelancer with a staffed agency The owner-led example has a $1,800 retainer, $150 contractor cost, $40 software, $20 other cost and $54 percentage fee, leaving $1,536 contribution . Fixed overhead is $800 with zero staff payroll; owner allocation is $4,000 and extra goal $1,000. Three retained clients plus one new $300-CAC client require four total clients. They leave $1,044 after owner allocation, beating the extra goal by $44. The owner has 84 productive hours and needs 72 for four clients at 18 hours each. Five clients would require 90 hours and exceed that capacity. 5. Use the minimum retainer as a cost boundary At ten planned clients in the default case, four are new and acquisition expense is $1,600. Required net contribution per client is ($10,500 + $4,000 + $2,000 + $1,600) ÷ 10 = $1,810. Add $750 other variable costs and divide by 0.97 to allow for the 3% revenue fee: $2,639.18 minimum retainer , rounded upward to a cent. This price supports the stated goal only at the entered volume, scope, hours and acquisition pattern. It does not establish buyer demand or a value-based market price. Records and next decisions Reconcile paid invoices with contract scope, time records, staff payroll, contractor bills and qualified-inquiry outcomes. Track revisions and account management even when they are not separately invoiced. Compare scope-creep cost , agency billable utilization , client profitability and client concentration risk . Use the hourly-rate calculator for an hourly offer, and a 13-week cash forecast for payroll dates and late receipts. OpenStax explains the fixed-cost and contribution basis of break-even analysis . The separate owner constraint, whole-client retention assumption and new-client acquisition treatment here are explicit planning additions. This is a monthly contribution model, not an accounting net-profit statement, payroll compliance calculation or cash forecast. Currency labels do not convert amounts. Method and original examples reviewed November 16, 2026. Gather the records for your agencies plan Use one consistent completed-sale unit and reporting period. Replace illustrative defaults with records you can reconcile. A new-client acquisition cost entered against every monthly retainer would overstate recurring cost if it occurs only once. Use a clearly allocated recurring-unit allowance or a separate new-client acquisition scenario; the calculator does not model acquisition timing automatically. INDUSTRY-SPECIFIC UNIT ECONOMICS What this agency break-even analysis includes This model calculates contribution per client after delivery labor, contractors, client software, payment fees and sales acquisition . It then determines the exact volume and revenue required to cover monthly operating overhead, owner compensation and an optional target profit. Because a financial target is useful only when the business can deliver it, MyBreakeven also compares required volume with productive team hours and estimates the customer inquiries needed at your conversion rate. Exact financial target See fractional break-even volume, exact revenue and the minimum practical whole-unit target separately. Operational feasibility Compare required clients with estimated monthly delivery capacity before committing to the plan. Private and transparent Inputs stay in your browser, while the formula trace explains how each result was calculated. Formula, assumptions and rounding — quick estimate Contribution per client = average price minus direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and percentage payment fees. Required monthly clients = (operating overhead + owner pay + target profit) divided by contribution per client . For a traditional operating break-even calculation, set owner pay and target profit to zero. Keep owner pay if you want the business to cover your compensation, and add profit only when calculating a profit target. The example values are illustrative USD inputs, not industry averages. The example contribution is $916.20 per client . The exact target is 16.59 clients ; rounding up gives 17 whole clients and $37,400.00 in monthly sales. Costs entered per client must not also be included in monthly overhead. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 / 12 × productive utilization ÷ delivery hours per client . Delivery hours mean total team labor hours per client , including preparation and travel where relevant. Whole-unit capacity rounds down, while required sales round up. Inquiry estimates use your assumed conversion rate, not a prediction of demand. For recurring work, count existing customers separately from new customer acquisition. The full calculator supports other currency labels; it does not convert exchange rates. Read the agencies break-even guide Read the calculation methodology · Browse business planning guides QUESTIONS THIS MODEL ANSWERS Agency break-even questions What does one client mean in the detailed calculator? One active retainer client for one month, with a consistent service scope. Exclude client ad budgets and other pure pass-through amounts from both revenue and delivery costs. One-off projects need a separate scenario. Where should salaried agency staff go? Enter committed loaded monthly delivery payroll in Payroll, once. It remains payable when client numbers fall. Only genuinely client-dependent contractors and software belong in variable cost. Owner compensation is separate. How are retained clients and acquisition costs calculated? The model conservatively rounds down existing clients × (1 − monthly churn rate). New clients are the positive gap between a modeled total and that retained count. CAC applies to those new clients once in this modeled month, not to every active retainer. Why are there three client targets? Operating break-even covers fixed overhead, committed payroll and modeled new-client acquisition. Owner coverage adds the owner allocation. The full target also funds the extra profit goal. Each uses whole clients and its own required new-client count. What if new-client acquisition costs more than monthly contribution? Retained-client contribution may still cover the target. If it does not, and contribution per added client is no greater than CAC, no finite total can cover the selected target in this one-month acquisition model. Longer-term lifetime value and cash timing need a separate cohort forecast. Does a capacity result prove the agency can serve that many clients? No. Staff and owner productive hours are separate aggregate limits. The lower whole-client capacity controls, but specialist roles, review bottlenecks, skills and demand still require a delivery schedule. What happens when conversion is zero? No finite inquiry estimate is shown when new clients are needed and conversion is zero. If no new clients are needed, required new inquiries are zero. A conversion assumption never forecasts demand. Can I export or print my agency scenario? Yes. Download a CSV of the entered assumptions and results, or print/save the page as a PDF. The detailed mode stays on this page; switching to the quick estimate does not transfer detailed inputs. Run a downside case using a lower realized price or higher delivery cost. Add new commitments if the operating range changes. Check a dated cash forecast before treating a profitable target as available cash. From the original charge to expected contribution Let P be merchandise revenue after discounts, S customer-paid shipping, r the fully refunded-order fraction, q the fraction of shipping refunded on a return, C landed product cost, and k the recoverable share of returned product cost. All fractions below are percentages divided by 100. Exclude pass-through sales tax from revenue. Expected net revenue = P × (1 − r) + S × (1 − r × q) Expected product cost = C × (1 − r × k) Percentage fees retained = (P + S) × fee rate × (1 − r × fee-refund fraction) Flat fees retained = flat fee × (1 − r × flat-fee-refund fraction) Contribution = expected net revenue − all included variable costs Included variable costs also contain outbound freight, packaging, sale-linked labor, acquisition, other costs and r × extra return-handling cost. Rates apply to the original item-plus-shipping charge, not automatically to post-refund revenue. Assume 10% of orders receive a full merchandise and shipping refund, and all returned product cost is recoverable as usable stock. Landed product cost is $40; outbound freight $8; packaging $2; fulfillment labor $3; acquisition $10; other variable cost $1. Percentage fees are 3% of the original $105 charge plus a $0.30 flat fee, neither refunded. Extra handling is $6 for each returned order. INDUSTRY-SPECIFIC UNIT ECONOMICS What this e-commerce break-even analysis includes This model calculates contribution per order after COGS, fulfillment labor, shipping subsidy, return allowance, payment or platform fees and customer acquisition cost . It then determines the exact volume and revenue required to cover monthly operating overhead, owner compensation and an optional target profit. Because a financial target is useful only when the business can deliver it, MyBreakeven also compares required volume with productive team hours and estimates the customer inquiries needed at your conversion rate. Exact financial target See fractional break-even volume, exact revenue and the minimum practical whole-unit target separately. Operational feasibility Compare required orders with estimated monthly delivery capacity before committing to the plan. Private and transparent Inputs stay in your browser, while the formula trace explains how each result was calculated. Formula, assumptions and rounding — quick estimate Contribution per order = average price minus direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and percentage payment fees. Required monthly orders = (operating overhead + owner pay + target profit) divided by contribution per order . For a traditional operating break-even calculation, set owner pay and target profit to zero. Keep owner pay if you want the business to cover your compensation, and add profit only when calculating a profit target. The example values are illustrative USD inputs, not industry averages. The example contribution is $25.25 per order . The exact target is 586.19 orders ; rounding up gives 587 whole orders and $50,482.00 in monthly sales. Costs entered per order must not also be included in monthly overhead. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 / 12 × productive utilization ÷ delivery hours per order . Delivery hours mean total team labor hours per order , including preparation and travel where relevant. Whole-unit capacity rounds down, while required sales round up. Inquiry estimates use your assumed conversion rate, not a prediction of demand. For recurring work, count existing customers separately from new customer acquisition. The full calculator supports other currency labels; it does not convert exchange rates. In the quick estimate: At the example price of $86.00, each order contributes $25.25 after direct costs and fees. Covering $14,800.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 587 whole orders, or $50,482.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. This is the combined funding target; the detailed mode separately displays operating break-even, owner-pay coverage and the extra profit target. What revenue covers overhead and advertising? In the quick estimate: At the example price of $86.00, each order contributes $25.25 after direct costs and fees. Covering $14,800.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 587 whole orders, or $50,482.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. This is the combined funding target; the detailed mode separately displays operating break-even, owner-pay coverage and the extra profit target. How do returns and shipping affect contribution margin? In the quick estimate: In this example, each order contributes $25.25 after direct costs and fees. Changing the price or a per-order cost changes that contribution and therefore the number of orders needed. Enter your own assumptions to see the effect. This is the combined funding target; the detailed mode separately displays operating break-even, owner-pay coverage and the extra profit target. Can I use this for handmade products and small batches? Yes. Preview and load the jewellery, ceramics, clothing or art-print example, then replace every assumption. Include making and packing worker-hours, allocate batch costs consistently, and keep owner compensation either in monthly owner pay or the relevant labor cost, once. The examples are illustrative USD inputs, not industry benchmarks. How should I enter shipping, returns and platform fees? In detailed mode enter customer shipping income, outbound shipping, fees, full-refund share and recovery assumptions separately. Revenue starts before the modeled refunds. In quick mode use a representative retained-sale unit and include any remaining return allowance once in costs. Do not deduct a refund again from revenue already net of that refund. Do I need Pro to calculate, and where can I save my plan? No. This page calculates free without an account. In quick mode, Continue with these numbers carries valid inputs to the full calculator in the same browser tab. A free account supports up to 3 saved scenarios; Pro supports up to 100 saved scenarios, three-plan comparisons and CSV/PDF reports. Opening the pricing page alone does not save inputs. What is the difference between operating break-even and my profit target? Operating break-even covers entered monthly fixed operating costs. Owner-pay coverage adds the separate owner allocation. The profit-target threshold adds your extra monthly remainder goal. The detailed calculator displays all three separately. Does the detailed calculator count returned orders twice? No. Its denominator is original paid orders, including those later fully refunded. Expected refunds reduce revenue once. Recoverable product cost reduces expected inventory consumption; outbound costs, retained fees and additional return handling are included separately. Does recovered inventory mean I received a cash refund? No. It means part of the product cost is assumed restored as usable stock. It does not reverse paid courier, advertising or processing costs and is not a cash inflow. Are payment fees automatically returned when I refund an order? No universal fee reversal is assumed. Enter the portion refunded under your actual provider and marketplace terms. The detailed example defaults to no percentage or flat-fee recovery. Can I use the detailed model for COD failures or partial refunds? This model assumes initially paid and fulfilled orders and full merchandise refunds on a stated fraction. COD non-deliveries, cancellations, partial merchandise refunds and exchanges need separate cohort economics; do not interpret this input as their universal treatment. Can I download the detailed calculation without Pro? Yes. Download this scenario exports the detailed inputs and unrounded results as a local CSV without an account. The quick estimate keeps its existing route to the full calculator and saved Free or Pro scenarios. Does positive order contribution prove the store is profitable? No. Order contribution must cover monthly overhead and the stated owner-pay/profit requirement. Returns, acquisition mix and unentered costs can change the full result; the tool does not verify your order records. What if required sales exceed capacity? The target does not fit the productive hours you entered. Test price, costs, delivery time or a revised capacity plan. Recalculate any new monthly staffing or equipment commitment; more available hours do not prove customer demand. Is this a cash-flow forecast or net-profit statement? No. It models contribution, a monthly funding target and productive-hour capacity. Schedule collections, supplier payments, taxes, equipment cash and loan principal separately; reconcile any unentered items before interpreting accounting net profit. Review the target before changing your plan Record the entered unit, period and cost boundary alongside the result. Compare required whole sales with both capacity and evidence of demand. Run a downside case using a lower realized price or higher delivery cost. Add new commitments if the operating range changes. Check a dated cash forecast before treating a profitable target as available cash. documents.text: FREE INDUSTRY CALCULATOR Salon Break-Even Calculator Estimate appointments, revenue and customer inquiries using service price, product usage, stylist labor and chair capacity. Use the free calculator A salon planning model: use your own price, costs and delivery capacity. TRY YOUR OWN NUMBERS · USD Calculate your salon break-even point Replace the example inputs below. Results update in your browser as you type. Enter monthly totals for overhead, owner pay and target profit; enter direct costs per appointment separately. Average price per appointment $ Net revenue per defined unit after discounts. Exclude taxes collected for others. Materials / product cost per appointment $ Materials or product consumed per unit, using compatible quantities and purchase costs. Direct labor per appointment $ Labor that changes with a delivered unit. Keep guaranteed payroll in fixed costs and owner compensation once. Laundry + disposables per appointment $ Other sale-dependent costs, including flat fees. Exclude the percentage fee entered below. Marketing cost per booked appointment $ Acquisition cost allocated per modeled sale. Do not charge a one-time customer cost to every repeat visit. Monthly operating overhead $ Monthly commitments for this operating range, excluding costs already entered per unit. Monthly owner pay $ Monthly owner-compensation requirement. Do not repeat the same owner wage in per-unit labor. Target monthly profit $ Additional monthly profit goal beyond entered costs and owner pay. Zero means no additional profit goal. Payment and platform fees % Percentage of selling price. A flat transaction charge belongs in other variable cost. Active team members Positive whole team size contributing the modeled productive hours. Hours per team member / week hrs Available hours per team member per week before productive-utilization adjustment. Delivery hours per appointment hrs Total worker-hours per completed unit, including necessary preparation, delivery and allocated travel. Productive utilization % Share of available hours usable for the modeled delivery work. Do not subtract the same downtime twice. Inquiry-to-appointment conversion % Completed sales divided by comparable qualified inquiries. Enter a measured rate above zero. Build my costs Optional · work out the cost of one appointment + Contribution per appointment $37.24 Whole appointments for your target 425 Monthly sales at that volume $39,100.00 The whole-unit target needs approximately 1,119 inquiries at your assumed conversion rate. This is a planning requirement, not a demand forecast. At these assumptions, estimated delivery capacity is 399 whole appointments per month. The current capacity is below the required volume. These are planning estimates, not a sales forecast. Replace illustrative defaults with records you can reconcile. Input records and cost boundaries Input group Record to use Boundary to check Realized service ticket Paid appointments by comparable service Exclude tax/tips and keep retail sales separate from chair appointments. Product and variable staff cost Recipe usage and commission/payroll records Include waste once; fixed wages should not be repeated as variable commission. Productive time and monthly commitments Delivered service times, diary and overhead ledger Use total worker-hours; gaps and no-shows can reduce realized paid volume. For color services, preparation, processing work and cleanup can require different amounts of occupied stylist time. Enter the worker-hours actually required, then check any separate chair or station bottleneck. Retail contribution does not create extra chair appointments. Check the next business decision Check how many extra sales a discount needs before changing your plan. Use the cash runway calculator to compare available cash with expected receipts and payments. INDUSTRY-SPECIFIC UNIT ECONOMICS What this salon break-even analysis includes This model calculates contribution per appointment after service products, stylist labor, disposables, laundry, payment fees and appointment acquisition . It then determines the exact volume and revenue required to cover monthly operating overhead, owner compensation and an optional target profit. Because a financial target is useful only when the business can deliver it, MyBreakeven also compares required volume with productive team hours and estimates the customer inquiries needed at your conversion rate. Exact financial target See fractional break-even volume, exact revenue and the minimum practical whole-unit target separately. Operational feasibility Compare required appointments with estimated monthly delivery capacity before committing to the plan. Private and transparent Inputs stay in your browser, while the formula trace explains how each result was calculated. Formula, assumptions and rounding Contribution per appointment = average price minus direct materials, labor, other variable costs, acquisition cost and percentage payment fees. Required monthly appointments = (operating overhead + owner pay + target profit) divided by contribution per appointment . For a traditional operating break-even calculation, set owner pay and target profit to zero. Keep owner pay if you want the business to cover your compensation, and add profit only when calculating a profit target. The example values are illustrative USD inputs, not industry averages. The example contribution is $37.24 per appointment . The exact target is 424.27 appointments ; rounding up gives 425 whole appointments and $39,100.00 in monthly sales. Costs entered per appointment must not also be included in monthly overhead. Capacity uses team members × weekly hours × 52 / 12 × productive utilization ÷ delivery hours per appointment . Delivery hours mean total team labor hours per appointment , including preparation and travel where relevant. Whole-unit capacity rounds down, while required sales round up. Inquiry estimates use your assumed conversion rate, not a prediction of demand. For recurring work, count existing customers separately from new customer acquisition. The full calculator supports other currency labels; it does not convert exchange rates. Read the salon break-even guide Read the calculation methodology · Browse business planning guides Test salon appointments against productive chair hours Use complete appointment worker-hours and actual available productive time. Suppose a salon needs $6,000 contribution each month and leaves $60 per appointment. It needs 100 appointments. If each requires 1.5 delivery hours, that is 150 hours of work. A plan with only 135 productive hours has capacity for 90 whole appointments and does not fit the target. Retail purchases can add contribution, but they should not be treated as extra chair appointments. Model the service mix and product economics consistently. No-shows can consume reserved time without producing the planned paid service. Track cancellations and rebooked slots rather than assuming every diary entry creates revenue. Owner pay remains explicit in the monthly amount to cover. A booth-rental arrangement and an employee-service arrangement have different revenue and cost boundaries; avoid mixing their fields. The calculator shows an assumption-based capacity and contribution test, not a guarantee of appointment demand or salon profitability. Does a full diary prove the salon covers its costs? No. Entries can include unpaid gaps, no-shows and services with different contribution. Compare paid delivered appointments, their costs and productive hours with the monthly requirement. QUESTIONS THIS MODEL ANSWERS Salon break-even questions How many salon appointments are needed to break even? At the example price of $92.00, each appointment contributes $37.24 after direct costs and fees. Covering $15,800.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 425 whole appointments, or $39,100.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. What revenue covers rent and owner pay? At the example price of $92.00, each appointment contributes $37.24 after direct costs and fees. Covering $15,800.00 in overhead, owner pay and target profit requires 425 whole appointments, or $39,100.00 in practical monthly sales. Replace these sample inputs with your figures. Are stylist hours sufficient for the target appointments? The example requires 425 whole appointments and estimates capacity for 399 whole appointments per month, using 5 team members, 34 hours each per week and 76% productive time. Adjust those inputs to check your own delivery limit. Does retail revenue increase appointment capacity? No. Product sales can add contribution but do not become chair appointments. Model retail economics separately or use a clearly defined combined unit; preserve the service-time boundary. What if required sales exceed capacity? The target does not fit the productive hours you entered. Test price, costs, delivery time or a revised capacity plan. Recalculate any new monthly staffing or equipment commitment; more available hours do not prove customer demand. Is this a cash-flow forecast or net-profit statement? No. It models contribution, a monthly funding target and productive-hour capacity. Schedule collections, supplier payments, taxes, equipment cash and loan principal separately; reconcile any unentered items before interpreting accounting net profit. Review the target before changing your plan Record the entered unit, period and cost boundary alongside the result. Compare required whole sales with both capacity and evidence of demand. Run a downside case using a lower realized price or higher delivery cost. Add new commitments if the operating range changes. Check a dated cash forecast before treating a profitable target as available cash.
